Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings  13 51. Concerns further arise in the law and, by extension,  the legal profession , because 
laws are both ancient and living.  It would be difficult to use tools that have ‘cut-off 
dates ’ for training data and expect them to deliver ‘ justice ’.  It is critical that any 
reliance on GPAI in assisting to dispense the law is appropriate and proportionate.  
52. Other important aspects in the context of the administration of justice use cases are 
that the law : 
• is language- based;  
• often contains a mental or cognitive element in order to apply it ; and 
• is often open to interpretation or nuance . 
53. Rather than being codifiable or reduced to logical ‘ if this, then that ’ rules, the Australian 
legal system recognises the need for flexibility  when applying the law to the facts of a 
specific case .  We acknowledge, however, that this is not the case in all matters : for 
example, where Parliaments have passed strict liability laws . 
54. Nonetheless , in most cases , the law is applied by practitioners and judges using a 
process of interpretation and the exercise of professional judgment .  The application of 
the law is then relied on by clients, parties in legal proceedings and , ultimately , the 
broader community .  If the application of the law is incorrect, then l awyers and judges 
are answerable to the participants in the legal system . 
55. In 1881, O liver Wendell Holmes observed that ‘ the life of the law has not been logic: it 
has been experience’ .24  Not every experience, even today, is captured or represented 
in our digital lives by data or  a digital footprint .  Another way to see the law is ‘ open-
textured’ , as Professor Simon Chesterman notes; it is why a rule such as ‘ no vehicles 
in the park ’—an example first offered by H.L.A . Hart25—is open- textured enough to 
extend to cars, trucks, bicycles , and even  drones , but perhaps not toy trucks or toy 
trains.26  This demonstrates how  the law often requires interpretation and experience.  
56. Defining high- risk use cases in the administration of justice as those making 
determinations about an individual may benefit from the further assessment of the purpose or social utility underlying the use case.  For instance, i f the purpose 
(or outcome)  is to ease the burden on courts and increase efficiency in administering 
the law, does the margin for error or false convictions that using AI may bring, justify its 
use?  Or should a social utility dimension also require that the efficient administration 
of justice must not result in denying any  person justice?  
57. We consider that t he advantage of a risk -based, purpose- driven approach could help 
ensure that high- risk uses are limited to those having social utility (by reference to 
consistency with, or being complementary to existing Australian law) .  This approach 
could further minimis e any unintended, unforeseeable harms or outcomes that are 
inconsistent with the rule of law and our democratic processes.

58. If a general principles -based approach is to be retained, we suggest that certain 
categories of use should also be designed ‘ high- risk’.  Such designation would have 
the effect of imposing a requirement that such uses comply with the proposed 
mandatory guardrails.  
59. This approach would ensure greater clarity for organisations developing and deploying 
AI, and enhanced transparency for users, whilst ensuring that novel applications are 
appropriately regulated . 
60. We a cknowledge  work that is already underway at the Commonwealth level to reform 
the Privacy  Act, combat misinformation and misinformation, review the Online Safety 
Act 2021 (Cth), and develop a consistent legal framework for automated decision-
making by government .  In light of this work, we submit that consideration should be 
given to designating the following categories as high- risk: 
(a) Uses of AI systems to make decisions impacting people’ s health, safety and 
human rights, or which have an impact on an individual ’s legal rights or 
entitlements, or a similarly significant effect on an individual.  
(b) Uses of AI involving the input of sensitive data in medical and health 
environments (and in other industries involving sensitive information 
processing).  
(c) Uses of AI systems to generate or replicate personhood or aspects of 
personhood (i.e., appearances, voices, etc.) for any identifiable individuals, 
especially minors.  
(d) Uses of AI -generated content in political campaigns.  
61. Regardless, we suggest that the Department seek expert guidance from independent 
and appropriately qualified individuals as to the risk profile of categories of AI use.  
Options for introducing mandatory guardrails  
62. The Proposal  Paper poses three options for implementing the proposed mandatory 
guardrails, namely:  
• Option 1 : Adapting existing regulatory frameworks to include the proposed 
mandatory guardrails;27 
• Option 2 : Introducing framework legislation, with associated amendments to 
existing legislation;28 or 
• Option 3 : A whole -of-economy approach through the introduction of a new AI -
specific Act.29 
 
27 Proposals Paper, 46-48.  
28 Ibid 48-49.  
29 Ibid 49-51.   
 
Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings  15 General comments 
63. The Law Council has previously indicated a preference for a ‘ multi- faceted’ approach 
to the regulation of AI based on the following elements:  
• an initial focus on the regulation of high -risk AI technology and applications;  
• a strengthened and precautionary approach to Al regulation, where there is 
evidence that existing laws and regulations are insufficient to address the issues and harms arising;  
• comprehensive regulatory reform to ensure that the use of automated decision making, including by the Australian Government, is transparent, capable of 
review, and consistent with administrative law principles;  and 
• consideration of the regulatory models adopted by other jurisdictions to 
determine an optimal and bespoke approach for Australia that reflects the 
nuances of Australia’ s pre -existing constitutional and regulatory framework, 
and unique local market environment.30 
64. We have previously expressed support for the expansion of current legislation and, 
where necessary, new targeted legislation, rather than seeking to explicitly regulate AI 
via a comprehensive ‘ AI Act ’. 
65. The majority of responses we received in response to this consultation favour an 
approach that  minimises the potential for conflict—or duplication—with existing laws . 
Views  on the proposed options  
66. When consulting on the Proposals Paper, it was apparent that there  are differing views  
amongst the legal profession as to the appropriateness of each option, particularly the 
merits of a new AI -specific Act , as proposed in Option 3.  
67. For example, the Law Institute of Victoria and Queensland Law Society have  
expressed a preference for Option 3, supporting the approach taken by the EU AI Act, which presents a clear articulation of what  uses of AI pose the greatest risk , with a 
consequent regulatory focus in those areas .  These bodies submit that Option 3 would 
best address the use of AI in high- risk settings, and would allow for additional reforms 
to be undertaken, by way of legislative amendment, as AI development and use 
evolves over time.  
68. We acknowledge that Option 3 may allow for Australia to be more consistent with the 
broader global scheme, given the recent implementation of the EU AI Act, and the UK’s plan to introduce a standalone AI Act .  This comment is also informed by the 
consideration that the guardrails are intended to only apply to AI in high- risk settings, 
thereby limiting the scope of application to a limited set of AI uses and outcomes . 
69. Other contributors , however,  have  raise d concern s that the Option 3 approach will 
most likely result in overlap in existing laws and may require frequent amendment for 
currency to keep up with the fast -evolving pace of AI development .  We also recognise 
that the implementation of this option may not be feasible in the immediate short -term.  
 
30 See, e.g, Law Council of Australia, Submission  to Department of Industry, Science and Resources, Safe 
and Responsible AI in Australia (17 August 2023) 1 1; Submission  to Senate Committee on Adopting Artificial 
intelligence, Inquiry into the opportunities and impacts of the uptake of artificial intelligence technologies in 
Australia (20 May 2024).   
 
Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings  16 70. On the other hand, Option 1 appears to be beneficial for reducing the risk of 
inconsistency or duplication across regulatory frameworks .  However, it is likely to be a 
more time -consuming project, given the need to review and amend existing laws to 
embed the guardrails .  Further, this domain- specific approach could lead to 
inconsistent regulatory outcomes and enforcement mechanisms . 
71. We observe that Option 2 provides an appropriate middle -ground approach between 
Options 1 and 3, by creating a new framework legislation that mitigates risks , while 
allowing  AI development .  In addition, this option could potentially be implemented as 
an interim measure until new legislation prescribing specific uniform requirements is introduced.  
72. On balance, we  do not consider a comprehensive AI -specific Act is required at this 
early stage.  However, the gradual introduction of regulations that address high- risk AI 
and applications, having social utility, will be helpful in minimising risks, both known and unknown.  
73. We consider that the areas in which regulation is likely to be introduced earliest are the areas regulated by the:  
• Australian Competition and Consumer Commission; 
• Australian Communications and Media Authority;  
• eSafety Commissioner; and 
• Office of the Australian Information Commissioner . 
74. These four regulators have a mechanism for collaborating on digital platform regulations called the Digital Platform Regulators Forum ( DP-REG ).  The DP -REG is 
welcome initiative that is likely to facilitate the effective introduction of domain-specific 
solutions.  
Proposed mandatory guardrails  
General comments  
75. The Proposals Paper sets out proposed mandatory guardrails for AI systems used in 
high- risk settings, as well as high- risk GPAI systems.31  The guardrails are 
preventative measures that would require developers and deployers of AI used in 
high- risk settings to take specific steps across the AI lifecycle.32 
76. It is acknowledged that nine of the 10 proposed mandatory guardrails is  identical to 
the Voluntary AI Safety Standard .  The Voluntary AI Safety Standard has been 
mapped against Australia’ s AI Ethics Principles and broadly aligns with  relevant  
existing frameworks33 (such as the ISO 42001:2023 and the US National Institute of 
Standards and Technology ’s Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework) . 
77. We agree that  the guardrails should apply to all GPAI models in Australia.  As GPAI 
models may exceed even what are currently perceived as their potential uses, there 
should be a willingness on the part of the government to modify the regulatory 
approach as the technology becomes more sophisticated.  
 
31 Proposals Paper, 35-42.  
32 Ibid 19.  
33 See, e.g., the ISO/IEC 42001:2023  (Information Technology – Artificial Intelligence – Management system) ; 
US National Institute of Standards and Technology, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework  
(January 2023).   
 
Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings  17 78. As the mandatory guardrails are broadly framed, we suggest it would be beneficial to 
develop a more detailed set of minimum standards, derived from these guardrails .  
Organisations developing or deploying AI systems should subsequently be required to 
adopt these more detailed standards, unless they establish their own standards that 
are compliant with the overarching guardrails . 
79. For example, in respect of guardrail  3 (“protect AI systems, and implement data 
governance measures to manage data quality and provenance ”), we recommend that 
developers and deployers should be more specifically obliged to establish and 
implement measures that sufficiently protect the data that is involved in the 
development of AI systems, including personally identifiable information of any 
individuals .  We consider that it would be preferable if, unless an organisation 
developed its own standards to comply with guardrail 3, that organisation would be 
required to comply with the government -developed minimum standards, including one 
requiring the establishment and development of measures to protect personal data.  
Intellectual property enfor cement  
80. From an intellectual property enforcement perspective, proposed transparency in 
respect of the use and operation of AI (guardrail 7) will be of critical importance, as will 
establishing processes for people impacted (guardrail 8) .  The nature and accessibility 
of these processes will also be important to ensure that people or groups who are impacted can access information and exercise their rights . 
81. Specific  issues arise in relation to transparency in the context of intellectual property 
rights .  For example, there is a question whether a transparency obligation may 
require the disclosure of information concerning whether —and the extent to which—
copyright protected materials may have been used in the creation of an AI system  
(for example,  in training it ).  That is a question requiring detailed consideration of 
policy and practical matters , and we note that  it is currently being considered by the 
Copyri ght and Artificial Intelligence Reference Group . 
82. Further, questions  arise as to : 
• how any transparency obligation will avoid the risk of inappropriately requiring 
the disclosure of valuable trade secrets ; and  
• whether intellectual property rights holders should have a means of enforcing 
the transparency obligation.  
83. Consideration could particularly  be given to whether it is necessary to have an 
external means of reviewing the outcome of such a process .  Currently, in order to 
enforce legal rights, individuals would most likely be required  to resort to litigation, 
which is unlikely to be an efficient or affordable option.  
84. These matters illustrate the necessity for the proposed ex  ante guardrails to be 
accompanied by  reforms to  intellectual property law reform and  other forms of specific 
guidance.  
85. From a copyright perspective, we suggest that consideration be given to what remedies might be appropriate for an individual or group whose legal rights are 
impacted .  
For example, where a copyright work has been used as an input to train AI, 
or accessed in the process of answering a query, what remedy should be available to 
the copyright owner ?  We note that t hese questions are  currently  being explored in 
litigation in other jurisdictions .  However, those individual matters will not provide clear 
answers f or Australian copyright owners.   
 
Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings  18 86. We also note the ongoing wider discourse about whether copyright infringement 
issues associated with AI systems might be addressed, or mitigated, by some form of 
licensing framework, statutory exceptions or defences to infringement, or some form of 
sui generis legislation . 
Protections for domestic end -users  
87. Recent commentary has observed that, even if the mandatory guardrails have 
extraterritorial effect —recognising that many AI developers are based outside of 
Australia —their efficacy in protecting Australian deployers and end- users may be 
low.34 
88. We suggest that further clarity is needed about  the protections that would be in force 
for end users within Australia under the current proposals .  Whilst enforcement will be 
critical, so too will be  ensuring that the legislative framework includes sufficient 
protections and avenues to pursue overseas developers or deployers.  
Specific comments

Environmental harm  
90. The Proposals Paper observes that the precautionary principle is usually applied 
where a technology has significant uncertainty about its risks , including environmental 
harms .  Nonetheless , we are concerned that environmental risks may not be 
sufficiently addressed in the Proposals P aper. 
91. We submit that this should be a core issue for consideration.  For example, 
environmental protection is a core value put forw ard in the EU Al Act with the energy 
consumption of Al models a central consideration.35  We support  the inclusion of  
enhanced environmental impact considerations in the Australian G overnment ’s 
regulatory response (whatever form that takes).  
Oversight  
92. Compounding the abovementioned concerns regarding uncertaint ies with a principles -
based approach  are issues of  ensuring compliance and enforcement . 
93. It has been suggested to us  that a mechanism of licensing is most appropriate.

Tech Council of Australia www.techcouncil.com.au   Introduction Thank you for the opportunity to contribute to the consultation on the introduction of mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings. The Tech Council of Australia (TCA) fully supports the Government’s efforts in progressing this important work to clarify Australia’s regulatory model for AI, and to ensure that Australia’s regulatory environment builds public trust and promotes the adoption of AI across the economy. The Tech Council is Australia’s peak industry body for the tech sector. We represent over 150 companies from a diverse cross-section of Australia’s tech sector, including companies working in business enterprise software, consumer software, tele-communications, and fintech. This includes companies that build and deploy AI-driven products and venture capital funds with investments in AI. AI is one of the most transformative technologies of our time, with the potential to offer our nation significant economic, social, environmental and strategic advantages. AI is already driving major advancements in areas such as healthcare, industry and public safety, and the future holds even greater potential. Generative AI alone has the potential to add between $45b billion - $115 billion a year to the whole Australian economy by 2030.1 Our research forecasts that AI also has the potential to create up to 200,000 jobs in Australia by 2030.2 In order to realise the benefits of this transformative technology, we must make clear, informed policy decisions that embrace a risk-based, technology-agnostic, and outcomes-focused approach that fosters innovation and economic growth through AI adoption. This will unlock the transformative potential of AI for Australia by adopting safe and responsible AI.  Australia has a unique opportunity to design an innovative regulatory approach that could be world-leading and gives Australia a competitive edge in the global technology landscape, while embedding strong safeguards. It is important for Australia’s AI governance framework to be internationally interoperable and to draw from the experiences of other jurisdictions to anticipate potential pitfalls and complexities. While the EU AI Act and Canada's AI and Data Act offer valuable insights, there are already significant concerns about the EU’s framework for tech regulation in stifling innovation and competitiveness,3 and significant uncertainties about how these regulatory frameworks will operate in practice.  We should also align our regulatory approach with those of key trading partners, such as the United States, the United Kingdom, and countries across the Asia-Pacific region, which are the markets where Australian tech companies operate, expand and grow. While regulation is important, regulation alone is not sufficient to enable the adoption of safe and responsible AI. Meaningful engagement with industry is essential for ensuring accountability and effective enforcement. Further action is needed to leverage policy tools to support the development of Australia’s AI capability. This requires investment in AI research, enabling infrastructure, attracting and nurturing top talent.    1 Tech Council of Australia and Microsoft (2023), ‘Australia's Generative AI opportunity’. 2 Tech Council of Australia, Microsoft, LinkedIn and Workday (2024), ‘Meeting the AI Skills Boom’. 3 Mario Draghi, ‘The Future of European Competitiveness’ (2024’), European Commission.

Regulatory options  TCA support for Option 2 The TCA supports the adoption of Option 2 to introduce framework legislation that establishes common definitions and guardrails, ensuring consistency for a whole-of-economy approach. This is essential given that AI is a cross-cutting technology with diverse use cases and applications across various industries and sectors. As the proposals paper identifies, there are already existing economy-wide laws,4 as well as sector-specific laws that already apply to AI and its uses.5  In this context, Option 2 provides an approach that builds on our existing laws and regulatory architecture and leverages the distinct expertise that our well-known, trusted and familiar regulators have accumulated over time. It will also be the most efficient pathway to introducing the guardrails and enabling enforcement.  However, we acknowledge there are challenges to overcome in adopting Option 2:  • First, the maturity of regulators in addressing technology and AI-related issues varies significantly. Not all regulators possess the same level of capacity or technical expertise. There will need to be supporting technical resources to aid and assist in ‘pulling down’ the framework legislation.  • Second, coordination among regulators is crucial. Consistency in applying framework legislation across different regulatory bodies is necessary to prevent regulatory fragmentation in interpreting, applying, and enforcing AI laws. To resolve these issues, TCA supports a mechanism to support regulatory coordination. In addition to providing a single point to align, this would assist in providing necessary technical expertise, as well as enable efficient resourcing to ensure that regulations that flow from framework legislation align with the broader objectives set by Government and avoid fragmentation. Such a mechanism could, for example, support:  i) discovery of specific high-risk use cases; ii) interpreting framework legislation to apply to existing bodies of law and legislation; iii) development of regulator guidance on high-risk use cases; iv) coordination and continued alignment to prevent regulatory fragmentation v) recommendations for reform if required. We recommend leveraging or evolving existing bodies. This could include the AI Expert Group working alongside an expanded DP-REG forum, with technical support provided through the establishment of an Australian AI Safety Institute (which also has the benefit of further drawing on lessons learnt from international counterparts). In adopting a regulatory option, we encourage Government to undertake further  4 For example, privacy, administrative law, online safety, corporations, intellectual property, competition and consumer protection, and anti-discrimination laws. 5 For example, medical devices, motor vehicles, airline safety and financial services laws.

The TCA does not support option 3 As previously submitted, TCA does not support the creation of a new overarching AI act or single regulator for AI (Option 3), either through the creation of a single regulator of AI, or through designating an existing regulator.  The creation of a single regulator of AI will not only be time-consuming and costly, it is also likely to: • discourage the important but necessary broader uplift required in capability building for addressing digital regulation issues, including on matters beyond AI • result in siloed expertise and capability across government entities, and • limit our overall capacity to adapt and consider innovative ways to evolve our regulatory architecture and coordination mechanisms. Ultimately, the creation of a single regulator for AI will reduce Australia’s ability to participate in an increasingly dynamic technological future. In the alternate, Option 3 proposes designating an existing regulator. While we acknowledge the deep expertise that regulators possess, relying solely on one regulator entity presents significant limitations. Drawing from a single source of domain knowledge could lead to interpreting broad AI issues through a narrow lens, resulting in enforcement that fails to appreciate the full spectrum of risks adverse impacts on affected entities posed by AI.  While we appreciate the Government's efforts to address concerns about complexity and duplication with existing laws by proposing carve-outs to enable domain-specific laws to take precedence over an Australian AI Act, we continue to have strong concerns with this approach. Legislative design undertaken this way:  • would increase complexity and compliance burdens, which would have a particularly significant impact on startups and scaleups;  • risks creating an uneven playing field that favours certain industries, sectors, or use-cases; and, • is likely to introduce perverse incentives that may create loopholes. An effective legislative approach would design AI regulations that are technology-neutral and that can accommodate for changing circumstances without relying on carve outs. While we recognise the complexities associated with regulator coordination, the need for cohesive direction across regulatory bodies, resource capacity, and the risks of regulatory fragmentation, we believe that Option 2 represents a pragmatic path forward for considering the goals of Government in establishing whole-of-economy coverage.

Defining high-risk AI   Principles to define high-risk AI TCA supports the Government adopting a risk-based approach to AI regulation, which aligns with international approaches to AI governance and ensures that regulatory resources are allocated effectively and efficiently. We generally endorse principles (a)-(d) and appreciate their intent to address a wide array of harms. We make two recommendations for principles (e) and (f), which are outlined below.  Principle (e): The risk of adverse impacts to the broader Australian economy, society, environment, and rule of law.  We urge Government to further refine this principle, given the breadth of the principle and the uncertainty it creates. As currently proposed, it is overly expansive and could potentially apply to an unwieldy range of scenarios that makes it difficult for businesses to interpret and apply.  From the examples provided in the proposals paper, there is also potential overlap with other principles (e.g. amplification of content that promotes discrimination, overlapping with principle (d) impacts on groups; deepfakes and synthetic child sexual abuse material, overlapping with principle (d) health and safety). We consider that this principle should be further refined to focus on specific harms, reducing overlap with other principles and to ensure that it does not create confusion or uncertainty in its application.  6 United Nations, ‘Governing AI for Humanity: Final report’ (2024).

The TCA strongly supports the inclusion of principle (f) which is crucial to the operation of principles (a) to (e) as it provides the means for an entity to evaluate risk levels. We support including ‘severity’ and ‘extent’ as factors to consider. We also recommend including the word ‘likelihood’ and making this explicit within principle (f). While the proposals paper includes references to likelihood and probability, making this explicit will provide greater certainty for businesses. It will also align with established best-practice risk assessment and evaluation frameworks, as well as Government’s existing Risk Assessment Matrix for AI.7  Principles and a list-based approach When applied in isolation, the principles are broad and will pose challenges for businesses who seek to implement them effectively. Further guidance is needed to provide clarity on high-risk use cases. We note that a principles-based approach and a list-based approach are not mutually exclusive; in fact, they can work in tandem to provide a more comprehensive regulatory framework. The success of a hybrid approach, however, will hinge on the regulatory mechanisms to implement this arrangement effectively.  It is also important to clarify the terms in use and when defining high-risk AI, distinguishing between:   a) the contexts in which AI systems are deployed which are the broad circumstances, settings or domains where AI applications are used (e.g. public health, education, law enforcement, human rights) and, b) the use cases for AI systems which are the specific examples where an AI application is deployed to support an end-user achieve a goal or complete a task (e.g. image recognition to tag objects in images, an application that translates text between different languages). The AI tech stack TCA is pleased that the Government is considering the AI value chain and roles and responsibilities across the AI model lifecycle. In considering shared responsibility models, both developers and deployers play critical roles. While these are helpful conceptual distinctions, understanding the technology stack and the respective entities involved is crucial in determining levels of control, and therefore responsibility for adopting relevant guardrails.   The AI tech stack is comprised of a range of interconnected technical layers, each playing a crucial role in the use of AI technologies. Spanning from hardware and infrastructure to end-user applications and services, the tech stack includes the different stages and entities involved in AI systems. Notably, these are not mutually exclusive, and some entities may play more than one role across the tech stack. AI Services: These are entities that provide specialised skills and knowledge on how to leverage and adopt AI applications for specific use cases (for end-users), within business functions, operations, or industries. It includes entities that substantially modify existing models for a particular use case. Applications: These are the specific end-user products that use AI models as is, integrated, or fine-tuned to particular use cases. API Services: Application programming interfaces, or endpoints, through which applications access pre-trained models.   MLOps: Machine learning operations software, processes, or tools that curate, host, fine-tune, or manage the development, deployment and maintenance of AI models. AI Models: Pre-trained models hosted on cloud platforms from which AI applications can be built. Hardware & Infrastructure: Compute infrastructure forming the backbone of AI systems, including energy systems, networks, semiconductors, processors like CPUS/GPUs, data centers, and other components that enable AI systems.

 The levels of control and visibility over AI outputs to end-users increase higher up the stack. For example, at the infrastructure layer, hardware operators have the least control and limited insight into the outputs and potential adverse impacts of AI systems on users. In contrast, for those operating at the application or services layers, have greater control and visibility over AI outputs and interactions with end-users.  Most entities in the AI ecosystem do not own all parts of the stack and so defining the responsibilities required for each entity at each layer becomes important in operationalising the guardrails. Developers and deployers At the outset, the core tenet in assigning responsibility is that the individual or entity in control of any given step within the AI lifecycle—whether during development or deployment—should be held responsible for implementing the relevant guardrail(s) at that step of the process. This ensures appropriate accountability and oversight for risk mitigation specific to each phase of the AI lifecycle.   For instance, developers are primarily responsible for the design and technical aspects of AI systems. They bear responsibility in ensuring AI models are built on high-quality datasets and undertake testing processes to identify and address potential issues. Developers also have responsibility in providing meaningful information for deployers on model details (e.g. date, version, type of model), intended use (primary intended users, out-of-scope use cases), performance limitations, and ongoing monitoring that a model is operating as intended over time.  On the other hand, deployers are entities that enable AI models to be used as practical applications. They are often closer in proximity to end-users with responsibility for monitoring AI systems in action, collecting user-feedback, and making adjustments to 
  
Tech Council of Australia www.techcouncil.com.au   improve user experience, and address concerns or issues that arise in the context of the specific use case. We also acknowledge that developer and deployer obligations may also overlap and we are pleased to see Government recognise these distinctions not mutually exclusive. Definition of developers   The proposals paper defines developers as “organisations or individuals who design, build, train, adapt or combine AI models and applications”.  We recommend incorporating the concepts of "intentional" and "substantial modification" into the definition of developers, in line with the EU AI Act and Colorado’s AI Act (US). This will provide greater clarity to organisations in situations where AI models have been fine-tuned or re-trained. For instance, where an individual or entity has intentionally and substantially modified a low-risk AI model that subsequently becomes high-risk in its application, it is reasonable for that person or entity to assume responsibility for any adverse impacts that may arise. Definition of deployers Deployers are defined as “any individual or organisation that supplies or uses an AI system to provide a product or service”.  We are concerned that the term “AI system” is overly broad and subject to multiple interpretations. It could mean an AI model or application, it could encompass a wide range of AI components constituting a ‘system’, or include elements beyond the intended scope for applying mandatory guardrails (e.g. socio-economic features that enable AI systems). We recommend aligning the definition of deployers with the definition of developers which refers to “AI models” and removing this ambiguity by replacing the word “system” with “models”. The term "supplies" also warrants reconsideration. Although the proposals paper includes a helpful view of the AI supply chain, it categorises a ‘service provider’ as a deployer that "supplies access and integration of AI systems." A distinction should be made between access and integration. Depending on how an AI system is modified during integration, a ‘supplier’ may be better characterised as a ‘developer’.  Moreover, the construction of “supplies…AI system” could also be interpreted to include a wide array of entities at the hardware and infrastructure layer including energy, networks, semiconductors, CPU/GPU, data centres, and other suppliers of AI-related components beyond AI models. To address this ambiguity, we recommend the word ‘supplies’ to be removed. We also we recommend the definition of deployers to focus only on ‘use’ of AI systems.   Recommendation 11. Mandatory guardrails   TCA is supportive of introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings. We support guardrails that are outcomes-focused, as well as flexible and adaptable to ensure that the regulatory framework can respond dynamically to new challenges. To achieve this, we emphasise the importance that these guardrails avoid being overly prescriptive. This will minimise compliance burdens on businesses, while being open to new innovative techniques and standards for AI governance to emerge and be adopted.   We support the Government in acknowledging that guardrails should be adaptable and remain fit-for-purpose as technology continues to evolve. This will be crucial as innovative mechanisms for AI governance continue to take emerge as the AI assurance and auditing market develops globally. Interoperability becomes even more crucial to enable the sharing of best practices for safe and responsible AI adoption.   Specific guardrails Guardrail #3: Protect AI systems, and implement data governance measures to manage data quality and provenance. TCA supports the inclusion of data governance, privacy and cybersecurity measures in the guardrails. We also support the proposals for this guardrail to complement requirements under privacy, copyright, and security of critical infrastructure laws.  However, we are concerned that requiring the disclosure of data sources could  compromise proprietary data, models, or systems that are vital for maintaining competitive advantage. In adopting this guardrail, care should also be taken to ensure transparency requirements do not create vulnerabilities that could be exploited for scams, fraud, data breaches, or cyber attacks.  Guardrail #6: Inform end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content The TCA agrees that transparency is crucial for fostering trust and adoption in AI. It is equally important to ensure meaningful transparency is provided to users at the right level of detail - which will be context dependent - and to avoid circumstances where excessive notifications result in users ignoring information altogether.  We recommend that this guardrail be clarified to apply specifically to situations where the requirement to ‘inform’ end users for AI-enabled decisions should be limited in the context where there are significant consequences at stake. We also encourage the Government to clarify how this guardrail aligns with the proposed amendments to the Privacy Act which has overlaps with automated decision-making.   Guardrail #7: Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcome  At this time, the TCA is not supportive of the establishment of Guardrail #7. While the TCA is supportive of the intention to establish processes for people impacted by AI   
Tech Council of Australia www.techcouncil.com.au   systems to challenge use or outcomes, the existence of these rights remains a relatively novel concept and their effectiveness is largely untested. Current frameworks, including the EU AI Act and Canada’s AIDA, do not establish clear rights for appeal or challenge, and best practices remain to be defined.  This guardrail will be best operationalised by deployers who have the closest proximity to interactions with end-users who are closer to the AI ‘use or outcome’. Further consideration is needed regarding this guardrail; it may help to monitor and consider globally emerging practices, or other jurisdictions, for guidance on operationalisation and implementation.  Guardrail #8: Be transparent with other organisations across the supply chain about data, models, and systems to help them effectively address risks.  As above with Guardrail #3 and #6, TCA encourages meaningful transparency that does not compromise the protection of proprietary and commercial assets, adversely impact cybersecurity measures. Information provided by entities about data, models, and systems across the supply chain should be meaningful to enable shared responsibility.  Guardrail #9: Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails. Record keeping requirements are helpful to document the development of models and their evolution over time. It is important that any requirements to maintain records that as part of Australia’s mandatory guardrails to be interoperable with similar international governance mechanisms to better enable interoperability and prepare for common conformity standards to be recognised. We note the broader international work underway for led by the OECD on Reporting Frameworks for advanced AI systems arriving out of the Hiroshima process. Guardrail #10: Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with the guardrails  This guardrail includes reference to both ‘conformity’ and ‘certification’ processes. While these are related terms, they embody distinct practices that we urge the Government to consider. Conformity is an assessment which can be carried out internally or by a third party. It assesses the extent to which an AI system adheres to established guidelines, standards, and regulations. Whereas certification is a formal process where an independent third party evaluates an AI system against specific criteria and standards to provide assurance that an AI system meets these benchmarks.  Certification holds significant promise for fostering accountability in the medium- to long- term. International organisations such as ISO and IEC are also making strides in developing relevant technical standards, for example as ISO/IEC 42001. However, given the current landscape of the AI assurance and audit market—both in Australia and globally—there is a notable lack of providers equipped to conduct these assessments at this time. We also have concerns regarding Government and regulator capacity to effectively evaluate conformity assessments at this time, especially considering the overall AI skills shortage. Therefore, we recommend that the Government prioritise conformity over certification in Guardrail 10. This approach will better facilitate compliance and support innovation as the AI assurance market continues to evolve and mature.

General-purpose AI The proposals paper assumes that all General Purpose AI (GPAI) models are inherently high-risk. However, it is crucial to emphasise that levels of risk associated with any AI model, including GPAI models, is dependent on their application to specific contexts and the harms attached to their use cases.  The primary concern for oversight of any AI models, including GPAI models, should be on model capabilities rather than size or complexity. Large GPAI models do not equate to greater risk or danger; in fact, smaller, specialised models may pose risks that are equal to or even greater than GPAI models. As currently proposed, both the principles and mandatory guardrails will be sufficiently broad to encompass GPAI models. As such, the TCA does not support developing legislation based on compute thresholds and other technical criteria for GPAI models, including FLOPs, number of model parameters, quality/size of data sets,   
Tech Council of Australia www.techcouncil.com.au   inputs/modalities, number of end users etc. Legislation attached to technical criteria is likely to become outdated as advanced models emerge and researchers develop techniques requiring fewer computational resources.  Drawing lessons from California's SB 1047, it is also important that policy solutions are “informed by an empirical trajectory analysis of AI systems and capabilities…based on empirical evidence and science”.8 As such, TCA does not believe that a sub-set of guardrails, or a different set of guardrails is required at this time specifically for GPAI models. However, we acknowledge that GPAI models may present risks which are not yet well understood or unforeseeable. To this end, we recommend the establishment of an Australian AI Safety Institute which can help in better understanding and monitoring advanced AI models, including GPAI models. The Institute can also play a crucial role in coordinating with other AI Safety Institutes established globally. Open-Source AI Open-source AI models play a vital role in promoting transparency, enabling research, innovation and development, and experimentation in AI. They also help in progressing other responsible AI measures (e.g. explainability, bias, safety, and efficiency).9  The proposals paper raises an important concern on the issue of ‘open-washing’ with reference to an article discussing ‘openness’. However, it is crucial to ‘openness’ and genuine open-source initiatives. Open-source AI models have particular characteristics:  • publicly available source code / algorithms;  • modifiability where users can view, further develop and train;  • disclosure of architecture, training, documentation and datasets;  • licensing under open-source licences, usually at no cost and with attribution, and;  • levels of engagement from a community of users and developers.10  In contrast, ‘openness’ encompasses includes some of these practices above, but are crucially distinguished by the free and public availability of models and algorithms to users, which may not meet the standards of open-source practices.   Similar to the EU AI Act, we recommend that open-source AI models should be exempted from any Australian legislation. This will help preserve the culture of open technology development and innovation, as well as recent breakthrough techniques that have made AI safer. A. Proposed pr inciples  
Clubs Australia believes the proposed principles on high- risk AI are comprehensive but must be 
applied flexibly. We suggest  the following adjustments:  
• Low-risk AI : Clear guidelines on low-risk applications, such as administrative tasks and 
customer service chatbots, should be established to allow clubs  to use AI, particularly  narrow AI  
use without  unnecessary regulat ory burden.  
• Categories of Uses: Treat certain high- risk AI categories, like biometric -based exclusion 
identification in gambling, separately with specific regulations. This provides unique 
considerations and balanced flexibility when potential har m outweighs  conventional rights.  
The use of biometrics to assist clubs in managing their safer gambling obligations including exclusion 
identification  by AI -powered facial recognition technology ( FRT) is vital.  
These programs involve  the individual s signing deeds that prohibit  them from entering gambling 
areas  at the club (or the venue as a whole) . While certain principles must be in place throughout the 
AI life cycle to minimise false negative and false positive identifications which may be a result of the 
AI developing discriminatory or biased properties.  There must also be proportionate and sufficient 
flexibility in circumstances when potential harm may take priority over  tradition al civil rights . 
1. Recommendation:  Clubs Australia recommends  the proposed principles be non-
exhaustive and open- ended to allow flexibility for certain approved uses to be treated 
separately.  
 
B. Defining high-risk AI  
Clubs Australia believe that the proposed principles, supported by examples, provide a solid foundation for understanding high- risk AI settings and models. However, to enhance clarity and 
certainty, we recommend a hybrid approach that combines both principles -based and list -based 
elements.  
For a list -based approach, similar to the EU and Canada, we suggest including existing hi gh-risk use 
cases such as:  
• Facial recognition technology  
• Biometric data processing  
• AI in healthcare diagnostics  
• AI in financial decision- making 
To capture emerging uses of AI, the list should aim to be technologically neutral and regularly 
updated based on technological advancements and industry feedback.  
For a principles -based approach, the guidance should address:  
• Clear definitions  of high- risk AI settings and models  
• Examples  of both high- risk and low -risk applications  
• Criteria  for assessing risk levels  
• Best practices  for transparency, accountability, and testing  
2. Recommendation: Clubs Australia recommends  a hybrid approach that  includes an 
exhaustive list to capture existing high-risk uses and open- ended principle -based guidance 
in consideration of emerging uses of AI  and technological advancements .

C. Banned uses (unacceptable risk level)  
Certain high- risk AI use cases should be banned due to unacceptable risk levels.  
Lack of knowledge/ consent:  
Applications using personal data without knowledge or consent, especially exclusion systems in 
designated gambling areas at the club premises, should also be banned.  
As mentioned above,  self-exclusion involves the individual entering into a deed that allows clubs to 
prevent that individual from entering gambling areas , such as gaming rooms  or the venue.  State and 
Territory governments may also look to extend gambling- related exclusions to include involuntary 
exclusions in the future.  In addition, patrons banned for convicted or suspected criminal activities 
may be impacted.  
Exclusions and bans require the collection of biometrical data for use by systems using AI . The 
storage and use of this personal data should not be permitted without individual  consent or 
knowledge in the case of involuntary orders.  
Age-restricted/minors:  
Clubs operate in a highly regulated industry with a number of age- restricted  services. As a vulnerable 
group, AI may pose potential risks of misuse causing harm  to minors  
AI deployment in age- restricted services must protect minors from potential misuse. AI age 
verification systems in industries like online gaming and finance must adhere to stringent regulations.  
3. Recommendation: Clubs Australia recommends establishing clear definitions and 
criteria for high- risk AI applications to ensure the regulatory framework addresses the most 
dangerous uses while still allowing innovation.  
 
D. Application to General Purpose AI  The importance of a flexible and adaptable regulatory framework to capture new and emerging forms 
of high- risk AI, including GPAI. The principles'  emphasis on testing, transparency, and accountability 
throughout the AI lifecycle provides  a robust framework that can adapt to evolving technologies. This 
framework should be regularly reviewed to keep pace with technological advancements, ensuring 
continued relevance and effectiveness.  
Clubs Australia highlights  the need for stringent standards across all GPAI models, focusing on 
safety, transparency, and accountability  to ensure that clubs'  deploymen t can manage GPAI risks 
and comply with the relevant regulations .  
4. Recommendation:  Clubs Australia suggests a flexible and adaptive regulatory 
framework that is regularly reviewed and updated should be applied to high -risk GPAI 
models . 
 
E. Proposed mandatory guardrails  
The proposed mandatory guardrails effectively distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain 
and throughout the AI lifecycle. The requirements assigned to developers and deployers should be 
proportionate, ensuring that each party is accountable and informed about  their role in the 
development and deployment of AI systems.  
Clubs Australia believe that the proposed mandatory guardrails are generally adequate to address 
the risks associated with AI . Yet a more tailored approach is necessary for broad application, we 
suggest  adapting the guardrails based on the risk level of different AI models. For low -risk AI models, 
the focus should be on ensuring basic compliance with transparency and accountability standards. 
For high- risk AI models, more stringent measures should be implemented, including rigorous testing, 
continuous monitoring, and detailed reporting requirements.

2.  Version – Initial Public Draft (for public comments)

Cornerstone Strengths
The document outlines a strong commitment and a broad-based approach for AI regulation. It also advocated a risk-based approach to AI regulation. Strategic differentiator that is crucial in building a strong AI governance momentum to ensure a safe AI adoption across organizations and industry are listed below.
* AI Expert Group: Setting up of a focused group (broad skill based) to advise on mandatory guardrails for AI development and deployment in high-risk settings.
* High-Risk Settings: The document considers options for mandatory use of guardrails for AI in high-risk settings. Detailed assessment on the need to have guardrails to mitigate risks, principle-based approach to define high-risk AI with known or foreseeable uses, ensuring transparency across supply chain and AI life cycle by different actors and options to mandate by adaptation of Australia’s existing legal frameworks through to enacting new AI-specific legislation or framework legislation.
* Integrated Approach for AI regulation: The government aims to balance mitigating AI risks with supporting innovation through is various investment and funding programs and regulatory strategy for AI as below.
* AI Ethics Principles: There is a push for mandatory compliance with AI Ethics Principles in high-risk settings, moving beyond voluntary adherence. These principles provide important values-based guidance for the intent of regulatory design and align with internationally recognized principles on ethical and responsible AI.
* Best Practices and Standards: Establishing voluntary AI Safety Standards and promoting best practices for organizations using AI.
* Government Leadership: The AI in Government Taskforce and the Digital Transformation Agency (DTA) will lead by example, developing policies and piloting an AI Assurance Framework.
* International Engagement: Australia will engage globally to share regulatory approaches and learn from other countries.




Recommendations
We recognize that the underlying risk lies in the disparity between the pace of innovation and the evolving AI governance structures. Governments worldwide are assessing AI regulations to address existing gaps across various evolving technology domains and sectors. 
In line with First Nation and cultural protocols, a risk-based approach with preventive measures is recommended:
* Hazard analysis exposure and labeling of known risks. We are dealing with known risks which are consistent in its occurrence and its intended impact. This approach can also consider blending a list of risks that are unacceptable and high risk as prescribed in the EU AI act and other regulations.
* Anticipating and adaptive approach to effectively identify target risks and manage mitigation measures by ways of implementing principle that are interoperable.
* Secure-by-design principles are at the forefront of Preventive risk management approach. It is critical to mandating standards, and collaboration with industry and international partners.
With regards to Guardrails adoption in AI regulation, it involves setting up a framework of guidelines and controls which are overarching laws that provide a structured AI governance. 
This approach will place greater emphasis on implementing governance at each layer of the AI lifecycle, enabling supply chain actors to effectively manage identified risks.
Regulatory advice to implement mandatory guardrails for high-risk settings.
1.  Develop Clear Guidelines: Create comprehensive guidelines outlining the guardrails for AI development and deployment. These should be clear, accessible, and easy to understand.
2.  Encourage Transparency: Promote a culture of transparency where organizations voluntarily disclose their adherence to these guidelines. This can be achieved through regular reporting and public statements.
3.  Stakeholder Engagement: Involve all relevant stakeholders, including industry experts, policymakers, and the public, in the development and refinement of these guidelines.
4.  Monitoring and Feedback: Establish mechanisms for monitoring compliance and gathering feedback to continuously improve the guidelines.
5.  Recognition and Incentives: Recognize and reward organizations that voluntarily disclose their adherence to the guardrails, encouraging others to follow suit.
Legal recommendations - Model contract terms as stipulated in EU AI Act would be on risk allocation among different players. Standardize agreements will ensure that all parties involved in the creation, integration and deployment of high-risk AI systems adhere to best practices and ethical guidelines. This will also prevent the downstream players to not over boarded by uncontrollable risk transfer by upstream providers, esp. AI model providers. 
Final thoughts
This document can serve as a foundational framework for compliance guidelines from a risk management and AI governance perspective for high-risk settings. Indications from mandating 10 voluntary and enforcing a robust AI regulatory framework will prove to shield and manage Bias, transparency and explainability as preventive mechanisms for harm to citizens rights and economic welfare. Going a step further we will need guardrails to prevent unacceptable scenarios like manipulative AI, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring and biometric identification should be critical. Stakeholder management and inclusive discussion with international community will add to further refining AI standards.

specific
examples
and
use
cases,
particularly
for
“borderline”
situations.
End-of-Life
and
Maintaining
Functionality
Responsible
use
of
any
system
includes
managing
it
when
it
reaches
end-of-life
or
is
disrupted,
such
as
by
malicious
activity,
a
stakeholder
error,
or
supply
chain
issues.
The
proposal
paper
seems
to
have
a
rather
significant
blind
spot
regarding
such
issues.
It
is
suggested
that
specific
mention
be
made,
perhaps
in
guardrail
8,
regarding
transparency
across
the
supply
chain
to
handle
such
issues.
In
particular:
●
It
should
be
clear
if
and
how
an
organisation’s
data,
which
might
become
incorporated
into
an
AI
system,
can
be
migrated
at
the
system’s
end-of-life
or
end-of-support.
●
It
should
be
clear
if
and
how
an
organisation
can
ensure
business
continuity
and
perform
disaster
recovery
when
the
AI
system
fails.
This
will
become
increasingly
important
as
AI
systems
are
used
in
critical
business
functions,
be
it
explicitly,
such
as
an
organisation
built
around
an
AI
system,
or
implicitly,
where
the
efficiencies
brought
by
AI
systems
result
in
the
organisation
no
longer
having
the
staffing
resources
that
allow
it
to
function
in
the
absence
of
the
AI
system.
4Means
of
Enforcement,
Appeal
and
Oversight
Mandatory
guardrails
must
have
meaningful
enforcement,
appeal,
and
oversight
avenues
at
several
levels.
While
we
may
hope
that
organisations
will
apply
the
guardrails
effectively
and
in
good
faith,
this
may
not
be
guaranteed,
be
it
due
to
deliberate
efforts
to
circumvent
them
or
under-resourcing
their
compliance.
Most
of
the
guardrails
listed
sound
reasonable
in
the
abstract
but
need
to
be
accompanied
by
technically
meaningful
and
enforceable
standards
and
language.
For
example,
an
organisation
should
not
be
able
to
satisfy
guardrail
6
on
informing
end-users
by
simply
telling
every
customer
that
AI
might
have
influenced
their
decision.
Some
of
the
guardrails
do
reference
current
and
ongoing
work
on
standards,
which
is
applauded,
although
we
must
be
vigilant
for
loopholes,
particularly
with
new
technologies.
At
a
different
level,
an
organisation
may
satisfy
guardrail
5
on
human
control
or
intervention
by
having
an
understaffed
department
in
charge
of
receiving
reports
that
its
system
is
making
incorrect
decisions
about
people,
such
as
regarding
loan
applications.
Meaningful
standards
must
be
placed
on
such
human
interventions
and
strong
regulatory
oversight,
along
with
the
ability
for
those
impacted
to
appeal
to
a
well-resourced
and
knowledgable
government
agency
and
ombudsperson
with
investigatory
and
enforcement
powers.
Now
is
the
time
to
make
this
clear,
so
that
organisations
build
this
into
their
decision
on
if
AI
is
worth
deploying,
potentially
at
the
expense
of
human
workers.
AI
in
Cyberphysical
Systems
and
Critical
Infrastructure
The
proposals
paper
appears
to
have
somewhat
of
a
blind
spot
regarding
the
types
of
AI
used
in
cyberphysical
systems,
such
as
robots,
drones,
self-driving
cars,
and
critical
infrastructure.
Critical
infrastructure
itself
is
mentioned
as
a
high-risk
or
impact
application.
Still,
there
appears
to
be
little
focus
in
the
proposals
paper
on
the
types
of
AI
used
in
such
applications,
which
focus
less
on
big
data,
GPAI,
generative
AI,
and
other
systems
based
on
deep
neural
network
models.
Instead,
they
tend
to
rely
more
on
AI
techniques
such
as
planning,
optimisation,
various
forms
of
machine
perception,
and
other
forms
of
machine
learning.
A
specific
feature
of
such
systems
tends
to
be
their
ability
to
take
knowledge
that
is
more
symbolic,
such
as
analytical
models
or
equations
describing
system
behaviour
rather
than
or
in
addition
to
the
training
data
that
is
nowadays
more
commonly
associated
with
the
training
of
deep
neural
networks.
This
tends
to
be
due
to
a
combination
of
appropriateness
to
those
applications
(e.g.,
the
AI
specifically
for
routing
an
ambulance
has
little
need
for
GPAI
or
generative
AI),
inertia
within
the
sector
that
tends
to
delay
the
introduction
of
new
technologies
and
an
increased
aversion
to
risk.
Such
techniques
tend
to
have
different
risks
compared
to
newer
techniques.
The
guardrails
can
still
apply,
and
it
is
highly
recommended
that
the
guidance
and
commentary
around
them
be
expanded
to
be
more
useful
to
these
types
of
AI
systems.
5Hidden
AI
Risks
and
End
Users
As
AI
becomes
more
pervasive,
it
becomes
much
harder
to
determine
who
is
impacted
by
an
AI
system
beyond
the
traditional
end
users.
For
example,
a
lawyer
might
use
an
AI
system
to
summarise
and
allow
them
to
review
many
more
cases
than
they
might
otherwise
be
able
to.
However,
if,
unbeknownst
to
them,
the
AI
system
has
some
bias
that
results
in
vital
information
being
consistently
omitted,
misrepresented,
or
hallucinated,
this
can
profoundly
affect
their
client
4
.
A
more
ominous
situation
may
involve
nefarious
actors
deliberately
poisoning
AI
models,
perhaps
by
generating
fake
resources
that
they
know
will
be
scraped
by
the
builder
of
an
LLM
and
that
results
in
targetted
bias
against
certain
groups
of
people
in
such
applications.
It
is
difficult
to
square
this
with
the
glossary
definition
of
“end-user”,
which
would
consider
both
the
lawyer
and
their
client
an
“end-user”.
The
risk
of
AI
is
hidden
from
the
client
-
they
may
not
even
know
that
the
lawyer
is
using
AI.
To
this
end,
it
may
be
necessary
to
instead
define
an
“end-user”
as
someone
who
knowingly
uses
a
system
with
declared
AI
and
an
“impacted
individual”,
such
as
the
client,
who
may
not
have
a
choice
or
visibility
into
the
system
but
may
be
impacted.
This
may
mean
that
the
end-user
is
now
subject
to
additional
guardrails,
such
as
guardrail
6
that
may
require
them
to
inform
the
“impacted
individual”.
The
idea
of
the
use
of
AI
being
hidden
has
other
profound
implications
that
should
be
considered
when
implementing
guardrails.
For
example,
users
are
often
unaware
that
photographs
taken
with
modern
mobile
phones,
with
default
settings,
already
have
AI
enhancements
applied
to
them.
This
often
includes
generative
components,
particularly
when
objects
are
unclear.
The
underlying
intent
of
helping
users
to
capture
more
pleasing
images
is
in
good
faith.
However,
the
implications
are
problematic.
At
one
level,
to
fulfil
the
letter
of
guardrail
6,
it
now
becomes
necessary
to
label
all
photos
taken
with
a
modern
mobile
phone
as
AI-generated
or
augmented,
even
if
this
is
not
the
intent
of
the
end-user.
This
has
the
same
effect
as
the
aforementioned
“may
contain
traces
of
nuts”
labelling,
where
the
presence
of
the
label
becomes
meaningless
in
the
marketplace
without
the
requirement
of
additional
nuance.
At
a
more
concerning
level,
however,
is
the
risk
of
distortion
of
truth
across
critical
uses
of
such
technologies.
For
example,
images
from
mobile
phones
of
a
crime
scene,
license
plates,
labels,
and
the
like,
taken
as
evidence,
can
no
longer
be
relied
upon.
Similarly,
the
identification
of
faces,
particularly
where
they
are
blurry,
becomes
problematic
as
it
will
be
unclear
if
the
AI
“enhancement”
has
caused
the
face
to
look
like
someone
else.

for,

rails

Proposals paper for introducing mandatory  
guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
Consultation                                                                   
Australian Banking Association, PO Box H218, Australia Square NSW 1215 | +61 2 8298 0417 | ausbanking.org.au  1 
Overview  
The ABA thanks the Department for  their significant effort s in preparing this con sultation  and 
appreciates the opportunity to provide comment on the proposals . As the organisations entrusted 
with the safeguarding financial assets  of Austra lians, banks are acutel y aware of the im portan ce of 
effective risk management  processes .  
Banks have long leveraged technology to enhance customer service and strengthen banking 
security. Artificial intelligence (AI) is now enabling more personali sed services, making some 
offerings more cost -effective and accessible, streamlining administrative and analytical tasks, and 
improving the consistency and quality of consumer outcomes. However, as AI is increasingly 
exploited malicious acto rs to target consumers through technology -enabled crimes,  AI itself is 
becoming for banks to more effectively detect and combat  financial crime  and fraud.  
Key obser vations  and recommendations   
• AI has the potential to be a globally transformative  techno logy, however, th is potential needs to 
be balanced with practices that promote safe and responsible  use.  
• Regulation should be proportionate and targeted to specific risks. An unnecessarily high 
regulatory burden may have an adverse impact on innovation  and produc tivity, limiting 
Australia’s ability to compete internationally . 
• Well intende d regulatory reforms can often have the unintended consequence of imposing 
disprop ortionately expensive , or operational ly challenging o bligations on small and medium 
sized companies.  
• Assessing high -risk AI applications  should be done in a techn ology ne utral way  with 
consider ation given to the  specific na ture of harm  and its novelty . 
• Prior to consider ing new legislation  or regulatory obligations , a gap anal ysis should be 
undertaken to map the coverage of existing laws in relation to AI issues.  This gap analysis 
would consider the  specific harms and applications within individual sectors, rather than 
considering the harms as equally large in different sectors.  
• Where existing regulations are unable to address material risks, a targeted and pro -innovation 
approach to additional  regulation should be used to close the gaps, rather than legislating a 
comprehensive AI law.  
• For high ly regulated sectors, it ’s criti cal that g uardrails be commensurate and reflective of the 
incumbent regulatory environment of those industries/sectors.  Where there is existing and 
effective regulation, addition al AI specific regulation should be avoid ed.  
• As AI is rapidly evolving , proactive monitoring of emerging risks and gaps to existing regulation 
should occur.  A risk -based approach would allow for proportionate responses to new and 
emergin g AI use cases by targeting high risk applications of AI while still allowing for 
responsible innovations that drive economic growth.  
• Sectoral regulators would also be best placed to work with industry on future high -risk uses, 
ensuring that potential innovation isn’t categorically prevented, while ensuring AI uses are 
sufficiently regulated.

Balancing regulation with inno vation  
Kristalina Georgieva , Managing Director of the IMF , notes that  AI represents a technological 
revolution unlike any before it  – a shift that will fundamentally transform the global economy.1 While 
AI evolution poses risks and disruption , which call for prudent  risk management , these risks need 
to be managed in such a way that doesn’t excessively constrain innovation. Just as there are risks 
of inadequate regulation, well intended , but excessively restrictive regulation too poses substantial 
risks to economic development and prosperity.  
These risks are well evidenced . Mario Draghi – the former European Central Bank President – was 
tasked with identifying why ‘ on a per capita basis, real disposable income has grown almost twice 
as much in the US as in the EU since 2000 .’2 His observations include:   
• Business adoption of AI will be the defining variable in determining competitiveness.3 
• Regulatory barriers which seek to limit risk by regulat ing organisationa l processes  ex ante have 
significantly constrained economic growth.  
• AI has risks  like all new technologies;  however,  AI specific regulation has led to complex 
overlaps with other obligations. This has created substantial compliance burden s and risks 
excluding EU companies from AI innovation and deployment.4 
• These obligations have disproportionately impacted small and medium sized companies.  
• The impact on innovation and investment has been material – EU investment into cutting edge 
AI is only 1% of the US.  
Draghi’s conclusions have been supported widely, including by Santander – one of Europe’s 
largest banks – concluding that Europe’s slower economic growth is in a large part driven by a less 
flexible, more complex regulatory framework.5 
While not specific to AI, r esearch6 has shown in Europe that the introduction of GDPR has 
materially impacted competitive dynamics, productivity, and innovation. These burdens have 
disproportionately fallen on small and medium enterprises, and hastened consolidation amongst 
venders.  Economic studies7 on app development  innovation in the EU concluded  that despite one 
of GDPR’s objectives being to support innovation through certainty, imbalance between 
preventative and outcomes -based  regulation has led to a  material decline in app development. 
GDPR is an ambitious and importan t reform to enhance consume r privacy, however this example 
highlights the harm that can be done when an overly preventative approach is taken to enact 
important consumer protections.  
The Productivity Commission  has also raised these concerns, cautio ning:  
“These effects of regulation on economic activity — especially potential distributional effects 
on smaller firms — need to be considered when creating digital privacy regulations. An 
overly legalistic focus on the need for privacy safeguards that is not coupled with a 
consi deration of their costs in limiting data use, competition and technological innovation 
risks regulation swinging too far in the direction of restriction. ”8

Where there are common themes to potential risks (e.g. privacy), the ABA strong supports a 
detailed review of existing legislation and regulation , with any gaps addressed in via existing 
regulatory frameworks. As AI risks extend horizontally across the economy, establishing parallel 
obligations risks introducing similar challenges  to those identified in the EU. While o verly complex 
and overlapping regulatory obligations have implications on all organisations,  we are particularly 
concerned with the potential  disproportionate and anti -competitive impact they can have on small 
and medium enterprises.  
For example, the proposed reforms to the Privacy Act9 contained in  Part 15 , would impose 
transparency and communication obligations to individuals when  automated decision making  is 
used. It would be concerning if separate, but functionally similar privacy obligations were 
introduced in parallel.  
 
Defining high -risk AI  
The ABA recognises there are inherent difficulties in designing regulation to be responsive to 
unforeseen risks and this often requires an ex-ante approach . While we ackn owledge  the focus  of 
the framework  is therefore preventive based (versus outcome based),  the proposed methodology , 
which takes a macro view of risk , abstract  view of harm , and is technology -neutral , is very broad.  
Focusing on the specific technolog y under pinning  AI risks , rather than the anticipate harm, would  
embed  a legal system based on their current technology only , resulting in a rigid regulatory 
framework that may struggle to adapt as AI applications rapidly evolve. Such an approach could 
trap Australia in an outdated posture, unable to adapt to  emerging challenges effectively.  
 
Instead, new regulatory responses  should focus on addressing potential harms in a thematic, 
outcome -driven way, rather than targeting specific technologies. If a harm is significant enough to 
warrant legislative attention, that harm  – rather than its AI manifestation  – should be the primary 
focus.  There is long-standing  precedent for this approach in addressing harm  where there is 
significant  variability in  how and where it may man ifest. For example,  the Anti -Discrimination Act 
1977 (NSW) prohibits racial vilification  in a technology neutral manner, rather than applying 
separate vilification laws to online vs offline vilification.10  
 
The consultation paper provides a comprehensive assessment of the current and potential harms 
that AI poses.  Categorically, these can be summarised as:  
• Harms from discrimination/bias  in decision making, services etc. (particularly with respect to 
protected characteristics and marginalised communities).  
• Harms from inappropriate, malicious, illegal use of generative AI tools  – e.g. 
dissemination of misinformation/disinformation to erode social cohesion, democratic trust, 
weaponisation by malicious actors (i.e. scams and fraud, creation of dehumanising, exploitative 
deepfakes etc .). 
• Intentional or unintentional intellectual/cultural property infringement through use of 
generative AI tools – e.g. through misappropriation of First Nations cultural material.

• Harms from polarisation, exposure etc. from engagement with AI  – e.g. through 
algorithmic content recommendations on social media.   
While the above categories present clear cases of the harm AI can cause, each harm is distinct 
and an extension of a preexisting harm  or offen se (e.g. IP infringement occurs without AI , hateful 
content creation doesn’t require generative AI). There is no doubt  that AI will accelerate th ese risks 
and add new complexity, however it is important to ensure regulation identifies whether the risks 
are novel or a step up on existing risks.  
Clear identif ication and cat egorisation o f potential  harms is an important input in ensuring 
responses effect ively target the  appropriate part of a process  and/or risk. For exampl e, it is unlikely 
that the guardrails  would be adhered to foreign domiciled  firms without a  local presence , that 
nonetheless  offer publicly  accessible generative AI tools  to consumers . Therefore, it’s likely that 
measures would need to be taken to regulate the use of the output by an end user to mitigate 
copyright risks  and harms a ssociat ed with extreme  content generation.  
The ABA strongly supports the development of a clear taxonomy of the categorical harms , which 
then assesses whether AI introduces risks  that are sufficiently incremental and/or novel , and maps 
this back to existing legislation through a gap analysis.  
 
Experiences of other jur isdictions  
As AI continue s to evolve, the community rightfully  expects government to consider policy opt ions 
to support its safe usage. While this is translating  to increas ed focus  on policy reforms b y 
governments  globally, this is a fast-moving  space , with significant variability. While jurisdictions like 
the EU have taken a particular approach,  this model has not  yet been  emulated else where , and it 
remains unclear what , if any, consensus  approach will emerge.  Some examples have been  
provided below to demonstrate th is:    
United States  
As home to 32 of the top 50 AI companies, regulatory developments in California  are naturally 
watched closely. After t he California State Sen ate approved Senate Bill 1047  – a landmark piece o f 
AI regulation – on September 29 , 2024, the Governor of California, Ga vin Newsom , vetoed the bill . 
There are several  commonalities between Senate Bill 1047 and proposed reforms in Australia:  
• A focus on high -risk AI specifically  through defining ‘covered models .’  
• A prevent ative, ex ante  approach to r egulation.  
• A numerical threshold approach to determining what models are covered. SB 104 7 
references both computing  power and financial cost as  indicators of risk potential .11 
• Requirement t o conduct annual conformity assessmen ts.  
• Requirement to implement  comprehensive monitoring  and risk management processes.

“By focusing only on the most expensive and large -scale models, SB 1047 establishes a

more dangerous than the models targeted by SB 1047 - at the potential expense of 
curtailing the very innovation that fuels advancement in favor of the public good. ” 
“Adaptability is critical as we race to regulate a technology still in its infancy. This will

whether an Al system is deployed in high -risk environments, involves critical 
decision -making or the use of sensitive data. ” 
The Bill proposed a preventative  ex ante approach  to address unknown risks , and use-agnostic 
approach to assessing high -risk. These approa ches were both widely critic ised – including  by 
prominent politic ians like N ancy Pelosi, leading  AI ac ademics13, and the influential voices in the 
media (e.g. newspaper s of record l ike the  Financial Times).14 
Japan  
The consultation p aper notes  that the proposals go beyond the principles agreed in the Hiroshima 
AI Process. While standards  agreed to in international agreemen ts should not be default define the 
regulatory ceiling, it should  be noted that J apan is not seeking  to materially regulate AI b eyond t he 
agreed principles in the H iroshima AI Process.  
Japan’s guidance for AI implementation - the Social Principles of Human -Centric AI15 – explicitly 
includes innovation as a core principle, alongside risk and privacy.  In practice, this involves Japan 
regulat ing AI primarily through existing laws rather than specific industry legislation . This means 
that the development, deployment and use of AI are subject to laws, including:  
• The Copyright Act  
• The Personal Information Protection Law  
• The Unfair Competition Prevention Act  
• The Economic Security Promotion Act  
Specific legislation has been amended as required to address specific risks as they emerge or are 
foreseen. For example, the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act regulates advanced 
algorithmic models deployed for high -speed trading through additional compliance and 
transparency oblig ations.16  
The Japan Fair Trade Commission routinely considers the risks of new technologies to unfair 
competition and cartel conduct. To date they have concluded potential AI harms are broadly 
addressed under the existing Anti -monopoly act17 and conduct targeted consultation to assess 
emerging risk (e.g. through a current Generative AI inquiry).
