United Kingdom  
To date, the develop ments in the UK suggest no significant  departure from the  pro-innovation 
approach to AI regulation contained in the UK’s AI white paper.  This approach  involves:  
• a cross -sector and outcome -based framework  for regulating AI, underpinned by five core 
principles: safety, security and robustness, appropriate transparency and explainability, 
fairness, accountability and governance, and contestability and redress.  
• A framework that would be implemented by sector -specific regulators  by applying existing laws 
and issuing supplementary regulatory guidance. Selected regulators  are required to publish AI 
annual strategic plans , providing businesses with much -needed direction  that is responsive to 
the existing regulatory environment.  
• Not intention to enact horizontal AI regulation. Instead, the White Paper and the Response 
support a "principles -based framework" for existing sector -specific regulators to interpret and 
apply to the development and use of AI within their domains.  
We strongly support an integrated approach to AI, ensuring the risks and opportunities of AI are not 
considered in isolation of each other . We support this joint approach, as noted by the current UK 
Minister The Rt Hon Peter Kyle in July:18 
“We have already commissioned our  AI Action Plan which will set out how we can make the 
very best use of artificial intelligence to grow the economy and improve public services, and 
the relationship between citizens and the public services that they depend  on.” 
 
Responses to specific questions  
Note th at some questions have been responded to categorically.  
1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high -risk AI? Are there any principles we should 
add or remove? Please identify any:  
- low-risk use cases that are unintentionally captured  
- categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for defence or national 
security purposes.  
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations 
people, communities and Country?  
3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high -
risk AI settings and high -risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative 
uses, needed?  
- If you prefer a list -based approach (similar to  the EU and Canada), what use cases should we 
include? How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?  
- If you prefer a principles -based approach, what should we address in guidance to give the 
greatest clarity?  
4. Are there high -risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory 
response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)? If so, how should we define 
these?

Generally, principles -based approach es to regulation of risk are preferred  when the risk is 
understood. Howev er, w hile we appreciate the intention of enabling flexibility , we are concerned 
that the wide breadth of the principles as proposed would introduce an intolerable level of 
ambiguity and uncertainty to businesses.  This could have the unintended effect of causing 
organisations with conservative approaches to risk management, to avoi d deploying AI where they 
identify ambiguity.  
Where a principles -based approach is taken, the ABA strongly  recommends that greater detail and 
clarity around the scope and sector -specific application of the proposed principles be provided to 
ensure they produce the intended outcome. This detail would be best supported through provision 
of illustrative examples, and sector -specific guidance to ensure the principles are not applied too 
broadly to low -risk uses.  It is also important t hat the harms as they pertain to a particular sector, 
should be specifica lly identified and assessed against existing regulatory controls , crucial to 
avoiding the unintended consequences of regulatory overlap.  
In absence of clear sector -specific applications and  defined harms, the broad scope of potential 
harm  and the  intention of taking a preventative approach to unknown risks , may mean a degree of 
prescriptiveness is required. It may be useful to consider whether the proposed high -risk 
framework and associated regulation would in theory prevent the deployment of specific AI uses 
altogether. This exceptionally high -risk applicati ons could become candidates for inclusion in a 
prohibited use list. For example, the  EU AI Act prohibits AI systems deploying capabilities that:  
• Use subliminal, manipulative, or deceptive techniques to distort behaviour  
• Exploit vulnerabilities  
• Use biometric categorisation systems  
• Develop or use social scoring  
• Assessing the propensity of an individual to commit a crime  
• Compile facial recognition databases  
• Infer emotions in workplaces or educational institutions  
• Use ‘real -time’ remote biometric identification (RBI) in publicly accessible spaces (for law 
enforcement)  
While further discussion would be required, the ABA in principle support the inclusion of a clear list 
of high -risk, or very -high risk, uses of AI, as seen in the EU AI ACT, to provide  appropriate clarity to 
businesses and the community. It is suggested  that either domain -specific lists and illustrative 
examples are included alongside proposed principles, or that a list -based definition is pursued to 
define high -risk AI, to ensure clarity.  Separating these highest risk uses from all other uses may 
additionally support a principles -based  approach, as it could theoretically ensure the risk -based 
framework is not required to address uses which categorically pose much high harm.  
 
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high -risk AI, 
such as general -purpose AI (GPAI)?  
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?  
We have significant concerns with the breadth of the proposed technology -specific  approach  to 
GPAI  – which is understood as  a response to concerns that all model s with ancillary, multipurpose 
capabilities represent an unknown, and therefore high -risk. As GPAI evolve over time, w ithout 
reference to the specific use of a model, the regulatory environment of the sector, and the potential 
harms, there is potential that the principles result in all GPAI application being considered high -risk.                                                                  
Australian Banking Association, PO Box H218, Australia Square NSW 1215 | +61 2 8298 0417 | ausbanking.org.au  9 
A harm -based approach should be taken with respect to the constituent risks of any sophisticated 
AI model, with necessary regulation to address gaps then informed. For example, c oncerns raised 
about generative AI  could be categorically defined as:  
• The training data (such as bias or inappropriately sourced training data)  
• User interaction  (such as users deliberately trying to generate offensive, malicious, illegal 
content etc. ) 
• The outputs (such as sharing of sensitive information , copyright material, misinformation)  
Consideration should be given to each of these concerns with respect to specific harms and 
sectors. The output of general AI would have very different risks and regulatory needs based on 
different uses: e.g. generative AI  
 
7. What are suitable indicators for defining GPAI models as high -risk? For example, is it enough to 
define GPAI as high -risk against the principles, or should it be based on technical capability such 
as FLOPS (e.g. 10^25 or 10^26 threshold), advice from a sci entific panel, government or other 
indicators?  
There are material challenges with using technical references to assess the risk of GPAI models  
that are agno stic to how AI w ould be used, and the types of harms that could emerge through use 
(e.g. FLOPS).  Techn ical capability does not necessarily denote or correlate with more harmful 
outputs and is highly specific to the context or scenario in which the AI/GPAI is deployed.  Many AI 
models would already exceed predefined computational thresholds, and the rate of growth may 
render fixed thresholds unviable.  
EU reviews19 have identified the flaws in arbitrary threshold -based approaches to regulating 
general purpose AI , instead calling for specific sector and harm -based approaches.  
Indicators of high -risk should refer to the potential harm of a specific AI model with respect to its 
deployment, intention and the regulatory environment of a sector.  
 
Mandatory Guardrail s 
Note that  comments have bee n provided  thematically and  on individual guardrails  rather than in 
direct response  to the consultation  questions.  
The ABA recognises the importance of  ensuring there is a degree of  cross -economy commonality 
in regulation.  
In principle, we support the intention of the proposed guardrails, but these should not seek to 
introduce AI specific regulation over a process, where the existing outcome is already sufficiently 
regulated. As the consultation paper acknowledges, the use of AI is subject to several existing 
laws. For example : 
• Existing IP and privacy laws provide compliance obligations over the use of data to train a 
model  
• A model’s outputs must comply with existing discrimination laws.

• For banks and financial service providers, the development or use of AI is also subject to 
specific legislation that provides strong consumer protections. In addition to existing legislation, 
banks have well established and sophisticated risk governance frameworks which consider 
many of the operational  and technology risks that arise in non -AI contexts which equally apply 
in the implementation of AI tools.  
For highly regulated sectors like banking, the determination of the need for, and implementation 
requirements of , the guardrails should reside with existing regulators. AI risks in banking are 
already covered  by comprehensive, principles -based regulation and legislation. These include 
competition and consumer laws, duty of care obligations, Design and Distribution obligations, the 
Privacy Act, and prudential standards regulated by APRA.  
Banks are responsible for ensuring compliance with laws and regulations, regardless of the 
technology used . Regulators hold institutions accountable for compliance failures, including those 
involving AI.  This allows for flexibility even where the regulation was not specifically designed for AI  
(e.g. APRA regulation is generally principles -based and outcome  oriented ). While we support the 
objectives of the guardrails, the guardrails should not introduce separate or new obligations on 
banks were there is no identifiable incremental risk. We strongly support the technology neutral 
approach to  AI regulation in banking outlined by  APRA:20 
“we believe our prudential framework already has adequate regulations in place to deal with 
generative AI for the time being. Our prudential standards may not specifically refer to AI 
but nor do they need to at the moment.  They have intentionally been designed to be 
high-level, principles -based and technology neutral. ” 
“ Having monitored developments in this area over several years, our advice now is that  
entities with robust technology platforms and a strong track record of risk 
management are good candidates to experiment with AI and should feel confident 
proceeding. ” 
“So while we are watching closely, we are confident for now that we have the tools to act, 
including formal enforcement powers, should it be necessary to intervene to preserve 
financial safety and protect the community.”  
Using a harms -based  approach to regulation, an outline  is provided below to illustrate some of the 
existing regulatory coverage of potential AI harms that could arise in the banking sector .  
 
1. Discrimination and Bias  
Harm: AI systems can perpetuate or amplify existing biases in data, leading to discriminatory 
outcomes in  decisions (e.g. credit) and customer service.  
Existing regulations/obligations:  
• Anti-Discrimination Legislation prohibits discrimination based on race, sex, disability, etc.  For 
example:  
o Racial Discrimination Act 1975  
o Sex Discrimination Act 1984  
o Disability Discrimination Act 1992  
 
20 ‘Member Therese McCarthy Hockey’s remarks to AFIA Risk Summit 2024 ’, APRA.

• Australian Securities and Investments Commission Act 2001 – Section 12CB : Prohibits 
misleading, deceptive, or unconscionable conduct in financial services.  
• Banking Code of Practice : Commits banks to treat customers fairly and ethically, ensuring 
services are provided without discrimination.  
 
2. Financial Exclusion  
Harm:  AI could inadvertently exclude or fail to meet the specific needs of vulnerable customers  
(e.g., low -income individuals, First Nations customers ) from accessing financial services.  
Existing regulations/obligations:  
• Anti-Discrimination Legislation : Prohibits exclusion based on protected characteristics.  
• ASIC’s Indigenous Financial Services Framework:  Regulatory engagement on ensuring 
banking practices promotes accessibility and inclusion for First Nations peoples.  
• Banking Code of Practice:  Commits banks to additional obligations in dealing with vulnerable 
customers – e.g. services tailored to specific needs and cultural sensitivities of First Nations 
customers.  
 
3. Privacy and Data Protection Concerns  
Harm: Generative AI and LLMs require significant amounts of data, increasing the risk that 
personal data is used inappropriately.  
Existing regulations/obligations:  
• Privacy Act 1988:  Governs the handling of personal information by organi sations, mandating 
lawful and fair collection and use.  
o Australian Privacy Principles (APPs):  Provide guidelines on the collection, use, 
disclosure, and security of personal information.  
• Notifiable Data Breaches (NDB) Scheme : Requires organi sations to notify individuals and the 
Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) of data breaches.  
• APRA Prudential Standard CPS 234 (Information Security): Requires financial institutions to 
maintain robust information security to protect against cyber threats.  
 
4. Transparency and Explainability Issues  
Harm:  AI algorithms can be complex and opaque, making it difficult for customers to understand 
decisions made about them.  
Existing regulations/obligations:  
• ASIC Regulatory Guide 209 (RG 209):  Requires lenders to make reasonable inquiries 
about a consumer's financial situation and assess whether credit contracts are unsuitable. 
Requires statements be produced to explain decisions with records kept for compliance 
(RG 209 Part D ).  
• Australian Consumer Law (ACL):  Prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct and requires 
transparency in transactions.                                                                  
Australian Banking Association, PO Box H218, Australia Square NSW 1215 | +61 2 8298 0417 | ausbanking.org.au  12 
• Banking Code of Practice:  Obliges  banks to communicate clearly and effectively with 
customers.  
 
5. Cybersecurity and Systemic Risks  
Harm:  AI systems can introduce new vulnerabilities, potentially leading to cyber -attacks  and 
systemic risks to financial stability where AI behaves unpredictably, without mitigation.  
Existing regulations/obligations:  
• Cybersecurity and information security risks in the banking sector are already comprehensively 
managed, primarily by, but not limited to, the SOCI Act and Prudential Standards.  
o CPS 234 (Information Security ): Requires financial institutions to maintain robust 
information security to protect against cyber threats.  
o CPS 220  sets out risk management standards, including risk management plans. 
Section 11CA, contained in  subdivision A, division 1BA of the Banking Act 1959  
empowers APRA to issue directions to comply with a prudential standard where APRA 
has reason to believe the ADI is non -compliant or will become non -compliant.  
o Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018  imposes significant risk management 
protocols on banking infrastructure.  
 
6. Irresponsible provision of credit or other products  
Harm : AI might recommend or approve unsuitable financial products to consumers, leading to 
financial hardship.  
Existing regulations/obligations:  
• National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009 (NCCP Act):  Mandates lenders to assess 
whether a credit contract is unsuitable for a consumer.  
• ASIC Regulatory Guide 209 .207:  Prohibits reliance on unreliable information (e.g. false 
information, information not about a customer) . 
• Australian Securities and Investments Commission Act 2001 – Section 12CB : Prohibits 
misleading, deceptive, or unconscionable conduct in financial services.  
• ASIC’s Design and Distribution Obligations : require s firms to design financial products to 
meet the needs of consumers and to distribute their products in a more targeted manner.  
 
7. Lack of Accountability over AI systems  
Harm:  Difficulty in assigning responsibility for decisions made by AI systems can lead to a lack of 
accountability.  
Existing regulations/obligations:  
• Financial Accountability Regime (FAR):  Requires clear lines of accountability within banks and 
holds senior executives accountable for misconduct and breaches of obligations.  
• APRA Prudential Standards:  Require clear governance and accountability structures within 
financial institutions.  
                                                                 
Australian Banking Association, PO Box H218, Australia Square NSW 1215 | +61 2 8298 0417 | ausbanking.org.au  13 
8. Third party AI risks  
Harm:  Reliance on third party suppliers (e.g. AI developers) can introduce risk into an organisation.  
Existing regulations/obligations:  
• APRA Prudential Standards  (generally) : Outcomes based regulation which requires banks to 
manage risk regardless of how they undertake a process.  
• CPS 230 Operational Risk Management : risk management obligations on managing risk when 
dealing with suppliers.  
 
Comments on individual guardrails  
1. Establish, implement and publish an accountability process including governance, internal 
capability and a strategy for regulatory compliance  
2. Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks  
3. Protect AI systems, and implement data governance measures to manage data quality and 
provenance  
4. Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the system once 
deployed  
We support guardrails 1 – 4, however note that APRA Prudential Standards and other regulation 
already requires these to be met to a high standard across a bank’s operations and data 
management practices. It would be appropriate for APRA to consider any supplemental AI risks 
and whether existing regulation is sufficient to address incremental risk.  
 
5. Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight  
The intent of guardrail 5 should be to ensure strong accountability and oversight of an AI system  
and its outcomes,  rather than pr oscribing specific requirements for human intervention. This is 
aligned to the views express by APRA21 regarding AI oversight in banking:  
“Entities must have, to use the industry jargon, a “human in the loop”: an actual person who 
is accountable for ensuring it operates as intended. This doesn’t necessarily mean 
human involvement in  AI decisions – for example, stopping a potentially fraudulent 
transaction requires fast action. Instead, it is about someone being accountable  for the 
algorithm, its sound operation, and the outcomes it delivers.”  
 
6. Inform end -users regarding AI -enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI -generated content  
7. Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcomes  
There are  already  comprehensive, regulated processes for customers to make complaints, 
challenge decisions, and seek redress when dealing with their bank. For example, the Banking 
Code of Practice establishes obligations on banks to provide Internal Despite Resolution 
processes. Where customers are unhappy with the outcome of a dispute, they can have the 
 
21 ‘Member Therese McCarthy Hockey’s remarks to AFIA Risk Summit 2024 ’, APRA.                                                                  
Australian Banking Association, PO Box H218, Australia Square NSW 1215 | +61 2 8298 0417 | ausbanking.org.au  14 
Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) review the case and make a determination. 
AFCA decisions are binding on banks.   
Banks have been using machine learning and automated decision making for many years. It’s 
important that where customer decisions are already regulated, the guardrails do not impose 
parallel regulations over a process, that would in effect produce divergent obligations over the 
outcome.  
Using credit approval as an example: banks currently deploy sophisticated machine learning and 
ADM capabilities to support  lending decisions. For low risk and simple credit assessments, the 
approval may be granted without any human intervention – with banks implementing appropriate 
portfolio, customer level risk management controls as oversight. Were these processes to be 
enhanced through GPAI models, then guardrails 6 and 7 would suggest a separate set of 
obligations for decisions done in this way – even though the outcome has not changed and 
remains regulated in a technology neutral manner.  
Taken at face value, guardrails 6 and 7 may require notifying customers of AI use that inadvertently 
undermine s key risk management processes . For example, AI is used extensively in scams and 
fraud detection and prevention. Guardrails 6 and 7 would appear to require banks to alert 
customers that a payment was blocked due to AI – which while expected by many, could 
undermine customer protection whe re highly confidential and sophisticated fraud model s were 
subject to challenge.   
We support notifications to end -users of AI interactions in cases where they are directly interacting 
with AI  and could reasonably assume it  is a human  – e.g. chatbots. Generally,  such notifications 
are already provided or made clear to a customer  in banking channels.  
8. Be transparent with other organisations across the AI supply chain about data, models and 
systems to help them effectively address risks  
9. Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails  
10. Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with the guardrails  
APRA sets clear obligations and requirements on banks regarding their data storage, transparency, 
and compliance practices. This includes obligations regarding engagement with suppliers. The 
intent of these guardrails should be assessed by APRA and reflecte d in existing information and 
security prudential  standards where necessary.  
In keeping with our position that existing regulatory frameworks should provide the basis for risk 
management, separate compliance assessments  outside existing frameworks  should not be 
introduced.

Implementation options  
Note that the consul tation questions  have been responded to  thematically . 
Implementation of the mandatory guardrails should be sector specific and reflective of the existing 
regulatory environment and assessment of harm. As AI risks are generally not novel, but rather 
refer to existing harms (e.g. Privacy), the existing regulato ry frameworks should be amended 
instead of introducing new AI specific obligations. Option 1 would appear to be most aligned to this 
position.   
However, we are conscious that the regulatory environment of the banking sector is unique, and 
that AI regulation needs a degree of interoperability across the economy. We would also support 
option 2  introducing this  to the extent that it provided for common terminology, objectives, and 
expectations regarding the desired outcomes of AI regulation only. It is important that flexibility is 
given to sector -specific regulators regarding the guardrails, ensuring that any n ew obligations are 
targeted and aligned to existing regulatory requirements.  
AI regulation should be informed by a detailed gap analysis , harms -led, and sector -specific . 
Therefore, t he ABA does not support option 3  insofar that it would conflict with this view – 
introducing a separate regulator and parallel , standardised  obligations on a sector -agnostic basis.  
However, it is essential that any regulatory obligation s to promote safe and respon sible AI apply to 
all sectors of the economy equally.  In absence of a dedicated regulator and legislation  as proposed 
under option 3 , there is potential difficulty in implementing the reforms over sectors without robust 
regulatory and enforcement mechanisms.   
Where this challenge  cannot be resolved, the ABA would support new regulatory capabilities being 
established  that address sector -specific gaps, while ensuring that parallel obligations are not 
introduced on other sectors . Existing economy -wide regulators and legislation should be 
considered for this purpose  ahead of a standalone AI regulator  – e.g. the Privacy Act and OAIC.   
Determining the  optimal  approach to implementation , will to a large degree, be reliant on 
understanding the exact nature of  how high -risk AI will be assessed  and how the guardrails would 
apply on a sector basis. The ABA looks forward to continu ed close engagement with the 
Department as these reforms progress.

Australian Payments Network (AusPayNet) welcomes the opportunity to respond to  the proposals  
paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for artificial intelligence (AI) in high -risk settings.   
AusPayNet is the industry association and self -regulatory body for the Australian payments industry. 
We manage and develop standards and guidelines governing payments in Australia. Our purpose is to 
create confidence in payments by setting enforceable industry standards for a safe, reliable and 
effective payments system; leading transformation in payments to drive efficiency, innovation and 
choice; and being the home for ecosystem collaboration and str ategic insight. AusPayNet currently 
has more than 150 members including financial institutions, payment system operators, major 
retailers and financial technology companies.  
This submission builds on the feedback AusPayNet provided in response to the Department’s earlier 
consultation on safe and responsible AI in Australia in August 2023  (Appendix 1) . The views expressed 
in this submission are those of AusPayNet Management, and may not necessarily represent the views 
of each of our members.  
Introduction  
AI has the potential to deliver significant benefits across many areas of Australia’s economy and 
society . This has long been recognised by the payments industry, which has been integrating AI into 
payments systems and processes for many years to help drive efficiency, innovation and safety for 
businesses and consumers.  Many of the existing  use cases of AI in payments – including fraud 
detection, customer authentication, and process automation – are widely trusted and adopted by 
payment s service providers, businesses and customers across Australia.  
As AI models become more sophisticated in their ability to process vast amounts of data, recognise 
complex patterns, and generate intelligent insights, the potential applications of this technology 
across society and the economy also continue to evolve. For the payments ecosystem, t hese 
opportunities include further enhancing fraud detection and risk management capabilities, improving 
operational efficiency and resilience, and supporting innovation and improvements in payments 
technologies and services, inc luding through more personalised customer and merchant experiences.  
At the same time, we recognise that the ongoing developments in AI also have the potential to 
generate significant risks if not designed and deployed responsibly. As noted in the consultation paper, 
this could  deter adoption and limit Australia’s ability to capture the full benefits of this technology. 
AusPayNet therefore supports the Government’s continued work on ensuring that Australia has clear 
and proportionate governance frameworks in place to mitigate risks , while supporting the continued 
development  and adoption of effective and trustworthy AI technology. As a standards -setting body, AUSTRALIAN  PAYMENTS  NETWORK  LTD.  ABN 12 055 136 519  
Suite 2 , Level 17 , 225 George Street, Sydney NSW 2000  | auspaynet.com.au  |  2 AusPayNet recognises that appropriate governance mechanisms can support innovation and growth 
for the benefit of all stakeholders.  
AusPayNet generally supports the  proposed  implementation of mandatory guardrails for the use of AI 
in high -risk settings. The proposed framework broadly aligns with the feedback provided in our earlier 
submission, which detailed our support for adopting a risk -based and principles -driven approach to AI 
regulation that balances the need for both consistency and proportionality in regulating the many 
different AI use cases across different industries. We also welcome the broad alignment with emerging 
internat ional standards and best practice, which will support both the ability of Australian businesses 
to take advantage of AI technologies developed offshore , as well as  continued investment in 
Australia’s own AI capacity and capabilities .  
The intention of our submission is to provide some insights and considerations  about the proposed 
guardrails  from the perspective of the Australian payments industry, to help inform any further 
refin ements to the governance framework. We believe that such sector -specific insights can help 
ensure that the overarching  guidelines strike an optimal balance between ensuring safety and 
fostering AI innovation  in Australia.  
Defini ng High -risk AI 
AusPayNet broadly supports adopting a principles -based approach to defining high -risk AI. This flexible 
approach will facilitate consistency in interpretation across the many different applications of AI , and 
allow for ongoing developments in AI technology. While  providing  illustrative examples of high -risk 
use cases could serve as useful guidance,  a list -based approach  is unlikely to be effective , since the 
risks associated with  the use of AI can vary significantly even within a given domain or technique . For 
example, Table 1 lists ‘biometrics’ as a high -risk use case; however, the risks associated with using 
facial recognition technology to unlock a phone or even authorise a mobile payment would be much 
lower than when used for public surveillance.   
Additional guidance from sectoral regulators on the application of the definitional principles to key 
use cases within their industries would also be helpful. In particular, the assessment of the potential 
for adverse impacts to individuals’ mental health, and the thresholds for the ‘severity and extent’ of 
harms beyond which use cases would classify as high risk could potentially lead to subjective and 
inconsistent interpretation  across sectors , and even businesses within the same industry.  
We also query whether the risk assessment framework (or at least the subsequent application of some 
of the guardrails) should consider the counterfactual of not using AI for that particular application. In 
the context of payments, for example, not using AI for fraud detection would very likely lead to a 
significant increase in financial crime . There may be a case for weigh ing such factors against any 
potential risks posed by the AI system s, to help ensure that beneficial AI applications are not unduly 
restricted.  
Developers and Deployers  
We support the Government’s proposal that  both developers and deployers of high -risk AI systems 
should share responsibility for ensuring the safe development and use of AI technology , with the 
guardrails distributed according to which actors are best equipped to address the risks associated with 
a particular stage of development.  AUSTRALIAN  PAYMENTS  NETWORK  LTD.  ABN 12 055 136 519  
Suite 2 , Level 17 , 225 George Street, Sydney NSW 2000  | auspaynet.com.au  |  3 However, we do have some concerns about the breadth and clarity of the two definitions , and 
particularly the point at which a deployer might classify as a developer. Many entities in the payments 
ecosystem  – particularly fintech companies  – may not have the capacity to develop their own AI 
models, and would therefore chose to adapt or fine -tune existing models for their specific use cases.  
A prominent example would be fraud detection systems . These are often developed by larger 
businesses , such as payments system operators , but allow  entities leveraging those tools to make 
minor adjustments to certain parameters  of the model . The current ly proposed definitions  are unclear 
about the extent of such fine -tuning that would classify those smaller entities as developers, and 
potentially subject them to a disproportionate regulatory burden. We therefore suggest providing 
more detailed guidance on the degree of model adaptation that would classify an entity as a 
developer , perhaps with industry -specific examples  to help clarify this distinctio n. It may also be useful 
to consider a potential 'middle' category for entities that significantly adapt but do not fundamentally 
develop AI systems .  
AusPayNet also note s that many Australian entities, particularly smaller ones, are likely to rely on AI 
systems developed by large global tech nology  companies. These local entities may not have the 
bargaining power to enforce all of the proposed guardrails on these global developers. While the 
alignment of Australia’s  mandatory guardrails with international standards should help mitigate this 
risk, w e encourage the Government to consider how this potential dynamic might affect the practical 
implementation o f the guardrails for some entities.  
Relatedly, we also encourage the Government and/or sectoral regulators to implement regulatory 
sandbox es for AI applications . This would allow  smaller entities in particular to carry out controlled 
development and testing of innovative AI systems under regulatory supervision , without incurring an 
upfront regulatory burden that may inhibit innovation . 
Mandatory Guardrails  
AusPayNet supports the Government's commitment to establishing robust guardrails for high -risk AI 
applications. The proportionate and tailored implementation of these guardrails  should significantly 
enhance the safety and trustworthiness of AI systems.  As noted earlier, we also welcome the broad 
alignment of the guardrails with emerging international standards.  
A key concern for us is ensuring that organisations have appropriate flexibility in how they implement 
these guardrails, based on the specific context and application of their AI systems.  In particular, s ome 
use cases in the payments industry highlight that there may be instances where strict adherence to 
one guardrail could potentially compromise another . For example, in AI -based fraud detection 
systems , there might be tension between the requirements for explainability and those for system 
security and ef fectiveness. A highly sophisticated AI model would likely be more effective at detecting 
complex fraud patterns , but could be less explainable than a simpler model. In such cases, the ability 
to balance these requirements based on the specific use case and risk profile is crucial.  We suggest 
that the final guidelines explicitly acknowledge such potential trade -offs, and provide guidance on 
how organisations should approach such situations.  
We also s trongly support the emphasis on rigorous testing and ongoing monitoring of AI systems. This 
is particularly important in  the payments industry, where AI systems often operate in real -time and 
deal with sensitive financial data  and decisions . However, for AI applications  such as fraud detection  
systems , some of the most effective development and testing often occurs in real -world deployment , AUSTRALIAN  PAYMENTS  NETWORK  LTD.  ABN 12 055 136 519  
Suite 2 , Level 17 , 225 George Street, Sydney NSW 2000  | auspaynet.com.au  |  4 where the system can continuously learn from and adapt to actual transaction patterns and emerging 
fraud techniques  in real time . We suggest that the guidelines consider allowing for phased or limited 
real-world testing for certain types of AI systems, under close monitoring and with appropriate 
safeguards. This could be particularly valuable for adaptive AI systems that improve their p erformance 
over time based on real -world , real -time  data.   
Similarly, while we generally support the principles of explainability and transparency, we suggest that 
these should be applied proportionately based on specific use case s and risk profile s. In the case of 
AI-based fraud systems, for example, full explainability of each decision might not always be necessary 
or beneficial if other safeguards are in place  – such as rigorous testing  to ensure appropriate accuracy 
and bias mitigation. Moreover, too much transparency around the decisions made by fraud detectio n 
systems could potentially introduce new risks  and compromise the effectiveness of the system , by 
assist ing criminal actors in learning how to evade detection. We therefore suggest a nuanced 
approach that balances the need for explainability and transparency with other considerations such 
as system effectiveness and security.  
Finally, the effective implementation of Guardrail 6 , on informing end -users regarding AI -enabled 
decisions and interactions , should also be considered.  There are many cases in which s uch 
transparency might  be necessary from an ethical  and trust -building  perspective , particularly when 
customers should be able to make informed decisions about whether to engage in the AI-driven 
services . However, we believe that such notification would not be appropriate  or helpful in some 
circumstances . For example, in the fast-paced, high -volume payment s environment  – where most 
transactions have been approved or denied on the basis of AI -led decisioning  for many years – 
constant notifications about AI use could reduce payments e fficiency and lead to customer alert 
fatigue, potentially causing users to overlook important information  in the future .  
Noting that some consumers may have general anxiety or mistrust around the use of AI , explicit 
disclosure of AI use in every instance of fraud monitoring and similar decisioning could also lead to 
unwarranted concerns ab out fairness  and accuracy  – and a corresponding increase in complaints that 
business es needs to handle – even where the AI model has been proven to reduce bias and increase 
accuracy relative to human -based decision making . Where busines ses deploying AI systems conduct 
rigorous ongoing testing to ensure the ir accuracy and fairness , we consider that a customer ’s decision 
to challenge an outcome  should not be unnecessarily biased by whether the decision was made by AI, 
a human, or a mix of the two . Furthermore, it should not be possib le for a customer to opt out of AI -
based transaction monitoring , even if they wished to do so . Recurring notification would therefore 
not provide the customer with any actionable  insights regarding the use of AI to inform decisions 
relevant to them . We therefore suggest that the guidelines allow for a nuanced approach to 
disclosure, considering factors such as the specific use case, the potential impact on system 
effectiveness, and the overall user experience. For example, it might be more appropriate to pr ovide 
general information about AI use in terms and conditions or privacy policies for certain systems, rather 
than real -time notifications for each AI -driven interaction. The goal should be to ensure meaningful 
transparency without compromising security o r overwhelming users with excessive notifications.  
Regulatory Framework  
As detailed  in our earlier submission, we support a regulatory approach to AI that balances consistency 
of regulatory outcomes across the economy, with the flexibility to proportionately tailor the AUSTRALIAN  PAYMENTS  NETWORK  LTD.  ABN 12 055 136 519  
Suite 2 , Level 17 , 225 George Street, Sydney NSW 2000  | auspaynet.com.au  |  5 regulatory response to specific contexts and use cases . This is supported by the discussion above, 
which highlights the need for tailored implementation of certain guardrails to mitigate the 
introduction of new risks, undue regulatory burden, or other unintended consequences. Our earlier 
submission had also expressed support for maximising reliance on existing legislation  and regulatory 
expertise  where possible . 
AusPayNet therefore broadly support s the framework approach (op tion 2 ), which we believe  best 
balances consistency with flexibility , by ensuring that all AI systems are subject to the same baseline 
standards, while allowing for sector -specific implementation of those standards  through well -
established regulatory frameworks and expertise .  
As indicated in the consultation paper, standards can also play an important role in supporting this 
kind of regulatory framework, to ensure the effective practical implementation of the  overarching  
guardrails in specific settings. As the self -regulatory body for the payments industry, AusPayNet is 
ready to lead the development of any technical standards for the Australian payments industry  (or the 
adaptation of relevant standards developed by international working groups) , where the industry and 
our sector al regulators see a need for such technical standards to effectively comply with any of the 
mandatory guardrails . 
Finally, we note that implementing these guardrails will require significant adjustments for many 
organisations, particularly those with existing AI systems.  Appropriate transition arrangements will be 
crucial to minimi se disruption to existing services.  These arrangements might include phased 
implementation, with priority given to the highest -risk applications, and could potentially vary by 
sector and risk level.  
Conclusion  
AusPayNet appreciates the opportunity to respond to the Government’s consultation on mandatory 
guardrails for AI in high -risk settings. This is a critical step in ensuring that the potential risks of AI can 
be mitigated appropriately, while promoting the continued development and adoption of AI so that 
Australia can realise the full benefits of this technology . AusPayNet look s forward to continuing  our 
engagement with the Government as this work  progresses over the coming years. Please contact 
Kateryna Occh iutto, Head of Policy & Insights ( kocchiutto@auspaynet.com.au ) if you have any

Responses to consultation questions 

16. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI? Are there any principles we should add or remove

No, the proposed principles do not adequately capture high-risk AI

17.  Additional comments on proposed principles 

The proposed principles are inadequate in not including specific reference to risks of adverse impacts to individuals’ human rights not contained in Australian Human Rights Law. The principles should include clear and detailed requirements for regard to be given to other laws that provide for individual and collective rights. Rights recognised in other laws, such as rights in the Fair Work Act, must be specifically covered within the definition of high-risk. It is not adequate to rely on reference to international conventions to which Australia is a signatory.

A list-based approach to defining high-risk AI is preferred and will be far more effective in
achieving the intended aim “to secure efficient and effective international AI governance
structures” and to develop Australian regulations that “are interoperable where
appropriate” (p. 7 proposals paper). It is appropriate for Australia to provide protections in the areas identified in EU AI regulation. 

The proposed principles-based approach offers insufficient clarity and certainty and has
strong potential for generating confusion, on-going contestation and inaction, rendering
regulation ineffective. Of particular concern is the stated intention for the principles
to “guide organisations in deciding whether a particular use represents a high-risk”. This suggests a level of voluntarism that is not suitable for a system of mandatory guardrails. 

For example,
1) in relation to principle (a) it is entirely unsatisfactory for individual organisations to decide if circumstances (for example, commercial imperatives) warrant interference with traditional rights and freedoms. 

2) The example in the proposals paper of how to apply the principles to use cases in an employment setting (provided on page 27) offers a good illustration of the type of use case for which the principles-based approach would prove ineffective, resulting in inconsistencies in compliance and in protection of rights. As this example suggests, following a principles-based approach in an employment setting, an organisation would need to undertake an assessment to understand the potential impacts and make an assessment of their likely severity to determine if the use is covered by the regulation. There would likely be great inconsistency in outcomes in different organisations given the flexibility and ambiguity in the principles and the variable levels of knowledge, time, motivation and resources different organisations will apply to this effort,. There may be many instances where deployers of AI systems in employment settings will make judgements that intentionally or unintentionally do not take proper account of the risks and possible severity of impacts on individuals or groups of employees. This would likely lead the mandatory AI guardrails not being applied in many employment settings, despite broad recognition in Australia (and clear specification in international regulations) of employment settings as high-risk. 

3) The application of Principle (f) “The severity and extent of those adverse impacts …” could readily lead to decisions by organisations to use AI despite there being significant potential to infringe on individuals' rights at work. 

A list-based approach that specifically identifies the world of work as a high-risk setting should be adopted, as it is in both the EU AI Act and in Canada’s approach.

A suitable definition is that included in the European AI Act (Annex III, para 4):
AI systems intended to be used for recruitment or selection, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates
AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of the work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics and to monitor and evaluate performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships. 

18 Are there any principles we should add or remove?

Yes


19 Please provide any additional comments.

The proposed principles are inadequate in not including specific reference to risks of adverse impacts to individuals’ human rights not contained in Australian Human Rights Law. The principles should include clear and detailed requirements for regard to be given to other laws that provide for individual and collective rights. Rights recognised in other laws, such as rights in the Fair Work Act, must be specifically covered within the definition of high-risk. It is not adequate to rely on reference to international conventions to which Australia is a signatory.

23 Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?

No, the proposed principles, supported by examples, do not give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models. A more defined list-based approach is required. The proposed principles-based approach where the principles act as a “guide” for organisation to decide if they need to comply with the regulation is not suitable for the application of mandatory guardrails, as outlined in the response to question 17 above. 

25 If you prefer a list-based approach (similar to the EU and Canada), what use cases should we include? 

Use cases should include:
* Biometrics
* Critical infrastructure
* Education/training
* Employment
* Access to essential public services and products
* Access to essential private services
* Products and services affecting individual and public health and safety
* Law enforcement
* Administration of justice and democratic processes
* 
26 How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?

Regulation can provide for review and adaption, including through requirements for post-market monitoring and incident reporting, as in the EU AI Act.

27  Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?

Yes, 

28 If so, how should we define these?

AI systems posing unacceptable risk should be banned 

29 Please provide any additional comments.

AI systems that should be banned in Australia include those systems prohibited in the EU AI Act, including AI systems: 
* deploying subliminal, manipulative, or deceptive techniques to distort behaviour and impair informed decision-making, causing significant harm.
* exploiting vulnerabilities related to age, disability, or socio-economic circumstances to distort behaviour, causing significant harm.
* social scoring, i.e., evaluating or classifying individuals or groups based on social behaviour or personal traits, causing detrimental or unfavourable treatment of those people. 
* assessing the risk of an individual committing criminal offenses solely based on profiling or personality traits, except when used to augment human assessments based on objective, verifiable facts directly linked to criminal activity. 
* compiling facial recognition databases by untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage.
* inferring emotions in workplaces or educational institutions, except for medical or safety reasons.
* biometric categorisation systems inferring sensitive attributes (race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation), except labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets or when law enforcement categorises biometric data.  
* 'real-time' remote biometric identification (RBI) in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, with specific exceptions.

32 Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?

Yes

36 Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?

No

37 Please provide any additional comments.

In general the guardrails are weak including in relation to providing for accountability and
for genuine consultation with individuals and groups who are at risk of negative impacts.
Individuals and groups should have enforceable rights to challenge decisions regarding the use of AI.

The proposed guardrails applied to work settings are not suitable for effectively mitigating risks of AI applications in work settings:
* An overarching concern is that guardrails in work settings need to account for the special nature of workplace relationships and structures. There is a case for development of specific guardrails for work settings, There are also existing regulatory systems such as the work health and safety system that could provide the basis for guardrails models appropriate to world of work settings
* 
38 Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?

Yes

39 What guardrails should we add or remove?

See response to question 40

40 Please provide any additional comments

In work settings effective guardrails should provide for consultation and input into
decisions by workers and their unions regarding the application of AI, including providing
for right of entry and access to records systems. Workers should have rights to reject the
application of AI where risks are significant and/or not amenable to mitigation. Guardrails
should include a requirement for organisations to demonstrate meaningful human
oversight. There should also be stronger requirements for transparency of conformity
assessments including that they are able to be accessed by workers. Organisations must
be required to be transparent about actions taken in response to challenges to use and
there must be mechanisms for appeal.

49 Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small-to-medium sized businesses applying guardrails?

Yes

50 Please provide any additional comments

A list-based definition of high-risk settings would assist small to medium businesses by
providing certainty and clarity and enabling these businesses to benefit from the
development of regulator guidance and sector-wide responses including, for example, 
certification of systems designed to conform with guardrails in planned use cases. The vast majority of small to medium businesses are unlikely to need individualised organisation-specific processes to comply.
 
51 Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?

A whole of economy approach – introducing a new cross-economy AI Act

52 What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach?

While a whole-of-economy approach is the best of the three options identified in the proposal paper, it needs to be supplemented by the adaptation of existing domain-specific legislation as. This is essential to enable Australian workers, consumers and businesses to be adequately protected through the emergence of AI. For example, in labour law there is a need for greater rights of consultation and representation for workers in the introduction of technological change, including most prominently the introduction of AI. Without such rights workers will be unable to adequately influence AI’s operationalisation within organisations. European research indicates that employees typically facilitate the introduction of technological change when empowered to shape it, but Australian workers often lack the rights to do so. Enacting such changes may be beyond the scope of this process, but the need to consider it is something that can be established.

53 Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the Australian Government should consider?

Yes

 54 Please provide any additional comments.

The mandatory guardrails will only matter if there are adequate institutions and resources for compliance and enforcement. This includes a need for:
1.  Organisation-level institutions, and resourcing of those institutions, to provide an opportunity for workers and informed experts to independently verify the development and application of specific forms of AI within organisations, and ensure that it is compliant with the guardrails.
2.  Opportunities for auditing along the whole of the AI supply chain, to ensure that it is compliant with the guardrails, including resourcing of those audits; and 
3.  Penalties for breaches of the guardrails at a level that is large enough to genuinely discourage breaches.

These institutions are necessary because the volume of AI that will be generated in the
near future will be far greater than can be adequately assessed and managed by any
national or even industry-based institution. Organisational-level bodies, and audits, are
essential for tracking AI and monitoring its compliance with the guardrails. 

The size and resources of many of the tech firms that will be implementing AI means that anything other than very large penalties will have no impact on their behaviour, while the very large number of developers and players means that the quantity of AI will be too great for any single institution to respond to.

55 Which regulatory option(s) will best ensure that guardrails for high-risk AI can adapt and respond to step-changes in technology?

A whole of economy approach – introducing a new cross-economy AI Act with amendment of existing legislation 

57 Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps and inconsistencies with Australia’s existing laws for the development and deployment of AI?

The greatest risks arise in relation to:
* Some important rights, especially for workers, being ignored because of the absence of  a human rights charter or Act in Australia unless, for example, all work-related AI is classified as high-risk; and

* The potential inability to enforce the guardrails because of the quantity of AI produced and the resources of the large tech firms who will be major players in this area.

58 Which regulatory option best addresses this?
A whole of economy approach – Introducing a new cross-economy AI-specific Act (for
example, an Australian AI Act).

59 Please explain why.

As noted in the proposals paper, this approach provides for greater consistency and can
address gaps in existing regulation as well as providing for extension of regulation
upstream in the supply chain, interoperability with international approaches taken by the
EU and Canada and enforceable obligations. However this approach needs to be
accompanied by reforms to existing legislation as explained above.
