PROPOSALS PAPERThis submission is provided by Build Club, a global community of AI builders committed to
responsible innovation and practical applications of AI. Our community, which includes
developers, researchers, and entrepreneurs from Australia and around the world, is deeply
invested in shaping the future of AI regulation. Through extensive conversations, roundtables,
and written submissions, our members have explored the challenges and opportunities that
the proposed AI guardrails present. This submission highlights key recommendations from
these discussions, advocating for a balanced regulatory framework that both protects
society and promotes AI innovation. We support an approach that leverages existing
industry expertise while allowing for adaptability in the face of rapid technological change.Executive Summary
buildclub.aiBuild Club is a global community of AI builders who are working on cutting-edge AI solutions
across various industries. As a community, we have engaged in multiple discussions,
including roundtables and written submissions, where we explored the regulatory
implications of AI. Our diverse membership provides insights from across sectors, allowing us
to propose recommendations that reflect the practical needs of businesses and developers
while ensuring AI is deployed responsibly. We are dedicated to ensuring that AI regulations in
Australia and beyond strike the right balance between innovation and safety, fostering an
environment where AI can thrive while managing potential risks.Introduction to Build Club
buildclub.aiThe rapid evolution of AI technology presents a unique challenge for regulatory frameworks
that must remain adaptable to new and unforeseen applications. Across the discussions and
written submissions within the Build Club community, the consensus was that static lists of
high-risk AI applications would quickly become outdated, unable to capture the full scope of
AI's ongoing developments. Instead, a dynamic, real-time mechanism for updating
regulations and capturing emerging risks was recommended.
Dynamic Regulatory Mechanism
One of the key proposals to address this issue was the creation of a real-time portal or
reporting system, which would enable stakeholders to flag new or emerging AI use cases that
could pose risks. This portal could be managed by a dedicated regulatory body or expert
panel, tasked with reviewing submissions and acting on them swiftly. As one community
member suggested, “The speed of AI development means we can’t rely on static lists—we
need a mechanism to update regulations as soon as new risks emerge.”
This reporting system could be coupled with automated tools for preliminary risk
assessments, allowing regulators to evaluate the severity of new AI applications and
determine whether they should be classified as high-risk. This mechanism would also foster
collaborative feedback loops between developers, industry bodies, and regulators, helping to
ensure that risks are identified and managed in real-time without stifling innovation.
Role of an Adaptive Regulator
A central recommendation from the discussions was the establishment of a dedicated
regulatory body or advisory panel that is empowered to assess and respond to emerging AI
risks. This regulator should have flexibility and authority to update the list of high-risk uses
and guardrails on an ongoing basis, with input from industry experts. One suggestion was
that the regulator could regularly consult with scientific and technical advisory panels to
ensure it is equipped to evaluate the latest AI innovations, especially in fast-evolving fields
such as autonomous decision-making systems and generative AI.
This adaptive regulator would work closely with existing industry bodies, leveraging their
domain-specific knowledge to assess risks in their respective sectors. For instance, regulators
in healthcare or finance could evaluate new AI models or tools specific to their field and
determine whether they pose significant risks to safety or security.How can the guardrails capture emerging uses of
AI?
buildclub.aiBroad, Principles-Based Framework
Several Build Club members also emphasised the need for a broad, principles-based
framework rather than a rigid, rule-based approach. This would allow the regulatory system
to be flexible and responsive to changes in the AI landscape. As AI applications evolve,
particularly in areas like synthetic biology and autonomous systems, principles around
transparency, accountability, and safety can be applied to evaluate new technologies.
The principles-based approach would ensure that regulation is driven by the outcomes and
potential harm of AI systems rather than the specifics of their design or deployment. As one
participant noted, “It’s not just about the power of the model—it’s about how that model is
used and the risks it poses in real-world applications.” This approach aligns with the idea of
regulating AI based on risk, focusing on the specific dangers associated with each
application rather than trying to classify every AI model or tool under a single set of rules.
The Role of Industry and Public Consultation
Another recurring theme was the importance of industry involvement in defining high-risk
uses of AI. Various members advocated for industry bodies like APRA (Australian Prudential
Regulation Authority), ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission), and other
sector-specific organisations to play a leading role in identifying risks. “The people who
understand the nuances of their industry are best placed to define what constitutes high-risk
AI,” one member argued, highlighting the importance of leveraging existing regulatory
expertise.
In this vein, it was also recommended that regulators engage in regular public consultations
and work with industry panels to gather feedback from AI developers, users, and stakeholders.
This collaborative approach would ensure that the regulatory framework remains grounded
in real-world use cases and is informed by the latest technological advancements and
industry trends.
Emerging AI Risks
Our discussions also raised concerns about the challenges of predicting emerging risks in AI
development. In sectors such as autonomous systems, biotechnology, and generative AI, the
potential for harm is significant and often unpredictable. For instance, generative AI systems
capable of creating realistic synthetic content could be misused for disinformation, fraud, or
privacy violations.
To address these concerns, one community member suggested that the regulatory
framework should include provisions for proactive risk assessments and monitoring systems
that can detect and mitigate harmful applications before they are deployed at scale. This
would allow for an early intervention approach, where risks are identified and addressed
before they lead to widespread harm.
buildclub.aiHow can the guardrails capture emerging uses of
AI?International Standards and Global Collaboration
A significant point raised in the discussions was the need for Australia’s regulatory framework
to be aligned with international standards such as ISO 42001. This would not only help ensure
that Australia’s AI regulations are compatible with those in other jurisdictions but also foster
global collaboration in identifying and mitigating AI risks. One member stated, “Most AI
systems are being developed and deployed across borders. We need to ensure that our
regulations align with global best practices, or we risk falling behind.”
By contributing to and adopting international standards, Australia can benefit from the
collective expertise of AI researchers, developers, and policymakers around the world. This
approach would also help mitigate the risk of regulatory arbitrage, where companies move
operations to jurisdictions with more lenient AI regulations.
buildclub.aiHow can the guardrails capture emerging uses of
AI?The community’s discussions and written submissions around the definition of high-risk
General Purpose AI (GPAI) models highlighted a variety of perspectives. The majority agreed
that identifying high-risk AI requires a multifaceted approach, combining technical indicators
with principles-based evaluations that reflect the potential societal impact of the technology.
However, there was a clear consensus that focusing solely on technical capabilities, such as
FLOPS, would not be sufficient on its own.
Technical Capabilities as a Baseline
There were differing opinions on whether to define high-risk GPAI models based on
computational thresholds, such as the number of FLOPS (floating-point operations per
second). For instance, some members suggested that computational power should be a key
factor, citing that extremely powerful models, regardless of their specific applications, pose
inherent risks due to their capacity for unforeseen emergent behaviour. One participant said,
“If a model is capable of executing an astronomical number of computations in real-time, it
could potentially engage in autonomous actions that are difficult to predict or control.”
However, others pointed out the limitations of this approach, noting that smaller, highly
optimised models could be just as dangerous as larger ones. Quantisation techniques and
other advancements in AI could allow models to run with much less computational power
while still delivering impactful or harmful results. “Size does not always equal risk,” as one
participant put it, “Some of the smaller, fine-tuned models could be used in malicious ways,
even with limited computational resources.”
Therefore, while technical capabilities like FLOPS can serve as an initial risk flag for regulatory
focus, they should not be the sole determining factor for identifying high-risk models. Instead,
a hybrid approach was suggested, where technical benchmarks are combined with
principles-based evaluations to account for the broader potential impact of the model.
Principles-Based Evaluation and Risk Categorisation
The community strongly supported the idea of defining high-risk models against a set of
principles that focus on the potential harms AI could cause. These principles should
encompass societal, economic, and ethical dimensions, offering a broader view of risk that
includes but goes beyond technical specifications.
One of the core principles discussed was the nature of the tasks that AI models are capable
of performing. High-risk should not only be associated with the model’s computational power
but also its potential to engage in activities that could lead to harm. “You need to look at what
the model is actually doing,” one contributor said, “A model that predicts the weather might
not be high risk, but a model that provides legal or medical advice certainly could be.”
buildclub.aiSuitable indicators for defining General Purpose AI
(GPAI) models as high-risk It was suggested that these principles could include:
Autonomy: Does the model have the capability to act independently, potentially without
human intervention?
Impact: Could the model’s outputs or decisions result in harm, such as violating privacy,
safety, or fairness?
Explainability: Is the model’s decision-making process transparent and understandable
to humans, particularly in high-stakes applications like healthcare or law enforcement?
Scalability: Could the model’s deployment at scale lead to significant societal impacts,
such as manipulation through personalised persuasion engines or mass misinformation?
Participants widely agreed that principles-based evaluation would help address concerns
about the unpredictability of AI models. For instance, models that autonomously generate
content, make decisions, or interact with humans directly, especially in sensitive domains like
finance, healthcare, or law, should be flagged as high-risk regardless of their technical specs.
As one member pointed out, “The real risk isn’t just how powerful the model is but how it’s
used, and who it impacts.”
Role of a Scientific or Advisory Panel
Several discussions recommended the establishment of a scientific or technical advisory
panel to periodically review and update the criteria for determining high-risk AI models. This
panel would ideally include AI experts, ethicists, and domain-specific regulators who
understand both the technical details of AI and the practical impacts of its deployment
across industries.
Such a panel could:
Provide ongoing advice on emerging technologies and use cases, helping the government
and industry bodies stay up to date with the rapidly evolving landscape.
Adjust technical thresholds over time, such as FLOPS or other metrics, as AI models
become more efficient and computational power evolves.
Advise on emerging risks that might not yet be captured by existing principles, ensuring
that the guardrails remain forward-looking and adaptable.
As one roundtable participant noted, “We need a flexible, dynamic system where a scientific
panel can regularly assess what qualifies as high-risk AI. It can’t be a set-it-and-forget-it
system; we need continuous updates based on the technology’s evolution.”
buildclub.aiSuitable indicators for defining General Purpose AI
(GPAI) models as high-risk Domain-Specific Approaches
The majority of members agreed that defining high-risk GPAI models should also be
contextual. That is, while there should be overarching principles, the risk categorisation of AI
models should depend on how and where they are applied. This is particularly important for
high-risk industries such as healthcare, finance, and critical infrastructure, where the
potential for harm is greater.
For example, a general-purpose AI model might not be deemed high-risk when used in a low-
stakes environment (such as product recommendations), but it could become high-risk when
applied in high-stakes decision-making (such as determining eligibility for financial loans or
medical treatments). “The same model in two different contexts can pose very different levels
of risk,” said one participant. “We need to focus on the end application and who is using it, not
just the model itself.”
This context-driven approach allows regulators to be more targeted and nuanced in how
they apply AI guardrails. Industry bodies, such as APRA (Australian Prudential Regulation
Authority) for finance or AMA (Australian Medical Association) for healthcare, were suggested
as key players in determining what constitutes a high-risk AI model within their specific
sectors.
buildclub.aiSuitable indicators for defining General Purpose AI
(GPAI) models as high-risk Hub-and-Spoke Model for High-Risk AI
A central theme that emerged from the Build Club discussions was the need to adopt a hub-
and-spoke regulatory model to effectively manage and define high-risk AI. In this model, the
government would act as the central hub, setting broad overarching guidelines for AI
governance and establishing a foundational regulatory framework. The spokes of the model
would consist of sector-specific regulators or industry bodies, such as APRA (Australian
Prudential Regulation Authority) for financial services or AMA (Australian Medical Association)
for healthcare, which would tailor the high-risk AI definition and guardrails to their respective
industries.
This approach allows for flexibility in regulating AI across different sectors, ensuring that the
nuances and unique risks of each industry are taken into account. Industry experts, rather
than a centralised government body alone, would play a leading role in defining what
constitutes high-risk AI in their domain. As one participant noted, “It’s important that the
people who understand the specifics of their industry are the ones defining the risks—they
know where AI can cause the most harm.”
By delegating the detailed risk assessments to industry-specific bodies, this model can
provide a more accurate and adaptive regulatory framework. The hub ensures consistency
across the broader economy by establishing baseline principles for AI safety, transparency,
and accountability. The spokes then apply these principles to create detailed, context-
specific regulations that reflect the real-world risks posed by AI applications in their sector.
Technical Capability in High-Risk AI
Building on the hub-and-spoke model, our discussions also highlighted the importance of
combining technical capability and principles-based evaluations to define General
Purpose AI (GPAI) models as high-risk. While computational measures such as FLOPS
(floating-point operations per second) provide a useful starting point for understanding the
potential scale of an AI model, they are insufficient on their own to assess the true risks
posed by the technology.
As several Build Club participants observed, technical capability should be just one factor in
a broader, more comprehensive risk assessment framework. As one roundtable member put
it, “It’s not just about the size of the model or the computational power—it’s about how the
model is being used and whether it can cause significant harm.” This underscores the need to
consider context and impact, rather than focusing solely on a model’s technical
specifications.
To this end, we propose that the definition of high-risk AI should incorporate the following
factors:
buildclub.aiHow should technical capability be defined in
high-risk AI? Model Capabilities: Evaluating the model's ability to perform complex tasks and its
potential for autonomous decision-making is critical. Models capable of acting
independently or mimicking human behaviour in decision-critical areas (e.g., legal advice,
healthcare diagnostics) should automatically trigger a higher level of scrutiny.1.
Context of Use: The same model could have vastly different risk profiles depending on its
application. For example, a small, specialised AI model used in financial trading or medical
diagnostics could be just as dangerous as a larger, general-purpose model if it operates
without proper oversight. Therefore, the context and sector in which AI is deployed must be
a fundamental aspect of determining risk.2.
Potential for Societal Harm: AI models used in sectors such as healthcare, legal systems,
national security, or public administration carry heightened risk due to their potential for
wide-scale societal impact. Whether the model could cause individual or collective harm,
such as biased decision-making, discriminatory outcomes, or privacy breaches, must be
evaluated.3.
Autonomous and Agentic Behaviour: One of the major concerns raised was the potential for AI
models to exhibit autonomous or agentic behaviour—making decisions or taking actions
without human intervention. AI systems that are self-directed or act on behalf of users
present significantly greater risks and should therefore be classified as high-risk under the
regulatory framework. As one member noted, "The risk level dramatically increases when AI is
capable of taking actions without a human in the loop."
Balancing Technical and Principles-Based Assessments
While technical capabilities such as FLOPS thresholds can serve as benchmarks, they should
not be the sole criteria for defining high-risk AI. A principles-based approach, grounded in
ethical considerations and societal impact, is essential for a balanced evaluation. The
application of ethical AI principles such as fairness, accountability, transparency, and
explainability ensures that models are not only assessed on their computational power but
also on the real-world risks they present when deployed.
The Build Club community strongly advocated for the involvement of a scientific or technical
panel to continuously monitor AI developments. This expert group would be tasked with
assessing new AI models and recommending updates to the definition of high-risk AI based
on their impact and potential for harm. This panel could ensure that emerging risks—such as
those posed by self-improving AI systems or AI models capable of deception—are captured
early, long before they reach widespread deployment.
buildclub.aiHow should technical capability be defined in
high-risk AI? Use of FLOPS and Computational Thresholds
Several participants acknowledged that FLOPS thresholds or other computational metrics
could provide a useful starting point for identifying potentially risky models, particularly when
it comes to general-purpose AI. These technical benchmarks can act as red flags for models
with the computational capacity to perform at scale or operate autonomously in critical
settings.
However, the consensus was clear: FLOPS alone cannot determine risk. A high-powered
model may have limited risk depending on how it is applied, while a lower-powered model
used in a sensitive sector (like biotechnology or financial markets) could pose serious
threats. The key is contextualising the model's capabilities within the broader framework of
societal harm and ethical responsibility.
Scientific Panel for Continuous Risk Evaluation
To stay aligned with the fast pace of AI development, the Build Club recommends that
scientific or technical advisory panels be established to guide regulators on identifying and
evaluating high-risk AI systems. This panel would ensure that regulations are up to date,
flexible enough to adapt to new technologies, and based on the latest research into AI's
societal and technical risks.
As one member emphasised, "AI regulation can’t be static—we need ongoing assessments of
the technology and its potential risks, not just at launch but as it evolves." The establishment
of such panels would enable real-time monitoring and continuous adjustments to the
regulatory framework, ensuring that both technical parameters and contextual risks are
taken into account.
buildclub.aiHow should technical capability be defined in
high-risk AI? The role of human oversight in AI systems was a contentious issue in many discussions. While
some advocated for mandatory human oversight in all high-risk AI applications, others
warned that this could stifle innovation. “We don’t want to slow down the development of low-
cost, high-volume AI applications by requiring humans to oversee every decision,” one
participant argued. The consensus was that human intervention should be required only in
cases of extreme risk, such as life-and-death situations in healthcare or law enforcement.
A central theme of the conversations revolved around the idea that not all AI applications
require human oversight, and enforcing this across the board would be impractical and stifle
innovation. As one participant noted, “Requiring human oversight for everything dilutes the
effectiveness of AI and reduces its value, particularly in high-volume, low-cost applications
where AI can drastically improve efficiency.” The sentiment here is that over-regulating
human oversight could hinder the development of beneficial AI technologies, particularly for
industries that rely on speed and scale, such as finance, retail, or logistics.
However, for high-risk AI applications, particularly in sectors such as healthcare, defense, and
law enforcement, human intervention becomes critical. Some noted, “AI should support
human decision-makers while ensuring that responsibility and oversight remain with them,”
underscoring the importance of shared responsibility between AI systems and human
operators.
Innovative solutions to proof of human control were also shared with one group highlighting
the potential use of blockchain and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) to ensure that human
interventions are transparent and traceable. These mechanisms would allow organisations to
prove that human oversight occurred without compromising sensitive data, ensuring
accountability while maintaining confidentiality. This is particularly relevant in regulated
industries where audit trails are essential for compliance, such as healthcare and finance.
Defining Human in the Loop
A recurring point was the need for clear criteria on when human oversight is required. Several
contributors suggested that industry-specific frameworks would be best suited to determine
when and where human control is needed. For example, in healthcare, AI diagnostics should
always be reviewed by a qualified physician before any treatment is prescribed. Similarly, in
legal settings, AI-driven analysis should be used to assist lawyers or judges, but final
decisions should rest with a human authority.
There were suggestions that government regulation should not prescribe rigid human
oversight for all high-risk uses. Instead, it should mandate that for catastrophic or life-altering
decisions, human oversight must be enforced. One contributor summarised it well: “If the end
impact is catastrophic, then human in the loop is non-negotiable. If it’s a low-risk use case,
human intervention isn’t necessary.”
buildclub.aiHuman control and autonomy in AI systems Challenges with Continuous Human Oversight
One of the operational challenges discussed was that human oversight in all high-risk AI
applications may not achieve the desired result. Many AI systems are designed to handle
large amounts of data and make rapid decisions that would be impossible for a human to
verify in real-time. As a result, continuous oversight could introduce inefficiencies and
potentially reduce the benefits of AI in certain contexts. This was a concern particularly for
high-volume applications such as financial trading or autonomous logistics systems, where
speed and precision are critical.
Recommendations for Flexibility and Innovation
Several participants recommended that government regulations provide a broad framework,
leaving it to industry experts to define specific guidelines for human oversight. The
participants advocated for a flexible approach where industry bodies are empowered to
define what constitutes high-risk use cases and the appropriate level of human oversight.
This hub-and-spoke model of regulation allows industries to maintain innovation while
ensuring appropriate controls are in place where necessary.
buildclub.aiHuman control and autonomy in AI systems As AI technology rapidly evolves, new applications are emerging that present both
opportunities and risks. During our roundtables and discussions, several participants voiced
concerns that certain emerging AI applications, particularly in the realms of generative AI,
synthetic biology, and autonomous decision-making systems, are not adequately addressed
by the current proposed AI guardrails. These emerging technologies carry potential risks that
may not fit neatly within the existing regulatory frameworks.
Generative AI and Autonomous Systems
Generative AI, particularly models like GPT-4 and other large language models (LLMs), is a
rapidly advancing field. While the utility of these models in creating content, answering
complex questions, and generating code is clear, the unintended consequences of their use
remain largely unexplored. A common concern raised was that general-purpose AI systems
like these, when combined with autonomous decision-making systems, could lead to high-
risk outcomes if left unregulated.
For instance, generative AI can be used to create deepfakes, manipulate text or audio, or
generate harmful misinformation at an unprecedented scale. One participant observed, “The
risk with generative AI is that it can be weaponised to manipulate information, spread
falsehoods, or damage reputations without any real human oversight.” In certain contexts,
such as the media, political campaigns, and even corporate communications, this poses
significant ethical and legal challenges that need to be addressed.
Similarly, autonomous AI systems—those that are capable of making decisions without direct
human intervention—have emerged in sectors such as finance, healthcare, and
transportation. These systems can streamline processes and enhance efficiency but raise the
question of where responsibility lies in the event of an error or unintended harm. As one
roundtable participant stated, “The real challenge with autonomous systems is when they
make a decision that impacts lives—who is accountable? The system? The developer? Or the
user who deployed it?”
Synthetic Biology and AI
An even more novel and concerning use of AI is its application in synthetic biology. AI has the
potential to accelerate breakthroughs in drug development, gene editing, and even
bioengineering. However, the same tools that can be used to create life-saving treatments
can also be misused for developing biological weapons. Several contributors warned of the
risks associated with unregulated AI in synthetic biology, particularly the possibility of AI being
used to design pathogens or bioweapons without proper oversight.
buildclub.aiEmerging AI applications not currently addressed As one submission highlighted, “There's nothing stopping someone from open-sourcing a
model with dangerous capabilities for producing bioweapons without even taking the most
basic precautions.” The lack of explicit regulations around the use of AI in biotechnology
presents a significant national security risk and requires urgent attention.
Agents and AI-Driven Manipulation
Another emerging risk raised was the potential for AI agents—autonomous systems that can
act independently and make decisions on behalf of users—to be used for manipulation and
malicious purposes. These agents can access vast amounts of personal data and use it to
tailor actions or responses that exploit individuals’ psychological vulnerabilities. “The biggest
risk we see is in personalised persuasion agents—AI systems that can target individuals by
analysing their data and exploiting their weaknesses,” one contributor remarked. These
systems could be used for manipulation in sectors like advertising, politics, and even personal
relationships, posing significant ethical and legal questions about how far AI can go in
influencing human behaviour.
AI-Driven Autonomous Weapons
Though outside the traditional civilian sectors, the rise of AI-driven autonomous weapons also
came up as a critical area that lacks regulatory oversight. Several respondents expressed
concerns about the use of AI in military applications where autonomous systems could make
life-and-death decisions without human oversight. This raises ethical concerns about the
delegation of lethal authority to machines, and the lack of accountability in the event of a
tragic mistake. While this is more relevant to defense and national security contexts, the
implications for AI development in civilian settings are worth considering, especially as dual-
use technology—where civilian technologies are repurposed for military use—becomes more
common.
Cross-Industry Risks and Inconsistent Regulation
Many high-risk domains already have a significant regulatory burden, and the addition of AI-
specific guardrails must be carefully considered to avoid adding redundant or inconsistent
regulations. One participant remarked, “Many high-risk sectors like healthcare and finance
already have strong controls, and adding new AI regulations without considering existing
ones might create a compliance burden that slows down innovation.”
For example, the finance industry has strict anti-money laundering (AML) and know-your-
customer (KYC) regulations, which are already designed to mitigate risks related to fraud and
illegal activities. However, AI applications in finance, such as algorithmic trading or
automated credit scoring, may introduce new risks that aren't currently covered by these
regulations. Similarly, healthcare is heavily regulated, but the use of AI in medical diagnosis or
robotic surgery may present risks that aren't accounted for in the existing frameworks.
buildclub.aiEmerging AI applications not currently addressed There is also concern that different industries will experience disparate impacts from AI
regulations, which could hinder innovation in some sectors more than others. As one
participant noted, “While finance and healthcare are already used to a high level of scrutiny,
newer industries like autonomous driving or creative AI in the media space might find
themselves caught in a web of regulatory hurdles that could stifle their growth.”
Recommendations for Addressing Emerging AI Applications
Separate Categories for High-Risk Applications and Powerful General Models: Several
participants recommended separating high-risk applications (such as medical
diagnostics or financial decision-making systems) from general-purpose AI models that
can be used across industries. This ensures that regulations are targeted and don’t
impose unnecessary restrictions on lower-risk applications.1.
Proactive Monitoring and Licensing: Building on ideas shared in discussions, many
members proposed a proactive monitoring system for AI applications in emerging fields,
with the possibility of a voluntary licensing system. Such a system could provide incentives
for companies that follow best practices and uphold high standards of AI safety and
transparency. This would also allow the government to keep track of new developments
and quickly adapt regulations as technologies evolve.2.
Developing Risk-Based Frameworks for Emerging Technologies: As one respondent
noted, “AI is moving too fast to keep running back to the legislature.” Many contributors
recommended risk-based frameworks that can be flexibly applied to emerging AI
applications, allowing regulators to address risks without stifling innovation.3.
International Collaboration and Standards: Given the global nature of many AI systems,
respondents emphasised the need for Australia to contribute to international standards
(such as ISO 42001) and mirror those standards in domestic legislation where appropriate.
This approach would ensure that Australia remains competitive globally while adhering to
international best practices.4.
buildclub.aiEmerging AI applications not currently addressed Best legislative approach for high-risk AI 
Across our conversations, the domain-specific approach emerged as the preferred method
for regulating high-risk AI. Many argued that attempting a whole-of-economy AI Act would
risk overgeneralising the regulatory framework, potentially stifling innovation in sectors
already managing risks effectively. “We have existing regulators like APRA and ASIC who are
best placed to define what is high-risk in their industries. Why reinvent the wheel when we can
adapt current frameworks to include AI?” one participant commented.
Leveraging existing regulatory frameworks ensures that the unique characteristics of each
industry are accounted for, while reducing the administrative burden on businesses,
particularly smaller ones.
Opportunities in both legislative approaches 
The government should seize the opportunity to develop a local AI safety industry,
encouraging the growth of companies focused on AI ethics, compliance, and security. By
doing so, Australia can position itself as a leader in AI governance while supporting
innovation. One key recommendation was to leverage existing industry knowledge to develop
guardrails that protect consumers without creating unnecessary regulatory hurdles. “We
need to look at how we can both maximise protections and minimise regulatory burden,
especially in industries that are already heavily regulated,” was a common sentiment in these
discussions.
Regulatory options to ensure guardrails adapt to technology changes 
We strongly advocate for reusing existing regulators where possible, combined with the
creation of a new regulatory body for general-purpose AI systems. This dual approach allows
for specialised expertise to govern domain-specific applications while providing broader
oversight for systems that cut across industries. One member remarked, “It’s crucial that
regulators have the technical expertise to understand the risks in their specific industries, but
we also need a central body to manage the big-picture risks that span multiple sectors.”
Addressing gaps and inconsistencies in current laws 
Many contributors pointed out that Australia’s existing laws do not adequately regulate
powerful general-purpose AI. One major gap identified was the potential for open-sourcing
dangerous models, such as those capable of producing bioweapons. “There’s nothing
stopping someone from releasing a model with dangerous capabilities without taking basic
precautions,” one participant noted, urging the government to address this critical risk.
buildclub.aiOther Areas DiscussedTechnical and operational challenges 
The technical challenges of testing AI systems for unintended biases or harmful outcomes
remain significant. Many in the community feel that the current proposals do not fully address
these difficulties. One member stressed, “We need further research into how to develop better
tools and techniques for detecting biases within AI models.” There is a clear need for new
methods to interrogate the internal workings of AI systems, which would allow for more
accurate risk assessments.
Regulatory and compliance burdens for SMEs 
Several members highlighted the disproportionate impact of regulatory burdens on small
and medium-sized businesses (SMEs). One proposal was to offer specific incentives or
support for SMEs, allowing them to comply with AI regulations without stifling their innovation.
“Weak general-purpose AI should be excluded from high-risk categories unless it’s
demonstrably dangerous,” one roundtable participant argued, emphasising that simplified
compliance processes would help smaller firms navigate the regulatory landscape more
effectively.
Overall views on proposed guardrails 
While generally supportive of the proposed guardrails, many participants raised concerns
about the burden these regulations could place on small businesses and developers.
“Requiring constant reporting and compliance checks could overwhelm smaller companies,”
one contributor pointed out, suggesting that compliance processes be simplified. There was
also concern that guardrails should focus on outcomes rather than prescribing specific
technologies, with several members recommending that human oversight requirements be
applied selectively based on the level of risk.
buildclub.aiOther Areas DiscussedThrough extensive consultation with our members, Build Club supports a flexible, adaptive
approach to AI regulation that leverages existing industry frameworks while ensuring the
necessary guardrails are in place for high-risk AI applications. The proposed hub-and-spoke
model, where industry bodies define high-risk use cases within a government-set framework,
is a practical solution for balancing innovation with safety. By streamlining compliance for
SMEs, encouraging the development of an AI safety industry, and focusing regulation on high-
risk outcomes rather than technical specifications alone, Australia can establish itself as a
global leader in AI governance.

DEFINITION OF HIGH -RISK AI  
We support a nuanced approach to regulating the two broad categories of high -risk AI : 
  
• where the proposed use of the AI system or general -purpose AI (GPAI) model 
are known or foreseeable ; and 
• advanced, highly capable GPAI models where all possible applications and risks 
cannot be foreseen.  
Category One: Proposed uses are known or foreseeable  
Our view is that principles that are all encompassing of any risk of adverse impact are 
excessively broad and could potentially  classify  low-risk AI applications intended to support 
and enhance customer experience and outcomes  as high risk . 
 
As currently drafted, the  proposed principles defining high -risk AI would capture practices 
which have been in use by banks for years and are considered low risk, for example, credit 
decisioning using machine learning models.  How the various AI systems are used  present 
different levels of  risk, and this is not differentiated in the principles . In determining what is to 
be considered high -risk AI, the Government needs to focus on the type of harm it is trying to 
prevent  to ensure the regulatory regime is targeted  at those use cases with the potential for 
serious  harm , noting that some  of these  harms are already prohibited through existing  laws.  
 
In addition,  greater clarity  is needed  in relation to how risk should be assessed  where  there 
is an AI system with high impact but low probability, or low impact but high probability.  The

Category Two: Advanced GPAI models  
Similar to the Canadian approach, the mandatory guardrails in Category One should apply 
equally for Advanced GPAI models. A more nuanced approach is required for the 
developers  of the GPAI models  which should focus on areas where there is lower 
transparency , for example, data measures, testing measures and any known vulnerabilities.  
 
Definition of a developer  
Westpac would expect that as organisations scale,  they will  adopt AI systems to support 
their business processes . This would require them to alter AI models whether it is to adapt or 
combine models to suit their specific needs. An organisation or individual altering an AI 
model , should not then result in them being classified as a developer. Any definition of 
developer needs to include a degree of materiality, like in the United States of America, such 
that the AI model is ‘significantly’ altered before an organisation or individual is to be 
considered a developer.  
 
A distinction should be made between developers who are developing for consumption by 
other organisations (external) and those that are developing entirely for internal use. A 
higher degree of risk applies to those developing for external consumption, as there is 
generally less transparency and explainability for end users, and as such more stringent 
obligations need to apply to these types of developers . 
 
PROPOSED GUARDRAILS  
We have considered the proposed guardrails  and have focused our feedback on the 
following.  
 
Guardrail 6: Inform end -users regarding AI -enabled decisions, interactions with AI 
and AI generated content  
The proposed guardrail is currently designed to apply broadly, encompassing not only 
decisions made by an AI system but also those influenced by AI. Imposing an obligation on 
the organisations to provide the en d user with detail about AI -enabled decisions or 
interaction would be burdensome and could potentially stifle innovation.  
 
Additionally, there is no distinction between internal and external applications of AI. With 
such a wide scope, Guardrail 6 might unintentionally cover low -risk applications, where 
decisions are ultimately made by a human or when the AI is used internally,  which are low -
risk scenarios that should not require disclosure. Westpac recommends  that a distinction is 
made between external and internal uses, and between AI used by experts and non -experts 
of AI systems . The requirement to inform should be narrowed t o those use  cases where 
there is the risk of serious harm to the end user.  
 
Guardrail 7: Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use 
or outcomes  
The banking industry is already subject to a range of comprehensive, regulated processes 
for preventing customer harm and for resolving customer complaints. As an example, we are 
required by the Banking Code of Practice and the Australian Securities and Investments 
Commission Regulatory Guide 271 to implement internal dispute resolution ( IDR) 
mechanisms. There are also existing external dispute resolution mechanisms through the 
Australian Financial Complaints Authority that allow a customer to seek a review of the IDR 
outcome where they are unhappy with that outcome.

Proposed Guardrail 7  impos es regulations based on technology, rather than outcome s. The 
ability for the customer to contest should not be based on the technology and resources 
used to achieve the decision.  There are examples where banks use AI, such is in the

Banks currently deploy sophisticated AI capabilities to make lending decisions. Current

As outlined by the proposals paper , banks are heavily regulated organisations, and already 
have  existing obligations  that support the safe and responsible use of AI. These obligations 
apply across a range of laws including the Privacy Act 1988, Corporations Act 2001, ASIC 
Act 2001, National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009, APRA Prudential Standards, Age 
Discrimination Act 2004 , Disability Discrimination Act 1992, Racial Discrimination Act 1975 , 
etc. These laws and standards already require the bank to have multiple assessments and 
extensive documentation requirements in place, such that the  introduction of an additional 
conformity assessment to demonstrate compliance with AI guardrails would  result in 
unnecessary  duplicative obligations .  
 
More broadly, this requirement has the potential to disproportionately impact smaller 
organisations, which could find the imposition of conformity assessments too high a barrier 
given the prescriptive nature of the Guardrail. This would likely hinder innov ation and limit 
the organisation’s ability to adopt AI systems.  
 
We support some form of demonstr able compliance,  but we believe this will be materially 
achieved through existing laws and regulations.  
 
REGULATORY OPTIONS TO MANDATE THE GUARDRAILS  
The importance of balancing the safe and responsible use of AI and the enablement of 
innovation cannot be understated. A regulatory regime that is overly burdensome will have 
negative impacts on innovation and the productivity benefits that this technology  brings, 
while also hindering Australia’s ability to compete internationally.  
 
As a starting point, Westpac encourages the Government to conduct a mapping exercise of 
the application of existing laws relative to AI. Such an exercise  would allow  for the 
identification of any gaps . 
  
Westpac supports  the introduc tion of  framework legislation (Option 2) that defines guardrails  
and their thresholds. This framework legislation would provide  a consistent set of definitions 
and measures  that would then be implemented  through amendments to existing regulations.  
This approach would better support regulatory settings that balance innovati on with 
consumer protections.

Feedback on the Proposals 1. Unclear Scope [Guardrails #1-10] (i) Systems and Models The Proposals are not clear or consistent concerning what obligation(s) apply to systems or models, or both. To address this, we suggest that in the first instance, the Government looks to align with established definitions for systems and models found in the United States’ Executive Order on the Safe, Secure and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence.15   The Government should then specify which guardrails apply to the developer, deployer and/or end user of the generative AI system based on the use/setting. Model developers should not be responsible or liable for system-level assessments and mitigations contemplated in the guardrails. This is aligned with the intention in the proposals paper to take account of the AI supply chain, and accordingly imposes guardrails where they can be most effectively applied.  (ii) Traditional AI v Generative AI  As the paper notes, “In Australia, the development and use of AI is shaped by a range of legal frameworks, including areas such as consumer, privacy, anti-discrimination, competition, data protection, and copyright law. The Australian Government announced an investment of $4.2 million in the 2024–25 Budget to clarify and strengthen existing laws impacted by AI, with reviews in priority areas of health care, consumer and copyright law.”  In addition to the Government’s work on existing regulation and bringing a contemporary interpretation to that for the generative AI age, rather than risk creating overlapping, conflicting, or duplicative obligations by applying guardrails to both traditional AI and generative AI, the Government should focus its efforts on the guardrails on generative AI only. This is the approach that has been adopted through the White House Voluntary AI Commitments, which are “designed to advance a  15 The U.S. Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence, 30 October 2023, https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/10/30/executive-order-on-the-safe-secure-and-trustworthy-development-and-use-of-artificial-intelligence 9 generative AI legal and policy regime”, and the Seoul Frontier AI Safety Commitments which apply to ‘frontier AI’ only, where ‘frontier AI’ is defined as “highly capable general-purpose AI models or systems (otherwise known as ‘generative models or systems’) that can perform a wide variety of tasks and match or exceed the capabilities present in the most advanced models.”  (iii) Thresholds  The Proposals are not sufficiently clear on the threshold for systems that will be in scope. For example, the paper suggests that “adopting an approach that focuses on the most advanced AI systems would also build on commitments developers have made through the Hiroshima AI Process Code of Conduct and the Frontier AI Safety Commitments”.16 However, elsewhere in the paper it is suggested that all AI systems will be in scope. To reflect the intention of aligning with existing frameworks such as the Seoul Frontier AI Safety Commitments, the Government should clarify that the guardrails only apply to ‘frontier AI’, where “frontier AI” is defined as, “highly capable general-purpose AI models or systems that can perform a wide variety of tasks and match or exceed the capabilities present in the most advanced models.”17 2. Ex ante designation of ‘high-risk’ [Guardrail #4] The Government should take an evidence-based approach, and avoid ascribing ex ante risk labels based on the technology itself. However, the Proposals assume that GPAI by its nature is high-risk. This is not supported by the vast science and evidence of GPAI capabilities and performance and would, in fact, go against the Government’s stated intention to not undermine the benefits of innovation in AI in lower risk contexts. The Bletchley Park Declaration, to which Australia is a signatory, describes the risks of “highly capable general purpose AI models,” rather than the entire category of GPAI.19 Similarly, the Seoul Frontier AI Safety Commitments specifically address “highly capable general-purpose AI models” as high risk.20 There is no precedent globally of an in force regulation that defines the entire category of GPAI models as high risk, precisely because the evidence does not support this.   While the discussion of what the threshold should be and which models are and are not high risk is important, in order to even reach that, the Government’s proposal needs to move away from a blanket discussion of GPAI as high risk. GPAI models that do not meet the criteria for high risk should not have added guardrails, as the entire exercise of the proposal is to create guardrails for “AI in high risk settings”.   Specifically, Meta suggests that the Government might look to the threshold established in the United States’ Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence which creates a flexible, yet predictable, way to categorise which GPAI models above these thresholds21 could be required to comply with additional obligations.   19 UK Government, ‘The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit, 1-2 November 2023’, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-safety-summit-2023-the-bletchley-declaration/the-bletchley-declaration-by-countries-attending-the-ai-safety-summit-1-2-november-2023   20 UK Government, ‘Frontier AI Safety Commitments, AI Seoul Summit 2024’, Policy Paper, 21 May 2024,  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/frontier-ai-safety-commitments-ai-seoul-summit-2024/frontier-ai-safety-commitments-ai-seoul-summit-2024  21  The U.S. Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence, 30 October 2023, https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/10/30/executive-order-on-the-safe-secure-and-trustworthy-development-and-use-of-artificial-intelligence states in s 4.2(b) (Ensuring Safe and Reliable AI): (i) any model that was trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10*26 integer or floating-point operations, or using primarily biological sequence data and using a quantity of computing power greater than 10*23 integer or floating-point operations; (ii) enabling powerful offensive cyber operations through automated vulnerability discovery and exploitation against a wide range of potential targets of cyber attacks; or (iii) permitting the evasion of human control or oversight through means of deception or obfuscation.  11 (i) Risks Assessments The proposed guardrail that sets up risk assessment requirements is overly broad and vague, which would make it a very difficult to apply standard. We believe that its scope should be anchored to areas of emerging consensus (in the forums and frameworks mentioned above), and be limited to reasonably foreseeable or known risks within specific areas, such as human rights, safety or health.  Risks should be cognisable and measurable based on standardised benchmarking and a marginal risk assessment of the use case. Such evaluations help industry and others to understand model performance, enabling documentation of the model's capabilities and limitations. However, AI evaluations and benchmarks remain a nascent field and, at present, there is a lack of consensus about how best to measure and evaluate certain risks.    In particular, evaluating general purpose models is challenging because these models can perform a wide range of tasks and involve interactions between the systems into which they are integrated. Determinations around model evaluations need to be based on repeatable measurements. Helpfully, valuable work is underway and progress is being made by numerous research institutions, the United States Department of Commerce’s National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the United States AI Safety Institute, and the MLCommons initiative. The Australian Government should consider these efforts and focus on identifying if there are gaps that remain to be addressed. If there are gaps, the Government should consider various measurements related to the ability of the model in question.   The marginal risk of releasing a model should be the gold standard of measuring the risk of models, rather than relying on an ex-ante perspective and labelling it unsafe or inherently risky. A marginal risk approach is the generally accepted best method for measuring the risk as against potential benefits of generative AI models. In developing the guardrails, we believe that a marginal risk framework is the most appropriate framework through which to consider risks, and how they might be assessed and mitigated.  (ii) High Risk AI Systems  We believe that the best way to describe high risk AI is by providing a list of consequential use cases. That is, the list should enumerate specific use cases where the AI system plays a major role in a consequential decision. By focusing on consequential uses, there is a reduced likelihood of unintentionally capturing low risk use cases while also ensuring proper treatment of legitimate high risk uses.  12  In contrast, a principles-based approach as proposed by the government would generate legal and commercial uncertainty. Companies will likely interpret and apply each principle differently, and their interpretations will differ from those of any regulator. As a result, companies will not likely be able to confidently implement the guardrails and, to avoid enforcement risk, may over-apply the guardrails to low risk AI systems.   A vague principles-based approach may deter Australian businesses’ uptake of AI systems, even when these systems are low risk and would lead to productivity boosts. Businesses in Australia should be encouraged to harness the power of low risk AI. But any regulatory system that leaves companies in doubt about their compliance obligations is sure to undermine this goal. Thus, a list-based approach, rooted in consequential uses, would be a better approach. 3. Disproportionate allocation of responsibilities upstream in the AI supply chain [Guardrail # 2] In order to comprehensively and effectively address the risk of misuse for general purpose AI models, the guardrails must sufficiently cover not only model developers, but all entities in the AI value chain. We refer the Government to the PAI Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment,22 which sets out the various actors: model providers (who train general purpose models that others build on to create AI systems for specific applications); downstream developers (who use open source models to build AI applications for their own use cases, often using their own data for fine-tuning the model); model deployers (who can be the same as the downstream developer); and end users (those who use the final AI application). By outlining different phases of AI development and deployment, it is then possible to pinpoint opportunities for effective interventions and determine specific mitigation strategies that various actors can feasibly and appropriately implement.23    Due to technology's dynamic nature, as well as its potential risks and benefits, policy measures should focus on differentiating responsibilities across this value chain in order to provide legal and business clarity. In this regard, the Government should prioritise  22 Partnership on AI, PAI’s Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment: A Framework for Collective Action, https://partnershiponai.org/modeldeployment  23 Partnership on AI, ‘ Risk Mitigation Strategies for the Open Foundation Model Value Chain’: https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/2024/07/open-foundation-model-risk-mitigation_rev3-1.pdf 13 standardising the threat models and evaluations along the AI value chain, and clarifying when and where risk assessments and mitigations are most effectively applied.    The proposal for assessing responsibility across the AI lifecycle is not rooted in the fundamentals of how GPAI models and the generative AI systems built on top of such models work. Importantly, the developer building the model is creating an engine that is capable of powering a substantial number of uses, whereas the deployer is the one that makes specific choices on how and in what form the “engine” gets used.  Accordingly, risk is context-dependent, and many of the risks associated with GPAI models will only become apparent and amenable to targeted mitigations once they are used for a defined purpose. It is therefore important to empower downstream developers with tools they can easily and effectively use to assess and mitigate risks presented by their specific AI applications,24 while also noting that ultimately, these developers are responsible for using such tools as appropriate for their specific use cases.   Having to address all foreseeable future use cases would be an impossible obligation for developers, whereas deployers can more effectively address contextual risks because they understand the use case, and can apply mitigations at the system-level. Thus, Meta suggests a re-alignment of the responsibility, to take into consideration the importance of the deployers in the AI lifecycle.  In the specific case of open source GPAI models, while Meta’s own guardrails – such as our model license and limitations on volume of use – provide us with important ways to manage some risks, no open source AI developer can monitor downstream use of their models. Therefore, it is crucial that the guardrails take into consideration the technical feasibility of such obligations.  4. Conformity assessments [Guardrails #9, #10] We are concerned by the lack of clarity regarding the proposed requirement to “undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with the guardrails.”   The Proposals contemplate that prior to deploying a high risk AI system, developers will be required to conduct a conformity assessment either themselves, or via a third-party or government entities or regulators and “once completed, the organisation will attain  24 Meta open sources several safety tools which developers can use to build responsibly with Meta’s Llama models: https://www.llama.com/trust-and-safety/ 14 certification of compliance.” This suggests that deployers could be required to obtain certification by the Government before deploying high-risk systems in Australia.   The Proposals provide many examples of categories of systems that would be in scope as “high-risk”, in particular through the concept of “systemic impact”, with the result that deployers may have hundreds of different systems that  would require conformity assessments. Such an obligation at scale is neither proportionate nor warranted. We suggest clarifying that internal assessments would be sufficient for demonstrating  compliance.   Furthermore, as the Proposals would classify all GPAI models as high risk, the conformity assessment guardrail would create a disproportionate impact on the deployment of all open source AI models, because such models would be subject to “passing” the conformity assessment by the regulator before being made available in Australia on an open source basis.   A pre-deployment certification requirement could be incompatible with releasing an open-source AI model for several reasons: i) Restrictions on modification: A certification requirement might imply that the model cannot be modified or changed in any way once it has been “certified”, which is incompatible with the principles of open-source.  ii) Testing protocols and evaluation metrics: The certification process might involve testing protocols, or evaluation metrics that are not publicly available, making it difficult or impossible for open-source developers to replicate the testing process or evaluate and improve their models.  iii) Cost and accessibility barriers: The certification process might be costly and/or require significant resources, creating a barrier for open-source developers who may not have the necessary funding or infrastructure to obtain certification. iv) Time-consuming and bureaucratic process: The certification process might be time-consuming and bureaucratic, which could slow down the development and deployment of open-source AI models.  By requiring pre-deployment certification, the Proposals may inadvertently create a situation where open-source AI models are at a disadvantage compared to proprietary models. This could stifle innovation and limit the adoption of open-source AI solutions.  In addition to the points made previously regarding ex ante designation of all GPAI models as high risk, Meta suggests clarifying that any such certification be considered optional and limited to “frontier AI”, as stated above. 15 5. Feasibility [Guardrails #3, #4, #5, #6, #8] (i) Technical Feasibility : Provenance and Risk Assessments / Evaluations (red-teaming)  (a) Provenance The labelling / watermarking guardrail seems to apply indiscriminately to all generative AI outputs and is not, contrary to the Government’s stated goals, indexed to risk. Meta believes an approach that follows that stated goal would be to take such steps that are reasonable in the circumstances (if any), taking into account the risk of actual harm to individuals associated with the outputs. As such, outputs that are very low risk would not be subject to this requirement. One clear low risk output would be AI-generated stickers that are not photorealistic and that users interact with in a particular context. Such stickers pose a low risk of harm, even if used maliciously.   Any measures which should apply to the outputs of an AI system are most effectively applied by the developer of that system. This is particularly the case regarding provenance measures, such as labelling and watermarking, and is why the Proposals should clearly reflect the allocation of responsibility along the AI supply chain.   Further, Meta suggests that the Government add to the guardrail language that explicitly limits requirements to those that are technically feasible and commercially reasonable. The state of the science around provenance and watermarking is still in its infancy. Because so many of the tools available today are still in “beta” form, proscriptive rules are largely not yet appropriate or technically feasible. In addition, identifying photo-/audio-realistic AI-generated content is an industry-wide issue that requires industry-wide solutions.   Meta is committed to doing our part, both on our platforms and through our products, to ensure people can understand when they are engaging with AI-generated content. This includes investing significantly in disclosure mechanisms, including perceptible and imperceptible watermarks.25   When photorealistic images are created using our Meta AI feature, we put visible watermarks on the images, and both invisible watermarks and metadata are embedded  25 Meta, ‘Our Approach to Labeling AI-Generated Content and Manipulated Media’, Newsroom, 5 April 2024, https://about.fb.com/news/2024/04/metas-approach-to-labeling-ai-generated-content-and-manipulated-media; Meta, ‘Labeling AI-Generated Images on Facebook, Instagram and Threads’, Newsroom, 6 February 2024, https://about.fb.com/news/2024/02/labeling-ai-generated-images-on-facebook-instagram-and-threads  16 within image files. These disclosure mechanisms help both people and other platforms identify AI-generated images. We are also building industry-leading tools that can identify invisible markers at scale (specifically, the “AI generated” information in the C2PA and IPTC technical standards), so that we can label images from companies like Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Adobe, Midjourney, and Shutterstock as they implement their plans for adding metadata to images created by their tools.26  In order to place political or social issues ads on our platforms, an advertiser is required to go through a verification process. We are also requiring advertisers to disclose when they use AI or digital techniques to create or alter ads when 1) the ad contains a photorealistic image or video, or realistic sounding audio, and 2) it was digitally created or altered to depict a real person as saying or doing something they did not say or do.27   Finally, since AI-generated content appears across the internet, we are also working closely with partners to develop industry-wide solutions, such as signing the Munich Tech Accord to Combat Deceptive Use of AI in Elections,28 joining the C2PA Steering Committee,29 and working with other companies to develop common standards for identifying AI-generated content through fora like the Partnership on AI (PAI).  (b) Risk Assessments / Evaluations (red-teaming) While we believe that red-teaming is an important evaluation tool, it should not be the sole evaluation method used or required in all instances.   Responsible development should include robust risk assessments and evaluations (which may include red-teaming for certain models) that are: commensurate with the potential risks involved; transparent; and include minimum guardrails. Common standards should be based on existing frameworks (e.g., the PAI Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment) and take into account the extensive work in the field of international partners, such as that of the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) and NIST in the US, the UK AI Safety Institute, and Australia’s own AI Expert Group.   26  Meta, ‘Our Approach to Labeling AI-Generated Content and Manipulated Media’, Newsroom, 5 April 2024, https://about.fb.com/news/2024/04/metas-approach-to-labeling-ai-generated-content-and-manipulated-media; Meta, ‘Labeling AI-Generated Images on Facebook, Instagram and Threads’, Newsroom, 6 February 2024, https://about.fb.com/news/2024/02/labeling-ai-generated-images-on-facebook-instagram-and-threads  27  Meta, ‘Helping people understand when AI or digital methods are used in political or social issue ads’, https://www.facebook.com/government-nonprofits/blog/political-ads-ai-disclosure-policy  28 Munich Security Conference, A Tech Accord to Combat Deceptive Use of AI in 2024 Elections, https://securityconference.org/en/aielectionsaccord  29 C2PA, ‘Meta Joins the C2PA Steering Committee’, 5 September 2024: https://c2pa.org/post/meta_pr/ 17  The Government should not anchor on red-teaming as the most important – or only – evaluation methodology in all circumstances. Red-teaming is a costly undertaking, and is limited by the expertise and scope of the red-teamers. For example, if a red-team group is only composed of experts in one particular area, it will not be best equipped to test for vulnerabilities outside of that scope. Developers need to be able to deploy a range of evaluations, including tools like benchmarking, human evaluation, A/B testing, cross-validation and adversarial attacks.   We encourage the Government to consider how it might facilitate establishing common standards for risk assessments, benchmarks and evaluations informed by science and in collaboration with the global network of AI Safety Institutes.  (ii) Trade Secrets Information within model evaluations can be highly commercially sensitive. Therefore, mandatory public disclosures should be carefully tailored to avoid compelling model developers to disclose commercial secrets, and be limited to areas where there is a significant public benefit. One possible solution might be to disclose information to authorities only.  Building datasets to train foundation models requires proprietary research into what data is effective and techniques for collection and preparation. While it makes sense for companies to provide high-level summaries about the type of data used (such as, for instance, time of collection or domain level info), many details about how data is collected, processed, and the final data composition are competitively valuable and sensitive. Flexibility is important. Because of how models are developed, the data used and the confidential business practices adopted will vary across different model developers. Any requirements to provide dataset transparency should not be overly prescriptive and should provide optionality for developers to provide lists or narrative descriptions as appropriate to preserve trade secrets and confidential information. 6. Options for introducing mandatory guardrails There are an increasing number of voluntary initiatives, domestic regulations, and international laws and principles emerging around AI, in particular generative AI. Given the increasing potential for regulatory fragmentation globally, it is important to ensure consistency and interoperability, particularly around definitions, taxonomies, risk identification, assessments, and mitigations. In this regard, the Government might usefully look to the US Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy 18 Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence, or the Seoul Frontier AI Safety Commitments. We also note the work of the EU-US Trade and Technology Council on taxonomies, the report of the UN High Level Advisory Board on AI, the UN Resolutions on AI governance, and UN Global Digital Compact.   Finally, the Government has sought feedback on which of the three options would be the most successful in mandating the guardrails. We believe that the best way forward would be Option 2 (a framework approach): Adapting existing regulatory frameworks through framework legislation.   This Option, which recognises that Australia’s existing laws may be capable of giving effect – or can be amended to give effect – to one or more of the proposed mandatory guardrails in individual regimes, would take cognisance of the applicability of existing laws and regulations already to AI and look to address gaps by providing a consistent set of definitions, defining the guardrails to apply and establishing thresholds for when they would apply. This is the most appropriate for achieving the policy outcomes being pursued - namely the safe and responsible use of AI in Australia in a manner that is aligned with emerging international consensus on AI governance.                  19 Annex A: Table of Responses to Specific Consultation Questions  No Question Summary of Meta Response Defining high-risk AI 1 Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI? To: Department of Industry, Science, and Resources – Australian Government  
From: Jaime Noda   https://www.linkedin.com/in/jaime -noda/  
Subject: Feedback on mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
 
Sydney, Australia 4 October 2024  
 
Dear AI guardrails consultation team,  
I am an Australian member of the public who is interested in our AI future laws. As such, I 
appreciate the opportunity and the invitation to provide constructive feedback on the proposal 
for mandatory AI guardrails in Australia.  
The guardrails paper is easy to read, and I was pleasantly surprised with the breath and coverage 
you included. In general, I feel you have put a lot of effort to get to this stage.  
Leaving that aside, t here are four suggestions I would like to make : 
1. There is an opportunity for the government to put in place an AI legislation with similar 
aspects to the way Cyber Security law has been established in Australia, establishing 
linkages to criminal codes.  
2. I would suggest the use of a Risk Taxonomy ( e.g. MIT's. See https://airisk.mit.edu/) to 
determine/guide the amount of governance or compliance required for an AI use -case. This 
approach could be more effective than a "one size fits all" for high -risk valuations.  Large, 
medium, and small organisations would benefit with this approach.  
3. The AI principles you list seem flexible enough, although I would place more accountability 
on the AI developers, since they can set controls (e.g. in code or configuration settings) on 
what an AI system can and cannot do. Deployers of AI systems will have a more limited 
ability to set those controls due to their restricted access to code and architecture.  
4. I appreciate the following is a difficult task, as I would like to see a proactive leadership  of 
the Australian Government to work with other nations like the US, UK, EU and Canada to 
start a world organisation that enforces AI laws regardless of the geographies where risks or 
incidents exist. Today we have international laws, and I feel they can be extended to 
incorporate AI legislations.  
 
I should point out this submission is made on my behalf as an individual and Australian citizen, 
and not on behalf of any organisation where I am affiliated . 
I look forward to seeing further developments of this great initiative.  
Jaime Noda

  3 1. Executive  Summary  
 Free TV Australia (Free TV) fully supports the Government’s  comprehensive  approach  to designing  
regulation  of high‐risk uses of AI to ensure they are safe and responsible.   
 The issue of how AI is adopted, used and regulated  in Australia is inextricably  linked to the health 
of Australian  democracy  and the sustainability  of the Australian  news media sector. 
 The Government  appropriately  seeks to take a risk‐based approach  to regulating  AI. The definition  
of ‘high risk’—which  warrants a mandatory  regulatory  response—should  include uses which pose 
a risk of harm to democracy  and local media industry sustainability.   
 Under this graduated  approach,  the use of AI in low‐risk settings by the creative sector should be 
enabled to flourish unimpeded.  
 Proposed  principles  for designating  an AI system as high‐risk due to its use should specifically  refer 
to risks to access to accountable  news and current affairs and associated  risks of harm to 
democratic  processes.  
 The guardrails  for high‐risk use of AI should include clear transparency  requirements.  Free TV 
agrees that organisations  across the AI supply chain should be informed  about data models and 
systems—this  includes those whose data (like news content) is ingested, not just those who 
deploy AI systems. 
 Technical  considerations  about how to provide transparency,  such as via the use of tokens to 
denote how much content has been used, would be considered  once the mandatory  guardrail 
relating to transparency  was put in place. 
 The domain‐specific knowledge  of existing industry regulators  should be preserved.  
Implementation  options which enable the application  of their expertise  by reference  to an 
overarching  AI regulatory  framework  and principles  are preferred.   
 While these matters are being considered,  Government  should direct the ACCC to conduct a 
market study of the impact of generative  AI on the creative and news media sectors.  
 The ACCC should be given new powers under an ex ante regulatory  framework  for digital 
platforms  that should be applied to address AI‐related risks set out in this submission,  and as 
informed  by the ACCC market study. 
 This should include mandating  transparency  of inputs to AI modes and support remuneration  
when content, such as news and current affairs content, is used by AI.

The key policy problems  to address in relation to AI and news media relate to: 
 Risks to democracy —there is a significant  risk that citizens will consume AI‐generated  or AI 
summarised  news without transparency  as to its source. They will not know if is accurate and 
reliable and will not be able to assess if a diversity of viewpoints  and sources have been used to 
train the AI. They may be exposed to misinformation  and disinformation,  including from AI‐
generated  fakes, which will impair their ability to make informed  decisions about public interest 
issues, and most concerningly  when forming voting intentions.  
 
 Risks to the sustainability  of the Australian  media sector —the sustainability  of news media and 
other content businesses  will be at risk if content, the production  of which they have funded, is 
used to train AI without transparency  or remuneration.1 
As a starting point, Free TV is seeking a regulatory  scheme which: 
 mandates  transparency  of inputs to AI models —so that both citizens are aware of the source of 
the information  they are consuming,  and so that Free TV members  can see if, and to what extent 
their content has been ingested to train the models; and 
 supports remuneration  when content, such as news and current affairs content, is used by AI—
where Free TV’s members  bear the cost of producing  content and being held to account for it 
under robust regulatory  arrangements,  while the AI providers  otherwise  benefit from it without 
paying, including by selling advertising  against it. 
Following  its extensive  expert work on the impact of major digital platforms  on consumers  and 
competition  in Australia—and  in particular  the production  of local, trusted and accountable  news and
