What this means is that any definition of high-risk GPAI is likely to need to change over time . 
We have argued throughout this submission that an entity (an AI Body), informed by technical 
and socio-technical expertise, will need to play a role in dynamic adjustment of any system 
for AI governance: for example, in updating any indicative or prescribed list of high risk AI 
systems or uses. That is, we will need a regulator body or scientific body with the power to 
independently declare certain specific models as high risk or very high risk (or systemic risk, in 
the EU parlance) GPAI, and therefore subject to more stringent regulation. For more, see Topic 5 
below.
Question 6 : Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
Question 11 : Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI? 
How could we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for example low risk and high 
risk GPAI models? Questions 6 and 11: The Mandatory Guardrails and GPAI
Can the proposed Mandatory Guardrails apply to GPAI?
The important implication of GPAI’s general purpose  nature is that it is difficult to predict uses 
and impacts. Their general nature means we cannot know in advance what all the uses (variety 
of purposes) will be, with the result that there might be increased risk that is not foreseeable. 
While for the most part the Guardrails are use case agnostic, and so capable of application 
to GPAI, applying some guardrails will be challenging when combined with the predictive 
difficulties introduced by GPAI. Specifically, we highlight:
• Guardrail 2 (risk management and mitigation): Identification of risks stemming from an AI 
system will be more difficult for GPAI systems where the potential applications, let alone 
risks, are harder to identify a-priori.
• Guardrail 3 (data quality and provenance): Protecting GPAI systems from poor quality 
or malicious data sources may be more difficult, due to the unforeseeable ways these 
systems might operate on data. For example more advanced LLM models are known to 
have a largern ‘attack surface’ for prompt injection attacks — that is, the general purpose 
nature means malicious users have more ways of tricking the model into performing 
forbidden actions.91
• Guardrail 4 (testing and monitoring): Testing GPAI systems may be much more difficult, 
as you can’t test specific use cases in advance, or you might need to test very many use 
cases, or the tests must be are very general and therefore lose predictive power.
• Our proposed Guardrail 11 (stakeholder engagement): Engaging effectively with the 
right stakeholders may be very difficult for GPAI systems where the question of which 
stakeholders are relevant is itself difficult to answer.
91Yupei Liu et al, ‘Formalizing and benchmarking prompt injection attacks and defenses.’ 33rd USENIX Security 
Symposium (USENIX Security 24) (2024).40
We have assumed throughout this submission that the Guardrails are intended to have some 
internal flexibility, and that risk management, risk mitigation, oversight, disclosure and the like 
are all intended to be applied in a way that is proportional and adapted to the AI systems, and 
risks involved. If this is correct, it may be mostly possible to apply the Guardrails flexibly to GPAI 
(and we note the adjustments specifically noted in Attachment E to the Paper). In any event, as 
we have noted above in our discussion of Question 8, there will be more work to do drafting the 
particular requirements that are to be mandated as part of each Guardrail, and more specific 
adjustments and flexibility can be included at that stage. Ongoing work via the Working Group 
on trustworthy GPAI in Europe will also be relevant in providing more detailed guidance on how 
the Guardrails apply to GPAI. One possible avenue to deal with this is to insert in any legislation 
an obligation for providers of GPAI to cooperate with government to identify risks, similar to 
what is envisaged in the EU AI Act in article 53(3).
Are additional protections needed, perhaps for ‘very high’ or 
‘systemic’ risk GPAI’? 
Another question is whether there are additional requirements that ought to apply to very high 
risk or very large models — beyond the ‘standard’ Mandatory Guardrails. Specific, additional 
obligations have been included in the EU AI Act (art 55) and were proposed in California’s 
(recently vetoed) SB1047. We note that the position in the US is fluid: while SB1047 has been 
vetoed, the developers of the largest models have engaged in some voluntary cooperation with 
the federal government; being voluntary it is inevitably unclear how long such cooperation will 
last, or how effective it will be.
The crux of additional existing or proposed requirements is that for GPAI that has potential 
large-scale, systemic risks, there should be additional cybersecurity and testing obligations, 
as well as deeper levels of engagement with government (such as reporting incidents). The 
recently vetoed SB1047 in California would have also included a requirement that such systems 
have capacities for shutdown built in. In Europe, further development of standards is expected 
to be developed through Codes of Practice (see art 56). 
We make the following brief comments on this question:
• Given that the Mandatory Guardrails will mostly involve organisations engaging in internal 
processes such as risk assessment and mitigation and testing, it makes sense that 
further external requirements including reporting to government should apply for some 
subset of very high-risk models. To the extent that systemic risks arising from large 
models or incidents relating to large models pose cyber security risks or risks to critical 
infrastructure, reporting and cooperation obligations already exist under other legal 
regimes. Cybersecurity or critical infrastructure-related risks however do not cover the full 
range of risks arising from AI (as discussed above in relation to the definition of high-risk 
systems).
• Any model which poses systemic risk within Australia is likely to pose similar risks beyond 
Australia. This is therefore an area where it is especially critical that Australia promote 41
international cooperation, and that any national regulation be developed in such a way 
as to ensure effective interoperation with global efforts, including with efforts following 
on from the Bletchley Declaration92 and the recent final UN Report on Governing AI for 
Humanity.93
• It will be important that Australia develops effective mechanisms for genuine engagement 
with international AI Safety cooperation, including via the growing network of AI Safety 
Institutes. 
Question 2 : How could the principles better capture harms to First Nations people, 
communities and Country?
Question 9 : How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural 
protocols to ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve ICIP? Topic 4: First Nations Australians rights 
and interests
It is critical that Australia take active steps to manage the particular risks, and any particular 
opportunities that arise from use of AI impacting on Australia’s First Nations people. 
Current models are trained on data and embedded with values that tend to be white, Western, 
English-speaking, Global North skewed, and so on. Far from being universal, AI is perhaps 
better understood as ‘artificial Western ethno-intelligence’.94 Such models have the capacity 
to reinforce historical injustice, to amplify labour precarity, and to cement forms of racial and 
gendered inequality. To avoid this bias and its concrete impacts on lives and livelihoods, models 
must be redesigned to include more expansive ways of being and knowing, including those of 
the Indigenous and First Nations peoples in Australia. An alternate set of values and visions 
could be used to both design and evaluate AI models, as nascent research has explored in the 
context of Aotearoa New Zealand.95
While such a project is certainly ambitious and long-term, there are existing frameworks in 
parallel disciplines (e.g. environmental impact) and parallel contexts (First Nations peoples 
in Canada, the United States) that could be used for integrating some of this Indigenous 
perspective. One immediate need relates to the breadth and depth of data around Indigenous 
knowledge, customs, and practices. This issue in some respects replicates that of ‘low-
resource’ languages, where inference, accuracy, and veracity all suffer due to a lack of training 
data. Of course, any generation or collection of such data in Australia should not employ the 
‘scraping’ or harvesting model prevalent in Silicon Valley, but rather work alongside Aboriginal 
and Torres Strait Islanders to collect, curate, and order data in ways that are both ethical and

Assuming that we accept that mandating guardrails is something Australia should do, a key

The Paper canvasses 3 options:

Option 1, 2, or 3?
In summary, our view is that a combined approach is inevitable, but that, in light of rapidly 
changing technology, the fact that regulatory frameworks are already in place in a number 
of important jurisdictions, and the need for Australia to take action sooner rather than later, 
some form of horizontal legislation (identified in the Proposals Paper as Option 3) will be 
required. Horizontal legislation would not necessarily cover the entire economy: the EU AI Act 
for example carves out many areas where domain specific rules continue to apply, especially in 
heavily regulated sectors (transport, finance, energy etc).98
Option 1  is unlikely to achieve the goal of safe and responsible AI, or building public trust, at 
least in the near term. Option 1 poses a number of problems: 
• Time and delays: the time available on the agenda of both government, and Parliament, is 
limited. It is simply unrealistic to think we could, within the kind of timeframes necessary, 
develop specialised legislation across a wide range of areas, undertaking the necessary 
further stakeholder consultation each piece of legislation would require, followed by 
separate Parliamentary consideration and negotiation of passage. 
• Gaps : while some regulators and departments are likely to be active and engaged with 
questions relating to AI, there are others where the issue is likely to fall much lower down 
the priority list. This is not a criticism: in the area of work and employment, other priorities 
such as ensuring people are fairly paid; addressing workplace health and safety; and 
tackling modern slavery are all high priority areas requiring significant attention. Where 
there are other priorities, we would anticipate gaps in addressing AI risks would be 
likely to persist for some time. In other areas there may not be an obvious regulator with 
responsibility and powers to address issues arising in relation to AI.
• GPAI: domain-specific rules, possibly with variations across domains (since that is the 
point that justifies Option 1), is a poor way to address cross-economy issues raised, for 
example, by GPAI. 
• Complexity and regulatory burden: many Australian firms operate across or offer services 
to more than one industry. System developers, for example, would have to be able to 
certify to deployers that they met any Mandatory Guardrails across every sector, which 
will become more challenging, the more variation there is.
 98EU AI Act (n 19) annex I.44
• Incoherence : it would likely lead to incoherence. As Weatherall has noted elsewhere,99 
there is already a lack of coherence developing around AI regulation and governance 
within and across Australian governments. 
The chief argument in favour of Option 1 is that domain expertise, and domain-specific rules are 
required, because AI is used differently in different domains. This argument, however, misses 
the point of the Mandatory Guardrails. What they mandate are not general substantive rules 
regarding what AI can and cannot be used for (which might require domain specificity), but 
processes , which lend themselves to more ready standardisation, even across industries or 
domains. And while, for example, the particular risks or mitigations will vary across (and notably, 
within) sectors, particular risks or mitigations cannot be addressed at the level of legislation, 
which cannot be easily changed. We have argued throughout this submission for high level, 
generalised guardrails with flexibility, supplemented with updates (via disallowable instruments) 
and guidance.
Option 2  is unclear, but so far as we understand it, the Guardrails would exist at a central level, 
but would not apply to any given industry, or in any given context, until some kind of action 
were taken by a responsible regulator or Minister. 
This seems to have many of the problems of Option 1. In particular, we will likely still have 
problems of delay and gaps . Responsible government agencies would need to engage in 
consultation prior to activation, and would be urged not to ‘activate’ Guardrails until detailed 
guidance on the application of the guardrails in the domain context has been developed. 
This risks making the promise to the Australian people, implicit in the passage of legislated, 
Mandated Guardrails an empty one. This would be destructive of already low public trust. 
As noted by Weatherall elsewhere, Option 2 would seem to require coordinated action on the 
part of the Commonwealth government that is not supported by evidence to date.100
If Option 2 is preferred, it would need to:
• establish common terminology, processes and rules for AI systems that can be applied 
across domains;
• include rules to deal with conflicts of competence for situations where more than one 
regulator has jurisdiction; 
• include rules for GPAI, which is inherently domain-crossing.
If all these matters are addressed, we are close to doing the work necessary for Option 3, but 
without gaining the benefits Option 3 provides. This strengthens the case for Option 3.
We also note that an advantage of Option 2 is that it allows for a federal approach, where 
states could also potentially ‘activate’ the guardrails: ie adopt the same guardrails as the 
Commonwealth? Many areas of regulation are state-based (eg property and rental laws are the 
domain of the States and this could be an important area). This is certainly an advantage over 
Option 1, but it may also be constitutionally possible to build mechanisms for state adoption 
model into Option 3. Consumer protection law, for example, operates via a cooperative scheme

where the Commonwealth and States have agreed to legislate the same law, which is a 
schedule to legislation.
Option 3 : This analysis would seem to suggest that some version of Option 3 — horizontal 
legislation that applies Mandatory Guardrails — is the most realistic means of mandating  
Guardrails for the purposes of ensuring safe and responsible AI development and deployment 
in Australia, and to protect Australians as well as equip Australian businesses to engage with 
developing global rules and frameworks. The Mandatory Guardrails applied this way are 
analogous to consumer protection law, or privacy law which applies across public and private 
sectors.
We understand that some may take the view that guardrails need to vary across different parts 
of the economy, or different issues. For example, it might be argued that risk assessment or 
mitigation should look differently for banks, than it might for a university or a company involved 
in cutting-edge medical research. The concern is that ‘whole of economy’ guardrails will lead 
to silly results (guardrails that are simply inapplicable), or won’t capture the unique risks that 
arise in different areas, or will mean that guardrails must be expressed at such a high level of 
generality that they are largely meaningless: little better than the AI Ethics Principles we already 
have. 
We think these concerns are more apparent than real. The Guardrails would require processes 
and governance (testing, transparency, accountability, processes for risk identification and 
mitigation), rather than specific directions how  to test, or how AI should or shouldn’t be used 
(beyond perhaps a small subset of prohibited uses). To the extent that detail is required, it 
should be provided by a mix of disallowable instruments, and guidance, including from domain-
specific regulators.
Importantly, having horizontal legislation does not necessarily mean the Mandatory Guardrails 
will be identical for all sectors. First: there is inherent flexibility within each of the Guardrails. 
Second, the Guardrails could be subject to staged introduction and/or variation between the 
private and public sectors. In particular, it may be advisable at an early stage to establish more 
constraining or detailed rules for public sector uses. Australian governments (Commonwealth, 
state and territory governments) have committed to being exemplars  in the safe and 
responsible use of AI, and to adopting a lawful, ethical approach that places the rights, 
wellbeing and interests of people first.101 This is appropriate.102 Addressing public sector use 
immediately and at a higher standard is consistent with the only existing treaty on AI use to 
date, the Council of Europe’s Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, 
Democracy and the Rule of Law ,103 which imposes stronger obligations in relation to government 
use. And both in Canada and in the US there are already quite strong binding rules for 
government AI use:104 rules that have come in advance of any regulation for the private sector.

Third, we could design option 3 Mandatory Guardrails as a default minimum set : a set which 
can be expanded upon (in terms of additional detail, or additional guardrails) through industry

superseded by more tailored industry-specific detail provides incentives for stakeholders to 
cooperate in designing domain-specific detail, rather than seeking an unattainable perfect 
ruleset. It would be important to ensure that any negotiated alternative to the default does not 
provide less/reduced protection for Australians: this could mean that the responsible entity or 
agency should have both involvement in, and power to refuse approval to, negotiated domain-
specific variations.
We note that Option 3 requires consideration of constitutional issues. In relation to State 
public sectors, all the States and Territories have committed to the National AI Assurance 
Framework ; we would urge all Australian governments to follow up on that commitment, and in 
a coordinated way. AI is not a technology that can or will be constrained by state borders, and 
all Australian stakeholders — especially industry but extending to Australian people and civil 
society — will benefit from avoiding duplication, overlap and gaps which will arise if a national 
approach is not adopted.
Another key issue which will need to be determined in Option 3 is how questions of 
interoperability with the domestic frameworks of other jurisdictions  will be addressed.105
The critical question of institutional structure and the need for 
ongoing, iterative design
A key message at every point in this submission has been that any regulatory framework 
imposing Mandatory Guardrails will need ongoing, iterative development . In the context of 
rapidly changing general purpose technology fuelled by significant investment; unpredictable 
future technologies; and shifting business models and societal attitudes, successful 
government intervention requires:
• Action as soon as possible, to join equivalent countries in offering protection to citizens 
and residents from unsafe, and irresponsible development and adoption of AI. 
• An understanding that Guardrails adopted now will need to be clarified, iteratively as 
circumstances change. Perfection now is not attainable and should not be sought. We will 
need to act, and iterate; designing a regulatory framework is as much if not more, in this 
context, about developing processes as it is about rules;
• Access to appropriately broad and independent technical and socio-technical expertise. 
Addressing issues around safe and responsible AI is a whole-of-government endeavour: it 
would be a problem to isolate all expertise and responsibility in a single entity, and there is 
much good expertise in various parts of the Commonwealth government. The Commonwealth 
government has already moved to appoint accountable officials, who can take on a larger role 
than currently envisaged. 
105 Here we refer to the separate submission on this point by J-M. Bello y Villarino and K. Weatherall.47
But equally, government action, especially at the Commonwealth level at present lacks 
coherence : as Weatherall has explained in some detail elsewhere.106 One reason for this lack 
of coherence could be the absence of any entity within the Commonwealth Government with 
the resources to develop coherent, technically- and socio-technically well-informed and hence 
authoritative positions, and the power, on the basis of those positions to impose stronger 
obligations, and/or the willingness to use that power.107
The imperatives identified above — the need to act; the need to develop processes and powers 
to update and iterate — should drive institutional and regulatory design. This could require an 
AI Body (Commission, Regulator). Such an entity would coordinate with agencies and regulators 
across government, but to be most effective, would need to be the ‘final word’ on safe and 
responsible AI, with authority across government uses of AI.
A key role of such a Body would be the further updating, development, adjustment and 
refinement of aspects of the regulatory framework as set out elsewhere in this submission. 
Broadly we imagine such a Body would play a role in:
• Developing guidance on the systems that are considered high-risk (including in 
consultation with domain-specific regulators);
• Developing an understanding of which GPAI systems should be considered high risk (and, 
if necessary, very high or systemic risk, including updating or developing any technical 
metrics that might be used to identify such systems);
• Adding to or refining any list of prohibited AI systems/uses; or offering pre-licensing/
registration of especially high risk systems if prohibitions are not adopted;
• Developing and refining the content of the Mandatory Guidelines;
• Helping develop, and approving, alternative guidelines for specific domains, in cooperation 
with domain-specific agencies or regulators and industry (secondary role in development; 
final say in approval);
• Helping develop AI aspects of regulatory frameworks for regulated industries where the 
Mandatory Guardrails do not apply (secondary role);
To fulfil these roles, we would suggest that such a body have power to issue disallowable 
instruments: sufficient to keep the rules current but maintaining ultimate authority in the 
Parliament.108
Beyond managing the regulatory framework, an AI body would ideally also have broader roles, 
in connection with broader networks of researchers, industry and civil society:
• Advising and/or determining on questions related to maturity levels as an element of any 
adjustment adopted for small business;
• Identifying emerging risks arising from shifts in technology;
• Scanning (and possibly commissioning) research on the impact of AI on human rights, 
democracy and the rule of law, as well as broader societal and environmental impacts of 
AI, and considering the import of such research for policy; and

how to use AI.
108See generally, Commonwealth Office of Parliamentary Counsel, Instruments Handbook  (2022).48
• Being a source of knowledge, and expertise on AI, its regulation and its impacts (often 
an underrated role, but across complex organisations like government, knowing there is 
someone to turn to for both knowledge, and networks of experts beyond government, 
could be of real assistance to the Public Service, and members of Parliament).
These roles should be separate from (but able to cooperate/work with) the existing National AI 
Centre, which plays an important promotional and facilitative role (enabling the adoption and 
responsible use of AI).
Given these roles, such a Body will need to:
• Have strong technical expertise, and the resources to access to further external technical, 
sociotechnical and legal/regulatory expertise;
• Be supported with appropriately skilled staff;
• Hold a mandate to monitor and require responsible technology design, procurement and 
use across all parts of the Commonwealth government
Such a body may not, in the end, be a permanent fixture within government: increasingly AI 
is likely to be ‘everywhere’. But in the current period of (possible) transition, and for the near 
future, there is a need for a coordinating body.

Response to the ‘Proposals Paper for introducing mandatory

Submission made by the Australian Research Council (ARC) Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child , 
prepared by Professor Tama Leaver (Curtin University) . 
 About The ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child  
 The ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child is shaping an environment with children, families, and communities so they can navigate their own digital worlds. We know that children’s lived experiences are rapidly changing, and that every childhood is  now fundamentally digital. Our mission is to create positive 
digital childhoods for every child in Australia.  
  
The Digital Child is a national research centre comprised of over 200 researchers from across Australia in addition to national and international partners. Our research is focused on:  healthy digital lives , understanding 
how digital technology intersects children’s lived experiences and providing guidance to families, educators, and policymakers as they navigate this space;  educational empowerment , equipping children with the skills 
they need to live their best digital lives; and  safe digital spaces , making online engagement safer while 
promoting healthy digital relationships.  
  
The Digital Child is funded by the Australian Research Council. Our research includes the world -first Australian 
Children of the Digital Age longitudinal study, which is tracking digital engagement of more than 3,000 
Australian families for four years.  
 
Genera l Response  
 We commend the development of the Man datory Guardrails approach , and the resou rcing and speed at which 
this process is happening. For the most part, the p roposed principles and guardrails do ext remely important 
work and will go a long way toward p rotecting Australians using AI tools .  How ever, looking through  the lens 
of Australian children, there is some specific lan guage required to delineate the potentially differentiated 
experience of children  using AI tools. This language  should ensure that any t ranspar ency in how AI tools 
operate should be accessible in a ge-appropr iate language , meaning that if, for example, a n AI tool i s being 
useful commercially or in edu cational settings by 8 or 1 3 year olds, then desc riptions of how it o perates, what 
data it collects, and so forth, should be understandable in terms those child end -users can readily understand 
and base meaningful action on  (such as the action to not use the tools).  
 
Defining high -risk AI   
 
The principles are doing a lot of work to try and flag who is exposed to risk, but does not specifically flag the question of risks to children.  Explicitly flagging risk in age -appropriate ways which notes the different 
experiences of children should be i ncluded in the proposed principles.  It's worth noting that as they stand, 
almost all educational uses in the K -12 sector would seemingly be high -risk. This is probably appropriate.  
2 
 
Submission form the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child. 6 December 2021.   Explicit mention of Indigenous Australians is needed, especially in terms of addressing culturally specific uses 
of data which may impact Indigenous peoples differently given their cultural traditions.  
 We recommend  an additional axis of risk be added: “The risk of adverse impacts on children in terms of age -
appropriate uses and understandings ”. 
 Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of AI  
 Any AI tool operating in Australia that can generate content about Indigenous Peoples should have a specific guardrail preventing the creation on outputs that might compete with intellectual property or outputs by Indigenous Australians.  It's very hard to know in advance. Hence the guardrails should be reviewed annually

 The fact that AI tools pretend to be agentic (ie human -like decision makers) is especially difficult for younger

Clarity Betwe en Deployers and Developers  
 A line is draw between the companies creating AI (developers) and those using AI as a tool (deployers), but there is an aw kward grey area in some of the lan guage . It is not clear, for example, if additional t raining is

Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) (ABN 72 002 692 944) P: (02) 8569 1144  
Phonographic Performance Company of Australia (PPCA) (ABN 43 000 680 704) P: (02) 8569 1100  
Level 4, 11-17 Buckingham Street, Surry Hills, NSW 2010  
PO Box Q20, Queen Victoria Building, NSW 1230  
Page 1 
 
Safe and Responsible AI in Australia - PPCA / ARIA response to the proposals paper 
for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
October 2024  
The Phonographic Performance Company of Australia ( PPCA ) and the Australian Recording Industry 
Association ( ARIA ) (together, we, us, our ) thank the Department of Industry, Science and Resources 
for the opportunity to provide a response to the Proposals Paper for introducing mandatory guardrails 
for AI in high -risk settings ( Mandatory Guardrails Proposals Paper ).  
Executive Summary  
• PPCA and ARIA support the application of mandatory guardrails to regulate artificial intelligence 
systems in high -risk settings and general purpose AI models. However if a principles or list -
based approach is taken in defining ‘high -risk’, further work is needed as the current proposals 
fail to adequately consider detrimental impact generative AI has on copyright and the significant 
risk unregulated AI systems present to a rtists and rightsholders within the music industry.  
• Mandatory guardrails must apply to all general purpose AI models, not just ‘high -risk’, due to 
their enhanced capabilities and unforeseen uses.  
• PPCA and ARIA support the implementation of all proposed mandatory guardrails, particularly 
those which address risk mitigation, data governance, disclosure and transparency.  
• PPCA and ARIA support disclosure requirements (per guardrail 3), however propose that AI 
developers must publicly disclose sufficiently detailed information about the use of copyright -
protected material in training, but also must provide full access to training data for parties with 
legitimate interests (such as where copyright owners are seeking to enforce t heir legitimate 
rights).  
• Labelling requirements for AI -generated content (per guardrail 6) must be amended to apply 
only to wholly -AI generated content (versus where AI systems have been used as just a tool in 
the human -driven creative process). Labelling requirements must also be  mandatory – the use 
of ‘best efforts’ will only erode public confidence and place a burden on consumers to attempt 
to identify wholly -AI works.  
• PPCA and ARIA support the regulation of AI through a standalone AI -specific Act which can 
address gaps in current legislation and ensure a consistent approach to regulation across 
different industries and areas of law. This approach will improve interopera bility with other 
jurisdictions and create a level playing field for Australian businesses.  
Introduction  
PPCA and ARIA embrace the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence ( AI) for the Australian 
music industry, including the opportunities to enhance how artists make music, how platforms organise 
music in playlists and recommendations, how artists connect with fans, and how fans access music. 
We also recognise the potential for AI to enh ance and accelerate many of the tasks behind the scenes 
from production, mixing, mastering, scheduling, planning, administration, understanding consumer 
trends and tackling piracy. However, the ability of generative AI models to ingest, copy and appropriat e 
copyright protected works and subject matter without authorisation from the copyright owner poses a 
very significant risk to Australian artists and creative industries. The creation of certain AI generated 
outputs (including deepfakes and AI -voice clones ) also has a significant potential to spread 
disinformation , distort culture  and adversely impact the broader Australian economy and society.  Page 2 
 It must be recongised that use of music by generative AI is not fundamental to the core business of AI 
platforms. For example, training on music does not enhance the AI assistance with booking travel or 
improving medical research. The use of music is a bus iness adjunct for AI companies (without as yet 
anywhere near fully formed business models) as they seek to monetise the copyright of third parties. It 
is by no means essential or a “need”.  
While music can be ingested by a computer as data, it is not defined to be the method in which it is 
carried. Music is culture and art and must be respected as such. It is not data simply to be blindly or 
intentionally sucked into giant digital hoovers without regard for the creators or copyright.  
Against this background, PPCA and ARIA welcome the introduction of mandatory guardrails in Australia 
to establish a framework for AI developers and deployers across the AI life cycle. We strongly support 
the introduction of Australian AI -specific legislati on to strengthen Australia’s existing legal framework, 
particularly the requirements to implement data governance measures to manage data provenance. 
Given the fast -evolving nature and broad use applications of generative AI, mandatory guardrails should 
apply to any Generative AI model used in Australia (not only those designated high risk). Application of 
mandatory guardrails to all Generative AI models will address risks and harms from AI, build public trust 
and provide businesses with greater regulatory certainty. Appropriate guardrails will ensure that 
Australian AI companies operate on a level playing field with foreign competitors while protecting and 
valuing the Australian creative industries.  
Defining High -risk AI  
1 Do the proposed principles adequately capture high -risk AI? Are there any principles we 
should add or remove? Please identify any:  
 low-risk use cases that are unintentionally captured  
 categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for defence or 
national security purposes.  
The proposed principles adequately capture high -risk AI “use” cases, and we support the Department’s 
proposal to regulate these use cases, particularly in relation to the risk of adverse impacts to the broader 
Australian economy, society, environment and r ule of law. The Mandatory Guardrails  Proposals Paper 
acknowledges the risk of AI -produced content (including content which uses voice cloning technology) 
on disseminating mis - and disinformation and manipulation of mass public opinion, and we strongly 
agree with the need for guardrails to manage this use case.  
 
However, these principles do not address the significant risk that generative -AI (that is, AI models with 
the capability of learning to generate content such as images, text, music and other media with similar 
properties to its training data) poses to crea tive industries in Australia arising from the creation and 
operation of generative -AI platforms, regardless of an intended use.  This is a critical issue that impacts 
the broader Australian economy, society and rule of law as well as impacting individual r ights of creators 
and copyright owners.  For example, under the taxonomy used, a generative AI model that allows a 
user to create “novel” sound recordings is not “high risk”. However, the process through which the 
system was trained (using mass amounts of copyright protected material, often without authorisation) 
should be considered high risk and would have significant adverse impacts on the creative industries, 
artists and copyright owners through degradation of their rights (loss of control over how thei r works are 
used) and loss of renumeration (if licensing is not acquired). To add insult to injury the output of 
generative -AI models (i.e., massive amounts of wholly AI -generated works) produced by unlawfully 
appropriating copyright -protected works and su bject matter also poses an economic and existential risk 
to Australian artists and creative industries by competing with the very content that it unlawfully trained 
on. This is in addition to the fact that, if left unchecked, it can supercharge illegal beh aviours1. The 
consequences to Australian society, the creative economy and the rule of law cannot be overstated; it 
is critical that guardrails be introduced to ensure that existing laws and freedoms, including intellectual 
 
1 See https://www.justice.gov/usao -sdny/pr/north -carolina -musician -charged -music -streamingfraud -aided -artificial -intelligence .  Page 3 
 property rights,  which are human rights are respected and that Australian creative industries are 
incentivised to continue to create and innovate.  
 
The potential adverse impacts of AI, regardless of use, necessitate mandatory guardrails to apply to all 
generative AI models (subject to certain exceptions which are described below).  
 
2 Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First 
Nations people, communities and Country?  
PPCA and ARIA support Government consultation with First Nations people and community groups on 
the likely harms, including the harm caused by the appropriation of Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual 
Property (ICIP). We acknowledge that ICIP is vulnerable  to exploitation. Mandatory guardrails, including 
robust record -keeping rules, will be beneficial to all rightsholders, including First Nations people and 
communities. Guardrails must also address the potential harm of artificial intelligence on First Nati ons 
knowledge and cultural expressions, including for example the harm caused by fake AI -generated 
Indigenous art or vocal clones of First Nations voices and artists.  
3 Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on 
high -risk AI settings and high -risk AI models? If you prefer a list -based approach (similar 
to the EU and Canada), what use cases should we include? How can this list c apture 
emerging uses of AI? If you prefer a principles -based approach, what should we address 
in guidance to give the greatest clarity?  
For the reasons set out above and described in more detail below, PPCA and ARIA consider that all 
generative -AI systems that are available in Australia should be subject to the proposed mandatory 
guardrails . This approach would be aligned with the EU approach in that ,, under the EU Artificial 
Intelligence Act (EU AI Act ), all General Purpose AI models – not only high -risk models  – are subject to 
basic obligations, including an obligation  to keep records of and disclose material used to train a model 
to enable right holders to exercise and enforce their rights, as well as  an obligation to implement 
copyright policies to ensure compliance with existing copyright law. However, if the Department intends 
to adopt a regulatory model based on high -risk cases, it should include consideration of the risks to 
creative industries in either a list or principles -based approach .  
 
(a) List-based approach : We submit that a list -based approach must include consideration of the risk 
to the creative industries, which is not explicitly referred to in the EU AI Act  and Canadian Artificial 
Intelligence and Data Act ( AIDA ).  
(b) Principles -based approach : Similarly, if a principles -based approach is taken, clarity must be 
provided by the Department that risks of adverse impacts on legal and economic rights refers to, 
amongst other matters, copyright law.  
4 Are there high -risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory 
response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)? If so, how should we 
define these?  
We agree that the Government should consider banning high risk use cases that present an 
unacceptable level of risk. The unauthorised production  of ‘vocal clones’  and ‘deepfakes’ using 
generative AI models poses an unacceptable significant risk to both Australian society (through the 
dissemination of mis - and disinformation) and artists (through the erosion of the rights and degradation 
of their reputations). We re commend that the Department enact a regulatory ban on unauthorised uses 
of a person’s voice, image, or likeness, including to create ‘vocal clones, or ‘deepfakes’ .  
We also support the introduction of a ban on manipulative AI, social scoring, and criminal profiling, 
which are ‘Prohibited AI Practices’ under Article 5 of the EU AI Act.  Page 4 
 5 Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new emerging forms of high -risk 
AI, such as general -purpose AI (GPAI)?  
The proposed principles are not flexible enough to capture new emerging forms of high -risk AI, such as 
general -purpose AI ( GPAI ). The fast -evolving nature of GPAI means that it has the capacity to be used 
for unforeseen uses, and that an approach based on “uses” currently known or foreseen, will prevent 
the consistent application of these mandatory guardrails. For the reasons set out above and described 
in more detail below, PPCA and ARIA consider that all generative AI that is available in Australia should 
be subject to the proposed mandatory guardrails.  
6 Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?  
We strongly support the introduction of mandatory guardrails to all GPAI models.  GPAI models pose a 
particular risk due to their versatility and unintended uses and consequences , especially considering  
the ability of GPAI models to generate highly sophisticated images and sounds, and content that can 
substitute demand for the original works they were unlawfully trained with.  This highlights a need for 
strict data governance and recordkeeping requirements , irrespective of the use or purpose of the model.  
However, even  generative -AI models that are intended to perform a limited purpose, such as the 
creation of sound recordings, have a capacity to produce misleading or deceptive content, or content 
that unfairly competes  with the content they were trained on, with the same or even more harmful 
impacts as a GPAI model , since they are specialised tools.  Given the rapidly evolving AI landscape, it 
is necessary to apply these mandatory guardrails consistently across the industry. We recommend that 
the mandatory guardrails apply not just to GPAI models, but to all Generative AI models, using the 
definition adopted in the Mandatory Guardrails Proposals Paper.  
Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of AI  
 
7 What are suitable indicators for defining GPAI models as high -risk? For example, is it 
enough to define GPAI as high -risk against the principles, or should it be based on 
technical capability such as FLOPs, advice from a scientific panel, government or other 
indicators?  
As set out above, given the high volume of data required, capacity of unintended use and consequences 
and unpredictability of Generative AI models, all Generative AI made available in Australia should be 
subject to mandatory guardrails. This step will ensure consistency across the broad spectrum of 
Generative AI models operating in Australia and prevent a lacuna in the regulation for narrow purpose 
AI which presents similar risks to GPAI.  
8 Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high -
risk settings? Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?  
Mandatory guardrails are an important step to (1) ensure that existing fundamental rights and laws are 
being respected and adhered to, and (2) give downstream businesses and users the means to know if 
Generative AI models have been created and trained lawf ully.  
To be effective in mitigating the risks of AI, these guardrails should be applied to all generative AI 
models put on the market in Australia regardless of the jurisdiction in which the generative AI model 
was created and trained or stored. These guardrails  should also extend to the beginning of the training 
of the Generative AI model to provide a full chain of use and ensure the guardrails are effective in 
practice. This would ensure accountability in instances where Generative AI providers try to avoid 
liability by forum shopping, e.g., by training AI applications in a jurisdiction in which it may be difficult to 
enforce rights. The viability of this approach has been demonstrated in the EU AI Act, which sets out 
the need for GPAI models placed on the marke t in the EU to comply with EU laws, including copyright 
laws, regardless of where they acquired data or trained and developed the models. In Australia, an 
approach could be adopted similar to that in the Australian Consumer Law , which applies to anyone 
who “carries on a business” in Australia (regardless of where that business is located).    Page 5 
 PPCA and ARIA support the proposed mandatory guardrails, and in particular strongly support the 
introduction of mandatory guardrails in relation to risk mitigation, data governance, disclosure, and 
transparency (guardrails 2, 3, 6, 9 and 10). The specific proposals in relation to guardrails 3 and 6, 
which are most relevant to the music industry, are addressed in more detail below. However, we note 
that in respect of Guardrail 9, records of training data need to be maintained to ensure Guardrail 3 is 
complie d with (which includes data quality, ensuring data has been legally obtained).  
Guardrail 3: Protect AI systems and implement data governance measures to manage data quality and 
provenance.  
Infringing AI models are “trained” on copyright works including text, image, audio and video . without 
authorisation.  At present we understand there is no statutory requirement  in Australia for deployers and 
developers to disclose the data source used to “train” models .  In order to try and avoid liability for their 
infringing actions Many  operators of Generative AI models do not voluntarily provide sufficient 
information on the data used in this process. This gives rise to significant issues across the AI lifecycle. 
In the copyright context, transparency around use of copyright protected m aterial is critical to ensure 
that right holders can effectively enforce or license their rights. Without it, rights holders have no means 
to ensure  AI developers have lawfully accessed their content for use in training ,  including  obtaining 
appropriate licences and permissions from right holders.  
PPCA and ARIA strongly support the introduction of a new statutory obligation for AI developers to 
disclose their data sources with sufficient detail to enable rightsholders to enforce their rights . We submit 
that AI developers and deployers should be required to:  
(a) make publicly available sufficiently detailed information of the use of training data and other 
material or content protected under copyright law to enable parties with legitimate interests, such 
as copyright holders, to make a prima facie  determination if and how their rights have been 
engaged and, subsequently, to take appropriate action if necessary ; and  
(b) upon request by parties with legitimate interests, including rights holders seeking to enforce 
and/or license their rights, provide access to full records of training data for which the party has 
a legitimate interest, including works or other protected su bject matter.  
This two -tier approach would ensure that parties with legitimate interests may enforce and/or license 
their rights while protecting AI developers and deployers from frivolous requests from parties with no 
legitimate interests or competitors seeking to impr operly obtain commercially valuable  information  
In relation to the first tier (a publicly available sufficiently detailed summary), detailed model cards for 
the express purpose of boosting transparency including in relation to training data, could  provide an 
existing basis for this summary – if sufficiently detailed. Data records could be kept in a delimited text 
file, database, or a machine learning data management or monitoring system.  
However, it would also be essential that the mandatory guardrails include a second tier  that includes a 
requirement to hold full records of training data which is disclosable to those with legitimate interests, 
such as copyright holders . This will enable a rights holder to establish if an element in the training is a 
recording or a work for which they control the copyright. For example, in recorded music, at the 
minimum, the name of the recording artist and track title information would be needed, ideally along 
with standard identifiers  such as the ISRC where available . For lyrics, a work title and information about 
the artist (performing or songwriting) would be needed. This level of detail is entirely feasible . Automatic  
content recognition technologies (e.g. Audible Magic) already enable this level of identification within 
even very large datasets  and some generative AI providers  already implement these type of services , 
e.g. see the Stable Audio  and Stable Audio Open .   
 
PPCA and ARIA also welcome the proposal to include a requirement that  training  “data must be legally 
obtained”. The Mandatory Guardrails Proposals Paper notes that the guardrail is intended to 
complement existing requirements under other legislation, including the Copyright Act 1968  (Cth) 
(Copyright Act ). Consistent with the approach taken in the EU AI Act, the mandatory guardrails should 
explicitly require  GPAI model providers to implement policies to comply with Australian copyright law to Page 6 
 ensure a level playing field  where model developers cannot simply go elsewhere to develop a model 
but then bring it to Australia and avoid complying with Australian rules . This will enhance the 
effectiveness of existing protections under the Copyright Act. It will be important for responsible 
deployers and users of Generative AI systems who want to know that the AI tools they are using are 
safe, ethical, and do not give ri se to risk for them, including by infringing third -party content.  Off-the -
shelf technologies (e.g. Audible Magic) already exist that enable businesses, including SMEs and start -
ups, to ensure that the content used for training does not include sound recordings protected by 
copyright. Such technology has been long implemented in the streaming ecosystem by large and small 
players, and has more recently been adopted by AI developers, e.g. Stability AI to ensure its Stable 
Audio Open model did not include material to which Stability AI did not have the rights. The cost of this 
is low , particularly as compared to other model development and training costs.  
Guardrail 6: Inform end -users regarding AI -enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI -generated 
content.  
We support the introduction of a requirement to inform end -users on how AI is being used and where it 
affects them, in a clear, accessible, and relevant manner. Internationally, the music industry has seen 
a proliferation of deepfake AI “voice cloning” mod els that are capable of generating  synthetic content 
that mimics an artist’s voice, image, and likeness without authorisation. Unauthori sed deepfakes is a 
gross appropriation of an individual's personal data and identity, and can mislead fans and cause 
potentially serious harm to an artist’s and record label’s reputation. It also distorts competition by 
allowing those generating the clones to unfairly compete with artists whose music and likeness has 
been used to train the AI m odel, unfairly leveraging the goodwill the artist has built with their fans, as 
well as the significant label investment which has been made in that artist’s career. The introduction of 
a labelling requirement for solely AI generated content will provide i mportant protection for creative 
artists as well as consumers. Requirements to identify the content as AI -generated in a clear, 
conspicuous, appropriate, and permanent manner are being introduced in several jurisdictions, 
including the EU AI Act.  
In order for Guardrail 6 to be effective, we propose the following two amendments:  
(a) Only solely AI -generated material should be subject to labelling requirements to inform 
consumers and enable them to differentiate between solely AI -generated content and human 
generated works. We acknowledge that many creative industries, including the mu sic industry, 
may use AI as a tool in the creative process, and do not consider that content where AI is a mere 
tool in a human creator’s process rather than generating the output should be subject to these 
requirements.  
(b) The labelling requirement should be mandatory. The proposal that organisations are required to 
apply “best efforts” to ensure AI generated output, including synthetic text, image, audio or video 
content, can be detected as artificially generated or manipul ated will not adequately protect artists 
or consumers from the risks associated with AI generated output. A “best efforts” labelling 
standard will erode consumer confidence in the labelling as not all AI -generated content will be 
labelled. Moreover, if the  requirement is only to ensure AI -generated content “can be detected”, 
that will potentially put all of the burden on consumers to use an AI detection tool or similar to 
establish whether content has been solely generated by AI. In practice consumers will not spend 
their time doing so and will not be effectively protected. Instead, companies developing or 
distributing content solely generated by AI should be under a clear obligation to label content as 
AI-generated in a manner that will come to the attentio n of a reasonable consumer, before they 
engage with that content. The Department must take into consideration the role of distributors of 
solely -AI generated material (who may not necessarily fall into the developer/deployer category) 
and the adverse impac t they have in disseminated content. To ensure consumers are protected, 
it may be necessary to extent labelling obligations to entities to distribute such content.  
9 How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols to  
ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve ICIP?  
Refer to question 2 above.  Page 7 
 10 Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain 
and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately? For example, are the requirements 
assigned to developers and deployers appropriate?   
To be effective, responsibility for data governance and transparency must be distributed across the AI 
supply chain. AI is often developed between multiple actors including entities that compile datasets; 
entities that develop and pre -train foundation mode ls; entities that fine -tune models; entities that  
develop or train generative models, entities that deploy these models by making them available to end 
users and entities which host or make available the outputs from AI models. Many types of AI models 
are licensed or open sourced for use by others. Entities involved in these various processes may be 
located in different jurisdictions. This complex ecosystem gives rise to unique challenges in the 
application of the mandatory guardrails.  
We acknowledge the recognition by the Department of the need to apportion accountability across the 
AI supply chain and support the Department’s proposal to apply guardrails to both AI developers and 
deployers. In order to distribute responsibility and ens ure that AI developers and deployers are able to 
comply with the mandatory guardrails, we propose that:  
(a) The data governance measures in guardrail 3 should apply throughout the entirety of the AI life 
cycle (including to the compilers of datasets used by the model) and continue to apply to 
downstream entities that provide a foundation model to provide a full chain of use and ensure 
that the obligation cannot be easily circumvented. It should also be clarified that distribution of 
responsibility for guardrail 3 and 8 needs to be extended to bodies that create training datasets, 
including research or educational  institutions and open -source generative AI systems, which may 
later be used for commercial and infringing purposes.  
(b) The mandatory guardrails apply to all Generative AI systems that are made available in Australia, 
or that generate output used in Australia, regardless of the nature of the jurisdiction in which the 
development may have taken place, in order to ensure that  there is a level playing field.  
These measures will ensure that developers and deployers are effectively able to comply with the 
guardrails and give downstream businesses and the wider public the means to know the models that 
they are using have been trained using lawfully obtained data.  
11 Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI? How could 
we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for example low -risk and high -risk GPAI 
models?  
Refer to question 6 above.  
12 Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small -to-medium sized 
businesses applying guardrails?  
The introduction of mandatory guardrails throughout the AI -lifecycle (as proposed in question 10 above) 
will reduce administrative burden for small -to-medium sized businesses, as these businesses will have 
the confidence that Generative -AI models and the d atasets they are trained on comply with the 
mandatory guardrails. The level of risk presented by an AI model does not depend on the size of the 
developer. A small entity can produce a system that presents an unacceptable public risk. The 
guidelines should be outcome -focused and tailored to address the level of risk of th e system, not on the 
characteristics of the developer.   
In relation to the data governance measures in proposed guardrail 3, entities conducting development 
and deployment of Generative AI systems operate extremely sophisticated processes. Many large  and 
small developers and deployers of Generative AI systems are already keeping records of the training 
sets used . Industry developments and academic research already provide tools, establish best 
practices, and demonstrate practical benefits from careful monitoring and curation of training data. Page 8 
 Examples of these tools include Whylabs2, Nucleus3, SuperAnnotate4, Apache Airflow5 and Splunk6. 
Accordingly, it is entirely feasible for small -to-medium sized AI developers and deployers that train on 
the content and data of others to generate, keep and disclose records of such data.  
For music, ACR (Automatic Content Recognition) technology is already available and used by AI 
developers to identify recordings and ensure protected content is not used (without authorisation) by 
their systems (see for example Audible Magic7). The cost of using ACR technology is relatively low and 
insignificant when compared to the other research, development and training costs already undertaken 
by AI developers.  
Regulatory options to mandate guardrails  
13 Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high -risk settings? 
What opportunities should the government take into account in considering each 
approach?  
We support the introduction of a new AI -specific Act to implement the proposed mandatory guardrails 
for AI (Option 3). This option allows the Government the opportunity to develop a clear and centralised 
framework for regulating artificial intelligence, co nsistent with the approaches taken in the EU and 
Canada. The approach would provide consistent regulation to AI developers and deployers, reducing 
the administrative burden which would be required from adhering to a variety of industry -specific 
standards a nd regulations (under options 1 and 2). It would also allow for consistent regulation and 
enforcement across the entirety of the AI -life cycle (including through the establishment of a single 
regulator responsible for enforcing the guardrails).  Finally, i t provides flexibility to enact AI -specific 
legislation, tailored to address the unique challenges of artificial intelligence in Australia (which are not 
adequately addressed in existing legislation).  
Conversely, Option 1 (adapting existing frameworks) and Option 2 (adapting existing regulatory 
frameworks through framework legislation) will require the amendments to multiple pieces of legislation. 
This process will be time consuming and has the signific ant potential to lead to gaps across industries 
where the Mandatory Guardrails are not consistently applied. The enforcement of the Mandatory 
Guardrails by different agencies, across different sectors, pursuant to different legislation will inevitably 
lead to inconsistent application of the Mandatory Guardrails.   
14 Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the Australian 
Government should consider?  
While the approach taken to regulating AI may be inline or comparable to certain jurisdictions (such as 
the EU and Canada), the Mandatory Guardrails must apply to generative AI systems that are made 
available in Australia, or that generate output used in A ustralia, regardless of the nature of the 
jurisdiction in which the development may have taken place. This will ensure that developers and 
deployers offering a generative -AI product in Australia cannot circumvent these important safeguards. 
This problem co uld be resolved in an AI -specific Act, which could apply to all generative AI modes 
placed on the market in Australia (consistent with the approach adopted in the EU AI Act) which will 
assist with creating a level playing field model  
 
15 Which regulatory option/s will best ensure that guardrails for high -risk AI can adapt and 
respond to step -changes in technology?  
The enactment of an AI -specific Act will provide the greatest flexibility to adapt and respond to step 
changes in technology. An AI -specific Act can be tailored to the unique challenges of artificial 
intelligence, which may not be adequately captured by ex isting regulatory regimes. If changes are 
required to address developments in AI, it will be simpler and more effective to amend an AI -specific 
 
2 See whylabs.ai/about.  
3 See scale.com/nucleus.  
4 See www.superannotate.com/data -curation .  
5 See airflow.apache.org/.  
6 See www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/learn/data -observability.html .  
7 See https://www.audiblemagic.com/ .  Page 9 
 Act rather having to make amendments across multiple pieces of legislation, each of which would 
require review and debate.  
 
16 Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps or inconsistencies with Australia’s existing 
laws for the development and deployment of AI? Which regulatory option best addresses 
this, and why?  
As the Mandatory Guardrails Proposals Paper notes there are very few regulations targeting the 
upstream development and deployment of AI technologies in Australia. The unique challenges faced 
by the rapid creation and commercialisation of generative AI in Australia in relation to both input and 
output are not adequately addressed in existing legislation. For example:  
 
(a) In relation to input : the lack of transparency in terms of how generative AI models operate, the 
data specific models use and how that data is obtained is a significant gap in Australia’s existing 
laws. There is no requirement in the Copyright Act requiring the data sources t o be disclosed, 
and/ or requiring models to necessarily even retain records.  
(b) In relation to the output : Australian Consumer Law prohibits misleading and deceptive conduct; 
it does not necessarily require indication to be given as to when a work is the sole product of a 
wholly generative AI process. A labelling or disclosure guardrail across all GPAIs would  assist in 
preventing any deception or confusion among consumers.  
For the reasons set out in questions 13 – 15 above, an AI -specific Act is the best regulatory option to 
address these issues.
