Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback  on this Proposals Paper .  
It is indeed important to recognise  that AI use is growing and will continue grow , and as AI 
use grows  in turn this will enable  businesses to grow.1 However, t his growth needs to be 
carefully monitored to ensure appropriate conduct by business ; and the protection of 
individuals , businesses , and society as a whole .2 A key consideration is whether existing  law, 
legislation and common law, can be adequately applied  to AI , or whether specific laws are 
needed . As with previous  technological issue s and  technolog ies3 the law , when compared 
with both current and future technologies, is and will be in a constant state of  playing ‘catch 
up’.4  
Importantly, whatever  measure  is adopted needs to be easily understood and consistently 
applied.  Equally important is the need for ongoing governance  oversight by the businesses 
that use AI , as well as those who create and deploy AI . Similarly to the harm it is designed to 
guard against, a guardrail itself could fail in that the party responsible may be without the 
necessary means to compensate those who have suffered harm  if there is a breach . It is 
important t herefore that there are in place appropriate provisions to enable any individual or 
business adversely impacted to recover  for any harm  they have suffered.  And for those 
obligations  to be easily  understood by all stakeholders.  
 
Concerns  
This submission supports a ‘whole  of economy approach ’ regulatory approach , however, 
such an approach will take time to implement . In the interim, it is incumbent  upon Parliament 
to implement measures  now to ensure that : all those involved in business decision -making  
take those decisions seriously and ensure they are appropriately informed before making any 
decision to adopt  or use  any AI system; and to ensure there is appropriate recourse for those 
who suffer harm  when there is a breach .  
While a company is a separate legal entity, it is important to remember it relies on its directors 
and other officers to function. Therefore,  liability for a business ’ AI adoption and use  should 
rest with those who control it , and those persons should have a positive obligation to ensure 
they make full  informed  decisions and should not be able to escape liability as accessories 
where , through their own inactions,  they have no direct knowledge  of relevant information .5  
This submission presents suggestions for changes to existing laws to reinforce that ultimate 
responsibility for  business  decision -making  rests with those controlling that business.  
Specifically, that those who are the controlling minds of a business should  be held perso nally 
accountable  for losses from conduct caused by  its AI use.

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
Please note that for all answers in this submission, due to the tight timeframe for consultation we were not able to properly consult with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander experts in our sector and our responses to this submission, especially regarding ICIP and data sovereignty have not been endorsed. We strongly recommend that the Department speak with experts in data sovereignty and ICIP from the library and archive sector, which have both deep experience in related areas and hold some of the most significant collections containing ICIP, Indigenous data and traditional knowledge in Australia.
With that said, ALIA strongly recommends that explicit reference to ICIP, traditional knowledge and Indigenous data are included in the principles. This principle should make it clear that the use of ICIP, traditional knowledge and Indigenous data are in and of themselves high risk uses, not dependent on the intended use of these materials. The addition of this principle needs to be in conjunction with a strengthening of guardrails to specifically address the safeguards needed when dealing with these materials.
Are there any principles we should add or remove?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
A specific principle regarding any use of Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP), traditional knowledge or Indigenous data.
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
When First Nations people are not able to exercise ownership and control over their ICIP, traditional knowledge and Indigenous data then this in and of itself can cause harm. Libraries, as custodians of significant collections containing these materials are very well aware that often legal rights and cultural rights are held by different people, and also that much of the content may not even be mislabelled (often with racist terminology) and therefore not easily identifiable as containing ICIP, traditional knowledge or Indigenous data. The library sector has a number of key protocols and guidelines to try to deal with materials in a respectful and appropriate way, in consultation with communities, and acknowledges there is still much work to be done to ensure Indigenous sovereignty in collections.
The principles should make it clear that the use of these materials in and of itself can cause harm, and then the guidelines should be strengthened to ensure that any use of ICIP, traditional knowledge and Indigenous data are done appropriately as befits the communities, materials and uses. This doesn’t mean that these materials can never be used, and there are several good examples of projects utilising AI in a respectful ways, for example in language revival, however there needs to be an onus on developers and deployers to treat ICIP, traditional knowledge and Indigenous data appropriately.
See for example the library sector guidelines the ATSILIRN protocols https://atsilirn.aiatsis.gov.au/protocols.php

Guardrail 1 should specifically require accountability processes and policies to include ICIP, traditional knowledge and Indigenous data with appropriate policies and processes, and these must be implemented.
Guardrail 3 could be strengthened by specifically requiring ICIP, traditional knowledge and Indigenous data to be proactively identified (as opposed to consideration of the principles of Indigenous Data Sovereignty and ICIP) and dealt with appropriately, which may include the possibility that data is not able to be ingested.

An undue stress on legal rights without recognition of other rights, such as ICIP, has the potential to override First Nations interests in material, for example if a publisher makes bulk deals with AI companies. Dear Department of Industry, Science and Resources. I wish to express my deep concern over the catastrophic risks posed by General Purpose Artificial Intelligence (GPAI). As a concerned individual, I am eager to share my thoughts on the Australian Government's proposed risk-based approach to regulating high-risk AI.
4. Are there high-risk use cases that Government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Absolutely. Yes, the government should consider banning certain high-risk use cases of AI systems. Specifically, AI systems that technical evaluations demonstrate could cause "critical harm", or where "systemic risks" are deemed unacceptable, should be prohibited.
There are already some appropriate definitions of these in other pieces of legislation or statements.
The California SB1047 bill aimed at avoiding "critical harm", defined it as mass casualties, at least USD 500 million in damage, or other comparable threats to public safety. The EU AI Act, in Recital 110, outlines systemic risks from general-purpose AI, including those that can lead to widespread or catastrophic harm. These include dangerous capabilities such as weapons development, persuasion & deception, and self-replication.
The International Dialogues on AI Safety Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence (https://idais.ai/idais-beijing/) also advocates for international coordination to enforce certain "red lines" on AI capability, like those in SB1047 and the EU AI Act. I believe AI systems that cross these red lines should be banned, except for being used for the purpose of improving future AI safety, and in those cases, must be done carefully.
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
Not necessarily. Australia should indeed impose significant obligations on GPAI with systemic risk as this will contribute to global safety standards and encourage AI developers to internalise these risks. However, GPAI that we can confidently deem safe is less critical to regulate.
The risks presented by future highly capable models differ from those posed by narrow AI in high-risk applications. Guardrails that proportionately match the risks of the AI system can strike a balance between safety and innovation.
The RAND report “General-Purpose Artificial Intelligence (GPAI) Models and GPAI Models with Systemic Risk” suggests that harmonising reporting and evaluation standards across the USA, UK, and the EU could help mitigate the unique risks posed by future models. Australia could contribute to this global standard by adopting this approach.
Mandatory guardrails on GPAI with systemic risks could draw inspiration from SB1047, incorporating AI evaluation standards, tracking risk management practices and incident mitigations.
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI?
In my opinion, the proposed guardrails are inadequate in addressing the risks posed by the development of advanced AI models. Australia needs to create a specific definition to identify AI models that might exhibit dangerous behaviours capable of causing widespread or catastrophic harm, as mentioned above.
Once these models are defined, tailored guardrails must be put in place to mitigate their risks during development. For example, under SB1047, developers of highly capable models were required to have shutdown capabilities should these risks become possible.
In conclusion, while I appreciate the Australian Government's proactive approach to regulating high-risk AI, I believe the proposed guardrails require further refinement to effectively address the potential risks of GPAI.

The Australian National University  2 Introduction  
The Australian National University (ANU) School of Cybernetics was established in January of 
2021 by Distinguished Professor Genevieve Bell AO FTSE FAHA with the aim of empowering us 
all to navigate major societal transformations. Here in Australia, and gl obally, we are facing 
many challenges from growing wealth inequality to climate change, diminished trust in social 
institutions and the role of new and emergent technologies in our daily lives, economies, and 
democracies, just to name a few.  
Whilst our school is comparatively new, it builds on the pioneering work of the Autonomy, 
Agency and Assurance Institute (3Ai) founded at the ANU in 2017. 3Ai was established to help 
scale AI safely, sustainabl y and responsibly; and its focus on cyber -physical systems inform s 
our current approach.  
To support the Government’s proposal to implement mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk 
settings, we offer some insights from our experiences developing research and education. Our 
definition of AI is taken from the 2019 Australian Council of Learned Ac ademics (ACOLA) Report 
on The Effective and Ethical Development of AI1:  
Artificial intelligence can be understood as a collection of interrelated  
technologies used to solve problems that would otherwise require human 
cognition. Artificial intelligence encompasses a number of methods, including 
machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP), speech recognition, computer vision and automate d reasoning.
 
In our submission, we focus on the following  key areas of opportunity to support how the 
guardrails for high -risk AI may be shaped. These include:  
• Taking a systems view of AI to identify and govern risk;  
• Accounting for cumulative and cascading impacts of existing and new AI systems;  
• Focusing on harms to the environment and society in the AI guardrails; and  
• Bringing a First Nations perspective  to the AI guardrails, which we propose needs to 
become part of a broader program of intentional engagement with Indigenous leaders 
and technologists.2

A systems approach to informing AI governance  
At the ANU School of Cybernetics we have come to realise that we need to lift our focus from 
specific and individual technologies to the systems of which they are always and already a part. 
From this vantage  point , technology components do not exist in isolation, but always in relation 
to other technology, social and ecological systems.  
We believe that cybernetics –  an approach to complex dynamic systems that celebrates the 
relationships between the human, the technical and ecological, as well as the individual 
component pieces –  is our best way to unpack and navigate the complexity of sy stems.  
When we consider AI, therefore, we are interested in AI systems as a collection of components, and the interactions of these components with each other , and with broader systems of people 
and the environment, which are dynamic, contingent and constantly in flux.  
One of the ways that we unpack this complexity within the School is through the ‘technology 
stack’ (see Figure 1). The four layers of the stack help unpack the ways in which components of 
AI assemble and interact, and each of these layers become an entry -point to unfurl the many 
agents, supply chains, markets, rules and regulations, and environments that an AI system is shaped by or is a part of.

The technology stack helps to convey that AI is not a singular thing –  it is a complex, dynamic 
system that relies on a collection of technologies, requiring data, human labour, cultural 
perspectives, physical resources from the environment, and a collecti on of processes, 
regulations, and rules.  Seeing AI as an interdependent system also reveals the many legacy 
sites of influence and intervention from past rules and regulations.  
In turning our attention to AI governance, we are interested in these multiple interacting 
systems that shape the component parts of AI, alongside the systems that develop, produce, 
deploy, and decommission AI -powered products, tools, and services. From th is perspective, a 
risk- based approach to AI governance sees the adverse outcomes of AI as a product of these 
systems interacting over time. Thus, r egulating this level of complexity will require an adaptive, 
iterative regulatory framework that imagines and  can respond to multiple possible future 
scenarios.  
Accounting for cumulative & cascading impacts  
Paying attention to the systemic impacts posed by AI will mean focussing on the ways that risks can compound and cascade beyond any single component, application, use case or context. This 
is particularly relevant to the burgeoning ubiquity of General Purp ose AI.  
Given that Machine Learning (ML) components can now be easily “swapped in” or “assembled” 
into new workflows that drive AI products, tools, or services, there are multiple opportunities for 
risks to accumulate and compound across end-to -end workflows. If we take voice assistants as 
one example, typical voice assistants use multiple ML components, including: (1) a  wake word 
engine that is used to listen for a wake word (like ‘Hello’) to activate the device; (2) a  speech 
recognition engine used to transcribe the user’s spoken command into text once activated; (3) 
natural language processing algorithms to identify the user’s intended command; and (4) a  
synthetic speech engine to provide voice confirmation back to the user.

Moreover, a risk -based approach should acknowledge that impacts from AI  systems frequently 
cascade beyond the end user of an AI -powered tool, service, or product. For example, when AI 
workflows do not operate as expected, such as in the cases of  automated decision -making in  
government and large -scale corporates , fallouts tend to impact families and broader social 
groups connected to the end use r. In these cases, the impacts can expose  vulnerable 
populations to further vulnerabilities.7 Taking a systems -view of AI risks needs to acknowledge 
that impacts can extend beyond end -users to larger social groups.  
Highlighting Environmental Harms  
Environmental harms –  including excess water use, land degradation, and emissions – are 
another key area of systemic risk, and should be highlighted among definitions of high-risk AI. 
As AI models become larger, energy, water, and resource costs grow with t hem. This is 
highlighted by the large, physical footprints of data centres that are used to train and support AI systems. When infrastructures such as data centres are in areas already competing for 
resourcing (such as land, water, housing) this can create  system -scale risks, and exacerbate 
injustices for local and global communities, especially in the contexts of environmental 
damage.

The Australian National University  7 dualistic approach will not suffice in bringing a First Nations perspective to guard  against the 
adverse impacts of  AI. We need to include Indigenous people's perspectives in every stage from 
designing and developing AI, to deploying and decommissioning AI systems. To guard against 
high -risk AI for Indigenous Australians, we must bring First Nations perspectives to the 
architecture of AI systems, consider data as a derivative of embodied knowledges, and develop 
cultural protocols which govern the intention,  affect and effect of AI systems . 11 
This needs to start with genuine and considered consultation with First Nations leaders and 
technologists. Consultation with these two First Nations cohorts is essential to ensure that subject matter expertise can define how AI systems should be considered within the diverse 
and complex social, cultural, and geographica l affordances pertaining to First Nations peoples. 
These invaluable insights can then be embedded across all guardrails
12.  
To enable and support genuine consultation with First Nations perspectives and bring these 
perspectives into the guardrails, we recommend the following:  
Country must be centred in the guardrails.  This is not currently the case. Country includes land , 
water and sky combined. Centring Country acknowledges that each of these elements  and 
society are inextricably linked and should not be considered as separate issues, unlike for 
example: “ The risk of adverse impacts to the broader Australian economy, society, environment 
and rule of law."  Additionally, Country should be referenced alongside groups of individuals and 
collective rights of groups of individuals i n the following guardrail: “The risk of adverse impacts 
to groups of individuals or collective rights of cultural groups," to highlight the ways in which environmental damage is inextricably linked to harms to First Nations peoples.  
The guardrails should reference and align to existing reforms, such as the National Agreement 
on Closing the Gap. The fourth agenda of the National Agreement on Closing the Gap reform 
relates to Shared Access to Data and Information at a Regional Level13, which is highly relevant 
to ensuring appropriate protections for First Nations people during the development and use of AI systems. The Australian Government has a responsibility to enact the Close the Gap targets,

entire AI system that it has influence and or interconnect to;  
• Ensure associated cultural18, social and environmental rights are protected along each 
stage of the AI lifecycle;  
• Ensure there is an equitable return on investments for Indigenous peoples and their 
cultural knowledges that are commensurate to the gains associated with 3rd party 
business models; and  
• Incorporate contractual arrangements to distribute revenue generated by the AI system 
to collectives and communities for ICIP, and other intangible cultural knowledges19. 
Any principles developed to incorporate First Nations perspectives should evidence that 
consultation has occurred, and consultation should extend beyond initial input to include 
regular reviews of AI risk profiles, and the guardrails themselves.20  
Lessons Learnt

Australia and beyond21. We have been using cybernetics –  with its strong focus on both the 
components of a system (the human, technical and ecological) and the dynamic relationships 
between them (connections and feedback) –  to orient us towards better decision -making in 
complex  AI-systems.

Re: Response to Proposals  Paper – Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-Risk Settings  
Amstelveen welcomes the opportunity to provide feedback on the proposed  Mandatory Guardrails for 
AI in High -risk Settings . 
Amstelveen is a specialist risk and compliance consultancy which operates across Australia and New 
Zealand. Our clients include public and private sector organisations at the forefront of AI deployment 
and which generally have a high degree of exposure to technology  and data -related  risks, such as those 
in financial services, government, telecommunications  and energy . 
In this submission, we have responded to a subset of the questions listed in the proposals paper titled 
“Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings” . 
1.  Do the proposed principles adequately capture high -risk AI? Are there any principles we should  
add or remove? Please identify any:  
• low risk use cases that are unintentionally captured  
• categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for defence or 
national  security  purposes.  
To further improve the breadth and specificity  of the principles we suggest  the following :  
1. Consideration of i ntention, in addition to outcome :  
It is suggested  that the purpose  and intent  behind the development of AI models and system s 
should  be specifically referenced in a principle. This could be achieved by adding a  principle which 
designate s an AI system  as high -risk, when its use is in a high -risk context , e.g. facilitating or enabling 
a high -risk activity, such as human safety, defence, national security , etc. In doing so, the framework 
would :  
• Demonstrate recognition of the importance and impact of key goals and objectives  beyond  
outcomes ; and    
 
Amstelveen  | Response to Proposals  Paper – Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High -Risk Settings  | Page 2 of 8 • Ensure greater alignment with global AI standards and re gulations . For example,  the EU Artificial 
Intelligence Act  places obligations on developers of high -risk AI systems  to have robust risk 
management , data governance , and technical documentation.  
This reflects recent industry developments, including findings from the 2023 Royal Commission into 
the Robodebt Scheme, that demonstrated the way in which relatively simple automated decision -
making can drive widespread and severe consequences, which cannot be predicted but could have 
been better governed at the planning and design stages.  
2. Protection of vulnerable communities : 
Whil e Principle  D reference s “groups of individuals ” and “cultural groups ” (p. 19) , we suggest  
consider ing the  explicit inclusion of  particular vulnerable communities , on the basis of age 
(particularly children  and the elderly ), disability  and socio -economic sit uation . This would support 
additional protections for specific vulnerable community groups , at higher risk  of influence or 
impact as a result of adverse AI solutions . 
3.  Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high -
risk AI settings and high -risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative 
uses,  needed?  
• If you prefer a list -based approach (similar to the EU and Canada), what use cases 
should  we include? How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?  
• If you prefer a principles -based approach, what should we address in guidance to give 
the greatest clarity?  
In order  to clarify  what constitutes high -risk AI  and how this may evolve  in future , both approaches may 
be necessary . While  a principles -based approach supports the identification of  current and potential  
high -risk A I scenarios , this may introduce a degree of subjectivity . The provision of examples to support 
the principles may mitigate this , however  a list -based approach  would provide more precise guidance  
commensurate with  the low-trust behaviour  Australians demonstrate with AI (p. 3 ; Ipsos, 2023; Roy 
Morgan, 2023 ). 
It is worthwhile to note  that the Security of Critical Infrastructure (SOCI)  Act 2018  takes a list -based 
approach through the recognition of 11 critical  sectors . However, a list -based approach alone is more 
likely to be  outpaced by the rate of AI’s development  and will fail to capture emergent high -risk uses.  
A dual approach can be presented as a comprehensive list which clearly define s and capture s current 
understandings of high -risk AI domains , supported by a list of  the principles , allowing emerging use 
cases of high -risk AI not explicitly mentioned to be captured, assessed and managed in accordance with 
these principles .

4.  Are there high -risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory 
response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)? If so, how should we 
define these?  
Given AI technologies are rapidly changing , accurately determining a complete listing of use cases 
posing unacceptable risk levels  is complex . Amstelveen’s determination of prohibited cases is through 
evaluation of  our proposed “ high-risk domain areas” and considers  niche use cases  that represent the 
most significant level of harm to the safety and security of individuals and the nation . We recognise the 
limitation of only prohibiting cases with current awareness and international case studies, rather than

actively occurring  and have material impact .  
To further the interest of achieving “International Engagement” (p. 7), Amstelveen proposes the 
Australian government adopt the listing of the detailed and practical  Prohibited AI Practices  detailed 
within Article 5 of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act . These bans are  narrowed versions of  domain areas 
listed in high -risk AI use cases  and would be executed to affirm  Australia’s alignment with  international 
prohibition s on: 
• Using subliminal, manipulative, or deceptive techniques to distort behaviour  and impair 
decision -making, causing significant harm ; 
• Exploiting age, disability, or socio -economic vulnerabilities to distort behavio ur, causing 
significant harm ; 
• Inferring sensitive attributes (race, political opinions, etc.) from biometric data, except for lawful 
purposes or law enforcement ; 
• Social scoring based on behaviour  or traits, leading to negative treatment ; 
• Assessing criminal risk based solely on profiling or personality traits, except to support human 
assessments with verifiable facts ; 
• Creating facial recognition databases by scraping images from the internet or CCTV ; 
• Inferring emotions in workplaces or schools, except for medical or safety reasons ; and  
• Using real -time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement  (with some

In addition to the use cases identified and listed within the EU Artificial Intelligence Act , Amstelveen

responding to high -profile cases of PEPs  likeness es being altered by AI in comprising situations . The US

Amstelveen would encourage  the pursuit of  a Framework Approach (p. 6) , actively amend ing legislation

Opportunities in Presen t Legislation  
It would be remiss to not utilise the effectiveness of existing regulatory infrastructure  beyond the listed 
“regulatory arrangements”  (pp. 43 -45). The following is a list  of regulations that  should be review ed and 
updated  to better address  high -risk AI  scenarios : 
• The SOCI Act : As identified in responses to Q1 and Q3, 11 sectors are oblig ed to ensure 
protections over systems that are critical to t he nation . The communication of how AI impacts 
these obligations from a cyber perspective  is required to achieve the regulatory clarity 
necessary.  
• The Privacy Act and Bills: Current and future legislation around the data lifecycle hold  
implication s on how AI systems can be developed, and already provides individuals certain 
levels of protection and rights regarding their privacy.  
• Commonwealth Prudential Standards: While only applying to Financial Services, there are 
legislative requirements which may intersect with AI use, especially from an operational risk 
perspective.  Here,  AI risks relevant to the listed domain area “ access to essential private 
services”  can be better captured to ensure appropriate governance on the use of AI systems by 
organisations in this sector.  
• Crimes Act(s):  In July of this year, a man in Victoria was sentenced for the production of AI -
generated child abuse images under pre-existing criminal legislation (S51c of the Crimes Act 
1958 (Victoria) ) (Aus tralian Federal Police, 2024) . This example was chosen to demonstrate 
there is already some level of  regulatory protections over high -risk AI domain areas , that are 
significant to Australians that do not reference AI and were certainly not written with AI in mind .  
• Discrimination Act(s):  At the federal level, unlawful discrimination is prohibited through the four 
legislative pieces  of Age Discrimination Act 2004 (Cth), Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (Cth), 
Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth), and Sex Discrimination Act 1984 ( Cth). Here, some of the

It would be  practical and reasonable for organisations t o be compliant with AI legislation through the 
lens and enforcement of frameworks and regulatory bodies  (e.g. the Courts, OAIC, APRA/ASIC,

Justification of a Dedicated AI Framework  
Dedicated  AI-based  legislation would help  organisations make more informed decisions on how their 
current compliance obligations could be leveraged  to better manage AI , as well as provide coverage on  
governance decisions idiosyncratic to AI usage. The following reasons support specialised  regulatory 
oversight beyond current regulations and laws : 
• Governance is inherently process -oriented, thereby creating an emphasis on the traceability of 
decision -making  to determine how incidents eventuated . People and Machine Learning  systems 
can be interviewed and/or audited , whereas AI cannot be; demonstrating the key risk that there 
are significant challenges  to monitor and govern AI ; 
• Our increasing reliance  on AI  systems increases the likelihood that there are negative impacts 
from its use ; and 
• To align with global standards, as other  jurisdictions have or are exploring dedicated AI 
legislation .

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
No
Please identify any:
The proposed principles could be refined to ensure a more comprehensive and nuanced approach.
The principles effectively highlight the importance of transparency, accountability, and risk assessment in high-risk AI applications. However, they may need to be expanded to better encompass certain aspects:
- Contextual Sensitivity: High-risk AI should consider the context in which it operates. Not all applications of AI in sensitive domains (e.g. health) pose the same level of risk, and principles should allow for this variability.
- Human Oversight: While the importance of human oversight is often mentioned, it should be explicitly stated that human involvement before reaching the end stage of any process where AI systems are involved, is essential.
Low-Risk Use Cases Unintentionally Captured
Certain low-risk use cases might be unintentionally captured by high-risk AI regulations. For example, in therapeutic goods manufacturing, efficient inventory management is crucial to ensure that the production process runs smoothly and that therapeutic goods are available when needed. An AI system might be implemented to optimise inventory management by predicting stock levels, monitoring supply chain dynamics, and automating reordering processes. This example of an AI system does not directly interact with consumers or the manufacturing process itself (like drug formulation). Instead, it supports the logistical side of production.
Similarly, the use of predictive AI analysis in pharmaceutical manufacturing would use historical data to forecast demand for raw materials and finished products. While accurate predictions can improve efficiency, errors in the model are unlikely to lead to direct harm to consumers.
Finally, the underlying manufacturing processes are governed by strict regulations and quality control measures through the TGA, which serve as safeguards against potential AI errors.
3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?
YES the principles give enough clarity and certainty
If you prefer a principles-based approach, what should we address in guidance to give the greatest clarity?
The proposed principles provide a solid starting point for addressing high-risk AI settings and models. However, we believe that incorporating a principle of human intervention between the AI system and the end-user output would enhance clarity and accountability, thereby providing an important safeguard against risks.
While a more defined list of illustrative use cases—similar to those used in the EU and Canada—could offer additional clarity, we advocate for the principles-based framework that is adaptable to emerging technologies. Central to this approach should be a contextual risk assessment that integrates risk-benefit models.
Specifically, the guidance should address:
1. Human Oversight: Clearly defining the role of human intervention in monitoring AI outputs and making informed decisions, ensuring that human judgment remains a key component.
2. Contextual Risk Assessment with Risk-Benefit Models: Providing a framework for evaluating risks in relation to the potential benefits of AI applications. This allows for a more nuanced understanding of when and how to assess the severity of risk in AI systems.
3. Dynamic Adaptation: Encouraging regular evaluation of AI technologies and principles to keep pace with rapid advancements and evolving use cases.
The proposed principles lay a strong foundation, however, emphasising human intervention and incorporating risk-benefit models into contextual risk assessments would significantly enhance clarity and effectiveness in managing high-risk AI settings.
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
Overall, we believe the proposed mandatory guardrails for AI safety are a positive step toward managing risks in high-risk settings. These guidelines are essential for ensuring that AI is used responsibly, especially in critical areas like healthcare.
However, we recommend incorporating a risk-benefit ratio model to better assess the severity of risks associated with different AI applications. This approach would allow us to weigh potential risks against the benefits that AI can offer, promoting innovation while still prioritising safety.
Additionally, we suggest a few areas for improvement:
1. Tailored Assessments: Recognising that different AI applications carry different levels of risk can help refine the guardrails to address specific challenges more effectively.
2. Adaptable Guardrails: As AI technology continues to evolve, the guardrails should also adapt. Establishing a process for regularly reviewing and updating these guidelines will help keep them relevant.
While the proposed guardrails are a significant advancement in AI safety, integrating a risk-benefit analysis and ensuring ongoing adaptability will enhance their effectiveness.

For instance, it is fair and proper that AI that has a medical purpose be subject to robust scrutiny in order to demonstrate safety and effectiveness. However, while AI challenges existing medical device regulation, these risks are best mitigated by updating medical device regulation. In this way, patients and healthcare professionals benefit from regulation that is tailor made for healthcare rather than rules that must generalise across all sectors. Currently, the proposed mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI are highly duplicative of existing requirements for AI that qualifies as a medical device.
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
Roche will defer to organisations specifically recognising First nations people, communities and Country.
How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
With respect to the broad principle of ‘The risk of adverse impacts to an individual’s physical or mental health or safety’ (b). This principle, compared to existing sectoral regulation as well as international comparators such as how the classification functions under the AI Act, is extremely ambiguous. It appears that this principle would be modified by Principle F (f) but there is likely no bright line to be drawn and these two principles would be difficult to interpret for healthcare as well as craft clear guidance for industry.
4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
No
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
It is anticipated that these principles would be extremely difficult for a developer of GPAI to answer as it characteristic of these models that they have a wide set of intended uses, the models being notoriously difficult to constrain. While GPAI is still relatively new, the approach taken by the EU to separate out GPAI on the basis of compute is perhaps blunt but both clearer and better addresses the wide intended uses for these models.
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
The majority of these guardrails are already present or highly overlap where the AI qualifies as a medical device.
With respect to Guardrail 10, careful thought with regards to how the conformity assessment process would be conducted is required. Shortage of conformity assessment body expertise, results in a lack of access to AI or an inability to swiftly update models. Such delays themselves can cause safety issues for patients in the healthcare sector. Roche Diagnostics also counsels that specific attention should be paid to how the conformity assessment process functions in the post market phase. Automatic reassessment at frequent intervals where there is robust post market surveillance which indicates a lack of adverse incidents is likely disproportionate. Notoriously, making any significant changes to medical devices in most jurisdictions requires reauthorisation of the device. Leading jurisdictions such as the US FDA, Singapore’s HSA, and the UK’s MHRA are now considering authorisation of a scope of changes as this reauthorisation process is often slow but also burdensome for regulators, especially in the context of AI.
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
We note that the definition of ‘deployer’ as proposed would likely cause confusion with sectoral regulation of medical devices, being misaligned with the definitions contained within that regulation. For instance, as is the case with the EU AI Act, as written, those conducting a clinical trials for a medical device would be a ‘deployer’ under this proposal, meaning they would have to meet the requirements of this legislation at the time of the trial, unless there was a specific exclusion for such AI devices.
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
The guardrails should reflect a risk based approach in accordance with proposed principle (f). This would of necessity then cover high, low and medium based risks.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A domain specific approach – adapting existing regulatory frameworks to include the proposed mandatory guardrails
What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
Option 1 is favoured. The regulation of AI should be proportionate to risk but also fit the products which it regulates. The best chance of fit-for-purpose regulation is to bolster, enhance, and support existing sectoral, vertical regulation, with the possible exception of regulation for GPAI in particular. For the healthcare sector, ensuring TGA has support and resource is the best way to swiftly and directly consider immediate gaps that may need to be filled for medical devices.
15. Which regulatory option(s) will best ensure that guardrails for high-risk AI can adapt and respond to step-changes in technology?
A domain specific approach – Adopting the guardrails within existing regulatory frameworks as needed
Please provide any additional comments.
See response to Question 13 above.
16. Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps and inconsistencies with Australia’s existing laws for the development and deployment of AI?
This Proposal Paper, unlike the US Executive Order and the UK Pro-Innovation Approach, does little to consider how to support existing regulators and existing regulatory frameworks to consider AI. Regardless of what cross-sector, horizontal regulation is implemented, it is Australia’s sectoral regulators such as the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) that know the specific products, know the sector, and know the users. Those sectoral regulators are best positioned to have the largest safety impact for Australian citizens.
Which regulatory option best addresses this?
A domain specific approach – Adopting the guardrails within existing regulatory frameworks as needed
Please explain why.  
See above.

Response to Proposal for Mandatory AI Guardrails 
Author: Sean Johnson FGIA, Lakeﬁeld Drive Pty Ltd

Executive Summary  
Executive Summary  
This response to the Australian Government's proposal for mandatory AI guardrails seeks to balance 
the imperative of ensuring safety, transparency, and accountability in high -risk AI applications with 
the need to foster innovation, particularly among small -to-medium enterprises (SMEs). It advocates 
for a nuanced, risk -based r egulatory framework that avoids excessive regulation and a one-size -ﬁts-
all approach.  
Key Recommendations:  
1. Outcomes -Based Compliance:  Adopt a ﬂexible, outcomes -focused regulatory model that 
allows developers to tailor compliance measures to speciﬁc AI use cases.  
2. Risk -Based Diﬀerentiation:  Implement diﬀerentiated guardrails based on the risk level and 
context of each AI application, ensuring that only genuinely high -risk applications face 
stringent oversight.  
3. Support Mechanisms for SMEs:  Introduce speciﬁc measures to assist SMEs, including:  
o Regulatory Sandboxes:  Establish controlled environments where SMEs can trial AI 
technologies with limited regulatory obligations.  
o Simpliﬁed Reporting Procedures:  Allow SMEs to submit simpliﬁed reports, especially 
when using vetted AI products.  
o Compliance Assistance:  Provide government -supported resources such as training, 
fee reductions, and tax credits to make compliance more accessible.  
4. Tiered Transparency Approach:  Recommend a tiered model for transparency requirements 
to prevent "disclosure fatigue" and ensure that information remains meaningful for end-
users.  
This response also critically evaluates the challenges of implementing transparency measures 
(Guardrail 6) across complex AI systems and suggests a practical, user -centric approach to enhance 
accountability without imposing impractical disclosure requireme nts.

Response to Proposal for Mandatory AI Guardrails 
1 Introduction  
The Australian Government's proposal for mandatory AI guardrails in high -risk settings aims to 
ensure safety, transparency, and accountability throughout the AI lifecycle. While the intent is 
commendable, the proposed approach raises concerns about potential regulatory overreach that 
could stiﬂe innovation and impose unnecessary burdens, especially on SMEs. This response 
addresses these concerns and proposes a measured approach to achieve both safety and innovation.  
 
2 Challenges and Risks  
2.1 Importance of Regulation and Risks of Overreach  
AI-speciﬁc regulations are essential for mitigating risks such as algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, 
and systemic harm. However, the current proposals suggest a one -size-ﬁts-all approach across all 
high -risk AI categories and even general -purpose AI  (GPAI) models like ChatGPT. This raises signiﬁcant 
concerns about regulatory overreach, potentially leading to excessive compliance costs that could hinder innovation and aﬀect both developers and end -users.  
The broad application of these guardrails could impose unnecessary burdens on SMEs, limiting their 
ability to innovate and compete eﬀectively due to compliance costs and resource limitations. It's 
crucial to avoid overreach that could hinder the adoption of AI solutions oﬀering considerable 
societal beneﬁts [2].  
2.2 Economic Impacts and the Risk of "By -Catch"  
The economic impacts of the proposed compliance framework on end -users and developers must be 
considered. Mandatory guardrails may inadvertently stiﬂe innovation by capturing applications that 
do not present signiﬁcant risks but are still subjected to he avy regulatory burdens —a regulatory "by -
catch" [3]. Such blanket measures could create a chilling eﬀect on AI adoption, limiting the 
competitive capacity of Australian businesses and impeding the development of sectors that could 
beneﬁt from AI, such as healthcare and ﬁnancial services.  
Studies on SME adoption of circular economy principles indicate that SMEs face signiﬁcant 
challenges in complying with complex regulations due to resource constraints and inconsistent 
policies. Similar issues could arise for SMEs adopting AI technologies under a rigid compliance 
framework.  
Applying stringent, uniform measures across diverse AI applications risks making valuable 
innovations unviable due to prohibitive compliance costs, leading to lost economic opportunities. 
Smaller ﬁrms operating in high-risk areas are particularly vulnerab le, as compliance costs can cascade 
through the supply chain, especially in sectors reliant on government funding.  
2.3 Balancing Innovation and Accountability  
While regulating AI is necessary to ensure accountability and mitigate risks, an overly prescriptive approach may unintentionally stiﬂe innovation. The current guardrails propose extensive 
requirements for transparency, testing, and accountability across all stages of the AI lifecycle. Such 
measures should be calibrated based on the speciﬁc context and risk level associated with each AI 
system [6].  Response to Proposal for Mandatory AI Guardrails

 A risk -based diﬀerentiation in regulatory requirements, tailored according to the severity of potential 
risks and the context of use, is essential [ See 7]. Focusing on proportionality will help ensure that 
compliance costs are reasonable and justiﬁed in relation to potential risks, encouraging responsible 
AI adoption rather than deterring it.  
 
3 Recommendations  
3.1 Outcomes -Based Compliance  
Adopting a ﬂexible, outcomes -focused regulatory approach allows developers to adapt compliance 
measures according to speciﬁc use cases, rather than adhering to rigid requirements that may not be applicable across all AI applications. For example, Australia uses outcomes -based approaches in 
environmental performance standards, where companies can adapt innovative rehabilitation 
techniques suited to the landscape and type of disturbance caused.  
3.2 Risk-Based Diﬀerentiation  
It's crucial to distinguish between diﬀerent levels of risk in AI applications. A diﬀerentiated approach 
that categori ses AI by its intended use and potential harm ensures that only genuinely high -risk 
applications are subject to the most stringent guardrails. This helps avoid capturing low -risk uses that 
do not necessitate strict oversight [7].  
Applying a Responsive Regulation Theory approach ensures ﬂexibility and adaptability to varying levels of risk associated with diﬀerent activities and entities. Regulators should match the severity of 
interventions to the risk level posed by a regulated entity's actions.  
3.3 Support Mechanisms for SMEs  
Encouraging SME participation will foster a diverse ecosystem of innovation and ensure that the 
beneﬁts of AI are broadly reali sed. Consideration should be given to SMEs operating in areas of 
health, with a focus on reducing economic compliance burdens in areas of need.  
 
4 Critical Evaluation of Guardrail 6: Informing End- Users Regarding 
AI-Enabled Decisions  
Guardrail 6 mandates that organi sations inform end -users about the use of AI, including AI -enabled 
decisions, interactions, and AI -generated content. While the intentions behind this guardrail are 
commendable, there are challenges and potential overreach concerns regarding its implementation, 
especially given the complexity and pervasive integration of AI in various services.  
4.1 Complexity and Pervasiveness of AI in Decision -Making  
The requirement assumes a level of simplicity in AI applications that doesn't reﬂect reality. AI 
systems often involve intricate processes where decisions are shaped by multiple layers of models 
and algorithms. Expecting organi sations to fully disclose every instance of AI involvement risks 
overwhelming end-users with excessive information, potentially leading to "disclosure fatigue" where users disregard information perceived as overly complex or redundant. [11][5] 
4.2 Disparity in Onus of Disclosure Based on Context  
There's an inconsistency in how the onus of AI disclosure might be applied across diﬀerent contexts. For example:  Response to Proposal for Mandatory AI Guardrails

 • Publishing House:  Producing a general recipe book using AI may warrant a simple 
acknowledgment of AI involvement.  
• Dietitian:  Providing personali sed dietary advice using AI might require more detailed 
disclosures due to personal health implications.  
The proposal doesn't clearly delineate the boundaries of such obligations, leading to confusion about 
the extent of required disclosure and potential inconsistencies across industries.  
4.3 Challenges with the Extent and Clarity of Disclosure Requirements  
The extent to which organi sations must trace and disclose the use of AI through their supply chains is 
unclear. In complex AI systems, AI is deeply embedded and may be layered over several stages. 
Requiring detailed disclosures at every stage may be impractical and could result in o rgani sations 
resorting to generic disclaimers that provide little meaningful information to users.  
Moreover, there's a need to consider the commercial implications arising from disclosure 
requirements that may venture into areas of signiﬁcant intellectual property investment.  
4.4 Building Practical and Eﬀective Transparency 
To align with the proposal's goal of fostering accountability and building public trust, a more context -
speciﬁc and tiered approach to disclosure should be considered:  
• Tiered Disclosure Requirements:  Vary the level of required transparency based on the 
context of AI use. General content may warrant a simpler acknowledgment, while critical 
decisions aﬀecting individuals should include more detailed disclosures.  
• Focused User Education:  Invest in educating users about the meaning of these disclosures, 
providing simple explanations of how AI decisions impact them and oﬀering options to seek 
further information.  
4.5 Encouraging Accountability through Realistic Guardrails  
Ensuring that disclosures are both meaningful and comprehensible is crucial to empowering users. 
Implementing practical guardrails that focus on user education and context -speciﬁc transparency can 
better serve the proposal’s goals. For instance, AI -genera ted content could include notes clarifying 
limitations and encouraging users to seek professional advice when necessary. 
 
5 Impact on Health and Allied Health Sectors  
With the health sector speciﬁcally targeted as "high -risk," it's essential to consider the impact on 
SMEs operating in health and allied health sectors, who are primarily "deployers" rather than 
developers of AI technology. Tailoring regulatory requiremen ts ensures safety while maintaining 
business viability.  
5.1 Proportional Compliance Requirements  
5.1.1 Risk-Tiered Requirements  
Establish a tiered system of regulatory requirements based on the risk proﬁle of the AI technology. For example:  
• Low -Risk AI (e.g., Administrative Tools):  Minimal reporting and documentation 
requirements, focusing on transparency.  
• Moderate -Risk AI (e.g., Financial Advisory Tools):  Medium- level audits and periodic 
assessments.  Response to Proposal for Mandatory AI Guardrails

 • High -Risk AI (e.g., Medical Diagnostic Tools):  Extensive testing, mandatory human oversight, 
and regular audits [1][8].  
This helps balance the need for safety while avoiding unnecessary regulatory burdens on applications 
that pose minimal risks.  
5.1.2 Use-Case Speciﬁc Guardrails  
Tailor compliance requirements based on the speciﬁc use of AI. SMEs deploying AI for administrative 
tasks or initial patient screening carry diﬀerent risk levels compared to those using diagnostic tools. 
Aligning guardrails with speciﬁc use cases ensure s that regulatory obligations are appropriately 
scaled [2].  
5.2 Regulatory Sandboxes  
5.2.1 Health -Speciﬁc Sandbox Initiatives  
Support the development of regulatory sandboxes, providing controlled environments where SMEs can deploy AI technologies on a trial basis without the full burden of compliance. This allows SMEs to 
demonstrate safety and eﬃcacy while receiving guidance on  improving compliance without facing 
penalties [4].  
For example, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has implemented an Enhanced Regulatory Sandbox (ERS) for ﬁnancial technology companies. A similar model could be 
adapted for AI in health or administrative purposes, supporting SMEs in proving the safety and utility 
of new AI technologies before scaling under full compliance.  
5.3 Compliance Assistance and Training  
Provide accessible guidance and tools, such as templates for risk assessment and regulatory 
checklists speciﬁc to SMEs in health and allied health. Simplifying the understanding and meeting of 
guardrail requirements without needing speciali sed legal expertise is crucial.  
5.4 Reduced Fees and Incentives  
5.4.1 Fee Reductions for Low -Risk Deployers  
Reduce or waive registration and compliance fees for SMEs using AI in non -invasive, administrative, 
or low -risk health applications. Diﬀerentiating between high -impact developers and lower -risk 
deployers can spare SMEs signiﬁcant costs.  
5.4.2 Tax Incentives for Compliance Investments  
Provide tax credits or grants to help cover costs related to achieving compliance, such as hiring data 
protection oﬃcers or acquiring software to enhance AI safety and data privacy [8].  
5.4.3 Simpliﬁed Reporting and Centralis ed Compliance Platforms  
Allow SMEs, particularly those acting only as deployers, to submit simpliﬁed regulatory reports, especially when using well -established, vetted AI products. This could include pre- ﬁlled templates or 
self-declaration forms outlining the intended use and r isk assessment of the AI tool.  
5.5 Clear Guidance and Real -Time Assistance  
5.5.1 Industry -Speciﬁc Guidelines  
Publish clear and practical guidelines focusing on speciﬁc subsectors, like allied health, which might have diﬀerent deployment models and needs. Provide use-case scenarios to guide SMEs in understanding the required compliance steps for diﬀerent types of AI deployment [13].  Response to Proposal for Mandatory AI Guardrails

Establish a helpline or consultancy services funded by the government to provide real -time 
assistance with compliance queries, particularly helping SMEs with limited capacity to navigate 
complex regulations. 
5.6 Public -Private Partnerships for Shared Compliance Resources  
5.6.1 Consortium for Health AI Compliance  
SMEs in the health and allied health sectors could form consortia to pool resources for compliance 
purposes. By jointly hiring data protection oﬃcers, sharing standardi sed risk assessment frameworks, 
and collectively developing compliance strategies, SMEs can reduce individual costs and better 
navigate complex regulations. Collaborating with organi sations like the Australian Digital Health 
Agency can enhance these eﬀorts [10].  
5.6.2 Partnering with Allied Health Industry Groups  
Work with industry groups to oﬀer compliance solutions that align with guardrails, potentially 
building industry -standard solutions that SMEs can adopt readily [16].  
 
6 Conclusion 
To reduce the regulatory burden on SMEs in the health and allied health markets, a combination of practical and targeted solutions must be implemented. These include creating risk -based compliance 
tiers, regulatory sandboxes, fee reductions, and simpliﬁed  reporting procedures. By ensuring that 
compliance is proportional and aﬀordable, SMEs can continue to innovate and deliver value in the 
health sector without facing prohibitive regulatory costs.  
The proposed mandatory guardrails must be reﬁned to avoid regulatory overreach that could stiﬂe 
innovation and hinder the economic beneﬁts of AI. A balanced regulatory framework that is 
outcomes -focused, risk -diﬀerentiated, and supportive of SMEs will more eﬀectively ensure both 
safety and the ﬂourishing of AI in Australia. This approach enables AI to contribute to economic 
growth, societal well- being, and improved quality of life while ensuring that risks are eﬀectively 
managed.

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
Please see my answer in question 5.
4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Yes
If so, how should we define these?
The Government should ban any AI system where technical evaluations show that it could cause “critical harm” or where there are unacceptable “systemic risks”. The EU AI Act, in Recital 110, describes systemic risks from general-purpose AI, including those that can lead to widespread or catastrophic harm — namely dangerous capabilities such as weapons development, persuasion & deception, and self replication. For instance, if a technical evaluation shows that an AI model could assist people in making cyber, chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapons or could engage in self-replication, deception and, ultimately, loss of control, it should be urgently banned.
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
For regulation to be effective at risk mitigation, we need to distinguish between high-risk uses of narrow AI, risks from current general-purpose AI systems, and the systemic or catastrophic risks associated with future general-purpose AI systems with powerful capabilities. It might be valuable for Australia to adopt the EU AI Act’s definition of general-purpose AI with systemic risk, distinct from just general-purpose AI. Although I don’t really like the phrase “systemic risk”, I think the meaning of it is valid & useful, and it may be wise for countries to be consistent with the language & terminology of emerging global practice. The EU AI Act defines “systemic risk” as “a risk that is specific to the high-impact capabilities of general-purpose AI models, having a significant impact on the Union market due to their reach, or due to actual or reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or the society as a whole, that can be propagated at scale across the value chain”.
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
Yes, but with different levels of severity depending on expert, technical evaluations of the model. Guardrails should be proportionate to the risks posed by the AI system. Australia should follow the EU AI Act in distinguishing between GPAI and GPAI with systemic risk, and applying the strictest mandatory guardrails for GPAI with systemic risk.
7. What are suitable indicators for defining GPAI models as high-risk?
Base on technical capability
What technical capability should it be based on?
Other
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
No
Please provide any additional comments
The guardrails should focus more obligations on developers, because they control most of the risks. The MIT AI Risk Repository, as well as similar analysis from the USA’s National Institute of Standards (NIST), show that AI developers control most risks of AI. Decisions during model development are key to safe and responsible AI. The authors of the MIT AI Risk Repository observe that technology companies have far better knowledge about capabilities and risks than regulators. As such, nations must find effective ways to incentivise action by developers. Mandatory guardrails should single out specific obligations — such as those proposed by the EU AI Act, the US Executive Order 14110, or California state bill SB1047 — and find specific ways to impose them on the developers of AI products that would be deployed in Australia. The Government should create incentives that force AI developers to internalise risks – ensuring they do not dodge obligations using the opaque nature of AI or legal manoeuvres such as end-user licence agreements.
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI?
No
How could we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for example low-risk and high-risk GPAI models? 
Australia needs a specific definition to capture AI models that might display dangerous behaviours that could lead to widespread or catastrophic harm. These dangerous behaviours include weapons development, persuasion & deception, and self-replication. Global norms are developing around how to define these “red lines”, including in EU AI Act Recital 110, SB1047, and the Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence. For instance, SB1047 would have required developers of highly capable models to be able to shut them down if these risks become possible. We need to be ready to deal with future systems with catastrophic risks.
Guardrail 1 should specifically require developers and deployers of GPAI to report accidents or incidents to the regulator, as is currently the case in the aviation industry. Many domain experts think safety incident reporting and security information sharing is the most effective risk mitigation for general-purpose models. Guardrail 1 should also include an obligation for AI developers to share models with national AI Safety Institutes. Media has reported AI developers have made commitments to share models with governments – including Australia – for evaluation. But AI developers have either reneged on those agreements or been slow to comply. We should require that AI developers follow through with these commitments.
The regulator should have powers and obligations to conduct investigations and publish reports that inform ongoing safety practices.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A whole of economy approach – introducing a new cross-economy AI Act
What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
Legislation should be a combination of options 1 and 3 (domain-specific and whole-of-economy approaches). I could only select one option, so I randomly chose option 3.
Importantly, Australia needs an AI Act that can shape the behaviour of overseas AI developers. Research, including from MIT and RAND, shows that AI developers are best placed to control the most severe risks from AI during model development. Regulating offshore activity can be challenging, but it has to be our top priority. We need an AI Act that has enforceable provisions targeting offshore developers.
The best regulatory approach may be to let established regulators - like the Therapeutic Goods Administration or the Civil Aviation Safety Authority - lead within their fields of expertise. At the same time, an AI-specific Act would cover any gaps (regulating any new products, services or anything else that is not within the domain of an existing regulator) and focus on shaping the behaviour of offshore AI developers.

 1. Introduction  
Australian workers  do not trust the artificial intelligence (AI) rollout . The Stanford AI Index 
2024 ranks Australians as one of the most AI -sceptical populations  in the world - only 44% 
consider  AI’s benefits to outweigh the risks , and just 6% oppose the establishment of a new 
regulator.  Australians trust business the least out of all organisations when it comes to 
responsible AI , and 92% of the public call for transparency about where and how AI is used.1 
 
VTHC is concerned that t he proposed guardrails will not improve public confidence in the 
AI rollout  because they are an exercise in self -regulation. To date, w orkers have been 
excluded from the consultation process – resulting in a proposal that seemingly  
misunderstand s the problem it is intended to solve. Throughout this submission, VTHC will 
include the stories of workers who have been subjected to AI in their workplace, gathered 
for the 2024 Victorian inquiry into workplace surveillance.  
 
AI increases the relative power of any one person or organisation controlling it  and AI 
regulation should consider  how best to  prevent this power from being abused.2 In order to 
accomplish this, the proposed guardrails will need to be substantially amended . 
 
Throughout 2024,  employer federations have argued that Australians’ low  trust is due to AI 
being ‘generally misunderstood by the community ,’ patronis ing workers  about digital 
literacy while simultaneously asking  the taxpayer for handouts to run trust building 
exercises  and investigate the causes of concern . 3 
 
Since 2021 , the Federal  Government has survey ed Australian  executives about their 
organisations ’ use of responsible AI practices – compiled  in the form of a ‘responsible AI 
inde x’ (RAI).4 The index is not ambitious : it tracks compliance with  practices that are little 
more  than  basic due diligence  - supervising autonomous systems, reviewing  algorithms for 
bias, verifying  claims made about a system by the vendor , and monitor ing harmful incidents.

Australian  businesse s using AI :

 4.1 Guardrail 1: The Accountability  Process  
 
Currently, t he proposed guardrails will only apply to a system  classified as high -risk. 
However,  it will be up to organisations to ‘assess … whether the use of an AI system is 
high -risk.’42 This means the guardrails are  an opt -in regulatory structure  that will provide 
workers with little protection.43 
 
Guardrail 1 requires organisations who use an AI system that they deem to be high -risk to 
make publicly available an ‘accountability process’ for that system. The accountability 
process consists of documenting how the business is going to approach regulatory 
compliance, develop policies for risk management, and set structures for reporting. As the 
propos ed guardrail states , ‘new processes for managing risks’ are not necessarily required 
and should be integrated to existing structures w here possible.44 At bare minimum, 
businesses will document  their  internal reporting structures and their  planne d approach to 
compliance .45 This is the only component of the proposed regulatory model which involves 
any form of public reporting , but i t is also the least detailed.   
 
Guardrail 1 is equated with the accountability process mandated by the EU AI Act , but m ore 
accurately, the two approaches sit at opposite ends of the regulatory spectrum.46 Employers 
who use high -risk AI in the EU  are compelled by law  to undertake a full impact assessment 
on fundamental human rights . Results from the assessment must  be publicly available 
before any high -risk deployment can occur.47 When serious incidents occur, there is a 
mandatory 2 -day reporting period for organisations.48 Public authorities must be informed 
without delay, and corrective actions taken.49 A risk assessment specifically concerning the 
incident is also submitted.50 Failure to take corrective action results in penalties and may 
cause the system to be recalled. This sits alongside the EU’s existing, culture of human rights 
and privacy with extensive national -level laws and regulations.51 No such measures are 
present in the Australian  ‘accountability process’ provided  in the proposed guardrails .  
 
Recommendation  1: Legislate  a national  AI authority  
Introduce economy -wide legislation (Regulatory Approach 3) to establish a new regulator 
with the power to enforce compliance with the guardrails and any other AI regulation, via a 
National AI Authority. Risk identification  and mitigation must be overseen by the regulator,  
to reverse the presumption of compliance and better protect workers .52

Australian  workers  do not trust the AI rollout because the AI rollout doesn’t deserve their

 1. Introduction: Digitalisation and the Future  of Work  
 
Workers, their unions and the public at large have been encouraged to think about 
workplace digitalisation as an issue of profound complexity and nuance.  
 
The novelty of these technologies is constantly emphasised: their total lack of a precedent, 
the impossibility of predicting their consequences. Through jargon, obfuscation and 
deceptive framing, many working people have been led to feel simply unqualified  to 
participate in the AI discussion – let alone have a say on the specific role it will take in their 
working lives.  
 
For all we hear about complexity and nuance, the self -reported experience of workers 
actually exposed to these technologies has been remarkably straightforward.  AI is a new 
technology causing old problems.1 In the hands of employers, it makes it possible for 
union workers to be added to blacklists, for worker’s private conversations to be used 
against them, for their personal life to fall under perpetual scrutiny. In other words, 
digitalisation risks making ‘the future of work’ look very similar to the past which they fought 
hard to escape.  
 
For several decades,  innovations in  information technology have  transformed  Australian 
workplaces.  Until recently , these transformations have concentrated on the production 
process – with machines  taking over  work previously performed by humans . Today’s crucial 
development  is that  AI has made it possible for  managerial  and productive functions to be 
automated. This has profound implications for  the future of work  in Australia . 
 
AI, algorithmic management  (AM),  automated decision making (ADM) and automation are 
starting to impact  every dimension of Australians’ working lives: from their day -to-day 
experiences in the workplace, to the ir relationship with managers and their position in the 
wider labour market.  
 
Although  human  worker s still drive  cars, deliver packages,  answer calls, and pack  goods  – 
an increasing number  receive their instructions  from an app  or software program . 
Pioneered by digitally based  food delivery and ride -hailing services, this system of 
management -by-algorithm  is spread ing to manufacturing, transportation, logistics , legal 
services,  banking, telecommunications, healthcare,  public administration  and retail .  
 
AM refers to the use of algorithmic systems to undertake managerial functions at work . It is 
closely tied to automation, because data collected through AM often guide s the automation 
process.  The functions performed by AM technologies  include:   
 
People analytics : 
• Monitor ing, evaluating and ranking  worker  performance .  
• Calculating and ensuring  adherence to schedules and deadlines . 
• Informing decisions  on hiring, firing, disciplining,  and promoting .

Digitalisation, ADM , and automation  have the potential to relieve workers of repetitive  tasks 
and generate historic productivity gains.  AI could pre -emptively address risks to wor kplace 
health and safety, streamline  the work process, improve organisational decision -making 
and enhance the quality of jobs . The se possible benefits are much discussed  and the 
Committee  is likely to hear about them from a number of responses to this inquiry. What 
may not currently be as salient are the extensive risks AI poses to workers – and it is here 
that this submission will focus .   
 
Just as digitalisation may transform workers lives for the better, it may also systematically 
deprive them of fundamental rights, secure livelihoods and the ability to take collective 
action. The outcome will depe nd on decisions taken today at all levels of government.  
 
All Australian  worker s should be able to share in the benefits of digitalisation . This means 
making sure that employers are not the only voice in the room when it comes to 
implementing t his technology  – workers must be front and centre on  decisions about AI, 
AM and ADM .  
 
So far, employers have been given relatively free reign to impose AI, AM and ADM 
technologies in their workplaces.  This has put Australia  out of alignment with other 
advanced economies and  leaves us vulnerable to a number of serious risks.  
 
At the workplace level, the employer -led AI rollout is reduc ing transparency and job quality 
while height ening surveillance and work intensification. At the workforce  level , this risks 
causing widespread deskilling, fragmentation  and polarisation. This w ill heighten  power -
differences in the workplace so significantly that labour rights may become increasingly 
difficult for workers to exercise  in any capacity.  
 
In 1856, Victorian unions were the first place in the world to fight for and win the 8 -hour day 
– setting a historic standard for every worker to enjoy 8 hours of rest and 8 hours of 
recreation after 8 hours of work. Workers have  a fundamental right to spend time with family, 
pursue education, explore creative pursuits, appreciate nature, participate in arts, culture 
and public affairs, or simply, to relax however they  please to. Digitalisation is undercutting    
 
Page 5 of 41 
 this basic principle - the principle which has civilised capitalism in Australia for nearly two 
hundred years.  
 
Workers take pride in their work. Workers want to improve their skills, become more 
efficient and contribute to better outcomes. Victorian unions are not opposed to 
technological progress. However, we also recognise that workers deserve to share in the 
wealth that they create.  Since 1994 -95, there’s been increase of 16.6% in the hours worked 
by Australians – but labour’s share of national income has only shrunk.2 The question of 
digitalisation needs to be considered in this context.  
 
Workers must be participants in  rather than victims of  the AI rollout. This will require 
proactive action from the Federal Government to harness workers’ voice, regulate the worst 
uses of this technology and prevent irreversible distortions to the structure of our workforce 
and society at large.  
 
This submission will make a number of recommendations about issues relating to 
workplace digitalisation. All of these share a common reference point: that workers deserve 
to have a say over how technological advancements affect them, and that all of societ y 
benefits when this happens.  
 
2. Digitalisation at the Workplace Level  
 
2.1 Current forms of digital transformation of the workplace are harming workers  
 
Unfortunately,  this inquiry ’s terms of reference  assumes  that digitalisation , on-balance, is 
going to be beneficial  for workers, communities, the economy and the national interest. 
Although widespread in elite policy -making  circles, this is not how the  average Australian  
worker is thinking about AI. In fact, concern with these technologies is higher here  than  in 
almost  any other developed country.3 Working Australians are seei ng firsthand  how these 
digital technologies are actually being  deployed  in the workplace . Their anxieties are well -
founded and need to be taken seriously.   
 
Narratives around futuristic technologies always presented a vision of utopia. In 1930, John 
Maynard Keynes predicted in the future there would be such extensive technological 
benefits, that living standards would increase to the point where workers would have so 
much leisure time, they would only need to work the hours they chose, around fifteen per 
week.4

higher than the OECD average . Inequality is worsening  - 90% of Australians receive just 7%
