PART 1 : Overview of AI   
 
 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly emerging as the defining technology of our time.  
It has transformed industries from ride -sharing to radiology, with ongoing advancements 
poised to unlock economic and societal benefits across a wide range of sectors and social 
domains. By improving predictive capabilities, optimising operations and resou rce 
allocation, and personalising service delivery, AI can drive positive social and environmental 
outcomes at scale, enhance the efficiency of government services, and provide significant 
competitive advantages for businesses and the Australian economy.  
 
However, concerns about AI’s potential negative impacts are also growing in the absence of 
regulation. These include risks to privacy, intellectual property, national security, and critical 
infrastructure, as well as the erosion of democratic values throug h the amplification of 
social discord and the potential for undermining meaningful work and human social 
interactions.  
 
Given the rapid pace of AI development, there is a pressing need for regulation to ensure 
its safe and responsible use in Australia.  AI technologies vary widely in complexity and 
application, resulting in a broad spectrum of associated risks, from negligible to severe. For 
instance, using a generative AI chatbot to summarise a long magazine article presents 
significantly different risks  when compared to using the same technology to offer medical 
advice. Similarly, simpler technologies can carry vastly diffe rent risks depending on their 
application  – such as the difference between using coded logic for calculating a family 
budget, versus implementing a nation -wide welfare system like the controversial Robodebt3 
scheme.  
 
Given A I’s complexity and diverse applications, nuanced and proportionate regulation is 
required to address a wide spectrum of risks, from low -level concerns to critical threats .4  
 
The Government’s proactive approach of engaging with industry, civil society, academia, 
and the community is reflected in the proposed mandatory guidelines for high -risk AI. It’s 
now vital to take action and build momentum by implementing mandatory AI regu lation.

PART  2: Defining high-risk AI   
 
 
The proposed approach to defining high -risk AI is based on two categories. The first 
category addresses AI systems with known or foreseeable applications, where risk is 
determined by the context of use. Guidance is provided to help organisations identify high -
risk scenarios. The second category targets advanced, highly capable General Purp ose AI 
(GPAI) models, which pose broader risks due to limited understanding of potential 
applications and the associated risks. A set of six principles have been proposed to guide 
assessment of whether an AI system is high -risk and therefore subject to man datory 
guardrails.  
 
Deloitte proposes a principles and rules -based approach to defining high -risk AI.  
 
Principles provide the flexibility needed to account for diverse use cases and evolving 
technology. A principle -based definition allows AI systems to be assessed holistically, 
considering various risks such as impacts on human rights, health and safety, le gal 
standing, and societal wellbeing. By using these guiding principles developers, deployers 
and regulators have a flexible and nuanced approach to distinguish between novel high -
risk applications and low -risk applications. This prevents unintended regula tory burdens on 
low-risk use cases while capturing new and emerging risks as AI technology advances.  
 
However, the proposed principles for defining high -risk AI on their own lack the precision 
needed to provide regulatory certainty. Their expansive nature leaves too much room for 
subjective interpretation.  This ambiguity can lead to inconsistent application and regulatory 
uncertainty – in which low -risk applications could be swept into high -risk scrutiny and high -
risk applications might be overlooked.  
 
A contrasting approach to defining high -risk AI is a rules -based approach , which explicitly 
defines which AI applications are considered high -risk by providing lists of high -risk AI 
applications (examples can be found in th e EU, Canada and Singapore ). High -risk 
applications might include, for example, those involving biometric surveillance, facial 
recognition in policing, or health diagnostics. A rules -based definition of high -risk AI offers 
clarity, predictability, and consistency, reducing uncertainty for developers and businesses . 
This enabl es them to more confidently assess whether their AI systems fall under a high -
risk category. However, on its own, this approach is not flexible to new technologies and 
applications in a rapidly transforming field. Lack of flexibility could lead to the uninte nded 
impact of constrai ning our ability to adopt new technologies to benefit Australia’s national 
interests.   
 7 
 
 
We know from our interactions with clients that regulatory uncertainty has stymied 
innovation in new technologies here in Australia. A list -based definition of high -risk AI will 
provide high regulatory certainty for those applications of AI captured. Howev er, new and 
emerging technologies will not be covered. Regulatory uncertainty will remain and continue 
to hinder innovation.  
 
A combined principles and rules -based approach is a practical way to provide clarity and 
certainty in defining high -risk AI .5 This is, in essence, a principles a nd list -based approach. 
Principles are the binding precept to define high -risk AI, which would be supported by clear 
rules – a list of context -specific AI applications. The list of high -risk AI applications is not 
exhaustive, which is implausible with the rate of AI technological advancement and breadth 
of possible applications , but does provide explicit guidance for defining the common high -
risk AI applications.  
 
A principles and rules -based approach is applicable to all possible regulatory options (see 
PART  4 of this submission). Principles can be centrally mandated with rules (lists of high -risk 
AI applications), maintained and implemented by existing industry regulators. Or , principles 
and rules may be overseen by an AI Regulator.  
  
 
5 John Braithwaite, ‘Approach Based on Rules and Principles: A Theory of Legal Certainty ’ (SSRN Paper No 
329400)  https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstr c_id=329400 . 
  
 8 
PART 3 : Guardrails ensuring testing, 
transparency  & accountability  of AI   
 
 
The proposed mandatory guardrails for high -risk AI and GPAI systems aim to reduce 
potential harms, build public trust, and ensure accountability throughout the AI lifecycle. 
These guardrails include requirements for rigorous testing, transparency and risk 
management, aligning with international regulation. The guardrails are designed to be 
flexible and adaptable to evolving technologies, promoting interoperability with global 
frameworks to ease compliance. The Australian Government emphasises integrating th ese 
measures within existing regulatory frameworks and across the AI value  chain, with shared 
responsibilities for developers and deployers.  
 
Deloitte supports the proposed mandatory guardrails for high -risk AI as a framework for 
good AI governance . 
 
The primary benefit of mandatory guardrails is that they define an approach to AI 
governance and establish consistent expectations for organisations involved in developing 
and deploying high -risk AI systems.  
 
Deloitte has found that uncertainty around the management of AI risk and compliance has 
led to stifled innovation. When companies know what is expected of them in engaging with 
and managing these risks, they are better equipped to implement robust AI gover nance – 
which supports experimentation, innovation and scaled deployment – and delivers on the 
promise of AI.  
 
“When we proactively and accurately regulate high -risk use of AI with mandatory 
guardrails, we will start to realise the benefits that AI and GPAI technologies have 
to offer – both in delivering organisational value, and  by putting Australia back on 
the map for innovation.”  
                                                                                                         Dr. Kellie Nuttall  
 
The need for good AI governance is not limited to organisations developing or deploying 
high-risk AI. However, a one -size-fits-all approach would create excessive red tape, stifling 
Australia’s innovation and ability to compete globally. Every organisation  working with AI 
should have an AI governance framework that is tailored to their AI ambition, maturity, and 
risk profile. The key is to craft governance structures that are right -sized, aligned to each 
organisation’s unique use and adoption of AI to deliv er on their AI ambition and create 
value.   
 9 
PART 4: Regulatory options to mandate 
guardrails   
 
 
Three regulatory options to mandate guardrails have been proposed:  
 
1. Integrating guardrails into existing sector -specific laws;  
2. Establishing a new overarching framework to adapt existing regulations; or  
3. Creating a comprehensive, AI -specific Act for uniform regulation across the economy.  
While the first option is incremental and focuses on sectoral adjustments, the second aims 
to streamline AI governance with a cohesive framework but uses current enforcement 
mechanisms. The third option offers the most comprehensive approach by consolidati ng all 
definitions, thresholds and guardrails in a single Act, providing clarity and dedicated 
enforcement.  
 
Deloitte supports an approach to AI regulation that provides certainty and consistency.  
 
Australia’s regulatory environment is complex, and AI is already governed under a range of 
existing legal frameworks including consumer protection, privacy, anti -discrimination, 
competition, data security, and copyright laws. Incorporation of AI regulation  into the existing 
regulatory landscape (options 1 and 2) has the potential to exacerbate complexity with 
mandated guardrails being dispersed across numerous statutes.  
 
This is likely to result in differential implementation and enforcement, making compliance 
challenging for businesses and increasing the risk of unintentional breaches. This fragmented 
approach can also heighten public concern that AI risks are not being a dequately addressed, 
particularly in high -risk applications. A more cohesive regulatory framework would provide 
clearer guidance and ensure responsible AI practices are upheld across all sectors.  
 
An AI -specific Act would provide certainty and consistency for compliance by 
establishing clear definitions and requirements for high -risk AI applications across all 
sectors, unlike fragmented sector -specific regulations.  
 
 
   
 10 
 
 
This approach minimises ambiguity by consolidating rules, definitions, and enforcement 
mechanisms in one piece of legislation, reducing confusion for organisations navigating 
multiple regulatory regimes. It offers a single, unified framework, making it eas ier for 
businesses to understand and adhere to their obligations.  
 
Additionally, this structure aligns with global best practices, promoting international 
interoperability and ensures that Australia has a cohesive and predictable regulatory 
environment that fosters safe and responsible use  of AI .  
 
It is paramount that Australia moves at pace to provide the regulatory certainty needed to 
promote AI -fuelled innovation in our country and not lag other developed nations in doing 
so. Every effort must be made to finalise a well -crafted AI regulation as swiftly as possible to 
balance the promotion of innovation with robust governance, creating a regulatory 
enviro nment that safeguards public trust while encouraging responsible AI development.  
 
Organisations need clarity today, so they can focus on investing in the right talent and 
resources to drive their growth and secure Australia’s position as a global player in AI.  
 
“The Government needs to quickly introduce clear and consistent AI regulation 
and provide the certainty Australian organisations need to set themselves up for AI 
success – so they can innovate with confidence.”  
                                                                                                      Dr. Elea Wurth  
   
 11 
PART 5: Closing comments   
 
 
The absence of a clear legal framework is slowing down the nation.  
 
We have heard many Australian leaders comment on the fact that Australia is lagging the 
rest of the world when it comes to AI regulation – at a time when there is a strong appetite 
to build the nation’s sovereign AI capabilities.  
 
Regulatory certainty is required to support a confident AI future in Australia and mandatory 
guardrails are a step in the right direction. However, if these guardrails are not tied to a 
broader investment in innovation and development, Australia will continue to lag other 
countries.  
 
Other economies’ regulation around AI is developed hand -in-hand with AI industry 
development policies. For example, both the EU Artificial Intelligence  Act and the US Executive 
Order  on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence  are a combination of regulation 
and economic stimulus. Therefore, any proposed AI regulation should be developed in 
concordance with a vison for both AI use and AI industry development.

support the Voluntary Safety Standard (replicated in the Mandatory Guardrails) applying to all AI

o be enforced with tough penalties to deter non -compliance; and  
o apply extraterritorially even though enforcement may be unsuccessful, there is a

The principles -based definition of high -risk AI systems should be 
accompanied by specific prohibitions  
 
We broadly agree with using the proposed principles on page 19 to determine high risk AI systems. The 
context -dependent nature of these principles make them flexible and wide reaching enough to make 
businesses assess all AI systems to determine whether the y are high risk or not according to how they 
are used. They do not differentiate between internal and external deployment of AI systems which is 
beneficial because AI used in internal processes can have significant impacts on end users.  
 
We suggest the following enhancements to work alongside the principles:  
• There should be some explicit mention that low -risk AI is not captured  in the proposed 
principles such as customer support chatbots, educational games and spam filters. This will 
enhance clarity and avoid administrative burden for businesses using low -risk AI technology.  
• Prohibit the most threatening uses of AI , specifically:  
o All applications that the draft EU AI Act lists in Title II26 (“Prohibited AI practices”, such as 
“subliminal techniques”) including untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet 
or CCTV footage to create facial recognition databases, emotion reco gnition in the 
workplace and schools, social scoring, predictive policing and AI that manipulates human 
behaviour or exploits people’s vulnerabilities should be prohibited.   
• Prohibit development of truly general AI  and self-sustaining learning machinery : 
o This type of AI includes systems that can make and execute long -term plans 
autonomously. It is referred to as general AI, “AGI”, or “self -sustaining learning 
machinery”, “artificial superintelligence”, “strong agentic AI” and other names.  
o We acknowledge that the possibility of creating such AI in the near term is still up for 
debate in the expert community. However, a significant number of people (including 
prominent scientists) not only believe in the possibility, but predict that such AI can be 
developed in a matter of years, not decades.  
o The in -principle uncontrollability and ungovernability of such systems has been 
demonstrated in research. Therefore, R&D aimed at creation of general AI , such that 
undertaken by OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and others, must be strictly prohibited 
in Au stralia.

national security and law enforcement. Extraterritorial application of the ban, even if 
unenforceable, should be considered as a signal against attempts to develop 
uncontro llable AI overseas.  
o The Australian Government should work towards an international treaty prohibiting 
attempts to develop dangerous general AI and instituting a strong global compute P. 5  
 governance mechanism.  
• Prohibit use of general -purpose AI or AI that exhibit dangerous capabilities  in critical 
infrastructure  and government services.

Feedback on mandatory guardrails  
 
Overall, we agree with the proposed mandatory guardrails for high -risk AI as described on page 35 of 
the proposals paper. They seem to align with international standards or global initiatives in the EU, 
Canada and the UK. They seem as a whole adequate enou gh to pre -emptively address potential harms.  
We also agree with the proposed definitions of developer and deployer on page 32 of the proposals 
paper and with the allocation of responsibility for guardrails implementation according to where it is 
most capable of addressing risk. Those with the most co ntrol over a model should bear the most 
responsibility which would typically be the developer, and not a business or end user buying models 
“off the shelf” with limited or no ability to adapt the model for their own purposes. Exceptions should 
be made for open -source where end users or players downstream should be responsible for using AI 
appropriately.  
 
We make suggestions to enhance the following guardrails:  
 
• On Guardrail 7, information about the AI system (for example, how it makes decisions) is 
essential for victims to seek compensation in court but it is insufficient. We believe reforms to 
liability and product safety laws are needed to adequately seek redre ss for damages or harms. 
We refer to the Shine Lawyer’s proposal for implementation details. An additional benefit of 
making it easier for individuals to seek redress is that it will incentivise AI developers to prioritise 
safety and ensure accuracy and qu ality in the systems they develop.  
• On Guardrail 9, the issue of the burden of record keeping on SMEs should not be a problem 
because the development of high -risk AI and frontier models is almost exclusively dominated by 
large corporations as currently only they have the vast resources requi red to develop these 
models. The focus of these mandatory guardrails is on high risk technology so this does not pose 
a barrier for SMEs from innovating towards lower risk AI.  
• On Guardrail 10, we support conformity assessments to certify compliance with the mandatory 
guardrails prior to deployment including repeating them if the AI system changes significantly. 
This additional guardrail represents a strengthening of the Voluntar y Standard.  
Apply the mandatory guardrails extraterritorially  
The proposals paper is silent on the territorial application of the guardrails. As the majority of the 
guardrails fall within the responsibility or control of developers who are mostly based outside of 
Australia, regulators will need to be able to enforce the guardrails extraterritorially. We believe this is 
achievable because Meta, Google and Microsoft have offices and a significant business presence in P. 6  
 Australia to supply services. Regulatory action will have an impact on reputation and raise awareness 
globally - a good example of this is the Online eSafety Commissioner’s civil penalty proceedings against 
X Corp. which was reported widely and was followe d by Brazil’s ordering of the suspension of X 
accounts for allegedly spreading disinformation.  
Apply tough penalties to enforce mandatory guardrails  
Penalties need to be serious enough to act as a deterrent and not be considered a ‘cost of doing 
business’ especially in an industry with large financial resources.  
We propose tough penalties for non -compliance, such as percentage -of-worldwide -turnover fines) and 
criminal penalties against corporations, their employees and directors, similar to sanctions under EU 
GDPR31.  
 
We ask the Government to consider implementing a penalty regime similar to the vetoed Safe and 
Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act (SB 1047) in California which includes:  
• fines amounting to up to 10% of the cost of the quantity of computing power used to train a 
covered AI model,   
• joint liability on affiliated entities  
• recovery of monetary damages, punitive damages, attorney’s fees and injunctive relief.  
Option 3 is the preferred implementation option  
As mentioned in our previous submission by Campaign for AI Safety, where possible, it is most efficient 
to update and strengthen existing legislation to cover risks that fall through regulatory gaps. However, 
new laws are needed to regulate high -risk AI sy stems and uses with unacceptable risk. These need to be 
enforced by a specialised AI regulator.  
 
On option 3’ s analysis of limitations, we believe these can be minimised through adequate resourcing, 
coordination and knowledge sharing with other regulators responsible for domain -specific legislation 
related to AI technology. The Government could consider imposing a levy on the largest players in the 
AI industry to resource a new regulatory regime. The broad alignment with international approaches 
should make it not extra cumbersome for businesses to comply and not undermine confidence in using 
or developing AI.  
 
Below are some proposed functions and powers to help enforce Mandatory Guardrails and stop 
unacceptable risk development:  
• Surveillance powers to monitor AI data centres in Australia for unauthorised training runs and 
powers to issue very large fines (page 42 of the proposals paper discusses compelling 
organisations to disclose to the Australian Government training runs of mod els with potentially 
dangerous emergent capabilities).  
• Establish a know -your -customer (KYC) scheme for cloud compute providers in Australia.  
• Compel data centres to report compute activities to the regulator.  
• Track dealing in computer chips that can be used in deep learning.  
• Fine and/or prosecute companies or individuals that attempt to develop AI with unacceptable 
risk.

As detailed later in this submission, DP -REG members have undertaken joint work

Against this backdrop, we believe i ntroducing an AI -specific Act will likely present 
significant practical challenges.  
• The growth of AI is rapid and unpredictable. This creates considerable risks that a 
technology -specific regulatory framework will not keep up with the pace of 
technological change.

not know when, how, or even whether they can complain about a decision that a 
company made with the support of AI.

implementation issues, DP -REG members consider that a framework that guides how 
AI is defined and regulated across government would be useful.  3

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
In my view, the current principles do not sufficiently capture the complexity of high-risk AI. While they serve as a practical starting point, they must be complemented with a regulatory pathway that includes technical evaluations of AI systems before training, deployment, and usage. These evaluations are crucial to uncover unexpected or unintended behaviours that might not be apparent until after deployment. Furthermore, such assessments could provide clarity when it is uncertain if the general principles encompass a particular AI system, thereby reducing regulatory burden for systems deemed safe.
Are there any principles we should add or remove?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
The Canadian Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA) has a procedure in s 36 for the Governor in Council to add new high-risk AI use cases even if they don’t align with the use cases included in the legislation. Australia should give our regulations similar flexibility in dealing with unexpected future developments.
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?
No
4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Yes
If so, how should we define these?
I believe there are cases where the government should consider banning the use of AI systems. Specifically, AI systems that could cause critical harm or pose systemic risks should be prohibited, much like what has been proposed in California's SB1047 bill and the EU AI Act (Recital 110). For example, if a technical evaluation reveals that an AI model could aid in the creation of weapons of mass destruction or engage in self-replication, deception, and loss of control, it should be promptly banned. Similarly, the International Dialogues on AI Safety Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence calls for international coordination to impose certain “red lines” on AI capability, similar to those in SB1047 and the EU AI Act.
Legislation must therefore establish an intolerable risk threshold.
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
The current principles are not flexible enough to accommodate emerging forms of high-risk AI such as GPAI. It would be beneficial to adopt the EU AI Act's definitions of GPAI and systemic risk GPAI, as they provide robust guidelines that are compatible with future technologies. Future AI systems could be powerful and unpredictable, and these definitions will allow Australia to prioritise the regulation of systems with particularly dangerous capabilities, ensuring global compliance safety.
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
Mandatory guardrails should not apply to all GPAI models, but instead should be proportionate to the risks posed by the AI system. Principle f factors in “the severity and extent of adverse impacts”, but it only applies to the classification of a narrow-AI systems as being “high-risk AI”. The severity and extent of adverse impacts should be taken into account when defining GPAI and implementing specific guardrails. A targeted set of mandatory guardrails that address potentially catastrophic risks from future AI models could balance safety with innovation and reduce regulatory burden where evaluations show models are safe.
7. What are suitable indicators for defining GPAI models as high-risk?
Base on technical capability
What technical capability should it be based on?
Other
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
The proposed mandatory guardrails do not fully mitigate the risks of AI in high-risk settings. We need tailored guardrails that match the extent of the risks. Current guardrails are inadequate to address novel and catastrophic risks from future advanced AI systems. We need specific guardrails for the most capable future AI models.
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
No
Which of the guardrails should be amended?
Establish, implement and publish an accountability process including governance, internal capability and a strategy for regulatory compliance OtherEstablish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks
Please provide any additional comments
We need to focus on developers and prevent them from shifting risks to others. The authors of the MIT AI Risk Repository noted that the complexity of AI systems makes it very difficult to understand how an AI arrives at a decision, and therefore who is responsible for the consequences. Without regulatory or legal incentives to take safety engineering seriously, developers may release poorly designed AI systems, leaving people harmed by those systems without recourse.
The "black box" nature of AI systems means that imposing substantive obligations on Australian deployers is unlikely to effectively mitigate risk in many cases. This is because deployers do not have the information needed to understand or control the underlying AI models.
The government should create incentives that force AI developers to internalize risks—rather than dodging obligations using the opaque nature of AI and legal maneuvers such as end-user license agreements.
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI?
No
How could we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for example low-risk and high-risk GPAI models? 
The proposed guardrails are insufficient to address the risks of General-Purpose AI (GPAI). Future highly capable models need targeted mitigations specific to these advanced systems. Securing model weights is crucial because if they are stolen, safeguards can be easily removed, leading to catastrophic harm—this aspect should be considered in Guardrail 3, "Protecting AI Systems." Most importantly, certain levels of model capability should not be permitted to be reached at all. The risk of theft by a motivated nation-state actor could make a dangerous, jailbroken GPAI system widely accessible. To truly mitigate these risks, we must ideally prevent the development of models that possess such potentially harmful capabilities.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A whole of economy approach – introducing a new cross-economy AI Act
What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
In my view, Australia needs an AI Act that can shape the behaviour of overseas AI developers. Regulating offshore activity can be challenging, but it should be our top priority. An AI-specific Act would have enforceable provisions targeting offshore developers, which is crucial. The best regulatory approach would be to let established regulators lead within their fields of expertise, allowing an Australian AI Act to cover any gaps and focus on shaping the behaviour of offshore AI developers.

Background  
Australia has a well -developed, robust regulatory framework for regulation  of 
therapeutic goods that  includes both pre -market (ex  ante) and post -market (ex  post) 
measures to ensure the ongoing safety, quality , and performance of all therapeutic 
goods.  
Key features of this framework include:  
• independent assessment and certification from approved third party regulators 
and assessment bodies  
• use of the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) as the basis for 
maintaining regulatory  oversight of the majority of therapeutic goods that are 
imported into, exported from , or otherwise supplied within Australia 
• ongoing reporting and surveillance requirements after a product  is approved for 
entry  in the ARTG to ensure products continue to be safe and perform as 
intended 
• a range of criminal and civil penalties that can be applied where there is failure to comply with regulatory requirements  
• legislative mechanisms which  ensure alignment with existing Australian data 
and privacy laws, as well as capability to require alignment with cybersecurity strategy requirements.

  These engagements , combined with our internal review , have led us to conclude that

Responding to the DISR consultation  
Defining high- risk AI  
The TGA agrees the use of AI in healthcare settings represents a  high- risk 
environment, and there is strong potential for adverse impact s on an individual’s 
physical or mental health . We further agree that regulatory requirements for safe and 
responsible use in these settings should be mandatory.  We note, however,  that the 
proposed principles are focused on the setting AI models and systems are used in,  as 
opposed to the specific kinds of AI models or systems  that may be used within the 
setting.  This approach differ s from that taken in the EU and Canada, where the risk is 
focused on the kind of application or the purpose of an AI model rather than the 
particular setting it is used in . 
It is crucial to note  risks associated with AI models and systems in these settings occur 
across a spectrum and are dependent on a range of factors including:  
• what the model or the system does (whether it is diagnostic, supportive of an 
administrative function, recommends a treatment plan or intervention, etc)  
• whether review of the output from the AI is regularly monitored or assessed by 
a human  
• to what extent the performance and outputs of the AI have been validated and 
verified before the AI system or model was deployed 
• the degree of influence or control which the AI exerts over an individual’s 
healthcare, and  
• to what extent intervention from a human (particularly a health care 
professional)  is able to occur when decisions are made or actions are taken by 
the AI . 
Therefore, it may be more appropriate to consider addressing the range, likelihood,  and 
severity of potential harms associated with specific AI models and systems rather than 
the setting alone. F or example, using a risk -based approach similar to  that used within 
TGA’s medical devices framework, rather than grouping all high -risk applications of AI 
into a single category.   Page 10 of 58 
  Consultation q uestions 
1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high- risk AI? Are there any 
principles we should add or remove? Please identify any:  
• low-risk use cases that are unintentionally captured 
• categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for 
defence or national security purposes.  
Yes, the proposed principles adequately capture high -risk settings where AI may 
be implemented.  However, w hile the proposed principles adequately capture 
high- risk settings, it is not accurate to say the proposed principles capture high -
risk AI  models and systems . 
No distinction between the different kinds of AI models and systems available is made 
in the proposed principles. It is therefore possible to inadvertently capture low -risk 
cases  used in high- risk settings . Digital a dministrative assistants in healthcare settings 
that do no t provide decision- making capability or suggest a diagnosis or treatment for 
individuals, for example, would not be considered to present the same level of risk as a diagnostic AI charged with reviewing patient scans and referring patients for further treatment such as a biopsy.  Under the proposals, i t would seem that there is no 
distinction between the two.

national priority.  In particular , the principles could be enhanced to ensur e the 
appropriateness and applicability of AI systems and models for First Nations 
people, through requirements for the specific inclusion of training and testing data representative of First Nations people, for AI models used within Australia.  
The Department works in partnership with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people 
to develop and implement strategies, programs , and initiatives to improve health and

decision making and Priority 4, shared access to data and information at a regional

• If you prefer a list -based approach (similar to the EU and Canada), what

Yes. The proposed principles give sufficient clarity and certainty on high- risk AI 
setting and high -risk models.  
A principles -based approach is preferred to the reduced burden when compared with 
the development of infrastructure or dedicating resources to support the development 
and maintenance of current, relevant content in a list -based approach.  A principles -
based approach also allow them to be applied strategically to account for emerging considerations.  
Guidance should include examples from real world use cases in each sector 
demonstrating how principles are applied. In our experience, providing evidence of the 
logic or reasoning behind a particular use case is more important than defining the 
explicit circumstance or product. Stakeholders must be empowered to understand and 
apply the underlying principles to their own real -world circumstances.  
The use of a list -based approach is not preferred due to the cost and administrative 
burden likely to be imposed on regulators who are required to ensure ongoing currency 
of information included  in the list . This is particularly relevant with AI in the healthcare 
sector because use cases and technologies are developing at a rapid pace.  If a list -
based approach were to be introduced, it is likely the TGA would need to dedicate 
resourcing to the development of infrastructure allowing auto- propagation of relevant 
information. Dedicated funding would need to be assigned to enable the development 
of this kind of infrastructure.  
4. Are there high -risk use cases that government should consider banning in its 
regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)? If so, how should we define these?  
No. The TGA does not support the banning of pr oducts.  However , use of AI and 
its appropriateness for any particular purpose or setting may require consideration. The importance of encouraging a strong culture and requirements 
for reporting issues and post market adverse events will be needed.  
Regulatory processes exist to ensure a risk  and evidence- based approach to the 
management of medical devices in the Australia market.  The TGA explicitly adopts a 
technology -agnostic approach where all therapeutic goods are assessed on a case -by-
case basis. This includes ensuring the AI model or system is appropriate and fit for purpose within the intended use setting, that there is adequate information made 
available to the intended user, and there are processes in place for reporting and follow 
up of any is sues, concerns or adverse events. Our approach is intended to prevent 
outcomes that will stifl e innovation, driv e questionable practices underground,  and 
reduce the likelihood that Australians will be able to access important emerging 
technologies that deliver better health outcomes . 
Furthermore, a ban on any  technology from use in therapeutic goods on the basis of 
particular features or technologies may become  problematic later on when 
technological advances  improve  the accuracy of the AI models and systems available, 
along with the ability to verify and validate their performance . Taking a risk  and 
principles -based approach to the regulation of AI and allowing for the setting of 
minimum requirements for demonstrating performance will allow regulators to 
moderate the entry of innovativ e models and systems  to the Australian market . This , 
ensur es that  any technology as it emerges and evolves, can enter the market providing 
appropriate risk mitigation occurs.

high- risk AI, such as general -purpose AI (GPAI)?   Page 12 of 58 
  Yes. As currently drafted, the proposed principles are flexible enough to capture 
new and emerging forms of high- risk AI . 
The proposed principles are broad enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-
risk AI within th e specifically defined high- risk settings.  However, as the current 
principles are centred on settings  and not specific technologies or risks associated with 
those technologies , it is conceivable that a new and emerging form of high -risk AI may 
not be captured because it is deployed in a setting that is not currently considered high-

No. All guardrails should be applied on a risk, rather than setting , basis.  
The TGA  consider it likely GPAI can be used safely in certain settings , providing 
appropriate information is available to the consumer/user.  Examples include the use of 
ChatGPT for general conversational and information purposes where appropriate 
boundaries are enforced limiting content which might be considered high-risk.

NIL response from the TGA. 
Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and 
accountability of AI  
Broadly the TGA agrees:  
• with the need for guardrails to be applied to AI models and systems used in 
high- risk settings  
• the use of guardrails in these settings aligns with international standards and approaches to governance of AI in some jurisdictions , and 
• it is critical mandatory guardrails are flexible and adaptable.  
Current alignment with the guardrails 
The TGA’s review of our existing legislation against the proposed guardrails, coupled with the targeted stakeholder workshops, indicate: 
1. Our existing regulatory framework generally aligns with the intent of the 
proposed guardrails  (see Attachment B
). 
2. Some amendments to the existing regulatory framework may be required to 
ensure all risks and opportunities associated with AI are addressed, and the 
mandatory guardrails are met . 
3. The intent of the proposed guardrails may not deliver the desired outcome depending on how they are applied.  
Emerging concerns and the need for change 
Australia’s regulatory approach to the regulation of medical devices is technology -
agnostic , an approach achieved through a risk and principles -based framework 
intended to deliver appropriate measures for risk mitigation depending on specific 
features of a medical device and/or its intended purpose. This approach provides 
flexibility and responsiveness to emerging technologies, allowing lower risk devices to  Page 13 of 58 
  enter the market expeditiously while requiring higher risk devices to undertake more 
pre-market assessment and approval procedures to ensure quality, safety , and 
performance throughout the device life cycle.  
Our concerns with the  proposed mandatory guardrails include:  
• lack of scalability to the level of risk posed by AI models and systems ; and 
• the limited information available explaining explicit requirements that will be 
imposed on specific models and systems  captured under the proposed high- risk 
principles . 
We also have further concerns with some of the terminology proposed in the 
document. In Australia, there are two main legal entities associated with medical 
devices who are regulated:  
1. Manufacturers  are generally responsible for the design, production, packaging, 
labelling , and first point of supply of a medical device under their name . Under 
our legislative framework, m anufacturers : 
a. assign an intended purpose to a medical device  
b. ensure their device is safe and fit for its intended purpose by meeting 
the essential principles , and 
c. obtain conformity assessment documentation or market authorisation evidence demonstrating their device is designed and constructed in a 
manner compliant with all regulatory requirements . 
2. Sponsors are responsible for the first point of supply of a medical device within 
Australia, whether through importation, download, sale,  or deployment from the 
place of manufacture. Under our legislative framework, sponsors:  
a. ensure all pre- market approval processes have been undertaken by 
obtaining the necessary documentation from the manufacturer  
b. ensure the device meets all relevant regulatory requirements prior to 
supply include ensuring advertising material is compliant with the 
Therapeutic Goods Advertising Code and the device is included in the 
ARTG, and  
c. meet ongoing responsibilities associated with the supply of the device as outlined above.  
Currently the Australian regulatory framework does not directly regulate agents , 
vendors , or distributors working on behalf of a sponsor . Sponsors remain responsible 
for these entities and are expected to ensure their  activities occur within established 
boundaries that will allow the sponsor to continue to meet their regulatory obligations.  
The TGA does not regulate end users of medical devices, including consumers or 
clinicians (unless they change the intended purpose of a medical device and therefore meet the definition of a manufacturer).  In this respect the current regulatory framework 
seeks to place regulatory requirements with those making and supplying devices , while 
removing burden from those who use them.  
Under the proposed definitions contained in the DISR consultation paper, t he definition 
of a manufacturer is likely to align with the “developer” term. The term “deployer” , 
however, does not align with the definition of a manufacturer or a sponsor. Its current 
scope is problematic as it appears to incorporate entities who would currently be 
considered agents, vendors, distributors , and end users of AI models and systems  
under the current framework . In health care settings this may mean regulatory 
responsibi lity for ensuring the safety, quality , and performance of medical devices is 
placed on health care professionals, practitioners , and facilities.  
Requiring these entities to engage with regulatory requirements for the integration, 
deployment , and monitoring of AI models and systems is unlikely to mitigate risks 
appropriately , primarily because many of these individuals are unlikely to have the 
appropriate resources or knowledge available to fulfil their obligations.   Page 14 of 58 
  If given effect, these current definitions will : 
• place regulatory requirements and obligations on those least likely to be able to 
meet them in the supply chain 
• increas e regulatory burdens to a wide number of stakeholders across the 
Australian economy, and  
• inevitably lead to either low rates of compliance or low uptake of emerging and 
innovative technologies.  
Consultation questions 
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used 
in high- risk settings? Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove? 
Yes. The TGA’s review of our existing regulatory framework against the 
proposed guardrails suggest the intent of the guardrails has largely already been 
met with respect to therapeutic goods (see Attachment B). There are, however, 
critical differences between what is proposed in the DISR paper and how the TGA 
currently approaches the regulation of therapeutic goods. Whether the proposed 
guardrails will appropriately mitigate risks of AI used in high- risk settings is therefore 
likely to depend on the manner in which any new  legislation is given effect to impose 
explicit require ments for  the guardrails to be met.  
Using Guardrail 5 Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve 
meaningful human oversight  provides an example : Currently , the manufacturer of a 
medical device is required to identify risks associated with features of the device and 
must then take steps to appropriately mitigate those risks or alert the end user to residual risk s which cannot be appropriately mitigated within the design and 
construction of the device.  For the purposes of Guardrail 5, there are likely to be 
examples of AI systems  used in healthcare settings where it is important that intended 
human control or intervention cannot be modified because it will interfere with the 
validated and verified performance of the device  as determined by  pre-market testing.  
Other similar e xamples include where systems intended to support radiographers with 
reviewing patient scans have had their functionality altered by healthcare facilities to 
limit features , thereby potentially inhibiting the intended performance of the AI system 
and giving rise to risks that have not been appropriately assessed and mitigated in real -
world settings . 
Such examples in the healthcare setting further demonstrate the importance of 
ensuring any guardrails that are established account for existing regulatory 
frameworks.  
 
9. How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols 
to ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve ICIP?  
As noted under consultation question 2, the TGA suggests DISR work closely with Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Stakeholders to ensure the principles are in line with the priorities for the National Agreement for Closing 
the Gap, particularly Priority 1, formal partnerships and shared decision making 
and Priority 4, shared access to data and information at a regional level.  
 
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI 
supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately? For example, are the 
requirements assigned to developers and deployers appropriate?   Page 15 of 58 
  No. As noted above, the proposed approach to lifecycle systems is appropriate 
the use of the definitions places regulatory responsibilities with entities who may 
not be able to meet those responsibilities . This document describes the full 
lifecycle approach in the Background as well as Attachment A.  
In Australia, devices are regulated across their lifecycle through two main legal entities:  
1. Manufacturers  
2. Sponsors  
The definition of a manufacturer includes the person who assigns an intended purpose 
to a medical device. This definition is likely to include the scope of the proposed 
“developer” term. Sponsors are responsible for the first point of supply of a medical 
device within Australia, whether through importation, download, sale , or deployment 
from the place of manufacture. Australian regulatory requirements currently place 
manufacturer obligations on an individual who alters a medical device’s intended 
purpose, but do not place obligations on agents , vendors , or distributors who are 
operating on behalf of the sponsor , or at subsequent steps within the supply chain.  
The term “deployer” as outlined in DISR’s proposals document may prove problematic 
as it would seem to place regulatory obligations  for ensuring the safety and ongoing 
performance of a medical device on entities who would currently be considered agents, 
vendors, distributors or indeed end users of AI models and systems. Requiring these 
entities to engage with requirements for the integration, deployment , and monitoring of 
AI models and systems is unlikely to mitigate risks appropriately, primarily because many of these individuals are unlikely to have appropriate resources or knowledge to 
fulfil their obligations.  
 
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI? 
How could we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for example low -risk 
and high- risk GPAI models?  
Whether the proposed mandatory guardrails are sufficient to address the risks of 
GPAI will depend on how they are applied to GPAI products. If the mandatory 
guardrails are considered to be guiding principles associated with specific risks 
that must be mapped and addressed on a product -specific basis, they will be 
sufficient to address associated risk s. All mandatory guardrails should be 
adapted to apply only “where applicable” with the onus for establishing where 
and when they should be applied placed on th e manufacturer (developer)  with 
documented justification.  
The TGA is of the view that all guardrails should be applied but the extent to which they 
will apply should be determined on a case- by-case basis depending on the risk posed 
by the intended purpose or foreseeable use of the device.  Our current framework for 
the regulation of medical devices does align with the intent of the proposed mandatory 
guardrails but  is applied only when a risk arises with the device.  
Again, using Guardrail 5 Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to 
achieve meaningful human oversight as an example. If a GPAI model that is a medical 
device were to be validated and verified with appropriate confidence margins in place, 
those margins would need to be maintained while the device was supplied. Which 
would only be possible providing human control is not enabled during use of the device 
by a consumer. In this instance, the intent of the guardrail (to achieve “meaningful 
human ove rsight”) is only met when human control has not been enabled.  
 
12. Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small -to-medium 
sized businesses applying guardrails?  Page 16 of 58 
  Yes. The ability to leverage existing regulatory frameworks will be a critical 
factor in limiting the regulatory burdens all businesses will experience when 
applying the guardrails.  
International models and applications should be considered along with, wherever possible, utilising and enhancing existing regulatory systems. For medical devices, all 
guardrails will need to apply on a case- by-case basis depending on the risk  associated 
with the device in question, and its intended or foreseeable use . For therapeutic goods, 
and medical devices in particular, the ability to maintain the current internationally harmonised approach to regulation,  while simultaneously  limiting the duplication of 
existing regulation through new legislative frameworks , will be a critical factor in 
ensuring regulatory burdens are minimised for small -to-medium businesses.  
Regulatory options to mandate guardrails  
The TGA acknowledges there are advantages and disadvantages associated with all 
three proposed approaches to the regulatory options for implementing the guardrails. 
With respect to the regulation of therapeutic goods and, in particular, medical devices, 
there are key concerns that must be addressed regardless of which option is chosen , 
the primary one being ensuring international alignment of medical device regulation is 
not disrupted,  thereby limiting supply . 
As discussed above, in Australia we recognise and accept appropriate pre- market 
evidence from comparable overseas regulators who are bringing medical devices to 
the Australian market. Currently the ARTG is comprised of more than 60,000 inclusions 
for medical devices. Of these inclusions:  
• Nearly 31,000 are medical devices requiring evidence of conformity 
assessment documentation from an independent third party.  
• More than 95 % are currently supported by evidence from a comparable 
overseas regulator.  
In this respect, t he implementation of mandatory guardrails through Option 3, the 
introduction of a cross -economy AI Act , is likely to cause significant and serious 
misalignment between Australia’s regulatory framework for medical devices and approaches taken in other jurisdictions. Without the ability to use pre- market evidence 
from comparable overseas regulators , which is accepted on the basis of harmonised 
requirements with other jurisdictions , costs associated with bringing medical devices to 
the Australian market will increase. The supply of medical devices is likely to be 
impacted as sponsors either choose not to enter the Australian market or increase 
costs to meet the increased burden associated with compliance.  
Option 3 , through the introduction of mandatory guardrails applicable to AI used in 
high- risk settings , will result in misalignment with internationally harmonised 
requirements by making therapeutic goods subject to further conformity assessment and compliance activities specific to Australia. This  will also have the effect of creating 
a duplicative regulatory framework by imposing similar  regulatory requirements on 
medical devices without contributing to any further risk mitigation. For this reason the 
TGA strongly recommends Option 1 or Option 2 , with a preference for Option 1.  
Option 1  – a domain -specific approach  
We consider the first option to be the safest in terms of limiting market disruption for medical devices that are, or incorporate, an AI model or system. Option 1  is also the 
most flexible in terms of providing the capability for sector -specific regulatory  Page 17 of 58 
  requirements to be introduced that will meet specific risks associated with each sector , 
whilst still aligning with the true intent of the mandatory guardrails .  
The TGA’s current public consultation process  for the clarification and strengthening of 
regulation includes proposals for regulatory refinements that would align our framework 
with the proposed mandatory guardrails.  A copy of the consultation paper is at 
Attachment C. 
We note this approach is similar to that taken by MHRA in the UK, under  the AI 
regulation: a pro -innovation approach – policy proposal  white paper , which was  
released i n March 2023. The UK’s approach was intended to provide support to 
regulators with the implementation of five principles developed to deliver safe  and 
responsible AI use , acknowledging regulators “…understand the risks in their sectors 
and are best placed to take a proportionate approach to regulating AI. This will mean 
supporting innovation and working closely with business, but also stepping in to 
address risks when necessary. By underpinning the framework with a set of principles, 
we will drive consistency  across regulators while also providing them with the flexibility 
needed. ”16 
Key advantages to Option 1 include: 
• Minimal disruption to the therapeutic goods sector in terms of administrative 
burden for sponsors of impacted therapeutic goods and, consequently, supply 
of innovative technologies to Australian consumers . 
• Retaining international harmonisation where appropriate. 
• Delivery of appropriate r efinements to existing regulation that have been 
tailored to fit the therapeutic goods sector. 
Option 2 – a framework approach  
Option 2 is likely to deliver the most consistent approach to AI regulation across the 
whole of government and the economy, while simultaneously providing a flexible outcome aimed at minimising market disruption. 
Advantages to this approach include:  
• provision of blanket policy approval from government for individual regulators to 
make refinements to their individual framework s on a case -by-case basis , which  
is likely to result in faster adoption of regulation with a reduced impact on 
resources for individual regulators; and  
• the introduction of consistent definitions and structures through an overarching 
legislative framework that can be leveraged by each regulator in their sector  is 
likely to result in a more consistent approach to the regulation of AI across the 
economy.  
In the event Option 2 is chosen, a cautious approach will need to be taken, as  
introducing an over -arching legislative framework  has the potential for broad disruption 
to the therapeutic goods sector . Disadvantages to the approach under Option 2 include 
the potential for unintended outcomes and impacts where there is a misalignment 
between proposed definitions and current definitions taken by individual regulators 
(manufacturer and sponsor versus developer and deployer, for example) . Furthermore, 
this option would require the Australian Government to make separate changes to the 
existing legislative framework for medicines, medical devices and biologicals that will 
 
16 https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai- regulation-a- pro-innovation- approach/white-
paper   Page 18 of 58 
  likely impact the application and scope of the Therapeutic Goods Act  and subordinate 
legislation.  
Option 2 will also require extensive engagement from regulators from across the 
economy to support the development of framework legislation to ensure the scope and 
intent of the guardrails are introduced appropriately  and consistently  without 
unintended consequences .  
Option 3 – a whole of economy approach  
Option 3 is the least preferred by the TGA due to the likely impact on the Australian 
therapeutic market . While there may be benefits for regulators who are new to the 
regulation of AI models and systems, Australian therapeutic goods regulation is already 
well-developed, robust , and flexible. If implemented, Option 3 is likely to result in 
problematic outcomes with serious consequences for  the therapeutic goods sector, 
including disruption to the current internationally harmonised approach Australia takes to medical device regulation.   
The flow on impact from this outcome will almost certainly lead to longer lead times for 
Australian access to medical devices that are, or incorporate, AI models and systems 
or, indeed, inability to access these kinds of devices at all.  
Consultation questions  
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high- risk 
settings? What opportunities should the government take into account in 
considering each approach? 
While t here are opportunities and risks associated with each of the three models, 
the TGA prefers Option 1 on the basis that it is the option most likely to allow 
flexible, responsive , and appropriate regulation of AI models and systems in 
therapeutic goods . 
Allowing sector -specific refinements to existing legislation to harmonise with a 
proposed strategy or policy is likely to be the fastest  solution in the therapeutic goods 
sector with the lowest amount of impact on resourcing and minimal disruption to 
supply . 
In the event that Option 2 is chosen , care will need to be taken to ensure the TGA is 
afforded flexibility with the adoption and/or enforcement of regulatory requirements . 
There are insufficient details available to understand the full impact  associated with the 
adoption of Option 2, however it is expected the Australian G overnment would be 
required to make changes to the existing regulatory framework  for therapeutic goods, 
to accommodate additional requirements established under the framework . 
It is critical that if Option 3 is chosen , therapeutic goods regulated by  the TGA are  
carved out of mandatory compliance so the current regulatory framework , and its ability 
to harmonise international ly, can be maintained.  Adoption of Option 3 would result in 
duplicative regulatory requirements and the need for additional conformity assessment 
and compliance activities, potentially by a separate regulatory body. This would lead to 
significant misalignment with international ly harmonised requirements and significant 
disruption to the sector and access to goods that incorporate AI technologies.  
  Page 19 of 58 
  14. Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the 
Australian Government should consider?  
The TGA’s framework for the regulation of therapeutic goods (and in particular, 
medical devices) is robust, flexible,  and has been developed over time to 
adequately capture the risks associated with regulating these kinds of goods . 
The Australian Government will need to consider that not all regulatory frameworks are 
as well developed with respect to existing measures that align with the guardrails.  
Regardless of the option chosen, there will be significant and extensive resourcing 
implications for all regulators and work will need to be undertaken with in each sector to 
ensure appropriate introduction of measures , with a view to minimising negative 
outcomes , for all stakeholders.  
15. Which regulatory option/s will best ensure that guardrails for high- risk AI can adapt 
and respond to step- changes in technology?  
Option 1 and Option 2 will allow flexibility for the guardrails to be applied in each 
sector in a responsive manner. Option 3 is likely to result in lost opportunities 
for flexibility and adaptability, particularly as these technologies continue to develop. It is likely Option 3 will prove more costly over time as the ramifications of 
changes are assessed across the whole of government and economy each time a 
change to the legislation is made.  
 
16. Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps or inconsistencies with Australia’s 
existing laws for the development and deployment of AI? Which regulatory option 
best addresses this, and why? 
The biggest gaps and inconsistencies with existing laws arise from the sector -
specific approaches taken to the regulation of AI . This results in adjustments to 
legislation needed to account for risks and opportunities associated with the 
introduction of these kinds of technologies. Introducing a whole- of-government 
approach through a strategy/policy paper or framework legislation (Options 1 and 2) is 
likely to address these concerns , while affording sector -specific flexibility to ensure 
ramifications for the market are managed appropriately.  
A further consideration with respect to gaps and inconsistencies is the current lack of information available for stakeholders about how existing laws are applied to AI models 
and systems. Stakeholders are universally reporting that confusion and lack of 
information are the primary source of failure to understand the risks associated with AI 
models and systems, and failure to meet their existing regulatory requirements.  
Regardless of the legislative option adopted within Australia, a dedicated, cohesive,  
and joined- up approach needs to be taken with  the communication of legislative 
requirements and their real-world impact for all cohorts of stakeholders .

V1.0 September 2024   Page 27 of 58 Introduction  
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has already made a difference to many lives, providing the potential to solve 
problems faster, and opening up opportunities to get things done in smarter and better ways. If safely 
deployed, its development and adoption can improve wellbeing, quality of life and economic growth. 
At the same time, caution is needed as AI presents a potential to create or amplify harms to 
individuals, organisations, communities and social cohesion through risks associated with its use 
including inherent bias, accuracy and data quality. These harms may disproportionally affect 
vulnerable and marginalised groups including people with cognitive disability, displaced workers, older 
people, culturally and linguistically diverse communities, regional communities, women, girls, gender diverse people and people who are mentally or physically unwell.  
Due to the number of unknowns around how AI works in the general public, there is low public trust that AI systems are being designed, developed, deployed and used safely and responsibly, 
particularly in high -risk settings.
17 People are concerned about personal privacy, the impact of bias 
and errors, and a near future where people can’t tell real from fake.  
In the 2024- 25 federal Budget, the Australian Government provided $39.9 million over 5 years for the 
development of policy and capability across government to support the adoption and use of AI 
technology in a safe and responsible manner. Through the budget measure for Safe and Responsible 
AI, the Australian Government is acting to ensure the design, development and deployment of AI 
systems in Australia in legitimate but high- risk settings, is safe and can be relied upon, while ensuring 
the use of AI in low -risk settings can continue to flourish largely unimpeded.  
The measure includes clarifying and strengthening existing laws to address risks and harms from AI, through an immediate review of the priority areas of health and aged care sector regulation, the 
Australian Consumer Law and copyright law.  
As part of the Australian Government’s Department of Health and Aged Care (the Department), the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) regulates therapeutic goods, including AI models and 
systems when they meet the definition of a medical device under Section 41BD of the 
Therapeutic 
Goods Act 1989 . T he TGA has issued this consultation paper as part of the review of priority areas in 
the health and aged care sector. The Department is concurrently completing a broader review  of the 
health and aged care regulation and legislation.  
This consultation seeks feedback on proposals identified for mitigating risks and leveraging opportunities associated with the use of AI models and systems across our regulated environment, and complements the Department’s broader review
.  
High-risk settings and proposed guardrails 
The Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR) is leading the whole- of-government Safe 
and Responsible Use of AI agenda. One proposal is to establish “guardrails” for the development and deployment of AI systems in high- risk settings, while allowing AI use in low -risk settings within the 
bounds of existing laws.  
The proposed principles underpinning the concept of an AI system designated as high- risk due to its 
use are:  
a) The risk of adverse impacts to an individual’s rights recognised in Australian human rights law 
without justification, in addition to Australia’s international human rights law obligations  
b) The risk of adverse impacts to an individual’s physical or mental health or safety

V1.0 September 2024   Page 28 of 58 c) The risk of adverse legal effects, defamation or similarly significant effects on an individual  
d) The risk of adverse impacts to groups of individuals or collective rights of cultural groups  
e) The risk of adverse impacts to the broader Australian economy, society, environment and rule 
of law  
f) The severity and extent of those adverse impacts outlined in principles (a) to (e) above.  
These principles set a foundation for defining high- risk AI where the proposed uses of an AI system 
are known or foreseeable. Ten mandatory guardrails are currently proposed for AI models and 
systems in high- risk settings. The guardrails are intended to place obligations across the AI supply 
chain and throughout the AI lifecycle to effectively prevent harms before people interact with, or are 
subject to, an AI system. These obligations are intended to primarily apply to developers and 
deployers of AI models  and systems.  
The proposed guardrails are:  
• Establish, implement and publish an accountability process including governance, internal 
capability and a strategy for regulatory compliance.  
• Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks.  
• Protect AI systems and implement data governance measures to manage data quality and 
provenance.  
• Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the system once deployed.  
• Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight.  
• Inform end- users regarding AI -enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI -generated 
content.  
• Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcomes.  
• Be transparent with other organisations across the supply chain of an AI system or model to 
help them effectively address risks.  
• Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails.  
• Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with the guardrails.  
 
The DISR consultation on proposals for principles to define high- risk settings, mandatory guardrails 
that should apply in those settings and options for applying the guardrails is now open
.

encouraged to provide a response directly to the DISR public consultation to specifically address the high-risk settings principles or the impact of proposed mandatory guardrails on therapeutic goods,

The TGA is Australia's government authority responsible for evaluating, assessing and monitoring 
products that are defined as therapeutic goods. The TGA regulates therapeutic goods including medicines, medical devices and biologicals to help Australians stay healthy and safe.  
Products that meet the legislative definition of a therapeutic good under the 
Therapeutic Goods Act 
1989  ( the Act) are regulated by the TGA. These products generally require pre- market approval and 
inclusion in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods  (ARTG) before they can be imported, 
exported or supplied in Australia.  Therapeutic Goods Administration

Potential changes to the Act  
The increasing use of AI models and systems across the regulated environment, as well as the rising 
number of software products that meet the definition of a medical device, means a review of the 
language used in legislation, regulations and associated legislative instruments is required. The 
Therapeutic Goods Act 1989  (the Act) and subordinate legislation were drafted using definitions and 
language intended to capture activities in the sector including:  
who is responsible for the manufacture and supply of therapeutic goods  Therapeutic Goods Administration

Currently the focus of the Act is centred on activities conducted by human beings. Technological 
advancements mean many of these activities are increasingly performed by complex algorithms, 
including AI models and systems.  
There are two key potential changes of language and definitions currently in use within the 
Therapeutic Goods Act 1989  and subordinate legislation:  
1. Potential changes to definitions to further clarify regulatory responsibility where software and 
products that are, or incorporate, AI models and systems are therapeutic goods.  
2. Potential changes to language about activities previously performed by human beings when they are now performed by engineered systems, including AI models and systems.  
 
The following proposals are intended to clarify responsibility for the deployment and use of AI models 
and systems.  
Definitions  
While definitions used in the Act may still adequately describe the entities and activities responsible at 
the appropriate time, stakeholders have indicated potential changes to the definitions would provide 
clarity and strengthen regulation. Similar language changes have been included in other jurisdictions, including the EU’s  AI Act  2024 and Canada’s proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act
. Examples 
of definitions that potentially could be recommended for change include:  
“Supply”, to include language about the availability of software products from virtual platforms, for 
example website or app stores.  
“Manufacturer” to include the appropriate legal entity responsible for the development and 
deployment of software products that are medical devices.  
“Sponsor” to include a person who provides, hosts, or facilitates access to software products that 
are medical devices, particularly when they are accessible through data transfer or online 
platforms only.  
Language  
AI models and systems have changed the way therapeutic goods are deployed and used. Not only 
are some medical devices now able to be accessed online, AI models and systems are replacing 
some services and activities traditionally performed by human beings. Who is responsibility for these 
activities is an emerging challenge, particularly with continuous learning and generative AI. For 
example, outputs are not always continuously validated as the system evolves over time, and the original deployer or user of the system may not have sufficient awareness or oversight of the activities 
the software performs. In other circumstances, a software system may be deployed or configured by 
an administrator, a medical clinic or health service, but a health professional using the software is not 
made aware of the performance or limitations of the software.  
Clarity is required for who is responsible and liable for the outputs of these systems, particularly when 
their activities constitute a breach of the Act or other laws. The Therapeutic Goods Act 1989
 (the Act) 
and subordinate legislation is no exception. Within the Act there are civil and criminal offences including many that are strict liability (where responsibility for an offence is not dependent on the 
ability to show fault or intent). In addition to a review of definitions to ensure clarity for stakeholders, 
we are proposing to review the current language used to define responsibility for meeting legal 
obligations. This will ensure penalties for civil and criminal offences can continue to be applied to the 
most appropriate legal entity associated with the use of an AI model or system.  Therapeutic Goods Administration

Potential changes to medical device regulation  
The TGA regulates AI when it meets the legislative definition of a medical device in Section 41BD of 
the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 . AI products likely to meet this definition include those that are 
intended to be used for the diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, prediction, prognosis, treatment, or 
alleviation of a disease, injury or disability.  
Regulatory requirements for medical devices, including software, are principles -based and apply 
regardless of whether the product incorporates components like AI, chatbots, cloud, mobile apps, or 
other technologies. As such, software that incorporates generative AI such as large language models 
(LLMs), text generators, and multimodal generative AI are all regulated as a medical device  if they 
meet the definition  under the Act.  
Clinical and technical evidence must be available to demonstrate the safety, reliability and performance of the product using AI to the same standard as other medical devices – for higher risk 
products, clinical and technical evidence requirements are more stringent. For AI products that are regulated as medical devices, feedback from our targeted workshops indicated:  
Australia’s current approach to the regulation of medical devices, which relies heavily on 
international harmonisation, should be maintained.  
The current classification rules and requirements for medical devices are generally sufficient to 
allow appropriate regulation and adequately mitigate risks associated with AI.  
The current exclusion of some software products may no longer be appropriate, given their 
increasing complexity and the rising use of AI.
