Medical devices are regulated based on the risk they pose when used as intended. In Australia the 
risk posed by a device is determined using “classification rules”, where factors impacting the 
classification of a medical device include:  
Where in the human body the device is intended to be used.  
How long the device is intended to be used continuously.  
Whether the device is intended for use by a consumer or a health professional.  
Whether information is provided for monitoring, or to inform a diagnostic or treatment decision.  
 
The classification rules are detailed in Schedule 2 of the Therapeutic Goods (Medical Devices) 
Regulations 2002 . T here are specific rules for programmed or programmable medical devices or 
software that is a medical device which will apply to devices that are, or incorporate, an AI system or 
model. An extract of Schedule 2 containing these specific rules is at Attachment A . 
Classification rules 4.5(1) and 4.5(2)  
All AI models and systems that:  
meet the definition of a medical device  
are solely intended to provide a prediction or prognosis for a disease or condition  
are currently regulated as Class I medical devices.  
AI-enabled devices are increasingly being used to predict clinical outcomes or provide prognostic 
information about a particular disease or treatment. The existing classification rules do not explicitly 
account for products intended for prediction or prognosis, meaning a default risk classification of 
Class  I currently applies. This is not considered appropriate in cases where this information is used to 
determine treatment plans or interventions which could have a significant and detrimental impact on patients if the prediction or prognosis is not accurate.  
A potential amendment of the current classification rules 4.5(1) and 4.5(2) to include prediction or 
prognosis would mean these devices would be classified at a higher level, depending on how serious 
the disease or condition they are providing information about is and whether the information is being 
provided to a clinician or a consumer.

The essential principles are safety and performance requirements for all medical devices, including 
in vitro diagnostic (IVD) devices. These requirements are detailed in Schedule 1 of the Therapeutic 
Goods (Medical Devices) Regulations 2002 . Manufacturers must ensure their devices meet all 
relevant principles  a nd sponsors must either hold or be able to obtain this evidence from their 
manufacturer on request.  
Principles -based regulation, as opposed to prescriptive or rules -based regulation, provides flexibility. 
This approach accommodates the broad complexity and diversity of medical devices regulated, 
including as new technologies like AI emerge. A rules -based approach may, for example, require 
compliance with prescribed requirements including international standards.  Demonstrating compliance with the essential principles may include compliance with relevant international standards, but for emerging technologies where an appropriate standard may not yet exist, other approaches 
may be used. The flexibility to adapt the principles to the unique circumstances of a medical device, 
particularly those incorporating emerging technologies, allows approaches to evolve over time without 
continuous review and updating of legislative frameworks.

Software exclusions 
In 2021, changes to the Regulations commenced that “carved out” out a number of software- based 
products from TGA oversight on the basis that:  
they presented a very low risk to users and/or  
they were not medical devices to begin with, and clarity was required for stakeholders and/or  
existing oversight measures were available through other regulatory frameworks to ensure these 
products were safe and fit for their intended purpose.  
 
These exclusions are detailed in the Therapeutic Goods (Excluded Goods) Determination 2018 .  
 
Since 2021 the TGA has been monitoring the exclusions and has received feedback from interested 
stakeholders, as well as through the targeted workshops that indicate the increasing complexity of 
some excluded software products and the increasing use of AI mean the exclusions may no longer be 
appropriate for:  
Consumer health products (Schedule 1, Item 14B)  
Digital mental health tools (Schedule 1, Item 14E)  
Software that is a calculator (Schedule 1, Item 14L)  
Laboratory information management systems (Schedule 1, Item 14O)

Laboratory information management systems  
Laboratory information management systems are software- based products intended to support the 
operation of a laboratory. Functionality includes managing samples and associated data. These kinds 
of systems are excluded in certain circumstances under Schedule 1, Item 14O of the Therapeutic 
Goods (Excluded Goods) Determination 2018:  
software that is a laboratory information management system (however named or described) and 
is not intended by its manufacturer to:  
(a) manipulate information or data to change, or generate new, diagnostic outputs (other than automating simple calculations or generating report comments); or  
(b) prevent, monitor, predict, make a prognosis of, treat or alleviate a disease, condition, ailment 
or defect  
As with other software exclusions, increasing functionality and changes to the way these kinds of 
products are used mean exclusion may no longer be appropriate.  
Potential changes to exclusions  
There are two reasons for proposing potential changes to the current exclusions:  
1. Where an exclusion has been given for clarity, increasing complexity and technological 
advancements means these products have evolved and may no longer be a general 
consumer good and – in many cases – now meet the definition of a medical device and may 
pose risks to users. Many developers are not recognising this shift and therefore, not seeking regulatory approval.  
2. While many of the exclusions would remain appropriate if they were utilised within the original conditions of the exclusion, there is scope creep where the intended purpose of the excluded goods changes over time as functionality becomes available, introducing a higher level of risk Therapeutic Goods Administration

Potential options for change include:  
1. Removing the exclusion for some of these kinds of products and regulating them under the 
medical device framework.  
2. Removing the exclusion of these kinds of products and introducing an exemption for certain products (more information about exemption versus exclusion can be found on the TGA website here
). 
3. Changing the current conditions of exclusion for these kinds of products.  
 
Exemption of products rather than exclusion provides a pathway to the supply of medical devices with 
a reduced regulatory burden for sponsors as exempt products are regulated by the TGA but are not 
required to be included in the ARTG before they are supplied. Advantages of this approach include 
the TGA’s ability to take post -market action against these kinds of products when they do not meet 
the requirements for medical devices in terms of demonstrating safety, quality and performance; or 
where adverse events warrant a recall activity.

Transparency  
Transparency has been raised as a consistent issue with the use of AI across all stakeholder groups, 
particularly consumers and clinicians, who would like to be able to identify the use of AI models and 
systems more easily. Identifying what transparency about AI use means, and the expectations of 
different stakeholders, has been difficult because:  
AI is a broad term covering multiple capabilities, functionalities and technologies  
the use of AI is already prevalent and integrated within existing systems, to varying degrees  
the application of AI within these models and systems is so varied that identifying the use of AI 
may not always contribute meaningfully to the mitigation of risks. For example, knowing 
where AI has been used to manage quality control in the manufacture of  a medicine is 
unlikely to provide a real -world benefit or significant risk mitigation to consumers or clinicians.  
 
Stakeholders have identified there is unlikely to be one approach that would adequately address the 
need for greater transparency. They have indicated the ability to identify the use of AI is more 
important where an AI model or system has been used to generate a result or propagate data that may require their review or input to ensure accuracy. For example, where a digital scribe product is 
suggesting a diagnosis based on the information provided during a consultation with the patient.

12.1  Programmed or programmable medical device or software that is a medical device  
 (1) A programmed or programmable medical device, or software that is a medical device, 
that is intended to make use of either or both of data and information must be designed 
and produced in a way that ensures that:  
(a) the safety, performance, reliability, accuracy, precision, useability, security and 
repeatability of the device are appropriate for the intended purpose of the device; 
and 
(b) any consequent risks, or impairment of performance, associated with one or more 
fault conditions is eliminated or appropriately reduced; and  
(c) the device is resilient with respect to interactions that could occur during the use of 
the device and that could result in unsafe performance of the device; and  
(d) if relevant to the safety of a patient, or the safety and health of the user or any other person, the device provides suitable warnings in a timely manner:  
 (i) following the disruption to services upon which the device is dependent for the device’s operation; and  
 (ii) following the performance of the device being adversely affected; and  
(e) if relevant to the safety of a patient, or the safety and health of the user or any other person, the device provides a means by which the user can verify correct operation of the device; and  
(f) if relevant to the safety of a patient, or the safety and health of the user or any other person, the integrity and quality of the data or information is maintained; and  
(g) if relevant, the privacy of the data or information is maintained.  
 (2) A programmed or programmable medical device, or software that is a medical device, must be developed, produced and maintained having regard to the generally 
acknowledged state of the art (including for design, development life cycle, development 
envir onment, version control, quality and risk management, security, verification and 
validation, change and configuration management and problem resolution).  
 (3) A programmed or programmable medical device, or software that is a medical device, that is intended to be used in combination with computing platforms must be designed 
and developed taking into account the capability, resources and configuration of the 
platforms and the external factors (including information technology environments) 
related to the use of the platforms.  
 (4) The manufacturer of a programmed or programmable medical device, or software that is 
a medical device, must provide instructions or information with the device that sets out requirements (including requirements about hardware, software, information technology 
environments and security measures) necessary to operate the device as intended.  
 (5) A programmed or programmable medical device, or software that is a medical device, 
must be designed, produced and maintained with regard to best practice in relation to 
software, security and engineering to provide cybersecurity of the device, includi ng 
where appropriate the following:  
(a) protection against unauthorised access, unauthorised influence or unauthorised manipulation;  
(b) minimisation of risks associated with known cybersecurity vulnerabilities (including 
either or both of remediation of known vulnerabilities and application of 
compensating controls);  
(c) facilitation of the application of updates, patches, compensating controls and other 
improvements;  Therapeutic Goods Administration

The following definitions are provided to assist in your understanding of the concepts and terminology 
used in this consultation paper or that may be included in your submission to the consultation.  
Artificial Intelligence (AI) system: a machine- based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, 
infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, 
recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. Different AI 
systems vary in their levels of autonomy and adaptiveness after deployment.19 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) system and model20: 
• AI model:  the raw, mathematical essence that is often the ‘engine’ of AI applications.  
• AI system:  the ensemble of several components, including one or more AI models, that is 
designed to be particularly useful to humans in some way.  
For example, the ChatGPT app is an AI system. Its core engine, GPT -4, is an AI model.  
AI lifecycle : All events and processes that relate to an AI system's lifespan. This spans from inception 
to decommissioning, including its design, research, model development, training, deployment, 
integration, operation, maintenance, sale, use, and governance.   
AI supply chain: the complex network of actors and organisations that enable the use and supply of AI 
throughout the AI lifecycle from model design, testing and fine tuning to deployment and integration 
into the local IT system.  
General -purpose AI (GPAI) : a type of AI system or model that addresses a broad range of tasks and 
uses, both intended and unintended by developers.  
Generative AI model:  an AI model with the capability of learning to generate content such as images, 
text, and other media with similar properties to its training data.  
LLMs : Large language models are a type of AI model trained on language datasets so they can 
recognise and generate text emulating human language.  
Machine Learning: a set of techniques that can be used to train AI algorithms to improve performance 
at a task based on data. Real -world examples of AI and machine learning technologies include21: 
• An imaging system that uses algorithms to give diagnostic information for skin cancer in 
patients.  
• A smart sensor device that estimates the probability of a heart attack.  
Narrow AI system : a type of AI system or model that is focused on defined tasks and uses to address 
a specific problem. Unlike GPAI models, these types of AI systems cannot be used for a broader 
range of problems without being re- designed.

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high -risk AI? Are there any

a. low-risk use cases that are unintentionally captured  
The principles focus on adverse impacts to human rights, health, legal effects, and 
systemic risks, but risk overgeneralisation without distinguishing contextual factors that 
lower the risk of AI use.  
A broad principles -based approach risks capturing AI applications in sectors where 
automation and AI serve low -stakes functions, such as AI -driven scheduling tools or 
customer service chatbots used in benign contexts like retail. These systems, while 
automated, do not pose significant risks to human rights, safety, or the broader societal

Overregulation of such systems could stifle small -to-medium businesses that rely on 
these tools for efficiency. Another low -risk case involves AI in weather pattern 
monitoring —an important function but one where transparency and human oversight 
already reduce ri sks.  
The principles should be refined to exclude AI systems with minimal legal or societal 
implications and low probability of harm in contexts where human intervention already 
mitigates risks.  
b. categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for defence or 
national security purposes.  
Defence and national security AI applications are highly context -specific and can carry 
different implications compared to civilian applications.  
AI in defence and national security contexts should be regulated separately due to unique 
considerations like classified data, national security implications, and the risk of state 
actors leveraging AI for intelligence or cyber warfare. The broad applicati on of the 
proposed principles to these domains may conflict with the operational secrecy required 
in these fields. For instance, AI systems used in military decision -making or autonomous

while providing little additional safety or ethical assurance.  Public Submission : Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings

such as automated land management systems that disregard traditional ecological

communities.

Indigenous Data Sovereignty, and the need for AI systems to align with First Nations

exploitation and marginalisation of Indigenous communities and ensure AI respects

Department of Industry, Science and Resources 
Industry House 
10 Binara Street
Canberra, ACT

Submission by the Uniting Church in Australia, Synod of Victoria and Tasmania, and U Ethical to the Safe and responsible AI in Australia. Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings
 4 October 2024

The Uniting Church in Australia, Synod of Victoria and Tasmania, and U Ethical make the welcome the opportunity to make a submission to the Safe and responsible AI in Australia. Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings. 

The membership of the Uniting Church in Australia is deeply concerned about child sexual abuse. There is an explicit statement opposing child sexual abuse from the Uniting Church National Assembly Standing Committee meeting of March 2013 (ASC Minute 13.07.03): 
The sexual abuse of children is criminal behaviour that is totally abhorrent and unacceptable.

The Synod and U Ethical are deeply concerned about serious human rights abuses that occur online or are facilitated online, including child exploitation. 

A growing body of behavioural science research shows that our interaction with technology changes our behaviour as people. This branch of psychology has been labelled cyber-psychology. Clinical psychologist Michael Seto has stated concerning our engagement with the online world because the technology companies rolling out products that have not been tested for their behavioural impact: "We are living through the largest unregulated social experiment of all time…." Generative AI is another phase of the online social experiment.

Turning to investment risks and opportunities present in generative AI, there is no doubt that predications of generative AI outline future financial gains across almost every sector of the economy. They also bring a variety of risks and harms that are occurring in the here and now. The human rights and environmental risks in particular offer harms at a societal level both here in Australia and globally.

As an ethical investor, we engage with portfolio companies on a range of environmental and social/human rights issues where we see that using our voice to seek assurances of enhanced management of ESG risks and opportunities is of material value. We will also use our entitlements, such as proxy voting, to support or oppose corporate actions in accordance with our ethical policy.

Some risks and opportunities, however, present at the systems level, leading us to use our voice to advocate for systems-level change to mitigate risk and maximise opportunity.

Generative AI, in particular, is one of those issues. The risk that generative AI can be used in the production of child sex abuse material poses a real and potent harm to a wide variety of economic institutions and companies in Australia, risking damage to companies’ social licence to operate and grow, as well as potential legal risks. Companies at risk are not only in the IT and communications sectors but, in the case of child sex abuse material, touch on sectors such as banking and financial services as potential facilitators of payment for said material. We cite as an example the $1.3 billion fine levied against Westpac by AUSTRAC for breaches of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act, including failing to conduct due diligence on suspicious transactions associated with possible child exploitation. 

We agree with the Australian Government’s view that the current Australian regulatory system for AI is not fit for purpose to respond to the distinct risks that AI poses.

We support the Government’s proposed application of the precautionary principle with a balance between ex ante (preventative) and ex post (remedial) regulatory measures to effectively target and mitigate known risks. Given the severe, widescale harms identified in the proposals paper for AI developments that carry such risks (such as weaponization, the widescale spread of disinformation that undermines our democracy and promoting large scale discrimination against minority groups in society), we strongly support the regulation erring on the side of caution to prevent such harms before they happen.
1.  Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI? Are there any principles that we should add or remove?
We support the existing proposed principles to determine if an AI system is high risk, while recommending the following amendments:
* Under (a) it should be explicit that the impact on an individual rights should apply to people located overseas as well as in Australia, to capture, for example, an AI tool that would allow Australian perpetrators to sexually abuse children online where the children are located overseas; and,
* Under (e) the risk of adverse impacts to Australian or foreign democracies (Australia should not be a jurisdiction that allows for foreign interference in the democracies of other jurisdictions) and to social cohesion.
4. Are there high-risk use cases that the government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk). If so, how should we define these?

The Government should ban generative AI apps developed with the purpose of removing a person’s clothing from an image of a real person that is not the user or a person who has clearly consented to their image being used, especially images of children who can never consent to the production of child sexual abuse material.

AI-generated child sexual abuse material can also be used in the sexual extortion of children. A child threatened with AI-generated sexual images of them can be coerced to provide real sexual abuse images of themselves. 

The eSafety Commissioner stated of such apps:
It is difficult to conceive of a purpose for these apps outside of the nefarious. Some might wonder why apps like this are allowed to exist at all, given their primary purpose is to sexualise, humiliate, demoralise, denigrate or create child sexual abuse material of girls according to the predator’s personal predilection. A Bellingcat investigation found that many such apps are part of a complex network of nudifying apps owned by the same holding company that effectively disguises detection of the primary purpose of these apps in order to evade enforcement action.

In March 2024, it was reported that ClothOff had more than four million monthly visits and invited users to “undress anyone using AI.” It charged £8.50 for 25 credits and did not provide meaningful age verification for users.

Many AI apps will provide nude images without the consent of the person being portrayed. Many allow for free trials before charging for ongoing use.

Recent investigations have uncovered the existence of organised sexual extortion groups. These groups operate across borders and use call centre-like operations in order to communicate with hundreds of potential victims at once. 

In December 2022, the US FBI issued a public safety alert about an “explosion” of financial sexual extortion schemes targeting children and teenagers. The number of reports the US National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) received on that form of cybercrime increased by 7,200% between 2021 and 2022.

The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) has reported that perpetrators are taking images of their ‘favourite’ child sexual abuse victims and using generative AI to create images of the victim in any setting, scenario or sexual activity they can imagine. One offender shared links to fine-tuned generative AI models for 128 different named real victims of child sexual abuse. 

The negative psychological impacts of sexual extortion include feelings of low self-esteem, withdrawal, worthlessness, anger and guilt. In some cases, victims have engaged in self-harm or killed themselves. In Victoria alone, 13 young Victorians have ended their own lives as a result of online sexual extortion or image-based abuse in the last decade. 

The Government should ban generative AI chatbots that allows for sexual communication with a simulated child. There are generative AI models and apps that provide an AI chatbot girlfriend who can give advice on how to kidnap a child to sexually abuse them. The apps offer advice on coercive control, what drugs to use on the child and where to obtain them. They also provide advice on counter-measures against law enforcement investigations, such as destroying evidence and manipulating artifacts of abuse, or advice on ensuring victims do not disclose. Some of these chatbots themselves simulate children. Some of these AI chatbots have few or no limits to the topics or content of conversation. The Government should ban chatbots that provide advice on how to use AI tools to make child sexual abuse material or advice on how to abuse children sexually. 
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
As noted in the proposals paper, GPAI can:
* generate and disseminate disinformation at an unprecedented scale that is difficult to detect;
* be used to increase the scale and sophistication of scams and frauds and generate fake compromising content; and,
* create biased systems that discriminate against people based on race, gender, age and disability status causing substantial harm.
Thus, the mandatory guardrails should apply to all GPAI models, as has been required in the draft Canadian legislation.
Definitions of Developer and Deployer
We support the proposed definitions of AI “developer” and “deployer”. Where it is not clear where an individual or organization is clearly a developer or a deployer, then the requirements of both categories should apply to them to avoid people seeking to game the requirements by seeking to find loopholes in the definitions and obligations.
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI in high-risk settings? Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?
While the existing proposed guardrails are worthwhile, additional safeguards are needed. We believe that there should be an over-arching guardrail for developers that requires them to ensure their product is “safe by design”. Further, where children are able to use an AI product or be subjected to an AI product, the developers and deployers of the product should ensure that it is designed with the best interests of the child as a guardrail.

There should be an additional guardrail for developers, to require them to modify their product if it is found to have unacceptable harmful impacts after it is made available for use, which goes beyond the monitoring outlined in proposed guardrail 4. The eSafety Commissioner has stated that generative AI developers must keep improving their models to engineer out harmful or illegal outputs as they emerge, as it is unlikely all harms will be mitigated before release.

There is a need for additional specific guardrails to protect against the use of AI products being used to generate child sexual abuse material. To that end:
* developers should be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the products they are developing have safeguards against misuse and cannot be easily used to generate child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate images. Such safeguards should include not training generative AI on databases that include child sexual abuse material and not allowing users to enter requests that would result in the generation of child sexual abuse material, as outlined in proposed guardrail 3. There needs to be a power for a regulator to take down a generative AI model until such time as it can be made safe from generating child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate images; 
* Developers should be required to have nominated individuals or teams accountable for ensuring the safety of their product; and,
* Developers should be required to add points of friction, such as educative prompts and nudges, when users attempt to generate illegal or harmful content, which can be an important method of reducing misuse.

AI developers can restrict how their technology can be used, and so the guardrails need to be thorough enough that developers are required to build in safeguards that would be reasonable to include. For example, text-to-image AI companies generally seek to disallow the production of pornography and extreme violence material. It can be possible to limit what some AI models can generate by limiting the training data they have been exposed to. In some cases, if the developers have not exposed the model to pornography, it will not be able to generate pornography. In some cases, developers may be able to block the entry of certain terms into the AI software to prevent the generation of child sexual abuse material.

Thus, generating child sexual abuse material and pornography more generally, has been blocked on some generative AI models with closed source.

CivitAI has stated that resources needed to train the AI to generate the likeness of a specific individual on their site must be non-commercial and non-sexual and may be removed upon request of the person depicted. While such a policy offers some limited protection, it is disappointing that the onus of permission to use an image is reversed. The person needs to complain to get an image of them removed rather than CivitAI needing to assure itself that an image is being used with the consent of the person in question.

Research from December 2023 discovered that the LAION-5B image dataset contained 3,226 entries of suspected child sexual abuse material. Much of that material was confirmed as child sexual abuse material by third parties. LAION-5B was used to train the Stable Diffusion generative AI model. Thus, a version of the Stable Diffusion model had been trained to generate child sexual abuse material for users who request it. The developers of LAION-5B did seek to detect child sexual abuse material in the dataset. Stable Diffusion 1.5 was trained on sexually explicit material. In the subsequent 2.0 version of Stable Diffusion, “unsafe” content was filtered out of the training dataset. Thus, it became difficult to generate sexually explicit material with version 2.0. A significant proportion of users, therefore, preferred Stable Diffusion 1.5 for generating sexually explicit material. Subsequently, Stability AI released Stable Diffusion 2.1, which took 2.0 as a base and further trained it on both “safe” and moderately “unsafe” material.

As evidence of the need for thorough guardrails to require developers to do all they reasonably can to make their products safe by design, the IWF has reported that child sexual abuse perpetrators on a dark web forum are looking forward to further advancements in the ability to use AI to generate child sexual abuse videos. One stated:
How long until we can get this new Sora software to make whatever video we want? I want to put my sister’s photos in from when she was a kid and make her do nasty things.
Another stated:
Am seeing the video trailers that were generated by AI, and my mind is blown… The ability to create any child porn we desire … our wildest fantasies… in high definition.
Such evidence makes the case for governments to get ahead of the harm that will result if developers are not adequately regulated to provide safeguards against the misuse of their products.

Proposed guardrail 7 will need to specify that complaint handling systems must be highly accessible, easy to find, easy to use, transparent and timely in their processing of complaints. Public trust in complaint handling mechanisms will be undermined where these standards are not met. 

While it is likely that technically sophisticated perpetrators will be able to defeat safeguards and misuse some generative AI software with built-in safeguards, it is likely to restrict the proportion of perpetrators that will be able to generate child sexual abuse material. To argue against safeguards is like arguing that we should have no firearm restrictions in Australia because some criminals will always be able to circumvent them. 
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately? For example, are the requirements assigned to developers and deployers appropriate?
We believe that there needs to be clear obligations of service providers that host or provide access to AI products and services. For example, app hosts should not sell or make accessible harmful AI apps. Search engine platforms should be required not to return results to users for generative AI services to produce child sexual abuse material or other harmful material, in addition to the existing obligations under the Search Engine Services Code not to return search results that contain child sexual abuse material. Search engines should be provided with a defence that they have taken meaningful steps to ensure they are not returning such results.
12. Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small-to-medium sized businesses applying guardrails?
Any reduction in the need for regulatory compliance by small-to-medium sized businesses should not undermine the need to prevent harmful AI products being developed and made available. Where a business is not able to meet the obligation to develop or provide safe AI products and services, it is better they are not able to operate in the AI space than compromise community safety and pass on the costs of their non-compliance in the form of harms inflicted on others. 
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings? What opportunities should the government take into account in considering each approach?
Given the serious harms that can occur from AI development and deployment, we strongly favour Option 3 that would see the creation of a comprehensive Australian AI Act for the reasons outlined as to the benefits of such an approach in the proposals paper. Such an Act would be best placed to address gaps, inconsistencies and fragmentation in the regulation of AI. As pointed out in the proposals paper, the risk of duplication can be minimised by well-designed legislation with appropriate regulation-making powers to allow for flexibility as AI technology further develops. Having a well-resourced regulator to ensure implementation and compliance with the Act will reduce regulatory uncertainty where it is not clear which regulator is responsible for an action.

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
While the proposed principles are broad and cover high-risk AI use cases, it will be important to ensure that they are not so broad as to inadvertently capture many low-risk use cases unintentionally as high-risk (particularly with respect to medical devices).
Importantly, risk assessment/ risk management in line with internationally recognised standards such as ISO 13485 – Medical Devices – Quality management systems – Requirements for regulatory purposes - and ISO 14971 – Medical Devices – Application of risk management to medical devices will be critical for appropriately defining high-risk within the framework of medical devices incorporating AI.
Are there any principles we should add or remove?
No
Please identify any:
It is essential for the ongoing access to latest technology in Australia that the framework and guardrails align to avoid unintentional capture of low risk medical devices. It will also be important that the guardrails align with international requirements for medical devices to ensure that there is no regulatory barrier, thereby ensuring that the Australian public can continue to have access to the latest technology. This situation can be avoided by adopting either regulatory option 1 or 2, and using the TGA framework for medical device assessment. This could be achieved relatively simply, as the DISR 10 guardrails align with TGA's guidelines.
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
Recommend consultation with First Nations people, communities and Country.
3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?
YES the principles give enough clarity and certainty
If you prefer a principles-based approach, what should we address in guidance to give the greatest clarity?
A principles-based approach is preferred.
Regulations need to be detailed and ambiguity removed so they can be applied consistently and enforced easily.
Guidance documents would also benefit from including a (non-exhaustive) list of examples of high-risk use cases in specific areas, including for medical devices.
How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
Existing TGA definitions are technology agnostic and therefore provide adequate coverage of emerging uses of AI. This framework should be used to ensure continued harmonisation with global requirements for these types of products and avoid any unintended consequences of the introduction of a separate framework.
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
A risk management approach is required and TGAs (total lifecycle) approach that encompasses ongoing monitoring of safety and performance and includes reference to international standards and quality management system (QMS) certification are required as part of the appropriate mitigation of risks for medical devices. TGAs processes also already align with international regulatory and conformity assessment processes, therefore these should be leveraged to ensure the appropriate balance between mitigating risk and facilitating access to new technology.
Further clarity of how the guardrails will deal with those health-related devices that are not ARTG medical devices or excluded/exempt will be required.
Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?
No
9. How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols to ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property?
Recommend specific consultation with First Nations peoples, communities and leaders
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
Responsibilities need to be shared across all stakeholders appropriately. For medical devices, intended use must be considered. Individual users can utilise systems for unintended purposes and in ways and methods unknown to the original developers, thus, individual users must bear responsibility for potential adverse consequences.
The TGA framework should be looked to for guidance in these areas. Existing frameworks should be leveraged in favour of creating new frameworks with potential unintended consequences and duplication of oversight with no benefit.
The TGA would also be best placed to capture and receive reports on post market surveillance from users, including performance changes, both desirable and unhelpful.
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
Once again, a risk management approach is required to appropriately mitigate the risks of GPAI, and the TGAs (total lifecycle) approach that includes the ongoing monitoring of safety and performance, that includes reference to international standards and quality management system (QMS) certification should be leveraged to appropriately mitigate risks while facilitating access to new technology. The TGA systems also ensures an appropriate focus on ensuring ongoing compliance.
12. Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small-to-medium sized businesses applying guardrails?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
Regulatory burden is not just a concern for small to medium sized businesses, but for all businesses, particularly in the dental sector, therefore it is critical to ensure that there is no duplication of regulation in medical devices by enabling the current regulator to manage medical device regulation, in alignment with regulators globally. Global harmonisation is critical, to ensure that there are no additional requirements for the local market. This is the key to ensuring patient access to medical devices is not adversely impacted, now or in the future.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A domain specific approach – adapting existing regulatory frameworks to include the proposed mandatory guardrails
What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
For medical devices, regulation via the current regulator, the TGA, should continue. Work and processes already in place and functioning well around Software as a Medical Device should continue (and be expanded where necessary). There is no need for wholesale revisions to regulation that is already in place and working effectively. The TGA already has a framework that maps almost directly to the DISR 10 guardrails. The TGA definitions and essential principles are technology agnostic and designed for future innovation. They are also harmonised with the International Medical Device Regulatory Forum. Harmonisation with other key markets is key to ensure that no additional regulatory burden for medical devices in the Australian market is introduced.
Options 1 and 2 are optimal for medical devices - as outlined above, by enabling the existing TGA framework - which is aligned with global requirements, to continue. This would ensure the definitions and (technology agnostic) essential principles to remain in place. Australia is a very small part of the global medical device market and continuing to harmonise via the International Medical Device Regulatory Forum (IMDRF) will be important to minimise risk while facilitating access to new technology.
14. Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the Australian Government should consider?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
It is critical that duplication of regulations is avoided at all costs - with medical devices continuing to be regulated by the TGA as outlined above.
15. Which regulatory option(s) will best ensure that guardrails for high-risk AI can adapt and respond to step-changes in technology?
A domain specific approach – Adopting the guardrails within existing regulatory frameworks as needed
Please provide any additional comments.
Option 1 and 2 will work if the TGA remains responsible for managing all healthcare (as outlined above).
16. Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps and inconsistencies with Australia’s existing laws for the development and deployment of AI?
It is critical that duplication of regulations is avoided at all costs - with medical devices continuing to be regulated by the TGA as outlined above.
Which regulatory option best addresses this?
A domain specific approach – Adopting the guardrails within existing regulatory frameworks as needed
Please explain why.  
Ensures all regulatory requirements for medical devices can be met by a single regulator thereby minimising regulatory burden.
Make a general comment
As outlined above, the TGA already has a framework that maps almost directly to the DISR 10 guardrails. The TGA definitions and essential principles are technology agnostic, allow for capture of future innovation and are internationally harmonised (with the International Medical Device Regulatory Forum). Global harmonisation is key to ensure that no additional regulatory burden is introduced for medical devices in the Australian market. This ensures that risks are mitigated while access to innovative technology is facilitated.

PAGE  1 Mastercard ’s contribution  to Australia’s 
proposals paper on mandatory guardrails 
for AI in high -risk settings  
October 2024  
 
Mastercard welcomes the opportunity to provide its views to Australia’s Department of Industry,  
Science and Resources on its proposals paper1 for “Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk 
settings”  (hereafter referred to as 'the proposals paper' ), outlining approaches to regulating AI.  
Mastercard is a global technology company in the payments industry that develops and leverages AI 
products and solutions to make everyday commerce activities - such as shopping, travelling, running a 
business, and managing finances —easier, more secure, and more efficient for everyone. We harness  AI 
to protect over 140 billion transactions every year, preventing billions of dollars from being lost to 
cybercriminals, and detect fraudulent activity by verifying people are who they say they are. Last year 
only, our AI-powered cybersecurity solutions have stopped over AU$ 26 billion in fraud losses,  helping to 
deliver superior digital experiences so consumers can interact with businesses confidently .   
Our company is committed to responsible AI development and use, and we take a human -centric 
approach to AI. Our Data & Tech Responsibility principles2 guide the design, development, and 
application of all data -driven technology at Mastercard, especially AI. They are also embodied in our 
robust AI governance and Privacy by Design frameworks, which include accountability tools and 
technical controls that advance AI principles such as transparency, fairness, and explainability.  
Mastercard welcomes the risk -based approach proposed by the proposals paper which is in line with the 
approach followed by the EU Institutions in the EU AI Act. This alignment will facilitate AI -based business 
collaboration between these core jurisdictions  which value trustworthy AI.  
In this context, M astercard respectfully submits its views, focusing on the topics  outlined below:  
1. Regulatory options for high -risk AI settings  
2. Defining and categorizing high -risk AI  
3. Requirements for high -risk AI  
 
1 https://consult.industry.gov.au/ai -mandatory -guardrails   
2 https://www.mastercard.us/en -us/vision/corp -responsibility/data -responsibility.html   
 
 PAGE  2 1. Regulat ory options for  high -risk AI  
An AI framework must be driven by respect for individuals’ fundamental rights, health and safety. As 
such, it should consider the potential negative impacts that any AI development or use may have on 
individuals and society and should not lose sight of the  potential benefits.  
When regulating AI, the first step should be to leverage existing technology -agnostic laws, as many of 
these frameworks already address potential consumer harms —such as data protection, responsible 
lending  in financial services , human rights, and consumer protection. While AI -specific policies may be 
needed in certain situations, many existing Australian laws provide  a robust foundation and continuing 
to modernize and develop these  should be prioritized over wholesale changes to ensure consistency and 
adap tability in regulatory protections  into a future where technological advancement will continue to 
challenge the ability of legislatures to keep pace . Under Option 1, i ssuing guidelines on how existing laws 
should apply in the context of AI systems is likely to require  less time than  introducing a whol ly new 
legislative framework or overarching  AI Act , while still guaranteeing protection for consumers and legal 
certainty for businesses.   
While  Option 2  has the potential to support consistency across existing regulatory frameworks , we 
would welcome further clarity on how this option can help to reduce regulatory burdens  on industry; for 
example, in the case where organizations  are regulated under multiple regulatory frameworks and by 
multiple regulators.  We believe it is critical to have one regulator taking the lead and operating as a 
single point of contact for any AI -related matters. Considering the inextricable connection of AI with the 
processing of personal information and the impact on individuals’ privacy, the Office of the Australian 
Information Commissioner ('OAIC') should be in the leading position and the single point of contact for 
the organization  in question, but with the possibility to collaborate with other regulators where 
necessary.  For A I systems not involving the processing of personal information (e.g., AI used in 
manufacturing), it could be envisaged that the regulator with the most relevant expertise (e.g., because 
of the sector in which the AI is deployed) takes the lead and cooperates with other regulators where 
needed.  If Option  2 is pursued further, we strongly encourage  the government to identify the specific 
gaps in existing regulatory regimes, and to allow industry an opportunity to provide feedback by 
consult ing in these area s.  
Should the need for AI -specific regulation arise  (under Option 3) , adopting a principles -based and risk -
based approach would be the most advisable. A principles -based framework focuses on key ethical 
guidelines, such as fairness, transparency, and accountability, allowing for flexibility as technologies 
evolve. A risk -based approach that encompasses both the design and deployment of AI systems is an 
appropriate mechanism to strike a balance between the protection of individuals and technological 
development  which can foster economic growth. Rather than applying a one -size-fits-all framework, 
regulations should consider the varying levels of risk across different AI applications, and providing  
 PAGE  3 organizations with sufficient flexibility to adapt the requirements to the specific contexts in which the 
AI system can be deployed. Furthermore, such horizontal and technology -neutral approach will also 
ensure that  the regulation can adapt to future advancements and variations in AI technology . It will also 
avoid the adoption of different sectoral rules, which may result in confusion and legal uncertainty.  
Additionally, Mastercard supports and encourages efforts to converge AI specific policies and laws 
globally. While countries may have distinct legal environments, legal convergence can help reduce 
divergent or contradictory legal frameworks and promote leg al certainty and compliance.   We agree 
that AI policy must be driven by respect for an individual’s fundamental rights, health, and safety , no 
matter where they are . As such, it should consider the potential negative impacts that any AI 
development or use may have on individuals and society while  not los ing sight of the potential significant 
benefits  that are derived from innovation . 
2. Defining  and categorizing  high -risk AI  
In line with our call for global convergence on AI regulation, we believe it is important the definition of AI 
aligns as closely as possible with the OECD definition3. This alignment will ensure consistency and 
interoperability between regulatory approaches ; and enhance consumer protection while also 
supporting  companies operating globally . 
In this context, we recommend aligning with the  EU AI Act for defining and categorizing high -risk AI 
systems. This approach involves prohibiting certain use cases deemed unacceptable , for intrusive use 
cases that only bring harm to individuals or society, and imposing stricter requirements on high -risk AI 
systems , which are  defined as AI systems with  “a significant harmful impact on the health, safety and 
fundamental rights of persons ”. 
In order to correctly and effectively categorize AI systems, it is absolutely crucial to adopt a flexible and 
context -based approach, taking into account the specific circumstances of each use case. For example, 
under the EU AI Act, Annex III establishes a  list of AI systems that are considered as high -risk, but also 
offers the abovementioned flexible and context -based approach in Article 6(3), if it is proven that the 
AI system actually does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fund amental rights 
of natural persons . This is the case when:   
- the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task;  
- the AI system is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity;  
 
3 https://oecd.ai/en/ai -principles    
 PAGE  4 - the AI system is intended to detect decision -making patterns or deviations from prior decision -
making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human 
assessment, without proper human review; or  
- the AI system is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the 
purposes of the use cases listed in Annex III.  
If overly broad and rigid categories of high -risk AI systems are defined , then low risk use cases may be 
unintentionally captured. On the other hand, a flexible and context -based approach can enable the 
specific circumstances of each use case to be  taken into account, in order t o correctly determine the risk 
level of AI systems. For instance:  
- Banks using AI to monitor their total line of credit in accordance with legal requirements entails 
lower risk compared to AI used to evaluate creditworthiness when granting credit to an 
individual.  
- AI used for recruitment can be sensitive, but there may be recruitment use cases where the risk 
is low because there is no appreciable impact on future career prospects and livelihoods. For 
instance, an AI system that scans whether the word “python” in a C V is used to refer to an 
individual’s Python programming language skills rather than their work experience at a zoo with 
a particular type of snake, wherein the scan would take place to help identify relevant skills for a 
recruiter to evaluate.  
- AI which processes biometric data can be quite intrusive if used to identify an individual among 
an indiscriminate number of individuals without their knowledge, whereas the use of AI for 
verifying the identity of an individual based on a previously record ed and legally stored biometric 
template is much less intrusive.  
Importantly , consideration should be made as to the need for relevant exceptions for those AI 
applications that benefit individuals and society (e.g., fraud prevention, cybersecurity, anti -money 
laundering, etc.). Indeed, over -regulation in these areas could hinder t heir ability to protect society, to 
detect fraud, mitigate cyberattacks, and protect sensitive information, ultimately compromising 
security efforts and leaving vulnerabilities unaddressed.  
3. Requirements for high -risk AI  
AI Governance and accountability  
We strongly support the implementation of AI governance frameworks by all companies involved in the 
development and deployment of AI technologies. Establishing such frameworks is crucial to ensure that  
 PAGE  5 AI systems are developed and operated in a manner that is transparent, ethical, and aligned with 
societal values.  
Mastercard established its AI Governance framework already in 2019. It demonstrates our commitment 
to responsible AI development and enhances the reliability and trustworthiness of our AI -powered 
solutions. Mastercard’s AI Governance framework  outlines concrete steps and requirements for the 
development and application of ethical AI, including oversight of AI by Mastercard’s executive leadership 
and minimization of bias and risk in models and underlying data, ensuring compliance with existing 
regulations. I t has been built upon our experience and best -in-class approach to Privacy by Design to 
embed strong controls and guardrails into the design of all our AI innovations upfront and throughout 
their lifecycle. As part of our Program, we evaluate the intended purpose for which we want to use AI  
and the data quality (incl. accuracy, veracity, completeness, timeliness, source, and lineage) to ensure 
integrity of the AI outcomes while protecting individuals and guarding against data misuse  and 
discriminatory outco mes in the design of our AI solutions. This structured approach fosters innovation 
by encouraging best practices, promoting accountability, and facilitating continuous monitoring and 
improvement of AI systems. Consequently, Mastercard’s program ensures the development of 
advanced AI solutions t hat are capable of delivering fair, ethical and responsible outputs, ultimately 
fostering trust and confidence in using AI.  
Transparency  
Transparency requirements for high -risk AI systems are essential for ensuring accountability and public 
trust, as they provide insights into the functioning and decision -making processes of these technologies. 
However, it is crucial to balance transparency  with the need to protect proprietary information and 
guard against potential misuse by malicious actors  – for example, trying to bypass the AI system in the 
context of a fraud prevention tool. Excessive disclosure could reveal sensitive details that might  
undermine the effectiveness of the AI system. Therefore, while transparency promotes ethical use and 
oversight, it must be carefully managed to safeguard intellectual property and maintain the integrity of 
security measures, ensuring that transparency doe s not inadvertently compromise the system’s 
effectiveness or encourage attempts to bypass it.  
Bias  
Policymakers should encourage AI actors to proactively research and employ bias mitigation practices 
and procedures, but regulations should not include overly prescriptive requirements for bias testing and 
mitigation because such requirements can be flawed  or become outdated, which can lead to legal 
uncertainty for businesses and unintended consequences.   
 PAGE  6 Consequences of poorly designed AI systems include inaccuracies, inconsistent outcomes, discrimination 
against protected groups, and other harms. AI systems can be biased due to unfair historical data, non -
inclusive design, and a number of other reasons.  
Standards/interoperability  
Mastercard agrees with the importance placed on interoperability and standards, which aligns with 
our support  for efforts to converge AI specific policies and laws globally. While countries may have 
distinct legal environments, legal convergence can help reduce divergent or contradictory legal 
frameworks and promote legal certainty and compliance.  We must encourage public -private 
exchanges, cross -border government collaboration, and cross -industry knowledge sharing to foster 
cooperation, deepen understanding, and supp ort interoperable approaches to AI regulation.  
*** 
Mastercard looks forward to further contributing to discussions on safe and responsible AI in Australia. 
We would welcome an opportunity to meet with the Department to engage further on this policy 
area. Our Vice President of Public Policy and Government R elations, Tanya Stoianoff, would be happy 
to arrange a call with Mastercard’s global practitioners on AI Regulation who have been working in this 
field for several years. Tanya can be contacted at tanya.stoianoff@mastercard.com  or 0413127039.

Proposals Paper for Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-Risk Settings
4 October 2024
Recommendations
This submission supports:

* The introduction of a mandatory, ex ante, whole of economy approach to high-risk AI guardrails (option 3). This will provide a default baseline for government and the private sector with the option of domain-specific rules as needed.

* The empowerment of an independent, capable regulator to enforce the Mandatory Guardrails. Effective regulatory schemes require a well-resourced regulator to ensure adequate enforcement.

About this submission
The Australian Communications Consumer Action Network (ACCAN) is pleased to provide this submission to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (the Department) on the Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings (the paper).

1

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a rapidly evolving and broad technology that, with the right regulatory settings, can provide material benefits for consumers. AI can offer tailored services for consumers and potentially drive efficiencies in business, lowering the cost for consumers. However, as the paper notes, AI also carries risks of consumer harm through discrimination and data breaches. 
We thank the Department for the opportunity to comment on the paper. Should you wish to discuss any of the issues raised in this submission further, please do not hesitate to contact Samuel Kininmonth, Senior Policy Adviser, at Samuel.kininmonth@accan.org.au.

Dr Natalie Sheard

Dr Natalie Sheard
1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
The principles-based approach to defining high-risk AI set out in the Proposals Paper is not supported for the following reasons:
1. It is not appropriate for organisations to be given responsibility for determining whether their AI system is high-risk (and it is not clear from the Proposals Paper whether it is the developer, the deployer or both who bear this responsibility). The assessment of whether an AI system is high-risk determines whether that system is subject to the mandatory guardrails which may have significant resource and cost implications. It is therefore the most critical decision that will be made by an organisation developing or deploying an AI system. Experience from other jurisdictions indicates that when too much discretion is given to organisations to make such an assessment, they are likely to err against finding that their AI system requires compliance with AI guardrails (see Lara Groves et al, 'Auditing Work: Exploring the New York City Algorithmic Bias Audit Regime (Conference Paper, Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency, June 3-6 2024)). A determination of this importance must be made by the government as it has democratic accountability.
2. Australia lacks the well-developed legal framework needed to make a principles-based approach meaningful or effective in practice. Federal anti-discrimination laws are not fit-for-purpose and need reform: see the Australian Human Rights Commission's ('AHRC') 'Free and Equal: A Reform Agenda for Federal Discrimination Laws' report (2021) and the recommendations of the Royal Commission into Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation of People with Disability (2023). Australia does not have modern and comprehensive privacy and data protection laws or national human rights protection.
3. The proposed principles are too vague, and organisations are ill-equipped to apply them in practice. For example, principle a. requires organisations to have regard to an individual's rights recognised in 'Australian human rights law' and 'Australia's international human rights law obligations'. Principle d. requires organisations to assess the risk of adverse impacts to the broader economy, society and the environment. Both of these principles require organisations to consider and weigh complex and difficult legal and ethical issues and organisations are unlikely to have the expertise to do so with any rigour. Further, the principles provide little guidance as to relevant thresholds. When is a risk an 'adverse' one? When will the 'severity and extent of the adverse impacts' be high enough to warrant a system's classification as high-risk?
4. The principles do not provide for transparency regarding the methodology used by organisations to conduct high-risk assessments and there is no indication in the Proposals Paper that there will be regulatory oversight of this risk assessment process. If a principles-based approach is adopted, at a minimum, there should be mechanisms for an independent regulator to review, and individuals to challenge, an assessment by an organisation that their AI model/system is not high-risk.
A list-based definition is preferred as:
1. It is appropriate for the government, a democratic institution, and not organisations conflicted by profit motives, to decide which AI systems are high-risk. It is best placed to make assessments of the human rights, economic, societal and environmental impacts of particular applications of AI.
2. This approach enables interoperability with regulation in other jurisdictions including Canada and the European Union ('EU'), and the ability to learn from those jurisdictions
3. It is transparent
4. A list provides greater clarity and certainty for organisations and is therefore more easily applied in practice and at less cost.
5. Mechanisms can be adopted to ensure that low-risk AI uses are not inadvertently captured.
3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?
NO a more defined list-based approach is needed
If you prefer a list-based approach (similar to the EU and Canada), what use cases should we include? How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
Employment Access to essential public services and products Access to essential private services Law enforcement
How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
This should not be a static list. Instead, there should be mechanisms for: (i) an annual review of this list; and (ii) for the list to be amended and updated as necessary.
4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Yes
If so, how should we define these?
The following high-risk use cases should be banned:
1. AI systems which utilise facial analysis techniques. These techniques rely on machine learning to identify and infer human characteristics, emotions and/or behaviours from an individual’s facial features and movements. They lack scientific reliability and validity (see, eg, Lisa Barrett et al, ‘Emotional Expressions Reconsidered: Challenges to Inferring Emotion From Human Facial Movements’ (2019) 20(1) Psychology Science Public Interest 1) and lead to discrimination. The EU AI Act bans emotion recognition in the area of 'workplace and education institutions' (article 5(1)(f)). However, it is submitted that all AI systems which employ facial analysis should be banned including those used in immigration and the criminal justice system.
2. Biometric categorisation systems which use protected attributes under anti-discrimination laws.
3. 'Real time’ remote biometric identification systems in commercial settings and publicly accessible spaces. Biometric identification has been proven to have low accuracy rates and high potential to infringe human rights.
4. Predictive policing systems (based on profiling, location or past criminal behaviour) including facial recognition systems as they have low accuracy rates and high potential to infringe human rights.
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
A list-based approach is preferred.
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
These guardrails need to apply to developers of GPAI models, GPAI systems and deployers.
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
1. This question raises central issues in a risk-based approach to the regulation of AI: how do we determine if an identified ‘risk’ is 'appropriately mitigated' and who makes these decisions? There are many gaps and uncertainties in the guardrails. For example, for Guardrail 4, what is the ‘objective and measurable performance metric’ for discrimination by an AI system? What are the relevant ‘test/s’ which must be conducted to evaluate whether an AI system has discriminatory impacts? The Proposals Paper indicates that standards will support the implementation of this guardrail. However, determining thresholds for discrimination by AI systems and how to ‘appropriately’ mitigate any discriminatory impact are normative and value-laden decisions and it is not appropriate for them to be made by standards bodies. These bodies lack democratic legitimacy and the expertise to make decisions about competing rights and interests and they are usually dominated by industry organisations to the exclusion of civil society and experiential experts. Decisions about these and other relevant issues must be made by government and relevant regulators, with meaningful engagement and input from civil society and experiential experts. There is much work to do done in this area to make the guardrails effective.
2. The proposed mandatory guardrails need to clearly and separately delineate the responsibilities of developers and deployers across the high-risk AI supply chain.
3. A holistic legal framework is required for the mandatory guardrails to be effective in mitigating the risks of AI used in high-risk settings. As stated above in this submission, this requires, at a minimum, anti-discrimination laws which are fit-for-purpose, modern and robust privacy and data protection laws and national human rights protection.
Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?
No
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
No
Which of the guardrails should be amended?
Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the system once deployed Inform end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with the guardrails Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails
Please provide any additional comments
It is submitted that the existing guardrails in the Proposals Paper should be amended as follows:
Guardrail 2 - this is a key guardrail. It should be strengthened by: (i) making an AI Impact Assessment mandatory before a high-risk system is placed on the Australian market and at regular intervals thereafter. Such an assessment should use human rights as a framework to identify AI harms; and (ii) creating a mandatory obligation to consult with impacted individuals, groups and communities. For example, workers and unions must be consulted before any AI system is deployed in their workplace.
Guardrail 10 - a conformity assessment regime must be overseen by an independent and resourced regulator empowered to: (i) establish a process for the accreditation of third party assessors. This guardrail will not be meaningful unless conformity assessments are carried out by independent third parties. This is particularly essential for developers of GPAI; (ii) investigate and determine individual complaints of non-compliance with the guardrails; and (iii) conduct 'own motion' investigations and audits regarding compliance by organisations with the guardrails.
As drafted, the current guardrails do not create sufficient transparency obligations for high-risk AI systems on the market in Australia. Transparency is required to give agency and autonomy to individuals as to how and when to interact with an AI system and is a pre-requisite to meaningful contestability of AI decisions and outputs. The guardrails should therefore be amended as follows:
Guardrail 4 - should create a requirement that a 'test' (or audit) of the performance of AI systems across standardised metrics be made publicly available.
Guardrail 6 - does not include any right to an explanation. The Government Response to the Privacy Act Review Report (2023) made it clear that a 'right to request meaningful information about how automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effect are made' is supported. This must be reflected in this guardrail.
Guardrail 9 - this guardrail should be strengthened by: (i) requiring that all high-risk AI systems be registered in a public database; and (ii) creating a notifiable adverse incident reporting requirement for all high-risk AI systems (not just GPAI models). This could be similar to the notifiable data breach regime in the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth).
12. Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small-to-medium sized businesses applying guardrails?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
The mandatory guardrails are needed to protect against the potential of high-risk AI systems to cause harm at speed and scale and impact fundamental rights, the economy, the environment and society. There should, therefore, be no 'watering down' of these obligations for SMEs. Instead, SMEs can manage the obligations created by the mandatory guardrails through their contractual arrangements with AI developers. For example, an SME deployer could require an AI developer to fund any conformity assessment required prior to deployment by them. There should also be mechanisms which enable SMEs, where appropriate, to rely on an AI developer's compliance with the guardrails.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A whole of economy approach – introducing a new cross-economy AI Act
What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
The third option has the benefit of establishing a monitoring and enforcement regime overseen by an independent regulator with expertise in AI systems.
15. Which regulatory option(s) will best ensure that guardrails for high-risk AI can adapt and respond to step-changes in technology?
A whole of economy approach – introducing a new cross-economy AI Act
16. Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps and inconsistencies with Australia’s existing laws for the development and deployment of AI?
1. Anti-discrimination law: the Proposals Paper recognises that discrimination is one of the primary risks of AI systems and that the Australian community has 'consistent concerns' regarding it. However, no evaluation has yet been undertaken by government or the AHRC of whether federal and state anti-discrimination laws adequately protect against AI harms and how legal liability might be apportioned between developers and deployers. Further, no guidance has been provided as to how existing laws apply to AI systems and automated decision making. These are significant omissions and ones which the Australian Discrimination Law Experts Group argued in its submission in response to the 'Safe and Responsible AI in Australia: Discussion Paper' need to be urgently addressed.
2. Any of the three legislative options will be ineffective unless there is reform of the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and the implementation of all of the reforms set out in Privacy Act Review Report (2023).
3. Remedies: we must ensure that there exist appropriate remedies across all existing Australian laws. In some cases, the individual remedy of compensation will be appropriate but, in others, systemic and collective remedies will be necessary. When the harm is at a group-level or to society, new remedies must be developed including those requiring the mandatory redesign of a system, temporary bans and mandatory external audits.
Which regulatory option best addresses this?
Other
Please explain why.  
The regulatory approach should be:
1. Close the gaps and uncertainties in existing laws. For Australian anti-discrimination law, this requires: (i) an evaluation of whether federal and state anti-discrimination laws adequately protect against AI harms and how legal liability might be apportioned between developers and deployers; and (ii) enactment of the reforms set out in the AHRC's 'Free and Equal: A Reform Agenda for Federal Discrimination Laws' report (2021) and the recommendations of the Royal Commission into Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation of People with Disability regarding disability discrimination laws (2023).
2. Provide guidance and enforcement of existing laws. For example, we urgently need the AHRC to provide regulatory guidance regarding how anti-discrimination laws apply to AI systems and automated decision-making.
3. Enact new cross-economy AI-specific laws overseen by an independent regulator with the necessary resources, capabilities and capacity to undertake this role.
Make a general comment
A research and evidence-based approach should be taken to all legislative and regulatory reforms.
