When AI is engaged to depict the voice, image, movement or likeness of Aboriginal and Torres 
Strait Islander ancestors and/or deceased persons, all companies and entities must follow the 
applicable Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander protocols and cultur al Lore of those ancestors 
and/or deceased persons.  
These protections must also apply to international sources seeking to appropriate the intellectual 
property of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.  
 
3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on 
high-risk AI settings and high -risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of 
illustrative uses, needed?  
As is mentioned above, if the proposed principles clearly define the use of AI systems that affect 
work processes, working relationships, and the rights and conditions of working people as high 
risk, then that approach can be a meaningful means to ensure working peoples ’ rights are 
protected in the context of the introduction and utilisation of AI systems.  8 We do note, however, that in recent best -practice legislative examples the list -based approach 
has been deployed in a manner that explicitly recognises workplaces and the employment 
relationship, such as in European and Canadian legislation, as is outlined in the example 
identified on page 26 of the consultation paper.   
This is indicative of the potential positives of this approach. We would note, however, that the 
example listed on page 26 is overly restrictive as it does not explicitly reference AI systems that 
lead to changes in work processes and practices, which will also be necessary to ensure 
meaningful consultation and engagement, and to ensure that AI applications are targeted 
towards boosting productivity by augmenting the skilled work undertaken by well -trained and 
supported workers, and not towards a race -to-the-bottom on wages and standards propelled by 
forms of automation and work intensification . 
It is also important to note the difference i n regulatory frameworks and settings between Europe 
and Australia  in particular .  
In Europe, the new AI Act is underpinned by a specialised and well -funded European AI Office 
with the power to enforce the Act . The Act works in concert with national jurisdictions, a number 
of which have their own significant legislation operating to safeguard the implementation of AI 
systems, including in the workplace.  
Many constituent EU states have substantial recognition of worker voice across both the 
enterprise and the industry level - for example, through co -determination in some large German 
companies.  
This is worth noting because the success of AI regulation in the EU will rely upon all these 
different levers functioning cooperatively. The Australian context is quite different to this , 
including a more restrictive system of collective bargaining and worker voice to manage the AI 
transition than exists in many European jurisdictions.  
These practical realities need to be accounted for in any discussion of a principles/ list-based 
definition of high -risk AI settings and how they are operationalised with a bias towards finding 
and enhancing means for the collective voice of workers to be embedded in these regulatory 
responses.  
 
 
 9 4. Are there any high -risk use cases that government should consider banning in its 
regulatory response? If so, how should we define these?  
The government should ban high-risk cases that:  
- Undermine the quality of human life , including mental health . 
- Do not have appropriate levels of human oversight  and where an accountable human 
being in a position of designated authority is not responsible for the outcomes of a 
system they have developed or deployed . 
- Involve automated decision making over the employment relationship that substantially 
affects the rights and interests of an employee.  
- Undermine the legal and human rights of citizens, workers, and consumers.  
- Are applied into employment and work processes without the meaningful knowledge and 
consent of workers (as defined by an appropriate consultation process  that allows for 
input by workers before decisions have been made ). 
- Are used for the purpose of intrusive monitoring or surveillance of workers without their 
knowledge or consent.  
- Co-opt or utilise data or creative content without the knowledge and consent of the 
producers of that date or creative content.  
- Are models/systems that seek to create a digital replica using the biometric data of an 
individual without their informed consent.  
 
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high -
risk AI, such as general -purpose AI (GPA) ? 
Australia continues to lag behind in preparing to adapt to the significant challenges posed by the 
latest AI systems, and to anticipate the  further  emergence of general -purpose AI  systems . We 
posit that GPAI  models should be considered inherently high risk because they can be applied to 
a wide range of applications, some not possible to foresee, to a potentially very broad audience 
at very high speeds.  
The consultation paper has recognised that “As GPAI  models become more powerful, and 
‘frontiers’ o f AI continue to advance, it becomes more difficult to predict all the foreseeable 
applications and risks of AI”  (p. 14).  
The ACTU agrees with this statement, and the significant risks recognised  in the consultation 
paper . 
The problem we have is that our established laws and regulatory regimes (outside of certain 
specified sectors that have been identified in the consultation paper)  do not necessarily  10 anticipate the scale, pace, and type of transformation that AI is instituting  already, let alone 
future potential GPAI  applications.  
For example, the workplace bargaining regime in Australia is notably restrictive when compared 
to international jurisdictions within comparable economies. There is a tightly defined set of 
permitted matters upon which bargaining can take place. To genuinely anticipate and prepare for 
unforeseen risks these systems may pose, restrictions on collective bargaining must be removed 
to enable workers to collectively bargain on the actual or potential use of artificial intelligence 
and associated issues (such as d ata ownership and privacy) in connection with their work.  
The general approach towards AI is unbalanced when we are providing the best possible means 
for business to innovate in the development and deployment of AI models with results and 
effects that we acknowledge we cannot anticipate, while maintaining overly onerous regulation 
on workers that prevents them from bargaining in a manner that will protect their interests 
against potential negative effects of AI systems, including GPAI . 
As such, the definition of high -risk settings and response to GPAI  and the implementation of 
guardrails needs to be conducted concurrently with a review of workplace laws around 
bargaining with the intention of removing those restrictions that might prevent workers from 
bargaining around any matters pertaining to the implementation and use of AI systems at work.  
 
Section two: Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of 
AI 
 
6. Do the proposed mandator y guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high -
risk settings? Are there any guardrails we should add or remove?  
The proposed guardrails make a  number of  positive contribution s in managing the use of high -
risk AI systems.  
At present, there are a number of areas in which these guardrails do not adequately recognise 
the need of protections for working people in the context of the introduction and utilisation of AI 
systems.  
To be effective, the guardrails need to embed worker protections such as the right to meaningful 
consultation before decisions on the introduction of AI systems are made, and measures to 
ensure that decision on the allocation of work and the conduct of wor k are being made by 
responsible and accountable human decision makers.  11 We are also concerned that the guardrails as currently framed suggest a great deal of employer 
discretion in formulating their own processes to satisfy the guardrails.   
We are also conscious that some industries and sectors have established regulatory regimes, 
codes, and standards, that incorporate responsibilities pertaining to AI systems that could be 
utilised by some enterprises as the basis for compliance, but not all  do. This risks creating 
fragmentation, inconsistencies, and exacerbating regulatory gaps and differentiations in 
enforcement and penalties. We also note that GPAI  systems may not overtly conform to industry -
based regulatory regimes, necessitating broader coordination.  
We believe there should be an explicit list of stipulated minimum requirements for each of the 
mandatory guardrails that is enforceable by the relevant regulator.  These minimums should be 
developed through a tripartite mechanism that ensures workers’ voice is included. The proposed 
National Artificial Intelligence Authority could play a role in developing these stipulated minimum 
requirements.  
We note that the guardrails have been designed to sit alongside the Voluntary AI Safety 
Standards, and that these standards list more specific processes that can be undertaken to 
manage risk.  
We express  with concern that the extensive consultation process undertaken to inform the 
Voluntary AI Safety Standard included substantive input from employer representative 
organisations while unions, and the worker voice, was almost completely excluded, and believ e 
further review is required to ensure these standards also embed worker protections.  
The tripartite National Artificial Intelligence Authority could play a supportive role in bringing 
industry leaders, unions, and government, to assist in the development of these minimum 
requirements for the satisfaction of the guardrails , while remaining sensitive to industry -specific 
regulations, codes, and standards .  
This level of coordination would recognise the fundamental reality that while the use and 
application of AI systems will differ according to industry, sector, and type of work,  and while the 
existing level of regulation of necessity differs by industry, the innate rights of workers in the 
context of the introduction and utilisation of AI systems does not.  
In addition to this general observation , which is applicable across  all 10 proposed guardrails , we 
also note the following points for development in regards to specific guardrails.  
 
Guardrail 2: Establish  and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks  12 This guardrail  correctly states that risk assessment requires contributions from experts from 
multiple domains, and representatives of impacted communities.  We note with great concern 
that when it comes to workers , the guardrail only states: ‘Consideration should also be given to 
including workers  when assessing the impacts of adopting AI in the workplace ’ (page 37).  
Workers must have the right to be meaningfully consulted about the introduction of AI systems  
that relate to their work  before decisions have been made, and provided the capacity for input 
into these decisions. Such consultation is vital to the management of risk . This current phrasing , 
‘Consideration should also  be given to including workers when assessing ’, undermines this 
fundamental right and proposes worker involvement instead as simply a potential consideration 
that employers may or may not accept. The extent of this involvement is limited to assessing 
impacts, rather than genuine and meaningful contribution about decisions to introduce AI 
systems into work processes.  
It is imperative that wo rkers are provided this opportunity  for meaningful consultation as part of 
the risk management process before decisions have been made through their representative 
organisations as both experts in work processes and as communities impacted by AI 
applications. There should be a guaranteed right for meaningful consultation for workers prior to 
decisions being made, and the recognised right for unions as representative organisations of 
workers to be involved in these processes when requ ested by any employee affected or 
potentially affected by the introduction and utilisation of an AI system.  This would bring Australia 
in line with international best practice, such as the EU’s AI Act, which enshrines rights and 
protections for workers and for unions as the representatives of workers . 
We would also recommend that “eliminate” is added to the guardrail, consistent with WHS law. 
The paper rightly suggests that risk mitigation strategy might involve “identifying such severe 
risks that they ought to reconsider whether to deploy the AI system ”. This is a critical part of a 
genuine consultation system, but it reflects an emphasis on risk elimination. The language of 
mitigation suggests employers might bring in harmful, high -risk AI, provided they can point to 
minimal measures further down the h ierarchy of controls.  
In addition, we strongly recommend that designers of AI systems should have explicit 
responsibility for ensuring at the development stage that systems comply with relevant and 
necessary industry regulations, codes, and standards. For instance, an enterprise developing 
systems for medical imaging should have responsibility for ensuring their systems comply with 
the relevant standards during the pre -market stage , and there should be clear evidence that 
reference has been made to ensure the system complies with these standards.  This would be in 
addition to, not in replacement of, the responsibility of deployers to comply with relevant industry 
standards.  13 Guardrail  3: Protect AI systems, and implement data governance measures to manage data 
quality and provenance  
There is a significant issue raised in these guardrails about the obtaining of data. The proposed 
guardrail quite correctly stipulates that all data must be legally obtained. There are, however, 
significant gaps that currently exist in privacy and workplace law s that mean workers have little 
to no control over their own data. Current far-reaching exemptions allow employers to use data 
without restriction after the initial point of collection . 
This guardrail should be broadened to address this gap and to provide further protection to 
consumers by stipulating that data must be legally obtained with its use consented to by those 
who have provided it, including employees. Clear measures for redress should be outlined in 
instances where data is used without this consent being provided. This should include measures 
that ensure  that consent is meaningful, as providers of data are fully informed of what is being 
collected, how, to what purpose, and what  controls (if any) they will have of its further use. It 
should also be made clear if the data is being monetised in any way.  
We also note that a large number of AI systems (and not just those that may be deemed as high -
risk or as operating in a high -risk setting) utilise data that has been copyrighted. It is necessary to 
ensure protections for creators of this data, and to ensure transparency over which systems are 
utilising copyrighted data (including those not designated as high risk).  
Knowing that much of the training of AI models has already occurred, we are interested in 
potential mechanisms to apply this guardrail retrospectively , and would like to see this option 
further explored . 
 
Guardrail 5: Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human 
oversight  
We endorse this emphasis on human control or intervention in an AI system.  We recommend, 
however, that in the language of the guardrail ‘Enable’ be replaced with ‘Ensure’ – this is to 
clarify that human oversight is not discretionary, but should be mandator y in the utilisation and 
application of these AI systems.  
When it comes to decisions made over the employment relationship and/or the engagement of 
work that substantially affects the rights and interests of an employee, such decisions must be 
made by a human decision -maker who has accountability and responsibility for the decision 
made . This guardrail should explicitly reference this.  14 When it comes to the employment relationship  and/or the engagement of work , no AI system 
should ever be charged with making a decision about the work performance of a human being.  
As is noted in the consultation paper, it has already been witnessed in Australian workplaces that 
methods of rostering and assigning work through AI systems has failed to take into account 
specific and important human factors and fundamental rights, such as caring responsibilities. AI-
infused rostering systems have also contributed to work insecurity and the creation of a ‘digital 
hungry mile’, for instance, by allocating additional shifts on a first -come -first-serve basis over an 
app that forces workers ( disproportionately casual workers) to be constantly monitoring apps. 
Without human oversight and intervention, such practices can quickly degrade work rights, 
work/life balance, quality of life, and perpetuate discrimination against those workers who have 
caring responsibilities (responsibilities that disproportionately are  undertaken by women, posing 
the risk of perpetuating gender inequality).  
To assist in protecting against such outcomes we recommend that human oversight include the 
right for unions as representative bodies of employees to request and be provided information on 
the systems that are being utilised in places where workers they represent are employed, the 
level and extent of human oversight over these systems, and measures taken to ensure that an 
accountable human decision -maker has responsibility for decisions being made. There should be 
a right to appeal to a relevant regulator o n behalf of represented workers where necessary steps 
to ensure meaningful and accountable human oversight has not been taken by a company.  
 
Guardrail 6: Inform end -users regarding AI -enabled decisions, intersections with AI and AI -
generated content  
We are concerned about the narrow application of the requirement for labelling to high -risk AI 
only. We are also concerned that a ‘best efforts’ approach will lead to sub -optimal outcomes 
when it comes to transparency, ensuring trust, and ease of use for e nd-users/consumers.  
We support the three distinct requirements that are outlined.  
We are concerned, however, that due to established precedent and action, some employers may 
fail to understand that these requirements apply to employees as well as the general public  when 
AI systems are used in a work setting or through work processes, and in which a worker is the 
‘end user’ .  
We recommend further clarification within the guardrail to ensure that it is clear that these three 
requirements refer also to the rights of workers , and that employers and managers and those 15 who engage labour have a responsibility to fulfil these requirements in regards to their 
workforces if they adopt AI systems  that people will interact with.  
We are also concerned that not enough attention has been paid to the differing communication 
needs of end users. For example, older Australians, people with disability and mental health 
consumers are entitled to choice and control over their supports, but they also might also require 
extra support to navigate and make those decisions. Meaningfully “informing” end -users in these 
contexts will need to look considerably different than in other markets.  
 
Guardrail 7: Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcomes  
Unions as the representative organisations of workers should have the standing right to be a 
party to the dispute resolution processes on behalf of affected employees when requested by any 
employee affected or potentially affected by the introduction and/o r utilisation of an AI system in 
the workplace.  
The relevant regulator  (where it exists) should also ensure an ultimate right to appeal to the 
regulatory agency exists to ensure that there is an avenue for address if a complaint cannot be 
resolved through internal processes. This right to appeal should be clearly communicate d to all 
those who initiate a challenge based on the impact of an AI system.  
We also believe that strong protections need to be instituted for ‘whistleblowers’ to report 
instances in which enterprises are not adhering to the guardrails, or in which AI systems are 
posing substantial harm or risk of harm to individuals, particular groups, and broader society.  
 
Guardrail 8:  Be transparent with other organisations across the AI supply chain about data, 
models and systems to help effectively address risks  
While we support these measures we believe they can be improved substantially by explicitly 
stating that unions will have the right to request and be provided with this information in any 
instance where AI system use does or may effect workers for whom the y have coverage.  
 
 
 16 Guardrail 9: Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with 
guardrails  
While we support these measures  we believe they can be improved substantially by explicitly 
stating that unions will have the right to request and be provided with this information in any 
instance where AI system use does or may effect workers for whom they have coverage.  
We also note that to make this guardrail effective there should be specific requirements that all 
documents necessary for third parties to assess compliance need to be kept and maintained  and 
provided to the relevant third party when required. The records kept and maintained must be 
suited to this assessment, and not be chosen at the employers discretion.  
 
Guardrail 10: Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with the 
guardrails.  
We strongly support the right for a relevant regulator to conduct conformity assessments and 
certify compliance by both developers and deployers with the guardrails. Without such a power 
these guardrails risk becoming perfunctory and ineffective.  
We also recommend the recognised right for unions as representative organisations to request 
that an assessment be undertaken by the regulator where reasonable suspicion exists that an 
organisation or enterprise is non -compliant.  
We also note that best international practice includes a requirement for enterprises to register a 
high-risk AI system into an appropriate public register before placing such a system into the 
market place or into service.8 We recommend that a similar public register, administered by the 
appropriate regulator, be established with the same requirements.  
 
7. How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols to 
ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve ICIP  
 
 
 
 
8 See Article 49: Registration of the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act : 
https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/49/#:~:text=This%20article%20states%20that%20before,system%20in%2
0the%20EU%20database.  17 The ACTU refers to the position of the ACTU Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Committee  on 
these important points . This is a self -determining committee, democratically elected, that drives 
policy development in the union movement on matters pertaining to Aboriginal and Torres Strait 
Islander workers and communities.  
We respect and encourage Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples rights to maintain, 
control, protect and develop their intellectual property over their cultural heritage, traditional 
knowledge, and traditional cultural expressions.  
It is vital that appropriate legislation and regulation establish Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander 
peoples Cultural Intellectual Property, sovereignty, self - determination and rights.  
Protocols for using Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples Intellectual and Cultural Property 
(ICIP) must be embedded into AI legislative protections and Australian copyright law.  These 
protocols must establish Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander  peoples sovereign rights of 
ownership of: data, lands, language, culture, art, stories, music, song, dance, voice, image, 
likeness, body, movement and intellectual and creative output.  
When AI is engaged to depict the voice, image, movement or likeness of Aboriginal and Torres 
Strait Islander ancestors and/or deceased persons, all companies and entities must follow the 
applicable Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander protocols and cultur al Lore of those ancestors 
and/or deceased persons.  
These protections must also apply to international sources seeking to appropriate the intellectual 
property of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.  
 
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain 
and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?  
We believe that the distribution of responsibility is well considered and appropriate.  
We particularly note the need, as captured in the guardrails, to ensure that appropriate 
responsibilities are designated for developers of these systems. This brings the guardrails in line 
with best international practices and ensures that developers canno t avoid accountability for the 
potential negative ramifications  of their systems, while also ensuring that dep loyers cannot 
abrogate their responsibilities for the functioning and operating of these systems by blaming 
negative ramifications on the de velope rs. A sensible and responsible approach is necessary to 
ensure that both developers and deployers are accountable at the relevant stages of the 
development, implementation, and application of these AI systems.  18 9. Are the proposed mandator y guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI ? 
The proposed mandatory guardrails are a positive step towards managing the risks of GPAI .  
We note that a defining feature of GPAI  and other largescale AI systems that may be in place in 
coming years is that their operability and potential applications and effects are unknowable. 
While the guardrails make a positive contribution to managing the risks of the unanticipateable 
effects of these systems, a truly comprehensive approach will require broader coordination, and 
a greater capacity for workers to bargain over the introduction of AI, its application, and its 
effects ,m than is currently the ca se.  
 
 
 
Section three: Regulator options to mandate guardrails  
13-16. In this section we take questions 13 – 16 together to provide a single comprehensive 
response.  
To rise to the challenges posed by AI, it is necessary for there to be a coordinated national and 
unified approach  across government and across the economy  that balances innovation , 
development, risk, regulation, and the fundamental protection of the rights of workers, citizens, 
and consumers.    
In consideration of the proposed regulatory options, the ACTU’s position has been determined by 
asking the simple question: to what extent will this option protect the rights of working people 
and ensure that AI systems are not used to diminish existing rights, protections, quality of work, 
and quality of life?  
We posit that regardless of the option adopted, there are vital and necessary steps the 
government should immediately take to ensure that workers, consumers, and citizens are 
appropriately protected from the potential harm of the use of high -risk AI system s.  
To this end, the ACTU recommends : 
- The establishment of a tripartite National Artificial Intelligence Authority to coordinate 
policy responses  across government . 
- Regulation that protects the fundamental rights of workers, citizens, and consumers, that 
ensures human oversight over these systems, and that ensures alignment between 
human objectives and goals and the technological development of AI systems.  19 - Tripartite consultations aimed at promoting the safe and responsible use of AI in order to 
harness its potential for positive effects on productivity , workplace health and safety, and 
the creation and protection of meaningful work.  
1. That the government engage with unions with a view to ensuring that the framework of 
industrial law is sufficiently robust to deal with the use of Artificial Intelligence  in 
connection to work.  This includes a review of the Fair Work Act to ensure it is fit for 
purpose.  
- The creation of a new Division of the Department of Employment and Workplace 
Relations be established to oversee the development by tripartite means of new 
regulation and training as it pertains to AI and work.  
2. That Australia’s work health and safety laws be reviewed to ensure they are fit for 
purpose and the role of Workplace Health and Safety Representatives strengthened.   
- That the government act to implement  adequate safeguards are in place for the 
utilisation of AI systems in government services to ensure these systems do not displace 
human decision -making and do not lead to negative outcomes for the users of 
government services.  
- That the government examines and amends existing consumer protection framework to 
afford the best protections for consumers.  
- That the government examine and where necessary amend existing privacy protections 
for workers and other persons.  
- That the government implement legislation that protects Aboriginal and Torres Strait 
Islander peoples ’ intellectual and cultural knowledge against the threat of AI.  
These measures will ensure that workers fundamental  rights, conditions, quality of work, and 
quality of life, are protected amid the introduction and application of AI systems in Australian 
workplaces.  
In assessing the outlined options, it is clear that Option 1 is insufficient to the level of 
coordination required  with a great potential to exacerbate gaps and inconsistencies within the 
regulatory response to AI systems in high -risk settings , and we do not support this approach.  
The ACTU believes that both Option 2 and Option 3 could serve the fundamental purposes of 
protecting working peoples’ quality of work and life amid the introduction and utilisation of AI 
systems, if appropriate steps and measures are taken to embed the pro tection of workers within 
these regulatory frameworks.  We favour Option 3 due to the greater level of coordination it offers, 
its emphasis on also covering the responsibilities of developers of AI systems with enforceable 
regulation, and as it better refle cts the urgency required to ensure protections are in place .  20 If either Option 2 or 3 is adopted, it will still be necessary to undertake the steps we have 
outlined above to ensure that working peoples rights, conditions, quality of life, and quality of 
work is protected.  
We suggest that a useful model for comparison is in the management of risk in the realm of 
workplace health and safety, where there is a positive duty on employers to identify risk, with 
prescriptive  regulations for managing high risk settings. A similar approach in regards to the 
introduction and utilisation of AI systems would make a meaningful contribution to managing  
challenges of the AI transition. Both Option 2 and Option 3 could potentially operate in this 
manner, if workers’ rights are appropriately  embedded within these regulatory frameworks  
alongside employer responsibilities.  
 
Option 2  
If this option is adopted , it will have the benefit of creating framework legislation to define the 
guardrails that would apply and the threshold for their application. This would assist with the 
necessary review of existing legislation and regulatory frameworks to ensure they are suited to 
purpose.  We are concerned that this Option may not be comprehensive and strong enough to 
guarantee the necessary protections for working people.  
In particular, we note the need to review the Fair Work Act  to ensure it remains fit for purpose in 
the context of the rapid adoption of AI systems, and the potential risks of GPAI ; and the need to 
review workplace health and sa fety laws to ensure they respond to the specific needs of the AI 
era and are strengthened accordingly.  
Considering the risk of fragmentation across industries due to differing regulatory regimes, it is 
imperative that a tripartite National Artificial Intelligence Authority is created to coordinate 
responses across government.  
Option 3  
If this option is adopted it, it will have the benefit of introducing a specific AI Act that would 
implement the proposed mandatory guardrails, would include a clear definition of  the high-risk 
applications of AI, and establish a monitoring and enforcement regime overseen by an 
independent regulator.  
If this option is adopted, it will be vital to define the scope of the legislation and the jurisdiction 
and powers of the new regulator against existing approaches.  21 In particular, we note the need to review the Fair Work Act  to ensure it remains fit for purpose in 
the context of the rapid adoption of AI systems, and the potential risks of GPAI ; and the need to 
review workplace health and safety laws to ensure they respond to the specific needs of the AI 
era and are strengthened accordingly.  
We also note that regulators are only effective when they are appropriately funded and 
supported. Government commitment to Option 3 must be matched by an appropriate level of 
funding to ensure that the regulator is effectively able to undertake its responsibilities.  
 
Whether Option 2 or 3 is selected, it is absolutely vital that  a comprehensive review of existing 
workplace laws and protections  is undertaken to ensure that working people are protected in the 
context of the rapid implementation of and utilisation of AI systems.  
This includes, but is not limited to:  
- Ensuring that workers are meaningfully consulted before decisions about the introduction 
and application of AI systems into workplaces and work processes are made.  
- Ensuring that workers have the right to refuse to work with AI systems where these 
systems pose a risk of harm to workers, consumers, and/or the general public.  
- Ensuring workers have the right to bargain to all current and potential applications of 
artificial intelligence.  
- Ensuring that workers’ data is covered by privacy protections.  
- Ensuring that anti -discrimination law is fully covering all workers in the context of the 
utilisation  of AI systems, including in hiring and firing.  
- Ensuring that decisions that affect working peoples work processes, distribution of work, 
quality of work, conditions of work, and all aspects of the working experience, are made 
by accountable human beings – not AI systems and/or algorithms.  
- Ensuring that WHS laws are providing appropriate protections for the AI era.

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
The definition of high-risk AI is far too broad.
Are there any principles we should add or remove?
Yes
Please identify any:
a. AI is increasingly integrated into many basic tools such as digital image capture (e.g. to automatically adjust light levels and other imaging quality parameters) and it is of concern that when these everyday tools are used in health care they will then potentially be subject that an additional layer of unnecessary and burdensome regulation simply because it is being used in the health care setting.
Similarly, voice-recognition dictation has been specifically used in the consultation paper as an example of narrow use AI. Such voice recognition systems have been used for decades now and should be considered low risk in their traditional form involving simple transcription of speech to text, that is subsequently checked by the user, regardless of the setting in which they are used.
Automated image analysis systems have been in use in the pathology sector for decades (e.g. ThinPrep imager for cervical cytology screening, Kiestra microbiology workflow automation system, CellaVision for blood film screening) and are already clinically validated and regulated as medical devices. These devices all essentially use a form of AI (usually expert systems rather than neural networks) although they are only recently being described as such, primarily for marketing purposes. There is a great concern that these sorts of programs will be captured under the definitions in the consultation paper and will be subject to additional regulations when their safety has already been clinically demonstrated. There should be a mechanism to grandfather in applications that have been in widespread use for a long time.
b. Categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for defence or national security purposes. It should be taken into consideration that the existing software exclusions as defined in Schedule 1, Item 140 of the Therapeutic Goods (Excluded Goods) Determination 2018, in particular pathology Laboratory Information Systems (LIMS), including any calculator functions present. The existing software exclusions remain appropriate for pathology Laboratory Information Management Systems (LIMS), including any calculator functions included therein. In general, these software platforms receive data from testing equipment and present this for both review and reporting by medical specialists. It may also perform simple calculations such as converting units of measurement. Results are sent to a medical professional prior to this being discussed with the patient or uploaded to MyHealth record. The LIMS itself is not used to generate new diagnostic outputs, nor is it used to prevent, monitor, predict, make a prognosis of, treat or alleviate a disease, condition, ailment or defect. Pathology staff are still key to providing a diagnosis based on the results generated.
Current LIMS do not engage an AI system/software, and thus, there is no potential harm to patients from risks from the use of AI. The LIMS is a pre-defined static environment that functions to transfer test results from the analyser to a referring (clinical) doctor’s Practice Management System (and thence to the patient). Interpretative comments are applied to results directly by Pathologists or Scientists, which may be automated using defined rules to reduce manual tasks. All rules are simple e.g. . if result is X then do Y. This includes both adding comments to reports and reflex testing based on other or previous results. Limited memory AI systems and machine learning is not used. In any regulation, there should be a distinction between:
1. Software that was modelled using AI and deployed with an AI function; versus
2. Software that was modelled using AI but is deployed without an AI function.
The latter option should be included in any exemption as the deployed software is not a learning environment based on ongoing data input. Current LIMS do not engage limited memory machine learning AI systems/software. There also should be an exclusion for basic digital imaging which is not AI generated but might in fact use an element of AI to enhance the image, i.e. improve brightness, in the same way that just about every personal use digital camera (phone or other device) can now do.

NO a more defined list-based approach is needed

Other
How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
a. The principles-based approach can result in ambiguity and a defined list-based approach is preferred. If a list-based approach is adopted the exclusions are probably more important than the inclusions. This will need frequent review by appropriate professionally-led bodies to ensure they remain fit for purpose.
However, modern AI tools in pathology are likely in many cases to be high-risk AI, whether it is by principle or by list. So, if a list approach is adopted, such lists should be extensive and comprehensive for every domain, compiled by domain-led professional organisations, because the range and capacity of AI tools can vary significantly within every domain.
If a list-based approach is adopted the exclusions are just as important than the inclusions. This will need frequent review by appropriate professionally-led bodies to ensure they remain fit for purpose.
b. If you prefer a principles-based approach, what should we address in guidance to give the greatest clarity? A principles-based approach has the potential to lead to problems as the principles can be very broad and could unintentionally capture existing systems, which may appear to be AI but are not really, or new simple tools being marketed as AI. Dictation software is an example of a product that some might describe as AI, but is really just a tool for simplifying a repeated task.

Yes

GPAI models applied to healthcare/pathology would be high risk and hence subject to guardrails. While the distinction between a GPAI model and a non-GPAI pathology (domain) specific large framework developed model could be debated/articulated more clearly, it is likely that both would be high risk in the health care setting and subject to guardrails so could make this distinction unnecessary (in the health domain at least).

Please provide any additional comments
There are still some questions about the guardrails (see below):

37. One of the most pressing concerns surrounding AI in the creative industries is the industrial -scale 
copying of content during the input stage of AI training. AI platforms are frequently trained on massive 
datasets, often scraped from the internet, without the consent of the original creators. These datasets 
contain copyrighted works that are essential to the creative process. While these works serve as the 
foundational input for AI systems, the outputs generated by these platforms are, in many cases, mere 
derivatives or adaptations of the original content.  
38. The outputs derived from these AI platforms are not entirely new creations. Instead, they are 
compositions that blend and remix elements from the original works used in training, often closely 
mirroring the style, structure, or essence of those works. Desp ite the derivative nature of these outputs, 
they are released into the same markets, competing directly with the original creators whose content 
was copied in the first place.  
39. It is essential to implement a compensation  regime not only at the input stage  – when AI models are 
trained on copyrighted works  – but also at the output stage. There must be a mechanism whereby AI 
platforms are required to compensate the owners of  the creative content which has been  both  a) used 
to train these  systems ; and b) forms part of the output of these  systems. This approach would ensure 
that the creators of the original works maintain a stake in the value chain of derivative creations.  
40. APRA AMCOS makes the following recommendations to support the implementation of the guardrails 
and ensure that AI is used responsibly in the music industry:  
1. Licensing for AI Systems:  AI systems that use copyright works in their training datasets 
should be required to obtain consent from and pay reasonable compensation to rights 
holders  for the use of their works . This will ensure that creators are compensated for the use 
of their work and that their intellectual property rights are respected.  
2. Auditable AI Models:  AI systems should be subject to regular audits to ensure compliance 
with licensing agreements and guard against the unauthorised use of copyrighted material. 
These audits should be conducted by independent third parties to maintain transparency and 
accoun tability.

distinguish it from human -created works. This will ensure that consumers are fully informed

services available in Australia, regardless of where the AI model was developed or trained. 
This includes imposing sanctions on overseas platforms that fail to comply with Australian 
regulations.  
5. Protection against cultural misappropriation:  AI systems should be trained on datasets 
that respect cultural integrity, particularly when it comes to Indigenous creators and 
communities. Guardrails must be in place to prevent AI from perpetuating cultural biases or 
misappropriating cultural works without proper attribution and consent.  
6. Global Collaboration for AI Regulation:  Australia should work with international bodies such 
as the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO) to develop global standards for AI 
regulation in the creative industries. This will ensure that Australian creators are protected 
globally and that  international platforms operating in Australia are held to the same standards 
as domestic platforms.  
Addressing AI assumptions and overreach  
41. APRA AMCOS submits that whilst  the Proposals Paper offers valuable insights into the potential 
benefits and risks AI in high -risk settings, it also contains several assumptions about AI capabilities that 
warrant further scrutiny. Some of these assumptions overstate the current abilities of AI or overlook the 
limitations and nuances of AI technologie s. 
1. AI’s Creative Capabilities:  The Proposals Paper suggests that AI has the potential to replace 
human creativity in industries like music, film, and the arts. However, this assumption 
overlooks the fact that AI systems, while adept at pattern recognition and data analysis, lack 
the emotional depth, cultural understanding, and contextual awareness that human creators 
bring to their work. AI -generated music, for instance, can mimic existing styles, but it cannot  
replicate the human experiences and emotions that drive artistic innovation.  
2. Bias and Cultural Representation:  The Proposals Paper downplays the risks associated with 
AI perpetuating bias, particularly in culturally sensitive areas like music creation. AI models 
trained on datasets lacking diversity are likely to amplify existing cultural biases, leading to 
misrepresentation or margin alisation of minority groups. It is misleading to assume that AI 
systems can produce unbiased outcomes without addressing the biases inherent in the data 
used to train them.

alignment with ethical guidel ines. The notion that AI can seamlessly and autonomously 
manage complex tasks without human input is an overreach and fails to acknowledge the 
significant limitations of current AI technologies.  
Conclusion  
42. The rise of AI presents both opportunities and challenges for the Australian music industry. Whil st AI 
technologies have the potential to enhance creativity and streamline production processes, they also 
pose significant risks to creators ’ rights, cultural representation, and economic stability. To mitigate 
these risks, it is essential that the Australian Government implements strong, enforceable guardrails 
for AI, particularly in high -risk settings such as music creation.  
43. AI guardrails and transparency obligations must apply universally to all AI services available in 
Australia, regardless of their origin. This is a global industry, and regulatory frameworks must reflect the 
international nature of AI technologies to ensure  fair competition and protect the rights of Australian 
creators.  
44. By imposing sanctions on platforms that fail to comply, including those based overseas, the 
government can safeguard the future of Australia's music industry in the face of AI disruption.

13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high -risk

The third option – a whole -of-economy approach, introducing a new AI Act – would be the most 
efficacious approach to applying the guardrails across all sectors of the economy, and ensuring 
consistency of application, without the risk of diverging approache s in sector -specific

Nevertheless, taking into account the interplay between Commonwealth and State/Territory

which are rigorously regulated and have their own regulatory oversight bodi es and 
mechanisms (e.g. TGA for health), these should be exempted from the horizontal AI Act.  
Definitions may be adopted where practicable for greater consistency across legislation. Please 
see question 16 for a more detailed response to concerns around intersection with

14. Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the 
Australian Government should consider?  
 
Given the constant evolution of the state of the technology, and the AI market both globally in 
Australia, and the need for Australian businesses to develop and compete, regulatory 
sandboxing mechanisms should be made available in the legislation to encour age innovative 
development and deployment of new AI solutions.  
 
15. Which regulatory option/s will best ensure that guardrails for high -risk AI can adapt 
and respond to step -changes in technology?  
 
As mentioned above, in order for the regulations to keep up with the state of play of the 
technology, the list of high -risk AI applications needs to be equipped with a mechanism 
whereby the regulator or the legislator can amend that list, taking into accou nt technological 12 | ACCI S ubmission:  Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
 evolutions and newly -identified risks, or risks which are no longer to be classified as such, and 
therefore can be removed from the high -risk list of applications to which the guardrails apply.  
 
16. Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps or inconsistencies with Australia’s 
existing laws for the development and deployment of AI? Which regulatory option best 
addresses this, and why?  
 
As mentioned above, the biggest regulatory issues lie with consistency of regulations at the 
Commonwealth and State/Territory levels: this would be most keenly felt in areas such as Work 
Health & Safety (WHS), and in Employment law.  
 
The model WHS laws are risk -based  and flexible enough to address emerging AI risks. The risk 
management process set up under this legislation is well -known and methodical. The 
proposals in this paper would create a parallel assessment process that is duplicative in parts 
and may result in two risk assessments with two different risk ratings and outcomes. This would 
ultimately undermine the objectives of both pieces of legislation and result in only further 
confusion from SMEs. Existing WHS risk identification and assessment processes as it relates 
to AI use and WHS should prevail with any bespoke AI legislation and guidance mirroring this.   
Attempting to implement these guardrails in employment settings,  with particular reference  to 
obligations and entitlements arising under the Fair Work Act or discrimination frameworks, 
would be immensely difficult due to the high level of duplication that would ensue. ACCI 
strongly recommends against imposing the guardrails on employment through designating 
employment uses as automatically high -risk. The textbox on page 27 makes particular 
reference to several instances where AI might be used in workplace settings : 
 
CV-scanning services / AI applications used in hiring   
 
The paper suggests that  CV-scanning services may create the risk of discrimination  in 
assessing individuals’ suitability for employment opportunities. The legislative framework 
already protects workers from discrimination in recruitment, across multiple acts and multiple 
jurisdictions.1  
 
Under the Australian anti -discrimination framework, both direct and indirect discrimination are 
unlawful. Direct discrimination occurs when a person, or a group of people, is treated less 
favourably than another person or group because of their background or certain personal 
characteristics. Indirect discrimination occurs when there is an unreasonable rule or policy that 
is the same for everyone but has an unfair effect on people who share a particular attribute. In 
an Australian Human Rights Commission (AH RC) Technical Paper from 2020, it was established 
that the use of AI would already lead to “unlawful discrimination and other forms of human 
rights violation”.  Meaning the existing legal infrastructure is already effective.  
 
 
1 Australia's anti -discrimination framework is broadly governed by the following regimes: the Age 
Discrimination Act 2004 (Cth), the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (Cth), the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 
(Cth), the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth), t he Anti -Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW), the Equal Opportunity 
Act 2010 (VIC), the Anti -Discrimination Act 1991 (QLD), the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA), the Equal 
Opportunity Act 1984 (SA), the Ant -Discrimination Act 1991 (TAS), and the Anti -Discriminatio n Act 1992 (NT).  13 | ACCI S ubmission:  Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
 The Fair Work Act 2009 (FW Act) specifically deals with discrimination in  the hiring process. 
Under the general protections in section 351, an employer must not take adverse action against 
an employee or a prospective employee based on any of the following characteristics: race or 
colour, sex, gender identity, intersex status, or s exual orientation, marital status, pregnancy, 
breastfeeding, or family or caring responsibilities, age, physical or mental disability, religion, 
political opinion, national extrac tion or social origin, and because they are experiencing family 
and domestic violence. Section 342 of the FW Act clearly states that adverse action against a 
prospective employee includes refusing to employ the prospective employee. This means that 
it is a lready unlawful for a business to not hire someone because of the above characteristics. 
Importantly, the FW Act covers any action taken by an employer, including the implementation 
of AI technologies. The FW Act mandates that the person alleged to have en gaged in the action 
is presumed to have engaged in the alleged action with the alleged intent unless they can prove 
otherwise.  If AI technologies have caused an incident of discrimination to occur during 
recruitment, then they are captured by the FW Act and may be dealt with accordingly. The 
requirement of a person to prove they have not engaged in adverse action is an additional 
element of accountability. Employers are not absolved if a contravention occurs through the 
use of AI. Hence, where risks to empl oyers’ obligations arise from using AI, then there must be 
oversight and review systems in place to ensure that there is not a failure to comply with 
legislation , such as the discrimination framework (because it is already effective). The approach 
outlined in relation to this possibility at page 27 is hence unwarranted – the current framework 
is rigorous.  
 
Not only is any risk already dealt with appropriately under anti -discrimination laws, but the 
proposals paper’s desire to designate the use of AI in recruiting as high -risk might make it less 
attractive to employers thereby dismantling the potential benefits that might be obtained from 
its use. The use of AI in the hiring process may have material impacts on driving down 
inequalities in the employment system. Studies whi ch examined the biases of recruiters and 
managers with respect to ethnic groups have shown that those with non -English names are 
less likely to progress through a hiring process than those with an English name . AI presents 
an opportunity to overcome the challenges associated with the unconscious bias in human 
decision making, which research from the UK suggests is present in hiring processes . ACCI has 
also previously heard feedback to that effect from its membership network. One member 
observed earlier this year that ” the use of this technology in hiring which blindly -screens 
candidates has secured results of more diverse staff being hired within my organisation than 
ever -before.” Naturally, where blind screening tools can be used through AI, the unconscious 
bias that wo uld be present in a human’s decision making will not be present. Research has 
shown that a recruiter may only scan a CV for seconds, meaning  that their preconceptions may 
play a strong role in who they invite for an interview. AI can help remove these preconceptions 
by only dealing with specific criteria and inputted information.  
 
Automated rostering systems  
 
The paper suggests the case of  automated rostering system s not adequately factor in caring 
responsibilities of employees. Implementing such systems does not abrogate employers of 
their obligations to consult with employees about changes which impact their rosters under 
their award or EA as is required by sections  145A and 205 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (FW Act). 14 | ACCI S ubmission:  Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
 Nor could it possibly overcome any flexible working arrangement made under the National 
Employment Standards.  As the FWO outlines, where an employer wants to change an 
employee’s regular roster or ordinary hours of work, they have to discuss it with them first, 
provide information about the change, invite their views, and consider those views.  Employers 
are still  required to meet these consultation obligations regardless of whether they used an AI 
application to create the roste r. Naturally, where risks do  arise with respect to employers’ 
obligations, then there must be oversight and review systems in place to ensure that there is 
not a failure to comply. Importantly, automated rostering can be programmed to consider 
compliance rules, reducing the risk of h uman error and ensuring that staff are scheduled 
accordingly.  
 
AI is already being used lawfully and carefully by employers to implement more efficient 
processes with respect to rostering arrangements. Instituting these mechanisms increases 
efficiency and reduces administrative burdens on employers and managers at an economy -
wide scale. Furthermore, these systems may help to decrease unconscious bias. Some 
employers or managers may unconsciously roster others more frequently, or at times more 
often, due to personal relationships, for example, and AI makes decisions bas ed on pre -defined 
rules and data, mitigating the potential for bias in scheduling. One business from ACCI’s 
membership network made the following observation : “Managers within my organisation will 
roster shifts for 200 -300 employees, this was not at all possible before the use of this rostering 
technology. This technology allows managers to not be bogged down in these administrative 
duties, and instead to free up time for other employees within the team. Employees really 
benefit from this technology as they  can simply input availability and preferences, and the 
technology can effectively accommodate staff needs”.  
 
Monitoring and surveillance  
 
This example is twofold – one that it might impose unlawful monitoring, and two it might lead 
to an unfair determination about the employee’s employment. These are problems with several 
existing solutions that do not need to be further duplicated by way of the guardrails. Firstly, in 
relation to monitoring and surv eillance as a practice. Businesses invest significant amounts of 
money into employees and their equipment, they have a right to assure themselves that they 
are being used in the appropriate way. The Fair Work Ombudsman, on its website, elucidates 
on the us e of monitoring technology, advising that businesses are increasingly using 
technology to lawfully monitor such things as work output, how business property is being used 
and employee attendance. The mechanism through which monitoring (i.e., AI  applications ) 
occurs is not necessarily the key factor : as the Australian Privacy Principles are technology -
neutral, the principal factor is whether these actions are occurring in a lawful manner and that 
the employer is conforming to their privacy obligations. Priva cy law applies, regardless of how 
monitoring occurs (as such employers should always have review and oversight mechanisms 
in place to ensure compliance).  
 
Secondly, in relation to decisions taken about an employee’s employment due to monitoring 
and evaluation by an AI, ACCI would draw attention to the  rigorous protections and unfair 
dismissal laws present in the Fair Work Act. Simply because an AI application was used in a 
decision, employers cannot obviate their obligations and entitlements under the Fair Work Act. 15 | ACCI S ubmission:  Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
 Section 387(e) of the Fair Work Act is clear : a consideration that must be taken into account as 
to whether a dismissal was unfair (harsh, unjust or unreasonable) when it occurred because of 
unsatisfactory performance, is whether the person had been previously warned about their 
performance. This cons ideration does not evaporate because AI was used to assess that 
performance. Hence, where an AI  application  was used to monitor performance and take a 
decision about an employee’s employment, it still needs to be fair in that context (i.e., the 
employees should be given a chance to ameliorate their performance issues). If the proposed 
guardrails also seek to deal with these obligations, they will introduce duplication. For example, 
as recently as a few months ag o, the FWC ruled a dismissal unfair after an employer used 
generative AI to draft a text terminating an employment relationship. The employer was not 
able to avoid their obligations by using AI in the workplace.  The guardrails hence would have 
very little  work to do in employment settings beyond imposing unnecessary new burdens on 
businesses. This would serve to make AI less attractive to employers (thereby reducing their 
proliferation) when they might actually be of some benefit to employees. Some employe rs or 
managers may unconsciously promote employees due to personal relationships, for example, 
and AI could make decisions based on pre -defined rules and data, stemming from such 
monitoring. This would actually mitigate the potential for bias.  
 
Other employment -specific situations  
 
In addition to the three examples listed above, the paper makes  further reference to specific 
employment settings that might give rise to a high -risk designation for the purposes of the 
guardrails and/or potential legislation. Those settings are “recruitment and hiring, promotions, 
transfers, pay and termination.” Rec ruitment, promotions, and termination have already been 
addressed in this submission and it has been evidenced that there is no new risk or challenge 
that AI might create, which is not already addressed by anti -discrimination laws and the Fair 
Work Act. With respect to pay (wage setting), ACCI submits that this is not a high risk setting as 
the proposals paper argues.  
 
Wage setting  
 
With respect to the use of wage setting in employment contexts, the risks of AI are minimal. 
The guardrails will only add to the complexity of the industrial relations system if it seeks to 
impose on how AI might interact with pay. Australia has a substant ial minimum safety net of 
terms and conditions through the National Minimum Wage (NMW) and modern award 
minimum wages, which are reviewed annually to assess their adequacy. An employee cannot 
be paid less than their applicable modern award minimum wage, ev en if they agree to it, and if 
no modern award applies, they cannot be paid less than the NMW.  Furthermore, in contexts 
where an identifiable pay point is available such as in modern award -reliant businesses and 
those with an enterprise agreement, the ris ks of AI are minimal and may simply present an 
opportunity to increase the efficiency of clerical tasks. Most independent contracting 
arrangements also bear minimal risk as the contractor can set or negotiate their own pay.   
 
 
 
 16 | ACCI S ubmission:  Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
 Transfers  
 
While the  reference  to transfers  is vague, it could be taken to have its meaning in section 311 
of the Fair Work Act, a transfer to a new position , or it could be taken to mean physical location 
(geographical transfer). If it is the latter, although this is an operational decision that is firmly 
within managerial prerogative, certain relocations would be taken to be a repudiation of the 
contract and would allow the employee to receive redundancy pay. For example, as recently as 
September , the Fair Work Comm ission (FWC) has rendered workers entitled to genuine 
redundancy because an employer sought to transfer their location of work.  If it is taken to 
mean a transfer to a new position, then protections already exist in that instance as well. The 
FWC has previ ously held that an employer does not have the right to transfer an employee 
from one position to another without his or her consent and  forcing them to do so would 
thereby enliven section 386(1)(b) of the Fair Work Act (namely that a dismissal has occurred).  
Finally, if it is within the meaning of section 311 then subclause (1)(a) clarifies that a termination 
must have occurred, which at  the outset means the unfair dismissal regime is in effect. Hence, 
it is clear that the guardrails do not have any work to do with transfers – it does not matter if AI 
is used in a decision about a transfer, the relevant protections apply.  
 
In conclusion, ACCI submits that the guardrails do not offer any additional protections not 
already provided to employees under employment law in Australia. The application of the 
guardrails to the employment context, which is already highly regulated, would cause 
duplication, leading to new complexities and unnecessary administrative burdens . 
 
 
We thank you for your consideration of our feedback. Should you require any additional 
information or clarification of any points contained within, please contact Jennifer Low, Director 
Health, Safety, Resilience and Digital Policy at jennifer.low@acci.com .au.

Aboriginal and Torres Strai t Islander peoples, locally and nationally. A core priority area for ALIGN is data; the 2

Intellectual Property (ICIP) in the deployment of genomics is central to this work, and highly relevant to this 
consultation on the regulation of AI. ALIGN acknowledges the tension between these principles, and the need to 
share data to ensure that models are developed which are not bias ed against Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander 
peoples and other minority groups and  seeks to work with Government in the development of platforms and policies. 
ALIGN also recognises the expertise in the Government’s Artificial Intelligence Expert Group under Ministers Husic 
and King, especially Dr Terri Janke who is an international reco gnised authority on ICIP.  
Australian Genomics   
Australian Genomics  is an Australian Government initiative supporting genomic research and its translation into 
clinical practice. Through broad engagement and a national collaborative approach, Australian Genomics achieves 
two key objectives: to improve efficiency, reach an d timeliness of genomic research projects, and to support 
Commonwealth, State and Territory health departments in the implementation of genomics research outcomes by 
refining and communicating evidence to inform policy development.  Australian Genomics engages with current and 
emerging government policy and priorities to identify gaps and opportunities, to support policy and action for 
integrating genomic technologies into the health system. By interfacing with consumers, government, industry and 
global geno mics initiatives, Australian Genomics drives change and growth in the sector.

 Summary of recommendations  
Defining high-risk AI   
We recommend a principles -based approach to defining high-risk AI. The proposed 
principles do not yet adequately capture high -risk AI, and we recommend amending  
Principle (b) to better protect autonomy and informed consent,  Principle (c)  to address 
discriminatio n, and Principle (f) for clearer risk assessment criteria. Recommendations 
from Indigenous health and genomics experts for this submission  also suggest adding a 
principle for AI systems using Indigenous data. This should incorporat e Indigenous data 
sovereignty and governance  approaches  that align with  the United Nations  Declaration 
on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP ) and Closing the Gap  framework . We 
further recommend that the Australian Government consider banning harmful AI 
applications  in line with the EU AI Act, and that general-purpose AI (GPAI) should be 
defined based on  risk principles , not solely on technical capabilities .  
Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of AI   
Given the short consultation period, w e recommend further review and revisions to 
Guardrails 1, 2 , 8, 9 and 10 to ensure  practical implementation and enforceability.  
Compliance and reporting requirements should be proportionate to the risks of harm 
and size of the organisation , balancing AI safety with the sector's economic viability to 
maintain innovation incentives . Unbiased and represen tative AI training data to support 
safety validation and quality assurance  requirements should be embedded in 
Guardrails 3  and 4. We support Guardrail 5 and  strongly recommend revision to 
Guardrail 6 to cover informed consent before AI-enabled decisions  are made . 
Distribution of responsibility across the AI supply chain for developers and deployers 
requires further guidance and clarification. Incorporating First Nations knowledge and 
cultural protocols, including the adoption of UNDRIP and self -determination principles, 
will help ensure that AI systems are culturally safe.  
Regulatory options to mandate guardrails   
We recommend the whole -of-economy approach in Option 3 for AI regulation  to 
minimise conflicting rules and enhance  national and  international AI collaboration and 
innovation . This option  would also deliver greater consistency in  legal enforcement , 
interoperability  and oversight, supported by a dedicated regulatory office  with diverse 
stakeholder expertise . We ask the Australian Government to consider integrating open 
access standards  to promote equitable  and transparent AI deployment , while 
protecting  community -specific guidelines and First Nations cultural safety.  
The mechanisms  underpinning the Australian Government’s approach to AI regulation  
should be consistent with  existing industry standards  to adequately protect Australians 
from harm and build  confidence among AI adopters as they navigate an increasingly 
complex legal and regulatory environment .   5 
 Responses to the Proposals Paper questions  
Defining high -risk AI  
Proposed principles:  
In designating an AI system as high -risk due to its use, regard must be given to :  
a. The risk of adverse impacts to a n individual’s rights recognised in Australian 
human rights law without justification,  in addition  to Australia’s international 
human rights law obligations  
b. The risk of adverse impacts to an  individual’ s physical or mental health or safety  
c. The risk of adverse legal effects, defamation or similarly significant effects on an  
individual  
d. The risk of adverse impacts to groups of individuals or collective rights of cultural 
groups  
e. The risk of adverse impacts to the broader Australian economy, society, 
environment and rule of law  
f. The severity and extent of those adverse impacts outlined in principles (a) to (e) 
above.  
 
1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high -risk AI? Are there any 
principles we should add or remove?  
Please identify any:  
• low-risk use cases that are unintentionally captured  
• categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for 
defence or national security purposes.  
The proposed principles do not yet adequately capture high -risk AI. 
Proposed Principle (b)  should be amended as follows  to explicitly protect 
autonomy in decision -making and the right to informed consent , in line with core 
tenets of the Australian Charter of Healthcare Rights : ‘The risk of adverse 
impacts to an individual’s physical or mental health, safety, autonomy, or right to 
informed consent. ’ This proposal  and future public consultation  would greatly 
benefit from a more thorough discussion on the critical issues of confidentiality  
and informed consent  in settings that are generally considered more high-risk 
like healthcare and clinical research.  The AASGARD and similar programs  rely on 
new and validated  AI methods to be developed and deployed  at a population 
scale and in ways that are accurate, robust, and compatible with  informed  
consent and ethical standards .  6 
 While Principle (d) covers adverse impacts to groups, d iscrimination should be 
specifically mentioned in Principle (c)  to cover the risk of discrimination against 
individuals.  AI in healthcare significantly enhances clinical decision support and 
treatment capabilities  as seen in the rare disease  and genomics  realm, but the 
risk of discrimination must be carefully managed  due to its impacts on patient 
outcomes, equity, and trust.  We applaud the Australian Government ’s recent 
commitment to ban genetic discrimination in life insurance, but prevention of 
high-risk biased data  that can result in other forms of discrimination  and further 
inequalities  must also be a priority in AI regulation . Lack of diversity  in training 
datasets regarding ethnicity, race, and gender  significantly  increases the risk of 
AI exacerbating systemic discrimination  in access to clinical care .1 In the case of 
rare disease genomics research , concerns specific to AI include:  
• Historical underrepresentation: Indigenous and other linguistically and 
culturally diverse populations are often underrepresented in genomic 
datasets due to limited healthcare access , as well as  historical mistrust 
and lack of substantive engagement by researchers . When training data 
does not adequately represent diverse populations, AI models may fail to 
accurately diagnose, treat, or provide clinical recommendations for them. 
This can lead to unequal treatment outcomes and perpetuate existing 
health disparities, undermining public confidence in AI applications.  
• Spurious correlations: incomplete  and/or biased  training data can  also 
result in AI models identifying false correlations  and incorrect 
conclusions  between genetic markers and traits , particularly affecting 
small, underserved  populations like many Indigenous and minority 
groups. 
We also recommend adding another principle that explicitly protects First 
Nations knowledge and cultural protocols  – see our response to question 2 
below.  
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture 
harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?  
Including First Nations consumers and knowledge holders is crucial for 
transparent, fair, and socially licensed AI use in high -risk settings. Our 
consultation with  leading Indigenous health and genomic experts for this 
submission suggests expanding  the principles to specifically set out: 
• a distinct principle that applies to AI systems  using Indigenous data  and 
incorporates  Indigenous data sovereignty and governance best practice

• alignment with Closing the Gap  national strategy to improve the health

3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and 
certainty on high -risk AI settings and high -risk AI models? Is a more defined 
approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?  
• If you prefer a list -based approach (similar to the EU and Canada), 
what use cases should we include? How can this list capture 
emerging uses of AI?  
• If you prefer a principles -based approach, what should we address in 
guidance to give the greatest clarity?  
AI applications are developing at an extremely rapid pace , in ways that are often 
unforeseen. Whether the  chosen approach is based on lists or principles, it 
should be adaptable to this future trajectory.   
We prefer and recommend a principles -based approach , as a list-based 
approach may : 
• require continuous updates ; 
• fail to adequately capture new and emerging forms of high -risk AI; and  
• allow for new systems to be designed in ways that render them exempt 
from compliance with the principles  and mandatory guardrails .   
Risk levels need to be explicitly defined and categorised to enable effective 
application of the proposed principles and guardrails . For Principle (f) , we 
recommend clear er assessment  criteria to distinguish high -risk AI settings from 
low-to-medium risk AI and their  potential application to GPAI models. This 
additional clarity in guidance will help  ensure consistency and fairness in policy 
interpretation and  application so that low -risk use cases, such as basic 
automation tools that do not handle sensitive information like health records, 
are not unintentionally captured.

4. Are there high -risk use cases that government should consider banning in its 
regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of 
risk)? If so, how should we define these?  
The Proposal s Paper does not explicitly outline the uses of AI that should be 
prohibited. In contrast, Article 5 of the EU AI Act provides a list of prohibited AI 
systems where exploitative, subliminal, manipulative, or deceptive techniques 
are deployed to distort behaviour and impair informed decision -making, causing 
significant harm.  We recommend that Australia adopts a similar approach to 
support interoperability  (see our further recommendation under question 14) . 
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging 
forms of high -risk AI, such as general -purpose AI (GPAI)?  
As above, further consideration and revisions are needed  to ensure flexibility . 
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
