7. What are suitable indicators for defining GPAI models as high -risk? For 
example, is it enough to define GPAI as high -risk against the principles, or 
should it be based on technical capability such as FLOPS (e.g. 10^25 or 
10^26 threshold), advice from a sci entific panel, government or other 
indicators?  
Risk indicators should be applied against principles. Defining GPAI as high-risk 
solely based on  computational capabilities and performance thresholds of AI 
systems is insufficient. While technical capability  is an important factor, it does 
not capture the full scope of potential harms and impacts associated with AI -
enabled decisions  in high-risk settings . If the high -risk AI classification depends 
solely or primarily  on technical capability, this could introduce a perverse 
incentive to keep that capability  at or just below threshold levels to avoid 
compliance  with the guardrails.  For systems that do have effective principles -
based guardrails in place, limits based purely on technical capability could also 
have the undesired effect of constraining progress without materially reducing 
risk.  
In the context  we are most familiar with - medical genomics  in both clinical and 
research settings  - rapid shift s in data generation and  analysis technologies are 
occurring against a backdrop of changing cultural attitudes towards AI among 
clinicians, policymakers, and the wider community, as evidenced by the rapid 
uptake of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT. For Australians to 
benefit from advances in AI technology applied to genomic medicine  and other 
rapidly changing domains of healthcare , both the principles and mandatory 
guardrails must be flexible and adaptable  enough to evolve with technological 
advancements  and public adoption.  
We recommend that t he Australian Government continue to review and revise 
the principles and guardrails based on  diverse engagement with : 
• key stakeholder groups  including  scientific panel s, researchers, 
government, First Nations experts, the wider public  (including other 
underrepresented communities)  and industry partners ; and  
• real-world deployment  of GPAI models  in critical sec tors like healthcare  
to refine risk definitions and evidence -based regulatory strategies.  10 
 Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of AI  
Proposed mandatory guardrails for high -risk AI  
Organisations developing or deploying high -risk AI systems are required to : 
1. Establish, implement and publish an accountability process including governance, internal 
capability and a strategy for regulatory compliance  
2. Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks  
3. Protect AI systems, and implement data governance measures to manage data quality and 
provenance  
4. Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the system once 
deployed  
5. Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight  
6. Inform end -users regarding AI -enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI -generated content  
7. Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcomes  
8. Be transparent with other organisations across the AI supply chain about data, models and 
systems to help them effectively address risks   
9. Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails  
10. Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with the guardrails   
 
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI 
used in high -risk settings? Are there any guardrails that we should add or 
remove?  
We recommend  further public consultation and  revision of  the proposed 
mandatory guardrails to address AI  risk levels  in high-risk settings  more 
effectively . 
While we understand that Guardrails 1 and 2  aim to establish accountability 
and capture emerging risks in the AI lifecycle, their broad and high -level nature 
may inadvertently promote a compliance -driven culture rather than enhancing 
transparency and responsibility  in practice . Further specific guidance is needed 
to clarify the followin g gaps:  
• the extent to which compliance  and reporting requirements need to 
respond to corresponding development and deployment  risks  
• how the Australian Government plans to enforce the mandatory 
guardrails for overseas developers  (extra-territorial application)  whose AI 11 
 solutions and capabilities are often adopted  and favoured by Australian 
businesses ;4 and  
• how the governance and risk management obligations under these 
Guardrails may complement existing laws and regulations , such as the 
Corporations Act 2001  requirement of directors to assess and govern  
risks to the organisation . 
We strongly agree with the Proposal s Paper that internal accountability 
processes mandated under Guardrail 1 should be proportionate to the specific 
risks of harm (as mentioned above  under questions 1 -7) and the size of the 
business . This, however, is not reflected in Guardrails  2, 8, 9, and 10  to form a 
consistent compliance framework.  Guidance should also be  clear about testing 
and evaluation criteria to demonstrate sensitivity, specificity , security  and safety 
of AI models and systems throughout the AI l ifecycle.   
We agree with the alignment of Guardrails 3 and 4  to relevant ISO/IEC 
standards, and further recommend that g uidance for  these Guardrails should be 
clear about the Government’s expectations regarding the use of an individual’s 
personal information  as part of a training dataset . Similar to our 
recommendation under question 1, t he guardrails need to mitigate the risk of AI 
use compounding existing inequities  in critical sectors like healthcare , as some 
populations remain underrepresented in the datasets used to train AI algorithms. 
The need for unbiased and representative data for AI training  to support  ongoing 
validation and quality assurance of data should be considered . Further, while 
guidance for Guardrail 3 provide s that data must be ‘legally obtained’  with 
disclosed sources , a significant concern with generative AI  models is their 
potential to expose personal  information  included in training datasets . Effective 
approaches to protect against sophisticated querying methods and other 
malicious attacks on  generative AI  models trained on sensitive data  (such as 
individual -level genomic and healthcare information)  remain unclear , and 
guidance in this area is likely to evolve rapidly alongside changes in the 
technology .  
We support Guardrail 5  which ensures human oversight for high -risk AI 
applications . This is crucial in research and clinical settings where diagnostic 
accuracy is paramount , and substantial  risks of AI models like LLMs such as 
“hallucinated” results , data leakage, error and bias  may impact acceptability  
and adoption . Healthcare decisions are inherently complex, encompassing not 
just medical data but also patient preferences, social and cultural contexts, and

9. How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural 
protocols to ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve ICIP?  
There is a paucity of legislation in Australia that protects Indigenous peoples ’ 
cultural knowledge and protocols , and their personal  and health data that are 
derived from multiple sources and biological samples , including genetic and 
genomic data . Without appropriate Indigenous -led and developed data 
sovereignty protection mechanisms and models, mandatory guardrails will not 
be adequate in being able to protect or provide the appropriate governance  and 
stewardship required.  
In addition to our recommendation under question 2, t he UNDRIP has not been 
embedded within Australian sovereign law despite numerous calls for specific 
legislation to be drafted and implemented (including a Joint Senate Committee 
into the application of UNDRIP in Australia). This legislative vacuum creates 
opportunities for exploitation by AI bad actors and developers. Mandatory 
guardrails  can only ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve 
IDSov/ICIP if specific legislation  and recognition  is drafted to enable adequate  
protection.  
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI 
supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately? For example, are 
the requirements assigned to developers and deployers appropriate?   
The proposed guardrails currently place greater obligations on developers, but 
there is a lack of clarity on how these requirements would be enforced for those 
currently based overseas , as well as  Australian -based SME developers and 
deployers  with limited re sources. Real regulatory effectiveness hinges on 
specific guidance  on how developers and deployers can adhere to them and 14 
 what criteria will be used to assess adherence.  We recommend further guidance 
and clarification to address  these critical gaps.  
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of 
GPAI? How could we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for 
example low -risk and high -risk GPAI models?  
Not fully, for the reasons outlined in our responses above. A cornerstone of these 
guardrails should revolve around the appropriateness, fairness, and 
representation of the training data, and ensure that it is obtained and used with 
appropriate consent  from individuals  and adherence to First Nations protocols . 
Adaptation of the guardrails to different GPAI models should follow clear risk 
assessment and evaluation criteria as previously recommended.

• potential exemption for SMEs based on  an annual turnover threshold, and 
non-applicability of this exemption in the event of high-risk AI used in 
certain high-risk business contexts  such as health services (similar to the 
approach taken by the Privacy Act 1988);

 Regulatory options to mandate guardrails  
 
Proposed mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI at a glance  
3 options for implementing the proposed mandatory guardrails:  
Option 1 – Domain specific approach – adapting existing regulatory frameworks to include the proposed 
mandatory guardrails

13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high -
risk settings? What opportunities should the government take into account 
in considering each approach?  
Recommended legislative option  
We acknowledge the strengths and limitations of the proposed options and 
support the government's efforts to align with AI policy frameworks of other 
leading democracies.  The AASGARD  consortium , like many of its counterparts in 
the Australian and global research and clinical communities, operate s as a large-
scale collaborative network that facilitates the identification of key datasets of 
diagnosed patients and best practices for rigorous AI tool validation and safe 
adoption to maximise clinical impact. A recent Productivity Commission report 
shows that Australia's innovation gap with leading global firms is widening, with 
the country  lagging most OECD nations in adopting advanced technologies .10 
This calls for an urgent need to avoid a patchwork of conflicting regulations  that 
impede national and  international AI collaboration and innovation  – a crucial 
aspect not recognised  in this paper.   
While all options would unavoidably result in consequential regulatory 
coordination challenges and complexity, the whole-of-economy approach 
provided in Option 3  would deliver greater consistency in enforcement and 
appears to be the most viable and sustainable legislative option. We note that 
the risk of duplicate obligations with existing legislative frameworks has been  
acknowledged as a challenge in all three proposed options and  recommend a 
legislative design that aims to achieve strong consistency with  sector-specific 
regulatory bodies (e.g. TGA) that are tailoring regulations to their assigned

sike.aiAs artificial intelligence (AI) continues to advance at an unprecedented rate, governments
around the world are recognising the need for regulatory frameworks that ensure AI’s safe
and responsible use, particularly in high-risk settings. The Australian Government’s proposed
introduction of mandatory guardrails for AI is a crucial step in this direction. However, to
avoid stifling innovation or imposing impractical regulations, it’s important that we take a
measured, evidence-based approach. At sike.ai, we believe the key to effective regulation lies
not in controlling the technology itself but in regulating its applications, supported by trials,
collaboration, and continuous feedback from industry stakeholders.
Much like how we don’t regulate maths because it can be misused, AI itself should not be
subject to restrictive regulation; rather, the focus should be on the outcomes and
applications it powers. Rapid technological advancement, combined with the complexities of
AI, means we need a framework that is both flexible and capable of adapting to future
developments. The approach of simply setting rigid rules, as seen in other jurisdictions, can
lead to obsolescence and inefficiency as the technology improves. To avoid this, we propose a
thoughtful, step-by-step approach, grounded in trials across different industries and the
continuous involvement of industry bodies in defining what constitutes "high-risk AI."Introduction SYDNEY | NEW YORK | VANCOUVER
sike.aiOne of the key challenges in AI regulation is the lack of clear definitions around high-risk AI,
particularly in the case of general-purpose AI (GPAI). This ambiguity can lead to
inconsistencies in how regulations are applied, creating uncertainty as AI technologies evolve
and new use cases emerge. A one-size-fits-all approach, where high-risk AI is centrally
defined across all sectors, may not be practical or effective.
To address this, we propose a Hub and Spoke approach to AI regulation:
Hub (Centralised Framework): The government sets overarching guidelines and broad
standards for AI regulation. These include requirements for risk management,
transparency, traceability, and operational practices, especially for high-risk AI
applications. The Hub provides a consistent regulatory foundation across the economy.
Spokes (Decentralised Implementation): Specific industry bodies and departments
define and adapt regulations to their respective sectors. These entities determine what
constitutes high-risk AI within their industries, ensuring the regulatory approach reflects
the unique risks and challenges of each domain.
This model allows for a more adaptable regulatory framework that evolves alongside AI
technology, tailoring rules to fit specific industries while maintaining core safety and
accountability principles.
Example: Finance Sector (APRA, ASIC, and Industry Bodies)
In the financial services sector, high-risk AI applications may include those used in areas such
as fraud detection, algorithmic trading, credit scoring, and anti-money laundering (AML)
activities. AI is also increasingly being integrated into decision-making processes for
customer interactions, loan approvals, and investment advice.
Under the Hub and Spoke model:
Hub: The government would establish general AI governance principles, such as
transparency, accountability, and risk management. For instance, there would be baseline
requirements for testing AI models before deployment, ensuring explainability, and
maintaining traceability in decision-making processes.
Spokes in Finance:
APRA (Australian Prudential Regulation Authority): APRA could define the specific
AI-related risks in banking, insurance, and superannuation, including areas like
systemic risk, solvency, and cybersecurity. For example, APRA could mandate more
stringent oversight for AI systems used in risk modelling or stress testing, ensuring
that these systems are transparent and that humans can intervene when necessary.The Hub and Spoke ApproachSYDNEY | NEW YORK | VANCOUVER

sike.aiIn the context of AI guardrails, traceability and explainability are critical components that
ensure the safe and responsible deployment of AI systems. These elements are particularly
relevant to several guardrails, including Guardrails 4, 6, 8, and 9.
Scaling Transparency with Risk
The transparency of AI decisions should scale with the associated risk. Higher-risk
applications necessitate greater transparency and traceability in decision-making processes.
This ensures that stakeholders can understand and trust the AI's outputs, especially in high-
stakes scenarios. For instance, in healthcare or autonomous driving, where decisions can
have life-or-death consequences, the need for transparency is paramount. This scaling
approach aligns with the risk management processes outlined in Guardrail 2, ensuring that
the level of transparency is commensurate with the potential impact of the AI system.
Explainability in AI Models
Models like OpenAI's ChatGPT (O1 model) have made strides in explainability, but they still fall
short compared to systems that can point to actual sources. This is where Retrieval-
Augmented Generation (RAG) systems excel. RAG models can provide source attribution,
allowing users to trace the origins of the AI's outputs. This capability is crucial for applications
requiring high levels of accountability and transparency. For example, in legal or academic
settings, the ability to trace information back to its source is essential for verifying the
accuracy and reliability of the AI's outputs.
Hybrid Approaches for Context-Specific Solutions
A hybrid approach that combines fine-tuned models for general questions with RAG systems
for specific workflows can offer a balanced solution. This approach ensures that general
queries are handled efficiently while maintaining rigorous source attribution for tasks that
demand it. The best approach will depend on the context and the specific problem being
addressed. For instance, a customer service chatbot might use a fine-tuned model for
general inquiries but switch to a RAG system when providing detailed product information or
troubleshooting steps.Traceability and ExplainabilitySYDNEY | NEW YORK | VANCOUVER

the need for maintaining records to demonstrate compliance with guardrails.
Compliance: Transparent systems are better equipped to comply with regulatory

From a technical point of view, we also flag an area where humans in the loop is an

surpass human decision-making capabilities. In such cases, having humans too involved

This calls for a more nuanced approach to human involvement. While high-risk scenarios will
still require human oversight and final sign-off—ensuring accountability remains with

sike.aiThis is not unlike systems in modern airliners, where pilots use highly automated systems for

The proposed mandatory guardrails make significant strides in addressing the risks
associated with AI in high-risk settings, but there are opportunities for refinement to better
mitigate these risks without stifling innovation. The following considerations highlight areas
where the guardrails could be improved or adapted:
Application-Focused Regulation: While the guardrails do well in addressing the
technology itself, a shift towards regulating the outcomes and applications of AI, rather
than just the technology, would ensure that the framework remains adaptable as AI
continues to evolve. For example, industries such as healthcare, law enforcement, and
finance each face unique risks, and the Hub and Spoke model would allow sector-specific
regulations to evolve alongside AI developments. This ensures relevant industry experts
shape the regulations and that they remain practical.
Scalable Transparency and Traceability: The current guardrails, particularly around
explainability and transparency, are necessary for building trust in AI systems, but they
should scale with the associated risk. In high-risk settings, such as healthcare or law
enforcement, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems that offer traceability and
source attribution should be prioritised. These systems allow for better decision-making
oversight and can act as a safeguard in sectors where explainability is critical.
Testing and Continuous Monitoring: Guardrails around model testing (Guardrail 4) are
robust but could benefit from deeper integration of ongoing human oversight and digital
attestations to ensure continuous reliability. These mechanisms would ensure that AI
outputs remain accountable over time, mitigating risks as systems evolve or new data is
integrated into models.
Human Oversight in Critical Decisions: Guardrail 5 rightly emphasises human control in AI
systems, but the implementation of augmented intelligence—where AI supports human
decision-making—should be strengthened. In high-risk environments, such as healthcare or
autonomous driving, AI should serve as a companion tool, with final decisions being made by
qualified professionals. This helps avoid over-reliance on AI systems and ensures that
responsibility for outcomes remains with human operators.Expanded answers from submissionSYDNEY | NEW YORK | VANCOUVER

government to take in order to refine and implement AI regulations effectively. These steps
focus on testing, feedback, and ongoing adjustments to ensure the regulatory framework is
adaptable, inclusive, and future-proof.
International Benchmarking
Compare trial findings with global AI regulatory developments (e.g., EU AI Act) to
ensure alignment with international standards.
Base the framework on ISO standards to ensure domestic and international
consistency.
Create a Flexible Regulatory Framework
Draft adaptable regulations based on trial outcomes, allowing room for future AI
advancements.
Implement a phased approach, starting with high-risk sectors and expanding based
on lessons from the trials.
Scale Successful Approaches
Develop guidelines and best practices based on successful pilot programs, which can
serve as a foundation for formal regulation.
Continue to allow industry bodies to define high-risk AI within their domains for

Update regulations as new AI capabilities emerge, ensuring the framework remains
relevant and effective.a.Action PlanSYDNEY | NEW YORK | VANCOUVER
sike.aiIn conclusion, the proposed guardrails for AI regulation represent a significant step towards
ensuring the safe, responsible, and ethical deployment of AI technologies in Australia. By
focusing on regulating the applications and outcomes of AI rather than the technology itself,
we can foster innovation while safeguarding societal and economic well-being. 
The Hub and Spoke model, combined with adherence to international standards like ISO/IEC
42001:2023, provides a flexible and adaptive framework that can evolve alongside
technological advancements. 
The integration of traceability, explainability, and human oversight mechanisms ensures that
AI systems remain transparent, accountable, and trustworthy. By leveraging advanced
technologies such as blockchain and Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs), we can address
potential weaknesses in data management and transparency, further enhancing the
integrity and security of AI deployments. 
Our proposed step-by-step action plan, which includes industry-specific trials, public
consultations, and iterative feedback cycles, ensures that the regulatory framework is
practical, grounded in real-world experiences, and responsive to industry needs. This
approach not only aligns with the broader goals of the AI guardrails but also promotes a
culture of continuous improvement and collaboration. 
At sike.ai, we are committed to building solutions that embody these principles, providing
businesses with the tools they need to adopt AI safely and effectively. By working together,

and unlocks the immense potential of AI to improve social and economic well-being.

Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
 
The Community and Public Sector Union - PSU Group (CPSU) welcomes the opportunity to make 
a submission to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources consultation process for the 
introduction of mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings.  
As the primary union for workers in the Australian Public Service (APS), CPSU members work in 
a range of settings that are considered high -risk for the use of AI including making 
determinations about social security benefits, migration and border protectio n, national 
security and defence, law enforcement and the administration of justice.  
The uptake of AI technologies must be done in a manner that fosters accountability, 
transparency and confidence in the public sector, serves the public interest and engages 
workers.  
The CPSU supports the introduction of the proposed mandatory guardrails for the use of AI in 
high-risk settings, however as detailed in this submission there are several areas where they 
can and must be strengthened.  
We note that guaranteeing a strong, well -resourced regulator will be critical to the success of 
the mandatory guardrails and in ensuring deployers and developers of AI are held accountable.  
Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High -Risk Settings: CPSU submission  
Page 2 of 5 
 
Authorised and printed by Melissa Donnelly, Community and Public Sector Union (PSU Group), Level 3, 54-58 Foveaux St, Surry Hills, NSW, 2010.  We support  the Government’s commitment to developing an appropriate and coordinated 
response to the rapid adoption of AI in Australia and the challenges it presents and look 
forward to continued engagement with Government on these much -needed reforms.  
 
Section one: Defining high -risk AI  
The CPSU echoes the Australian Council of Trade Union’s (ACTU) concern, detailed in their 
submission to this consultation, that the proposed definition of high -risk AI fails to provide 
certainty that the use of AI in relationship to work is high -risk. 
As discussed in the proposals paper1, the introduction of AI in a workplace setting can have 
substantial impacts on workers including recruitment and promotion, pay, rostering, workplace 
surveillance and the way in which work is conducted.  
It is our view that the use of AI in the workplace is high -risk and that should not be open to 
interpretation. To avoid ambiguity, we recommend the creation of an additional principle that 
explicitly recognises workplaces and the employment relationship as  high-risk, as is the case in 
many international examples such as the European Union and Canada’s approach to regulating 
the use of AI2. 
This should include the use of AI systems that in any way affect the work being conducted, 
work processes and practices, the employment relationship and the rights and conditions of 
workers and should be done in consultation with workers and the ir Unions.  
 
Section two: Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of AI  
The proposed guardrails are an important step towards ensuring ethical and effective measures 
for the implementation of AI . While we welcome these much -needed reforms, there are a 
number of areas where they must be strengthened.  
In particular, the guardrails must embed the rights of workers and guarantee a strong worker 
voice, guarantee human oversight of the use of AI in high -risk settings and provide 
whistleblower protections.  
At present, the guardrails rely on self -regulation from the organisations that are developing or 
deploying high -risk AI systems in terms of developing appropriate processes to meet the 
guardrails; we support the ACTU’s position for an explicit list of mini mum requirements for 
each of the mandatory guardrails that is enforceable by the relevant regulator.

Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High -Risk Settings (p.28)  
2 Australian Government Department of Industry, Science and Resources 2024, Proposals Paper for 
Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High -Risk Settings  (p.26)  Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High -Risk Settings: CPSU submission

Authorised and printed by Melissa Donnelly, Community and Public Sector Union (PSU Group), Level 3, 54-58 Foveaux St, Surry Hills, NSW, 2010.  Right now, the guardrails fail to effectively communicate to the user that the primary purpose 
of regulating AI is to protect citizens. Government regulation must clearly establish  that 
protecting citizens is an essential and non -negotiable guardrail in all development, 
implementation and use of AI.  
 
Guardrail 2: ‘Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks.’  
The meaningful inclusion of workers is critical to the successful adoption of AI and as such, a 
recognised right to worker consultation must be embedded in these processes.  
The proposals paper notes that, ‘consideration should also be given to including workers when 
assessing the impacts of adopting AI in the workplace.’ It is not sufficient to rely on employers to 
include workers in these discussions at their discretion. Currently, the Fair Work Act 2009  does 
not provide for mandatory consultation with workers about the introduction of AI and 
automated technologies in their workplace, and too often we see decisions being made without 
the meaningful involvement of workers.  
The CPSU recently surveyed APS workers on the use of AI in their workplaces. Only 21% of 
respondents who are using AI technology at work indicated consultation had occurred  and, 
even where consultation had occurred , the overwhelming majority of  workers were not 
satisfied with the level of consultation.  
Workers must be provided with the necessary information and be involved in decisions that 
impact them and their work. Where AI is adopted, workers who interact with the new systems 
must help drive the design and use of these programs and be supported to de velop the new 
skills required in their changing roles.  
 
Meaningful consultation must be ongoing, particularly considering the constantly evolving 
nature of emerging technologies and their impact. We refer to the Essential Research Report, 
Invisible Bystanders  that recommended new mechanisms to ensure a ‘worker voice is embedded 
in innovation and change is negotiated. ’3 
 
The use of AI, particularly in government, must also be accessible and inclusive. Ensuring 
diverse perspectives and needs are considered in the development and deployment of AI can 
prevent the creation of biased systems, promote equality and enrich its dev elopment.  
 
As such, we recommend strengthening the proposed guardrails to mandate genuine and 
ongoing consultation with workers and their representatives, as well as involvement from 
diverse groups and underrepresented communities.  
 
 
 
3 Essential research and the UTS Human Technology Institute (May 2024), ‘Invisible Bystanders’: How 
Australian Workers Experience The  Uptake of AI and Automation (p.12)  Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High -Risk Settings: CPSU submission  
Page 4 of 5 
 
Authorised and printed by Melissa Donnelly, Community and Public Sector Union (PSU Group), Level 3, 54-58 Foveaux St, Surry Hills, NSW, 2010.  Guardrail 5: Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human 
oversight.  
We strongly support the intention of guardrail  5 to ‘ ensure that humans can effectively 
understand a high -risk AI system, oversee its operation and intervene where necessary  ’ to allow for 
meaningful human oversight and mitigate risks associated with AI’s speed, scale and increasing 
autonomy4. 
We recommend strengthening the language used in the guardrail so that human oversight of AI 
in high -risk settings is mandatory.  
The ability for a human to review outputs and reverse decisions where necessary is essential 
and should not be left to the discretion of the deployer. This is particularly critical for the APS 
where decision -making processes have the potential to significantly affect people’s lives. The 
Robodebt Royal Commission documents the extensive harm caused by errors in automated 
decision -making and highlights the challenge of rebuilding trust in government and the public 
service afterward. Government decisions must be explainable to maintain trust and credibility 
in the APS and in the institution of government.  
 
The need for human oversight of AI systems extends to decisions affecting workers such as 
recruitment, promotion, rostering and allocation of work where AI systems may fail to 
adequately consider relevant factors and fundamental rights.  
Without proper controls, the CPSU is concerned that AI could discriminate against workers 
exercising their rights, such as taking personal leave, or those with protected attributes, leading 
to missed opportunities in rostering, recruitment, and promotion, and increased workplace 
surveillance. There must alw ays be an accountable human decision -maker.  
As such, we strongly recommend amending the language in the proposed guardrail to 
guarantee human oversight of the use of AI in high -risk settings.  
 
Guardrail 7: Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcomes  
The provision of an appropriate process for individuals to challenge t he use of AI where 
necessary is crucial. This can be strengthened by providing strong whistleblower protections, 
which are essential to allow for individuals to report instances in which organisations are 
failing to meet their obligations or where an AI syst em poses a risk of harm to individuals, and 
to act as a deterrent to organisations not complying with the guardrails.

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
No
Are there any principles we should add or remove?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
A1: The definition of high-risk AI should follow the EU AI Act and explicitly exclude the use of biometrics for liveness and face matching for one-to-one identification.
Extract from EU AI Act - Annex III, para 1 (a):
“This [High Risk] shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be;”
We suggest that Australia follows this approach, though perhaps adds the condition that the person has consented: "High Risk shall not include AI systems, used with consent, for identity or authentication services whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be".
The rationale for the exclusion is that the user has given express, free and informed consent, and so the use of AI is highly targeted and for a specific use case. There is no longer a high risk of the AI being used for harm. The consumer knows AI is being used to assess them, and if the AI falsely indicates the consumer has committed fraud then the consumer knows who to appeal to and can prove their identity another way.
Page 28 of the Proposal highlights that Facial Recognition has its own particular considerations. An additional consideration is that where Facial Recognition is solely used for identity verification or authentication, and provided there is a fall back option (eg entering a PIN or verifying identity another way), there is no high risk of harm. It is only where Facial Recognition is used for other purposes, eg categorization based on skin tone or gender, that there is likelihood of harm.
A2: The justification in the Proposal for “Legal effects” (part c) as a High Risk consideration highlights the weaknesses in Australian privacy law.
The Proposal quotes Article 22 of the GDPR which covers automated processing. The Australian government has not followed Article 22 GDPR in its Privacy Act overhaul. If the Australian government is concerned about automated processing it should address it in the Privacy Act rather than AI guidelines since the automated processing is wider than use of AI. The draft Privacy Act only enforces transparency.
This AI Framework should not be used to remedy the inadequacies of the Privacy Act. That should be a matter for Parliament.
Please identify any:
AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be.
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?
No
4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Yes
If so, how should we define these?
IDVerse favours outcome-based categorisations of AI to be banned, rather than process-based categorisation. This is because if the Australian government seeks to define AI based on process there is a real risk that non-harmful AI systems may be caught. Further, outcome-based assessment solves the problem that the Proposal identifies as an issue; that AI used in some contexts is fine, but the same AI used in other contexts is harmful.
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
A: The guardrails are generally strong and aligned with IDVerse’s understanding of developing international norms.
A weakness of the guardrails is that they do not make clear whose job it is to ensure compliance with the guardrails in the typical B2B2C relationship - ie when there is a supplier of AI technology to an entity, and that entity is dealing directly with the consumer. Under the EU AI Act and the GDPR it is clear that it is the entity dealing with the consumer that is directly responsible for compliance. This is because the EU and UK have the helpful concept of a ‘data controller’ and a ‘data processor’. Australian law lacks this distinction. In its absence, the Guardrails needs to make clear that it is the responsibility of the entity making decisions about how to process a consumer’s data to meet the Guardrails.
There are three Guardrails that at first sight appear very onerous for an SME to comply with, but on further reading of the guidance appear more acceptable.
Guardrail 5: Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight
This Guardrail is requiring human oversight. It needs to be clear that this applies to deployers only and not developers.
This needs a lot of more detail of exactly what the Australian government is requiring. The Singaporean government’s paper on AI distinguishes carefully between human in the loop and human over the loop decision making. Modern neural networks do not allow humans to understand every step in the AI decision making process, and so human in the loop is not appropriate, but instead human over the loop should be permitted.
In practice, this means that rather than mandating oversight of the actual working of the AI, it is more appropriate to mandate human oversight of the end-to-end process that the AI works in - and that is under the control of the deployer and not the developer. For example, in an identity verification journey with an AI powered component, it is not the AI component that needs human oversight but the end to end process needs to allow an appeal process or alternative verification journey so that, if necessary, a human is involved in the overall decision making process.
The Proposal explanation of Guardrail 5 appears to agree with the above reasoning, so it is the drafting of the actual Guardrail that needs amending, rather than a change to the overall intention.
Guardrail 6: Inform end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content
This Guardrail makes sense. For it to be workable in practice, it needs to make clear exactly which entity (AI supplier or the entity dealing directly with the consumer) needs to inform the consumer.
Guardrail 9: Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails
This requires businesses to allow “third parties” access to assess compliance. The notes assume that third parties is understood to mean regulators and other authorities with legal powers. It would be helpful if the Guardrail could make this more explicit.
Guardrail 10: Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with the guardrails
This strongly suggests the need for external certification. This goes further than the EU AI Act and therefore is an additional burden for Australian businesses that will impact on competitiveness.
If this is not the intention then Guardrail 10 should be amended to make clear that internal assessment is adequate.
Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?
No
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
No
Which of the guardrails should be amended?
Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with the guardrails
Please provide any additional comments
Clarity is needed that it is the deployer only that should be bound by Guardrail 5. This is essential to allow AI tech to be developed in Australia.
12. Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small-to-medium sized businesses applying guardrails?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
See comments above in Q8 on certification and external review.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A framework approach – Introducing new framework legislation to adapt existing regulatory frameworks across the economy
What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
An AI Act would be a huge regulatory burden for SMEs.
Even though our technology is carved out of the EU AI Act, and we only have a few clients in the EU, we spend a considerable amount of time answering questions about the EU AI Act.
See Mr Draghi's comments on the EU AI Act driving tech unicorns out of the EU.
15. Which regulatory option(s) will best ensure that guardrails for high-risk AI can adapt and respond to step-changes in technology?
A framework approach – Introducing new framework legislation to adapt existing regulatory frameworks across the economy

MEAA Submission  
Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High -Risk Settings  
 
The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA) welcomes the opportunity to make a 
submission to the Department of Industry, Science, and Resources’ consultation process for 
its proposal paper on the introduction of mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings.  
This submission engages with questions raised in the Department’s proposal paper. We have 
opted to respond to questions 1 -4 and 6 in section 1 of our submission, 8 -9 in section 2, and 
13-16 in section 3 . 
MEAA is the largest and most established union and industry advocate for workers in the 
media, film, music, and arts industries, with a history going back more than 110 years. We 
endorse the submission of the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU), of w hich we are 
an affiliate, and seek to provide additional feedback specific to the creative and media 
industries.  
 
Introduction  
The emergence of generative Artificial Intelligence comes with significant potential risks for 
Australia’s creative industries. MEAA’s recent member survey showed that a majority of 
members (56%) are extremely concerned about the rise of AI, whereas only o ne in fifty 
members (2%) are not at all concerned about the rise of AI.  
If left unchecked, it is conceivable that the increased use of AI tools could lead to a 
significant  loss of jobs and the degradation of conditions for Australia’s media and creative 
sector workers. AI also poses unique threats in its potential to digitally replicate a  
performers’  voice or likeness, as well as in its ability to replicate a creators’  technical and/or 
creative style. This has the capacity to alienate that persons’ unique style, likeness, or voice 
from them without compensation, credit, or cons ent. 
The basis for the development of these tools is the mass ingestion of creative and 
intellectual works by AI machines. Creatives, writers, and journalists from Australia and 
around the globe have had their work scraped, largely without any compensation or 
consent, and used to train AI. In this sense, the theft of creatives’ and journalists’ work is 
directly related to the development of the very tools designed to replace them.   
These risks are not just theoretical. MEAA  has already  seen cases where performers’ voices 
have been reproduced without their consent, while First Nations artists have had their styles 
replicated in AI -generated copycat works without permission or disclosure to buyers in the 
marketplace.  2 
 
 It’s not just AI’s impact on workers that are a concern. The Australian public  need s to be able 
to trust that the news they read, the film and television they watch, and the music they 
listen to has been produced by artists and journalists whose work has not been 
compromised by AI.  
For these reasons, MEAA holds that it is critical that Australia adopts a comprehensive, 
economy -wide AI Act. This AI Act must be underpinned by a specialised and well -funded 
independent regulator to ensure compliance.  
Last, as a general comment, MEAA is concerned about the application of the guardrails to AI 
developers who have developed models abroad – outside of the Australian jurisdiction for 
the purposes of AI regulation. It is critical that the Government ensure th at developers 
acting abroad are subject to the same requirements for transparency, the legal collection of 
data , and labelling as those operating inside Australia’s borders.  
 
Section 1: Proposed definition of high -risk AI  
Developing a comprehensive and clear definition of high -risk AI is crucial for the success of 
the Departments’ proposed mandatory guardrails approach. In general, MEAA endorses the 
definition of high -risk developed by the Department. However, we have a num ber of key 
concerns about the definition as it currently stands. First, MEAA is concerned that the stated 
principles do not provide sufficient clarity and certainty regarding the definition of high -risk 
in relation to a) work, and b) Australia’s creative a nd media sector.  
First, we endorse the ACTU’s view that any AI that impacts the nature of work, the 
conditions of workers, or the means through which work is allocated and/or managed and 
distributed should be considered inherently high risk. This would remove ambiguities i n the 
definition and make it explicit that the guardrails apply not only in the case of consumers 
and end -users but in the case of workers also.  
Recommendation 1: That a further proposed principle be included: ‘The risk of adverse 
effects on workers in regards to the employment relationship, the allocation of work 
(including through digital platforms) work processes and in all matters pertaining to rights 
at work and rights while conducting work.’  
In addition, MEAA is concerned about the lack of attention given to Australia’s cultural and 
media landscape in the proposed definition of high -risk. This is for two reasons. The first is 
the critical importance of these sectors for the health of Australia ’s democracy and for our 
unique cultural identity. Australia’s storytellers, artists, actors, dancers, musicians, and 
technicians form the heart of our country’s culture, and the health of our democracy and 
civil society is reliant on the commitment and te nacity of our journalists who deliver public 
interest journalism that scrutinises power, informs the public and provides a bulwark against 
the proliferation of disinformation and misinformation.  3 
 
 The second reason  is that generative AI poses significant and particular risks to the creative 
and media sectors which fundamentally threaten the sustainability of these sectors. 
Generative AI has the potential to dislocate and devalue the work of artists, creators, and 
journalists. If left unchecked, it is conceivable that the increased use of AI tools in the media 
and creative industries could lead to a loss of jobs and the degradation of conditions in 
creative and journalistic work. Furthermore, while AI  advocates spruik the technology’s 
capacity to improve the productivity of workers and “democratise” the production of 
creative content, the reality is that businesses are utilising AI tools to replace their workforce 
with automation products. This means t hat the jobs of those working in the production of 
digital content – including actors, musicians, set and costume designers, and voice artists – 
are under significant threat. With that threat comes a broader threat to the production of 
distinctly Australia n cultural work and journalism.  
It is critical to note the impact of generative AI on First Nations art and culture. MEAA is 
aware that generative AI is being used to train AI software used to mimic the artistic style of 
Australia’s First Nations artists and performers. There are now numerous reports of AI -
generated ‘Indigenous art’ being commodified and sold online, including on Adobe, Etsy, 
and eBay.1 These are adding to the competition Indigenous artists already face from the fake 
‘Indigenous art’ market, threatening to further undermine their livelihoods and the 
sustainability of the sector.  
Recommendation 2: That a further proposed principle be included: ‘the risk of adverse 
impacts to Australia ’s cultural and media landscape .’ 
In addition, MEAA holds that there are several ways in which the proposed principles could 
better empower to First Nations people to protect culture , communities and country from 
exploitation. First, protocols for using Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples 
Intellectual and Cultural Property (ICIP) must be embedded into AI legislative protections 
and Australian copyright law.  It is critical th at these protocols must be incorporated into 
existing legislation to ensure proper enforcement.  
These protocols must establish Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ sovereign 
rights of ownership of data, lands, language, culture, art, stories, music, song, dance, voice, 
image, likeness, body, movement, and intellectual and creative output. I n addition, if AI is 
engaged to depict the voice, image, movement or likeness of Aboriginal and Torres Strait 
Islander ancestors and/or deceased persons, all companies and entities must follow the 
applicable Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander protocols and cultural Lore of those 
ancestors and/or deceased persons.  
Recommendation 3: that Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) be embedded 
into law.  
Our view is that all general -purpose AI (GPAI) models should be considered inherently high 
risk because they can be applied to a wide range of applications, some not possible to 
foresee, to a potentially very broad audience at very high speeds.  
Recommendation 4: categorise all general -purpose AI (GPAI) as high risk.  4 
 
 MEAA also holds that certain kinds of AI applications should be banned, including that which 
is used for exploitative and deceptive purposes. MEAA endorses the ACTU’s list of proposed 
unacceptably high -risk cases of AI use that should be, in our view, bann ed. These include 
cases where they involve automated decision making over the employment relationship that 
substantially affects the rights and interests of an employee, where they are applied into 
employment and work processes without the meaningful knowl edge and consent of workers 
and where they are used for the purpose of intrusive monitoring or surveillance of workers 
without their knowledge or consent. MEAA would also add to this list any use of  an AI 
system to create a digital replica using the biometric data of an individual without their 
informed consent.  
Recommendation 5: that the government ban unacceptably high -risk AI.  
 
Section 2:  Proposed Guardrails  
The proposed guardrails provide an important first step in managing the risks of AI in high -
risk settings. In particular, MEAA strongly supports efforts to mandate transparency in the 
collection of training data, to ensure that datasets are obtained legall y, and in efforts to 
ensure a system of labelling or watermarking for AI -generated outputs. These guardrails 
speak to key concerns raised by our members.  
Guardrail 2  
Workers must be involved in formulating the risk assessment and management process 
within an organisation , and  it is also imperative that meaningful consultation and consent be 
obtained from workers prior to decisions about implementing AI systems in the workplace 
being made. We believe that there are circumstances where workers may identify or be 
exposed to risks f rom the use of AI in their work which may conflict with the priorities of 
their employer  and that these can be avoided by ensuring meaningful co nsultation and 
engagement with workers . 
The media and creative industries bring with them a range of unique challenges when 
considering and mitigating risk. Film and TV productions  for example,  are large undertakings 
that involve a diverse range of teams of experts responsible for aspects of the overall 
production. Therefore, there are many possible different uses of AI within a single 
production with the potential to expose workers to different  kinds of risks. For instance, 
Generative AI tools could be used in post -production and editing, visual  effects, 
photography, script writing, score writing, sound production and of course, in the 
performance of actors, dancers and musicians.  
There are clear risks in the possible use of AI tools which have been developed using illegally 
obtained training data, and there are risks to workers (regardless of them being a performer, 
crew, technician or other member of staff) having their biometric data obtained with 
consent or compensation for the use in the production or used in other productions or even 5 
 
 commodified and on -sold. These are only two of the many possible risks associated with 
employing AI in film and TV productions.  
Journalism is also exposed to a number of significant risks specific to the industry. Public 
interest journalism requires journalists to be able to verify and protect sources and 
interrogate information provided to them to ensure they are factual. Addition ally, journalists 
who are members of the MEAA are bound by the Journalist Code of Ethics2 which binds 
them to a set of professional standards in the production of public interest journalism.   
The potential use of AI systems in newsrooms whether they are ‘off the shelf’ tools or ‘fine -
tuned’ in -house AI systems present significant risks to the ability for journalists to uphold 
their professional standards. Risks to future work and appropriate compensation  also arise 
when media companies wish to on -sell or license the work of journalists for use by AI 
developers.   
Guardrail 3  
MEAA holds that all AI models, not just those which are deemed high risk, should be subject 
to transparency requirements around the collection and use of training data. This is because 
copyright violation is an inherent risk of all AI models.  
Second, MEAA holds that these datasets should be made publicly available – or at a 
minimum, that the copyright holder and original author are notified about any use of their 
work for the purposes of training. This is necessary because of the profound ways in which 
the theft of such work for the purposes of training is impacting creative  worker s, writers, 
and journalists.  
Third, MEAA strongly believes that this guardrail should be applied retrospectively. We know 
that huge amounts of data have already been ingested for the purposes of AI training. For 
example, we know that the Books3 database (estimated to contain 196,640 b ooks3) and the 
LAION -5B database (containing an estimated 5.85 billion images4) have been ingested by a 
range of major LLMs. Creators deserve to know whether their work has been used to build 
these models.  
Last, we echo the ACTU’s concerns about existing gaps in privacy and workplace laws, as well 
as the use of far -reaching exceptions which allow employers to use employees’ data without 
restriction following the initial point of collection. We reiterate the ACTU’s call to broaden 
this guardrail to further stipulate that this data must be legally obtained, with its use subject 
to informed consent. This should include clear avenues for redress where proper 
authorisation has not been obtained.  
Guardrail 6  
MEAA is concerned that a ‘best efforts’ approach will lead to sub -optimal outcomes when it 
comes to transparency, ensuring trust, and ease of use for end -users/consumers. Further to 
this, MEAA believes that, at a minimum, attempts should be made to standar dise labelling 6 
 
 systems across industries and be incorporated into existing classification systems and 
practices where possible.  
Furthermore, MEAA is strongly concerned about the narrow application of the requirement 
for labelling to high -risk AI only. We believe that labelling should apply to all content 
generated by AI, including those applications not designated ‘high -risk’. This  is necessary to 
ensure that, as a general rule, audiences can be informed about whether content – for 
example, a film, television show, media article, or musical composition – has been generated 
by AI.  
Last, we echo the ACTU’s concerns about employers potentially failing to recognise 
employees as end users – as well as the general public. We agree with the ACTU’s 
recommendation that the government provide further clarification that employers have a 
respo nsibility to fulfil the obligations under this guardrail in relation to employees.  
 
Section 3: Preferred Regulatory Options to Mandate Guardrails  
In order to meet the community’s expectations of government to ensure the safety and 
security of AI systems, it is necessary for there to be a comprehensive and coordinated 
approach across government and the economy that protects workers, citizens, and 
consumers, provides clarity and simplicity for users and businesses of all sizes, and is 
enforceable.   
Our approach is guided by these criteria:  
• That the need for regulation is urgent,  
• That the regulatory response must ensure the strongest possible protections for 
workers citizens and consumers,  
• That the regulatory response must be comprehensive and work seamlessly with 
other economy -wide regimes such as workplace, copyright and privacy laws,  
• That the regulatory regime must be clear and simple,  
• That the regulatory regime must be enforceable, and  
• That the regulatory regime must allow scope for alignment with similar regimes 
from international jurisdictions.  
On this basis, we endorse Option 3: an economy -wide AI Act. This option is the only one that 
will deliver on the ambition to deliver safe and responsible AI in Australia in line with the 
criteria mentioned above. Much like the implicit rationale for other comprehensive 
regulatory regimes in Australia, the case for a comprehensive approach to regulating AI 
through an Act is clear. AI -enabled applications are already installed on devices sitting in 
most homes and workplaces. AI systems are already being used across business, academia 
and government, and plans are being put in place to use AI tools to replace thousands of 
jobs in the coming years.5 We also know that AI is turbocharging the spread of 
disinformation and propaganda contributing to the decline of trust in democratic institutions 
and undermining the work of journalists .6 7 
 
 We are concerned that options one and two would force government to take a piecemeal 
approach to amending laws and regulations and this would greatly inhibit the government in 
implementing regulations with the urgency required to match the speed of the rol lout of AI 
systems in Australia. It is our view that government must act with urgency because of the 
rate at which AI is developing and setting new norms in the absence of comprehensive 
regulation. Not only would these approaches be slower to enact than a comprehensive AI 
Act, but it would also make Australia’s AI regulatory regime complex, difficult to understand 
and prone to unnecessary duplication. This would hinder the successful implementation of 
AI regulation, it would leave workers, citizens and cons umers unsure if their rights and it 
would be a disincentive for small and medium sized enterprises to positively embrace 
regulation.   
It is also our view that options one and two contain inherent limitations which would impair 
the ability for government to bring the guardrails into effect. We concur with the analysis of 
DISR in the proposals paper7 that both options one and two will retain gaps across regimes, 
will leave industries siloed, will limit regulation to the scope and powers of current 
regulatory arrangements and will be largely unenforceable. Option three presents the best 
opportunity for  a coordinated approach to regulation. Some of the proposed guardrails go 
hand in hand and would be much less effective if implemented in isolation or with different 
effect industry by industry.  
Option three also presents the best environment for ensuring that all related regulatory 
regimes such as copyright and privacy are linked together as seamlessly as possible. As we 
have stated in other sections of this submission, we believe that there is a  gap in the 
proposed guardrails when it comes to ensuring protections for workers. We endorse the 
position of the ACTU on the need for a comprehensive review of workplace laws, particularly 
the Fair Work Act, to ensure they remain fit for purpose in the co ntext of the rapid adoption 
of AI systems, and the potential risks of AI.  
Such piecemeal approaches would also add complexity to Australia’s regulatory landscape, 
encouraging litigation and adding to the costs of doing business. It would enable well -
resourced companies to game the system to suit their interests over the interest s of the 
community. Such scenarios have precedents overseas where big tech companies – who also 
count amongst the most significant developers and deployers of AI – have been accused of 
flouting competition laws and other regulations in the European Union a nd United States8.  
Examples like this highlight the need to ensure the enforceability of these regulations, and 
only a comprehensive AI act can achieve that. It is our view that an AI regulator must be 
instituted and properly funded to oversee this regime and to make sure th at there is 
sufficient oversight. Self -regulation cannot to be depended on to ensure that comprehensive 
safeguards are enacted and upheld. Considering the enormity of the scale of change that AI 
is predicted to have on our society, we cannot afford to impl ement a regulatory regime that 
is limited unambitious .  
Recommendation 6: The government adopt Option 3: an economy -wide AI Act  as the 
preferred option for mandating the guardrails.   8

Medicines Australia submission to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources’ ‘Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings: proposals paper’ 4 October 2024 Medicines Australia welcomes the opportunity to respond to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources’ consultation on introducing mandatory guardrails for artificial intelligence (AI) in high risk settings. As the peak body representing the innovative pharmaceutical industry in Australia, our response will focus primarily on AI used in therapeutic goods. Australia's medicines regulation system is highly regarded both domestically and internationally for its rigorous standards and robust oversight. The Therapeutic Good Administration (TGA) regulates AI where it is used in a medical product (technically referred to as a device), for the purposes of diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, prediction, prognosis, treatment, or alleviation of disease, injury or disability.1  The TGA collaborates with international regulatory agencies such as the FDA (US), EMA (Europe), and comparable international regulatory counterparts wherever possible to ensure global consistency in the regulation of medicines. This harmonisation is beneficial for global manufacturers and ensures that Australian standards are in line with international best practices, while promoting timely access to medicines by streamlining registration processes.2 Medicines Australia believes that creating bespoke regulatory requirements could be a barrier to Australia being able to benefit from innovations and efficient regulatory procedures. Bespoke regulatory frameworks could negatively impact both Australian owned and overseas owned companies and should therefore be avoided. A sizeable number, around 250, global and local research-based pharmaceutical companies operate in Australia. Australian owned companies export therapeutic goods which totaled $8.2 billion and ranked 8th largest in Australia in 2019.3 While Australia ‘punches above our weight’, we produce only a very small proportion of medicines that Australians use. Due to the competitive nature of the larger international economies, we rely heavily on imported medicines, particularly for innovative drugs and treatments not yet developed or produced locally.  1	https://www.tga.gov.au/how-we-regulate/manufacturing/manufacture-medical-device/manufacture-speci8ic-types-medical-devices/arti8icial-intelligence-ai-and-medical-device-software	2	https://www.tga.gov.au/resources/resource/international-scienti8ic-guidelines	3	https://www.mtpconnect.org.au/images/2020%20MTPConnect%20Sector%20Competitiveness%20Plan.pdf

Over the 2014-2016 period, the largest exporters of pharmaceuticals were EU countries, as well as Switzerland, the United States, India, China, Singapore, Israel and Japan. Together, these economies represented more than 92% of the total value of global exports of pharmaceuticals.4 Given the global supply chain, maintaining international harmonisation of regulatory frameworks for AI in therapeutic goods is paramount in ensuring Australians continue to have access to safe and effective innovative medicines. Medicines Australia has very close ties with international pharmaceutical industry associations, including in Europe, the US, Canada and the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations (IFPMA). As the therapeutic goods sector and regulators in Australia and overseas explore the use of AI in the medicines lifecycle, we look forward to collaborating with the Australian Government, the TGA and other relevant regulators. We would be happy to facilitate collaboration and share learnings from our overseas industry colleagues regarding the development of AI governance frameworks to maintain safe, effective and sustainable supply of innovative medicines to Australia. Medicines Australia’s position and proposed principles are outlined below. They align with the OECD principles, which the Australian Government has committed to, that set standards for AI that are practical and flexible enough to stand the test of time, and promote use of AI that is innovative and trustworthy and that respects human rights and democratic values.5  Our position is also consistent with the IFPMA’s and Australia’s AI ethics principles.6,7  We hope that this may help to guide the development of appropriate mandatory guardrails for AI use in therapeutic goods. Position and Proposed Principles • Medicines Australia believes in the potential of applying AI to deliver benefit for patients, life-science companies and society.  Avant submission to the consultation on introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in 
high risk settings  
 
Avant is a member -owned doctors’ organisation and Australia’s largest medical indemnity 
insurer, committed to supporting a sustainable health system that provides quality care to 
the Australian community. Avant provides professional indemnity insurance and  legal 
advice and assistance to about 90 ,000 healthcare practitioners and students  around 
Australia (more than half of Australia’s doctors). Our members are from all medical 
specialities and career stages and from every state and territory in Australia.  
 
We assist members in civil litigation, professional conduct matters, coronial matters and a 
range of other matters. Our Medico -legal Advisory Service provides support and advice to 
members and insured medical practices when they encounter medico -legal issues. We 
aim to promote quality, safety and professionalism in medical practice through advocacy, 
research and medico -legal education . 
 
General comments  
 
Avant welcomes increased governance in relation to the implementation of safe and 
responsible AI in Australia and acknowledges the delicate balance required between 
regulation for safety and consistency, and promotion of innovation.  
 
While we acknowledge that this consultation adopts a whole of economy approach, our 
focus is on the need to promote safe and clinically appropriate regulation of AI in the 
context of health care.  We will be making submissions  to sector -specific consultations 
conducted by  the Department of Health and Aged Care  and the Therapeutic Goods 
Administration.  
 
Avant supports the need for clearer frameworks and guidelines to address the 
complexities of AI in healthcare, ensuring that responsibility and liability are properly 
managed and that both doctors and patients are adequately protected.  
 
In summary, our key points are:  
 
• We are broadly supportive of the introduction of guardrails as outlined by DISR  and we 
agree that they should be mandatory in high -risk settings . 
• We agree that the use of AI in health  care is high -risk, based on the potential for 
adverse impacts on an individual’s physical or mental health or safety.  However, there 
is a scale of risk for the AI products that might be used in the health care setting.   
• We acknowledge that existing regulatory frameworks are ill -equipped to address the 
unique challenges posed by using  AI in health  care. Current regulations may not 
sufficiently cover the safety, efficacy, and ethical use of AI , and will need to be 
adapted.  
• The regulatory settings for AI products used in health  care should  be commensurate 
with the scale of risk associated with the type of  product . Not all uses need to be  
3 
 treated in the same way . The regulation  of some produc ts such as AI scribes may also 
need to be reconsidered . 
• Clinicians may be both deployers and users of AI in settings  such as  medical practices . 
It is essential that there is clear guidance about the obligations on  clinicians  and how to 
comply with the guardrails to limit  regulatory burden  and enable adoption.  
• We agree with the preventive approach to accountability and risk management, but if 
harm does occur, there should be mechanisms for appropriately determining liability 
and obtaining redress, beyond the complaints handling processes outlined in relation to 
guardrail 7.  
• Liability should be appropriately apportioned and should not be shifted away from 
those who are able to control the risks, for example, through contractual indemnity 
clauses and disclaimers.  
• The guardrails must also allow for appropriate insurance and indemnity arrangements 
for developers, deployers and users in the health care sector so that there is 
accountability and responsibility for patient safety across the AI lifecycle. Both 
practitioners and patients alike need to have the confidence that insurance issues can 
be appropriately addressed should they arise.   
• Further consideration is required about the best regulatory approach to implement the 
mandatory guardrails so that they are applied consistently and without duplication. We 
broadly support having a principles -based framework, supported by guidance on how 
to apply the principles in practice which might be sector specific. A relevant comparison 
is Australia’s privacy regime model.  
• Ongoing consultation will be  essential  and we recommend that sector -specific working 
groups are formed, made up of key stakeholders including insurers .

Mandatory guard rails should apply to a ll GPAI models because there is the potential for
