6 
 Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of AI  
 
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in 
high risk settings?  
 
Yes.  
 
Please provide any additional comments.  
 
 
We agree that the introduction of the proposed mandatory guardrails  is an appropriate 
means of responding to the risks of AI in high -risk settings . The guardrails themselves are 
comprehensive , address ing the AI lifec ycle and the AI supply chain . The principles -based 
approach is also effective, enabling consistent application across the whole economy  as 
well as  sector -specific application and responses.   
 
We also agree that the use of AI in health care is high -risk, based on the potential for 
adverse impacts on an individual’s physical or mental health or safety.  These additional 
sensitivities should be considered so that AI is adopted safely and in a way that enhances 
public and professional trust.   
 
However, there is a scale of risk for the AI products that might be used in the health care 
setting . Uses in healthcare range from providing and collecting information,  triage and 
prioritisation , document summarisation, prediction  and clinical decision support , to 
diagnosis , treatment and ongoing clinical management . Our view is that t he regulatory 
settings for AI products used in health  care should be commensurate with the scale of risk 
associated with the type of product. Not all uses need to be treated in the same way. The 
regulation of s ome products which  are currently unregulated, such as AI scribes  for clinical 
notetaking , may also need to be reconsidered.  We will provide further commentary in our 
submission to the Department of Health and Aged Care consultation.  
 
Given that the mandatory guardrails are to apply to developers and deployers of high -risk 
AI systems  across the AI lifecycle , we support the  following requirements  to mitigate the 
risks:  
• The ongoing obligation on developers to monitor and refine their AI system once 
deployed ( guardrail 4 ) 
• Deployers  to inform  developers of any adverse incidents or risks that emerge while the 
system is in use (guardrail 8)  
• The requirement on developers to undertake a new conformity assessment i f the AI 
system changes in a way that affects compliance with the guardrails (guardrail 10). 
This should not be the responsibility of deployers as implied in the table on page 67 of 
the proposals paper.  
  
7 
 While the proposals paper indicates that the guardrails will operate “ alongside laws and 
regulatory instruments to hold organisations accountable when harm does occur ”, we look 
forward to considering the details of how this will operate in practical terms .    
 
Ongoing consultation will be essential and we recommend that sector -specific working 
groups are formed, made up of key stakeholders including insurers .  
 
Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?    
 
 
No. 
 
9. How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols to 
ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve Indigenous Cultural and 
Intellectual Property?     
 
No response .  
 
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply 
chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately? For example, are the requirements 
assigned to developers and deployers appropriate?  
 
Yes.  
 
Please provide any additional comments.  
 
 
We make two comments  from a health care perspective in relation to  responsibility and 
assigned requirements  in the proposed guidelines : 
1) responsibility , liability and insurance considerations  
2) responsibility for conformity assessments.  
 
Responsibility, liability and indemnity considerations  
Avant supports a risk -based approach to promote the apportionment of liability and 
responsibility to those who have the ability to affect outcomes  and control the risk . In 
particular, we support the intention that the mandatory guardrails require developers and 
deployers of high -risk AI to take specific steps across the AI lifecycle to:  
• test to ensure that the systems perform as intended and meet appropriate performance 
metrics  
• ensure transparency in relation to product development and use  
• promote accountability for governing and managing the risks of AI systems.  
 
Currently, there is legal uncertainty around accountability, responsibility and liability across 
the AI lifecycle in healthcare. It can be difficult to determine who is accountable when AI -
driven decisions result in errors or adverse outcomes. The complexi ty of AI algorithms  
8 
 makes it challenging to trace the decision -making process, creating medico -legal risks and 
complicating the implem entation of risk management processes  and the assignment of 
liability.  
 
There is a risk that responsibility for the design or function of AI could be unfairly shifted 
onto doctors. This has been exacerbated by the presence of broad indemnity clauses in 
some AI provider contracts, which attempt to absolve these companies of res ponsibility 
and liability and place the burden on doctors  using the AI system . This not only gives rise 
to moral hazard , but also it  exposes doctors to legal risk and raises concerns about 
whether their professional indemnity insurance will cover liability  under such contracts.  
 
The guardrails must also allow for appropriate insurance and indemnity arrangements for 
developers, deployers and users in the health care sector so that there is accountability 
and responsibility for patient safety across the AI lifecycle. Both practitioners and patients 
alike need to have the confidence that insurance issues can be appropriately addressed 
should they arise.   
 
The challenge of ensuring proper accountability is amplified by the need for accessible 
and historical data on AI performance. If the data and operational information the AI 
systems rely upon are not properly recorded, stored and maintained  (as required under 
guardrail 9) , it becomes extremely difficult to trace the source of the error that has caused 
patient harm and determine liability at a later date.   Guardrail 9 should encompass the 
need to keep historical data.  
 
In guardrail 7, the discussion refers to complaints handling . However, redress for harm is 
broader than that and includes appropriate compensation. We note also that the table on 
the last page the box outlining what this means for developers is blank .  
 
We recommend the following:  
• That developers of high -risk AI software are prevented from contracting out of their 
responsibilities under the guardrails.  This may prevent  those who have the capacity to 
reduce risk from avoiding  responsibility through indemnity clauses . 
• Developers and/or deployers not based within Australia should be required to have an 
Australian base or nexus to ensure that they will fulfil  their accountability and reporting 
requirements under the guardrails.  
• That standards be adopted to ensure that the guardrail obligations for developers and 
deployers remain in force for the period that the developer or deployer maintains their 
involvement with the AI system. Developers and deployers should be required to 
ensure they have insurance to cover  future liability. This is particularly important in the 
health sectors given limitation periods under civil liability legislation.  
• In guardrail 4, standards should  be adopted to identify  relevant time frames for 
responding to feedback from deployers about changes to the AI system. Failing to 
provide some guidance on the time frames may result in delays and increased risk.  
• Guardrail 9 should encompass the need to keep historical data  for relevant time 
periods, given  limitation periods under civil liability legislation.   
9 
 Responsibility for conformity assessments  
We agree that developers must undertake a conformity assessment before the ir AI system 
is deployed , as outlined in guardrail 10.  This should also be required  of developers when 
the AI system is retrained  or changes in a way that affects compliance with the guardrails .  
This should not be the responsibility of deployers as implied in the table on page 67 of the  
proposals  paper.   
 
Responsib ility for performing  the conformity assessment  is currently unclear . In our view 
conformity assessments should be performed by third -parties or government entities as 
this would be  more independent and objective than  self-assessment . This  would  need to  
be supported  by the requirement to maintai n records and a documented accountability 
process as outlined in the  proposals  paper .   
 
11. Are the  proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI?  
 
 
Yes. 
 
If yes, p lease provide any additional comments.  
 
 
Avant supports mandatory guardrails for all GPAI models to protect against unforeseeable 
risks to user s and the public at large.  
 
12.  Do you have any suggestions for reducing regulatory burden on small -to-medium 
sized businesses applying guardrails? Please provide any additional comments.  
 
Yes.  
 
Clinicians may be both deployers and users of AI in settings such as medical practices , 
which are often small businesses . The guardrails will create  many  obligations  on clinicians, 
and with it a significant regulatory burden. The accountability processes suggested under 
guardrail 1 are a n example  of this . There will be a barrier to adoption  if the regulatory and 
compliance burden is too great.  
 
We recommend th e following:  
• It is essential that there is clear guidance about the obligations on clinicians and how to 
comply with the guardrails to limit any regulatory burden and enable adoption.   
• Guidance should acknowledge the potential overlap between a clinician’s obligations 
as a deployer and a user of AI in health care.  
• Under guardrail 9, r egulatory and compliance requirements  should align with existing 
practice standards for clinicians ( e.g. RACGP accreditation standards) .  
• Requirements should also integrate into existing risk management processes wherever 
possible.  
  
10 
 Regulatory options to mandate guardrails  
 
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high -risk settings?   
 
 
No response.  
 
What opportunities should the government take into account in considering each 
approach?  
 
See response to Q15 below.  
 
14.  Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the 
Australian government should consider?    
 
See response to Q15 below.  
 
15.  Which regulatory option(s) will best ensure that guardrails for high -risk AI can adapt 
and respond to step -changes in technology?    
 
Other . 
 
Further consideration is required about the best regulatory approach to implement the 
mandatory guardrails so that they are applied consistently and without duplication  across 
and within sectors .  
 
We broadly support having a principles -based framework, accompanied  by guidance on 
how to apply the principles /guardrails  in practice which might be sector specific. A relevant 
comparison is the Commonwealth  privacy regime model.  
 
We also believe that the regulatory regime should not be overly burdensome nor be a 
barrier to innovation  or adoption . However, the balance between regulation and innovation 
needs to be appropriate to achieve this.  
 
Option 1 – the domain specific approach – could be beneficial because:  
• It leverages the existing economy wide and sector specific laws to apply the guardrails . 
• Adoption of the guardrails in the context of existing legislation capitalises on the 
associated familiarity and knowledge of the legislation . 
• It will allow for the introduction of the guardrails at the earliest possible opportunity, 
supported by tailored regulation for each specific area.  
 
However, we agree that option 1 is likely to encourage gaps between regulated sectors 
and regulatory silos.  
  
11 
 We agree that option 2 – the framework approach – would be more flexible and able to 
respond to step -changes in technology  but also has limitations and , like option 1,  could 
lead to regulatory gaps  and silos .  
 
16.  Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps and inconsistencies within Australia’s 
existing laws for the development and deployment of AI?     
 
• There are scales of “high -risk” depending on the nature of the risk and the sector in 
which it arises. How these are treated in regulation across sectors may create

• If options 1 or 2 are adopted, there is a risk of inconsistency between Commonwealth

• There may be a gap in ensuring appropriate responses (such as override or shut down)

• There is a need to ensure that there are appropriate and harmonised penalty

RMIT welcomes the opportunity to provide feedback on the Proposals Paper for Introducing 
Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High- Risk Settings , published by the Department of Industry, 
Science and Resources in September 2024. We are pleased to provide our support for the 
recommendations, which are largely consistent with the Australian AI Ethics Principles  and mark a 
significant step toward ensuring the safe and responsible evolution and implementation of AI 
technologies in Australia.  
 
RMIT  has established our own detailed AI Governance Framework , which  addresses many, if not 
all, of the proposed guardrails stated in the paper and reinforces our commitment to ethical AI 
practices.  In our 2023 submission to DISR, we stated that RMIT stakeholders see a need for 
adopting a common proportionate risk -based and principles -based regulatory approach to promote 
and foster the safe and responsible design,  development, deployment and use of AI in Australia. 
We supported t hese regulations being mandated across all sectors (given the potential risks , and 
recognising self -regulation is not appropriate or  justifiable). We also suggested that  there may be a 
need for more specific and limited regulations to apply to particular AI technologies , particular 
sectors , or in particular contexts.  
 
The following detailed feedback, from RMIT’s Data & Analytics  team, RMIT’s Centre for Education, 
Innovation and Quality (CEIQ) team , and the ARC Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision-
Making + Society (ADM+S) led by RMIT, represents perspectives from researchers and 
practitioners who have significant experience and knowledge in the domains of educational 
practice, data science, ar tificial intelligence, internet policy, data management and data 
governance.  
Key points  
Overall, RMIT commends the proposals as an advancement in the growth of AI systems 
development in Australia and strongly supports the need for action to address potential harms. 
However , we have some concerns and recommendations regarding some aspects of the proposal:  
 
• The definition and use of ‘AI system’ is too general. We recommend that the AI Supply 
Chain perspective be more widely adopted within the proposal paper.  
• Enhanced definition of deployers. We suggest that deployers who significantly modify AI models, particularly by manipulating system and user prompts to control outputs, should be 
considered "developers" under the proposed guardrails.  
• A clear definition of "substantial modification" be provided in the context of “prompt 
engineering” for GPAI models  
• Guardrail 1 could have a stronger emphasis on logging, recording or cataloguing AI assets or an enrolment mechanism to register generative AI platforms.

In addition, a key message from the ADM+S Centre, put forward in detail in their submission to this

Defining High -Risk AI  
Overall, RMIT commends the proposals as an advancement in the growth of AI systems development in Australia and strongly supports the need for action to address potential harms . The 
paper proposes six principles to define high- risk AI use.  
 
While we continue to support this principles -based approach , we would suggest that  the “Key 
definitions ” section  (p. 8) may require tightening to avoid inadvertent unnecessary restriction of 
some activities . For example, one of the proposed principles state s that "In designating an AI 
system as high- risk due to its use, regard must be given to …". We suggest that the term "AI 
System" here is too general  (even for use in a principle) since it glosses over the detailed 
interaction between activities in the AI lifecycle and the AI model when determining risk levels. This 
is also apparent in Figure 2: AI Lifecycle, where a singular model -to-system relationship is implied, 
focusing exclusively on the model without addressing the "ensemble of several components" 
inherent in the system definition. Conversely, the AI Supply Chain example (Figur e 3) provides a 
more effective mechanism for identifying high-risk situations, compared to the terminologies “AI 
system” or “AI lifecycle” used in the principles.   
 
Importantly, w hen the term “AI System” encompasses multiple models with varying data sets, 
algorithms, autonomy levels, adaptability, and goals (both implicit and explicit), we feel that 
potential risk  is only partially addressed through mandatory guardrails for “high- risk” AI. Thus, it is 
crucial to fully leverage the definitions and terms provided to enhance the interpretation and criteria of high- risk use cases, minimi sing the potential for misinterpretation or misuse through the 
principles -based approac h.  
 We also note that in the area of higher education and research training, the proposal paper’s 
designation of an “AI system ” as high- risk when “used in determining admission to education 
programs, evaluating learning outcomes or monitoring student behaviour” might inadvertently 
encompass many low -risk applications under compulsory , and unnecessary,  regulations.  
 
The following are examples of low- risk applications  in education and training that may be caught in 
this broad definition:

Enhanced definition of deployers  
We suggest that deployers who significantly modify AI models, particularly by manipulating system 
and user prompts to control outputs, should be considered "developers" under the proposed 
guardrails. This reclassification is crucial because:  
 
• Impact on Risk Profile:  Significant modifications can fundamentally alter an AI system's 
risk profile, potentially introducing new biases, vulnerabilities, or unintended consequences. 
Holding deployers accountable as "developers" in such cases is essential for ensuring that 
the guardrails effectively mitigate these risks.  
• Alignment with International Approaches:  This approach aligns with the EU AI Act, 
which designates deployers as "developers" if they make "substantial modifications" to a 
high- risk AI system or offer it under their own branding. This alignment promotes 
international consistency and avoids loopholes in the application of guardrails.  
 
Accordingly, w e recommend that a clear definition of " substantial  modification" be provided in the 
context of  “prompt  engineering” for GPAI models . This could involve considering factors like:  
 
• The purpose for the modification by the deployer (i.e. to connect this with relevant ex post 
implications in domain areas such as education, law enforcement, or democratic purposes)  
• The degree to which modifications alter the intended purpose or functionality of the AI 
model.  
• The potential for modifications to introduce new biases or discriminatory outcomes.  
• The technical complexity of the modifications and the level of expertise required to 
implement them .

Guardrail 10. Conformity assessment  
This draft Guardrail could also include making allowance for independent third parties, such as 
researchers, to assess the AI model or tool. As platforms have grown they have increasingly 
tended towards the development of ‘walled gardens’ that limit interoperability and aim to retain 
users within their domains. In recent years platforms have shut down or significantly limited access 
to their APIs for researchers. This has reduced visibility and transparency into how their algorithms 
operate. As AI systems b ecome increasingly integrated into various everyday platforms and 
systems there is an urgent need to ensure greater transparency about all facets of these systems 
and their operations. Such requirements include the need for mechanisms to provide access for  
independent researchers for evaluation, which can be achieved in ways that do not compromise 
commercially sensitive or private data.

Impact on First Nations People  
While the principles do highlight  potential adverse impacts to groups of individuals or collective 
rights of cultural groups, we feel that there should be greater emphasis o n impacts to  First Nations 
peoples.  
 
The Framework for Governance of Indigenous Data4 published in May 2024 refers  to issues with 
data collection and management of indigenous datasets . Specifically , it states that :  
‘Cultural, Language Group, and First Nations affiliations tend not to be included 
in standard  administrative datasets resulting in Indigenous people not seeing 
themselves within the data.  Some datasets are decontextualized and lack 
additional information that makes them meaningful for researchers or Indigenous 
people and their communities’ . - National Perinatal Data Collection case study  
It is therefore clear that a ny AI system that seeks to make decisions or recommendations involving 
First Nations people may be inadvertently introducing generalisations and unintended biases 
towards specific cultural and language groups . The Framework acknowledges the historical 
marginalisation of Indigenous peoples within data systems and aims to remedy data gaps and 
biases. This objective complements the AI guardrails’ emphasis on testing (Guardrail 4), 
specifically in assessing AI model  performance acros s different social groups to reduce bias and 
prevent discriminatory results.  
Consideration of Severity and Likelihood of  Impacts  
As stated above, under a principles -based approach, clear and definite criteria to assess the scale 
and severity of impacts need to be provided.  This, c oupled with criteria to assess the likelihood of 
risks occurring, aligns with common risk assessment frameworks that are used in many industries 
today.  In determining which AI use cases require mandatory guard rails, we suggest that a 
combination of consequence and likelihood factors be considered in determining which models and 
systems will be subject to additional  mandatory requirements.   
 
We recommend that in using common risk assessment frameworks  evaluating for models and 
systems, there be  sufficient attention placed on applying these frameworks across the full AI

First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols  
We also recommend incorporating further  guidelines from the Framework for the Governance of 
Indigenous Data in the proposal. As we suggest  above regarding data gaps and bias, t here are 
already clear alignment  between these guidelines and some of the suggested Guardrails. For 
example:  
 
• Recognising Indigenous Data Sovereignty: The Framework prioritises Indigenous Data 
Sovereignty, recognising the right of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples to control 
their data. This aligns with the guardrails’ focus on ethical data governance, especially 
Guardrail 3, which stresses data quality, provenance, and respect for Indigenous Data 
Sovereignty and Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP).  
• Partnership and Consultation : The Framework highlights the need for collaboration with 
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities throughout the entire data lifecycle. Similarly, the AI guardrails encourage transparency and stakeholder consultation, ensuring 
responsible development and deployment of AI systems that consider potential impacts on 
Indigenous communities.  
• Transparency and Accessibility: The Framework supports making government -held 
Indigenous data accessible to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. This is in line with the AI guardrails' emphasis on transparency (Guardrail 8), requiring organisations to 
disclose information on h igh-risk AI systems to promote responsible utilisation.  
Regulatory options to mandate guardrails  
Finally, we believe that Option 3 offers the most comprehensive and future- proof solution for 
addressing the challenges of governing the responsible development and use of AI in Australia. As 
the ADM+S Centre Submission to the Proposal notes, Option 3 : 
 “is the most realistic means of mandating Guardrails for the purposes of ensuring safe and 
responsible AI development and deployment in Australia, and to protect Australians as well as 
equip Australian businesses to engage with developing global rules and frameworks. The 
Mandatory Guardrails appl ied this way are analogous to consumer protection law, or even better, 
privacy law which applies across public and private sectors."
5 
 
This option is compelling because it:  
• Creates consistencies across industries: e stablishes a unified set of definitions, risk 
assessment principles, and guardrails, similar to the EU AI Act and Canada's AIDA, 
ensuring a standardised approach across various sectors.  
• Promotes regulatory efficiency: introduces a dedicated regulatory body with specialised 
expertise in AI, thereby streamlining the regulatory process and improving oversight capabilities.  
• Fosters collaboration: e ncourages synergy between industry -specific regulators and a 
central AI regulatory body, enabling organisations to effectively implement guardrails within 
their unique contexts.  
 We note that having horizontal legislation in place  does not necessarily mean the Mandatory 
Guardrails will be identical for all sectors.  
 We suggest that a phased implementation be considered, prioritising high- risk sectors and public 
sector use, then gradually expanding coverage. This phased approach will help mitigate implementation challenges and allow for adjustments based on industry feedback. Another option 
suggested in the ADM+S Centre Submission is for Mandatory Guardrails as a default minimum

SBS submission  – Safe and Responsible AI in Australia: Proposals paper  
SBS appreciates the opportunity to respond to the Department of Industry, Science and 
Resources' Safe and Responsible AI in Australia  (Proposals Paper). As with many emerging 
technologies, artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) is delivering signiﬁcant beneﬁts acr oss the economy and 
society. However, as noted in the Proposals Paper, AI also ampliﬁes and creates new risks, such as AI -enabled disinformation campaigns, the misappropriation of First Nations cultural material, 
and inbuilt biases that disadvantage indiv iduals based on matters such as cultural background 
or gender.  
General approach to AI regulation  
SBS supports a risk -based approach to AI regulation, focusing on high -risk settings and 
activities that pose the greatest potential for individual and/or socie tal harm. Regulation must 
balance harm prevention with fostering innovation and evolving governance frameworks , 
without hin dering the potential soci etal and individual beneﬁts  that can be derived from  AI.  
The timely introduction of appropriate AI guardrails is vital, given th e pace of AI development  
and the potential harmful impacts  identiﬁed  in the Proposals pa per. It is promising that 
Governments around  the world are already acting quick ly to implement safegua rds in relation 
to the  use of AI.  The global  failure to regulate social media platforms eﬀectively and quickly  
has led to se rious  and widespread social and individual  harm  (including  to children)  that is 
proving diﬃcult to address  retrospec tively .  It is imperative that this  experience is not repeated  
in relation to AI. 
Any r egulatory framework must apply equally to multi -national entities and hold them as 
accountable as local entities , to ensure a consistent approach  that does not create competitive 
disadvantage in the development and use of AI .   
SBS’s position on many of the issues explored in the Proposals Paper was addressed in its 
May 
2024 submission  to the Select Committee on Adopting Artificial Intelligence, which is attached 
for reference.  This includes specifi c discussion of  issues such as algorithm transparency , bias,  
and copyright, which a re also addressed b riefly belo w.  
Noting the ne ed for time ly regulation, a  consultative approach in developing AI -specific 
frameworks is still  required , to prevent unintended consequences or stifle innovation.  
Existing frameworks must be considered 
Assessments of high -risk AI applications and the imposition  of new regulations must consider 
existing regulatory protections and frameworks, taking a n approach similar to Canada ’s AIDA 
Bill and avoiding regulatory duplication as ﬂagged  regarding  Option 3 of the Proposals Paper .  
 
 
 
2 
 It is possible that content creation and distribution can create harms, but this will not be 
consistent across the sector . Any guardrails or  regulatory framework must  therefore  be 
suﬃciently nuanced to target  potentially harmful activities that are not a lready subject to 
oversight or controls.   
For example, SBS, as a highly regulated media organisation, already has robust protections in 
place to prevent harms such as misinformation. It is crucial that AI regulations diﬀerentiate 
between professional med ia organisations like SBS and content creators /publishers  without 
similar protections or enforcement regimes.  
Guardrails must recognise intellectual property  
SBS has previously highlighted the critical need for regulatory frameworks to guide AI 
development, particularly concerning copyright and intellectual property rights. SBS expressed concerns about the rising number of AI -powered websites repurposing content 
from other source s without permission, credit, or compensation, thus exploiting the expertise 
and investment of others including media companies. These issues pose a significant threat to the sustainability of Australia’s news and media industry, necessitating the establis hment of 
guardrails to protect intellectual property.  
The intellectual property of media companies is also now being utilised to deliver AI -
generated search results on platforms such as Google , displacing native news sites.  When a 
user searches for a news  event or information, instead of being served a series of links to 
trusted news sites, a user will receive an AI -generated answer from Google that utilises 
information from unidentified and uncredited sources.  This is undesirable  both in terms of the 
unauthorised use of news organisations’ intellectual property, but also in terms of the reliability 
and transparency of information used to generate the answer –  which will be opaque to the 
end user.  This also escalates the risk of mis - or dis -information being spread, albeit 
unintentionally.   
Addressing bias in AI  
Both AI systems and their regulation should seek to reduce, not increase, biases. Agreements 
between AI providers and trusted content sources are key. However, relying predominantly on 
Western or English -language sources risks perpetuating bias and homogenising perspectives. 
AI systems should diversify sources to mitigate entrenched biases, fostering greater public 
trust in AI and the media industry  impacted by AI . A more inclusive deﬁn ition of credibility will 
lead to a more balanced and trustworthy AI ecosystem.  
Positive AI use cases at SBS  
There are positive use cases, of assistive AI tools that are able to further support SBS’s 
purpose of enhancing social cohesion in Australia, which may also be used to improve service 
delivery for Australians. Key examples of these tools are language technologies, which can 
further allow SBS’s unique in language  stories, views,  and opinions from across Australia’s 
multicultural, multilingual, and Firs t Nations communities to be understood and shared with 
the wider Australian audience, and vice versa. These technologies can help, at unprecedented speed and scale, millions of audience members overcome language barriers, and accessibility 
or certain healt h issues (further to the unique SBS News in Easy English service), to share and 
understand each other’s perspectives, thus strengthening social cohesion in doing so . 
SBS’s existing role in harm prevention  
As AI -driven algorithms intensify the spread of mis information, SBS's trusted, human -led 
content creation becomes even more vital to democracy. SBS strives to provide accurate,

languages, including valued services such as SBS  Examines , which seeks to directly address 
and combat misinformation circulating among communities in Australia.  
SBS is Australia's most trusted news provider1 with a proven track record in supplying high -

• Content authenticity , copyright,  and intellectual property concerns  
As AI becomes capable of producing artistic and journalistic content informed by the work of 
human creators, issues around copyright infringement, authenticity and ownership of AI -
generated content emerge. Determining issues of  infringement, authorship and  rights over AI -

ethical use of AI in creative fields . The SAG –AFTRA (Screen Actors Guild –American Federation of 
Television and Radio Artists ) union strikes in the US in 2023 demonstrated the significant 
discontentment and strong will by creative practitioners in gaining an appropriate level of control 
over  and being compensated for the use of their images or voices by AI  services .

 There have als o been multiple reports12, of the proliferation of websites that repurpose or 
repackage other websites’ content using AI. Audiences may not be aware at all that they are 
consuming AI -created content repurposed from others’ intellectual property. This puts legitimate 
news businesses in a position of losing traffic (and hence monetisation) to competitors who are 
monetising the news businesses’ own content. It  is a genuine threat to the viability of legitimate 
news media businesses , including SBS, and sufficient policy or legislative response including 
relevant guardrails are urgently required in relation to AI and copyright.  
• Privacy and data security concern s 
AI systems often learn from large datasets, which  potentially include sensitive, personal, and 
confidential information that they have accessed  with or without permission. There are issues and 
risks associated with how the data is accessed, collected, used and stored, potentially leading to 
privacy breac hes, or breaches of confidentiality. Without any guardrails, currently the onus is on AI 
users, including SBS, to be vigilant when considering the information shared  with AI systems. 
However, users including SBS do not know the full extent and mechanisms  of how AI systems 
access and deal with data, including when they potentially do so without permission. Guardrails in 
relation to data security robustness of AI systems are urgently required.  
As the appropriate possible legislativ e vehicle, t he implications of the lack of transparency around 
AI use of sensitive data should be considered as part of the Government's ongoing Privacy Review.  
• Increased difficulty in information -verification  
There have been multiple reports of AI ‘flooding’13 the internet with information, including multiple 
instances of information without attribution to their sources. This increases the difficulty of 
information verification, a process required to be performed by reputable news or media 
businesses including SBS. This is also related to the issues of intellectual property, and concerns in 
relation to data outlined immediately above, and should be addressed through industry -wide 
guardrails.  
• Amplified inaccuracies, b ias and discrimination  
Further to the issue of mis - and disinformation already outlined in the body of this submission, 
currently, s ources of AI -generated content are often undisclosed , meaning that such content may 
derive from a range of  sources including those that are  unreliable and unverified , and those 
influenced  by bias  or discrimination . 
Moreover , human biases have  been built into many AI technologies because th ose technologies  
have been trained on current and historical online material s, some of which  reflect  existing bias, 
inaccuracies, inequalities, inadequate representation , and discriminatory approaches . This result s 
in an accelerated perpetuation of dominant narratives  and viewpoints , and the exclusion of diverse  
perspectives and approaches . Many AI systems  are not trained to identify or correct these 
approaches . 
The nature of AI systems mean s these issues can become more ingrained as part of the ir 
algorithms , as they are repeatedly trained . The potential consequences could include  
amplification of mis - and disinformation,  and unequal treatments of groups based on —as 
examples —language,  culture, race, gender, or ethnicity . The severity of these issues  varies, 
depend ing on materials and data relevant to such groups being used by AI systems . 
Numerous domestic and international examples have demonstrated th is risk of algorithmic bias 
when AI is deployed , particularly  without human oversight.  A well -reported example in Australia in 
early 2024 was how Adobe  Photoshop’s  AI-assisted  tool could potentially  take differen t 
approaches when tasked to modify the appearances of female s and males.14

 Executive Summary  
“Software engineering is the key to both deep cost reduction and scalable network effects. Building 
an advantage around software engineering is the key to all platforms, drones, factory automation, 
robotics, quantum, enterprise, defence, government, and cybersecurity. Software engineering is the 
lubrication a competitive advantage around software requires .”1 
The Medical Software Industry Association (MSIA) exists to create the environment for a vibrant 
Australian health software industry to power positive health outcomes. Everyday efficiencies enjoyed 
by Australians today come from our members investment into innovations including electronic medical 
records2, electronic pathology and radiology3, telehealth4, automated administrative, payment and 
booking systems and a national electronic prescribing system. Our key purpose it to ensure certainty 
of a regulatory environment to enable sustainability, whilst encourages investment and innovation.  
Continuous innovation is critical to Australia maintaining a competitive world class health system. 
Health workforce shortages,5 pressure on the viability of clinical services and clinics,6 the cyber threat 
landscape, 7 productivity challenges,8 and mounting complex red tape jeopardise our current ranking 
as one of the most efficient and safe health systems in the world.9 The opportunities which AI provides 
to clinical and non- clinical healthcare are manifold.10 AI is not new to health care.11 What is novel is 
the widespread availability and popularity of enhancements like generative AI which has brought the 
use of AI in healthcare to the fore.  
The use of AI, like any other healthcare tool, can have the most extreme benefits or create 
considerable risk if not managed. The risks of using -and not using12 – AI all depend on the detailed 
scaffolding of laws, rules, regulations, practice, and education which currently exist in the multi -
faceted healthcare ecosystem.  
The lack of clarity about how AI can be used and  when it is used is not positive for users, consumers, 
innovators, developers, investors, or Governments. Contrary to urban myths about the “wild west ” of 
health software, companies actively seek certainty in the form of standards, rules, and requirements. 
The health software industry is the powerhouse of Australia’s world class health. The MSIA currently  
works  with Government , professional stakeholders and standards organisations to co-design safety 
standards and conformance profiles13. Doctors, Pharmacists, Allied Health workers, the Health 
workforce, Health Administrators, Researchers and Governments understandable need to know that 
the health software they are supporting and/or using is fit for purpose, safe and efficient. Software 
companies cannot survive unless they meet this demand.  
The key is to ensure that the regulation has the “Goldilocks”14 recipe – not too hard, not too soft – but 
just right. As usual, the devil is in the detail. Current   technical15, professional, legal, and 
administrative regulation has served Australia well . The added complexity of specific AI regulation needs consideration in this context . 
The Department of Industry Science and Resources (“DISR”) ask s three key questions which we 
have answered as follows:  
1. Do the proposed Principles for AI High Risk work? Not (b , )the health one . 
2. Are the proposed mandatory Guardrails fit for purpose? Not Quite . 
3. What is the best way or three proposed alternatives for the government to regulate AI in Australia? Option 2 - leave what is working,  but supplement with an overarching Act 
accessible to all  Australians,  referenced by existing working frameworks.  
The MSIA has answered the DISR Yes/No  survey questions  here. The complexity of health demands 
a more calibrated response.  
 Naturally every industry thinks it is “special.” No doubt it is.16 This is why we support an approach 
which builds on the decades of  specific deep knowledge- based  clinical  technical experience within 
our sector. Healthcare providers (deployers), developers and regulators have been navigating 
fundamentally the same questions asked by  DISR for decades. Byzantine in its complexity,   MSIA response - Department of industry, Science and Resources Consultation: Safe and responsible AI in

 Defining high- risk AI  
1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high- risk AI? Are there any principles we should add or remove? Please 
identify any:  
• low risk use cases that are unintentionally captured 
• categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for defence or national security purposes. 
The MSIA will only respond to proposed principle (b),  and (f).  
 In designating an AI system as high -risk due to its use, regard must be given to:  
(b) The risk of adverse impacts to an individual’s physical or mental health or safety  
(f) The severity and extent of those adverse impacts outlined in …(b)  
The physical and mental health and safety is in the DNA of MSIA  member companies and their 
clients.  
The Hippocratic Oath, taken by Doctors, is  
 First, do no harm.17 
The principles appear intended to cover crucial areas for Australians including harm or risk of harm to 
their  body, mind, environment, culture, legal standing, and autonomy. Australia does not have a Bill of 
Rights like some  other countries upon which to found its AI regulation,   so whilst these are key 
concerns, care needs to be taken not to use AI regulation as a default convention for such rights. The 
principles are overly broad as a result of this.  
The wording in principle (b)  is too all encompassing.  All healthcare requires some level of risk . This 
result s in an obligation to minimise that (first, do no harm , ) which  must be balanced against the 
beneficial impact of using available tools . This principle is reflected in current frameworks used by the 
TGA, and other regulator s overseas where the models used to assess risk work on two axes : 
1. Based on the inherent risk of the type of care, &  
2.  Based on the level of autonomy.  
 Interestingly, there is some variability in how those two axes are interpreted in different jurisdictions. 
Part of the problem is that there are currently no objective criteria for determining the associated level 
of functional risk. DISR’s paper on Safe and Responsible Us of AI in Australia published in June 2023 
described “Use of AI to generate patient records in care settings” as Medium Risk . Recent public 
debate on the use medical scribes might  now deem it l ow. This demonstrates the fluidity of the 
concepts and need for more specificity to enable the adoption of safe and efficient health software.  
This issue is currently being examined by ISO TC215  to see if more objective criteria can be 
developed. JWG3 is considering developing a healthcare extension of ISO/IEC 42001(quality 
management),  to include “lite” version of the quality management standard fit -for-purpose in smaller 
organisations such as research labs and start -ups. Irrespective of the ISO outcome, the wording in 
the principle (b), is not fit for purpose for application to health software.  
The potential for adverse impacts when interacting with individuals in a health setting is well 
established and understood18. From basic existing physical hygiene standards, evidenced with 
practices like hand sterilisation in GP waiting rooms, through to sophisticated medical devices like 
pacemakers, and everything in between. There is virtually no interaction in healthcare tra nsactions 
which could not be coloured with a risk of an adverse impact. Inaction as a result of complexity of 
regulation and reluctance to engage with innovation can likewise carry elevated risk.  
The use of AI in managing administrative load to maximise the use of the  critically low health 
workforce in areas like aged care has proven to be extraordinary in terms of increasing FTE numbers 
and filling gaps19. The example provided on page 27 of the DISR consultation paper demonstrates an  MSIA response - Department of industry, Science and Resources Consultation: Safe and responsible AI in 
Australia

 unintended consequence of deeming all rostering systems to be high risk, would be to lose the clear 
gains achievable for workforce efficiency  in areas like aged care. Detailed knowledge of each domain

The Therapeutic Goods Administration (‘TGA”)   has grappled with this issue and the need to balance

legislation and exclusions  are regularly updated and provide a crisp useful reference for policy

 5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high- risk AI, 
such as general -purpose AI (GPAI)?  
A technology agnostic approach is essential. In this case, our response above to question 4 could be 
reversed to respond to this question. That is, if there was a GPAI which was seen as universally 
useful in any environment, it probably would avoid Australia if all the proposed guardrails were to be 
implemented . “Catching ” technologies should not be the aim of the regulation so much as clarifying 
what the endgame of the technology renders. There may be GPAI which will have inestimable 
benefits in some appli cations, such as triaging children in emergency wards to expedite testing, but 
which could be equally successful in selecting substances for nefarious purposes. Outright bans in an 
international market have unintended consequences.  
Much like banning aeroplanes would solve the problem of crashes and airport security. Even more so 
here as governments are not well suited to being on the forefront of technology. The use of GPAI in 
National or international disasters could be high risk – or lifesaving.  
Research by Takeuchi  and Nonaka  found that knowledge acquisition is a process, and you don’t 
know everything in advance, so vision must be sufficiently vague  to ensure the team can 
translate that into their o wn rolling vision. At no time do you know less than at the start, or to 
quote Profe ssor Greenhalgh, “by deﬁnition,  a technological project is a ﬁction , since at the 
outset it does not exist. ”27 In fact it has been said if technology and regulation are both working at 
the same pace, then one, or both, are not going fast enough. Focusing outcomes , and whether they 
are desirable or not, seems to be a more achievable and sensible stance than technological 
specification which is unlikely to keep up with new technologies.

 Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of AI  
Questions for consultation  
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high -risk 
settings? Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?  
The purpose of AI in health is  the achievement of  goals including safety, efficiency, improved research 
and monitoring. The ten proposed guardrails are of themselves modifications of what is required 
under existing regulatory frameworks. For instance, Guardrail 3  refers to data quality, which is also 
required by the Privacy Principles31 and clinical data governance frameworks32 which are expanding 
to respond to AI33 Guardrail 4  refers to monitoring which is covered by the TGA adverse event 
reporting, Guardrail 5  refers to human control which reflects the Essential Principle of clinical 
oversight, and ability to trace the provenance of the algorithm and asses it for accuracy.34There is a 
gap in this guardrail in respect of who is the responsible person for overseeing the AI system in the 
supply chain,  which would make compliance difficult.  
Guardrails 1,2 and 9 are largely administrative reflecting current good practice.  Further 
consideration should be given to legalities around copyright and harmonisation with taxation laws, 35 
regulations around technical conformance,36to avoid excessive red tape and duplication.  
Guardrails  6 and 8  reflects the fact that there is a growing need for transparency for users and 
consumers about how, when and why AI is being used. This could be equally well addressed by 
amendments to the TGA requirements, with a possible extension to a “trust mark”, to remove onerous 
obligations on end users to make inquiries of complex systems, which they may not even know exist. 
This would place an onus on industry but  could have the benefit of improving public trust and use of 
AI in healthcare.  
Guardrail 7  appears to require every AI system to have a complaints process for negative outcomes 
which would more elegantly be replaced by reference to the existing compliant mechanisms in specific industries. For instance,  the TGA, and Medical Board of Australia. The process should be 
aligned to the outcome it aims to prevent and not technically specific, but domain specific. Having 
developers and deployers managing this is also inappropriate from a governance perspective
37,  other 
than to alert users of the various organisations which ought to be contacted to run disputes, e.g. ACCC.  
Existing complaints mechanisms like the banking and Insurance Ombudsmen could also be augmented to manage AI issues.  
Guardrail 10 reflects  the type of conformance currently conducted by Government entities including  
the TGA, ADHA and Services Australia. Having a generic conformance testing would not be helpful for 
the health software industry which demands a depth of knowledge over health d omains, technologies, 
terminologies, and settings. More comments on this in response to question twelve(12).

 Regulatory options to mandate guardrails  
Questions for consultation  
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high- risk settings? What 
opportunities should the government take into account in considering each approach?  
Option two is favoured by the MSIA because it  enables a regime that is:  
- the least disruptive,  
- most harmonious with existing regulatory frameworks  
- least confusing/inconsistent  
- enables an outcomes -based approach  
- overcomes transparency issues for deployers and end users – thus improves trust  
- able to provide a consolidated resource for all industries.  
- swifter transition periods which will assist alleviate community concern.  
-  the most future proof  
- the most relevant to health( and other specific industry)   complexity which will increase 
consumer trust - especially when benchmarked with the new framework.  
- able to leverage existing entities expertise and processes e.g. ACSQHC, TGA to enable focus on 
policy rather than industry specific operational issues . 
The need for industry specific requirements is reflected in the work on international standards for AI. 
JTC1 ISO/IEC SC42 Artificial Intelligence and ISO TC215 Health Informatics have established Joint 
Working Group 3  to develop healthcare specific extens ions of the horizontal AI standards such as 
ISO/IEC 22989  (concepts and terminology) and ISO/IEC 42001 (quality management).  
 This work is being mirrored in Australia through collaboration between the respective Standards 
Australia Technical Committees IT -043 Artificial Intelligence and IT -014 Health Informatics. The latter 
has established a subcommittee IT -014-21 AI in Healthcare whose expert membership is drawn from 
industry, academia and government (including CSIRO, TGA and DoHAC). Australia cannot ignore the 
international approach in respect of health, and Option 2 enables the optimal ability for harmonisation.  
Option One fails in that merely extending/varying the existing regimes of specific frameworks does 
not provide the clarity which consumers rightly require and puts the onus of compliance with complex regulation on the parties most familiar with the detail. It would require the same amount of work as 
option 2 and three without additional benefit.  
Option Three  is confusing in that it purports to maintain existing regimes and carve them out, but that 
in  and of itself would make it complex for say a health consumer which would then need to navigate 
the TGA or other requirements. A one size fits all solution does n’t work because all the issues are 
different and nuanced so their solution must reflect that.  
All options will require a co- ordinated response and need attention to duplication.  
Leveraging what works and creating clarity for consumers and existing regulators makes sense. It enables an outcomes -based approach most effectively  as it will facilitate definition of standards, 
thresholds and conformance via amendment to existing framew orks and for other reasons enunciated 
above.

Government should consider?

developers and deployers. It is unclear why this is not seen as possible, because like many of the 
other changes proposed, legislation will be required, so changes to existing laws are not only feasible, 
but essential irrespective of which option is adopted.   
Australia is unique in many ways, but the work it has done with the IMDRF has enabled 
harmonisation for industry and should be maintained and buil t upon rather than dismantled or 
threatened with the uncertainty of a fresh regulator without the specific skills and experience.   MSIA response - Department of industry, Science and Resources Consultation: Safe and responsible AI in

Conclusion  
Healthcare is a special case . It is more mature than other industries in its approach to the 
responsible use of AI in Health . This is  because it has been balancing   risks , including the 
adoption or non -adoption of technology which has been such a predominant force for positive 
change to healthcare outcomes.  
We endorse the  calibrated approach of Option Two, together with a targeted subsidies for 
piloting and  incentivising the  adoption of AI. Call it the Steven Bradbury approach39The 
Australian market is too small to ‘go it alone’ so harmonisation with the work already underway 
by the TGA with the IMDRF , is supported. Australia is in a unique position of being able to gauge 
the success or otherwise of regulation in other countries and should take advantage of the 
position to ensure it strikes the right balance between safety, efficiency and innovation.

NELA Submission on the 
Safe and Responsible AI for Australia: Proposals Paper for Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-risk Settings

About NELA and its interest in this consultation
NELA is the national peak body for advancing Australian environmental law and policy. It is an independent, multidisciplinary, member-based association focused on environmental law and sustainability. NELA is managed by a national board that includes directors with expertise in international and domestic legal frameworks for biodiversity conservation, ecological restoration, environmental and carbon markets, environmental regulation and regulatory theory, and natural resource management.
One of NELA’s core objectives is to provide a forum for, and to otherwise assist in, the discussion, consideration, and advancement of environmental law across the legal profession and the wider community. As a body with particular expertise and interest in environmental laws, NELA and its members recognise the importance of clear, strong, transparent and ambitious laws for safeguarding Australian environments, and we bring that recognition to bear in this submission. 
We are grateful for the opportunity to make a submission on this consultation paper.
1.  Summary of this submission
We thank the Department of Industry, Science and Resources for the opportunity to make a submission in response to the Safe and Responsible AI in Australia proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings. Our submission relates to questions 1, 8 and 13, and highlights the importance of greater attention to environmental issues associated with AI in both the proposed principles and guardrails. 
In this submission, NELA highlights three important considerations, including: 
* ensuring that the environmental impacts of AI are given appropriate prominence and weight by revising ‘principle e’ to remove reference to the environment, and creating a new principle that specifically addresses the environmental impact risks of AI development and use. This is discussed further under our response to Question 1.
* ensuring that environmental issues are appropriately factored into the binding norms of a new AI regulatory framework by proposed guardrails 2, 5, 6, 7 and 8 being updated to include more explicit focus on, and reference to, environmental considerations. This is discussed further under our response to Question 8; and
* supporting a new cross-economy AI Act as the best option for ensuring that environmental considerations are given appropriate consideration and weight in AI regulation. This is discussed further under our response to Question 13.

2.  Question 1: Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI? Are there any principles we should add or remove? Please identify any low risk use cases that are unintentionally captured, and categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for defence or national security purposes. 
The risk of adverse environmental impacts associated with AI is recognised in proposed ‘principle e’: ‘The risk of adverse impacts to the broader Australian economy, society, environment and rule of law’. However, there is a risk that environmental impacts could be overshadowed by a disproportionate focus on the economy and society. The accompanying information emphasises the economic and social impacts of AI, with only a brief mention of the risk of adverse impacts to the environment. At a minimum, there needs to be substantial attention to the environment as an element of ‘principle e’.
To better address the risk that the environment will not receive adequate attention if it is listed alongside the economy and society, we suggest that consideration should be given to creating a new principle that specifically addresses potential environmental risks. A new principle should recognise that potential adverse environmental impacts arise not only from the use of AI, but also from its development. The May 2024 Interim Report of the International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI was produced by a diverse group of 75 AI experts, including an international Expert Advisory Panel nominated by 30 countries, the European Union, and the United Nations. The Interim Report identifies the potential for significant risks to the environment arising from the growing demand for computing power (‘compute’) used for general-purpose AI development and deployment. These risks include: 
* Rapidly increasing energy usage associated with general-purpose AI, which is outpacing hardware efficiency improvements, and could potentially lead to ‘strongly increasing CO2 emissions’. Others have similarly predicted that data transmission networks and data centres, which currently account for 1% of energy-related GHG emissions, will consume approximately 21% of the world’s electricity supply by 2030.
* Increases in compute used for training and deploying AI models in turn lead to higher water consumption to meet increased cooling demands. Some researchers predict that billions of cubic meters of water could be consumed by AI by 2027.
To ensure that the environmental impacts of AI are given appropriate prominence and weight, we suggest revising ‘principle e’ to remove reference to the environment, and creating a new principle that specifically addresses the environmental impact risks of AI development and use:
* Suggested revised principle e: The risk of adverse impacts to the broader Australian economy, society, and rule of law
* Suggested new principle: The risk of adverse environmental impacts of AI development and use 
Foregrounding the importance of the environmental impacts of AI by creating a new principle would help to discourage continued reliance on unsustainable technologies, and lead to a greater focus on designing and choosing sustainable AI models that reduce the ‘digital carbon footprint’ and water consumption.
  
3.  Question 8: Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings? Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?
  
  Although the risk of adverse environmental impacts of AI are referred to in ‘principle e’, there is currently no reference to the environment in the proposed mandatory guardrails. This creates a significant risk that environmental issues will not be appropriately factored into the governance and binding norms of a new AI regulatory framework. As the European Commission High Level Group pointed out in their Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI, ‘AI systems should benefit all human beings, including future generations. It must hence be ensured that they are sustainable and environmentally friendly. Moreover, they should take into account the environment, including other living beings, and their social and societal impact should be carefully considered’. 
We suggest that the proposed guardrails need to include more explicit focus on, and reference to, environmental considerations. There are several ways this can be achieved. For example: 
* Proposed guardrail 2 is ‘Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks’. The accompanying information clarifies that ‘The risk management process is not just a technical risk assessment. It is crucial that developers and deployers consider any potential impacts on people, community groups and society before the high-risk AI system is in use’. We suggest that the environment should be explicitly mentioned in guardrail 2, and in the accompanying information about this guardrail, alongside consideration of potential impacts on people, community groups and society. One way this could be achieved is through requirements for ‘AI eco-impact assessments’ or AI environmental impact assessments to complement human-centric approaches to AI risk management. A benefit of AI eco-impact assessments is that alongside the assessment of risks associated with AI use, they would also allow for the identification of ways that AI can promote the realisation of sustainability benefits. Such benefits can be achieved through, for example, enhancing sustainable resource allocation, the prevention and management of natural disasters, and promoting carbon neutrality. Incorporating environmental considerations in proposed guardrail 2 would promote greater consistency with the current ‘principle e’ or the proposed new principle, discussed above. 
* Proposed guardrail 5 is ‘Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight’. We suggest that meaningful human oversight requires that those responsible for oversight must be sufficiently qualified to understand (i) the core capabilities and limitations of an AI model to accurately assess the accuracy of algorithmic outputs, as well as (ii) the impacts of AI on non-humans including the environment and animals. The proposals paper does not address (ii); rectifying this gap would again promote consistency with the current ‘principle e’ or the proposed new principle, discussed above.
* Proposed guardrail 6 focuses on ‘Inform[ing] end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content’. These types of notification requirements could be expanded to include duties to disclose information necessary for better understanding the impact of AI on the environment. This information would assist regulators to better allocate resources for addressing the risks associated with AI.
* In a similar vein, proposed guardrail 7 is concerned with ‘Establish[ing] processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcomes’. AI uses can affect the environment and animals, as well as people. Proposed guardrail 7 should therefore be framed more expansively to encompass establishing processes for organisations and regulators representing the environment and animals that are impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcomes. 
* Proposed guardrail 8 is ‘Be transparent with other organisations across the AI supply chain about data, models and systems to help them effectively address risks’. There is a risk that AI used to inform environmental decision-making may be relying upon poor quality data, or data collected at ‘different levels of temporal and spatial frequency’. There is therefore a need to coordinate and aggregate information across multiple data sources, and to remove incorrect, outdated or unreliable data. An explicit focus in guardrail 8 on encouraging organisations to improve data quality, as well as to ‘effectively address risks’, would strengthen the guardrail’s utility for diverse AI applications, including those affecting the environment. 
4.  Question 13: Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings? What opportunities should the government take into account in considering each approach? 
We suggest that a new cross-economy AI Act is the best option for ensuring that environmental considerations are given appropriate consideration and weight in AI regulation. As environmental protection is an issue that cuts across regulatory domains, effective monitoring and enforcement of environmental protections built into a new cross-economy AI Act would be best facilitated by a new AI regulator.  
A domain specific approach or a framework approach both pose a risk that environmental considerations will be overshadowed by the other goals prioritised in existing regulatory frameworks. Irrespective of the regulatory approach that is ultimately adopted, it is vital that there is more explicit focus on the environmental impacts of AI in both the proposed principles and mandatory guardrails, as outlined above.
NELA would be pleased to participate in ongoing consultation on the above matters.

Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high- risk settings  
The Insurance Council of Australia (Insurance Council) welcomes the opportunity to provide a 
submission on this important topic.  
The Insurance Council is the representative body of the general insurance industry in Australia and represents approximately 89% of private sector general insurers. As a foundational component of the 
Australian economy, the general insurance industry employs approximately 46,000 people, generates 
gross written premium of $6 6 billion per annum and on average pays out $159  million in claims each 
working day ($3 9.4 billion paid out per year).  
The Insurance Council and its members welcome the Australian Government’s commitment to a 
modern and efficient regulatory system as a critical input to unlocking innovative uses of AI in the Australian economy.  
We provide the following general comments , with further detail at Appendix A.  
First, we encourage the Government to consider  any potential  implication s which may arise from the 
creation  of new regulations, including the impact of cumulative administrative burden s, existing 
regulatory obligations, transparency requirements, and investigative and sanction regimes on 
insurance risks and costs. In particular, new artificial intelligence ( AI) regulation is likely to impact 
products and costs in the cyber, professional indemnity and directors’  and officers’  insurance markets.  
We would welc ome further discussion on these issues as regulation is further developed.  
We also encourage the Government  to consider a phased approach to new AI regulation, irrespective 
of which regulatory path it chooses.  We recognise that m uch of the techno logy discussed in the 
Proposal Paper is novel and crosses international jurisdictions . Phasing AI regulation in, starting with 
uplifting existing regulatory frameworks and  the highest- risk settings will allow the Government to 
monitor regulatory outcomes in Australia and internationally , and adjust  Australia’s approach 
accordingly.  Any n ew AI -specific legislation must take a cautio us approach, noting that it may bring 
unintended consequences, including lost economic opportunities.  
Finally, AI is a fast -moving environment with data sets, models and use cases evolving quickly. We 
expect this to continue.  It is important that the principles and guardrails are fit for future enablement . 
The International Monetary Fund recent publication Australia: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2024 
Article IV Mission  noted the importance of ongoing assessment, flexibility, agility and adaption in 
policymaking to maximise AI’s productivity benefits for Australia.

Appendix A  
Do the proposed principles adequately capture high- risk AI?  
The Insurance Council consider s that on balance,  the proposed principles would adequately capture 
high- risk AI .  
However, we  believe they  may also unintentionally capture lower risk AI applications.  Examples of low -
risk AI use cases in the insurance industry that may be captured include:  
• Fraud detection applications.  
• The coding and matching of invoices.  
• Code (software) development.  
• Security classification determining programs (e.g., for documents and shared folders).  
• Customer service chatbots.  
• Document processing (e.g., document ingestion and insight generation). 
• Analytics and decision trees for low complexity and high volume transactions (e.g., paying 
windscreen claims).  
As outlined below, we support the flexibility and adaptability that would be provided by a principles -
based approach, but we strongly support there being clear guidance,  and specific examples provided 
alongside the principles . Examples  will give clarity to organisation and assist them with 
implementation .  
Without this clarity, we are concerned investment in AI may be stifled as businesses opt to avoid 
regulatory risk . At a time when we are seeking to boost Australia’s productivity , it is important that any 
new regulation does  not reduce business investment in technology that will help arrest productivity 
losses and improve consumer outcomes.2 
Specific to the proposed principle “ The risk of adverse legal effects, defamation or similarly significant 
effects on an individual”, the Proposal Paper outlines an example from the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation that restricts entities from making solely automated decisions that have a legal 
or similarly significant effect on individuals. We support this and suggest that guidance should clearly 
give regard to risk mitigants and how they can be applied. Risk mitigants may include, for example, the extent of autonomy and human oversight in a decision -making process.  
We also note that potential harms such as bias, discrimination or accessibility issues are proposed to 
be address ed within the guardrails (e.g. Guardrail 2 relating to risk management, and Guardrail 8 
relating to transparency). We suggest that consideration be given to the principles specifically 
acknowledging these types of risks.  
Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?  
We support the proposed principle “ The risk of adverse impacts to groups of individuals or collective 
rights of cultural groups”, its acknowledgement of , and the need to protect marginalised groups

including Indigenous communities . For example, the well-documented potential of AI to embed , 
perpetuat e, and amplify existing  biases and stereotypes  about  minority groups underscores  the need 
for countermeasures against these biases . Particularly  as AI increasingly plays a role in decision -
making  and decision -support  developing and implementing safeguards will be essential  to minimis ing 
harmful  impacts on Indigenous communities .  
The Insurance Council’s Indigenous Advisory Committee is focused on advising the insurance industry 
on Indigenous -related issues to drive better customer outcomes, support reconciliation actions, 
increase industry understanding of vulnerable customers and increase knowledge of specific cultural 
and heritage concerns. We would welcome the opportunity to provide views on how the principle and 
supporting guidance, together with the guardrails, could address potential harms to First Nations 
peoples, communities  and Country as it relates to insurance as they are developed.  
Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high -risk AI 
settings and high- risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?  
We support the flexibility and adaptability that would be provided by a principles -based approach, but 
we strongly support there being clear guidance and specific examples to provide clarity and assist with 
implementation. We would especially support more detail and definition at a sector -specific level . We 
suggest more definition, guidance and examples will be imperative as any new regulation is introduced in this evolving landscape to ensure regular  business activities are not unintentionally captured by the 
principles .  
For example, we note the list of high -risk use cases identified in other countries includes “ AI systems 
used to make decisions that affect access to essential private services, including credit, insurance in a 
manner that poses significant risk”. Where  insurance is protecting an individual (in general insurance, 
this may include accident and health or workers compensation insurances for instance), the underwriting risk assessment process may need to consider an individual’s characteristics to facilitate 
the provision of the insurance that protects the individual. In other settings, considering an individual’s 
characteristics may be discriminatory but it is essential in the insurance underwriting process.  
Similarly, we note the listing of biometrics as high -risk in other countries and suggest that in certain 
circumstances this technology may in fact be low risk, with considerable benefit, particularly in improving consumer outcomes. For example, t he use of biometric voice data to perform sentiment 
analysis to detect stress and risk of self -harm during an insurance claims process, with appropriately 
managed human follow up care, would be very low risk and very high potential benefit.  However, this 
use would l ikely be captured under the description given in Table 1. It is important that Australia’s 
chosen approach does not preclude such opportunities.  
Specific examples of high- risk settings and models, as well as settings and models that are not high-
risk, can assist businesses in understanding and identifying when their AI use crosses the high -risk 
threshold. Similarly, examples could be used to show t he conditions under which the AI associated 
risks have been reduced such that a business’ use of AI is no longer considered high -risk. As also 
noted above, examples could be supplemented with sector -specific guidance, developed by the 
Government and indust ry, to assist entities with implementation of and compliance with the principles 
and mandatory guardrails.  
Are there high- risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for 
example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?  
While we do not propose any particular use cases the Government should consider banning , we do 
note some high- risk use  case s would be covered by existing regulation  and encourage consideration
