of how existing law can be strengthened . For example, discrimination in the employment process  is 
illegal and technology neutral legislation can reflect this . Where possible, regulation and legislation 
should deal with unacceptable practices in a technology neutral manner.  
Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high -risk AI, such 
as general -purpose AI (GPAI)?  
We understand the principles to be defined by outcomes and  on that basis  suggest they are 
appropriate. This allows flexibility for emerging forms of AI as the decision is based on the impact.  We 
do not consider GPAI to be inherently high -risk.   
Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?  
No. We recommend  the guardrails should apply  only where the use of GPAI is high -risk. We also 
recommend greater guidance  and examples are provided on when use of a GPAI model would be 
considered as high-risk. Applying guardrails to all GPAI models runs counter to the  purpose of the 
principles which are being designed to assist in determining i f the “use of an AI system is high -risk”. 
We suggest that there are GPAI models that are helping to promote greater efficiency and  productivity 
by helping people with everyday tasks, rather than making decisions . Broadly speaking, these should 
not be considered high -risk nor subject to guardrails. We are concerned that capturing all GPAI 
models , regardless of their use, will discourage dynamism and business optimisation with negative 
implications for productivity.  
Guardrails will be critical in the development and testing of models to avoid having biases built in .  
What are suitable indicators for defining GPAI models as high -risk? For example, is it enough to define 
GPAI as high -risk against the principles, or should it be based on technical capability such as FLOPS 
(e.g. 10^25 or 10^26 threshold), advice from a sci entific panel, government or other indicators?  
We believe that trying to regulate against technical specification s creates the risk that regulation 
quickly becomes outdated  or obsolete. This is particularly true in areas where  advancements are rapid, 
as is the case with A I. As much as possible, regulation should be technology neutral. Risk may be 
better managed through the regulation of what an AI model can do, rather than how it does a task . 
Given this, we support the use of the principles to define high -risk and would query the purpose of 
those principles if they are paralleled by an attempt to also use technological specifics to indicate high -
risk. 
In the alternative, we  propose a  compromise may be a more general categorisation of the technology, 
such as where a model is deterministic as opposed to non -deterministic.   
Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high -risk settings?  
The Proposals Paper notes that the proposed mandatory guardrails have been developed with a view 
to being aligned nationally and with comparable jurisdictions and international standards to reduce the 
compliance burden. While we welcome this approach, any new regulation will generally increase 
operating costs for businesses and create additional regulatory burden. This needs to be balanced against the ability for businesses to continue to compete and innovate whilst providing affordable 
products or services for their cust omers. Regulatory burden typically also has a greater impact on 
small to medium businesses. We therefore support the recognition in the Proposals Paper that organisations should integrate the guardrails into existing processes and suggest this should expli citly 
form part of any future regulation.

We also support the implementation of the proposed mandatory guardrails in a way that enables 
organisations to embed them as appropriate to the nature and extent of the activities they are 
undertaking. For example, while they are proposed to apply to high -risk settings, we would still expect 
there to be differences in these settings across sectors, and the application of the mandatory 
guardrails should therefore reflect this.  
We also welcome the intention that the guardrails will need to be adaptable to remain fit for purpose as 
AI technology continues to evolve and become more autonomous. We also support the intention as 
outlined in the Proposal Paper to provide further  clarity on the division of responsibilities between 
developers and deployers  will be necessary.  
We off er further comments on specific guardrails : 
• Guardrail  8. We believe this guardrail  may prevent Australian entities from creating models 
using their own intellectual property  and new small businesses from entering the market . 
• Guardrail  9. It may be appropriate to ensure businesses can utilise and augment their existing 
risk functions. Additional clarity of appropriately shared responsibility on developers and 
deployers will be critical to ensuring open access and availability of the benefits to AI across the 
economy and wider community.  
• Guardrail  10. We suggest additional guidance be provided that  highlights the risks that need to 
be asses sed when implementing a solution, allowing individual entities to tailor their 
implementation approach.  
Finally, w e also suggest two themes may be missing from the proposed guardrails.  
1. Consent . It is very possible to digitally duplicate a person or company’s image, communications 
and to forecast behaviour through AI techniques. The guidelines speak to letting customers know when they are interacting with AI content. However, nothing currently exists  to govern 
organisations using customer data to create AI content . Many “Terms and Conditions” today are 
broad in the permissions they grant, but an individuals’ current consent for us to retain their 
data for today’s business purposes may not be sufficient for tomorrow’s  business opportunities. 
Explicit consent from individuals  may be necessary for data about them to be used and consent 
may need to be asked again each time the information is used for something new. Models need 
to be able to track who has not consented an d eliminate this.   
This said, w e note that future tranches  of reforms to the Privacy Act  1988 are expected  to 
introduce a “fair and reasonable” requirement  which should deal with this issue. It would be 
appropriate for the Government to confirm this approach  and regulatory interaction  and 
consider if interim measures are required.  
2. Responsibility . We note Guardrail 6’s determination that end -users be informed regarding AI -
enabled decisions . We consider  this determination to be very broad and observe that it touches 
on an  ethical issue which may evolv e in the  general  insurance industry  and broader economy . 
As insurers ability to  access and utilise  larger and larger datasets increases , underwriting 
abilities may also extend to forecast ing events that have serious implications for underwriting . 
We query then an organisation’s responsibility to inform an indiv idual . The guardrails should 
consider an organisation’s  responsibility  in such a situation  and make guiding provisions .

How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols to ensure AI 
systems are culturally appropriate and preserve Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property?  
While we do not propose a solution, we do note that general AI is trained on vast amounts of publicly 
available data. While we understand that it is common practice for organisations in the AI development 
space to monitor their models for unfair bias, we r ecognise the not insignificant risk that First Nations 
people may not be prioritised through regular processes in a way that ensures culturally appropriate 
expression or best preserves indigenous cultural and intellectual property.  
Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?  
We agree that the AI deployer bears a level of responsibility,  however  we are concerned that the 
burden of responsibility will be placed too heavily on the eventual deployer of an AI model.  Of 
particular concern are models built overseas . These models  are likely to reflect differences to 
Australian populations, values and ethics .  
We recommend that the level of responsibility be commensurate with the various roles throughout the AI lifecycle.  
We also recommend the Government consider the interaction of any potential AI regulation with the 
use of AI in Australian businesses’ international supply chains , where Australian businesses  are not the 
deployer of the technology.  
Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small -to-medium sized businesses 
applying guardrails?  
As outlined above, we support implementation via existing processes and also in a way that reflects 
the nature and extent of use of AI in high -risk settings. These businesses could also be supported 
through the provision of additional guidance on deployment of AI in organisations to meet transparency 
and explainability requirements.

1.  Executive Summary
Western Power have undertaken a comprehensive review of the Safe and Responsible AI in Australia Proposals Paper For Introducing Mandatory Guardrails For AI In High-Risk Settings (‘Proposal’), and welcomes and supports the initiative to enhance the safety, transparency, and reliability of artificial intelligence (AI) applications. Establishing standardised measures for high-risk AI applications aligns with Western Power’s continuous efforts to embed robust cybersecurity and safety protocols within our operations, which is vital to maintaining the security and trust inherent in our services.
Western Power acknowledges the importance of the introduction of a regulatory mechanism to ensure that Australia protects both its citizens and its critical infrastructure, and that ensures consistency with other nations who are rapidly establishing robust legislative frameworks in the area of artificial intelligence. However, such regulation must be balanced with the practical impact on business and industry, and the cost of compliance. 
Western Power seeks further clarity on the definitions within the Proposal, and clear and pragmatic practical applications to organisations that operate in highly regulated sectors such as utilities. This is essential to preventing the inception of blanket regulations that could hinder technological advancements vital for operational efficiency and service improvements. A lack of clarity on some elements of the Proposal may result in overlapping responsibilities and complications to compliance efforts, undermining the effectiveness of the proposed regulatory framework. 
To address these issues, Western Power proposes adopting a framework approach to regulation that would allow for greater flexibility and adaptability, enabling the regulatory environment to evolve alongside rapid technological advancements without the need for frequent costly and time-consuming legislative updates. Additionally, ongoing engagement with stakeholders, including AI developers, deployers, First Nations representatives, and regulatory bodies, is essential. This collaboration will ensure that the guardrails reflect practical realities and incorporate industry and cultural expertise, which is critical for crafting effective, safe, equitable, and functional AI governance.
The impact of implementing the proposed AI guardrails on Western Power’s operations would be significant, particularly in how Western Power manage and deploy AI systems (as currently defined within the Proposal) across our systems. Western Power operate in an already highly regulated space, and pride ourselves on taking an industry leading approach to pertinent issues including cyber security, privacy, and the protection of Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP). Whilst Western Power are committed to measures that enhance safety and reliability, it is vital that these regulations do not inadvertently curb our capacity to innovate and improve the services we provide to the community. 
As a provider of essential services, our ability to responsibly and efficiently leverage AI systems directly influences our capability to meet and exceed the expectations of the communities we serve. Western Power supports the goals of enhancing safety and reliability through the proposed Mandatory AI guardrails, but also wish to highlight that it is imperative that their implementation is thoughtfully considered to address the unique needs and challenges faced by utilities such as Western Power. Through careful legislation that integrates comprehensive industry feedback and expert insights, we can establish a balanced regulatory framework that not only supports safety and public good but also fosters innovation and technological advancement.
2.  Introduction
Electricity Networks Corporation (trading as Western Power) is a Western Australian Government Trading Enterprise responsible for the transmission and distribution of electricity in the South West Interconnected System. Western Power is dedicated to connecting over 2.3 million customers to a mix of traditional and renewable energy sources and plays a pivotal role in Western Australia’s energy landscape. Western Power has consistently demonstrated a commitment to safety, reliability, and efficiency, underscored by a robust culture of innovation and forward-thinking strategies. As we navigate the complexities of energy transition and grid modernisation, our approach aligns with the highest standards of corporate governance and community engagement, ensuring that our practices resonate deeply with the values we uphold.
The proposed Mandatory AI Guardrails in the Proposal are of significant interest to Western Power, given our proactive stance on integrating advanced technologies, including AI where appropriate, into our operations. Our long-standing commitment to leveraging new technologies to enhance grid management and optimise energy distribution positions us uniquely to assess the implications of these regulatory changes. The guardrails, intended to enhance the safety and transparency of AI applications, must be crafted to support not only the ongoing technological evolution but also the dynamic needs of energy providers and controllers of other Critical Infrastructure Assets.
Artificial intelligence has been described as the biggest thing to influence humanity since the internet. It has been estimated that a greater utilisation of AI across some key Australian industries (including the utilities sector) has the potential to provide short-term boost to Australian GDP of more than $200 billion per year. Whilst Western Power acknowledges that AI has the potential to reduce operating costs and provide significant improvements in tasks such as repetitive administrative tasks, workflows, data analytics, forecasting and predictive modelling we also recognise the risks inherent in unregulated or inappropriate adoption across the sector.  Our understanding of the proposed guardrails centres on their objective to introduce rigorous standards for AI systems, particularly those deemed high-risk within essential services. These standards are crucial for ensuring that AI systems operate safely, transparently, and effectively, without compromising the security and reliability of the infrastructure services that depend on them.
This submission reflects Western Power’s commitment to safeguarding our operations against the risks associated with AI technologies while embracing the potential for innovation and efficiency improvements. By participating in this legislative process, we seek to ensure that the final regulations are balanced, fostering an environment conducive to technological advancement whilst upholding the highest standards of safety and accountability.
3.  Implications for the Utilities Sector and Critical Infrastructure
In electrical utilities technological tools can play a pivotal role in driving efficiencies and solving complex operational challenges. These sectors rely heavily on technology that utilises various forms of artificial intelligence for predictive maintenance, grid management, load forecasting, and energy distribution optimisation. AI applications in these fields can predict equipment failures before they occur, optimise the distribution of electricity based on real-time data, and enhance the efficiency of renewable energy sources by accurately predicting output levels. Such capabilities not only improve reliability and service quality but also contribute significantly to cost management and environmental sustainability.
The proposed list-based classification of "high-risk AI" in the Mandatory AI Guardrails could significantly hinder these advancements. By potentially classifying many AI tools used in these sectors as high-risk, the guardrails could subject them to stringent regulatory standards. This could lead to increased compliance costs and operational inefficiencies as owners or operators of critical infrastructure may need to navigate complex approval processes or redesign systems to meet new standards. 
The vague distinction between AI "deployers" and "developers" under the proposed guardrails further complicates this scenario. Many energy sector entities customarily adjust and configure AI tools to suit their specific operational needs. This standard practice could unexpectedly categorise them as developers, imposing on them a set of obligations and liabilities that are disproportionate to their actual role and the inherent risks of their AI applications. 
These proposed regulations, while aimed at mitigating potential risks associated with AI, may inadvertently stifle innovation. For instance, in the energy sector, AI's potential to enhance grid stability and integrate renewable energy sources more efficiently could be curtailed. Similarly, Government Trading Enterprises that utilise AI for public service optimisation might find their hands tied, unable to deploy AI solutions that can streamline operations and improve public outcomes without facing onerous regulatory hurdles. To address these challenges, it is crucial for stakeholders in these industries to engage actively with regulatory bodies. This engagement should help refine the definitions and scopes within the proposed guardrails to ensure they accurately reflect the risk profiles and operational realities of AI applications in critical infrastructure. By doing so, they can safeguard the continued innovation and efficiency improvements that AI tools bring to these essential sectors, ensuring that regulatory measures do not inadvertently hinder the very progress they aim to protect.
4.  Key Concerns and Suggestions
4.1  Definitions of High-Risk AI, Developer, and Artificial Intelligence
The categorical or list-based approach to defining "high-risk AI," particularly as it relates to critical infrastructure, raises several concerns for our business. This method, which involves pre-defined categories that dictate which AI applications must adhere to stricter regulatory measures, may include systems that, while technically sophisticated, do not pose significant practical risks. For instance, AI systems used for scheduling maintenance or managing logistics within a critical infrastructure framework might be unnecessarily classified as high-risk. This broad inclusion could subject benign applications to undue regulatory scrutiny, diverting resources from more critical areas where they are needed.
Another issue with this approach is its lack of flexibility. Once an AI system is categorised as high-risk, altering this classification in response to changes in technology or operational use may be challenging. This rigidity potentially hinders the ability of businesses to adapt swiftly to evolving technological landscapes or operational requirements. Additionally, the categorical approach often does not consider the context in which AI is used. For example, AI applications designed with robust safety features and deployed in controlled environments might still be classified as high-risk, ignoring the mitigating circumstances that substantially reduce their actual risk.
To address these issues, it would be more effective to assess AI systems based on specific functionalities and the direct impact they have, or by using the proposed ‘Proposed Principles’ approach. This approach would allow for a more nuanced understanding of what constitutes high-risk, focusing on factors such as the potential for adverse effect on human rights, mental or physical health and safety, and the impacts on marginalised groups. in decision-making. Moreover, regulatory frameworks could be enhanced by introducing flexibility to assess risks based on the specific operational contexts, distinguishing between AI used in critical decision-making processes and those employed in non-critical administrative tasks. In initial discussions surrounding the drafting of the EU AI Act, the European Commission contemplated more specific definitions of artificial intelligence systems that would effectively exclude the more traditional and lower-risk forms of artificial intelligence. Such ‘traditional’ forms of artificial intelligence include List Processing, Machine Learning, Robotics, Natural Language Processing, Automation tools, Predictive Analytics tools, Speech Recognition Software, and logic reasoning. 
AI applications that handle routine administrative tasks such as document management, employee scheduling, or basic data processing should be explicitly excluded from the high-risk category, provided they do not autonomously make decisions that could significantly affect infrastructure safety or security. Similarly, AI systems used for predictive maintenance, which schedule repairs based on data-driven predictions, enhance operational reliability without directly controlling operational systems and should also be considered for exclusion. Additionally, AI used for optimising energy consumption within facilities contributes to efficiency without impacting core operational controls and should not be categorised as high-risk but rather encouraged as part of sustainability efforts.
The EU AI Act contains specific carve-outs to facilitate the use of AI in administrative and procedural tasks within critical infrastructure sectors. While the EU AI Act generally classifies certain AI systems as high-risk—particularly those integral to safety components or involved in critical operational functions—it also acknowledges that not all AI applications pose the same level of risk.
Specifically, the EU AI Act allows for exceptions where AI systems are used for narrowly defined procedural tasks or for enhancing previously completed human activities without replacing human judgement. This means that AI systems used for administrative purposes, which improve efficiency but do not directly influence critical operations or safety components, might not necessarily be classified as high-risk. This carve-out is crucial as it acknowledges the varying impact levels of AI applications and aims to prevent unnecessary burdens on AI systems that pose lower risks.
Such distinctions are important for ensuring that AI regulations are proportionate to the risks presented, allowing for the beneficial use of AI in enhancing operational efficiency without the heavy compliance requirements reserved for high-risk applications. This regulatory strategy helps balance innovation with safety and accountability, particularly in sectors where AI can significantly contribute to operational improvements.
By advocating for more tailored criteria and the exclusion of certain low risk use cases from high-risk categories, we can ensure that AI regulation is both effective and proportionate. This approach supports innovation and efficiency without compromising safety or oversight, fostering a regulatory environment that nurtures technological advancement and operational excellence.
4.2  Impact on Technological Innovation and Competition
It is essential that we stop to consider how regulatory measures influence innovation and the competitive landscape for technology products. The proposed framework, with its broad application across all AI developers and technologies, may inadvertently stifle innovation and escalate costs. By imposing stringent guardrails universally, we risk burdening developers with compliance obligations that may not correspond to the level of risk their AI systems pose. This could deter startups and smaller enterprises, known for their innovative contributions, from developing AI solutions, thereby limiting the diversity and dynamism within the technology sector.
A more targeted approach, as exemplified by Singapore's regulatory framework for AI, could serve as a constructive alternative. Singapore selectively applies AI regulations, focusing on specific industries or sectors that are considered high-risk. This method not only ensures that the necessary safety measures are enforced where most needed but also fosters an environment conducive to innovation. By not over-regulating, Singapore continues to cultivate its status as a global technology hub, encouraging both local and international companies to develop and deploy AI technologies within its borders.
Adopting a similar strategy could allow us to safeguard essential interests and public safety without compromising our competitive edge in the global technology market. Such an approach would support a thriving ecosystem of AI development, attracting investment, and fostering innovation, while still addressing the critical areas where AI poses genuine risks.
Whilst we recognise the necessity of establishing guardrails for AI to protect public and infrastructural safety, it is equally important to ensure these regulations are thoughtfully crafted to avoid inhibiting the very innovation they aim to safely promote. A targeted regulatory approach, inspired by successful international models, could provide a balanced pathway forward, supporting robust economic growth and technological innovation alongside essential safety and privacy standards.
4.3  Impact on First Nations People and Communities
The integration of AI technologies in sectors such as utilities has profound implications for First Nations communities, necessitating robust regulatory measures to ensure respect for Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) and broader First Nations rights. AI's deployment in areas involving resource management, land use, and cultural heritage carries risks of bias that could lead to cultural misappropriation or other forms of cultural harm. This risk is exacerbated by potential biases in the data sets used to train AI systems, which can lead to AI outputs that further perpetuate existing inequalities or misunderstandings.
To address these challenges, the proposed AI guardrails must include specific mechanisms aimed at mitigating the risk of bias and ensuring the protection of cultural rights. Regulatory mechanisms should mandate the inclusion of cultural impact assessments in the AI development and deployment phases. These assessments would evaluate the potential impacts of AI systems on First Nations communities, aiming to prevent negative consequences such as the infringement of cultural rights. This process should involve meaningful consultation with First Nations stakeholders, integrating their perspectives and knowledge into the development of AI systems to ensure culturally informed and unbiased AI applications.
Moreover, AI guardrails should enforce strict adherence to protocols that respect ICIP. This includes ensuring that any AI system that interacts with or processes data related to First Nations communities does so in a manner that is fully compliant with ICIP guidelines, which protect the traditional knowledge and cultural expressions of these groups. Additionally, it is critical for developers, deployers, and end-users to be vigilant about potential biases in their datasets. Regulatory obligations could include requirements for routine bias audits, transparency in data sourcing and usage, and mandatory training for AI developers on cultural competence and bias mitigation.
By embedding these regulatory mechanisms into the AI guardrails, we can safeguard the rights and heritage of First Nations communities and enhance the societal acceptance and effectiveness of AI technologies. Such measures ensure that AI serves the good of all community members, fostering an inclusive, ethical approach to technological advancement that respects diversity and cultural rights.
4.4  Risks and Opportunities for Critical Infrastructure
It is integral that we emphasise the need for a balanced regulatory approach that adequately mitigates risks while fostering innovation, particularly in low-risk AI applications. We understand the importance of leveraging technological advancements to enhance the operational efficiency of forecasting, analysis, and management systems. AI applications play a crucial role in optimizing resource allocation, reducing waste, and improving system reliability, which are imperative for maintaining the sustainability and efficiency of our network.
The proposed AI guardrails, while necessary for managing potential risks associated with high-risk AI applications, should be designed to avoid imposing undue burdens on AI technologies that pose minimal risk but offer significant benefits. Overly stringent regulations could stifle innovation in areas where AI can provide substantial improvements to operational efficiency and service delivery. For instance, AI-driven analytics for load forecasting in energy sectors allows for more precise demand management, which directly contributes to energy conservation and cost reduction. Similarly, AI applications in predictive maintenance can significantly reduce downtime and maintenance costs by predicting equipment failures before they occur.
It is essential that the regulatory framework distinguishes between high-risk and low-risk AI applications or use cases, applying stringent controls where necessary but allowing more flexibility for low-risk scenarios. This approach would encourage continued investment and innovation in AI technologies that enhance the capabilities of critical infrastructure without compromising safety or operational integrity.
Moreover, fostering an environment that encourages the development of AI solutions for critical infrastructure requires collaboration between regulators, industry stakeholders, and technology developers. By working together to define clear, practical guidelines that reflect the varied risk profiles of AI applications, we can ensure that the guardrails support technological advancement while protecting public and environmental safety.
The proposed Mandatory AI Guardrails must strike a delicate balance between risk mitigation and support for innovation. Ensuring that this balance is appropriately managed will be crucial for maintaining Australia’s competitive edge in technology and infrastructure development, while also safeguarding the interests of the public and the environment. Such a balanced approach will not only support the growth of the technology sector but will also ensure that our critical infrastructure continues to operate efficiently and reliably.
5.  Regulatory Considerations and Alignment with Existing Frameworks
It is essential to ensure that the proposed Mandatory AI Guardrails are focused on ensuring these new regulations effectively integrate with existing frameworks. This integration is crucial for maintaining a coherent regulatory environment that enhances the security, privacy, and operational integrity of AI applications within critical infrastructure.
Alignment with Existing Regulations:
The proposed Mandatory AI Guardrails need to be closely aligned with existing regulations such as the Security of Critical Infrastructure (SOCI) Act, which governs the protection of vital infrastructure from external threats, and various privacy and cybersecurity laws that regulate data protection and security. The SOCI Act, in particular, sets out obligations for Controlling Entities responsible for Critical Infrastructure Assets to mitigate risks from external interference. The alignment of the proposed Mandatory AI Guardrails with these provisions is essential to ensure that AI technologies deployed within critical infrastructure sectors do not introduce new vulnerabilities or undermine existing protections.
Furthermore, privacy laws provide a regulatory framework for managing the privacy and security of data used by AI systems. Western Power is not subject to Commonwealth privacy legislation, but will soon be subject to Western Australian legislation regarding privacy and responsible information sharing. It is vital that the AI guardrails enhance these privacy protections rather than conflict with them, particularly in the processing and utilisation of personal and sensitive information by AI systems.
Regulatory Gaps and Areas of Inconsistency:
Despite these alignments, there are potential regulatory gaps, particularly in the nuanced application of AI in sectors not fully covered by the SOCI Act. For example, the current frameworks may not adequately address the emerging risks associated with advanced AI technologies, such as deep learning and autonomous decision-making processes, which could have far-reaching implications beyond traditional cybersecurity and privacy concerns.
There is also a risk of inconsistency in how AI risks are assessed and mitigated across different sectors. The broad application of AI across various industries—from energy to telecommunications—might encounter variable regulatory standards, leading to a patchwork of compliance obligations that could hinder cohesive risk management strategies. These inconsistencies could complicate the responsibilities of AI developers and deployers, especially those operating across multiple sectors.
To address these gaps, it is suggested that the proposed Mandatory AI Guardrails incorporate specific guidelines for continuous risk assessments and updates to the regulatory frameworks as AI technologies evolve. Additionally, establishing a centralised body or mechanism for overseeing AI regulation could help ensure uniformity and consistency across different sectors and regions.
By carefully considering these regulatory considerations and striving for alignment with existing frameworks, we can ensure that the deployment of AI technologies adheres to the highest standards of security, privacy, and operational integrity. This approach not only supports the robust development of AI within regulated frameworks but also safeguards the interests of all stakeholders involved in or affected by AI technologies in critical infrastructure.
6.  Suggestions for Legislative Options
Western Power believes that each proposed methodology for legislative enactment of the Guardrails has its merits and potential drawbacks, depending on the specific needs and operational realities of different sectors and that all are both valid and internationally demonstrated mechanisms. 
The domain-specific approach is being adopted by nations such as Singapore as a professed way to continually foster and support technology advancement without the imposition of burdensome regulation that acts as a barrier to entry to market. This approach tailors regulations to the specific needs and risks of individual industries or domains, allowing for precise and relevant regulatory measures. While this could ensure that regulations are highly relevant to the characteristics of each sector, this piecemeal approach could complicate compliance for AI developers and deployers working across multiple sectors.
The framework approach offers a balanced mix of uniformity and flexibility, providing a set of overarching principles and guidelines that can be adapted to various industries. This approach supports uniform definitions, penalties, and regulatory oversight, which can be integrated into existing legislative tools. The flexibility of the framework approach is particularly advantageous as it allows for regulatory updates and adaptations without the need for frequent legislative amendments. This adaptability is crucial given the rapid pace of technological advancements in AI.
The economy-wide approach can be seen in the European AI Act,and involves applying a uniform set of AI regulations across all sectors. While this offers consistency and simplifies the regulatory landscape, it may not adequately address the unique risks and needs of specific industries, particularly those involving critical infrastructure or highly sensitive data.
Western Power believe that the most appropriate option for the Australian introduction of Mandatory AI Guardrails is the is the framework approach. This approach allows for the establishment of uniform definitions and regulatory mechanisms that are essential for cohesive oversight across different sectors. The framework's adaptability makes it possible to reference and integrate with existing legislative instruments, enhancing the agility of regulatory responses to technological changes. For instance, just as privacy regulations have evolved under the umbrella of broader privacy legislation, AI regulations could similarly adapt within a framework approach.
The framework approach also enables the potential incorporation of internationally recognised standards like NIST or ISO 42001, which many industries may already be compliant with. These standards could be extended to include AI services, providing a robust foundation for ensuring that AI technologies are developed and deployed responsibly.
By adopting a framework approach, we can ensure that AI regulations are both comprehensive and flexible enough to accommodate future advancements in AI technology. This method provides the benefits of uniformity and consistency necessary for effective regulatory oversight while retaining the flexibility to adapt to rapid technological developments. This legislative strategy will support ongoing innovation and ensure that AI serves the broader interests of society while safeguarding individual rights and public welfare.
7.  Conclusion
Western Power appreciates the opportunity to provide feedback on the proposed Mandatory AI Guardrails. We commend the initiative's aim to enhance the safety, transparency, and efficacy of AI systems, particularly within critical infrastructure sectors. It is imperative that the final regulatory framework is carefully calibrated to balance safety and innovation without stifling technological progress.
We urge consideration of a more nuanced classification system for AI risks, one that accurately reflects the varying degrees of risk associated with different AI applications rather than a prescriptive list that fails to take into account the intrinsic detail implicit within the artificial intelligence space. Taking a principles base approach would prevent the unnecessary burdening of low-risk AI innovations that hold significant potential for enhancing operational efficiencies and service quality. Additionally, clear and precise definitions of terms such as those for “Artificial Intelligence”, "Deployers" and "Developers" are essential to avoiding ambiguities that could complicate compliance and enforcement processes.
Adopting a regulatory framework that is flexible and adaptable to rapid technological changes will ensure that regulations remain relevant and effective in the face of evolving AI capabilities. Continued stakeholder engagement is also crucial to harnessing industry insights and expertise, which will aid in refining and enhancing the regulatory proposals.
As we move forward, it is our hope that these guardrails will foster an environment where safety and innovation coexist harmoniously, supporting Australia's ambition to be a leader in the ethical development and deployment of AI technologies. Through thoughtful legislation and collaborative regulation, we can safeguard public and infrastructural safety whilst also promoting a vibrant and dynamic technological ecosystem.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) is an independent 
Commonwealth statutory agency that promotes competition, fair trading and product safety 
for the benefit of consumers, businesses and the Australian community. The primary 
responsi bilities of the ACCC are to administer and enforce the Competition and Consumer 
Act 2010  (CCA) and other legislation promoting competition, consumer protection, fair 
trading, product safety,  monitoring and disrupting scams , regulating national infrastructu re 
and undertaking market studies. The CCA includes the Australian Consumer Law (ACL)

under a one law, multiple regulator model (the ACL Regulators).  
The ACCC welcomes the opportunity to make a submission to the Department of Industry, 
Science and Resource s’ (DISR) consultation on the proposals paper for introducing 
mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings.   
Proposals for high -risk AI guardrails and regulatory options  
The ACCC strongly supports Option 2’s ‘framework approach’ as the preferred approach. 
This would provide for timely implementation and a flexible application that would help 
implement the guardrails appropriately and effectively, while leveraging existing regulatory 
expertise and providing greater certainty for business.   
Importantly, this option will provide flexibility to integrate with international frameworks and 
promote international coherence in the regulation of AI. This is important given many of the 
companies likely to be subject to regulation are based overseas an d are operating in many 
different jurisdictions.  
We encourage strong consideration of international frameworks  when developing  Australia ’s 
regulatory approach  to maximise consistency with  other jurisdictions . This was the 
approach taken when developing the ACCC’s proposals for a digital competition regime .  
We consider that Option 2’s framework approach would provide the flexibility needed to help 
promote the consistency of Australia’s approach to regulating high -risk AI with other 
international jurisdictions. The other options, particularly Option 3, may  not provide this 
flexibility , may lead to regulatory incoherence , and could increase the burden for businesses.  
In implementing guardrails, the ACCC considers that the following should be taken into 
account:  
▪ As stated in the Digital Platform Regulators Forum (DP-REG) joint submission  in 
response to DISR’s ‘Safe and Responsible AI in Australia’ discussion paper, the ACCC 
and other DP -REG members support a view that any regulatory or Government response 
to address the risks associated with AI should consider the extent to which Australia ’s 
existing regulatory frameworks provide appropriate safeguards. The ACCC is working 
closely with Treasury and DISR on these issues, including through Treasury’s Review of 
AI and the  ACL, discussed further below . 
▪ The ACCC considers that competition issues should be considered for inclusion as a 
future priority review. It is imperative that markets remain competitive for this technology 
to mature, drive innovation , and provide positive outcomes for consumers. Should 
markets or supply chains for AI development  and deployment become dominated by a 
small number of market participants, it may diminish innovation and raise prices in these 
or related markets.   
Submission to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources   2 ▪ It will also be important for the regulatory regime to provide appropriate remedies and 
redress to consumers and businesses impacted by the misuse of high -risk AI.  The ACCC 
supports DISR’s view that obligations under Guardrail 7 will need to work alongside 
existing avenues for complaints handling, such as  existing rights and obligations under 
the ACL , and notes that internal and external dispute resolution requirements for high -
risk AI should be compatible with a proposed independent digital external disput e 
resolution scheme , and external dispute resolution schemes required under the 
proposed Scams Prevention Framework. The Government should also consider who 
would be the best body to undertake an external dispute resolution function for high -risk 
AI, and whether this should b e a regulator enforcing the mandatory guardrails or a 
separate entity.  
▪ The ACCC considers that mandatory guardrails that require meaningful human 
supervision to oversee the operation of AI technology (including in the supply chain, as 
well as record keeping, documentation and audit requirements) are important to ensure 
accoun tability, responsibility and transparency. In turn, accountability, responsibility and 
transparency are important to foster competition.  
▪ The ACCC notes that the proposal to categorise all general -purpose AI as ‘high -risk’ and 
therefore subject to the mandatory guardrails is currently without reference to thresholds 
of a developer’s size or of a model’s technical capability. The ACCC considers that  this is 
an important question that requires further deliberation as it could have significant 
impacts on competition.   
▪ The ACCC observes that under the proposed principles for identifying high -risk AI based 
on intended and foreseeable uses, regard should  be given to the risk of adverse impacts 
to an individual’s human rights, health and safety, and the risk of adverse legal effects, 
defamation, or similarly significant effects on an individual. We consider that some 
consumer -facing AI systems may carry a h igh-risk as they could  cause significant 
financial harm and damage to consumers, particularly where there is not clear l iability. 
Consideration should be given as to  whether these risks would fall under existing 
proposed princip les, or whether additional  principles are needed to  appropriately address 
this risk.  
The ACCC holds concerns with options 1 and 3. Option  1’s domain specific approach raises 
concerns, both in principle and practical implementation. Option 1 would require substantial, 
overlapping consultation and legislative amendment processes to implement . This would be 
resource -intensive for government and risk ‘consultation fatigue’ among engaged industry 
and advocacy groups. Option 1 also carries the risk of inconsistency across domains as 
time passes and the AI landscape evolves. The ACCC considers that the risk of regulatory 
uncertainty, overlap and delay may outweigh the potential benefits of option 1’s bespoke 
regulatory approaches.  
The ACCC considers that option 3’s proposal to introduce new AI -specific legislation and a 
new AI regulator has the potential to add additional complexity to the established 
boundaries between regulators. We also note that this approach may unnecessarily 
duplicate existing regulation and regulatory functions . It will also  likely require significant 
engagement between existing and new regulators to address overlaps and divisions of 
responsibilities.  
It is also not clear to the ACCC what functions the new regulator would perform. For 
example, whether  the regulator would have a role in determining what AI goods and services

Consumer  protection  considerations   
The ACL is a national law that deals with consumer protection and fair trading issues arising 
across the economy.1 The ACCC’s consumer protection role includes enforcement of the 
ACL to ensure that consumers and small businesses are protected from misleading and 
deceptive conduct, unconscionable conduct, unfair terms and conditions and unsafe 
products, and to promote fair trading. The National Anti -Scam Centre (the NASC) , which is 
operated by the ACCC  seeks to identify and disrupt scams before they reach consumer s, 
and to raise consumer awareness on how to spot and avoid scams . 
The uptake of AI technologies in Australia could have serious implications for the work of 
the ACL Regulators, including the potential to exacerbate a range of consumer harms that 
the ACL Regulators are working to address. For example, the use of AI to cre ate and 
disseminate misleading or deceptive advertising, scams, fake reviews and harmful 
applications.  
Exploring risks associated with the use of emerging technology in consumer products, 
including the use of AI, is one of the ACCC’s product safety priorities for 2024 -25. The ACCC 
will better seek to understand these risks by engaging with stakeholders and considering 
how the ACL can be applied to support safe and responsible practices in relation to 
emerging technology and product safety.   
The ACCC notes that there are multiple processes currently underway that have the potential 
to strengthen the ACL to address AI -related risks and harms in consumer transactions with 
businesses.  
Treasury is  undertaking  a review to examine  whether the ACL remains fit -for-purpose to 
protect consumers and support the safe and responsible use of AI by businesses.  The ACCC 
acknowledges  the importance of this review, and considers that where gaps in the existing 
law are identified, changes to legislation should be made  expeditiously  to address them . The 
ACCC is actively contributing to this review, which will consider potential interactions with 
any proposed mandatory guardrails for high -risk AI.  
In addition, t he Australian Government  is considering possible reforms to the ACL to address 
currently unregulated unfair trading practices .2 The ACCC supports the introduction of an 
economy -wide prohibition on unfair trading practices  and notes that this  may be a further 
mechanism to address potential harms that might arise from AI use . 
The Government  is also considering possible options aimed at improving the effectiveness 
of the consumer guarantee and supplier indemnification provisions under the ACL .3 The 
ACCC supports reform to the ACL that would make it  a contravention of the ACL  for: 
• businesses to fail to provide a remedy for consumer guarantees failures, when they 
are legally required to do so under the consumer guarantees, and

Competition considerations  
The ACCC has been closely following the development and deployment of AI technologies 
and potential risks for competition, particularly in the context of an increasingly digitised 
economy . The ACCC  is actively monitoring AI developments around the world and is 
currently considering competition issues in  generative  AI as part of  the Digital Platform 
Services Inquiry  Final Report , discussed further below .  
Effective competition in the provision of AI models and services is important to ensure 
consumers and the economy fully benefit from the technology. Informed and confident 
consumers and businesses are essential to enliven and drive competition in markets where 
AI is  utilised.  
Among other things, the CCA regulates  anti-competitive behaviour across the economy. The 
CCA includes prohibitions against cartel activity,  misuse of market power, anti -competitive 
exclusive dealing,  resale price maintenance and certain conduct that has the purpose, effect, 
or likely effect of substantially lessening competition in a market. These prohibitions on anti -
competitive conduct apply to businesses which supply or acquire AI technologies.  
Competition risks or concerns may include:  
• market concentration and vertical relationships which may entrench or extend market 
power  
• control and/or access to key inputs  (including data)  and users, and exclusive dealing 
arrangements which may create or extend market power and barriers to entry or 
expansion  
• barriers to switching, including lack of interoperability, which may entrench or extend 
market power and barriers to entry or expansion   
• access to talent ; where no-poach  agreements or non -compete clauses  could hinder the 
mobility of the skilled labour force as companies may attempt to lock -in workers with AI 
experience and skills  
• self-preferencing ; where firms that offer a range of products and services as part of an 
ecosystem may engage in self -preferencing, funnelling users towards their own AI 
products  
• access restrictions or refusal to deal; where some AI model developers may impose 
restrictions  or block access to their model to rivals that want to use it to develop 
competing functionalities ; and  
• firms engaging in anti-competitive collusive behaviour , such as price fixing , through AI 
algorithms that may either unintentionally coordinate with other firms’ algorithms or be 
intentionally developed to do so .  
Submission to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources   5 Additionally, AI has implications for the current regulatory framework, which typically 
attributes the actions , knowledge or intention  of directors, employees or agents to the 
corporation when determining the state of mind of a corporation required for liability for 
contraventions of the CCA. There is an increasing ability for  businesses to use AI to make 
key decisions, and to make representations to consumers, rather than directors, employees, 
or agents.  Where businesses use AI in these ways, liability for  conduct that contravenes the 
CCA is potentially unclear .  
The ACCC’s work on digital platforms  
We note that digital platform firms such as Microsoft (through investments in OpenAI), 
Google, Meta , and Amazon  (through investments in Anthropic)  have been instrumental in the 
development and popularisation of generative AI services, as well as the provision of 
services necessary for its deployment, such as cloud computing. These firms , which already 
maintain a dominant position across a range of digital markets,  have also been increasingly 
incorporating AI functionality into their own consumer -facing and business -facing digital 
platform services . 
The ACCC has been actively monitoring these developments through the Digital Platform 
Services Inquiry (DPSI) as well as ongoing participation in DP-REG as outlined below.  
The September 2024 interim report  of the DPSI considers competition and consumer issues 
in relation to general search services in Australia, including search quality. As part of this 
report, the ACCC looks at the potential impact  of generative AI on the competitive landscape 
in general search services. This report has been provided to the Australian Government and 
we expect to publish it shortly.  
The March 2025 final report  of the DPSI will consider  potential and emerging competition 
and consumer issues which relate to digital platform services, including the impact of 
Generative AI models and services . The report will also consider recent international  
regulatory developments , and will update the ACCC’s observations made throughout the 
DPSI . An issues paper  for this report was published on 25 July 202 4. 
The September 2022 interim report  (the Regulatory Reform Report)  recommended new 
competition and consumer protection measures to address various harms observed in the 
supply of digital platform services. These included:  
• consumer measures applying to all digital platforms to address scams, harmful 
apps, and fake reviews, and to improve access to dispute resolution for consumers 
and business users of platforms  
• a new competition regime applying to the largest and most powerful digital platforms 
to address anti -competitive conduct and barriers to entry.  
On 8  December 2023, the Government provided in-principle support  for all of these 
recommendations and noted it would publicly consult on a legislative framework to 
implement the digital competition regime  in 2024. Many of these  reforms would 
complement mandatory guardrails for AI services.  
The Government has already implemented the report’s recommendation to strengthen the 
economy -wide unfair contract term laws, including by enabling penalties to be imposed for 
contraventions and, as mentioned above, is considering implementation of the 
recommendation to prohibit unfair trading practices . 
The Government has also announced that the Treasury and the Department of 
Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications and the Arts will consider  
Submission to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources   6 options to develop internal and external dispute resolution requirements for digital 
platforms, and has called on industry to develop voluntary internal dispute resolution 
standards as a first step.4 The ACCC welcomes the consideration of dispute resolution 
mechanisms, and considers that effective mechanisms will be crucial to providing avenues 
for consumers to resolve problems.   
Additionally, the new  digital competition regime would impose targeted obligations 
addressing specific types of anti -competitive conduct.  For example, existing large 
technology firms typically have superior access to critical inputs required to develop 
foundation models including access to vast datasets, long development lead times, 
sophisticated AI systems and talent, and substantial ongoing computing costs . These 
features of the AI supply chain can contribute to smaller firms depending  on these larger 
firms for access to their founda tion models . This has  raised concerns with other 
competition regulators that a small number of the largest technology firms  with market 
power in existing digital markets  ‘could profoundly shape the development of foundation 
model -related markets to the detriment of fair, open and effective competition’ .5 The new 
competition regime could  include obligations preventing firms leveraging their dominance in 
digital platform services to  related  markets , such as AI , which would otherwise stymie 
choice and innovation.  
The ACCC’s recommendations are also intended to be principles -based and adaptable 
enough to provide flexibility to address competition issues for emerging and future 
technologies, which could include AI services if significant competition issues arise . 
Addressing scams on digital platforms  
The Government has also committed to introducing mandatory industry scams codes for 
digital platform services through the Scams Prevention Framework, which would be 
introduced via an amendment to the  CCA . The Treasury released an exposure draft bill  to 
implement this framework for consultation between 13 September and 4 October 2024. The 
Government plans to have the Bill tabled in Parliament this year.  
The Scams Prevention  Framework would strengthen the work of the National Anti -Scam 
Centre (NASC), which is part of the ACCC and was established in July 2023. The NASC 
combines the expertise of Government and the private sector to disrupt scams and shares 
intelligence across Gov ernment and authorised industry participants to interrupt scams in 
real time. It also raises consumer awareness on the risk of scams and how to avoid them.  
Under the  Scams Prevention  Framework, the Treasury Minister intends to designate banks, 
telecommunication providers, and digital platform services (initially social media, paid 
search engine advertising , and direct messaging services) – as each represent significant 
vectors of scam activity. This  framework includes a mechanism enabling expansion to other 
sectors as scammers shift their activity to target consumers through other channels.  
The Scams Prevention F ramework would also require designated entities to participate in an 
external dispute resolution (EDR) scheme, and the Government intends that the Australian 
Financial Complaints Authority will operate a single EDR scheme for designated banks, 
telecommunications provider s and digital platform services.  
While the guardrails outlined in the Proposal Paper may mitigate some of the potential scam 
risks in high -risk AI services, it may also be appropriate  in the future  for high -risk AI services 
to be designat ed under the  Scams Prevention  Framework ’s digital platform services code .

regulatory or Government response to address the risks associated with AI should start by 
considering  the extent to which Australia’s existing regulatory frameworks provide 
appropriate safeguards. The submission also noted that where gaps are identified, the 
Government should consider how existing frameworks may be strengthened and enhanced 
(including thr ough existing regulatory reform proposals).

Executive summary  
Accenture appreciates the opportunity to provide a submission on the Proposals paper 
for introducing mandatory guardrails for artificial intelligence ( AI) in high -risk settings.  
 
The world is arriving at what might be technology’s biggest inflection point in history, 
and governments and industry are at the heart of shaping how we move forward. AI, 
particularly generative AI ( ‘gen AI’), has the profound potential to unlock economic value, 
and accelerate government and industry toward a new performance frontier.  
 
However, this potential must be balanced with a focus on mitigating risks and 
unintended consequences of AI , to engender  trust and improved outcomes needed to 
realise the economic advantages . As a global industry leader in AI systems, Accenture 
has worked with many governments and businesses to transform their organisations 
through the adoption of AI technologies, and ensure the appropriate governance and 
frameworks exist to responsibly manage AI risks and opportunities.  
 
At Accenture, we define “responsible AI” as the practice of designing, building and 
deploying AI in a manner that intentionally considers the potential impact on users , 
stakeholders,  and society , while also ensuring  AI systems are tested and monitored to 
optimise performance and reliability – allowing organisations to scale AI with confidence.  
 
By implementing clear guardrails  to use AI responsibly , the Government  will help all 
organisations better prepare to manage risk . AI regulation does not need to be perceived 
as a barrier to innovation. Businesses are empowered to make decisions around AI 
adoption and implementation when there is c larity around government regulation, 
expectations and measures that should be implemented around AI technology . 
Ultimately, these measure s protect Australian businesses and their  customers and  
reassure the  Australian public , which is increasingl y calling for caution  around the 
technology’s use .  
 
The regulatory approach need s to be  flexible  and consistent, but most importantly 
supported by practical guidance  and tools  for compliance.  Given the breadth of 
questions posed in the Department of Industry, Science and Resource’s proposal s paper, 
our submission focuses on addressing questions 1, 3, 6, 8, 10, 12, 13, 15 and 16 and 
provid es recommendations for the Department to consider as it progresses the 
development of regulations for the use of AI in high -risk settings.

Section A: Defining high -risk AI  
 
 
Question 1: Do the proposed principles  adequately capture high -risk AI?  
Questio n 3: Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty  
on high -risk AI settings and high -risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of 
illustrative uses, needed?  
Question 6: Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models ? 
 
Accenture is broadly supportive of the risk -based approach to defining high -risk AI usage 
and the principles listed in the proposals paper, which can flexibly adapt to emerging AI 
risks.  
 
Recommendation 1: Guidance on risk classification : For improved clarity and 
consistency of application, Accenture  recommend s a mechanism for obtaining 
additional guidance on risk classification . For example, a list of illustrative uses and 
examples, maintained by an AI Safety Institute, with the list developed and updated in 
consultation with regulators and with consideration of list -based definitions used 
internationally.   
 
Accenture supports the application of the guardrails to all general -purpose  AI (GPAI ) 
models . Effective risk mitigation has dependencies on foreseeability, explainability and 
transparency . With ‘black box’ GPAI models, risks may be unforeseeable to developers 
and explainability may not be available to deployers  as some of the challenges with black 
box models include difficulties in tracing the reasoning behind outputs and debugging. 
This lack of explainability can stop users from fully trusting system outputs.

Section B : Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of AI  
 
 
 
Question 8: Do the proposed mandatory guardrails  appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in 
high -risk settings?  
Question 10: Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply 
chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately? For example, are the requirements assigned to

Mandatory g uardrails 1 -2 (accountability)  
 
1. Establish, implement,  and publish an accountability process including governance, 
internal capability,  and a strategy for regulatory compliance . 
2. Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks . 
 
Accenture agrees with the need for greater accountability, risk management processes, 
and governance frameworks for compliance, and is broadly supportive of the proposed 
mandatory guardrails 1 -2. Appropriate AI governance and risk management is a core 
foun dation, and bare minimum requirement for responsible AI.  
 
In our experience, Australian organisations that are building the foundations for their AI 
journey are typically seeking help with responsible AI governance, including the 
development of AI principles, policies, processes, operating models, and risk assessment 
frameworks. Th e more mature AI users in Australia tend to already have AI principles and 
risk review processes, and their priority is to effectively operationalise principles into 
practices with systemic risk assessment, testing and monitoring technol ogy solutions.  
 
Mandatory guardrails 3-4 (testing)  
 
3. Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the 
system once deployed.  
4. Protect AI systems, and implement data governance measures to manage data 
quality and provenance.  
 
Accenture is broadly supportive of the proposed guardrails 3 -4. We agree that AI system 
security and good data governance practices are critical to safe and effective AI, and 
that AI system testing and monitoring, with consideration of the use case context  is key 
to identifying and managing risk.  
 
Many  Australian organisations already appreciate the need for cybersecurity and data 
privacy practices, however , there is still a need to advance maturity, particularly to 
achieve readiness for AI. Testing and monitoring are important for both developers and 
deployers, and it requires some AI/ machine learning ( ML) and data science capabilities 
to execute effectively .

Mandatory guardrails 5 -10 (transparency)  
 
5. Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human

7. Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or

guardrails . 
 
Accenture is supportive of the proposed guardrails 5 -10 relat ing to human oversight, 
transparency, user empowerment, record keeping and conformity assessments. These 
practices will help to maintain human -centred AI, empower users to understand and 
challenge how AI impacts their lives, and improve knowledge sharing across domains , 
regulators, global research networks, and the AI value chain to optimis e risk 
management effectiveness.  
 
Accenture supports the application of all guardrails to both developers and deployers, as 
the guardrails can be adapted to suit the role of the entity, there should be consistency 
across the value chain, and risks need to be both assessed and tested during  AI system 
development and within the use case context of deployment.  
 
Improved clarity on the  definitions and  practices of developers is welcomed, in addition 
to improved guidance on what risk mitigation practices  is expected  of developers . This 
could includ e practices the deployers could rely upon to reduce their own risk mitigation 
effort, for example, the issuing of a model card that show s details of the developer ’s 
testing and suitability of the model for identified use cases .

 3 INTRODUCTION  These submissions are made in response to the Government’s paper entitled ‘Safe and Responsible AI in Australia: Proposal Paper for Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-Risk Settings’ (the ‘AI Proposal’) dated September 2024.1 The Government is to be commended for taking the initiative in seeking to regulate AI to ensure that is safe and ultimately benefits individual citizens and society more generally, because as the Government observes, AI is already ‘permeating institutions, infrastructure, products and services’.2 Before addressing the Government’s specific questions on AI, this submission first addresses the a priori questions as to: 1. what a government’s goals should be in regulating AI;  2. how governments should conceptualise AI for the purpose of determining the regulatory challenges associated with its use and the appropriate regulatory response; and  3. the regulatory significance of the fact that AI operates at scale.  The purpose of this preliminary discussion is to aid the Government in identifying and tackling the regulatory challenges associated with the use of AI in an effective and comprehensive way.  1.1 Purpose of regulating AI  As the Government notes in the AI Proposal, each successive wave of technology raises difficult questions as to whether and how it should be regulated to ensure that society reaps the benefit of the technology whilst also minimising or avoiding both potential known and unknown risks associated with its use. Given these shifting sands, in addressing these questions, it is useful to adopt a high-level framework derived from the work of Roger Brownsword.3 Brownsword identifies three ideal regulatory responsibilities that can be used ‘to assess the fitness of the regulatory environment’4 and  1 Australian Government Department of Industry, Science and Resources, Proposals Paper for Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-Risk Settings (Commonwealth of Australia, September 2024). 2 Ibid 2. 3 Roger Brownsword, Law, Technology and Society: Re-Imagining the Regulatory Environment (Routledge, 2019). 4 Ibid chapter 4. Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024  
 4 which this submission argues can be used to guide the Government’s response to AI. These three responsibilities are developing regulations that:  1. ensures that the ‘preconditions (the commons) for any form of human social existence, for any kind of human community, are maintained and protected’;5 2. articulates and respects the ‘distinctive fundamental values of the community’6 such as the focus on human dignity in the EU or the proposed focus on human rights in the AI Proposal; and 3. maintains an acceptable balance between ‘the legitimate (but potentially competing and conflicting) interests of members of the community’.7 This includes maintaining ‘for example, an acceptable balance between the interest in innovation and technological progress and the interests in human health and safety, protection of the environment, preservation of employment options, and so on’.8 The articulation of these responsibilities as the ideal objectives for the regulation of new technology is significant because it suggests that, while there are some highly useful elements in the AI Proposal, the Government’s objectives are unduly narrow. They are unduly narrow firstly, because rather than privileging the preconditions for the commons necessary for human existence, although there is some concern for this issue in relation to the threats AI poses to democracy more generally,9 the AI Proposal Paper tends to focus predominantly on the economic benefits that may potentially be derived from the use of AI through the promotion of trust in it. In so doing, it fails to appropriately prioritise broader goals of not merely ensuring net economic benefits, but ensuring the appropriate distribution of those benefits and avoiding irreparable social harm.  Secondly, rather than articulating the distinctively Australian values, such as, for example, a ‘fair go for all’ that ought to be respected by any individual or entity designing, developing or deploying AI in Australia, the AI Proposal suggests merely that an AI system will be classified as a high-risk one having regard, amongst other things, to an individual’s ‘rights recognised in Australian human rights  5 Ibid 30. 6 Ibid. 7 Ibid. 8 Ibid. 9 Australian Government Department of Industry, Science and Resources (n 1) 23–5. Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024  
 5 law’.10 As the AI Proposal itself notes11 and as discussed further below,12 these rights are very limited. They do not, therefore, appropriately reflect Australian values of, for example, respect for human dignity or fairness and do not provide the desired certainty and clarity for those designing, developing and deploying AI in Australia by clearly delineating what lines must not be crossed. Further, the utilitarian flavour of some aspects of the AI Proposal suggests that the Government does not view itself as playing an important role in protecting Australian society and its citizens from harms caused by AI. Rather, it suggests that almost anything could be traded away as a result of the use of AI, such as the human dignity of older persons who may not be able to navigate an increasingly complex digital environment, provided the perceived economic benefits flowing from the use of AI outweighed these perceived – and often intangible - costs.  Finally, the AI Proposal is unduly narrow because it does not identify all of the relevant stakeholders in what this submission calls the ‘AI Project’. While it clearly identifies AI designers, developers and deployers as having a clear interest in AI regulation, it has not identified all those interested in it, including those whose industries or livelihoods might be impacted by AI. This is a concern for two reasons. Firstly, it means that the Government has not taken into account in its proposal the disruption that AI may cause to other parts of society, such as the disruption it is currently causing to the educational sector. Secondly, it means that the Government has not taken into account the distribution of both the benefits and detriments of AI. This includes the distribution of, for example: • any detrimental unemployment that may be caused by AI as software replaces jobs; and  • the economic benefits of AI, which, because of the economies of scale and Australia’s position in the AI lifecycle, may lead to the concentration of AI-generated economic value in only a small handful of potentially overseas individuals or firms.  Finally, the AI Proposal is unduly narrow because it does not recognise that the Government’s first order priority ought to be promoting fair and just AI. Rather, it appears that the Government has privileged the interests of designers, developers and deployers by designating regulatory clarity and certainty as the first priority for regulation. While regulatory clarity and certainty are desirable –  10 Ibid 19. 11 Ibid 20. 12 Section 2, qn 1 below. Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024  
 6 particularly for those who seek to promote AI – they should be seen as second-order priorities. This is because those who seek to disrupt the status quo in unknown ways with unknown consequences should not expect the Government to provide regulatory certainty. Rather, they should expect the Government to respond to their actions and hold them accountable when it becomes known that the AI caused disruption has resulted in outcomes that are neither fair nor just and may be potentially harmful.  A new regulatory bargain If the Government wants to ensure safe, responsible and fair AI, it should attend to all of these matters. More specifically, the Government should  approach the regulation of AI as a new regulatory bargain between AI technologists and society in which AI technologists will be permitted to experiment with new forms of AI and their impact on individuals and society more broadly, but only to the extent that AI technologists: • do so in a way that respects human dignity, Australian values and Australian society; and  • engage positively, openly and in good faith with an AI regulator and the Australian Government more broadly.  As part of that bargain, the Government should.  1. to the extent it can, clearly articulate what good AI looks like, beyond the motherhoods statements in the Government’s AI ethics framework,13 and require compliance of all AI systems with those principles; and 2. include two new pillars in the Australian Government’s approach that focus on: (a) positioning the Government as the promoter of responsible and fair AI, the protector of Australian citizens and society more generally; and  (b) ensuring the fair distribution of both the benefits and risks associated with the use of AI amongst all stakeholders.   13 ‘Australia’s AI Ethics Framework: Consultation’, Department of Industry, Science and Resources (Web Page, 22 June 2021) <https://consult.industry.gov.au/australias-ai-ethics-framework>.
