 7 1.2 The nature of AI This submission argues that for the purpose of regulatory analysis, it is important not only to define AI but also to conceptualise what is involved when AI is released into what developers sometimes call ‘the wild’ - by which they, in effect, mean human society. In conceptualising AI in this way, this submission recommends that the Government avoids conceptualising AI narrowly, as merely a particular form of software. Rather, it recommends that the Government conceptualise AI as socio-technical systems consisting of both a ‘product’ aspect (the AI software itself) and a series of social practices associated with both its production and use.  To some extent, the AI Proposal has conceptualised AI in this way by observing that the AI development process is complex14 and involves multiple individuals and entities who may participate as part of an AI lifecycle.15 This focus on the broader development process and the AI development chain is welcome, as is the very clear language used to describe each player in that lifecycle, especially when compared to that adopted in the AI Act 2024 (EU) (‘AI Act (EU)’).16 While the Government is to be commended for this analysis, its approach is nonetheless too narrow.  1.2.1 The implications of identifying AI as goal focused  The Government’s conceptualisation of AI is too narrow, firstly, because it fails to distinguish the different kinds of objectives that may be associated with AI’s character as software. The Government correctly identifies that all AI systems adopt technical objectives that are used as a key performance measure within an AI system.17 Just as importantly, if not more importantly, there are also likely to be broader objectives for the system as a whole, such as how to cure cancer by finding a new drug, how to monetise the AI system through the optimisation of user’s clicks, or how to kill a human through the use of automated drones. These broader objectives become operationalised into the AI system itself. Whilst they are not necessarily relevant to the question of whether or not the AI system  14 Australian Government Department of Industry, Science and Resources (n 1) 10. 15 Ibid 302. 16 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 Laying Down Harmonised Rules on Artificial Intelligence and Amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) [2024] OJ L 1/144 (‘AI Act (EU)’). 17 Australian Government Department of Industry, Science and Resources (n 1) 8 (definition of ‘Artificial Intelligence System’), 38. Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024  
 8 properly functions, they are highly relevant to the question of regulation because it is these broader objectives that determine both: • the more technical objectives of the AI system; and  • the degree to which AI systems are likely to be compatible with Australian values.  As a result, if Australia wants trustworthy AI, its regulation needs to pay attention to whose objectives are being served by AI in both the technical system objectives and the broader organisational objectives of those designing, developing or deploying.  This focus on broad objectives is particularly important for AI used in the generation or distribution of information – given the effect this has on human emotions and cognition and, therefore, on society as a whole - and in the emerging area of agentic AI. This is because, in those AI systems, there may be clear conflicts between the broader objectives of the AI system itself and those of the users. While a user might be looking for accurate and relevant content or an AI system that acts on their behalf in their own interest, the AI system may privilege the interests of shareholders by ensuring the AI system optimising a user’s attention for clicks or, in the case of agentic AI, directing the user to recommended products or services that may provide a benefit for the AI system’s owners, but may not necessarily be in the best interest of the user. Given this, the Government needs to: • treat AI systems that act on another’s behalf by retrieving information or be performing tasks as ones that are prima facie high risk; and  • include, as a fundamental AI Guardrail, one that provides clear direction to AI designers, developers and deployers that these kinds of conflicts of interest should include, at a minimum, clear disclosure of the AI’s commercial objective to any users. Ideally, however, this AI Guardrail should require AI designers, developers and deployers to resolve these conflicts in the users’ favour. In other words, the Government should require AI that is loyal to its users.18   18 Anthony Aguirre et al, ‘AI Loyalty: A New Paradigm for Aligning Stakeholder Interests’ (2020) 1(3) IEEE Transactions on Technology and Society 128 (‘AI Loyalty’); Anthony Aguirre et al, ‘AI Loyalty by Design: A Framework for Governance of AI’ in Oxford Handbook on AI Governance (Oxford University Press, 2023).  9 1.2.2 The implications of the practices of production  The Government’s approach to AI regulation is too narrow secondly because while the Government has some conceptualisation of AI being the product of an AI lifecycle, it does not take into account that all AI lifecycles may not be equal and some are more likely than others to develop AI systems that are consistent with Australian values. In other words, the Government’s approach fails to take into account the practices associated with the production of AI systems – who is involved and why - that are relevant to the types of AI likely to be designed, developed or deployed in Australia. For example, researchers in AI who are interested in a cure for cancer who operate within a university or other not-for-profit entity are likely to produce a very different kind of AI to AI researchers who are seeking to monetise AI intended to generate or distribute content by selling, for example, a user’s attention. Further, researchers operating in such different contexts are likely to be motivated by different incentives and subscribe to different values. These different incentives and values are, in turn, likely to be ultimately embedded in an AI system itself, including, but not limited to, the objectives discussed above. Further, depending on the context in which an AI system was produced, these values and incentives may or may not be consistent with Australian values of, for example, fairness.  Given this, if Australia wants trustworthy AI, the regulation needs to focus not only on the contexts or purpose for which AI is used. It also needs to focus on the practices of production of AI, recognising that only some practices of production are, therefore, welcome because they are likely to produce AI systems that reflect and embed values and practices that are consistent with Australian values. Others are likely to produce AI systems that do not, for example, respect human autonomy or dignity and ought not to be welcome in Australia.  1.2.3 The implications of the practices of AI’s use  The Government’s approach to AI regulation is too narrow, finally, because it fails to take into account that AI systems are not merely products of the social practices surrounding its design, development and deployment. They also produce social practices arising from use. These may be, for example, by: • replacing some workers;  Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024  
 10 • further encouraging a ‘digital first’ world and a permanent shift towards human-computer interactions rather than human-human ones - raising important questions not just about discrimination but about accessibility, inclusion and respect for those who may be compelled to deal with AI with little digital capability; or  • as the Government acknowledges, polarising society into distinct information bubbles with harmful effects on democracy and social cohesion.19  Given this, if Australia wants trustworthy AI, the AI Guardrails need to focus not just on the contexts of use but on the manner of use and the way it affects individuals and societies more broadly. As discussed below, some of these uses are undesirable and should be banned. 1.3 AI’s operation at scale, the new calculus of risk and the implications of a precautionary approach  One last aspect of the conceptualisation of AI that is vital to take into account is the ability of AI systems to operate at scale. Given this, the Government is to be commended for noting that the ability of an AI system to operate at scale has regulatory significance.20 It is vital, however, that the Government understand the regulatory implications of this fact. This is because the ability of AI to operate at scale creates not just a quantitative difference, but a qualitative difference associated with the risk of regulatory failure. As the Government observes, rather than that regulatory failure potentially only affecting a small number of users, the use of AI may have wide ranging detrimental societal effects. In the nomenclature of this submission, the use of AI, in fact, creates a new ‘calculus of risk’ relating to a failure of the regulatory model to prevent legal service providers from acting appropriately. This new calculus of risk is important firstly, because it means that it is not sufficient for the regulation to ensure that most AI systems are designed, developed and deployed appropriately. It is vital that all AI systems, especially those in high-risk categories, are designed, developed and deployed appropriately. This is because a single failure of even a single service provider to use AI appropriately may play out at scale. This new calculus of risk is important, secondly, because it has implications as  19 Australian Government Department of Industry, Science and Resources (n 1) 24. 20 Ibid 23. Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024  
 11 to what kind of regulatory strategy ought to be adopted. More specifically, as the AI Proposal welcomingly observes,21 the scale of AI implies a need for a precautionary approach where the focus is on preventing ex-ante harm rather than seeking to remediate ex post facto potentially irreparable harms to the citizens or the social fabric of society more broadly. This new calculus of risks is important thirdly, because it implies a need for a regulatory oversight model that includes an active regulator who can move quickly and proactively to prevent harms arising at scale. As a result, ideally, the Government’s regulatory model for AI should include an AI statutory regulator that is empowered to act proactively to exercise regulatory oversight of those that participate in the design, deployment and development of AI systems, including the design, development and deployment of high-risk AI systems. That statutory regulator should also be involved in a constant dialogue with AI stakeholders, including those that design, develop and deploy AI and those affected by its use, to help crystallise the risks involved in the use of AI - enabling them to become known risks and for the risk level of AI to be lowered22 - and to ensure that AI used in Australia upholds Australian values.  2 Response to Questions for Consultation With the above conceptual framework in mind, this submission now provides its response to the AI Proposal Paper’s questions.  Question 1: Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI? The proposed principles are a useful starting point for identifying high-risk AI. They are problematic, however, for three reasons.  1.1 Incomplete Regulating for the unknown  Firstly, the proposed principles are incomplete as they are written on the assumption that the risks arising from the use of AI can be known at the outset. One of the regulatory challenges with AI is that it is unclear at the outset what the potential issues and risks are associated with a particular form of AI, with a particular use of AI, or with particular social practices generated by AI’s use – such as  21 Ibid 16. 22 See the response to question 1 below. Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024  
 12 the polarisation of society. Given the new calculus of risk with the use of AI,23 this means that prima facie, any new form of AI, new use of AI, or new social practices associated with AI should be treated as high risk unless and until they can be demonstrated by those promoting its use that it is safe. This is essential to preventing harm arising before it arises – potentially at scale. Accordingly, the first principle that ought to be adopted to determine whether an AI system is high-risk, is how novel the AI system is, how novel the business model associated with the AI system is and the degree to which the impact of its use is known. Where the AI system or its business model is novel, and its impact is unknown, it should be treated as an AI system that is high-risk.  Regulating for the known propensities of different production environments Secondly, the principles are also incomplete because they ignore the fact that who is producing the AI system and the purpose of that production is a factor that impacts the degree of risk associated with its use. More specifically, as noted above,24 an AI system that is the product of a university research team designed to support a not-for-profit cure for cancer is likely to be a less risky form of AI than an AI that is designed to support a two-sided market that captures a user’s attention in order to sell it or to monetise their behavioural data.25 Accordingly, the proposed principles should include as a risk factor, one that focuses on the context and practices associated with the production of AI, not merely its use, and classify AI systems as potentially high-risk systems where the need to profit from AI may create a conflict with the interests of Australian users or society more broadly.  Ensuring accuracy as a goal  The principles are also incomplete because they fail to identify, as a risk factor, uses of  AI where accuracy is particularly important. Rather, through its focus on human rights, the principles tends to focus on discriminatory uses of AI. While it is important to ensure that AI does not amplify existing discrimination, discrimination is merely one manifestation of inaccuracy of AI. That is, an AI system that makes a recommendation about the likely rate of recidivism based on a factor such as gender or race that has no bearing on the likely rate of recidivism is not only discriminatory: at its simplest, it  23 See [1.3] above. 24 See [1.2] above. 25 ACCC, Digital Platforms Inquiry: Final Report:Executive Summary (Government Report No Executive Summary, ACCC, June 2019) 1, ch 2 <https://www.accc.gov.au/publications/digital-platforms-inquiry-final-report> (‘Digital Platforms Inquiry’). Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024  
 13 is one that is inaccurate. It may be similarly inaccurate if it finds, for example, a correlation in the data between recidivism and the colour of someone’s shoes, which has no real predictive power. While in many cases, it might be possible to tie this kind of inaccuracy back to a protected attribute (shoe colour might perhaps be an indicator of gender or race), it may not be possible in all cases. This is important because if an AI system produces an output that would significantly impact a person’s life, all inaccuracies are important, not just those that reflect broader discrimination in the society itself. Accordingly, the principles should include, as one indicia of a high-risk AI system, that an AI system will be used in a context where the accuracy of the system is important and inaccurate output of an AI system is likely to have a significant impact on individuals or society more generally.  Disruption  The principles should also take into account the impact of AI, including the degree of disruption it causes to existing industries. This is essential to ensure that, over time, an appropriate balance can be developed between the interests of all stakeholders.  1.2 The expression of the principles problematic The principles are not only incomplete. In some instances, the expressions of the principles are too narrow.  Principle (a) - human rights  The identification of human rights as one of the yardsticks by which to measure the likely risk of AI is valuable and is supported by this submission. Because Australian human rights are notoriously limited, the limitation of the proposed principles to adverse impacts on an individual’s human rights recognised in Australian human rights renders this principle overly weak. In effect, it gives a green light to AI designers, developers and deployers to ignore Australians’ human rights because they are not well-protected by Australian law. To remedy this, the AI regulation should, at a minimum, clearly articulate the Australian digital rights charter. Ideally, however, the Government ought to ensure that Australian human rights are protected by law more broadly.  Principle (c) - legal effect  The identification of adverse legal effects is useful, but again, it is too narrow. The limitation that the consequence of use has some legal effect raises difficult questions about what this means. Is the Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024  
 14 refusal to allocate a rental property to an applicant based on erroneous assumptions about their ability to pay an adverse legal effect, given that the rental applicants were seeking legal rights to rent the property but had no right to do so? Because of the impact that this type of use might have on individuals, this type of use of AI ought to be covered as a high-risk use of AI, but it is not clearly covered in this principle. The position is not remedied by the addition of the words similarly significant effects on an individual26 which are too vague. To cover this challenge, this risk should be written to identify not only AI’s potential to have legal consequences – whatever that might mean -  but its allocative and distributional function – such as in determining who gets to rent a house or receive priority for medical treatment. It should, therefore, include, as a high-risk form of AI, any AI system used to allocate or distribute resources to individuals or social groups that are necessary to participate with human dignity in modern social life.  Principle (e) - societal impact The approach to societal impact is also too narrow. The problem with this principle is one of priority. The risk of adverse impacts that operate on a societal level seems to suggest, through the ordering of the risks within the existing principle, that economic impacts are the most significant. Because the economy is merely one part of Australian society, this principle should be reordered to prioritise those aspects of Australia’s social infrastructure necessary for social life. It should, therefore, read: “The risk of adverse broader impacts to Australian society, the environment and the rule of law that sustains it, and the Australian economy which primarily attends to the distribution of goods and services.” Principle (f) - severity Given the submission above that it might not be clear at the outset what the likely risks are of the use of an AI system, this principle should be rewritten to include a caveat that this principle is relevant to the extent the risks are known. It should, therefore, read as follows: The severity and extent of those adverse impacts outlined in principles (a) to (e) above – to the extent they are, in fact, known.   26 Australian Government Department of Industry, Science and Resources (n 1) 19. If so, how should we define these?  Yes. There are high-risk practices in the use of AI systems. Question 5: Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?  For the reasons discussed above, to adopt a precautionary approach, all novel forms and uses of AI should presumptively be treated as high-risk uses unless and until those that propose to design, deploy or develop such AI systems can demonstrate that their use is consistent with the objectives of technological regulation discussed above. Under this principle, GPAI would necessarily be captured as a high-risk AI. Similarly, when agentic AI emerges ‘in the wild,’ it will also be captured as a high-risk AI unless and until it can be demonstrated to be a low-risk use.  Further, designers, deployers and developers of AI systems should be aware that even those uses of AI that initially seem low-risk, or have become accepted as low-risk AI, may nonetheless reveal themselves to be high-risk uses over time. As discussed above, designers, deployers and developers should, therefore, understand that they are involved in a new AI regulatory bargain in which: • they only have social license to use AI while it is clear that the use is, in fact, a low-risk use or the risks have become known and are considered acceptable by the legislature or regulator; and • they may need to alter their AI system ex post facto, alter their associated practices of production or even roll back or remove the reliance on AI30 to protect Australians and Australian society.   29 AI Act (EU) (n 16). 30 See, eg, s 17 in Canada’s Artificial Intelligence and Data Bill 2022 (Canada) contained in Bill C-27 An Act to Enact the Consumer Privacy Protection Act, the Personal Information and Data Protection Tribunal Act and the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act and to Make Consequential and Related Amendments to Other Acts 2021-22 (Canada). These guardrails should also include not just guardrails associated with the production and management of such AI systems but should include requirements for accuracy on matters for which there is an objective measure of accuracy and which are likely to affect humans. Question 8 Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings? Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?  No. The proposed mandatory guardrails are predominantly procedural and could easily be satisfied by an internal compliance system, which may not necessarily produce the kinds of AI systems that ought to be accepted within Australia. The guardrails also fail to set the standard for appropriate AI to clearly signal to the regulatee just what is acceptable AI. There is also a risk that Guardrail 5, enabling human control, will simply create a potential human scapegoat for defective AI that is a product of a collaborative effort. It also assumes that humans are not subject to the well-known problems of AI bias and automation complacency. Guardrail 6, informing users about only the use of AI in decision-making or the generation of content, is too limited. Users do not need merely knowledge about the use of AI. They need power – including the power to opt-out. There is also a need to ensure that automated decision-making is only used in appropriate contexts. For example, although it may be efficient, it may not be appropriate to use to determine, for example, the care plan for the elderly. Guardrail 7 is useful but does not address the likely inherent power imbalance between AI users and AI systems.  To remedy these deficiencies, the Guardrails should include: 1. an Australian digital rights charter that protects Australians and Australian society and clarifies for designers, developers and deployers what are the design criteria for acceptable AI;  2. a requirement for designers, developers and deployers of AI to not only be ‘AI literate’,31 but to understand their legal obligations under Australian law, including the Australian digital rights   31 AI Act (EU) (n 16) (art 3 (definition of ‘AI literacy’, para 56), art 4). Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024  
 19 charter and what constitutes ethical AI according to Australian standards. In other words, ethical awareness – or ‘ethical and legal literacy’ - is required in addition to technical competence and legal compliance; 3. a requirement for AI organisations that employ designers, developers and deployers to create an ethical infrastructure that ensures that everyone with an impact on the design, development or deployment of the AI system is aware of the Australian legal and ethical obligations in relation to AI, including the Australian digital rights charter. This should be accompanied by an appropriate whistleblower scheme to ensure that problems with AI can be identified early and prevented;  4. a requirement to notify the AI regulator of the use of AI in Australia;  5. mechanisms to ensure that any AI organisation that designs, develops or deploys to be used in Australia has a presence in Australia and is answerable, in a meaningful way, to Australian regulators and courts;  6. an AI compliance officer responsible for the AI system as a whole and for liaising with the regulator, alerting them to problems where necessary - with penalties for both the entity and individual for any failures;  7. a right for Australians to be informed about any use of AI, including AI enabled decisions;  8. a right to opt-out of AI enabled decision-making;  9. a requirement that where AI enabled decision-making is employed, the onus of proof is reversed if a person impacted by an AI system challenges its use or outcome. This should be seen as an acceptable trade-off as part of the new AI regulatory bargain for those advocating the use of opaque systems to make decisions affecting humans. That is, if AI technologists advocate AI’s use, they should bear the risks associated with its use and should therefore bear the onus of proving that its output is accurate and non-discriminatory;  10. exposure to appropriate remedies for harm caused by AI’s use, enforceable not only by an appropriate regulator but by individuals and groups;  11. a requirement for those participating in the AI supply chain to hold appropriate insurance to cover potential harms;  Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024

Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately? For example, are the requirements assigned to developers and deployers appropriate?  It is not clear from the AI Proposal how the responsibilities are assigned. It is also not clear from the paper what penalties might apply for any breaches of the responsibilities or whether individuals or groups will have access to appropriate remedies.  Question 11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI? How could we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for example low-risk and high-risk GPAI models?  No. There is nothing in the guardrails that requires GPAI to be accurate when it is asked questions of fact or that have a degree of objective truth to them. While the whole society bears the risks associated with the use of GPAI, there is also nothing in the guardrails that ensures that society will reap the benefits. Nor is there any obligation on those who benefit from GPAI to assist individuals and industries to adapt to the new environment through, for example, unemployment schemes or improved fraud detection. Further, in the current state of knowledge in relation to GPAI, there are no low-risk GPAI models. This is because it is only once we understand what they will be used for, how they will be monetised and how they impact human behaviour that GPAI can be classified as low risk – assuming that evidence ultimately suggests it is appropriate to do so. Accordingly, different guardrails are not yet required for low-risk GPAI.   32 See, eg, s 17 in Canada’s Artificial Intelligence and Data Bill 2022 (Canada) contained in Bill C-27 An Act to Enact the Consumer Privacy Protection Act, the Personal Information and Data Protection Tribunal Act and the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act and to Make Consequential and Related Amendments to Other Acts 2021-22 (Canada). No. Significant and influential AI systems could be designed, delivered and deployed by a small to medium business. X, formerly known as Twitter, was, after all, created by what, on one measure, was a small business at the time of its launch. Given this, and the importance in a precautionary approach of designing AI systems appropriately before they become entrenched in society, at this stage, there should be no exemptions for small-to-medium businesses.  Question 13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings? What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach?  This submission supports a whole of economy approach – which this submission suggests should be re-conceptualised as a ‘whole of society’ approach given that the economy is but one part of society - supported by a robust and proactive AI regulator. AI poses a new problem, is likely to have far reaching and transformational consequences, and requires, therefore, both its own legislation and a new AI regulator to oversee it. This approach will also provide greater clarity and certainty than the diffuseness of a domain specific approach.  While this submission recommends a whole of society (ie economy) approach, it also recommends that the domain specific legislation be reviewed at both federal and state levels to ensure that the regulatory strategies adopted in this other legislation are still appropriate to apply to the diffuse production environment associated with the AI lifecycle. This may not be the case where, for example: • the legislation relies on a licensing scheme to license human agents or advisers (lawyers, financial advisers, real estate agents) and the activities of those human agents are eventually replaced by AI. In these cases, there may be a regulatory gap if the existing legislation does not apply to the corresponding services provided by AI; or  • the legislation allocates responsibility to a specific human, such as a human driver. In this case, there may be a misallocation of responsibility once some tasks are performed by AI. Submissions: AI Proposal Paper Author: Jane Hogan Date: 4 October 2024

This will best be achieved by a whole of society (ie economy) approach which: 1. adopts a flexible definition of high-risk AI that presumptively treats any step-changes in technology as a form of high-risk AI;  2. creates a proactive AI regulator who can scan the AI landscape and respond as required; and  3. obliges designers, developers and deployers of AI systems to engage with the AI regulator in the manner outlined above. The greatest risks are: 1. a lack of a clearly articulated set of values that protects Australians and Australian society and also provides clarity for designers, developers and deployers of AI as to what constitutes acceptable experimentation on individuals and society through the introduction of new technology;  2. a lack of information about an appropriately constituted regulator and the means by which stakeholders (including AI designers, developers and deployers) can engage with the regulator; and  3. an over-emphasis on the possible economic benefits and an under-appreciation of the risks of AI, including the fact that those risks are not yet fully known.  To remedy this, an AI Act should be introduced that includes the features discussed above, including a well-resourced AI regulator. To the Department of Industry, Science and Resources,  I am an international student at the University of Melbourne. The development of Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) is a subject that deeply interests me, as the stakes involved are extremely high. AI has the capacity to bring about positive outcomes including the acceleration of medical research, potentially leading to longer, more fulﬁlling lives. However, the catastrophic consequences from AI, including possible human extinction, cannot be overlooked. Hence, I believe that ensuring the safe development of AI should be one of our highest priorities.  1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI? No While the proposed principles oKer a practical starting point, they fall short in addressing the regulation of high-risk AI systems. One potential approach is to establish a regulatory framework that classiﬁes AI systems as high-risk through technical assessments conducted at multiple stages—prior to training, before deployment, and during operation. This is crucial because AI systems can exhibit unexpected or unintended behaviors, and without thorough evaluation, these issues may go undetected until after deployment. The principle should therefore include a means to assess actual capabilities and behaviours. This approach would also reduce regulatory burden on AI systems proven not to possess dangerous capabilities.  4. Are there high-risk use cases that Government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)? Yes The government should consider banning AI systems when technical evaluations reveal the potential for critical harm or unacceptable systemic risks. For example, AI models that could facilitate the development of cyber, chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons, or those capable of self-replication, deception, and loss of control, should be urgently prohibited. This approach aligns with California’s SB1047 bill and the EU AI Act, both of which advocate for banning AI systems posing critical harm or systemic risks. Stricter legislation needs to establish an intolerable risk threshold.  5. Are the proposed principles ﬂexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)? No The proposed principles lack the ﬂexibility required to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as GPAI. To future-proof its regulations, Australia should adopt the EU AI Act’s deﬁnitions of GPAI and GPAI with systemic risks. These deﬁnitions would enable Australia to prioritize and target the regulation of systems with particularly dangerous capabilities.  6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models? No Meaningful obligations should only be imposed on GPAI models that present systemic risks. Guardrails that are proportional to the risks posed by the AI system would strike a balance between safety and innovation. The RAND report on GPAI models suggests that harmonizing reporting and evaluation standards across the USA, UK, and EU could address the unique risks posed by future models. Australia should follow this approach and enforce mandatory guardrails on GPAI with systemic risks, including AI evaluation standards, risk management practices, and incident mitigations.   7. What are suitable indicators for deﬁning GPAI models as high-risk?  Base on technical capability / other Instead of simply classifying all GPAI as high-risk, the law should use a combination of technical evaluation and expert advice to deﬁne whether a GPAI model carries signiﬁcant risk. The EU AI Act Article 51 provides a good example of this approach. We need ﬂexible, future-proof deﬁnitions that can be updated in response to evolving technological developments, such as advancements in algorithms or hardware eKiciency.   8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings? No The proposed guardrails fail to account for the varying magnitude of AI risks. AI presents a unique regulatory challenge, as it has the capacity to cause catastrophic harm, yet also has the potential to become ubiquitous. Applying a single set of guardrails to all AI systems in high-risk settings will inevitably lead to both over-regulation and under-regulation. What is needed are tailored guardrails that are proportional to the speciﬁc risks each system presents.  10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately? No The current guardrails place insuKicient obligations upon AI developers, who in fact control the majority of the risks. Both the MIT AI Risk Repository and the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) highlight that decisions made during model development are crucial for ensuring safe and responsible AI. Therefore, mandatory guardrails should focus more on obligations speciﬁc to developers of AI products intended for deployment in Australia.  11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails suPicient to address the risks of GPAI? No The proposed guardrails fail to adequately address the risks associated with the development of the most advanced AI models. Australia needs a clear deﬁnition to identify AI models that could exhibit dangerous behaviors, potentially leading to widespread or catastrophic harm. Once we have a way of deﬁning these speciﬁc models, we can implement targeted guardrails to mitigate their risks during development.  13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?  A whole of economy approach - introducing a new cross-economy AI Act  An AI-speciﬁc Act targeting oKshore developers would be the most eKective way to inﬂuence the behavior of overseas AI developers. Established regulators, such as the Therapeutic Goods Administration or the Civil Aviation Safety Authority, should lead within their ﬁelds of expertise. This would allow an Australian AI Act to cover any regulatory gaps and focus on shaping the behaviour of oKshore AI developers.  Thank you for considering my submission. I look forward to seeing progress in this important area of public policy.  Sincerely, Jake

LinkedIn is pleased to contribute to the Australian Government's proposals paper on introducing 
mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings.  As a leader in fostering responsible AI development, we

also mitigating risks.

the responsible development, adoption, and use of AI.  While we align with Microsoft ’s key principles,

workforce applications of AI.  
LinkedIn’s views, which complement those of Microsoft, emphasi se the critical need to address the risks 
associated with AI  in high -risk applications.  We support the development of robust guardrails to ensure 
AI’s safe and ethical use across all sectors.  
Our recommendations offer a pathway for building trust, transparency and accountability in AI, while 
enabling Australia to fully harness AI’s transformative potential.   We welcome ongoing collaboration with 
the Australian Government and stand ready to engage in further discussions to ensure AI’s potential is

At LinkedIn, we are committed to harnessing the transformative potential of AI to create economic

At LinkedIn, our member s’ trust  is fundamental - we call it “members first ”.  Our platform is designed to

International interoperability of AI regulations: ensuring 
global alignment  
As AI technologies continue to evolve at a rapid pace, regulatory frameworks around the world must work 
cohesively to mitigate risks, especially when dealing with high -risk AI systems.  For Australia, it is 
imperative to align its AI regulatory standards with internationally recogni sed frameworks to ensure 
consistency for businesses operating on a global scale.  This alignment not only helps in harmonising 
compliance obligations but also fosters international collaboration and reduces complexity.  
A critical element in achieving this harmonisation is by adopting established frameworks like the NIST AI 
Risk Management Framework, which is widely recogni sed for its comprehensive approach to managing AI 
risks.  By aligning with existing standards such as NIST,  Australia can ensure its AI regulations remain 
practical, innovative, and interoperable.  This would not only facilitate compliance across multiple 
jurisdictions but also promote regulatory alignment, reducing the burden on businesses and encouraging 
a consistent global approach to AI governance.  
One of the key messages from international AI regulation efforts  is the importance of clear coordination 
mechanisms and defined regulatory boundaries .  By adopting valuable practices like risk -based 
regulation of AI systems and clear allocation of responsibilities along the value chain - without 
necessarily implementing a singular, overarching  law - Australia can ensure coherent enforcement and 
reduce the risk of regulatory overlap.   Drawing on these practices, Australia should consider adopting a 
model that pools expertise to support  coordinat ion with existing technology -neutral and sector -specific 
regulators.   This approach would streamline the compliance process and ensure that AI technologies are 
developed and deployed responsibly.

 Excessive or overly prescriptive AI regulation can hinder innovation, particularly for emerging AI

could place Australian businesses at a competitive disadvantage.  By focusing on the intended outcomes 
of AI regulation —such as safeguarding public safety, fairness, and transparency —while maintaining 
flexibility for technological innovation, Australia can foster a regulatory environment that promotes both 
responsible AI  development and economic growth.  
LinkedIn recommends  that the Australia government’s approach to AI regulation should be focused on a 
risk -based  approach, zeroing in scrutiny on AI systems with the highest potential for negative impact, 
such as those used in critical sectors  where impactful decisions may occur,  or involving sensitive data.  
By concentrating regulatory resources on critical areas , Australia can reduce risks associated with AI 
deployment while still allowing businesses to experiment and innovate.  Importantly, proactive guidance 
and support for AI developers, including pre -deployment consultations, can help businesses identify 
potential compliance issues early, thus promoting a robust regulatory environment that is focused on the 
right outcomes for citizens.  
Public trust is key to the successful adoption of AI technologies, and transparent, well -communicated

detailed information on regulatory expectations, offering industry -specific guidelines to help businesses

AI technologies are implemented safely and effectively across different sectors.  
Offering regulatory clarity  and risk -appropriate guardrails , particularly to smaller businesses and 
startups, is crucial for ensuring that AI innovation flourishes.  This can be achieved by providing resources 
and support to help companies of all sizes navigate the complexities of AI regulation.  In doing so, 
Australia can strike a balance between fostering technological innovation and protecting public interests, 
ensuring that AI technologies contribute to economic growth while addressing societal risks.  
Aligning Australia’s AI regulations with international standards  will ensure that the country remains 
competitive in the global AI landscape.  By focusing on key regulatory principles such as transparency,

The economic opportunity of AI in recruitment  
AI has the potential to address significant economic inefficiencies in the Australian labour market by 
overcoming barriers to entry and reducing information asymmetry.  Well -designed recruitment tools can 
enhance the recognition of candidates’ skills, increase their visibility to employers, expand their 
networking opportunities, and strengthen their bargaining power.  This is especially beneficial for 
underrepresented groups and skilled migrants - a quarter of whom, according to the OECD, are either

 over - or under -skilled for their current roles1.  Addressing Australia’s gender pay gap, currently at 19 
percent2 for comparable positions, can be effectively improved through AI, fostering greater equity and

The economic benefits of AI -driven recruitment tools are substantial both in Australia and globally. 
Research shows that by optimising the matching process between job seekers and employers, AI

inclusive, and competitive economy.  By breaking down barriers to entry, AI can reduce inequalities in the 
labour market and fully utilise Australian talent, ensuring that national productivity is maximised.  
On a global scale, the impact of AI in recruitment is equally impressive.  Research  from Oxera found that 
in 2019, AI tools in recruitment generated $168 billion in the USA, €104 billion in the EU, and £22 billion in 
the UK, contributing significantly to GDP in each region.  By minimising wage disparities and improving 
transparency in labour markets, AI promotes equitable growth and enhances productivity across sectors 
worldwide.  As seen in Australia, the right AI tools and regulatory frameworks can minimise labour market 
inefficiencies globally, fostering more inclusive economies.   In this way, AI in recruitment has the 
potential to drive economic growth, both nationally and internationally, while addressing labour market 
imbalances.  
While the advantages of AI in recruitment are substantial, it is imperative that these technologies are

essential to ensure that AI enhances, rather than compromises, fair employment practices.  
Responsible AI in Recruitment: balancing innovation with 
human judgement  
At LinkedIn, the responsible use of AI is central to our vision of creating economic opportunity for every

Our approach is anchored in a "human -in-the-loop" philosophy, where AI enriches human decision -

LinkedIn’s focus is on the earlier stages of the employment lifecycle, particularly talent sourcing.  
Sourcing involves identifying potential candidates through AI -powered tools that expand the candidate

By adhering to this approach, LinkedIn maintains a framework that prioritises transparency, fairness, and

Building upon our commitment to responsible AI, we focus on ensuring trust and mitigating risks 
throughout the entire employment lifecycle.  This approach involves addressing these considerations at 
each stage of the employment life cycle.  
Ensuring trust and reducing risks in the employment life 
cycle  
The employment lifecycle spans multiple stages —from attracting and sourcing talent at one end of the 
cycle to employee performance evaluation and termination decisions at the other end.  Each stage 
carries distinct risks, especially when AI is involved.  LinkedIn’s primary involvement is in the earlier 
stages, particularly talent attraction and talent sourcing, through products such as LinkedIn Pages and 
LinkedIn Recruiter.     
 
  6 
 In the sourcing stage, LinkedIn helps organisations expand their candidate pool using AI -powered 
discovery and engagement tools.  These tools, such as LinkedIn Recruiter and job recommendations, 
allow talent professionals to search for candidates based on skills and experience, discovering 
individuals who might otherwise be overlooked.  This helps reduce information asymmetry and enhances 
diversity by mitigating human bias (e.g., hiding names and photos during searches).  With over 67 million 
job seekers vi siting LinkedIn Jobs every week and more than 9,000 members applying for jobs every 
minute, LinkedIn’s platform demonstrates its significant role in reshaping the talent landscape.  
Importantly, sourcing differs from hiring, as sourcing focuses on expanding opportunities and reaching 
out to potential candidates, whereas hiring involves evaluating and selecting applicants.  
Sourcing and hiring are distinct processes with different levels of risk.  Sourcing primarily expands the 
talent pool by identifying potential candidates that you may ask to apply for a role and  is generally 
considered lower -risk compared to the higher -stakes hiring decision phase, where final decisions about a 
candidate’s  future employment are made.   Importantly, the sourcing process does not have a lasting or 
dispositive impact on whether a potential candidate ultimately gets hired.  
In contrast, hiring decisions - which involve evaluating candidates  and determining outcomes like job 
offers - carry inherently higher risks related to evaluation accuracy and fairness.  To address these risks, 
LinkedIn continuously refines and monitors its AI systems, ensuring that both job seekers and recruiters 
benefit from fair, transparent, and equitable tools throughout the recruitment process.  This distinction 
between sourcing and hiring helps ensure that AI supports, rather than determines, critical employment 
decisions.  
In summary, our dedication to responsible AI use, international regulatory alignment, and risk mitigation 
across the employment life cycle underpins our support for the development of balanced AI regulations 
in Australia.

unique needs and priorities.  We welcome ongoing dialogue with the government, industry stakeholders,

Submission on introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings 
 
As the CEO of Safe Work Australia, I welcome the opportunity to make a submission to 
the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR)’s public consultation on 
introducing mandatory guardrails for Artificial Intelligence (AI) in high-risk settings. 
 
Role of Safe Work Australia  
Safe Work Australia is a tripartite national WHS policy body representing the interests of 
the Commonwealth, states and territories, as well as workers and employers. We lead 
the development of national policy and strategies to improve WHS and workers' 
compensation across Australia, including developing and maintaining the model WHS 
legislative framework. The model WHS legislative framework is the model WHS Act , the 
model WHS Regulations  and model Codes of Practice. 
 
As a national policy body, Safe Work Australia is not a regulator – it does not implement 
or enforce WHS laws or administer workers’ compensation schemes. The 
Commonwealth, states and territories are responsible for making, regulating and 
enforcing WHS laws and managing workers’ compensation schemes in their respective 
jurisdictions.  
 
For the model WHS laws to become legally binding, a jurisdiction must separately 
implement them as their own laws in their jurisdiction. All jurisdictions except Victoria 
have now implemented laws based on the model WHS laws. 
 
Application of model WHS laws in the context of AI 
The model WHS laws establish a comprehensive and robust legal framework to protect 
workers and others from risks to their health and safety while at work. 
 
The model WHS laws are principles-based and require duty holders to undertake a risk 
management approach to manage risks to health and safety. Duty holders must 
eliminate risks if it is reasonably practicable to do so, or if not possible, minimise it so far 
as is reasonably practicable. Importantly, the question of what is reasonably practicable 
is determined objectively, not by reference to a particular duty holder’s capacity to pay or 
other individual circumstances.  
 
As the primary duty holder, a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) has 
a duty to ensure the health and safety of its workers and other persons at the workplace. 
PCBUs who design, manufacture, import, supply or install products or plant used at a 
workplace also have duties to ensure their product or plant is without risks to health and 
safety.

2 Phillip Law Street, New Acton ACT 2601  
GPO Box 641, Canberra ACT 2601 
www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au  
 
 Broadly, the model WHS laws accommodate the emergence of transformative 
technologies such as AI. PCBUs have a duty to manage risks arising from the 
introduction of or exposure to digital technologies such as AI. That said, the development 
and deployment of AI has and continues to result in changes to the work environment 
and work processes which have the potential to impact work health and safety. 
 
The Australian Work Health and Safety Strategy 2022-2033 recognises the rise of AI and 
other new technologies as a key emerging challenge. It is an issue Safe Work Australia, 
in collaboration with our tripartite Member organisations, continues to monitor and 
assess closely to ensure national policy and regulation continues to support work health 
and safety. Importantly, the capability of duty holders must also be developed to ensure 
they understand and meet their WHS duties and responsibilities as the digital 
transformation of workplaces takes place.  
 
Proposed AI regulation options and mandatory guardrails 
Safe Work Australia supports the intent of the proposed guardrails to reduce the 
likelihood of harms arising from AI through the regulation of businesses developing and 
deploying AI in high-risk settings. Like the model WHS laws, the guardrails are 
underpinned by a risk-based approach which seeks to place obligations on those 
involved in the supply and ongoing maintenance of AI in high-risk settings.  
 
Safe Work Australia considers there is likely to be significant crossover and/or interaction 
between the existing WHS legislative framework with each of the three regulatory 
options proposed to mandate the AI guardrails. It is important any such crossover and/or 
interaction is understood, acknowledged and considered closely before settling the 
proposed guardrails and deciding which regulatory approach will be used to mandate 
them. 
 
Explicit consideration of potential interactions between the two frameworks will help to 
prevent unintended duplication and ensure consistency in the scope and application of 
any shared or similar provisions. In turn, this will help to ensure the effective enforcement 
and compliance of both frameworks by reducing potential confusion and uncertainty for 
policymakers, regulators and duty holders alike. 
 
To the extent that any new AI legislation or regulation will contain shared or substantially 
similar provisions to those in the model WHS laws, Safe Work Australia is particularly 
keen to prevent the possibility a duty holder may have to take two different approaches 
to ensure compliance with their duties under both frameworks. Even more concerning is 
the potential for any new AI legislation or regulation to set a lower standard of work 
health and safety than already exists under WHS laws.

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
Yes, the principles adequately capture high-risk AI by focusing on societal impacts, such as human rights, health, safety, and democracy. However, some aspects could be further refined. For example, both the EU's AI Act and the US Algorithmic Accountability Act include explicit references to legal rights and the potential for discrimination, making them more comprehensive. Similarly, Canada's Directive on Automated Decision-Making mandates impact assessments based on the severity of AI's effect on individuals, ensuring a broad coverage of high-risk settings.
Are there any principles we should add or remove?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
A principle specifically addressing algorithmic transparency should be added. In the US, transparency is a key focus, ensuring that decisions made by AI systems can be explained, especially in high-risk settings like healthcare and law enforcement. Similarly, the EU's GDPR emphasizes a "right to explanation," which could strengthen the proposed principles.
Please identify any:
Certain low-risk AI systems, such as decision support systems for non-critical tasks, could be unintentionally captured. For instance, systems used in administrative education settings should be exempt unless they impact legal or economic rights.
AI used for defense or national security purposes must be treated distinctly. In the UK, defense AI is subject to separate scrutiny under military regulations, given its high-stakes nature.
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
The current principles should incorporate Indigenous Data Sovereignty frameworks, which are increasingly being discussed in Australia and Canada. Incorporating First Nations protocols on governance and decision-making would ensure that AI systems respect Indigenous knowledge and heritage. This approach echoes Canada’s focus on preserving Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP), aligning AI systems with cultural appropriateness. The principles should also integrate free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) from the UNDRIP to ensure that First Nations communities are consulted before any AI systems affecting them are developed. Additionally, drawing from New Zealand’s Indigenous Data Sovereignty Network, provisions for Indigenous control over their data across the AI lifecycle must be included to ensure AI systems respect their rights and cultural integrity.
A more robust engagement process, where First Nations communities are involved in the AI design and governance processes, would help prevent potential harms. Integrating protocols that prioritize self-determination would safeguard against exploitation and historical inequities.
3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?
NO a more defined list-based approach is needed
If you prefer a list-based approach (similar to the EU and Canada), what use cases should we include? How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
Biometrics Critical infrastructure Education/training Employment Access to essential public services and products Law enforcement Access to essential private services Products and services affecting individual and public health and safety Administration of justice and democratic processesOther
How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
The proposed principles do not provide sufficient clarity, and a more defined, list-based approach is needed. While the principles provide a broad framework, clear illustrative examples—such as those found in the EU AI Act—would give stakeholders more certainty. The EU’s classification of AI into risk categories provides clarity for developers, users, and regulators.
To capture emerging AI applications, regular updates to the list should be institutionalized to account for advancements such as General-Purpose AI (GPAI) and AI’s role in social media moderation or public discourse. Additionally, to capture future AI use cases, a mechanism for real-time updates to the risk categories should be proposed. This could be achieved through stakeholder consultations and research, ensuring AI governance remains flexible and responsive to rapid advancements in AI technology, drawing inspiration from Canada’s Dynamic Impact Assessment framework.
4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Yes
If so, how should we define these?
Some AI systems, such as facial recognition in public spaces, predictive policing, mass surveillance or social scoring systems, pose risks to civil liberties and should be banned or heavily regulated. The EU AI Act is moving toward banning such uses due to the high likelihood of human rights violations, which Australia should consider replicating.
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
Yes, the principles provide flexibility, but they need regular reviews to remain relevant in capturing emerging forms of AI, like General-Purpose AI (GPAI). Both the EU and UK frameworks address adaptability by setting up bodies like the AI & Data Governance Board (UK) to oversee AI developments. Similarly, Canada’s Directive calls for dynamic regulatory approaches that evolve with technology.
Additionally, implementing regulatory sandboxes (as seen in the UK’s AI strategy) could help test new forms of AI in a controlled environment before widespread deployment. This approach encourages innovation while ensuring that safety and ethical considerations are addressed early in development.
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
GPAI models should be subject to mandatory guardrails. Defining GPAI as high-risk based on principles such as transparency or accountability, rather than solely on technical metrics like floating-point operations per second (FLOPS), would align with the EU and Canadian risk-based approaches. Technical capability, though important, should not be the only criterion. The systemic impacts, scalability, and potential for widespread harm should guide regulation.
7. What are suitable indicators for defining GPAI models as high-risk?
Define high-risk against the principles
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
The proposed guardrails effectively mitigate risks, particularly through its focus on testing, transparency, and accountability. However, more explicit provisions on bias mitigation and impact assessments—as incorporated in the EU AI Act and Canada’s Directive—would bolster the framework. Including a mandatory AI impact assessment (AIA), as required in Canada, would add robustness.
Additionally, the guardrails should include provisions for continuous human oversight in high-risk AI systems. Drawing from the US NIST AI Risk Management Framework, human-in-the-loop (HITL) processes should be mandatory for systems affecting legal rights or public safety, ensuring that AI decisions remain accountable even after deployment.
Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?
Yes
What guardrails should we add or remove?
Establish, implement and publish an accountability process including governance, internal capability and a strategy for regulatory compliance Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks Protect AI systems, and implement data governance measures to manage data quality and provenance Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the system once deployed Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcomes Inform end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content Be transparent with other organisations across the AI supply chain about data, models and systems to help them effectively address risks Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with the guardrails
9. How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols to ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property?
The guardrails should integrate First Nations knowledge by mandating consultation and co-design with Indigenous communities. The Canadian First Nations Principles of Ownership, Control, Access, and Possession (OCAP) could serve as a template, ensuring AI systems respect Indigenous sovereignty over data and knowledge. Such integration ensures AI aligns with Indigenous cultural protocols and safeguards Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP).
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
Yes, however they could be more explicit in outlining shared responsibility throughout the AI lifecycle, from development to deployment. The EU AI Act establishes clear obligations for AI developers, providers, and users, which Australia could emulate. By ensuring that accountability mechanisms are embedded at every stage, risks can be mitigated more effectively.
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI?
No
How could we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for example low-risk and high-risk GPAI models? 
The current guardrails are a good start but may not fully address the complexities of GPAI. Given GPAI’s broad applications and potential for misuse, additional guardrails—such as real-time auditing and continuous impact assessments—may be needed. The UK’s AI Strategy highlights the importance of dynamic regulation for future-proofing governance structures.
12. Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small-to-medium sized businesses applying guardrails?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
To reduce regulatory burdens on small-to-medium sized businesses (SMEs), adopting a tiered regulatory framework like Canada’s AI Impact Assessments would be beneficial. This approach can scale compliance requirements based on the risk level of the AI system, thereby preventing SMEs from being overburdened.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A framework approach – Introducing new framework legislation to adapt existing regulatory frameworks across the economy
What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
A framework approach is likely the most appropriate legislative option. It offers flexibility and the ability to adapt existing regulatory frameworks across industries. This approach aligns with the UK’s pro-innovation stance and the EU AI Act, where sector-specific regulations coexist within a broader AI governance framework.
14. Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the Australian Government should consider?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
One limitation is the risk of over-regulation, which could stifle innovation. Balancing regulatory oversight with room for experimentation is crucial. The US, for instance, opts for a sector-specific approach to regulate AI, emphasizing innovation while safeguarding public interests.
15. Which regulatory option(s) will best ensure that guardrails for high-risk AI can adapt and respond to step-changes in technology?
A framework approach – Introducing new framework legislation to adapt existing regulatory frameworks across the economy
Please provide any additional comments.
A framework approach offers the best solution for adapting to technological changes. This model allows for sector-specific updates, ensuring that the regulatory framework can evolve as AI technologies advance. It would allow Australia to mirror the flexibility incorporated in the EU’s AI Act while maintaining necessary safeguards for high-risk applications.
16. Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps and inconsistencies with Australia’s existing laws for the development and deployment of AI?
The biggest risks lie in the inconsistent application of AI laws across sectors and a lack of comprehensive data governance standards. By aligning with global standards and embedding continuous review mechanisms into regulations, Australia can avoid these gaps and ensure its laws remain effective amidst rapid technological advancement.
To further address these gaps, sector-specific guidelines, as seen in the EU AI Act, could be adopted to tailor AI regulations according to the unique risks of different industries. For example, AI in healthcare, finance, and education may require distinct regulatory approaches, ensuring that Australia’s AI laws are both flexible and context specific.

CAG  Response  – October 2024   1 CAG Response  to the ‘Introducing mandatory 
guardrails for AI in high -risk settings ’ proposals 
paper   
 
This response  is made by the Schools and TAFE Copyright Advisory Groups ( CAG ). Further 
information about CAG and its activities is set out in Attachment A  to this response.   
CAG welcomes  the opportunity to comment on the ‘Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in 
high-risk settings’ proposals paper (the Proposals Paper ), and thank s the Department of 
Industry, Science and Resources (the Department ) for its consideration of our response .  
Executive Summary  
In this response, CAG addresses four key copyright issues for education that arise in connection 
with the  Department’s proposed approach to regulating high -risk AI systems, particularly the 
mandatory guardrails (the Guardrails ). To assist the Department, CAG responds to relevant 
consultation questions in Attachment B . 
Overall, CAG recognises the need for safety, accountability and transparency obligations to be 
imposed on certain developers and deployers of AI systems  and supports the Department’s intent 
to introduce regulation to respond to high -risk applications of AI .  
However, CAG considers that there are four key issues  with the approach outlined in the 
Proposals Paper  that must be addressed in conjunction with developing regulation for high -risk 
AI systems : 
1. AI regulation  and mandatory transparency guardrails must be supported  by 
corresponding public -interest exceptions under Australian copyright law .  
The Department ’s proposed approach reflects AI regulations in the European Union AI Act  
(EU AI Act ) and Canada’s proposed amended AI and Data Act  (AIDA ), which w ere 
introduced in context s where copyright law s permit  some  AI activities under robust public 
interest exception s. Australia does not  have the same c ontext : our copyright framework does 
not include equivalent exceptions  to those that exist in the EU and Canada , to the detriment 
of researchers and educational institutions wanting to develop AI tools or teach AI skills for 
the benefit of Australian students . 
CAG urges the Department to adopt a holistic approach that carefully considers the copyright 
implications of any regulatory response to high -risk AI : transparency obligations make sense 
as long as there are copyright exceptions in place that provide legal clarity about beneficial 
uses of AI, including in education. If the Department  proposes to implement AI regulations 
that mirror those in the EU and Canada, then Australia’s copyright laws must also contain 
equivalent exceptions .  
CAG  Response  – October 2024   2 2. AI regulations  should reflect  a nuanced approach to risk  in the educational context .  
What is considered a  “high -risk” AI  system should not capture everyday educational 
applications of AI systems that are low-risk, such as the beneficial educational use of AI as a 
‘study bu ddy’ as recommended by a recent House Standing Committee . CAG encourages 
the Department to adopt an appropriate and nuanced definition of high -risk AI that avoid s all 
educational applications of AI being automatically categorised as high -risk with 
corresponding mandatory guardrails applied. Any approach to AI regulation should focus on 
developers of general purpose AI ( GPAI ) model s, which  are sophisticated, commercial 
technology companies like Microsoft, OpenAI and Google , rather than schools , TAFEs , 
Departments of Education or administering bodies , with limited r esources , who are deploying 
AI in an educational context .   
3. Transparency obligations should also apply to copyright collecting societies which 
administer licensing regimes allowing certain uses of copyright works in connection 
with AI.  
There are two aspects to transparency obligations for AI: firstly, transparency in connection 
with disclosure of training datasets, and  secondly,  transparency as to the management of 
any licensing schemes that may apply  to, or be developed for, the use of copyright works to 
train AI. Transparency is required to ensure that  licence fees paid by the education sector 
and governments out of public funds are being distributed appropriately , particularly when 
much AI training occurs in relation to public domain materi als, or on content for which there 
is no easily identifiable copyright owner . Where developers and deployers of AI systems are 
required to disclose what works were used to train AI systems, it is appropriate for 
transparency obligations to apply to copyright collecting societies , which administer voluntary 
collective or statutory licensing regimes covering uses of copyright works in connection with 
AI.  
4. Where appropriate, the Guardrails should encourage organisations to comply with 
ICIP policies and protocols in connection with AI.  
The Guardrails  do not currently require organisations to comply with ICIP policies and 
protocols that they have in place when developing or deploying AI systems. An effective way 
of improving protections for ICIP in the AI context would be to : 
(i) require developers and deployers to have ICIP protocols in place and comply with 
those protocols in connection with high -risk AI  
(ii) encourage developers and deployers to comply with ICIP protocols in connection with 
other applications of AI.  
CAG’s position in respect of each issue is addressed in further detail below.     
CAG  Response  – October 2024   3 1. AI regulation and mandatory transparency guardrails must  be supported 
by public -interest exceptions  in the Copyright Act  
Background  
The Department proposes to implement Guardrails that mirror  AI regulations in the EU AI Act and 
Canada’s AIDA , including transparency obligations in the Guardrails that are modelled on the EU 
AI Act as summarised in the flowcharts in Attachment C. In particular, g uardrail 3 is modelled on 
Article 53  of the EU AI Act and requires developers and deployers to identify “ the origin and 
legality of the dataset and collection processes ”.1 Guardrail 3 is intended to complement 
requirements under the Copyright Act.2 
While CAG welcomes the Department’s recognition that the Guardrails and Copyright Act should 
complement each other, it is important to recogni se that the guardrails in the EU were developed 
in a vastly different copyright context to that in Australia, where certain activities in relation to text 
and data mining  and AI are permitted under European copyright law.  
Copyright exceptions are an important part of the broader legal framework underpinning the 
approaches to AI regulation being taken in overseas jurisdictions including the EU and Canada. 
Other ju risdictions have  copyright frameworks with robust and flexible education exceptions 
permitting non -commercial uses of copyright works in connection with digital technologies 
including AI , as set out in Attachment D . Relevantly : 
• the EU has a TDM exception  and other broad education  exceptions3  
• Canada has a fair dealing for education exception4 
• Singapore has a TDM exception  and fair use5 
• the United Kingdom has a TDM exception and fair dealing for education exceptions.6   
However, Australia’s Copyright Act 1968 (Cth) (the Copyright Act ) does not  include equivalent 
public -interest exceptions that would permit certain non -commercial, educational use of copyright 
works. This has long been recognised as a problem that should be remedied by both the 
Australian Law Reform Commission and the Productivity Commission.7 Supporting appropriate 
use of copyright materials in the public interest, including education,  is enshrined in our

Australia’s copyright framework needs to be updated so that it is fit -for-purpose for the AI -driven 
future of education. The Copyright Act must reflect the well -recognised public interest in Australian

being required to  pay licence fees or face legal exposure for non -harmful uses of copyright works 
that cause no prejudice to copyright owners.  
CAG is not suggesting  that every educational application of AI will, or should be, free. Instead, 
CAG envisages that Australia’s copyright framework  as it applies to  AI will ultimately comprise :  
• public interest exceptions to copyright infringement permitting certain uses of copyright works 
without a licence in limited public interest circumstances

distributed to rightsholders to compensate  them for uses of their works  that have an impact 
on the market for their works  
• direct licensing between  rightsholders and developers of AI systems permitting  uses of 
copyright works in connection with AI , which is already occurring in commercial contexts .11 
Why is this an issue?  
Under the proposed Guardrails, Australian educational institutions who develop or deploy  high-
risk AI systems including GPAI models would be required to comply with transparency obligations 
that mirror those that apply in the EU and Canada, but they cannot rely on copyright exceptions

To avoid  these risks, a ny regulatory response to AI must be introduced alongside appropriate

CAG recommends that  the Department continue consultation on the issues addressed in the

process should be undertaken in Australia.  
CAG also considers that t he Department should follow a phased implementation process to allow

for educational institutions to comply with any new AI regulations . As summarised in the EU’s AI
