CAG  Response  – October 2024   7 2. AI regulations should reflect  a nuanced  approach to risk  in the 
educational context  
Background  
The Department’s proposal  would include the following applications of AI as “high -risk”:  
• AI systems designated as “ high-risk due to [their] use ” by reference to a set of principles or, 
alternatively, particular use cases  
• all GPAI models, which is broadly defined as “ an AI model that is capable of being used, or 
capable of being adapted for use, for a variety of purposes, both for direct use as well as for 
integration in other systems ”.13  
As acknowledged in the Proposals Paper, many “high -risk domains” can include  AI use cases 
that pose limited or minimal risk .14 CAG notes that the current proposed version of Canada’s AIDA 
does not expressly include education a s a high -risk class of use for AI systems, while the EU AI 
Act only lists certain  educational AI use cases as high -risk.  
What applications of AI are considered high -risk will have implications for obligations imposed on 
both developers and deployers under the proposed Guardrails. In particular, a s reflected in the 
flowcharts in Attachment C, the EU AI Act includes a nuanced, tiered approach to transparency 
obligations for different applications of AI  applications. However, t he Department’s proposed 
approach  appear s to impose the most stringent transparency obligations from the EU AI Act on 
both developers and deployers of  any high -risk AI systems.  
Further, CAG understands that the Department’s proposed approach could impose the same 
obligations under the Guardrails on:  
• sophisticated commercial technology organisations responsible for developing and deploying 
large -scale commercial GPAI models and AI systems, such as Microsoft, OpenAI and Google 
and EdTech companies  
• state and territory Departments of Education and administering bodies in the Catholic and 
independent sectors with limited budgets drawn from public funds who are deploying GPAI 
models in specific educational AI applications, such as NSWEduChat , or fine -tuning GPAI 
models  
• schools, TAFEs and their educators engaging  with AI on the ground, for example where a 
Year 12 class is building an AI system that leverages GPT -4 as part of an in -class exercise.  
CAG notes that the Study Buddy Report recommended that the Government “ regulate EdTech 
companies and developers  through a system -wide risks -based legal framework ” and “ require 
EdTech companies and developers  to share critical information about how their AI systems are 
trained, what data it has been trained on, and how algorithms function and affect users ” (see 
recommendation 11  – emphasis added). This recommendation would not be possible under the 
Department’s proposal which could potentially treat all educational uses of AI as high risk.

14 Guardrails proposals paper, p 26.   
CAG  Response  – October 2024   8 Why is this an issue?  
There are  two main issues relevant to  risk arising out of the Proposals Paper . 
(a) Not all educational applications of AI should be considered high -risk 
Irrespective of whether the Department adopts a principles or list -based approach, CAG considers 
that any attempt  to define  high-risk AI should not be overly prescriptive. CAG favours adopting 
discretionary factors for assessing risk that are supported by guidelines to ensure there is 
sufficient flexibility to reflect a variety of contexts.  
In CAG’s view, the Department’s approach to AI regulation needs to be nuanced enough to 
recognise the lower risk profiles of some educational applications of AI. As noted in the Study 
Buddy Report, it is important to recognise the complexities around risk and AI in the education 
context, and the diverse ways in which AI can be deployed across the sector.  
CAG agrees that some education applications of AI identified in the Proposals Paper are more 
clearly high -risk (eg using a system to determine access to educational institutions) . However, 
other educational applications of AI are not (eg a jurisdiction deploying a GPAI model that allows 
teachers to generate answers to basic questions, similar to the way they would use Google).  
If all educational applications of AI are considered  high-risk, then educational institutions may be 
subject to unnecessary regulatory burdens that could impact their ability to engage  with all of the 
opportunities and benefits of AI, including those recognised in the Study Buddy Report . For 
example, as a ‘co -designer’ to summarise research or concepts for lesson plans, personalising 
lesson plans to suit a student’s level of knowledge, or reducing teacher workload by performing 
“menial tasks, such as sortin g information under headings or in tables .” These low risk and 
beneficial uses of AI should not be classified as high risk simply because they occur in an 
educational context.   
(b) There needs to be clarity  around what obligations apply to  particular developers and 
deployers of high-risk AI  
As a matter of principle, AI regulations  should differentiate between particular developers and 
deployers of high-risk AI systems. CAG welcomes the imposition of appropriate mandatory 
guardrails  on large, commercial developers and deployers of AI systems, such as such as 
Microsoft, OpenAI and Google and EdTech companies.  
Schools and TAFEs need to be able to provide access to, and potentially in future build and 
develop, AI systems and models : for example, to “build students’ skills through project -based 
learning ” as envisaged by the Study Buddy Report (see recommendation 19 ). Educational 
institutions such as schools, TAFEs and administering bodies which are deploying GPAI models 
or developing AI systems for educational purposes should not be subject to equivalent, stringent 
obligations  to those that apply to sophisticated, commercial entities like OpenAI or Google . The 
obligations envisaged by the Guardrails are likely to be particularly burdensome for educational 
institutions with limited resources and school - or TAFE -level technical expertise.   
CAG  Response  – October 2024   9 CAG’s recommendations  
CAG strongly recommends  that any approach to regulating high-risk AI  recognises that : 
• not all educational applications of AI should be  considered “high -risk”. Low-risk educational 
applications of AI  systems  should be  excluded, in recognition of the strong identified benefits 
of those applications and the limited risk of harm occurring. Examples of low -risk applications 
of AI could include using an AI system  to ensure teachers are grading consistently across 
classes, using AI -assisted search to find a specific curriculum outcome, or where a teacher 
asks AI to “generate a list of Australia’s f irst 10 Prime Ministers”  
• the most stringent transparency obligations and risk settings should be targeted to 
sophisticated developers of commercial AI systems, such as  EdTech providers and  
OpenAI /Microsoft /Google. E ducational institutions should otherwise be subject to obligations 
that better reflect the actual risk profiles of the activities they are undertaking with AI systems 
(for example, by differentiating between administering bodies deploying GPAI models as part 
of systems such as NSWEduChat, and schools/TAFEs  deploying or developing AI systems ). 
CAG  also recommends  further consultation with the education sector to give their input and 
support about what educational applications of AI should be considered high-risk. Given the fast -
developing nature of this space, t here should  also be a process for continual assessment of what 
applications of AI are considered high -risk and what mandatory obligations apply to educational 
institutions.     
CAG  Response  – October 2024   10 3. Transparency obligations should also apply to copyright collecting 
societies that administer collective licensing regimes allowing certain  
uses of copyright works in connection  with AI  
Background  
As set out above, the Department’s proposed approach would impose transparency obligations 
on developers and deployers of high -risk AI systems to identify “ the origin and legality of the 
dataset and collection processes ”15 and complement requirements under the Copyright Act.16 
Information disclosed in compliance with those obligations would support rightsholders in seeking 
remuneration for prejudicial uses of their works in connection with AI models.  
Subject to  CAG’s comments above concerning  the necessity of introducing public -interest 
education exceptions in the Copyright Act , some uses of  copyright material in connection with  AI 
that would interfere with a copyright owner’s commercial market may ultimately  be subject to 
remuneration under collective licence schemes. Current examples of collective licence schemes 
that apply to  education include:  
• the Schools Music Licence  and the TAFE Music Licence , which are voluntary collective 
licences under which Australian schools and TAFEs respectively pay music collecting 
societies APRA, AMCOS and ARIA for certain rights to use music  in education  
• the Statutory Broadcast Licence  and the Statutory Text and Artistic Works Licence , which are 
set out in s 113P of the Copyright Act, and under which Australian educational institutions 
pay fees to declared collecting societies Screenrights and Copyright Agency to copy and 
communicate film and TV broadcasts and text and artistic works res pectively for educational 
purposes.  
CAG notes that t he education sector pays millions of dollars of public funds each year to collecting 
societies for the educational use of copyright material. In 2023, the total paid was over $94 million .  
Why is this an issue?  
There are two aspects to transparency obligations for AI: firstly, transparency in connection with 
disclosure of training datasets, and secondly, transparency as to the management of any licensing 
schemes that apply  to the use of copyright works in connection with AI .  
CAG appreciates that the intention behind  the proposed transparency obligations is to permit 
rightsholders, and collecting societies who represent them, to know when their works are used to 
train AI models . Equivalent transparency  obligations  should apply to collecting societies , which 
use that information to remunerate rightsholders in respect of prejudicial uses of their works in 
connection with AI.  This is critical where, as the ALRC has noted, “collecting societies have been 
said to have a ‘de facto monopolistic nature’” .17  
Under Australia’s current framework , the  education sector cannot  obtain information from 
collecting societies on how they distribute licensing fees because collecting  societies are not

16 Ibid, p 38.  
17 See ALRC Copyright and the Digital Economy Report (ALRC Report 122) , December 2013, at 8.64.   
CAG  Response  – October 2024   11 obliged to disclose that information. For example, limited to no transparency is given about the 
distribution of licence fees where copyright owners cannot be identified, or the rates charged for 
de minimis  and extensive uses of copyright materials respectively.  
CAG has long -standing concerns about the lack of appropriate governance arrangements for 
declared collecting societies, and the practical consequences of these deficiencies. Neither the 
Code of Conduct for Copyright Collecting Societies, nor the existing legislative framework 
applying to collecting societies, provide any enforceable mechanism requiring the collecting 
societies to address the se transparency concerns, which have been echoed by the ALRC and 
the Productivity Commission.18  
CAG wishes to avoid exacerbating this existing problem with Australia’s collective licensing 
system to the extent it might apply to AI  given the large volume of works involved in AI training, 
and the potential corresponding impact on public funds if there is lack of transparency surrounding 
payments under licences for these works . Introducing transparency obligations on collecting 
societies will ensure that public funds collected under voluntary collective and statutory licence 
schemes are being used approp riately and distributed to creators fairly. In addition, this would 
give the Australian school and TAFE sectors confidence that the copyright licence fees paid from 
already limited budgets  represent ‘value for money’ . 
CAG’s recommendations  
CAG encourages the Department to support mandatory transparency obligations on copyright 
collecting societies on distribution of funds collected under statutory licences in connection with 
educational uses of AI.  At a minimum, CAG considers that collecting societies should be required 
to publish information about recipients of distributions or what portion of fees have been 
distributed to particular classes of rightsholders . 
  
 
18 In September 2016, t he Productivity Commission’s Productivity Commission Intellectual Property

access the information needed to allow them to effectively negotiate directly with rights holders ” (p 160).   
CAG  Response  – October 2024   12 4. Where appropriate, t he Guardrails should encourage organisations to 
comply with their ICIP policies and protocols  
Background  
ICIP covers a bundle of perpetual rights that exist independently of statutory IP rights (such as 
copyright). That said, ICIP can be protected by copyright and other types of statutory IP in some 
circumstances (but this is usually quite limited). For examp le, copyright only protects expressions 
that have been reduced to ‘material form’ ie written down or painted – oral histories or spiritual 
knowledge passed down through generations might not meet this  criteria. This is why First 
Nations communities rely on  other mechanisms such as contracts and protocols to protect their 
ICIP.  
Many organisations , including state and territory Departments of Education,  already have ICIP 
policies and protocols in place addressing responsible engagement with ICIP rightsholders and 
use of ICIP.  
The Government, through the Office for the Arts, is separately working on introducing standalone 
legislation for protecting ICIP , in partnership with First Nations stakeholders and a First Nations 
Expert Working Group. The standalone legislation was announced in  2023 as part of  the National 
Cultural Policy  Revive: a place for every story, a story for every place .  
Why is this an issue?  
As set out in the Proposals Paper, AI systems may have been trained on content that is protected 
by ICIP rights and could be used to create outputs that incorporate ICIP without attribution or 
permission from the relevant custodians of that ICIP.19  
The Guardrails do not currently require organisations to comply with ICIP policies and protocols  
that they have in place when developing or deploying AI systems . An effective way of improving 
protections for ICIP in the AI context would be to require developers and deployers to have ICIP 
protocols in place and comply with those protocols in connection with high -risk AI, and encourage 
developers and deployers to comply with ICIP protocols in connection with other applications of 
AI. 
CAG’s recommendations  
CAG encourages the Department to consider whether it is appropriate to require  developers and 
deploy ers of high -risk AI systems that leverage content containing ICIP to implement , publish  and 
comply with ICIP protocols , and otherwise encourage developers and deployers to comply with 
ICIP protocols in connection with other applications of AI.  
  
 
19 Guardrails proposals paper, p 13.   
CAG  Response  – October 2024   13 Summary of CAG’s recommendations  
In responding to the risks and opportunities of AI, particularly in education, CAG encourages the 
Department to bear in mind that AI regulation works hand -in-hand with copyright law. As outlined 
above, there are several key copyright risks and challenges faced by education in adopting digital 
technologies  including AI . Copyright law now needs urgent reform, as recommended by various 
reviews over more than a decade.  
To address the issues raised above , CAG recommends that  the Department should : 
1. only implement AI regulations in the form of the EU AI Act if Australia’s copyright framework 
is amended to include public interest copyright exceptions covering education that mirror 
those already in place in the EU and other jurisdictions  
2. support efforts to introduce copyright exceptions to give the education sector the legal clarity 
required to enable full engagement with the educational opportunities of AI  
3. continue consultation on the issues addressed in the Proposals Paper, in line with the

About CAG  
The Schools Copyright Advisory Group reports to Australian Education Senior Officials 
Committee ( AESOC ) and is comprised of senior representatives from the Commonwealth, State 
and Territory Departments of Education, all Catholic Education Offices and Independent Schools 
Australia. On copyright matters, CAG represents the almost 9,550 primary and secondary schools 
in Australia and their approximately 4 million students.  
The TAFE Copyright Advisory Group is the peak body responsible for copyright policy and 
administration for the Australian TAFE sector (other than in Victoria), including the management 
of obligations under educational statutory licences.  
CAG is assisted by the National Copyright Unit ( NCU ), a small secretariat based in Sydney.  
The sector invests a significant amount of resources into promoting respect for copyright amongst 
students and teachers, as well as the broader community. Some of the copyright education 
initiatives undertaken by the NCU include:  
● the Smartcopying website , the official guide to copyright issues for Australian schools and

copyright presentations

delivered 5 webinars about copyright and AI in education  to 335 school and TAFE 
educators ) 
● provision of extensive copyright advice to administering bodies and schools.  
NCU’s experience with AI in education  
Over the past year , the NCU has provided general copyright advice and support to schools and 
TAFEs in relation to  their use of generative AI tools. It has published an information sheet for both 
schools  and TAFE  on its Smartcopying  website, and has presented at various committees 
considering the impact of AI in education. In particular, the NCU has provided specific guidance 
to: 
● a teacher using AI to re -write portions of a text  into simple English suitable for students 
with learning difficulties  
● a teacher using OpenAI to generate images for use in a math s quiz 
● a department of education staff member requesting assistance on how to attribute content 
generated by AI.

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
The principles outlined generally capture high-risk AI settings, however a clearer focus on copyright needs to be explicitly included.
Are there any principles we should add or remove?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
A clearer focus on copyright needs to be explicitly included.
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
We fully support the comments of APRA AMCOS that a more comprehensive integration of Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) as it relates to the digital economy is urgently required to safeguard First Nations’ cultural knowledge, stories, and music from being misappropriated by AI systems.
3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?
NO a more defined list-based approach is needed
If you prefer a list-based approach (similar to the EU and Canada), what use cases should we include? How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
Whilst the development of AI offers exciting potential, it also poses serious risks to creators' rights, economic stability, and cultural integrity. Accountable AI therefore urgently requires appropriate guardrails including transparency and accountability. We therefore recommend including a list of high-risk use cases involving the unauthorised creation, distribution, and replication of copyrighted works.
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
The development of AI presents both opportunities and challenges for the creative sector. To mitigate risks, it is essential that the Australian Government implements strong, enforceable guardrails for AI, particularly in high-risk settings such as music creation, including:
1. Licensing: AI systems that use copyrighted works in their training datasets should be required to obtain licenses from rightsholders. This will ensure that creators are compensated for the use of their work and that their intellectual property rights are respected.
2. Audits: AI systems should be subject to regular audits to ensure compliance with licensing agreements and guard against the unauthorised use of copyrighted material. These audits should be conducted by independent third parties to maintain transparency and accountability.
3. Labelling of AI-generated content: All AI-generated music should be clearly labelled to distinguish it from human-created works. This will ensure that consumers are fully informed about the origins of the music they are listening to.
4. Market access standard: The Australian Government should set AI guardrails as market access standards to ensure that AI service providers have to respect Australian rules irrespective of where the model training has taken place. This approach was also adopted in the EU AI Act (recital 106) in order to address forum-shopping. Moreover, we recommend that the Australian government considers including effective sanctions on overseas platforms that fail to comply with Australian regulations.
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
To be effective, AI guardrails and transparency obligations must apply universally to all AI services available in Australia, regardless of where the AI model was trained or developed creating a level playing field where all players are held to the same standards. This approach was also adopted in the EU AI Act (recital 106).
Equally, effective sanctions for non-compliance should be in place and must also be imposed on platforms based overseas but operating in Australia.
9. How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols to ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property?
We recommend ensuring that the entire AI lifecycle—from development to deployment—incorporates mechanisms for ICIP enforcement, preventing unauthorised use of Indigenous materials. We further refer to the submission from APRA AMCOS in this context.
12. Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small-to-medium sized businesses applying guardrails?
No
Make a general comment
A legally, politically, and commercially successful AI ecosystem depends upon all relevant parts working in tandem for this common goal: Coexistence of human created and AI generated works, competing on a level playing field, a fair market. The fundamental starting point for the maintenance of a fair market is the compliance with the law in the jurisdiction AI service providers operate, in our case mainly copyright law but also other rules such as data protection and contractual obligations. We therefore welcome this timely consultation and rest at your disposal should you require further feedback.

oaic.gov.au  Introduction  
1. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) welcomes the opportunity to 
comment on the Proposals paper  for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
(Proposals Paper) released by the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR).   
2. The OAIC is an independent Commonwealth regulator, established to bring together three 
functions: privacy functions (protecting the privacy of individuals under the Privacy Act 1988  
(Cth) (Privacy Act) and other legislation), freedom of information functions (access to 
information held by the Commonwealth Government in accordance with the Freedom of 
Information Act 1982  (Cth))  (FOI Act) , and information management functions (as set out in the 
Australian Information Commissioner Act 2010  (Cth)) . 
3. The Proposals Paper  seeks feedback on proposed principles for defining high -risk AI , proposed 
mandatory guardrails to apply across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle, and 
three regulatory options for implementing the guardrails.  
4. As the Proposals Paper acknowledges, AI has the potential to benefit the Australian economy 
and society, by improving efficiency and productivity across a wide range of sectors and 
enhancing the quality of goods and services for consumers. However, the data -driven nature of 
AI technologies, whi ch rely on large data sets that often include personal information, can also 
create new specific privacy risks, amplify existing risks and lead to serious harms.  The OAIC’s 
2023 Australian Community Attitudes to Priva cy Survey (ACAPS) identified significant 
community concern with the use of personal information in AI systems, with  43% of Australians 
consider ing AI using their personal information to be one of the biggest privacy risks they face 
today.1  
5. The OAIC welcomes  the Government’s aim  to strengthen  and clarify the laws that apply to AI in 
order to address the risks and harms from AI, build public trust, and provide greater regulatory 
certainty. We broadly support the Proposal Paper’s approach to defining high -risk AI, and the 
content of the proposed mandatory guardrails. The guardrails have a number of synergies with 
Privacy Act protections, including in relation to transparency, data quality and  accuracy, and 
information security. To the extent the  guardrails apply to Australian Government agencies, 
they will also support greater government transparency and accountability in respect of AI and 
have positive impacts on access to government -held information and the operation of the FOI 
Act.  
6. This submission highlights  the key role  already  played by the OAIC in the regulation of new and 
emerging technologies such as AI . It is important that in implementing the mandatory 
guardrails , the Government considers which option will  ensure the best outcomes for 
individuals . Rather than introducing an AI -specific regulator, which has the potential to create 
regulatory duplication and confusion, the OAIC suggests that a framework approach will help to 
uplift existing regulatory frameworks and support  coordination and consistency across the 
individual regulators.  
 
1 Lonergan Research,  Australian Community Attitudes to Privacy Survey 2023 , report to OAIC, August 2023, p 24 . October 2024  
 
 
Page 3 DISR Proposals Paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
oaic.gov.au  General position  on Proposals Paper  
7. The OAIC broadly supports the Proposal Paper’s proposed approach to defining high -risk AI and 
the content of the mandatory guardrails. A human rights -based approach to defining high -risk AI 
will require organisations to consider adverse impacts on privacy alongside other human rights 
when determining whether a proposed use or application of AI is high -risk. This approach also 
recognises the well -publicised risks of bias and discrimination in AI system outputs.  
8. As the Paper acknowledges , the human -rights based approach to defining high -risk AI aligns 
with the approach adopted or proposed in other jurisdictions, including Canada and the 
European Union .2 As discussed in our previous submission to the  Department’s Safe and 
responsible AI in Australia discussion paper , the OAIC supports the need for  robust and  
interoperable regulatory frameworks  to support effective cross -border regulation  of AI 
technologies, recognising that personal information flows across national borders .3 
9. As a general comment, we  also support the Proposal s Paper’s  recognition of the regulatory 
remits  that currently exist  in respect of AI, including in relation to privacy, copyright, 
competition and consumer law, and the nee d for the mandatory guardrails to work in 
complement with , rather than replace,  these existing frameworks .4  
10. The  OAIC ’s previous submission to the Department’s Safe and responsible AI in Australia 
discussion paper  pointed to the growing  intersections between domestic frameworks relating to 
data and digital technologies, including privacy, competition and consumer law, and online 
safety and online content regulation. While there are synergies between these frameworks, 
there are also variances given each regulatory framework is designed to address different 
economic and societal issues.5 An effective regulatory approach to AI will require institutional 
coordination between different regulatory bodies in different areas, given the need for 
complementary expertise.  
11. To this end, the  OAIC has entered into MOUs with other regulators and is also a member of the 
Digital Platform Regulators Forum (DP -REG), together with  the Australian Competition and 
Consumer Co mmission (ACCC), Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA)  and 
Office of the eSafety Commissioner. DP-REG has also made a joint submission to this Proposals 
Paper, which highlights the work already being progressed by DP -REG members in respect of AI 
technologies and how the existing regulatory frameworks and expertise could be applied to 
address the challenges of AI.  
 
2 DISR, Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings , DISR, September 2024, p. 19.  
3 OAIC, Submission to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources - Safe and responsible AI in Australia discussion paper , 
OAIC, 18 August 2023.  
4 DISR, Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings , DISR, September 2024,  pp. 17, 50.  
5 OAIC, Submission to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources - Safe and responsible AI in Australia discussion paper , 
OAIC, 18 August 2023.  October 2024  
 
 
Page 4 DISR Proposals Paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
oaic.gov.au  Proposed mandatory guardrails  and the preservation 
of the right to access information and the right to 
privacy  
12. The OAIC supports the proposed content of the mandatory guardrails which will set out clear 
expectations regarding  testing, transparency,  accountability and  data governance in relation to 
high -risk AI systems  which  apply across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle.  
13. The Proposals Paper acknowledges that the guardrails, which are largely aimed at preventing 
harms occurring from the development and deployment of AI systems, will need to operate 
alongside laws to hold organisations accountable and help people to exercise  their rights when 
harm does occur.6 This highlights the critical role that the existing regulatory frameworks will 
continue to play to protect individuals from harms arising from high -risk AI.  
14. We note that there  is significant intersection  between obligations under the proposed guardrails 
and existing obligations under the Privacy Act  and Australian Privacy Principles (APPs). In 
particular , Guardrail 3, which provides for the protection of AI systems and implementation of 
data governance measures  to manage data quality and provenance , substantially overlaps with 
Privacy Act obligations on entities to: 
a. Take reasonable steps to ensure the personal information they collect, use and disclose is 
accurate, up -to-date and complete (APP 10) ; and  
b. Take reasonable steps to protect  the personal information they hold  from misuse, 
interference and loss, as well as unauthorised access, modification or disclosure (APP 
11.1).  
15. There are also areas of strong alignment across the other  guardrails. For example, Guardrail s 1 
and 2, whi ch require organisations to establish and implement accountability and risk 
management processes , intersects  with transparency and governance obligations under APP 1 , 
which requires entities to take reasonable steps to implement practices, procedures and 
systems to ensure they comply with the APPs and any binding registered APP Code, and can 
deal with related inquiries and complaints . Guardrail 6, which  requires organisations to inform 
end -users regarding AI -enabled decisions, AI interactions and AI -generated content, will overlap 
with notification obligations under APP 5 . 
16. To the extent the mandatory guardrails will apply to Australian Government agencies  deploying 
high -risk AI , they have the potential to  improve  government transparency and accountability in 
respect of AI and enhance access to government -held information , by requiring agencies to take 
steps such as publishing details of their  AI accountability processes  and keeping and 
maintaining records about a high -risk system over its lifecycle. This aligns with other initiatives 
currently underway to ensure that the Aust ralian Government is an exemplar in best -practice 
approaches to AI governance  and transparency , including the Digital Transformation Agency’s 
 
6 DISR, Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings , DISR, September 2024, p. 30.  October 2024  
 
 
Page 5 DISR Proposals Paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings  
oaic.gov.au  Policy for the responsible use of AI in government  and draft National framework for the assurance 
of artificial intelligence in government .7 
17. These intersections highlight the way that due to the data -driven nature of AI technologies, the 
OAIC is in many ways the default regulator of AI with responsibility  for responding to many of 
the harms that flow from the use of AI systems. At the same time, the guardrails cut across a 
number of different regulatory areas , emphasising the need for regulatory collaboration and 
cooperation .  
18. The OAIC notes that these reforms, while important measures to enhance the transparency of 
decision -making involving the use of AI, will apply only in  the context of decisions  relating to an 
individual  and will not apply  more broadly  to government decision -making that is informed by 
AI.8 The mandatory guardrails play an important role in this regard by requiring  government 
agencies to be transparent about the broader deployment of high -risk AI systems, including 
through the publication of an accountability process and strategy for regulatory compliance, 
informing end -users about interactions with AI and AI -genera ted content, and being transparent 
with other organisations across the AI supply chain.   
19. This broader application extending beyond privacy to information access rights introduces a 
further need to adopt a human rights preserving framework manifesting in guardrails that 
promote and preserve both of the fundamental human rights oversighted by th e OAIC.  
20. The Freedom of Information Act 1982  (FOI Act) enshrines the right of access to information under 
Art. 19 of the UN Declaration of Himan Rights. The objects of the FOI Act include: to require 
agencies to publish information; provide a right of access to documents; and increase scrutiny, 
discussion, comment and review of the Government’s activities.9 
21. AI presents unique risks to the transparency of government policy and decision making. 
Mitigation of the se risk s has been actively addressed in other jurisdictions. In some jurisdictions 
a legislated mandate requires the provision of notice to the community that AI is in use  both 
proactively and reactively.10 The proactive provision of a notice to the community together with 
a general statement that provides an adequate description of its operation ensures that the 
community is aware of the use of AI systems. However, that foundational protection of the right 
to access information should be augmented by further detail provided reactively, upon request 
deliver a more specific explanation of the operation of the system. This more detailed 
explanation injects  a further rights preservation strategy, the right of review. In the government 
setting administrative review is integral to our democratic values and rights.  
22. Large language models derive data from multiple sources to provide an output. In 
circumstances where the output impacts the provision of government policy, services and

24. The FOI Act expressly recognises that the right to access information is preserved 
notwithstanding contractual arrangements between government and third -party providers.11 In

25. In these high -risk  sectors  which necessitate engagement of third -party providers  preservation of

of information access rights which mandate  proactive and reactive disclosure of information 
regarding the use of AI systems in government settings.   
26. Increasingly the right to access information is compromised in digital government settings that 
lack mature information governance frameworks. Consistent convention, storage and retrieval 
together with developed systems to assure data provenance are all re quired to safeguard the 
right to access information. The development of an AI regulatory framework should be informed 
by these foundational requirements.  
27. Additionally, Australia’s d igital sovereignty will be compromised unless extant rights and values 
are preserved,  and our existing regulatory ecosystem is optimised in our development of new 
regulatory approaches.  
28. Option 2 presented within the proposals paper provides an opportunity to harness existing 
regulatory controls and optimise their application through coalition within a new regulatory

accommodates that development under an AI regulatory model that provides a consistent set of 
high -risk definitions and guardrails.

30. As the  Proposals Paper acknowledges , the current proposals intersect with  a broader suite of 
government actions and reform processes underway, including  reforms to the Privacy Act to  
implement the proposals from the Attorney -General’s Department’s (AGD) Privacy Act Review .  
31. The Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2024  was introduced into Parliament on 12 
September 2024  and contains the first tranche of amendments responding to proposals from 
the Privacy Act Review.13 Relevantly , the Bill proposes amendments to APP 1  to require entities 
to include information in their privacy policies about automated decisions that significantly 
affect the rights or interests of an individual.14  
32. The proposed amendments are aimed at providing individuals with greater transparency about 
how an entity is handling their personal information , and the ability to take further action in the 
event of a breach of their privacy.15 This will complement work being led by AGD to develop a 
whole -of-government legal framework for the use of automated decision -making (ADM) 
systems , to ensure that government use  of ADM (including ADM systems involving AI) complies  
with administrative law principles .  
33. The OAIC anticipates that the second tranche of privacy reforms will implement  additional  
proposals from the Privacy Act Review  that will operate to further mitigate  and address  the 
privacy risks associated with AI  and enhance transparency in the use of AI .  
34. In particular, the proposal to establish a positive obligation on organisations to collect, use and 
disclose personal information fairly and reasonably will require entities to proactively consider 
whether their personal information handling activities are appropriate an d set a baseline 
standard of information handling that is flexible and adaptable as circumstances and 
technology change .16 A positive obligation for organisations to handle data fairly and reasonably 
would give individuals engaging with AI technologies greater confidence that they will be 
treated fairly, and that —like a safety standard —privacy protection is assured.  
35. Another key proposal to increase organisational accountability is that all APP entities would be 
required to complete a PIA prior to undertaking any ‘high privacy risk activity’.17 This is likely to 
intersect  with obligations under proposed Guardrail 2 for organisations to establish and 
implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks.  
Implementation of mandatory guardrails  
36. The Proposals Paper canvasses three options for implementing  the proposed mandatory 
guardrails.  Of the options presented, the OAIC  considers that the framework approach outlined

37. The  domain -specific approach  of Option 1 , which aims to embed the relevant guardrails in 
existing frameworks, may not provide these framework s with the uplift needed to effectively 
address the challenges posed by high -risk AI technologies. As recognised in the Proposals Paper, 
this approach is likely to lead to a number of regulatory gaps and inconsistencies  and would be 
limited to the current  law and enforcement powers of existing  regulators.  
38. The  introduction of an AI -specific  Act and  regulator, as proposed by Option 3, may lead to 
inefficiencies and risks creating duplication  and lack of regulatory coherence.  The regulation of 
AI will require  specialised knowledge of  a broad range of existing  regulatory systems  in place  – 
as an example, Guardrail 3 canvasses obligations that intersect with privacy, copyright and 
critical infrastructure laws.  It is not clear how a standalone AI  regulator will be able to operate 
effectively  across these diverse  areas , and as the Proposals Paper acknowledges, there is 
significant risk of overlap.  Establishing an AI -specific regulator alongside existing regulatory 
regimes is also likely to create confusion for the public about where to direct  complaints.  
39. Additionally, given  that many high -risk AI technologies are still emerging and the harms and 
risks are not fully realised, the gaps in existing frameworks are still not well understood. Existing 
regulators need time to develop their responses to high -risk AI and to understand and clarify the 
application of existing laws . To prevent a new regulatory model becoming outdated  quickly , it 
may be more appropriate to consider the option of a  new AI -specific regulator at a later point in 
time.  
Support for framework approach (Option 2)  
40. The OAIC is of the view that a framework approach, as set out in Option 2, is the most 
appropriate model  to support a coordinated approach to the regulation of high -risk AI  and 
create the best outcomes for individuals . As the Proposals Paper acknowledges, a framework 
approach  recognises the existing laws that can be used or amended to give effect to the 
proposed mandatory guardrails and leverage s familiarity that people and businesses have with 
Australia’s  existing  regulatory regimes . This approach enables  current regulators to bring their 
particular expertise to the enforcement of the mandatory guardrails.  
41. Given the centrality of our role in whole -of-economy regulation of AI, the OAIC is likely to be best 
placed to address many of the harms arising from AI technologies. Noting the synergies between 
the proposed mandatory guardrails and the APPs, discussed earlier in this submission, it may be 
possible to incorporate many of the requirements in the guardrails either t hrough AI -specific 
legislative amendments or using the APP codes mechanism under the Privacy Act.18 APP codes 
can adapt and particularise the APPs where appropriate, providing greater clarity about 
obligations where that is warranted by the entity’s particular circumstances .

Getty Images appreciates the continued opportunity to provide further comments in

Mandatory Guardrails – Public Consultation Questions  
 
 
Defining high -risk AI  
 
(1) Do the proposed principles adequately capture high -risk AI? Are there any 
principles we should  add or remove?  
Please identify any:  
• low-risk use cases that are unintentionally captured  
• categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for 
defence or national  security purposes  
 
The proposed principles pro vide a strong foundation for addressing high risk AI, in 
particular, the reference to ‘adverse  legal effects where an ind ividual ’s legal right 
may be impacted ’ – broadly respect s the intellectual property rights of content 
creators.  This underpins the notion that innovation should not come a t the expense 
of creators , as there are  certainly path ways that would allow the two to coexist and  
elevate each other in a balanced way.  It is vital to support the advancement of AI 
technology that is created responsibly, respects creators and their rights, protects 
users of such technologies, and ultimately sustains ongoing creation by obtaining 
consent from rights holders for training . 
 
The principles may benefit from stronger enforcement  mechanisms  and alignment 
with global standards , as international consistency would help manage cross -
border risks and prevent companies operating in countries with less stringent 
regulations , to avoid accounta bility. The proposed principles should expressly 
recognize the adverse impacts of AI on an individual’s right to privacy, specifically 
data privacy. Given, privacy  is recognized as a human right under the Universal 
Declaration of Human Rights , data privacy should be incorporated into the 
proposed principles for assessing high risk AI, either under  “Human Rights” or  as 
a stand -alone principle , given the sensitive nature and possible imp acts associated 
to such data.  
 
Transparency should be recognized as an overarching principle in assessing high -
risk AI. The EU AI Act recognizes transparency as one of several foundational 
principles of the legislation. AI risk assessments should consider whether organizations are transparent to the public regarding the type and use cases of 
data that is being collected , how certain decisions are made and any other 
implications for individual rights.  This transparency should extend to accurate 
record keeping of any data used to develop AI , for audit purposes.  
 
Categories of uses should be distinguished based on sector or industry. For 
example, different considerations may apply for AI that is used in administrative 
process compared to AI used for national security purposes of commercial AI.  
 
(3) Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and 
certainty on high -risk AI settings and high -risk AI models? Is a more defined 
approach, with a list of illustrative uses,  needed?  
• If you prefer a list -based approach (similar to the EU and Canada), what 
use cases should  we include? How can this list capture emerging uses of 
AI? 
• If you prefer a principles -based approach, what should we address in 
guidance to give the  greatest clarity?  
 
A comprehensive principles -based approach may offer greater flexibility than a list -
based approach  as certain uses may not be adequately covered by a prescribed 
list. Alternatively, the legislation could include both a list of high -risk uses and a set 
of guiding principles to inform risk assessments of uses that do not clearly fall 
within the prescribe d list of uses.  
 
(5) Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of 
high-risk AI,  such as general -purpose AI (GPAI)?  
 
New and emerging forms of high -risk AI, such as GPAI, pose heightened risks of 
data privacy violations. Data privacy and transparency should be principles of 
emphasis in AI risk -assessments.  Minimum safeguards for personal information  
(including incidental or inadvertent processing) , lack of transparency on what data 
is collected and how it is used and adverse effects on data privacy would be 
indicators of high -risk AI systems.    
 
Given the difficulty associated with predicting all possibl e risks extending from new 
and emerging forms of high -risk AI, the principles surrounding safety and security 
could be enhanced to include a focus on reviewing ongoing ri sks, and involve 
continuous monitoring of such GPAI systems  (to recognize the dynamic natur e and 
capacity to change behaviour after deployment ). This could be strengthened  
through certain levels of human oversight to avoid rogue systems that need to be  
paired back with human intervention when necessary . A dynamic review 
mechanism would ensure the principles remain relevant as new high -risk AI forms 
become more prevalent.  
 
(6) Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?  
 The mandatory guardrails should apply to all GPAI. The guardrails should 
prescribe minimum standards for safe and responsible AI development. 
Obligations under the mandatory guardrails may be heightened for GPAI models.  
 
Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of AI  
 
8) Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used 
in high -risk settings ? Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?   
 
Guardrail 3 – While general data governance principles may apply, GPAI systems 
pose a higher risk, as they may ingest vast and diverse datasets, potentially 
leading to unintentional IP and data privacy infringement . Tech nical measures 
should be implemented during the testing process to detect and mitigate biases 
and inaccuracies . The level of privacy and cybersecurity measures should 
correspond to the volume and sensitivity of data, particularly personal information, 
that is included in a given dataset.  Organizations should be required to enter into 
licensing agreements with content providers for data that is used to train AI models, 
as opposed to scraping content from the web.  This is to ensure that any content 
protected by copyright and the associated metadata that is included in datasets to 
train AI is adequately protected  and licensed for the intended purpose. This 
information should be included in the company’s model card . 
 
Guardrail 4 – AI models should be subject to rigorous 3rd party testing, both before 
and after deployment to the market  on a continuous basis . For example, during the 
deployment of AI -driven content recommendation systems, ongoing monitoring 
should ensure that recommendations respect content usage rights and do not 
promote pirated or unlicensed works . 
 
Guardrail 6 – To mitigate the risks of deepfakes and/or misinformation, any content 
generated by AI, partly or entirely, by AI should be labelled or watermarked 
accordingly . Users interacting with AI -generated content should be informed about 
its origins, especially when AI tools might use or reference licensed content. 
Transparency about the use of creator works is essential to maintain trust with 
rights holders and to ensure that end users understand the legal standing of the 
content . 
 
Guardrail 8 – Organizations should ensure that there are adequate safeguards 
(such as encryp tion) to protect data/information communicated between 
organizations  
 
Guardrail 9 – third parties should be responsible for implementing safeguards to 
protect collected data from misuse/unlawful access . 
 
10) Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the  AI 
supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately? For example, are the 
requirements assigned to developers and deployers appropriate?   
AI developers should be subject to the same degree of liability as deployers for 
safety risks. Developers should be required to conduct separate due diligence and 
testing of AI models. A I developers should be responsible for implementing internal 
safeguards.  One potential solution to increase accountability is to impose a 
statutory duty of care on AI developers and implement a government certification 
scheme. AI developers would be required to respect fundamental human rights 
and intellectual property rights and comply with minimum accountability and 
transparency requirements. Certificates could be awarded on an annual basis 
based on compliance with the statutory duty of care.  
 
 
12) Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small -to- 
medium sized businesses applying guardrails?  
 
Some guardrails can be tailored to the size of a business and the nature of the AI 
system. For instance, small -medium sized businesses could be subject to less 
extensive disclosure requirements and less burdensome human intervention 
requirements . Only guardrails that are truly necessary to ensure safe and 
responsible AI development should be mandated for small -medium sized 
businesses . However, it is al so important to consider the size of impact of the 
potential AI system and not purely the size of the business who developed or 
deployed such systems.  
 
Regulatory options to mandate guardrails  
 
13) Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high -risk  
settings? What opportunities should the government take into account in 
considering each approach?  
 
Option 3 – a whole economy approach – is the most suitable regulatory approach, 
given the broad and evolving nature of AI. AI laws should be consolidated  into one 
single piece of legislations so that they are easily accessible to businesses and 
consumers.  This allows legislatures and/or delegated authorities to pass 
regulations that apply specific aspects of the legislation. This approach would 
ensure that AI legislative requirements and obligations are consistent across 
sectors, which reduces the regulator y burden for multi -sector organizations. 
Overall, this option allows for the most consistency flexibility and enforcement.  
 
In considering each approach, the government should consult a broad range of 
stakeholders in both the public and private sectors on the design of a 
comprehensive AI regulatory framework.  
 
The government should consider which option best allows for a consistent, uniform 
approach to AI regulation that recognizes different ways that AI is applied across 
sectors.   
14) Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the  
Australian  Government should consider?  
 
An AI legal regime or framework should not conform too closely with existing 
Australian legal frameworks to the extent that they conflict with AI legal regimes in 
other jurisdictions, such as Canada and the EU. One danger is that organizations 
with operati ons in multiple jurisdictions may be subject to conflicting AI legal 
obligations and requirements across jurisdictions.  Therefore, the Australian 
government should model its regulatory framework on existing frameworks in other 
jurisdictions, such as Canada  and the EU. 
 
The broad and evolving scope of AI issues poses a risk for regulators, regardless 
of which regulatory option is chosen. The relevant laws and regulations must adapt 
to ongoing developments in AI and subsequent risks but organizations should not 
be overly -burdened with legal obligations and requirements.  
 
Ensuring compliance with the laws and appropriate enforcement is a challenge 
with any  legal and regulatory framework. Therefore, any laws or regulations that 
are enacted to implement the mandatory guardrails should be binding on 
organizations and the regulatory body should have appropriate enforcement 
powers to compel  compliance.  
 
15) Which regulatory opti ons will best ensure that guardrails for high -risk AI can  
adapt  and respond to  step-changes in technology?  
 
Option 3 – a whole economy approach – would enable the Australian government 
to adapt the guardrails to technological advances and developments in v arious 
sectors.  Option 3 would also allow for the creation of a regulatory agency/body that 
is tasked with overseeing and enforcing AI laws/regulations  and implementing new 
regulations to adapt to technological developments .  
 
16) Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps or inconsistencies with Australia’s  
existing laws for the  development and deployment of AI? Which regulatory option  
best addresses this, and why?  
 
Regulatory risk regarding  the development and deployment of AI stems from the 
absence of regulation that prohibits organizations from using publicly available 
content on the internet to train their AI models without  license  or consent  is a 
concern . Organizations should be required to enter into licensing agreements for 
the use of AI training data that is scraped from the internet. AI -generated content 
that is trained on unlicensed content may infringe  the copyright of those who 
created the content contained in the training data set.  One solution is to require 
organizations to maintain records of the source of its training data . These records 
should be made available to the relevant audiences, including IP owners and 
consumers  who want to understand the provenance of the data set on wh ich the model was trained . Additionally, the government should introduce a statutory duty 
or certification scheme that encourages organizations to enter into licensing 
agreements for training data.  
 
In parallel, and as mentione d above, data privacy is an adjunct human right that is 
under threat when discussing AI. Web scraping has managed to get around strict 
privacy laws, often on the basis that if data is publicly available online it is 
considered  fair game. But just because data is public should not equate to it being  
public domain. Privacy laws extend to publicly available information and even 
when many can access it the principles of privacy still apply.  
 
Scraping personal data serves purposes like web searches, archival, generative 
AI and academic research. But in AI applications scraping raises big ethical 
questions. Scraping increases the risk of surveillance, harassment and automated 
decision making which affects individuals and society in harmful ways directly and 
indirectly.  
 
The complexity of scraping cannot  be solved by just tweaking existing privacy 
frameworks. This requires a fundamental rethinking of privacy paradigms and new 
legal approaches than the ones in most regulations. The tension between scraping 
and privacy principles is clear. But eliminating s craping would break the internet, 
hinder AI progress and impede legitimate research and journalism.  
 
Trying to fit scraping into the existing patchwork of privacy laws will produce 
inconsistent and disjointed legal precedents. A better approach would be to create 
a unified theoretical framework that aligns scraping with privacy. This could start 
by drawin g from existing regulatory models like the GDPR which provides 
guidance by focusing on legitimate grounds for processing and clearly defining 
when and how scraping can be justified

1.2 Overview  
Overall, we support the advancement of AI as a tool in the video game industry to ultimately 
enhance player enjoyability, accessibility , and safety. Unlike most other contexts and use 
cases of AI, AI use in video games is focused on entertainment, safety, or innovation 
purposes and is, therefore,  low-risk. Noting that the consultation primarily focuses  on high -
risk AI and associated guardrails and regulatory responses, we do not consider that these 
should apply to the video game context.  
We reiterate from our previous submission that AI in video games is not a context that would 
benefit from , or require , additional regulatory oversight.4 Concerns with AI largely do not 
directly correlate to the use of AI in video games. While AI in video games will unlikely 
require regulation,  any regulation should be evidence - and risk -based, proportionate, 
carefully scoped and limited to what is practically necessary. Further, any regulation of AI 
should not inadvertently impact video games that contain or use low-risk AI technology. If 
specific AI regulation is to be established, AI regulation should be industry -focused, 
particularly given the lower risk of harm in video games compared to other sectors . 
Additionally, should the government decide to proceed with regulation, consideration 
should be given to ensure regulatory coherence  with international approaches, where 
appropriate . That being said, references to international regulatory arrangements such as 
the EU AI Act  need to be cognisant of the context in which it operates. This includes the fact 
that such legislation is relatively new, having only commenced operation several weeks ago  
on 1 August 2024,5 and therefore at its infancy in terms of implementation and addressing 
any teething issues that may very likely arise.  Further, the EU AI Act also operates along with 
other EU digital -related legislation such as the EU ’s General Data Protection Regulation 
(GPDR) , Data Governance Act, Digital Markets Act, Digital Services Act , and Data Act .  
Therefore,  it is essential  to take  a holistic approach when considering introducing  any form 
of regulation and how it interacts with existing legislation . Australia will be no different with 
our various regulations when having regard to AI such as online safety, privacy, security, IP 
(including copyright), and consumer and competition laws . 
We would also caution against introducing additional reforms that overreach and create 
regulatory uncertainty and complexity to the current Australian regulatory landscape 
without proper identification and assessment of the problems (if any) and potential 
solutions based on firm policy evidence. As a matter of good regulatory practice and policy

2. Defining high -risk AI  
Question 1 . Do the proposed principles adequately capture high -risk AI? Are there any 
principles we should add or remove? Please identify any:  low-risk use cases that are 
unintentionally captured ; categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as 
uses for defence or national security purposes.  
The discussion paper proposes principles to guide whether the use of an AI system is high -
risk, namely:  
a. The risk of adverse impacts to an individual’s rights recognised in Australian human 
rights law without justification, in addition to Australia’s international human rights 
law obligations  
b. The risk of adverse impacts to an individual’s physical or mental health or safety  
c. The risk of adverse legal effects, defamation or similarly significant effects on an 
individual  
d. The risk of adverse impacts to groups of individuals or collective rights of cultural 
groups  
e. The risk of adverse impacts to the broader Australian economy, society, environment 
and rule of law  
f. The severity and extent of those adverse impacts outlined in principles (a) to (e) 
above.  
Generally, we are supportive of a principles -based approach and adopting internationally 
recognised approaches, where it is appropriate to do so .

3. Guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability 
of AI  
The Proposals Paper proposes mandatory guardrails for AI systems used in high -risk 
settings, as well as high -risk GPAI systems.  Given that we do not consider video games to 
fall under the high -risk category, we have limited comments in this area . 
Question 10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across 
the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately? For example, are 
the requirements assigned to developers and deployers appropriate ? 
If we a pply  a risk -based approach, this implies that the regulatory requirements should be 
proportionate to the risk associated with any organisation or given point in the supply chain , 
as opposed to arbitrary definitions and thresholds. However, further considerations are 
needed to a ssess the risk appropriately and identify the  harm . There are already well -
established principles for conducting risk assessments based on severity and probability of 
harm.  
The purpose of a risk assessment is to evaluate the real risk of the harm on the service  or 
along the supply chain , taking into account current mitigation measures. Ignoring these 
measures would mean assessing a different service altogether. A proper risk assessment 
process should guide companies in identifying areas needing more attention to mitigate 
residual user risk s. Once these actions are taken, companies can update their risk 
assessments accordingly.  
Similarly, when evaluating the risk level of identified potential harm, a single occurrence 
should not automatically classify the harm as a higher risk. While such an incident may 
suggest a potential risk, this should be considered in the context of all av ailable evidence. 
Factors like the frequency or probability of incidents, the degree of harm, the proportion of 
verified complaints related to the harm, and the mitigation measures in place must be 
considered . It would be unreasonable to label a service as  a higher risk, and impose 
additional obligations, based solely on an isolated incident or even a technical possibility 
of an incident occurring.  
Regardless, we do not consider this issue applicable to video games, which are low -risk in 
nature with respect to AI.  
Question 12. Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small -
to-medium sized businesses applying guardrails ? 
Smaller  businesses face relatively higher burdens to meet any given obligation for any form 
of regulation. While there should be a risk -based approach, proportionality also means that 
weight should be given to the size of the business and its  capability  and resources  to meet 
any obligation.

Department of Industry, Science and Resources

The Reserve Bank of Australia appreciates the opportunity to provide feedback on the proposal s 
paper , ‘Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-risk Settings ’. We are not making specific 
recommendations . However , we would like to raise some concerns and seek clarity around certain 
aspects of the paper . 
1. Defining high -risk AI  
The proposals paper attempt s to clarify the concept of general -purpose AI (GPAI), including on page 8 
where it states:  
General -purpose AI (GPAI) models (that is, AI systems that could be used for a wide range of 
purposes) are the next evolution of AI. GPAI models, such as GPT -n, DALL -E, and Sora, can now 
generate ‘human -like’ text, images, and videos based on simple user prompts.  
This description  lacks specificity. F urther , the definition of GPAI on page 9 as ‘an AI model that is 
capable of being used, or capable of being adapted for use, for a variety of purposes, both for direct 
use as well as for integration in other systems ’ does not clearly distinguish it from narrow AI systems. 
Narrow AI is defined in the paper as:  
[A] type of AI system or model that is focused on defined tasks and uses to address a specific 
problem. Unlike GPAI models, these types of AI systems cannot be used for a broader range of 
problems without being re -designed.  
The distinction between ‘adapting’ a model and ‘re -designing’ it is ambiguous. For example, a logistic 
regression model designed to classify flowers – which is a narrow AI application – can be re -designed 
to classify trees. This re-design process could be interpreted as adaptation, thus falling under the 
current definition of GPAI.  
Given this ambiguity, we suggest dedicating a section of the paper  to clearly define GPAI and narrow 
AI. As it stands, the current definition risks unintentionally categori sing low -risk use cases as GPAI.  
In addition, the proposed principles -based approach to defining high -risk AI seems overly broad, 
potentially capturing low -risk applications. This could deter the use of models to produce rigorous 
assessments of public policies and/or deter cautious entiti es from investing in AI. For example, in an 
economics or finance setting, it is not clear if a machine learning model used as an input (among 
many) when assessing the impact of a public policy or producing a forecast would be classified as high 
risk. Witho ut greater clarity in the definitions of high -risk AI, broad regulations could inadvertently 
encompass long -standing applications of AI and machine learning models used as inputs (among D24/290068  GENERAL  2 
 many) for analytical purposes, leading to unintended consequences and inefficiencies in fulfilling our 
charter functions and thereby serving the public.  
There is also ambiguity about the role an AI model must play in decision -making to be considered high  
risk. For instance, if generative AI is used to produce a variable or indicator that constitutes just one of 
many inputs into a policy deliberation – including human judgement – would the use of AI in this 
context be considered high  risk? Clear er guidelines on the significance of AI in decision -making 
processes are needed.  
2. Guardrails  ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of 
AI 
A clear risk assessment methodology with examples of high -, medium -, and low -risk categories could 
make the guardrails more meaningful. The controls framework should align with and expand on 
existing guidance, such as the Australian Cyber Security Centre’s guidelines for deploying AI systems 
securely.1 This approach would allow for independent updates and ensure that existing investments in 
controls could  be reused and expanded.  
Establishing an AI provider certification framework would be helpful for independent testing and 
verification against a standard, indicating that AI technologies are safe to use. An example is the 
hosting certification framework for cloud providers managed  by the Australian government.  
There also needs to be clear guidance on the rules that apply to consumers, developers and 
platforms.  
Further, t here should be specific provisions addressing data leakage, data usage and attestation to 
ensure data security and privacy. Additionally, AI -generated content could be clearly labelled, similar 
to food labelling (e.g. ‘may contain nuts’), to inform consumers that the content was generated using 
AI. 
3. Regulatory options  to mandate guardrails  
We understand that the proposal s paper  outlines three regulatory options: adapting existing 
regulatory frameworks, introducing framework legislation and creating a new AI -specific Act. We do 
not prefer one option over the others. However, we would value further clarity on how each option 
would  be implemented and their potential impact on existing regulatory frameworks and industry 
practices.  
In conclusion, in our view refining the proposals in the paper to address the concerns raised above 
and to provide clarity on definitions, guardrails and regulatory options will help create a balanced 
regulatory environment that promotes innovation while ensuring the safe and responsible use of AI. 
We appreciate the o pportunity to provide feedback and look forward to continued engagement on 
this important issue.

 Introduction  
Engineers Australia welcomes the opportunity to continue supporting  the Australian Government with 
the ongoing work related to  safe and responsible use of AI  in Australia . Engineers are essential to the 
development, implementation, integration, utilisation and maintenance of artificial intelligent systems 
and products.   
Engineers Australia’s submission to the S afe and Responsible AI in Australia  consultation  called for a 
balanced, sector -specific, and risk -based approach to regulating high -risk AI applications, including the 
development of sector -specific standards, technology -specific regulations, and industry body 
guidelines and controls.  These measures are essential for maximising AI’s benefit for society while 
preventing harm, building public trust and ensuring international competitiveness.  
AI and the impact on the engineering profession  
Emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence are reshaping many professions globally. 
Businesses, the tertiary sector and governments need to keep pace with these changes. In engineering, 
this means equipping engineers and engineering businesses to effectively leverage technology 
advancements, while hav ing appropriate safeguards in place against associated risks. To address this 
need; it is crucial to build a holistic understanding of the challenges, risks and opportunities associated 
with emergin g technologies in engineering.    
A forthcoming report to be released by Engineers Australia  later this year  has been exploring the 
impact of AI and emerging technologies on the engineering profession.  Key findings from this report 
include:  
▪ AI is transforming the engineering profession , including GenAI  (generative AI)_ , however it is 
mainly being used to increase  productivity .  
▪ Over 70 per cent of engineers agree GenAI will increase productivity in engineering, however, 82 
per cent believe GenAI will always require oversight.  
▪ One of the main challenges the profession faces is how to keep pace with the changes, ensuring 
engineers can effectively leverage advancements while safeguarding against associated risks.  
▪ Clarity and understanding of AI  are crucial, including developing a clear understanding of 
appropriate use and risks . This helps to boost engineers’ confidence and ability to use GenAI and 
AI tools correctly.  
▪ Open communication and training , policies, guidance and support also help mitigate risk of misuse 
and data breaches.  
About this submission  
This submission provides feedback to the questions raised in the Department of Industry, Science and 
Resources’ (DISR) proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings . The 
submission has been developed in consultation with Engineers Australia’s members from Engineers 
Australia’s College of Information, Telecommunications and Electronics Engineers and the Risk 
Engineering Society .
