Prof Toby Walsh FAA FTSE Chief Scientist @ UNSW.ai 3 October 2024 Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-Risk Settings Introduction1.0. This submission is provided by the AI Institute of the University of New South Wales, UNSW.ai. The AI Institute is the largest research institute in Australia devoted solely to artiﬁcial intelligence. Over 300 academics from across the university are connected to the Institute, developing and using AI for a broad range of applications. We welcome the opportunity to provide input on the proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings. 1.1. Artiﬁcial intelligence offers an unparalleled opportunity for Australia to improve economic, societal and environmental outcomes.  A recent study by Microsoft and the Tech Council of Australia estimated that generative AI alone could contribute as much as $115 billion a year to Australia’s economy by 2030. The broader use of AI within the Australian economy could grow GDP by around 20%. There is perhaps no other technological change arriving in the next couple of decades that will be as disruptive or as valuable.1.2. However, as with any opportunity, this comes with signiﬁcant associated risks. The greatest risk by far is that Australia fails to adopt AI quickly enough, permitting the ﬁnancial beneﬁts of AI to ﬂow offshore and, lacking sovereign AI capability, risking Australia to be held hostage by outside interests. Unfortunately, in the last 15 years, we have seen signiﬁcant declines in R&D investment in Australia. Worrying, we are the only major OECD economy that reduced its percentage of GDP invested in R&D. 1.3. Other countries are making signiﬁcantly larger investments in AI compared to Australia. The last ﬁve years have seen the Australian government announce an additional $142 million in the AI space. However, if we are to be competitive in this area, we need to invest much more in fundamental AI and safety research, and not just in translating existing research into practice. Current research funding levels are uncompetitive compared to other nations. For instance, Canada, which has a similar population and economy to Australia, just announced an additional $2.4 billion for AI research. Unless we lift our game, we will miss out. The consequences will be dire.AI INSTITUTE, UNSW SYDNEY 11.4. This submission outlines our recommendations for implementing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings, focusing on deﬁning high-risk AI, implementing guardrails, and choosing an appropriate regulatory approach.Executive Summary2.0. Our key recommendations are:•Adopt an impact-based approach to deﬁning high-risk AI, using principles rather than a rigid list.•Adapt existing legal frameworks to mandate the guardrails, but add some focused and new regulations to deal with new harms (e.g. for deepfakes and for biometrics). •Establish an AI Ofﬁce to provide expertise in monitoring and enforcing AI regulations.•Provide ﬁnancial support and incentives to business, especially SMEs, to deploy current AI technologies like generative AI responsibly.•Substantially increase investment in fundamental AI research and AI safety to ensure Australia proﬁts from future waves of AI innovation and leads the way with the responsible use of AI.•Support efforts to improve AI literacy among the workforce and general public.Deﬁning High-Risk AI3.0. We largely support the proposed principles-based approach to deﬁning high-risk AI. This ﬂexible framework can adapt to rapidly evolving AI capabilities better than a ﬁxed list of high-risk use cases. However, we recommend providing detailed guidance and examples to help organizations interpret and apply these principles.3.1. We also suggest that high-risk AI should encompass not just AI applications like predictive policing where the impacts on an individual can be large, but also applications where the impact on an individual might be small but the number of individuals impacted is large (e.g. AI used for assigning gig work to workers, or for workplace surveillance). We describe this as an impact-based approach to deﬁning high-risk AI. 3.2. The proposed principles appear comprehensive, covering key areas of potential harm. We suggest adding explicit consideration of:•Impacts on vulnerable populations•Potential for large-scale societal disruption•Risks to critical infrastructure and essential services3.2. Regarding general-purpose AI (GPAI) models, we believe they should be subject to mandatory guardrails due to their wide-ranging potential impacts. However, the deﬁnition of high-risk GPAI should be based on capabilities rather than arbitrary technical metrics like AI INSTITUTE, UNSW SYDNEY 2FLOPs. We recommend establishing an expert panel to assess GPAI models and determine risk levels.Mandatory Guardrails4.0. We broadly support the proposed mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI systems. These align well with international best practices and cover crucial aspects of responsible AI development and deployment. We offer the following suggestions: •Transparency: As well as mandating clear disclosure of AI use to end-users and affected individuals [Guardrail 6], we suggest that AI systems should be designed explicitly not to mislead users (see the proposal for “Turing Red Flag” laws, https://cacm.acm.org/opinion/turings-red-ﬂag/). Additionally AI generated outputs should be digitally watermarked to facilitate transparency.•Fairness and non-discrimination: We propose adding a guardrail about the need to assess and mitigate bias in AI systems.•Human oversight: We propose replacing Guardrail 5 with a simpler and more stringent Guardrail in which we “Require meaningful human control of high-risk AI systems”. We need control not just oversight. And we do not want to specify explicitly how to obtain this.•Security and robustness: We propose adding a guardrail to require appropriate cybersecurity measures and resilience to adversarial attacks.Regulatory Approach5.0. Of the options presented, we believe Option 1 (adopting the guardrails within existing regulatory frameworks as needed) offers the best balance of comprehensiveness, ﬂexibility and speed. However, we also see need for a few pieces of new and specialised AI regulation to deal with novel harms (for instance, to protect against the misuse of deepfakes, or against the misuse of facial recognition and other biometric recognition technologies). 5.1. We recommend that a dedicated AI Ofﬁce be established to provide technical expertise and coordinate enforcement of AI regulation. Existing regulators often lack appropriate expertise and resources to police the AI space. Additional Considerations6.0. Research and Development: To maintain Australia's competitiveness in AI, we strongly urge increased government investment in fundamental AI research and AI safety. This is crucial for developing sovereign AI capabilities with future waves of AI innovations, and fostering a thriving AI industry.AI INSTITUTE, UNSW SYDNEY 36.1. We recommend government provide ﬁnancial support and other incentives to business, especially SMEs, to deploy emerging AI technologies like generative AI responsibly and in line with the proposed guardrails.6.2. AI Literacy and Workforce Preparation: We recommend government support for initiatives to improve AI literacy among the general public and prepare the workforce for AI-driven changes. This could include funding for education programs and retraining initiatives. We point to initiatives like “Day of AI Australia” which we have been involved in, and which has engaged over 100,000 students in Australia over the last few years, with a focus on under-represented groups like indigenous and female students. 6.3. International Cooperation: Given the global nature of AI development, we encourage the government to pursue international cooperation on AI safety and governance. Alignment with key partners on core principles and standards will beneﬁt Australian businesses and researchers.Conclusion7.0. Introducing mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI is a crucial step in ensuring the safe and responsible development of this transformative technology. With a carefully crafted regulatory approach, Australia can foster innovation while protecting against potential harms. The AI Institute stands ready to provide technical support to the government in further developing and implementing these important measures.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce (“Chamber”) is the world’s largest business federation, representing the 
interests of more than three million enterprises of all sizes and sectors  operating in over 50 countries, to 
promote free enterprise and advance trade and investment globally . The Chamber’s Australia Working 
Group promote s the bilateral economic relationship via high -level meetings, briefings, and other event s, 
while fostering a policy dialogue aimed at the removal of barriers to trade and investment and 
enhancing U.S. -Australia trade promotion ef forts. The Chamber is a longtime advocate for strong 
commerci al ties between the United States and Australia . 
 
We make this submission in response to the Australian Government’s discussion paper on guardrails for 
AI in high -risk settings.  
 
AI is an innovative and transformational technology. The Chamber has long advocated for AI as a 
positive force, capable of addressing major societal challenges and spurring economic expansion for the 
benefit of consumers, businesses, and society. It is vital to  promote rules based and competitive trade, 
and foster alignment around emerging technologies, including through  internationally -recognized  
standards  that encourage  the responsible use of AI. 
 
The Chamber has encouraged p olicymakers in multiple jurisdictions to refrain from instituting overly 
prescriptive regulations or regulations that do not account for the novel qualities of AI technologies. 
Potential negative examples include stifling innovation,  e.g., if regulations are too restrictive or 
prescriptive, they may impede the development and deployment of new AI technologies. This can 
hinder the ability of businesses to explore novel use cases, create disruptive solutions, and drive 
technologica l advancements.  Overly prescriptive regulations can also reduc e flexibility .  
 
AI technologies are rapidly evolving, and regulatory frameworks need to be adaptable to keep pace with 
these advancements. If regulations are rigid and fail to account for the dynamic nature of AI, they can 
limit the ability of businesses to adapt and iter ate their AI systems as new technologies and 
methodologies emerge. Furthe r, overly burdensome regulations can create a  competitive disadvantage  
for Australia . For example,  if regulations are inconsistent, fragmented, or overly burdensome in 
Australia compared  to its trading partners , it could  create a competitive disadvantage for businesses 
that operate and invest in Australia. This can lead to a diversion of AI investments and talent to more 
favorable regulatory environments, impacting the competitiveness of Australia.  
 
Interoperable  and globally recognized regulatory frameworks can help foster global cooperation.  
Additionally , regulations that fail to consider the unique qualities of AI technologies may not effectively 
address the risks associated with AI systems. One -size-fits-all regulations might not adequately account  
 
   
 
for the diverse range of AI applications, their varying levels of risk, or the roles of different actors in the 
AI lifecycle. This can result in either overregulation that stifles low -risk applications or under regulation  
that fails to adequately mitigate risks in high -risk areas.   
 
Excessive regulatory requirements can  also impose substantial compliance costs on businesses, 
especially smaller enterprises that may lack the resources to navigate complex regulatory frameworks. If 
compliance becomes too burdensome  in Australia , it could reduce  the adoption of AI technologies, 
particularly for Australian  SMEs , hindering their ability to compete in the global market and reap the 
potential benefits of AI.  
 
The better alternative , as highlighted in the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Principles on A rtificial 
Intelligence , is to  develop targeted rules  that effectively address the tradeoffs  associated with various AI 
use-cases and the roles of different actors in the AI developmental lifecycle . These rules should be 
proportionate and based on the risk of the intended use , technologically impartial , and technically 
feasible. These approaches not only increase safety and build trust, but also allow for necessary 
flexibility and innovation , given that AI is a rapidly evolving technology. Controls to reduce the risk of AI 
harm should focus on areas such as unintended bias mitigation, model monito ring, fairness , and 
transparency.   
 
As the  Australian government  proceeds with  the assessment of introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI 
in High -Risk Settings in Australia , we ask that you keep in the mind the following broad principles:  
 
Develop Risk -Based Approaches to Governing AI  
 
Governments should incorporate risk -based approaches rather than prescriptive requirements into  
frameworks governing the development, deployment, and use of AI. It is simply not feasible to  
establish a uniform set of rules that can adequately address the distinctive features of each  
industry utilizing AI and its effect on individuals. Indeed, we recognize  that AI use cases that involve a 
high risk should face a higher degree of scrutiny than a use case where the risk of concrete harm to  
individuals is low. New regulations should be risk-based and proportionate with a focus on “ high risk ” 
use cases rather than on entire sectors or technologies. Additionally, any risk assessment should account 
for the significant social, safety, and economic benefits that may accrue when an AI application replaces 
a human action.  
 
The Chamber advocates for policy makers to be mindful of existing rules and regulations when it comes 
to regulation of artificial intelligence. Governments do not need to create redundant legislation or 
regulation . It is crucial  to remember  that “high  risk” sectors like autonomous vehicles and healthcare 
diagnostics  are already subject to extensive regulation by established bodies such as the  Australian  
Department  of Industry, Science and Resources .  While the  integration of AI technologies within these 
sectors  can introduce new dimensions of complexity and potential risks , it is again crucial to recognize 
that if a gap in current law is found , they  need to  complement and align with  already  existing sector - 
 
   
 
specific regulations .  As opposed to duplicating efforts or creating conflicting requirements  which can 
increase risk.   
 
Alignment  and coordination between regulatory bodies is vital to ensur ing that AI technologies are 
adequately governed  to consider the unique challenges they present while avoiding unnecessary 
regulatory burdens. By leveraging the expertise and insights of established regulatory agencies ,   
Australia  AI-specific regulations can build upon existing frameworks and address the novel aspects and 
risks associated with AI applications within highly regulated sectors . 
 
Balanced Policy Approaches for Managing Risks in General Purpose AI Systems  
 
Instead of classifying all General Purpose AI (GPAI) systems as high -risk, policy approaches should 
balance innovation and risk management. These approaches should be risk -based, tailored to the 
specific risks associated with GPAI systems, fair, and equita ble, without placing an undue burden on 
providers. For example, classifying GPAI systems according to their risk level and applying different 
regulatory requirements to each class would allow for responsible development and use of GPAI 
systems while ensuri ng that associated risks are properly managed.  
 
Additionally, there should be a focus on transparency, accountability, and human -centered design. 
Providers of GPAI systems should be transparent about the risks associated with their systems and 
accountable for their use, ensuring that users are aware of the risks. GPAI systems should be designed 
with human needs in mind, meaning they should be transparent, explainable, and fair, and should not 
be used in ways that harm or exploit humans. These policy  approaches would allow for the responsible 
development and use of GPAI systems while ensuring that associated risks are properly managed.  
 
Embrace International Regulatory Cooperation  
  
It is critical to advance multilateral cooperation on AI governance by strengthening mechanisms  
for global coordination on AI transparency. This includes promoting interoperable approaches to AI  
governance to enable best practices and minimize the risk of unnecessary regulatory divergences  
and trade restrictive practices emerging in the digital economy. Additionally, endorsing transparent,  
multi -stakeholder approaches to AI governance is essential, including in the development of  
voluntary standards, frameworks, and codes of practice that can bridge the gap between AI  
principles and its implementation. Multi-stakeholder initiatives have the greatest potential to identify 
gaps in AI outcomes and capabilities, and to mobilize AI actors to address them.  
 
The Australian Government can look to examples such as the United States’ approach, which includes 
the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) Artificial Intelligence Risk Management 
Framework (AI RMF) and the Commission on Artificial Intelligence Competitiveness, Inclusion, and 
Innovation . These models both  emphasize a risk -based approach to AI governance, highlighting the need 
for proportionate regulations that account for  different use cases and actors in the AI lifecycle .  
 
   
 
NIST's framework promotes safety, transparency, and accountability while fostering innovation, making 
it a suitable model for Australia’s  AI governance approach.  The Australian government can draw 
inspiration from these models to develop a robust AI governance regime that aligns with international 
best practices and addresses the unique challenges posed by AI technologies.  
 
Accelerated Cooperation on AI  
 
The Chamber and our members recognize that AI has the power to significantly transform societies and 
economies . To that end,  we share a commitment to government action that unlock s the vast 
opportunities and address es the potential risks arising from the rapid advancement of AI technologies.  
We emphasize the importance of engaging with companies, research institutions, civil society, and our 
allies and partners to ensure a well -rounded perspective .  Our collective aim is to accelerate  
collaboration on AI, prioritizing the safe and responsible development of this technology.  
 
Non -Market Economies  
 
Collaboration between the Australian government and U.S. on AI frameworks is paramount to counter  
the efforts of non -market economies, particularly China, to dominate the AI landscape. By aligning our 
approaches and sharing best practices, the Australian government and the U .S. can leverage each 
other’s  expertise, innovation ecosystems, and regulatory frameworks to ensure a competitive and 
ethical AI environment. Strengthening cooperation not only enhances the global influence of market -
based economies , but also establishes a unified front in advocating for responsible AI governance that 
upholds democratic values, safeguards privacy and data protection, and promotes fair competition. 
Together, Australia and the U .S. can shape a global AI landscape that prioritizes innovation, 
transparency, and the well -being of individuals and societies, countering the influence of non -market 
economies and fostering an ecosystem that drives global AI advancement.  
 
In conclusion, as Australia strives to be a policy leader in AI governance, it possesses a unique 
opportunity to inspire and encourage other nations to adopt these broad -based approaches . By 
championing risk -based frameworks, promoting private and public investment in AI research and 
development, embracing internationally recognized standards, fostering international regulatory 
cooperation, and accelerating collaboration on AI, Australia  can set a powerful example for responsible 
and innovative AI governance. Through its leadership , the Australian government  can help  shape a 
global landscape that fosters trust, supports economic growth, and harnesses the transformative 
potential of AI for the betterment of societies worldwide.  
 
We appreciate your consideration of these points,  and look forward to further engagements with the 
Australian government on AI.

Napier AI welcomes the Australia Government’s proposed guardrails on the use of artificial intelligence. We believe all AI models must be explainable and auditable, allowing stakeholders to understand and audit all of its decisions. On the proposed guard rail 4 to ‘Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the system once deployed’:
Rigorous testing of representative and accurate data is essential to assess AI’s performance and fairness in real scenarios. AI predictions can include a measure of confidence in the result, and standard testing procedures can help define the justification metrics to some extent. What cannot be avoided is the transparency aspect that has to come from some means of explaining how the models work in a way that the end user can understand. Validation of training and testing is critical to have confidence before the system is deployed.
Building interpretability layers into AI models needs to be integrated early in the development process. This ensures guardrail 6 of informing end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content.
It is critical that the output is explainable not just for data scientists, but also for end users, ensuring transparency and trust. Ensuring the team can explain the AI and its outputs also encourages wider confidence within a company through knowledge diffusion. To maintain accuracy, models must undergo regular audits, retesting, and retraining to prevent drift from their original performance metrics.
Using open-source models for AI

The data used for anti-money laundering and financial crime compliance checks are often highly confidential with financial and personally identifiable information of individuals, improper use of which could violate intellectual property and privacy concerns.
Sharing and accessing information, data and methodologies on using AI in such high-stake industries can even be misused by financial criminals who exploit transparency to identify money laundering risk thresholds and circumvent risk management measures. With full access to data, code, and documentation, results can be consistently replicated, so there's no question as to what's actually happening behind the scenes.
For businesses reliant on such third parties and insecure cloud environments, malicious data scientists could employ Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, to disrupt the server, service or network by overwhelming it with a flood of traffic.
Napier AI also welcomes the proposed principle to give regard to ‘The risk of adverse impacts to groups of individuals or collective rights of cultural groups’.
We agree that ‘AI systems have the potential to create highly unequal or damaging outcomes for specific groups and perpetuate existing inequalities’ as mentioned in the paper. Especially in high-stake sectors such as financial crime compliance, it is crucial to ensure that impact of poor AI generated outcomes don’t disadvantage people who are in lower socioeconomic groups and whose transaction patterns may not fit what financial institutions consider ‘normal’.
One significant concern in the financial services industry is the risk of poorly implemented AI systems “hallucinating” wrong answers, which can lead to incorrect decisions and actions. For instance, a sub-par AI model might generate false positives in compliance checks, fraud detection or misclassify customers’ creditworthiness, leading to unwarranted account freezes or loan denials. Research on AI tools used for legal practices has shown that large language models can provide incorrect facts up to 30% or the time and omit data up to 60% of the time. This is why care needs to be taken with any AI models that do not provide clear testing results and decision explanations with links to the original source data.

service quality, and targeted predatory practices.
For any AI solution, it is important that developers assess the stakeholders who are likely to be most vulnerable to the outcomes of the systems you’re building, and fine-tune strategies to accommodate their needs. To achieve meaningful human oversight, the person responsible for overseeing the AI system while it is in use must be able to access and interpret information regarding the system’s outputs. Those responsible for oversight must be sufficiently qualified to interpret output and understand the core capabilities and limitations of an AI model to accurately assess the accuracy of algorithmic advice. There should be continous training of human agents in these roles so that they’re efficiently skilled and equipped to understand and challenge the workings, decisions and outcome of the AI systems without becoming overly reliant on them.

technologies, across their entire lifecycle. TGA’s risk -based regulatory framework already considers the 
evolving nature of AI, ensuring patient safety while prom oting innovation. Applying additional, cross -sector

Promoting Innovation Worldwide October 4, 2024  ITI Response to Australia’s Proposals Paper for Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-Risk Settings  The Information Technology Industry Council (ITI) is the premier voice, advocate, and thought leader for the global information and communication technology industry. Founded in 19161, ITI is an international trade association that promotes public policies and industry standards that advance competition and innovation worldwide. We represent companies that span the tech ecosystem, including developers, deployers, and integrators of AI technology.  ITI is committed to fostering the responsible development and deployment of AI. We have been actively engaged in shaping AI policy around the world. In 2021, we issued a set of Global AI Policy Recommendations, aimed at helping governments facilitate an environment that supports AI while simultaneously recognizing that there are challenges that need to be addressed as the uptake of AI grows.2 We also launched our AI Futures Initiative in 2023, which is an initiative comprised of technical and policy experts aimed at addressing challenging questions that are emerging in the global conversation on AI. We have published several policy papers via this Initiative, including on the AI Value Chain and Foundation Models3, and our latest AI Accountability Framework,4 both of which we think are particularly relevant to Australia as it considers developing a regime to implement mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI systems and general-purpose AI models. We have also actively worked to inform the efforts of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)5 to create an AI Risk Management Framework (RMF) in the United States and have been consistently engaged with the EU throughout the development its AI Act.6   We support Australia’s overall goal of facilitating trust in AI technology. ITI and its members agree that there are important questions that need to be addressed related to the responsible development and use of AI technology. At the same time, given the evolving nature of AI technology, crafting a future-proof legal framework is a challenge. In seeking to do so, believe that global alignment and regulatory coherence are key goals that Australia should seek to achieve in developing mandatory AI guardrails. We are committed to working with Australian  1 Learn more at https://www.itic.org/  2 Our complete Global AI Policy Recommendations are available here: https://www.itic.org/documents/artificial-intelligence/ITI_GlobalAIPrinciples_032321_v3.pdf  3 ITI’s Understanding Foundation Models & the AI Value Chain paper is available here: https://www.itic.org/documents/artificial-intelligence/ITI_AIPolicyPrinciples_080323.pdf  4 ITI’s paper on Authenticating AI-Generated Content is available here: https://www.itic.org/policy/ITI_AIContentAuthorizationPolicy_122123.pdf  5 See ITI response to RFI on AI RMF Concept Paper here: ITI Comments on AI RMF Concept Paper FINAL.pdf 6 See, for example, ITI’s response to the Commission’s Proposal for an AI Act here, our trilogue recommendations here, as well as series of blog posts written to inform trilogue negotiations. We also recently offered feedback on the GPAI Code of Practice being developed by the EU AI Office.   
  
2 policymakers as they seek to develop legislation to address AI-related risks while supporting innovation. Below, we offer perspectives in response to several of the questions that Australia poses in its Consultation Paper.  Responses to Specific Questions  1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI? Are there any principles we should add or remove?   Please identify any:  • low-risk use cases that are unintentionally captured  • categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for defence or national security purposes.   ITI comment: We believe that the proposed principles appropriately capture the criteria for assessing when the use of an AI system is considered high-risk. In general, as we outline in our AI Accountability Framework, we view a high-risk AI system as one that is specifically designed or deployed to make decisions that have a legal or similarly significant impact on a person’s fundamental human rights, safety, or fair access to basic services. The above criteria adequately capture the principles that make-up our definition. 3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models? Is a more deﬁned approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?  • If you prefer a list-based approach (similar to the EU and Canada), what use cases should we include? How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?  • If you prefer a principles-based approach, what should we address in guidance to give the greatest clarity?   ITI comment: We appreciate that Australia is considering what the most appropriate way to designate high-risk AI systems is. While we appreciate that a principles/criteria-based approach allows for greater flexibility, we do not believe that such an approach engenders enough legal certainty for companies. It is not clear in practice how this approach would work, and we are concerned it may result in inadvertently capturing low-risk use cases. Indeed, without specific guidance on how to measure and quantify the risk – including understanding what constitutes too much risk -- organizations may either overestimate or underestimate the risk presented by an AI application. Because of this, we have generally been supportive of a list-based approach, assuming that the list is appropriately nuanced to exclude low-risk use cases. Providing an initial list of covered uses allows organization to have clarity about what might be captured and enables them to proceed confidently with low-risk use cases. With that in mind, Australia should also endeavor to include criteria in any forthcoming legislative framework that allows organizations to understand how such a list was constructed and how it may be updated moving forward. 5. Are the proposed principles ﬂexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?   ITI comments: Yes, the proposed principles are flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI.   
  
3 6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?   ITI comment: We do not believe that mandatory guardrails should apply to all GPAI models, except for those relating to documentation, which can be shared with downstream deployers. The approach that Australia proposes is, in our view, not proportionate to risk. To be sure, as Australia recognizes, there are many different ways in which GPAI models can be used, and based on the current definition of GPAI model, we are concerned that obligations will be disproportionate, capturing models that do not have capabilities of concern. Indeed, the current definition is very broad, capturing a wide range of models that may be used in low-risk settings. In our AI Accountability Framework, we differentiate between a foundation model and a frontier model for this reason and suggest that certain practices should apply to frontier model developers.7 As we have advocated for more broadly regarding AI regulation, the obligations levied upon an AI system should be proportionate to the level of risk that it poses to health, safety, or fundamental human rights. This should hold true regardless of whether an AI system relies on a foundation model, because the end use is often where risk to individuals materializes, regardless of the underlying technology.   We recognize that highly capable or very advanced models may present unique risks and agree that providers of these models can take steps to increase safety and security, transparency, and reduce risk. As such, we encourage Australia to target obligations around general-purpose AI models, applying governance measures to the most advanced GPAI models, which is consistent with the recommendations we put forth in our AI Accountability Framework.   In further developing its proposal, we encourage Australia to review both our Guide to Understanding Foundation Models8, which includes a series of policy recommendations, as well as our AI Accountability Framework,9 which outlines practices we believe are appropriate to apply to frontier models.  7. What are suitable indicators for deﬁning GPAI models as high-risk? For example, is it enough to deﬁne GPAI as high-risk against the principles, or should it be based on technical capability such as FLOPS (e.g. 10^25 or 10^26 threshold), advice from a scientiﬁc panel, government or other indicators?   ITI comment: While the principles are flexible, they will be difficult to apply in the context of GPAI models, largely because there may be instances in which the deployment context is unknown, making it difficult to estimate, for example, the risk of adverse impacts to an individual’s physical or mental health.   While FLOPS is an imperfect indicator, we believe it is an appropriate starting point to provide clarity about which types of general-purpose AI models are intended to be  7 We encourage the Australian government to review our Framework in more depth, including the way in which we delineate throughout the Framework which practices are most appropriate for a developer and deployer to take on. Available here: https://www.itic.org/documents/artificial-intelligence/AIFIAIAccountabilityFrameworkFinal.pdf 8 ITI’s Understanding Foundation Models & the AI Value Chain paper is available here: https://www.itic.org/documents/artificial-intelligence/ITI_AIPolicyPrinciples_080323.pdf  9 See FN 6 for link to the document.   
  
4 captured by regulatory requirements. However, in leveraging this approach, Australia should keep in mind that compute is an incomplete measure of the size and capabilities of a model, and it is not necessarily always a good indicator of risk. Smaller models, or a mixture of agents approach, which leverages several open-source AI models, may demonstrate similar capabilities, or even outperform individual models.10 As such, technological developments may have the potential to undermine regulatory thresholds that are based solely on FLOPS.   Even so, in order to facilitate regulatory convergence, we encourage Australia to use the 10^26 FLOPS threshold as introduced in the AI Executive Order to capture those models at the frontier. We also suggest that Australia consider incorporating additional criteria, perhaps modeled after that suggested in the definition of a dual-use foundation model included in the United States AI Executive Order.11   The term “dual-use foundation model” means an AI model that is trained on broad data; generally uses self-supervision; contains at least tens of billions of parameters; is applicable across a wide range of contexts; and that exhibits, or could be easily modified to exhibit, high levels of performance at tasks that pose a serious risk to security, national economic security, national public health or safety, or any combination of those matters.   If Australia proceeds with leveraging FLOPS as an initial threshold, we encourage Australia to ensure that it builds in a process to update the threshold and definition based on technological developments. This process should be undertaken in consultation with industry and should consider developments around the world to remain aligned to the extent possible.  8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings? Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?   ITI comment: The proposed mandatory guardrails are aligned with many of the practices we outline in our AI Accountability Framework. To be sure, in high-risk settings, we highlight practices that are appropriate for developers and deployers to take on. Such practices include risk and impact assessments, testing, taking steps to facilitate downstream transparency about the AI system itself, providing notice to end-users and ensuring that data is high quality and relevant.12   Add guardrail around cybersecurity risk management. We also suggest that both developers and deployers consider cybersecurity risk in the context of an overarching risk management program, and design AI systems with cybersecurity in mind. Available here: https://www.itic.org/documents/artificial-intelligence/AIFIAIAccountabilityFrameworkFinal.pdf    
  
5 Australia consider whether it is appropriate to add a principle focused specifically on cybersecurity.   Clarify how impact assessments can contribute to the guardrail specific to implementing a risk management process. We appreciate that risk assessment and risk management play key roles in mitigating potential harms introduced by AI systems. We encourage Australia to clarify how impact assessments play a role in furthering risk management, and ideally differentiate between risk and impact assessment. Indeed, we understand risk and impact assessments to be two different tools, which serve different functions in the overall risk management process. A risk assessment is the process by which an organization considers the risks presented by the development, deployment, and use of an AI system. An impact assessment is a type of risk management tool, which is narrower than a risk assessment, and can help an organization evaluate the potential impact (both positive and negative) that an AI system might have on an individual or group that may interact with or otherwise be affected by an AI system. Adding clarity of this nature can help organizations better understand how both tools can be leveraged most helpfully in the overarching risk management process.   Considerations regarding the guardrail on publishing an accountability process. We appreciate the important role that accountability plays in fostering trustworthy AI. In considering how to operationalize this guardrail, particularly regarding publishing information, Australia should ensure it scopes such a requirement to avoid creating legal and/or strategic risks for companies.   Considerations regarding the guardrail on protecting AI systems and implementing data governance measures to manage data quality and provenance. As we highlight in our AI Accountability Framework and as Australia recognizes, high-quality data plays a critical role in the performance of an AI system. We therefore appreciate that Australia is considering how to best operationalize this guardrail, and that it emphasizes the key role of representative data that is fit-for-purpose. However, in its discussion of Guardrail 3, Australia specifically references the EU AI Act, which requires GPAI model providers to make publicly available a summary of the content used for training a GPAI model. If Australia takes a similar approach, we encourage it to consider comments that we provided to the EU AI Office’s Consultation on the first GPAI Code of Practice, which reflected the fact that such summaries should be high-level, and should exclude business sensitive information, data that were used based on licensing agreements, proprietary datasets, or other datasets acquired from third-parties, as these are commercially sensitive and the data is not relevant for other rightsholders.13  Considerations regarding the guardrail on informing end-users about AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI-generated content, and AI-generated content. We appreciate that Attachment E.6 includes phrases such as “as technically feasible” and/or “best efforts,” which reflect that many of the technical solutions for watermarking and/or labelling AI-generated content are still evolving.14 For example, there are not yet well- 13 See ITI’s comments responding to the EU AI Office Consultation on the Code of Practice here: https://www.itic.org/news-events/news-releases/iti-flexibility-engagement-with-industry-and-global-alignment-a-must-in-implementing-general-purpose-ai-models-rules  14 For a more robust discussion of practices that are currently being used to authenticate AI-generated content, their benefits, and their limitations, please see our Guide to Authenticating AI-Generated   
  
6 developed proposals for watermarking in text. As such, as Australia considers how best to operationalize this guardrail, it should take care to recognize the current technological limitations and seek to invest in further research and development around content authentication practices. We appreciate that Australia highlights the C2PA (and Content Credentials) as an example of a digital content provenance standard that can help with the implementation of Part 3 of this guardrail.     Considerations regarding the guardrail on enabling human control or intervention. We believe that human oversight can be critical in controlling risks in certain instances, though it is not always meaningful or needed and should reflect the specific context of the AI use case. However, Australia should recognize that human oversight is not an infallible solution, leading to a false sense of security and perpetuating unwanted results, if other issues, such as the quality and accuracy of the data used, are ignored. As such, clarifying when and how to leverage "human controls" will be important.  Considerations regarding guardrail on conformity assessment. We appreciate that conformity assessment can play a role in helping to foster trust. Conformity assessment systems include a suite of tools that provide for a range of approaches that can be calibrated to the level of risk associated with an AI system. However, whether the use of conformity assessment is appropriate in the context of AI systems should be carefully considered, and at a minimum requires identifying whether standards exist that can be used for conducting conformity assessment related activities such as certification of products or systems. Australia should clarify whether there are standards that it intends to leverage in order to underpin the conformity assessment regime it proposes introducing as a mandatory guardrail and delineate what those standards are. To promote global regulatory interoperability, which is critical for international research collaboration and global business operations, we recommend that Australia leverage international, rather than national or regional, standards. However, even international standards, which typically undergo updates every 3-5 years, struggle to keep pace with rapid AI innovation, which is one reason why we recommend broadly aligning policy requirements with international standards to promote voluntary adoption instead of mandating international standards adoption. If Australia proceeds with leveraging conformity assessments as one mechanism for demonstrating compliance and building trust, conformity assessments should not be the only mechanism for demonstrating compliance.   In rapidly evolving areas such as AI systems, the use of conformity assessments and/or other mechanisms for demonstrating compliance and building trust must be tailored in a manner that factors in the constantly evolving nature of AI systems. A static approach where an AI system or product is tested or certified at the outset may provide little assurance about the product’s operation after it has been in use. In any case, any conformity assessment scheme or other approach to facilitating compliance should be developed within already existing sectorial frameworks (e.g., medical devices, motor vehicles). 7 9. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately? For example, are the requirements assigned to developers and deployers appropriate?   Yes, we believe the proposed guardrails distribute responsibility appropriately.  10.  Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sucicient to address the risks of GPAI? How could we adapt the guardrails for dicerent GPAI models, for example low-risk and high-risk GPAI models?   We believe that the mandatory guardrails are largely sufficient to address high-risk GPAI models. They reflect the practices that we outline in our AI Accountability Framework that we believe frontier model developers should undertake, including 1) risk and impact assessments, 2) testing, 3) documenting and sharing information about the AI system; 4) disclosure to end users; and 5) ensuring that data is relevant and high quality and that safeguards are in place to protect privacy and IP. As we noted in response to q. 8, Australia may want to incorporate a guardrail around cybersecurity.   As we further reference earlier in our submission, we believe that it will be most beneficial for Australia to target these obligations to frontier models (and/or high-risk GPAI models), with a mandatory guardrail for all GPAI model developers around transparency and documentation to facilitate downstream risk management measures.   11. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings? What opportunities should the government take into account in considering each approach?   Of the three options presented, we believe Option 2 is the best choice, with Option 1 as an alternative. AI is a cross-cutting technology that can be used across sectors in very diverse contexts. As such, we believe that when sectoral authorities are appropriately resourced, sector-specific oversight is a more effective approach, given the fact that sectoral agencies better understand applications and risks within their sector and are therefore better positioned to assess compliance. With that in mind, it is also true that in the case of the proposed guardrails, there is the possibility that sector-specific regulators interpret their application differently, creating regulatory divergence or fragmentation in the Australian marketplace. Therefore, we believe that Option 2 will help to facilitate a common interpretation of guardrails, and foster consistency in their application across sectors. An overarching framework can create alignment based on a common set of underlying principles. We also appreciate that such an approach allows for the adaptation and amendment of existing laws and regulations to account for AI uses in lieu of the creation of a new set of rules.  In proceeding with such an approach, we encourage Australia to consider how it can streamline compliance processes, especially in instances where an organization is regulated under multiple regulatory frameworks and/or by multiple regulators. It may be helpful to consider creating a central coordinating body (similar to the UK’s Digital Cooperation   
  
8 Regulation Forum15) and/or centrally delivered functions that can help coordinate across sectors, similar to what the United Kingdom proposed it its AI White Paper.16  *** We appreciate the opportunity to provide feedback on Australia’s Proposals Paper for Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-Risk Settings. We encourage Australia to maintain global alignment in the development and implementation of the guardrails and stand ready to work with Australian policymakers to advance a tailored, risk-based approach to AI regulation. Response to the question
While broadly speaking we support the principles outlined in the consultation document, and agree with the Government that such an approach enables more flexibility and longevity, overreliance on principles could create ambiguity and open the regime to legal challenge. We therefore believe that a list-based approach, driven by and regularly reviewed against the principles, would be preferable.
That said, we would caution against the outright banning of AI applications or technologies, as this could risk stifling innovation in Australia, leaving it behind its global counterparts. Instead, we would propose that very high-risk applications or technologies could be tested and explored within limited testbeds, and under the close supervision of an independent watchdog that ensures the Government’s AI Ethics Principles are not breached.

8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
The proposed guardrails provide a solid foundation for mitigating the risks of AI used in high-risk settings. We are also pleased to see the Government’s commitment to developing a regulatory framework that aligns nationally and with likeminded jurisdictions. Such an approach will be key to minimising compliance burdens and ensuring the success of national regimes, regulating what is ultimately a global challenge.
That said, the application of the mandatory guardrails could be strengthened in the following ways:
Guardrail 2: Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks.
In addition to managing security vulnerabilities (as outlined in Attachment E), guidance should be provided on how developers implement secure-by-design and secure-by-default principles throughout the development lifecycle. Frameworks already exist which could form the basis of more detailed guidance, such as NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework and the cross-agency Guidelines for Secure AI System Development (https://www.cyber.gov.au/resources-business-and-government/governance-and-user-education/artificial-intelligence/guidelines-secure-ai-system-development).
Guardrail 4: Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the system once deployed. / Guardrail 10: Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with guardrails.
Such activities need to be undertaken on a continuous basis to ensure vulnerabilities are addressed and the latest threat landscape is understood and acted upon. In addition, where the risk profile necessitates (such as for high-risk systems or GPAI models), we believe independent continuous product validation should be mandated. In our experience, many claims made by AI product vendors, predominantly about products’ effectiveness in detecting threats, can be unproven or lack independent verification.
Guardrail 8: Be transparent with other organisations across the AI supply chain about data, models and systems to help them effectively address risks.
As the Government highlights in the discussion paper, most AI-based products in use today are ‘black box’ appliances that are placed onto networks and configured to consume data, process it and output decisions without humans having much knowledge of what’s happening. This means understanding and explaining why an AI system reached a certain decision can be very difficult and could be used maliciously by some organisations to provide cover for why a decision has been reached. To enable effective governance, contestability and redress, we believe that any new regulatory framework should ensure that organisations are transparent about:
• The algorithms they are using and the sources of their training data: There are two core components to AI-based applications: (1) the algorithms themselves and (2) the data they use. In the end, any application is only as good and fair as the algorithms used (i.e. the right questions must be asked) and the quality of data used to train it. Organisations should outline in general terms how the AI makes decisions, what factors it takes into account and any biases it may have. This could be standardised through a labelling scheme.
• The AI’s decision-making process: Explainability will be difficult to achieve for many AI-based systems. Indeed, there is an inevitable trade-off between the explainability of a system and its effectiveness as an AI-based product. Nevertheless, organisations should be able to provide insights into how the AI system makes decisions. This might not mean exposing the intricacies of the algorithm, but rather explaining the type of data inputs the AI uses and the broad logic it follows. For example, a bank using AI for loan approvals could explain that the AI uses information like credit score, income and employment history to make its decision.
• Performance metrics: Sharing metrics related to the performance and accuracy of the AI can be beneficial, particularly where end-users are not the developers of the system. For instance, an AI health diagnostic tool could share its accuracy rate or the percentage of diagnoses that are later confirmed by human doctors.
• Data handling: In alignment with existing data protection legislation, organisations should disclose what data the AI is using, how this data is being collected, processed and stored. It's also important to communicate whether data is shared with third parties and how the user's privacy is being protected.
• Alignment with human values: The Government should consider how it might address the issue of AI alignment. AI alignment refers to the challenge of ensuring AI systems act in accordance with human values throughout their operational life. This is especially important as AI technologies become more autonomous and sophisticated, increasing the potential for their objectives to diverge from those of human operators or society at large. In order to facilitate this, we recommend that any regulatory intervention incorporates an explicit requirement for the disclosure of details about how an AI system has been trained for alignment with human values, as well as the measures in place to maintain this alignment as the system learns and evolves. Such a requirement could help build trust and facilitate external oversight of AI systems, while emphasising the responsibility of developers and operators to continually monitor their systems and correct any misalignment that arises. However, it should be noted that AI alignment is a complex problem, and our understanding of it continues to evolve. The practicalities of regulatory implementation should be carefully considered, and the requirements should be flexible enough to adapt as our understanding of AI alignment improves. Regular consultation with the AI research community, as well as industries using AI, would be crucial to ensuring the continued relevance and efficacy of these regulations.
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
One area that requires further clarity is who owns, or has right of ownership over, the datasets that are used in generative AI systems. Many systems use web crawls to collate datasets available on the web, but not all publicly-available data is meant for public consumption. For example, confidential information may be intentionally or accidentally leaked on the internet, such as personal data we frequently see on the dark web. The Government should consider how scenarios where such data is (unintentionally) fed into AI systems are to be dealt with from a data privacy and legal standpoint.

Yes

A whole of economy approach – introducing a new cross-economy AI Act
14. Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the Australian Government should consider?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
While we support a context-driven, flexible approach to regulating AI, there is a risk of reinventing the wheel when regulating cross-sectoral AI systems. In the same way that a significant proportion of organisations use Office 365, it’s likely that some AI systems will be widely adopted across the economy. In such cases, there should be a concerted effort to pool resources and coordinate regulatory responses – otherwise there is a danger of regulatory overlap and/or conflict.
There is a danger that, under a sector-based approach, some AI systems will not fit neatly within one regulator’s remit, and as such their regulation and oversight may fall through the net. Lessons could be learnt from the world of cyber security, where the sector may dictate what types of activities need to be undertake to improve resilience, but coordination is required across sectors to avoid fragmentation. The Government could explore establishing a central function to oversee the implementation of AI regulations. Part of the function’s remit could include regular assessments of the AI landscape to ensure that there is sufficient regulatory oversight across AI applications. This responsibility may need to be established on a statutory footing to ensure effective implementation.
In addition, the Government must equip sectoral regulators with the resources and skills to effectively oversee the development and use of AI in their sectors. While some regulators are more advanced in their understanding of and ability to regulate AI, there remains a significant skills gap across authorities which will only widen as technologies and applications evolve. In addition to skills investment, a requirement should be established within all regulatory frameworks to regularly and systematically engage with the AI ecosystem to understand technological developments. This includes academics, incubators and accelerators, disruptors, and other innovation centres. This engagement could take a number of forms, including: secondment models; formal and informal government consultations and discussion papers; and regular sounding board mechanisms such as advisory groups and councils.

Submission to the call for feedback on introducing mandatory guardrails for ‘AI’ in 
high-risk settings: proposals paper  
 
by Dr Jean Linis -Dinco  
 
I would like to thank the Australian Government’s Department of Industry, Science and 
Resources for the opportunity to submit feedback  as part of the consultation process to 
introduce mandatory guardrails for ‘AI’ in high -risk settings. Before I go to my comments 
about the ten guardrails, I would like to comment on the text written on page 7. On this 
page, the five pillars of the Austral ian Government’s approach to supporting the adoption 
of safe and responsible ‘AI’ have been outlined.  
The second pillar ‘supporting and promoting best -practice governance’ relies heavily on 
the Voluntary AI Safety Standards. This approach is dangerous because this would render 
all our efforts on protecting human rights secondary to economic development. Th e 
voluntary nature of these standards, or any standards in that regard, tells corporations 
and companies that human rights is optional. As such, this will result in inconsistent 
adoption across different sectors and organisations. By making compliance volu ntary, 
we risk creating a digital economy where essential human rights measures is ignored, 
particularly by entities who prioritises speed to market over human rights.  
Australia, as a founding member of the United Nations, has a crucial role in ensuring that 
it follows a human rights -based digital economy wherein the people and the planet are at 
forefront of every economic  decision. This means we need to integrate international 
human rights obligations that the Australian Government has signed and ratified in the 
past seventy nine years. An ‘AI’ safety standard should not merely respond to market 
dynamics. Instead, it should actively foster human well -being and environmental 
sustainability. A human rights -based approach would commit all organisations, for -profit 
or otherwise, to using Australia’s human rights obligations as a compass rather than a 
suggestion when it  comes to the development and deployment of technologies to ensure 
substantial investments are made in ways that enhance public services.  
 
Page 11 explains why ‘AI’ is different as opposed to other technologies. I would like to 
caution that Australia should take a grounded approach to ‘AI’ regulation so that it is not 
sandwhiched between the hypes. By this, I mean that we should recognise tha t the 
current understanding of the technology we call ‘AI’ is highly contingent on how the 
makers of this technology marketed it, that it is existential and an uncontrollable force. 
This sets a dangerous precedence as policies might be informed by fear instead of actual 
needs of citizens. Australia must recognise that ‘AI’ is part of a technological evolution rather than a revolution. This argument will create a more nuanced understanding that ‘AI’ 
does not operate in a vacuum. Regulation, therefore, must take into account the larger 
political and economic operations especially the increasing control of a small  number of 
powerful corporations that have significant influence over global technology standards 
and practices.  
I would also like to present a counter argument regarding a risk -based approach to ‘AI’ 
regulation. While this may appear to be the best solution as it has been used in various 
countries and jurisdiction, I argue how a risk -based approach  falls significantly short of 
addressing the deeper human rights issues that these technologies pose.  By using a risk -
based approach  as outlined on page 16 -17, we create a certain quantified benchmark 
wherein risk is measured and managed according to existing policies and standards. This 
approach will then rely heavily on potentially superficial  benchmarks that do not capture 
the full spectrum of human rights impacts. As most human rights issue cannot be 
quantified, we might end up prioritising certain risks over others based purely on visibility 
or regulatory pressure rather than on actual impac t. In turn, we will have a regulatory 
framework that has a skewed perception of what constitutes a serious risk.  
Employing a risk -based approach also inadvertently demotes human rights, making 
them secondary to the allure of technological progress and economic gain. It does this 
by pitting human rights against business  risks, which often results in prioritising 
innovation and profit at the expense of essential  freedoms and societal well -being.  A risk-
based approach is also too focused on the short -term gains that addresses symptoms 
rather than the root causes of the problem and fails to take into account how continuous 
exposure to ‘AI’ decision -making can alter social norms and erode privacy standards or 
worse increase dependence on automated systems.  
What Australia needs is a  human rights -based approach  to tech legislation. One that 
truly navigates  the complexities and impacts of technologies on its citizens and society 
at large.  Guided by international treaties, Australia can create a human rights -based 
digital economy that will serve as the epitome of optimal technological regulation 
for decades to come . Australia has a unique opportunity to  step  away from the 
economy -first approach and position itself as a leader in effective tech  governance.  The 
EU's AI Act has been criticised for not going far enough   and the uncertain impact of its 
non-binding codes of practice. Australia could benefit from implementing stronger, 
legally binding regulations without relying solely on industry self -regulation. This 
approach would provide clearer consequences for violations to right to privacy, right to 
equality and non discrimination, freedom of expression and information, right to a fair 
trial, right to work a nd free choice of employment, amongst others.  
The guardrails presented on page 35 exhibits significant shortcomings when viewed 
through a human rights -focused lens. As previously mentioned, the emphasis on 
mitigating risks rather than fundamentally rethinking the structure of ‘AI’ development and deployment reflects a profound oversight in addressing the broader implications of 
technology's power dynamics. It is imperative that we do not depend heavily on the 
willingness and ability of corporations to self -regulate. This is problematic because it 
assumes these entities will prioritise public good over profit maximisation, which 
historically is seldom the case. Corporations have inherent interests in downplaying risks 
and amplifying benefits, which can lead to a significant underestimation of the  potential 
harms and exploitation of ‘AI’ technologies.  Thus, I propose a mandatory legally -binding 
guardrail against self -regulatio n, which will  implement clear legal frameworks that hold 
‘AI’ developers and deployers accountable for violations. This should include stringent 
penalties for non -compliance and mechanisms for individuals and communities to seek 
redress for grievances caused by ‘AI’ systems.  
Further, I would like to argue how the guardrails miss the most important part in the 
politics of ‘AI’: the concentration of power in the hands of a few multinational 
corporations that dominate the ‘AI’ landscape.  The Australian Government launched the 
AI Adopt Program and the National Reconstruction Fund  that provide funding to establish 
up to five “AI” Adopt Centres to support small -to-medium sized en terprises (SMEs) that 
engage in international and interstate trade to adopt responsible AI - enabled services 
and enhance their businesses . While a commendable effo rt, Nonetheless, I am 
concerned about recipients’ collaboration with  larger multi -national, well -resourced 
firms as these large firms may be able to disproportionately influence ‘AI’ adoption 
standards and practices within the SME sector  in Australia . Collaborations with  BigTech 
and Big consulting firms  risk solidifying the market position of these  large 
corporations,  which  could inadvertently perpetuate a market dynamic where smaller 
players are either marginalised or compelled to merge with larger entities due to 
competitive pressures and a lack of sufficient independent resources necessary for 
survival in today's market.  The concerns of interest for further investigation here extends 
to the types of ‘AI’ technologies used and the training methodologies employed, which 
can indicate a preferential pipeline where the tech and the methodologies are sourced 
from the  same  partner  big corporations.  These preferences are not conducive to 
the distribution of capital, development of local markets, and SME's independent 
innovation. In turn, this does not serve the public interest. Such approaches to funding 
can eventually sideline other technology providers that are not part of these established 
networks and render SMEs too reliant on specific technologies or platforms. As such, I 
propose the establishment of government -mandated regulatory oversight to monitor 
the influence of large firms within these programs  as a guardrail against monopoly.  
This oversight could include ensuring that no single entity can unduly influence the 
setting of standards or the direction of ‘AI’ development and adoption among SMEs. 
Working with big tech companies without stringent guardrails can inadvertently lead to 
their technologies and standards becoming the default in the industry. This underscores 
the need for guardrails that ensure the initiatives actively promote a diversity of sources and methodologies in ‘AI’ development and adoption. This could involve setting quotas 
or providing incentives for using ‘AI’ services and products from smaller or independent 
tech firms.  Effective regulation should also include mechanisms that ensure 
transparency in the lobbying efforts of these corporations and enforce strict conflict -of-
interest rules in policy -making processes. The concentration of power not only stifles 
competition but also limits the democratic governance of AI technologies. Regulations 
should challenge this by enforcing policies that ensure fair access to essential resources 
and data, thereby leveling the playing field for all stakeholders.   
 
There must also be a guardrail  against assumed consent.  This will address 
how  corporations use personal data including medical data and consumer data for 
training their ‘AI’ systems. As such, a legally-binding guardrail  must focus on ensuring 
explicit and informed consent for using individual data in AI development . This must go 
beyond the current standards of passive or implied consent mechanisms often buried in 
lengthy terms of service agreements.  Consent must be proactive . They are, after all , an 
affirmative action by the user . Therefore, t hey must  not be derived from pre -checked 
boxes or assumed after a certain period of inactivity. Users must engage actively in the 
consent process, ensuring they understand and agree to their data’s usage. Consent 
should not be considered indefinite.  Corporations  would need to periodically renew 
consent, especially when changes occur in the models or their intended use that could 
affect the original terms of consent. There must be easy and straightforward mechanisms 
for individuals to withdraw their consent at any time, with the assurance that their data 
will be removed from any current or fu ture training datasets promptly. An independent 
government body should have the authority to audit ‘AI’ developers and deployers for 
compliance with these consent requirements and have the power to impose penalties 
for non-compliance. This guardrail would help to shift the power dynamics currently 
favouring  corporations over data rights . This will ensure that personal information is not 
used to train ‘AI’ without clear, ongoing, and informed approval from the individuals 
concerned.  Another point wo rth considering is creating a legally -binding policy that 
would require all ‘AI’ developers  and actors to be transparen t and ensure that end  users 
are aware and duly informed of their interactions with ‘AI’ systems. This includes 
interaction in the  form of artwork, ‘AI’ -assisted video, healthcare, financial services, 
employment processes, education technologies, and any other application where ‘AI’ 
systems may influence decision -making or generate content.  
The guardrails has completely overlooked the environmental cost of developing and 
deploying AI technologies. The energy consumption of training large -scale AI models and 
the electronic waste from rapid obsolescence of technology should be critical 
considerations. We are at pivotal point in our Net Zero goals, and we cannot afford to miss 
out on this important milestone in the history of human kind just because we are pushing the boundaries some ‘sophisticated’ chatbot. We need guardrails with teeth that would 
enforce standards and demand energy -efficient design for any technological systems. 
For sense of transparency, companies must be mandated to disclose the environmental 
impact of their ‘AI’ systems regularly. This disclosure must detail energy consumption, 
carbon emissions, and other relevant metrics, akin to financial transparency 
requirements. I propose creating  a mandatory, legally -binding guardrail for economic 
and enviromental sustainability  that would focus on the sustainable development of 
technologies to assess their economic impact on job markets and their environmental 
footprint, such as energy consumption and electronic waste.  
The provision for human oversight  (guardrail 5)  in ‘AI’ systems is framed in a  vague manner. 
To be more specific, the guardrail does not provide detailed guidance on how human 
oversight should be implemented across different contexts and stages of ‘AI’ deployment. 
This vagueness could result in inconsistent applications of the rule  wherein a mere 
presence of a human during the deployment migh t be considered as a human oversight. 
Further, from  the way this guardrail is framed, it appears that human oversight is merely 
being considered as a procedural check. This should not be the case. Instead, human 
oversight should mean that individuals and communities should be able to have a say 
and decide if and how AI technologies are deployed on them. This includes the collection 
of their data to how these system s will affect them on a daily basis including workplace 
surveillance, amongst many other. Human oversight must include the community power 
to veto ‘AI’ deployments that communities deem harmful or inconsistent with their values.  
This is also in line with the conc ept of data sov ereignty. Specifically, this guardrail should 
also address the massive corporate surveillance in public spaces that disproportionately 
target specific ethnic or socioeconomic groups.  And more importantly, there needs to be 
a mechanism in the regulation that will cover the development and use of lethal 
autonomous weapons systems.  Australia should cr eate a legally binding prohibition 
against the abil ity of actors to design weapons of mass destruction  or one that would 
violate the 1925 Geneva Protocol  and the C hemical Weapons Conv ention. This must be 
a guardrail on its own, a g uardrail for protection against surveillance  and against the 
development of LAWS.  
While there is a nod towards Indigenous Data Sovereignty (guardrail 3), it lacks clear 
mechanisms to ensure that Indigenous communities can control their data and the 
interpretation of their cultural knowledge. To remedy this, there must be governance 
bodies comprised of Indigenous leaders who oversee the use of AI and data practices 
involving their communities. These authorities could grant permissions, monitor usage, 
and ensure compliance with cultural protocols. There must also be proper consent 
procedur es to ensure they are not only informed but also culturally tailored, granting 
Indigenous communities the time and resources necessary to make educated decisions 
about AI projects. It is therefore my recommendation to require  companies to conduct a 
legally binding comprehensive human rights impact assessment before the deployment of any ‘AI’ system. These assessments should be conducted independently by a 
government -mandated body and include consultations with potentially impacted 
communities. They should evaluate potential violations of rights such as privacy, non -
discrimination, and freedom  of expression.  
Finally, and probab ly one of my most crucial point s in this submission , I would like to 
caution with the use of the term "AI autonomy", for instance, implies that such systems 
have a form of agency or independent decision -making capability like that of human 
autonomy. This approach obscures the reality that all tech systems t hat we currently 
have are designed by humans.  We need a guardrail that would prohibit ‘AI’ developers and 
investors from shifting the responsibility for moral decision -making onto ‘AI’ systems . 
This means they also cannot transfer  to anything o r anyone  the accountability for the 
outcomes of decisions made by the technologies  they created.  By suggesting that ‘AI’ has 
its own autonomy, there is a risk of deflecting responsibility from the developers and 
operators to the technology itself. This also creates a form of dilution of accountability by 
suggesting that as ‘AI’ systems become more 'autonomous,' the responsibility for their 
actions shifts from the creators and operators to the systems themselves, which is a 
dangerous precedent for human rights. Accountability should always be clearly 
attributed to identifiable an d responsible human s, not to the systems they create.  This 
includes the creation of adaptive learning systems and evolutionary al gorithms that 
refine solutions based on performance.  
The guardrails presented in the proposal paper  too narrow and technical. It fails to 
consider the broader social, political, and economic impacts of these technologies, 
which can perpetuate inequalities and erode democratic norms. I suggest we follow a  
more grounded  approach  that would incorporate social impact assessments that 
evaluate ‘AI’'s effects on social structures, communal well -being, and individual 
freedoms. If we are to set up a mandatory, legally  binding guardrails, we only have one 
chance to make it right. There fore, we must ensure that all tech development aligns with 
social justice, environmental sustainability, and genuine democrati sation of technology. 
A reimagining of these regulations is necessary to ensure that tech serves the people, 
particularly the most marginali sed, rather than entrenched corporate interests.
