NTEU Submission on the Department of Industry, Science and Resource’s Consultation Process on
Safe and responsible AI in Australia: Proposals paper for introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings

Gabe Gooding, NTEU National Assistant Secretary
ggooding@nteu.org.au 
03.10.24



EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1.  NTEU recognises the potential of AI to enhance and enrich work and outcomes in our sector, provided that it is developed and implemented in an ethical manner that does not represent high risk to the sector, our members, or the national interest in maintaining a trusted high-quality higher education system.

2.  The list of activities within the education sphere that are identified as high risk is too limited and the following high-risk activities must be specifically included to reflect the unique character of academic work: 
a.  Content development and delivery
b.  Moral rights of authors
c.  Academic freedom
d.  Student support
e.  Use of AI generated metrics to assess the performance of academics

3.  NTEU supports the ACTU submission and in particular the position that all uses of AI in employment are high risk, as well as the call for a review of the Fair Work Act to ensure that provisions of that Act such as the requirement for consultation with workers, are appropriate to accommodate application of AI in the workplace.

4.  While the guardrails go some way towards addressing issues associated with the introduction of AI, they do not give us comfort that the needs of workers and the potential impact on the labour market will be sufficiently persuasive to protect the employment rights and safety of workers when decisions are made about designing and employing AI in our workplaces.

5.  NTEU recommends amendments to guardrails 2 – 10 as outlined in this submission to ensure that they provide meaningful protections to workers and students.

6.  We believe that having an independent umpire will be critical to ensuring that workers and the community more broadly, develop trust in the use of AI systems. On this basis, we strongly support the inclusion of an independent regulator in this scheme.

INTRODUCTION
We welcome the opportunity to comment on the Department of Industry, Science, and Resources’ consultation process on the introduction of mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings, as outlined in “Safe and Responsible AI in Australia”.
 
NTEU represents 28,000 workers in the tertiary education sector, principally employed in universities. Our members have a strong interest in ensuring that any introduction of AI into our sector is done in a way that preserves academic integrity and academic freedom, is bias-free, has the full confidence of students, staff and the Australian public, supports quality education and research, and is adopted in full consultation with employees.

NTEU recognises the potential of AI to enhance and enrich work and outcomes in our sector, provided that it is developed and implemented in an ethical manner that does not represent high risk to the sector, our members, or the national interest in maintaining a trusted high-quality higher education system.
 
We support the submission by the Australian Council of Trade Unions and make additional comments relative to tertiary education in this submission.

FOCUS AND CONSULTATION
NTEU notes that the intention of the risk-based approach adopted by the Government is to place “obligations on those across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle who can most effectively prevent harms before people interact with, or are subject to, an AI system (an ex ante or pre-market approach)”. NTEU has concerns that this focus principally on the technology choices does not take into consideration of the impact on individual workers and the public, and on the special case of the application of AI in what are largely publicly funded institutions who must be accountable to the Australian public. By focusing only on adoption of AI prior to interaction with people the approach runs the risk of failing to identify the effect on those who interact with those technological choices after decisions are made. This singularly utilitarian technological approach does not sit comfortably with protection of the human and labour rights of the community.

While we generally support the risk management approaches, e.g., in health and safety, in this case the pace of change in this field means that the risks we face tomorrow may be very different from the ones we face today. It is not clear to us how this approach can both flexibly cover as yet unseen developments and also be robust enough to ensure compliance.

As the only union covering all workers (and academic staff in particular) in higher education which contributed $48 billion to the national economy in 2023, and is the home of the bulk of Australia’s research in Science and Technology– we were disappointed not to be involved in the recent round table on education. We believe this was a significant missed opportunity for the Department to hear from those workers who have both theoretical expertise and are already implementing and working with AI in a significant sector of the Australian economy. We note in passing that the recently adopted resolution of the United Nations General Assembly, “Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development”, specifically names academia as a key stakeholder group who should be encouraged to be involved in the development of regulatory approaches.

HIGHER EDUCATION SPECIFIC ISSUES
Education is nominated in the Proposals Paper as being a high-risk field in relation to “admission to education programs, evaluating learning outcomes or monitoring student behaviour”. While these three elements are obviously high risk, we believe that other aspects of the use of AI in higher education are also high risk and should also be specifically included. These include the following:

CONTENT DEVELOPMENT AND DELIVERY
NTEU members believe that the use of AI to standardise and automate the “delivery of content” to replace genuine instruction is a high risk. Where teaching AI is off-the-shelf, this runs the risk of homogenising instruction, losing local knowledge and becoming unresponsive to local problems.
The ownership of these resources is already muddy, and broad AI use going forward will further muddy the waters. For example, we have already seen, during the pandemic, universities reusing recorded or pre-recorded lectures from previous years. With the widespread use of Zoom for teaching, and its AI-enabled capacity to provide closed captions and transcripts, it is not too farfetched to anticipate lectures being delivered online from material put together by AI from material scraped up from whatever is available on the internet. We have already seen industry-wide decreases in curation and ownership of material, “pre-recorded material” becoming static, and institutional support misinterpreting the need for maintenance of learning materials. Often little to no time is given to staff to review or update such material. This is sector-wide institutional failure that poses a high risk for the future quality of Australia’s higher education outputs.

MORAL RIGHTS 
Adoption of AI in curriculum and content development is likely to lead to the loss of the legal and moral rights of those who developed original content, as existing teaching materials are used to train these machines. Moral and intellectual rights are very important currency for academics, evidenced by an almost universal system that demands attribution. 
Again, the UN resolution, “Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development”, contains guidance here at point 6. i) “Encouraging, where appropriate and relevant, the implementation of appropriate safeguards to respect intellectual property rights, including copyright protected content, while promoting innovation“

ACADEMIC FREEDOM
Academic Freedom is a principal defining characteristic of universities and in its simplest terms allows academics to determine what and how they teach and research and how they do so, free from fear or favour. The introduction of AI in delivery and assessment, linked to AI generated metrics of the assessment of academic work, significantly undermines academic freedom by putting in place measures that effectively force academics to adopt AI. It is worth noting that universities are required under the Higher Education Support Act to have policies that protect academic freedom and freedom of speech and that the UNESCO Recommendation on the status of higher education teaching personnel contains the following statement:
“Higher-education teaching personnel should not be forced to instruct against their own best knowledge and conscience or be forced to use curricula and methods contrary to national and international human rights standards. Higher education teaching personnel should play a significant role in determining the curriculum.”

STUDENT SUPPORT
University students are provided with a broad range of support during their course of study. This support often requires human-to-human interaction for the simple reason that the circumstances of each individual student are unique. One example where AI is already being used and having a deleterious effect is decision making around student accommodations, i.e., waiving or altering course requirements based on the individual student’s needs. Use of a standardised matrix via AI systems increases the risk of failure and is again a high risk for the sector.

USE OF AI GENERATED METRICS TO ASSESS ACADEMIC WORK
The use of AI to introduce further metrics into the assessment of academic performance potentially leads to a reduction in diversity and a loss of expertise, both of which are high risk for the institution, but also the country as a whole. 

Academic work in Australian universities is already subject to extensive metrification but with human input in responding to the relevant model. For example, different disciplines can have different lead times from research to publication, this is accounted for in many models at an individual level. Outcomes of those exercises in counting output are used to determine promotion opportunities, workload allocation (e.g., the relative balance between teaching and research), and resource allocation. Where an AI system makes those assessments, and the academic is denied the opportunity to research as a result, Australia’s research output declines as does the diversity of that research.

EMPLOYMENT RELATED ISSUES
NTEU strongly supports the ACTU submission in relation to the Proposals Paper and specifically the guardrails as they relate to employment. We believe that all use of AI in employment is high risk, and is particularly high risk in our sector due to the unique characteristics of academic work.

We support the ACTU’s call for a review of the Fair Work Act and note in particular that the model term for consultation with employees about change, which includes technological change, requires consultation with employees after a decision has been made to introduce change. The need to ensure that appropriate systems are deployed within the workplace mandates consultation with the workers who have the best understanding of their work and the subtleties and intricacies that it may include, before a decision is made. We strongly believe that the guardrails should include reference to the necessity to engage with workers at the beginning of the AI life cycle, not at the end.

THE GUARDRAILS
Before turning to comment on the specific guardrails, NTEU is concerned that, as currently constructed, there would be little capacity to ensure that the employers in our sector, largely the universities, could be compelled to conform to a particular standard. This is because the guardrails appear to provide considerable latitude to the universities to interpret them as they wish and there appears to be no external regulatory oversight. While the guardrails go some way towards addressing issues associated with the introduction of AI, they do not give us comfort that the needs of workers and the potential impact on the labour market will be sufficiently persuasive to protect the employment rights and safety of workers when decisions are made about designing and employing AI in our workplaces.

Unions currently have rights to examine specific records relating to their members (e.g., wages), and this should be extended to having the right to examine the use of AI, including its data collection, and any records it generates in relation to employees. There should also be access to an independent body to whom a union or a worker may refer potential breaches of the guardrails, and this body should have the power to make a determination and, where necessary, impose a penalty or order restitution. 

Guardrails that organisations can freely interpret without the back-up of an independent body eventually become equivalent to self-regulation schemes which have, at best, a chequered history in this country. 
GUARDRAIL 1
ESTABLISH, IMPLEMENT AND PUBLISH AN ACCOUNTABILITY PROCESS INCLUDING GOVERNANCE, INTERNAL CAPABILITY AND A STRATEGY FOR REGULATORY COMPLIANCE

No comment
GUARDRAIL 2
ESTABLISH AND IMPLEMENT A RISK MANAGEMENT PROCESS TO IDENTIFY AND MITIGATE RISKS

This guardrail should explicitly include that the risk management process must be comprehensive and include all foreseeable risks, including risk to customers, employees, and third parties, as well as risks to the national interest. The risk management register should be accessible to employees as equivalent risk management registers relating to work health and safety are. As it is currently worded it is entirely open to the enterprise to produce a risk management register that only considers business risks (e.g., reputational risk), but does not consider risks of harm to others.

NTEU suggests:
Establish and implement a comprehensive risk management process to identify and mitigate all foreseeable risks, including risks to customers, employees, and third parties, as well as risks to the national interest.

GUARDRAIL 3
PROTECT AI SYSTEMS, AND IMPLEMENT DATA GOVERNANCE MEASURES TO MANAGE DATA QUALITY AND PROVENANCE

As described above, the issue of moral rights is highly significant in our industry. This guardrail needs to ensure that academic work in particular cannot be harvested without appropriate attribution. Consistent with the UN resolution, both copyright and moral rights must be protected, and the guardrail should require not only that no data has been collected that is subject to copyright, but also that no data is used in machine learning that is subject to copyright or other property rights.

With regard to employees, employers must be obliged to seek genuine informed consent from their employees before their data is used in AI systems and there should be a clear stipulation that there will be no adverse impact on an employee who refuses consent.

This guardrail is insufficient to protect the cultural knowledges, artefacts (including images), and cultural traditions of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Ownership and use must remain entirely within their control and the guardrail should include a prohibition on the use of such materials without permission from the appropriate individual or recognised cultural group.

NTEU suggests:
Protect AI systems from misuse, and implement data governance measures to manage data quality and provenance including ensuring that:
* All data is legally obtained
* the copyright moral and intellectual property rights of those whose data is being used is protected and attribution is made, 
* genuine informed consent has been obtained from employees for the collection and use of their data
* there are no adverse consequences for employees who refuse to consent to use of their data, and 
* all rights to cultural knowledge and images of artefacts of Aboriginal and Torres Strait islander peoples are only used with prior genuine informed consent.



GUARDRAIL 4
TEST AI MODELS AND SYSTEMS TO EVALUATE MODEL PERFORMANCE AND MONITOR THE SYSTEM ONCE DEPLOYED

An assumption is being made here that adequate testing has been conducted prior to the deployment of an AI model or system. This guardrail needs to specify that testing, particularly against the risks identified in guardrail 2 above, be conducted prior to deployment as well as after. When testing involves the collection and analysis of employee data that must be with informed consent (see guardrail 3 above).

NTEU suggests:
Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the system before and after deployment for performance against goals, reliability, and risks to customers, employees, third parties and the national interest ,in addition to any business risks. 




GUARDRAIL 5
ENABLE HUMAN CONTROL OR INTERVENTION IN AN AI SYSTEM TO ACHIEVE MEANINGFUL HUMAN OVERSIGHT

This guardrail is entirely dependent on the definition of meaningful as applied by each deploying organisation. For example, if AI is used to shortlist applicants for a position and then there is a human selection panel, does this constitute meaningful human oversight? We would argue that it does not, because if human oversight is dependent on or limited to material generated from AI, the oversight is entirely dependent on the AI system. This guardrail needs more detail and the introduction of oversight independent of the AI system, or its developers.

We strongly support the ACTU’s recommendation that human oversight include the rights of unions and workers to oversee the use of systems related to their working conditions and their workplace.

GUARDRAIL 6
INFORM END-USERS REGARDING AI-ENABLED DECISIONS, INTERACTIONS WITH AI AND AI-GENERATED CONTENT.

We note that the definition of end-user as applied in this Proposal Paper is broad and as such it should be included in the actual guard-rail as follows:

Inform end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content. An end-user is any intended or actual individual or organisation that consumes an AI-based product or service, interacts with it or is impacted by it after it is deployed, including workers in the organisation.

Without that explicit inclusion it would open to the employers in our industry, for example, to determine that the end users are students and not inform employees when AI-enabled decisions are being made that relate to them.

GUARDRAIL 7
ESTABLISH PROCESSES FOR PEOPLE IMPACTED BY AI SYSTEMS TO CHALLENGE USE OR OUTCOMES

We agree that an internal process in the first instance is appropriate, but this guardrail does not go far enough to protect those who have been negatively affected by AI systems. This guardrail should include the following:

Establish and maintain a timely disputes resolution process based on procedural fairness and natural justice for people who are impacted by AI systems in which the complainant may be represented by a third party and may challenge either the use of data in an AI system, the use of the AI system, or its outcomes.

Any system where an individual is challenging the decisions of another body needs to be independent of that body to ensure justice. While an internal process is acceptable as a first step, there must be regulatory bodies to whom individuals or groups may lodge complaints about the use of AI-enabled decision making and AI systems more broadly.
GUARDRAIL 8
BE TRANSPARENT WITH OTHER ORGANISATIONS ACROSS THE AI SUPPLY CHAIN ABOUT DATA, MODELS AND SYSTEMS TO HELP THEM EFFECTIVELY ADDRESS RISKS.

This guardrail needs to include those whom the AI system is collecting data from or about, including employees and customers.

NTEU suggests:
In order to allow third parties to effectively address risks, contribute to transparency across the AI supply chain by informing other organisations, people from whom data is being collected, and people about whom data is being collected, of the data, models and systems being used.

GUARDRAIL 9
KEEP AND MAINTAIN RECORDS TO ALLOW THIRD PARTIES TO ASSESS COMPLIANCE WITH GUARDRAILS

To be effective this guardrail needs to specify that the keeping and maintenance of documents applies to all documents necessary for a third party to assess compliance, and when and how those documents may be accessed. Without these stipulations, the record-keeping may be the bare minimum. There is also no obligation on the record keeper to provide those documents to third parties.

NTEU suggests the following:
Keep, maintain, and provide all records necessary to enable third parties to assess compliance with guardrails. Third parties may include relevant regulators, unions which have coverage or workers employed within the organisation, or civil organisations that have a legitimate interest in the development and deployment of specific AI systems.


GUARDRAIL 10
UNDERTAKE CONFORMITY ASSESSMENTS TO DEMONSTRATE AND CERTIFY COMPLIANCE WITH THE GUARDRAILS.
NTEU believes that it is important for organisations to regularly self-audit, but given the risks associated with AI and the stated need to ensure community trust, it is essential that there be the capacity for independent audit for compliance by an appropriate regulator.  There should also be capacity for the bodies listed in the amended Guardrail 9 above to request that an independent audit be undertaken when they have a reasonable belief that there is a failure of compliance. 

NTEU suggests:
Undertake conformity assessments regularly to test for compliance with the guardrails and provide all necessary information for an independent regulator to complete an external audit of its own volition or on request of employees, unions, or civil organisations, where there is a reasonable belief that there is failure of compliance with one or more guardrails.

CONCLUSION
The guardrails as drafted are a good start but they will be insufficient without the addition of further detail that reduces the current almost total capacity for an organisation to interpret the guardrails and assess their own compliance. 

In relation to higher education, the scope of high-risk activities is too limited and needs to include issues related to curriculum development and content delivery, moral rights, academic freedom, student support, and the use of AI generated metrics to assess academic work. 

The guardrails are at present effectively self-regulatory, in that the developers and those who implement AI systems have wide scope to interpret them and determine and test their own compliance. Australians understandably are very cynical about industries engaging in self –regulation and we believe that having an independent umpire will be critical to ensuring that workers and the community more broadly develop trust in the use of AI systems. On this basis, we strongly support the inclusion of an independent regulator in this scheme.

NTEU strongly supports the recommendations contained within the ACTU submission regarding aspects of the consultation process not covered in this submission.

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
Education Services Australia believes the principles provide good coverage of the potential areas of high-risk, however applying the principles to determine whether an application is high-risk or not is not obvious and could be open to subjective interpretation. This is evidenced within the proposal document itself within the section titled, “Examples of how to apply the principles to use cases”. ESA believes that high-risk use cases are required in support of the principles to provide guidance as to the application of the principles and to outline known high-risk applications of the technology.
ESA has concerns about who would make the determination of high-risk use cases. Given the room for subjective interpretation and the potential seriousness of the impacts, it is ESA’s view that such determinations should not be left to the market. However, ESA also notes that there is no obvious national education regulator who could make this determination. There is a risk that if determination of high-risk under these principles is devolved to states and territories, as is the case with a lot of education-related legislation, then there could be different approaches to the implementation of the proposed guardrails. A national approach could be considered under a program like ESA’s Safer Technology for Schools (http://st4s.edu.au/), which provides national assessments of education technology against a privacy and security framework that has been agreed by all states and territories.
In terms of risk, ESA would like to highlight a unique aspect of the education domain, which is the duration of the experience and its role in shaping the cognitive, social, emotional and physical development of Australia’s young people. The duration of education participation in particular raises a special risk dimension in that the aggregation of seemingly small, automated decisions over years could affect the outcome of students’ studies, their future career, and even their social and emotional wellbeing. As such biases within models may pass screening and training exercises designed to reduce risks in short-term, immediate impact environments (such as health) but over time could place student wellbeing and life prospects at risk. The risk of lifelong harm is acute in education in a way that it is different to other sectors and industries.
Are there any principles we should add or remove?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
Principles should be reviewed overtime to ensure they are aligned with legislation and policy changes as well as emerging risks
Please identify any:
ESA believes that education itself should be treated as a high-risk environment due to the impact this domain has on the lives of students and role it plays in forming citizens and society and due to the long-term nature of the educational experience and the vulnerability of students who are children for much of their educational journey.
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
ESA acknowledges that special protections and provisions are required to prevent harms to First Nations peoples, communities, culture, and Country and that this is pertinent in an educational context for both indigenous and non-indigenous students, however such protections need to be informed from First Nations cultural perspectives which are many and various; wide additional consultation is required.
3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?
NO a more defined list-based approach is needed
If you prefer a list-based approach (similar to the EU and Canada), what use cases should we include? How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
Education/training Biometrics Critical infrastructure Employment Access to essential public services and products Access to essential private services Products and services affecting individual and public health and safety Law enforcement Administration of justice and democratic processes
How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
ESA supports a principle-based approach since, by being focused on outcomes rather than technology it is more robust and sustainable. However, interpretation of the principles and the process of translating them to assess practical implementation approaches is not clear, obvious, creating the risk of miscategorisation, whether accidental or otherwise. This is evidenced within the proposal paper itself by the provision of example use cases, which demonstrate how the principles can be applied.
Since the national education sector does not have an industry regulator, implementation of mandatory guidelines will fall to state and territory education departments and Catholic dioceses and purchasing networks (such as CENet) through procurement controls for systemic schools. Such an approach would result in potential variances across the country in the interpretation and application of the principles in determining high-risk use cases and applications. Moreover, for the independent schools the onus would fall to the individual schools to make these decisions.
Due to these concerns, ESA strongly recommends that high-risk use-case examples mapped to principles are provided to enable more consistent application of the principles. In addition, the identification of known high-risk use cases would in themselves provide good guardrails. Such a list would need to be updated from time-to-time.
In addition, ESA recommends that consideration is given to a national agency (such as ESA) leading an education-specific assessment program for these principles, in line with the national Safer Technologies for Schools (https://st4s.edu.au) program.
4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Yes
If so, how should we define these?
In an education context, ESA recommends that education in and of itself be considered a high-risk domain due to nature of the sector and potential impact on student lives of automated decision-making. In terms of specific use cases within education which could be candidates for bans ESA, recommends the following are considered:
* AI used in surveillance technologies within school settings (both physical and virtual). There are issues around: privacy infringement, chilling effects on behaviour (inhibit natural behaviour, self-expression), inequitable impacts on students who exhibit atypical social behaviours (e.g. Autism, ADHD, neurodivergence etc), data security risks (breaches or misuses), overreach and mission creep: implementation for one reason extends to others over time, without oversight or evaluation; psychological impact on teachers and students: increasing stress and anxiety creating atmospheres of distrust and suspicion; consent and autonomy: children have or may not be providing consent.
* Use of student data for commercial purposes by vendors/deployers/developers
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
The principles are broad and flexible enough to cover high-level risks, however as noted in previous responses, specific use cases may not be correctly identified due to the challenge of mapping implementation to principles, particularly in education where risks which in single instances may seem low risk, but which aggregate over the duration of schooling could cause real and long-lasting harm to a student.
ESA recommends consideration be given to the practicalities of consistent risk assessment. In addition, ESA recommends that regular reviews of the effectiveness of the guardrails against existing and emerging use cases and risks are undertaken in the future.
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
The mandatory guardrails should apply to all GPAI. Focusing on principles which protect the rights and wellbeing of individuals and the safety and cohesion of society is critical. In other words, focusing on mitigating the potential risks and minimising potential harms is a more effective approach that creating arbitrary delineations in relation to technology. Should some models be excluded from the guardrails there is real risk that an unforeseen harm is caused.
ESA recommends that all GPAI models are considered high-risk. Arbitrary distinctions based on compute power create the illusion that harm cannot be cause by a machine just below the threshold. This is not the case. All AI models can cause harm, depending on a range of factors that are not connected to compute power (e.g. FLOPS). Such factors include low quality or biased training data, undertrained models, applications intentionally designed to cause harm, or ill-considered software design decisions.
The mandatory guardrails proposal paper itself presents five examples of real-world harm that has been caused by existing AI models, some indeed with very low compute power.
ESA recommends consideration be given to the arguments presented in this article: https://medium.com/@ingridwickstevens/regulating-ai-the-limits-of-flops-as-a-metric-41e3b12d5d0c

Define high-risk against the principles

Submission to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources – Options for Mandatory Guardrails:  AI High Risk Settings           3 Introduction Thank you to the Department of Industry, Science, and Resources for the opportunity to contribute again to this important consultation on the regulation of AI in high-risk settings. While I have provided specific feedback in response to the consultation questions, the primary focus of my submission is on the establishment of a regulatory sandbox—a flexible and adaptive framework that can be implemented irrespective of which legislative option is ultimately chosen by the government. This sandbox will ensure that AI innovation is fostered while maintaining strong safeguards for transparency, accountability, and public safety. Defining High-Risk AI 1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI? Are there any principles we should add or remove? The proposed principles appear comprehensive in their attempt to capture high-risk AI; however, some adjustments could enhance their precision: • Additions: Include principles that specifically address autonomous decision-making in critical systems such as healthcare, transportation, and law enforcement, where AI decisions can have life-altering consequences. Additionally, a principle that focuses on AI transparency and explainability should be emphasised to ensure that AI systems can be audited and understood by regulators, particularly in high-risk cases. • Removals: There are no obvious principles that need removal, but greater clarification could help avoid overregulation. Regarding low-risk use cases, such as AI used for personal assistants or content recommendation engines, it should be ensured that these do not fall under the stringent criteria for high-risk AI. For categories like defence or national security, these should be treated separately, as they involve additional layers of sensitive information, sovereignty, and national protection that may require specific regulations distinct from commercial applications. 2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities, and Country? AI has the potential to perpetuate historical biases and inequalities, especially if it is trained on data that reflects existing disparities. To better protect First Nations people, communities, and Country, the following adjustments are recommended: Cultural Sensitivity: Introduce a principle focusing on culturally informed AI to ensure that AI systems are developed and used in a way that respects First Nations traditions, languages, and perspectives. This should include consulting with Indigenous stakeholders when designing AI systems that impact Indigenous land, water management, or cultural heritage. • Inclusive Data Practices: Add specific requirements to include diverse and representative datasets when training AI systems. AI models should actively avoid perpetuating biases against Indigenous people and should be audited for potential harm or exclusions. • Environmental and Cultural Harms: Ensure that AI systems do not exacerbate environmental harms or cultural erasure by mandating impact assessments specifically focused on Country (Indigenous land) and how AI applications may affect sacred sites, resources, or cultural heritage. support government efforts to build trust in AI by ensuring students and the public  are 
educated in its ethical , responsible , and safe  use. 
2. The Government should continue to work closely with and consult leading experts on the 
risks of AI , including university academics and researchers . The Government could leverage 
this expertise to increase awareness of the types of risks that are specific to the higher 
education sector.  
The proposed guardrails  
3. UNSW supports a principles -based approach to risk management, which is more adaptive 
and technology -neutral  in its application . The proposed principles for guiding consistency  in 
assessment by organisations of whether the use of an AI system is high risk are appropriate, 
particularly if they protect existing rights , impacts  and protections .  
4. We support reinforcing existing regulatory mechanisms . As currently proposed , the 
guardrails amount to an entirely new regulatory regime, which we do not support. For 
organisations such as universities, which could participate in any level of the AI supply chain, 
there are existing regulatory regimes and legislative requirements that do or can be adapted 
to cover risks and harms posed by this emerging technology.  
5. We suggest focusing on  the core issues that need to be protected (fairness, privacy, etc) by 
extending  and/or modifying those protections to ensure they capture new ways of operating , 
rather than through a new regulatory or legislative regime which risks ageing out of relevance 
as these new technologies continue to develop  at pace . Defining high -risk AI  
6. We recommend implementing a technology -neutral approach which allows organisations to 
identify risk s and frame a policy response that is not dependent upon  the conception of the 
technolog y associated with th ose risk s. 
7. List-based use cases , as identified later in the proposals paper , have useful illustrative 
purposes for organisations seeking to assess their activities, and can be  helpful for 
governments and industry to identify and share best practice and new applications ( along 
with  their appropriate management) of AI and other technologies. However , no list of use  
cases can  provide full coverage for the proposed regulatory options being considered by 
government to mandate guardrails  for such a rapidly  evolving technology . 
8. In the case that list -based use cases are u tilised  by government, w e strongly recommend that 
education and training , including  higher education , are not considered as  de facto  high -risk 
across all of their activities . The use of AI in education  environments , such as UNSW , 
encourage s responsible, safe, and ethical experimentation  from both a teaching and learning, 
and a research and development perspective .  
9. Government should appl y a balanced approach to use cases and defining high -risk settings, 
so as not to  unintentionally capture some low  risk uses through generalisations, and  better 
enable  potential  future  use cases of AI during suitable periods of review . It should be noted 
that within some of the specified  high -risk domains, there may be individual use cases which 
would pose  limited or minimal risk.   
Regulatory options for mandating the guardrails  
10. Any proposed options for regulating AI should be flexible and adaptable to keep up with 
technological advancements.  The best way of achieving this is through analysis of existing 
regulatory and legislative functions that are designed to protect, for example, privacy,  identity,  
intellectual property rights, use of data, freedom from discrimination, consumer protection 
etc, and consider amendments that enable these protections  to be robustly maintained , 
independently of the emerging field that is AI , and future technologies  
11. The Government should focus primarily on Option 1 . This includes  adapting existing legal 
and regulatory frameworks to ensure they are effective in achieving their goals. The primary 
benefit of this approach is that it aligns the law with regulatory objectives and values , 
including protections,  rather than with a point -in-time conception of an evolving technology.  
 
About UNSW  
UNSW is ranked in the world’s top 20 universities. UNSW  is a world -leading  research and teaching -
intensive universit y, known for innovative, pioneering research and high -quality education with a 
longstanding global impact. Since our foundation in 1949  and through celebrating our 75th anniversary 
year , our aim is to transform all lives through excellence in research, outstanding learning and teaching  
experiences,  and a commitment to advancing Australia’s economic growth and prosperity.  
UNSW proactively equips both staff and students to navigate the realm of AI -assisted learning and 
professional practice , align ing with the UNSW mission of developing students  and researchers  who are 
globally -focused, are rigorous scholars, capable of leadership and professional practice in an 
international community.  Developments in the higher education sector  
AI has ushered in substantial transformations within the higher education  sector  – disrupting 
conventional assessment methodologies, altering student learning paradigms, and prompting 
evaluation of  research  conduct . The impacts of AI are complex and wide -ranging  for universitie s: 
• Learning and teaching : Through new and emerging technologies, academics  can reimagine 
learning and teaching practices. In similar ways to how the COVID -19 pandemic encouraged an 
accelerated adoption of digital technologies, the emergence of AI has encouraged staff to 
adapt their assessment methodologies (e.g. using oral assessments; in-class quizzes; and 
assessments where students reflect on what they have learnt ). With privacy safeguards, AI 
tools can assist with indicative marks and generating feedback. T he workload efficiencies AI 
promises may well mean that staff have more time to create personal connections with 
students, enhancing  the overall  student experience.  
• Research : For researchers, the availability of large language models can have both positive and 
negative implications for their work. On one hand, these models can assist with data analysis, 
text summari sation, and other tasks that can speed up the research process. On the other hand, 
there is a risk of researchers relying too heavily on these models, which can lead to unoriginal 
work and potential plagiarism. Additionally, the ease of generating realistic -looking text and 
data with language models raises c oncerns about the validity and reliability of research results.  
• Integrity:  AI tools can often produce reasonable responses, blurring the distinction between 
genuine understanding and algorithmic output.  One of the  key concerns expressed about the 
use of  AI in higher education relates to the potential for students to misuse the technology  (e.g.  
relying on AI rather than generating their own ideas , and  not referencing appropriately ). These 
concerns are being addressed by universities through a range of strategies to provide our 
students, regulator s and the public with con fidence in the world‐class education Australian 
universities provide ( e.g. through  student education campaigns to promote academic integrity 
and avoid ing cheating and academic misconduct1; using a  variety of assessment methods2; and 
encouraging critique of generative AI output ). On the other hand, AI is an opportunity for the 
fundamental purposes of university education to develop critical and reflective thinking. Used 
responsibly, AI provides the opportunity to develop these uniquely human skills.  Given the rapid 
pace of change, researchers, journals, and organisations are also considering their position on 
the appropriate use of these tools, especially in the context of research integrity.  
• Biases : A study by Gartner found that “85 per cent of AI projects will deliver erroneous 
outcomes due to bias in data, algorithms, or the teams responsible for managing them” . 
Engaging students in critical reflection on AI generated outputs encourages them to scrutinise 
the underlying assumptions, biases and limitations of AI technologies. This process not only 
sharpens their judgement but also cultivates a healthy scepticism and curiosity, essential for 
using generative AI responsibl y. For researchers, the text generated by language models can 
contain biased, false, or harmful information, and it can be difficult to determine who is 
responsible fo r this content. It is becoming increasingly important for researchers to use 
language models in an ethical and responsible manner and to be transparent about their use in 
their methods and reporting.  
 
1 For example, UNSW’s Key principles in AI usage and assessment , Six Categories of Permissible Use  of AI in Assessment ,  
  Supporting Academic Integrity  
2 For example, UNSW’s guide on designing alternative assessments in the world of AI  • Authorship : Academic authorship is generally reserved for individuals who have made 
significant contributions to the design, conduct, or analysis of a study or other research project. 
While language models can assist researchers in generating text, they do not have t he 
capability to independently design, conduct, or analyse research, and therefore should not be 
considered as authors. However, it may be appropriate to acknowledge the use of language 
models in the methodology or materials and methods section of a study or research paper, to 
ensure transparency and to allow for accurate interpretation and replication of results.  
• Students and equity:  While there may be students seeking an advantage by using AI  tools , for 
the most part we have found that students want to do the right thing and want to make sure 
that they are using emerging tools appropriately. Some students have reported feeling anxious 
and uncertain around the use of AI in their studies and assessmen t, without breaching 
university guidelines. A major issue raised in discussions regarding the use of AI in education is 
the impact on equity and diversity in education.  Assumptions are made that students coming 
into university are familiar with the use of AI. A critical gap for students and staff is training and 
increasing comfort levels with AI . 
Maintaining academic excellence and integrity in research, teaching, learning, and assessment will 
continue to be a priority for UNSW as it adapts to and leads in the responsible and safe use of AI, 
bearing in mind expectations from employers in an evolving AI world. We can support government 
efforts to build trust in AI by ensuring there is sound education for students and the public  in the 
ethical , responsible and safe use of AI , including policy professionals with responsibility around 
governance and int egrity . 
The Government should also continue to work closely with and consult leading experts on the risks of 
AI, including at universities such as UNSW. The Government could leverage this expertise to increase 
awareness of the types of risks that are specific to the higher education sector .  
The proposed guardrails  
We have a strong commitment to progress for all, supported by  world leading AI researcher s and 
ethicists, exceptional teachers and a thriving community that is deeply engaged in responsible 
experimentation.  In this context and more broadly from a societal perspective, we see our role is to 
help contribute to digital literacy  and developing the critical thinking skills  of our students and staff  to 
understand what AI is and ensure AI is used ethically, responsibly, and safely.  
As an early adopter, UNSW supports the ethical and responsible use of AI in research, learning, 
teaching, administration, and thought leadership. For example, UNSW’s Ethical and Responsible Use of 
Artificial Intelligence  guide assist s the University  in the development and deployment of AI. The 
principles are aspirational, outcomes -focused, and seek to effectively balance regulation with 
innovation . We recognise that we will need to continue to update our policies and guidelines to ensure 
they remain appropriate as new AI products and technologies emerge.  
Additionally, within the higher education sector, universities such as UNSW already have systems and 
processes in place that reflect the type of guardrails proposed. This includes robust mechanisms to 
identify and manage risk , and strategies for regulatory compliance , such as guidance for the 
safeguarding of data and organisational avenues to raise concerns or complaints.  
UNSW supports a principles -based approach to risk management, which is more adaptive and 
technology -neutral in its application. The proposed principles for guiding consistency in assessment by organisations of whether the use of an AI system is high risk are appropriate, particularly if they protect 
existing rights, impacts and protections.  
We therefore support reinforcing existing regulatory mechanisms.  As currently proposed, the 
guardrails amount to an entirely new regulatory regime, which we do not support. For organisations 
such as universities, which could participate in any level of the AI supply chain, there are existing 
regulatory regimes and legis lative requirements that do or can be adapted to cover risks and harms 
posed by this emerging technology.  
This includes focusing on the core issues that need to be protected (fairness, privacy, etc) by extending 
and/or modifying those protections to ensure they capture new ways of operating, rather than through 
a new regulatory or legislative regime which risks ageing out of relevan ce as these new technologies 
continue to develop at pace.  
Defining high -risk AI  
Firstly, d efining AI as a ‘regulatory object ’ is an almost impossible task. All agencies and governments 
that have attempted this task have struggled.  For example, t he E uropean Union’s  definition of AI has 
been amended multiple times throughout the drafting  process . The OECD ’s definition  of AI  on which 
the Australian definition is based has  also already been amended.  The struggle here is not that any 
given definition is ‘good ’ or ‘bad’, it is that we do not yet understand the object that we are trying to 
define.  
While defining AI is a difficult task at this stage of the technology’s development, there are risks with 
which government is rightly  concerned. Identifying high -risk scenarios is a useful exercise preliminary 
to law reform, particularly to better understand broader cluster s of problems . These include , for 
example , the bias that can result from machine learning approaches  which rely on inferences drawn 
from statistics,  issues relating to non-transparency  and accountability , and ownership and 
consumption of data, including public and individual data . For the purposes of regulation, however, a n 
adaptive,  technology -neutral approach  focus ing on mitigation of risks is likely to be more effective, as 
it is not dependent upon the conception of the technology associated with those risks.  
Secondly, we note that the paper has specifically identified ‘ education/training’  as a potential high -risk 
use case based on  international developments , where AI systems intend to be used to:  
• Determine access or admission to educational institutions  
• Evaluate learning outcomes  
• Assess the appropriate level of education that individual s will receive or can access  
• Monitor and detect prohibited behaviour of students during tests  
List-based use cases , as identified in the proposals paper , have useful illustrative purposes for 
organisations seeking to assess their activities, and can be helpful for governments and industry to 
identify and share best practice and new applications (along with their appropriate management) of AI 
and other techn ologies. However, no list of use cases can provide full coverage for the proposed 
regulatory options being considered by government to mandate guardrails for such a rapidly evolving 
technology.  
In the case that list -based use cases are utilised by government, we strongly recommend that 
education and training, including higher education, are not considered as de facto  high -risk across all 
of their activities. The use of AI in education environments, such as UNSW, encourages responsible, 
safe, and ethical experimentation from both a teaching and learning, and a research and development 
perspective.  Further, government should apply  a balan ced approach to use cases and defin ing high -risk settings , so 
as not to unintentionally capture some low risk uses through generalisations, and better enable 
potential future use cases of AI during suitable periods of review. It should be noted that within some 
of the specified high -risk domains, there may be indi vidual use cases which would pose limited or 
minimal risk.  
We therefore recommend that the most appropriate approach is to provide protections against 
potential harm s, rather than implementing a new regulatory regime.  This has the additional benefit of  
minimis ing operational disruption s for organisations  and businesses , so that they can integrate new 
regulatory compliance requirements into existing processes without developing and resourcing  entirely 
new processes  and procedures .  
Regulatory options for mandating the guardrails  
Any proposed options for regulating AI should be flexible and adaptable to keep up with technological 
advancements. The best way to achiev e this is by analysi ng existing regulatory and legislative 
functions that are designed to protect, for example, privacy, identity, intellectual property rights, use of 
data, freedom from discrimination, consumer protection etc, and consider ing amendments that enable 
these protections to be robustly maintained, independently of the emerging field that is AI, as well as 
future technologies . 
The Government should therefore focus primarily on Option 1 . This includes adapting existing legal 
and regulatory frameworks to ensure they are effective in achieving their goals. The primary benefit of 
this approach is that it aligns the law with regulatory objectives and values rather than with a p oint-in-
time conception of an evolving technology.  
Conclusion  
Thank you for the opportunity to provide a submission to this consultation.  
Should you wish to discuss any issue raised in this submission, please do not hesitate to contact 
our Senior  Government  Relations  Manager , Ms Cassandra Switaj , on 02 9348 2246 or 
c.switaj@unsw.edu.au .

Department of Industry, Science and Resources
Australian Government
aiconsultation@industry.gov.au 

3 October 2024

Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings

NAVA welcomes the opportunity to respond to the proposals paper Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-Risk Settings. 

The National Association for the Visual Arts (NAVA) is an independent membership organisation which brings together the many voices of the visual arts, craft and design sector to improve the fundamental conditions of work and practice. We do this through advocacy, education and the Code of Practice for the Visual Arts, Craft and Design. Our network comprises over 50,000 artists, arts workers, galleries, arts organisations and industry bodies. 

NAVA has been a longstanding advocate for copyright entitlements for visual creators and played a pivotal role in establishing Viscopy, Australia's visual arts copyright collecting agency, in 1995. Now part of the Copyright Agency, Viscopy was a critical step toward protecting artists' rights. Today, NAVA continues to champion the intellectual property rights, moral rights, and income-generating potential of Australian artists, creators, and cultural workers, particularly as AI becomes an increasingly significant factor in the sector.

Defining High-Risk AI

Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI? Are there any principles we should add or remove?

NAVA believes the proposed principles capture the broad concept of high-risk AI. However, we suggest an explicit inclusion of intellectual property (IP)-related risks. The use of visual artworks and other creative material in the training of AI models without proper consent or remuneration should be recognised as high-risk, given the significant implications for Australian artists. 
For individual artists to fully benefit from their creative work, their IP must be adequately protected against unauthorised exploitation or appropriation. The copyright held by visual artists and craft practitioners is crucial to their economic survival, and any undermining of these rights poses a serious threat to their livelihoods.

Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities, and Country?

NAVA strongly supports the inclusion of provisions that protect Indigenous Cultural Intellectual Property (ICIP). It is crucial that these guardrails explicitly safeguard Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities from the unauthorised use of ICIP, particularly in AI systems that generate artistic or cultural content. The misuse or appropriation of First Nations art for AI training or production violates cultural protocols, disrespects Traditional Owners, and risks perpetuating harmful misrepresentations.

By involving First Nations decision-makers and integrating Indigenous Knowledges into the machine learning processes that inform AI, this framework can uphold data governance and data sovereignty. This presents an opportunity for this continent to lead the way in advancing technology ethically, with respect for First Nations cultures, values and ICIP.  

Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models?

While the principles provide a helpful framework, it would be helpful to expand these examples to include AI applications in the arts, particularly where AI is used to generate content based on copyrighted material. This would highlight the risks AI poses to artists and creators, whose works are increasingly being used without consent for AI training and content creation.

Guardrails Ensuring Testing, Transparency, and Accountability of AI

Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings? Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?

NAVA supports the mandatory guardrails, especially those related to transparency and data provenance. We advocate for additional disclosure requirements for AI platforms, particularly those using copyrighted content for training purposes. This should include clear guidelines on how third-party copyright content was legitimately sourced, whether through:
* Open licensing (e.g., Creative Commons);
* Public interest exceptions;
* Content out of copyright;
* Specific licenses obtained for the AI development.

Further, NAVA asserts that transparency obligations should apply to all AI services operating in Australia, irrespective of where the AI model was trained, and that penalties for non-compliance should extend to platforms based overseas to maintain a level playing field for local businesses.

How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols to ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve ICIP?

To preserve and respect ICIP, the mandatory guardrails must include specific protections that ensure AI systems respect First Nations cultural protocols. This would involve ensuring that datasets used for training AI are not derived from First Nations cultural materials without proper consultation, consent, and compensation. Indigenous knowledge holders should be consulted, and their protocols integrated into AI development processes.

Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?

NAVA believes the proposed guardrails effectively distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain. However, we suggest stronger accountability mechanisms for developers who use copyrighted material in training AI models, ensuring that compliance with IP laws is consistent throughout the AI lifecycle.

Regulatory Options to Mandate Guardrails

Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?

NAVA supports a framework approach which includes creating new AI-specific legislation. This option allows for the centralisation of transparency obligations and ensures that AI-related copyright compliance measures do not burden the existing Copyright Act. AI-related risks extend beyond traditional copyright issues, and a dedicated AI framework will provide clarity and compliance across all sectors impacted by AI.

Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the Australian Government should consider?

NAVA cautions against any approach that fragments the enforcement of transparency requirements across multiple regulatory frameworks. This could lead to inconsistencies in protecting artists' rights. Centralising AI-specific regulatory obligations will streamline compliance and avoid placing the burden on artists’ to navigate complex legal frameworks.

Guardrail 3: Protect AI systems, and implement data governance measures to manage data quality and provenance. 

NAVA supports Guardrail 3, particularly its focus on ensuring that data used to train AI systems is legally obtained, fit for purpose, and representative, with measures in place to address bias and ensure cybersecurity. However, we believe the guardrail should go further in explicitly addressing intellectual property (IP) concerns, especially regarding the use of visual artworks and cultural materials in AI training datasets. NAVA advocates for enhanced transparency and protections to ensure that artists’ copyrights, moral rights, and cultural rights are upheld, particularly regarding the use of ICIP and visual artworks in AI systems.

The inclusion of data provenance and disclosure requirements is a critical step forward, but it is essential that these disclosures also cover copyrighted material used in training, including how third-party content is sourced and licensed. This is particularly important for visual artists and creators whose works could be appropriated without consent or proper remuneration. NAVA emphasises that datasets used to train AI models must comply with Australia’s copyright laws and provide transparency on how they were sourced. AI platforms must clearly communicate how artists’ copyrighted works, if included in datasets, were sourced - whether through open licenses, public interest exceptions, or specific commercial agreements.

NAVA is particularly concerned about the protection of ICIP. We are pleased to see this referenced and urge that the principles of Indigenous Data Sovereignty be carefully integrated into this guardrail. This means ensuring that First Nations knowledge holders are involved in decisions regarding the use and governance of their cultural data in AI, and that any use of ICIP is fully compliant with Creative Australia’s Protocols for using First Nations Cultural and Intellectual Property in the Arts. This guardrail should also align with the current consultation on standalone ICIP legislation through the Office for the Arts (OFTA). This alignment is crucial to prevent cultural harm and ensure adherence to the new ICIP legislation.


Guardrail 6: Inform end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content. 

NAVA strongly supports the principle of informing end-users about their interactions with AI systems, particularly in cases where AI-generated content is involved. This transparency is essential not only for building public trust in AI systems but also for safeguarding the rights of artists, creators, and cultural workers who are at risk of having their work used or imitated without proper consent or attribution.

Clear and accessible communication about AI use is especially important in the visual arts sector. We support efforts to develop AI detection and labelling techniques, such as Content Credentials, which embed information about the origin and creation of digital content. This helps ensure proper attribution for artists and allows consumers to verify the authenticity of the content they engage with.

Additional Recommendations

1.  Voluntary AI Safety Standard: NAVA recommends that the Voluntary AI Safety Standard be made mandatory for recipients of government funding. This will ensure that publicly funded projects comply with the highest levels of transparency and accountability.

2.  Government Procurement: NAVA suggests that, as part of government procurement processes, suppliers should be required to disclose any use of Australians' content in the development of AI products or services, ensuring artists' rights are respected.


Please contact me for any further information I can provide.


Yours sincerely,

Penelope Benton

SUBMISSION   
 
Safe and responsible AI in Australia : proposals paper for introducing 
mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings (Sep 2024)  
 
Submission to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources  
Prepared by  Peter Richard McDonald  and 
Associate Professor Selina Tually  
Centre for Social Impact , Flinders University  
3rd Oct 2023   
 
1 
 Executive Summary  
 
The Centre for Social Impact at Flinders University has a stream of their work centred on ensuring new 
technologies are used in appropriate ways and do not disadvantage or further reinforce disadvantages 
experienced by particular groups within our communities. This work is supported through a n industry  
partnership the Centre for Social Impact has with Uniting Communities (UC) – known as Data for Good. Our 
partnership brings together connections and influence across the community services sector and academia  
around issues of marginalisation and in ways of amplifying the voices and experiences of marginalised 
people .  
A key focus of partnership work is understanding and illuminating the impacts of data, artificial 
intelligence (AI) and automated decision making (ADM) on isolated and disadvantaged people.  The 
Data for Good research focus remains on the importance of saf eguarding marginalised people and 
communities from the negative effects of AI.  
 
This submission brings together some of our research and thinking around AI and its use in highrisk 
settings  as our response to The S afe and responsible AI in Australia: Proposals paper for introducing 
mandatory guardrails for AI in high -risk settings (proposals paper) . Our contribution to the current 
debates around AI regulation is important . Too frequently we overlook the impacts of such 
technologies and their deep and widespread uses on already marginalised and disadvantaged 
people, families and groups. We raise as a specific case in point here : the emerging issue of 
discrimination in the private rental market due to the application of AI and ADM in the o nline 
platforms people must now use to apply for, see and rent a home . We offer insights into this issue in 
our submission and thoughts around regulation, specifically the need for an AI and new technologies 
ombudsman  to be established to  respond to complaints which are unable to be  resolved directly 
with industry or government . 
 
   
2 
 Introduction  
 
The Centre for Social Impact Flinders University is  concerned about the many  ways A I is affecting 
vulnerable populations . AI and ADM has an influence over our everyday lives and it is imperative 
mechanisms are in place to scrutinise the impacts such technologies are having on humans and 
communities, especially more marginalised people and groups; those who traditionally have less of a 
voice in their lives and those of the communities in which they live. As researchers tightly connected 
to the community services sector we are concerned about the impact of AI and ADM inside rent 
technology (rent tech), the online platforms people use to rent a home in which to live.  Examples of 
rent tech include : 
• Real Estate.com https://realestate.com.au  
• IRE Pty Ltd: 2Apply: https://www.2apply.com.au  
• Tenant Options Pty Ltd : https://tenantoptions.com.au/  
• REA Group Ltd: https://www.realestate.com.au/  
• Sorted Labs Pty Ltd: https://www.sortedservices.com  
• Rent.com.au Ltd: https://www.rent.com.au   
 
Questions: Defining high -risk AI  
Responses to question s for consultation.  
 
Qu 1: Do the proposed principles adequately capture high -risk AI?  Are there any principles we 
should add or remove?  
The Proposals  paper seek s a more comprehensive understand ing of  the adverse impacts of AI.  The 
proposed definition of high -risk AI  requires the consideration of  six principles ( Proposals paper  items 
(a)-(f) p.19 .). We want to see rent tech considered as a high -risk technology. Our reading of the 
proposed principles is that it capture s rent tech  platforms  inside the definition of high -risk AI on at 
least five of the six principles . We describe our inclusionary reading of the principles as follow s. 
Principle A:  adverse impact to an individual’s  rights recognised in Australian human rights 
law 
Our unpublished research is gathering evidence of where rent tech discriminates against 
people on attributes such as g ender, rac e and income status. We have interviewed 
individuals who  report being discriminated against by rent tech platforms , even having their 
ability to view a property curtailed by ADM . We also note that there is existing research on  
3 
 the adverse impacts of discrimination in renting  (Wolifson, P ., Maalsen, S., & Rogers, D.  
2023) . 
The insights and experiences noted in o ur research , particularly when positioned  alongside 
the emerging body of academic evidence , reach th e definitional criteria  of Principle A  - 
adverse affects  on an individual ’s right access to housing  without discrimination . 
Principle B: adverse impact on individ ual’s physical or mental health and safety . 
There is a body of research which describes the adverse physical and mental health affects 
of renting  (Li, A. Baker,  E., & Bentley , R. 2022 ).  
Though not our specific research focus in terms of investigating rent tech , we have feel that  
the research evidence on the adverse effects of being excluded from renting would reach 
the definitional criteria of Principle B – adverse impact s on a n individual’s physical , mental 
health and safety.  
Principle D: adverse impacts to groups of individuals or collective rights of cultural groups . 
Our research project is gathering evidence of individuals who are being adversely affect ed 
by rent tech.   We have  particular groups  such as single mothers and Aboriginal and Torres 
Strait Islander people s reporting to us that they are f aced with discriminatory barriers from 
rent tech . 
Our evidence , alongside existing  academic research , would reach th e definitional criteria  of 
Principle C  – adverse impacts on groups and individuals  collective rights  of cultural groups.  
Principle E: adverse impacts on the broader Australian  economy, society , environment and 
rule of law  
The growing number  of people and families who can no longer afford to buy a ho me can be 
seen in an increase in the number of people renting  from 20% of the population in 1999 to 
26% in 2020 (Australian Bureau of Statistics, Survey of Income and Housing May 2022 ). This 
increasing proportion of the population who are reliant on renting  sits alongside an 
increasing number of renters in Australian society who are faced with the adverse impact of 
renting : lack of stability in their life circumstances due to constant threat of, or need to, 
move; housing affordability and cost of living stress etc  (Hulse, K., Morris, A., & Pawson, H. 
2018 ). Any applic ation of AI, including ADM, that makes the renting situation harder for 
people and families amplifies the stress and impacts of housing instability in people’s lives.  
There is a body of research evidence on Australian society and renting which would reach 
the definitional criteria of Principle E – the adverse impacts on broader Australian society .  
4 
 Principle F.  the severity and extent of those adverse impact s outline d in (a) to (e) . 
The severity of impacts of being excluded  from renting, or living in precarious housing 
circumstances, sits inside a body of academic work including longitudinal studies on the 
effects of housing and renting (Li, A. Baker, E., & Bentley, R. 2022 ). The severity and impacts 
of discrimination and being unable to rent are captured by Principle F.  It is our view that 
being left in tenuous housing or homeless ( without housing at all ) has a profound and 
lifelong impact on people , families, communities and Australian society, impacting the social,  
economic and cultural fabric of our country  (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare  
2024).  
We strongly support the inclusion of rent tech within the category of high -risk AI takes in rent -tech.  
This logical and necessary inclusion would see rent tech platform developers, owners and, hopefully 
also, users  (i.e. landlords and real estate agents) , more aware of the impacts they have in the lives
