SAP RESPONSE TO THE PROPOSALS PAPER FOR INTRODUCING MANDATORY GUARDRAILS 
FOR AI IN HIGH RISK SETTINGS  
 
SAP Australia Pty Ltd, a subsidiary of SAP SE (hereafter referred to as ' SAP'), a leading global software 
provider, thanks the Australian Government for the opportunity to contribute to the Proposals Paper 
for Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High -Risk Settings  (the Paper ). We appreciate the 
government’s proactive approach to developing best practices in AI regulation and value the 
opportunity to provide feedback on this crucial issue.  
 
Recently, SAP released the report Advancing Australia with AI , a copy of which is also submitted 
Attachment A . This paper outlines the significant opportunities AI technologies can unlock for the 
Australian economy, showcasing five real -world use cases where SAP Business AI is already helping 
our customers improve efficiency and effectiveness. Furthermore, this document sets out SAP's core 
AI principles on relevant, reliable, and responsible AI which is much in line with global AI regulations. 
These are our AI principles , which  have shaped our response to the Paper.  
 
About SAP Business AI  
SAP has been delivering AI enabled business solutions for well over a decade, including more than 100 
machine learning algorithms in SAP HANA since the product’s early days. Recent developments in 
Generative AI have resulted in a vast amount of new use cas es and solutions for our customers.  
 
SAP’s Business AI encompasses the tools we offer and are developing for our quarter -million strong 
global customer base. It is the deployment of these tools on our customers’ data that will help to 
elevate productivity across both, the Australian and globa l economy.   
 
Our Business AI is founded on three pivotal principles, known as the three Rs:  
• Relevant  - SAP Business AI is relevant from day one since it is built in across all SAP applications 
that customers already use to run their most critical business processes; in other words, AI to 
run companies.  
 
• Reliable  - SAP Business AI is grounded in the truth of customers’ business and leverages 
generative AI in context with real -time information to help ensure accurate and safe outputs.  
 
• Responsible - SAP Business AI is designed for people to get their best work done, valuing 
human oversight and agency to keep humans in the loop.  
 
For relevant, reliable, and responsible application of AI, data quality and context are critical. What sets 
SAP apart from many other solution providers is our experience and access to the wealth of high -
quality data used to train our models across our glo bal customer base, as well as our deep 
understanding of business processes.  
 
With SAP customers touching 87% of total global commerce, this means SAP Business AI is harnessing 
the immense power of the world’s largest and most comprehensive pool of business data.  
 
Recognition of Government Initiatives  
We commend the Australian Government for its early leadership in supporting AI best practices, 
particularly the Policy for the responsible use of AI in government  established by the Digital 
Transformation Agency (DTA) to guide the public sector's AI use. We also recognise the co -operation 
across Australian governments to established aligned standards with the National Framework for the 
Assurance of AI in Government . These actions taken by Australian governments are positioning 
Australian governments as a gl obal exemplar of responsible use of AI in Government.  2 
 
 
Additionally, we recognize the pivotal work of the National Artificial Intelligence Centre  (NAIC ) in 
establishing a Voluntary AI Safety Standard to support Australian AI users. This toolkit will facilitate 
the responsible adoption of AI, instilling businesses with the confidence that they can implement AI 
tools thoughtfully while being aware of criti cal considerations. As a global organisation we particularly 
welcome the close alignment between the Voluntary AI Safety Standard and ISO 42001.  
 
These initiatives are instrumental in promoting the wider adoption of AI across the economy. Given 
the current economic context, where Australia is grappling with declining productivity, the potential 
for AI to drive growth and efficiency among businesses and workers is essential.  
 
Position on Ex -Ante AI Regulation  
We recognise the Government’s intention to take a preventative approach to potential AI harms. 
However, SAP holds the view that ex -ante AI regulatory interventions —imposing regulatory structures 
in advance —are not the optimal solution for AI technology dev elopment.  
 
SAP has been a major industry stakeholder and contributor to the development of the EU Act. While 
we acknowledge the alignment between the Australian framework and ex -ante approaches in the EU 
and Canada, we believe the best approach to managing potential harms from AI technologies is 
through sector -specific regulation.  
 
It is worth noting that one of Australia's largest allies, the United States, which leads globally in AI 
adoption, has also chosen a sectoral approach to AI regulation rather than establishing an ex -ante 
framework. Similarly, New Zealand has also announced  that it will take a sectoral approach and ruled 
out AI -specific regulation in favour of pro -innovation policies focused on AI adoption and adaptation. 
This approach, which encourages innovation while monitoring potential risks within specific sectors, 
will support the US to maintain its leadership position in private AI investment.  
 
In contrast, the EU is significantly lagging behind the US in private AI investment. A recent audit by the 
European Court of Auditors  highlighted that AI investment in the EU is not keeping pace with global 
leaders. In 2023, the EU invested approximately $9 billion in AI, compared to around $55 billion in the 
US.1.  
 
We recognise that there are concerns about AI’s potential impact, particularly areas such as, but not 
limited to:  
• Automated decision -making and its effects on individuals or groups ; 
 
• Copyright -related issues ; 
 
• Anti-discrimination ; 
 
• Misinformation that could harm social cohesion or mislead consumers ; and  
 
• Security risks associated with AI systems . 
 
These concerns are valid and warrant further gap analysis to be undertaken. However, we believe the 
most prudent approach is to addressing these specific issues sector -by-sector before adopting broad, 
whole of economy, ex -ante regulatory frameworks.

Definition of High -Risk Use Cases  
SAP strongly opposes the proposal to define high -risk AI use cases through a principles -based 
approach. While flexibility is important, this method introduces significant uncertainty for businesses 
and creates variability in how AI risk is assessed across industries. There are several key issues with 
this approach:  
 
• Business Uncertainty : By relying on principles rather than a defined list, businesses are left to 
interpret the level of risk on their own. This leads to inconsistency in how different 
organizations apply the regulations. A use case that one business deems low -risk could be 
classified as high -risk by another, creating an uneven playing field.  
 
• Market Barriers : The ambiguity of the principles -based approach may result in hesitation 
among businesses to adopt AI solutions, fearing that their applications could later be 
categorized as high -risk. This creates a barrier to AI adoption at a time when businesses shoul d 
be embracing technology to improve productivity and innovation.  
 
• Assurance Challenges : The lack of clarity also makes it difficult for developers and vendors to 
provide consistent assurance to customers. If one customer considers an AI solution high -risk 
and another does not, vendors may face fragmented compliance requirements across their  
client base. This can lead to inefficiencies and added costs in development, testing, and 
deployment.  
 
SAP advocates for a list -based approach that provides clear and specific examples of high -risk AI use 
cases. This method offers certainty and allows businesses to operate with confidence, knowing 
whether or not their AI solutions fall under high -risk regul ations. Furthermore, the list should be 
dynamic, with a Ministerial process (such as a legislative instrument) to allow for updates to the list 
as new use cases emerge or as certain applications prove to be less risky than initially thought.  
 4 
 
 
To ensure consistency and minimize regulatory burden for global businesses, SAP recommends that 
in line with the Government’s intention to promote inter -jurisdictional interoperability, this list be 
aligned with the EU AI Act's definitions of high -risk AI systems. The EU has already laid out a clear 
framework, and aligning Australia’s definitions with international standards will help streamline 
compliance for businesses operating in multiple regions.  
 
2. Regulation of General Purpose AI (GPAI)  
SAP acknowledges the potential implications of General Purpose AI (GPAI), but we believe it is 
premature to regulate a technology that is not yet fully developed or understood. There are several 
concerns with the current proposal to classify GPAI as high -risk by default:  
 
• Prematurity of Regulation : Given that GPAI technology is still evolving, it is difficult to predict 
the specific risks associated with its use. Regulating GPAI now, before the technology has 
matured, could result in over -regulation or misalignment with the actual risks it presents . 
Instead, the focus should be on regulating the specific use cases of GPAI rather than the 
technology itself.  
 
• Unnecessary Burden : Automatically classifying GPAI as high -risk places an undue regulatory 
burden on businesses that utilize this technology. Many use cases of GPAI are likely to be low -
risk, such as customer service chatbots or basic language models used in non -critical 
applications (and GPAI models are restricted to the use case of the application). Imposing 
strict regulatory controls on all GPAI applications could stifle innovation and slow the adoption 
of AI across industries.  
 
We discourage the automatic classification of GPAI as high -risk. Instead, the government should 
remain engaged with the development of GPAI technology and reassess its regulatory stance as the 
technology matures and more use cases become clear. This approa ch allows for flexibility while 
ensuring that any regulatory intervention is based on evidence of actual harm rather than theoretical 
risks.  
 
3. Proposed Guard Rails  
SAP has foundational policies and principles being broken into:  
▪ Human Agency & Oversight  
➢ SAP follows a human -centered approach to Business AI  
➢ SAP puts in place appropriate governance mechanism to allow for human intervention 
and control of its AI systems’ decisions  
➢ The extent of oversight necessary for a specific AI system is evaluated depending on 
its context of use and risks of interference with the rights and freedom of affected 
individuals  
▪ Addressing Risk & Discrimination  
➢ SAP defines a clear scope for the AI system and ensure that AI system’s behaviour 
matches within that boundary.  
➢ AI systems go through SAP’s regular, continuously adapted quality assurance process  
➢ Throughout the AI system lifecycle, SAP assesses and monitors fairness by ensuring 
representation of all forms of diversity and making reasonable efforts to avoid 
discriminatory or biased outcomes  
▪ Transparency & Explainability  
➢ SAP clearly communicates input, capabilities, intended purpose and limitations of its 
AI systems to its customers  
➢ SAP ensures that end users are aware about their interaction with an AI system  5 
 
 
➢ SAP strives to provide clear and understandable explanations of recommendations 
and decisions of its AI systems  
➢ SAP actively supports industry collaboration and conducts research to improve 
transparency  
Hence, we are supportive of the 10 proposed guardrails proposed by the paper.

In relation to Guardrail 8 on specific prohibitions, foundational to SAP’s approach to AI Ethics is our 
commitment (through our Global Human Rights Commitment Statement) to uphold and support the 
Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and to respect, promote, and support internationally 
recognized human rights and widely accepted international norms.  
 
An essential part of this commitment is the prohibition of discrimination and harassment of humans 
based on personal factors (including for example culture, race, ethnicity, religion, age, gender, sexual 
orientation, gender identity, physical or mental dis ability etc.), with the goal to promote respect for 
human autonomy and to ensure that the moral worth and dignity of all human beings is respected.  
 
If the Government is considering the introduction of specific circumstances prohibiting AI, it could 
consider these prohibitions and goals . 
 
It is SAP’s view that AI should be developed to augment, complement, and empower human cognitive, 
social, and cultural skills, and not act to prevent or restrict activities that are commensurate with a 
free society.  
 
• AI systems should not be developed or deployed for human surveillance that is utilized for the 
targeting of individuals or groups, either by biometrics, facial recognition, or other identifiable 
features, with the purpose of disregarding or abusing the hum an rights of the individuals or 
groups.  
 
• AI systems should not be developed or deployed for purposes which cause individuals or 
groups to be discriminated against or excluded from equal access to AI’s benefits and 
opportunities that may be available to the wider population.    
 
• AI systems should not be developed or deployed for deception or unfair manipulation of 
individuals or groups via public forums, media, or moderation of other similar uses.     
 
• AI systems should not be developed or deployed to undermine human debate or democratic 
electoral systems.

• AI system development or deployment should be conducted with minimum to no explicit 
damage to the environment.   
 
4. Alignment with International Standards  
SAP fully supports the Australian Government’s commitment to ensuring global interoperability of AI 
regulations. As a global business, consistency in standards across regions is essential for efficient 
operations. The ability to reuse certifications / conf ormity assessments and demonstrate compliance 
across multiple jurisdictions is critical to reducing administrative and operational burdens.  
 
We welcome the government’s recognition of the need to align its proposed regulations with 
international frameworks, particularly those being developed in the European Union. The EU AI Act  
has set a strong foundation for AI governance, and aligning Australian regulations with the EU AI Act  
will enable businesses to operate more seamlessly across borders.  
 
• Cross -Jurisdictional Recognition : SAP encourages the Australian Government to explicitly 
recognize certifications and assurance frameworks developed under the EU AI Act. If an AI 
solution has met a conformity assessment under the EU’s compliance framework, this 
assurance should be accept ed within Australia without requiring additional certification. This 
would not only reduce duplication but also accelerate the adoption of AI solutions in the 
Australian market.  
 
• Best Practices : Aligning with international standards also ensures that Australia remains 
linked to global best practices in AI governance. The EU’s approach to risk management, data 
governance, and transparency is well -regarded, and Australian businesses would benefit from 
adhering to these principles.  
 
 
5. Lack of clarity on how the rules will be applied across the supply chain of deployers and 
developers.  
There is a lack of clarity regarding how the proposed regulations will apply across the entire supply 
chain of AI developers and deployers. While SAP supports the distinction made in the proposal 
between different organizations within the AI supply chain, including the delineation of 
responsibilities between developers and deployers as outlined in Attachment E  of the Paper, the 
framework remains ambiguous about its application to multiple developers involved in creating AI 
systems classified as high -risk. 
 
For example, SAP Joule, SAP's co -pilot, utilizes a Retrieval -Augmented Generation ( RAG ) process to 
enhance its capabilities. The approach enables Joule to provide more accurate and contextually 
relevant responses by incorporating information from various sourced stored directly within SAP 
systems. This co -pilot enables users to retrieve and  surface insights tailored to their specific data 
stored in SAP applications, offering relevant information and personalized insights based on that data.  
 
However, the generative responses are powered in part by third -party Large Language Models ( LLMs ), 
which help generate natural language responses. The proposal does not clearly outline how 
compliance checks or enforcement mechanisms would apply to such third -party LLMs, especially 
when these systems are developed and maintained by external providers.  This raises questions about 
the government's enforceable rights over third -party tools or businesses that are not directly 
controlled by or in a commercial rel ationship with the organization deploying the AI system, such as 
SAP.  
 8 
 
 
Moreover, the proposal does not sufficiently explain how the government intends to enforce 
regulatory compliance across the entire supply chain, which can involve multiple, sometimes 
international, developers. This creates uncertainty for companies like SA P that integrate third -party 
AI components, as it remains unclear who would be accountable for ensuring these components meet 
regulatory standards.  
 
Another area that should be clear in the distinction between Developers and Deployers is 
accountability during the lifecycle of a solution being in operation. For example, while a Developer 
may have an obligation to avoid bias in the data a model is traine d on, control is lost once the Deployer 
begins using the model and imputing their own data. Distinguishing the accountability between testing 
and operations should be made clear.  
 
Given the increasing complexity of AI ecosystems, the current proposal does not provide a clear 
strategy for addressing accountability gaps across the supply chain, which is critical when third -party 
tools play a significant role in AI development and depl oyment. Without clear mechanisms for 
monitoring and enforcing compliance across all participants —especially third -party providers —the 
proposed regulations could be difficult to implement effectively. This leaves developers and deployers 
uncertain about how  to manage risks and ensure compliance in multi -developer scenarios, particularly 
when third parties are outside Australia's jurisdiction.  
 
6. Preferred Ex -Ante Regulatory Approach  
As previously mentioned, SAP does not support the introduction of ex -ante regulation for AI 
technologies. Our preferred approach is to focus on sector -specific regulations that address identified 
harms rather than applying an economy -wide assurance process . However, if the government 
proceeds with ex -ante regulation, SAP considers the establishment of a new AI Act (Option 3) to be 
the most effective framework.  
 
• Regulatory Consistency : A dedicated AI Act would ensure consistency in regulatory 
application, avoiding potential conflicts between sector -specific regulations. By centralizing 
the regulatory framework under one Act, the government can ensure that AI guardrails are 
applied uniformly across industries.  
 
• Expertise Development : Establishing a dedicated regulatory body for AI through a new Act 
would allow for the development of specialized expertise in AI technologies. This would 
improve the quality of regulation and ensure that the guardrails are effectively enforced while 
supp orting AI innovation and growth in Australia.  
 
 
Furthermore, we agree with the limitations outlined in the Paper regarding the risks of applying sector -
specific regulations for AI, particularly the potential for conflicting authority between regulatory 
bodies. By adopting a unified AI Act, these issues can be mitigated, providing businesses with a clear 
and consistent regulatory framework.  
 
Conclusion  
In conclusion, SAP remains committed to engaging with the Australian Government on the 
development of a robust AI regulatory framework. While we advocate for sector -specific regulation, 
we also recognize the importance of ensuring global alignment, regulat ory clarity, and effective 
compliance mechanisms should the government pursue an ex -ante approach.  9 
 
 
APPENDIX A – SAP RESPONSES TO THE SPECIFIC QUESTIONS RAISED IN THE PAPER  
 
Question 1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high -risk AI? Are there any principles we 
should add or remove?  
SAP does not support defining high -risk AI through a purely principles -based approach . We 
recommend a list-based approach  with specific examples of high -risk AI use cases, similar to  the EU 
AI Act, to provide businesses with greater clarity and operational confidence.  
 
Question 3. Do the principles and examples provide clarity on high -risk AI settings? Is a more defined 
list-based approach needed?  
SAP strongly supports a list-based approach , similar to the EU and Canada, over a purely principles -
based one, due to the higher clarity it offers to businesses. In recognition that use cases may change 
over time, to address emerging issues the list could be dynamic list with updates through a legislative 
process.  
 
Question 4. High -risk use cases for potential banning?  
In relation to SAP own Business AI principles we prohibit the development of AI systems that violate 
human rights, such as AI used for:  
o Human surveillance  (biometrics/facial recognition targeting individuals or groups).  
o Discrimination or exclusion  from AI benefits.  
o Deception or manipulation  in public forums or democratic processes.  
o Environmental damage . 
 
Question 5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high -
risk AI, like GPAI?  
SAP cautions against the automatic classification of GPAI as high -risk, as the technology is still 
evolving. Instead we encourage  the government to monitor GPAI development and focus on specific 
use cases rather than regulate the technology itself.  
 
Question 6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?  
SAP does not support a blanket approach for regulating GPAI, instead guardrails should apply only to 
high -risk use cases rather than all GPAI applications, as some may be low -risk. 
 
Question 7. Indicators for defining GPAI models as high -risk?  
See SAP’s response  to question 6.  
 
Question 8. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails adequate?  
SAP supports the guardrails but recommends additional clarity in assigning responsibility across the 
AI supply chain , particularly where third -party AI components are involved.  
 
Question 10. Do the guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain appropriately?  
There is a lack of clarity in how responsibilities are distributed, particularly with third -party providers. 
We call for more detailed guidance on compliance checks  and enforcement mechanisms  across the 
entire supply chain, including international developers.  
 
Question 11. Are the guardrails sufficient to address GPAI risks?  
See SAP’s response to Question 5.  
 
Question 12. Reducing regulatory burden for small -to-medium businesses?  
SAP does not recommend variable application of regulation across the economy . 
 
Question 13. Preferred legislative option for high -risk AI settings?  10 
 
 
SAP does not recommend an ex -ante regulatory approach. However, if the government chooses to 
pursue an ex -ante approach, SAP recommend a new AI Act  (Option 3)  as this is most likely to deliver 
regulatory consistency  and the development of specialized expertise  and understanding  within 
government in AI technologies . 
 
Question 14. Additional limitations the Government should consider?  
When considering the creation of compliance and conformity assessment framework SAP strongly 
recommends mutual recognition of other like jurisdictions. This aligns with the Government’s stated 
purpose and goal of designing the proposed regulation to be aligned and interoperable with global 
standards. We are encouraged by the proposed amendments to the Privacy Act which will allow for 
recognition jurisdictions with similar privacy in relation to the overseas transfer of data.  
 
Question 15. Which regulatory option can adapt to step -changes in technology?  
SAP advocates for a centralized AI Act  that would provide a consistent, adaptable framework to 
manage the evolving landscape of AI technologies.

This starts with the principle that the focus should not be regulation of AI per se but a focus on the specific

We recognize the Australian Governments @consultation on Mandatory guardrails for safe and responsible AI. 
Our response to this consultation is informed by the following approach.With respect to regulation more generally, we acknowledge that there are 
potential societal harms that may exist outside of the adoption of AI into a 
business. Based on SAP’s engagement across jurisdictions globally, we 
recommend the following approach when considering regulatory intervention. 
Regulation to address specific harms
When considering the application of regulation to AI we have recommended the 
following approach.
Identify the specific harms that are a result of the use of AI technologies.
Assess existing regulation to determine whether the specific harms posed by AI are not already 
addressed. For example, data protection and privacy, consumer protection, product safety, security, 
export control, and liability, as well as sector -specific regulation, e.g., on critical infrastructures, 
medical goods and services, financial services, food safety, and motor vehicle safety.
•AI development often depends on the ingestion of large sets of data that are used to train 
algorithms to produce models that assist with decision -making. To the extent that any of the input 
for an AI model involves personal data or any output is used to make decisions that affect the 
rights or interests of individuals, the AI model and its applications are already directly subject to 
existing rules under the Australian Privacy Act.
If existing regulation is insufficient to address these specific harms –consider amendments to existing 
regulation to address the harm.
•In response to concerns around automated decisions that impact on individuals’ rights in 2023 the 
Australian Government agreed to legislate to define “types of personal information that will be 
used in substantially automated decisions” affecting “an individual’s rights” and enshrine “a right to 
request meaningful information about how automated decisions are made.”
If amendments to existing regulation are insufficient to address the perceived harm take a risk -based 
approach whereby proposed regulation is applied to specific high risk scenarios. These should relate 
to specific harms to the public.
Articulation of these high -risk scenarios to which proposed AI specific rules will be applied must be 
clearly and precisely defined and not generalized.
When applying the regulation , it must take into account the unique roles and responsibilities of the 
entities involved in the AI supply chain. Broadly speaking the supply chain consists of Developers 
and Deployers. The two roles can be distinguished as follows: 
•an organization that designs, codes or produces an AI system, for example a system integrated 
into an expense management solution to read digital images of receipts is a Developer  
•an organization that uses that AI system to make a decision for a customer, employee or for its 
own business operations is a Deployer 
•in some cases, the same organization may be both a Developer and a Deployer. 
Consequently , the responsibility and consequences of meeting those regulations should fall on the 
group best able to identify and reduce the risk of harm. Ideally there should be room for contractual 
freedom between equal parties to negotiate. This will typically be the organisation with direct 
relationship with the citizen or customer. 
Aligning with global standards , many AI solutions are offered worldwide can benefit from regulatory 
alignment across jurisdictions reducing duplication and cost through the recognition of existing 
standards and frameworks.

1.    SUMMARY
* Film and television (screen) content creates important cultural benefits for Australians, and significant economic impact. This submission focuses on Australia’s post-production, digital and visual effects (PDV) sector, which uses strong contractual and technological processes to operate ethically and safely. 
* 
* While some AI tools are generating concern in the global screen sector, several tools are used ethically and safely in the industry. An example is REVIZE, a world-leading machine learning platform developed in Australia and only used to create visual effects for film and TV content.
* 
* Such tools should be considered low-risk when evaluated against the principles outlined in the Proposals Paper, or other principles adopted by the Government. 
* 
* Ausfilm’s supports the use of a principles framework to avoid inadvertent capture of low-risk applications. If the Government adopts a list-based approach it is important that the list exclude low-risk, safe and ethical AI tools used for the creation of professional screen content, particularly in post-production and visual effects. 
Introduction
Ausfilm welcomes the opportunity to make this submission to the Australian Government regarding the introduction of mandatory guardrails for use of AI in high-risk settings.
Ausfilm is a unique government and industry partnership that promotes Australia as a leading film and television production destination and drives inward investment across the nation. We do this by marketing Australia’s suite of screen production tax incentives and connecting international filmmakers with Australia’s screen industry.
Ausfilm receives an annual grant from the Australian Government and reports to Government departments and agencies on issues that affect the screen industry. Ausfilm’s members include eight government screen agencies and 55 corporate businesses that work with global filmmakers across all aspects of content creation. Members include Australia's major studio complexes, production service providers, and picture, sound, music, visual effects, and animation studios. 
2.  Screen content is culturally and economically significant
Screen content is culturally important and economically significant. Australians spend more than 15 hours per week watching screen content, and going to the cinema remains the most popular cultural venue or event in Australia. 
The sector also creates important economic impacts, with expenditure on drama in Australia reaching $2.34 billion in 2022/23. Work in the sector includes: 
* physical production: the filming of content
* and post-production, digital and visual effects (PDV) work: editing of picture and sound, and the creation of digital effects and animations.
This submission focuses on Australia’s PDV sector. 
3.  Post-production and visual effects work relies on safety and security
PDV work is completed by specialist companies based around the world. Australian PDV companies commonly work on blockbuster projects shot in Australia and elsewhere. Packages of work are often worth millions of dollars. To win contracts, PDV companies must:
* create work that excels creatively and technologically 
* offer services at a competitive price
* provide a safe and secure work environment, usually certified under the Trusted Partner Network (TPN) accreditation 
* fulfill contracts with strict requirements around use, storage, confidentiality and disposal of footage, data and other information
* provide unencumbered outputs: work that a studio client can use free of any claim.
PDV work is high cost, high stakes, and subject to very strong safeguards. A data leak, privacy breach or other failure would be disastrous for any PDV company or worker. To manage risks, the industry has well-established processes regarding safety, security, copyright, privacy and consent. 
4.  AI screen sector tools vary - and include safe and ethical options
The screen sector is widely considered to be facing significant disruption by artificial intelligence. The creation of professional film and television is often a high-cost activity that involves thousands of people. AI tools can now be used to augment this process, and some AI platforms promise the creation of content entirely generated by AI. 
The provenance, quality and ethics of some AI tools and their training data is strongly debated by some stakeholders in the sector here and overseas. Ausfilm acknowledges important concerns about unethical and unsafe use of AI. However, it is not widely appreciated that some specific AI tools have been safely and ethically used by the sector for several years, particularly machine learning tools used by post-production and visual effects businesses. An example is set out below.
5.  Machine learning case study – REVIZE and Rising Sun Pictures
Rising Sun Pictures (RSP) is an Australian company that creates world-class visual effects for films and television. Created in Adelaide almost 30 years ago, RSP also has an office in Brisbane, and employs more than 350 people in Australia. RSP has contributed to more than 200 tentpole films and series projects, including Deadpool & Wolverine, Star Wars: The Acolyte and Elvis. 
RSP has used machine-learning techniques for several years to create visual effects. RSP’s REVIZE platform is a world-leading suite of tools empowered by machine learning. People and objects are ‘scanned’ and this information is input into REVIZE. The platform enables face replacement, facial performance modification, de-aging, body replacements, and other likeness adaptations. REVIZE was used to create ‘baby Thor’ in Thor: Love and Thunder, de-age Furiosa in Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga, and replace actors in dangerous scenes. 
Importantly:
* RSP is a developer and deployer of REVIZE
* REVIZE is a narrow AI system: it is only used for defined tasks
* Use of REVIZE is restricted. It is only available to vetted film and TV clients, and only used on RSP premises – no cloud or external services are used
* Use of REVIZE is governed by strict contracts that establish consent and security for all parties
* Source data is restricted and traceable. RSP does not maintain a generalised database for REVIZE: for each project, the software is trained on specific actors contracted for the project, and training data is archived or deleted as per client instructions. RSP can trace which data is used for any output. 
REVIZE empowers actors, filmmakers and visual effects artists to create better work. Demand for REVIZE is a significant factor in RSP growing its employee base: efforts that are enhanced by RSP’s training partnership with the University of South Australia. REVIZE is RSP’s latest product in a long history of research and development and is an example of Australian innovation that should be further encouraged.
6.  Feedback on mandatory guardrails
Tools such as REVIZE are empowered by properly sourced data, used safely and with the informed consent of stakeholders, and bound by clear and strong contracts as well as by compelling commercial and reputational incentives. These tools create strong creative and economic benefits for Australia, and place Australian businesses at the forefront of global innovation. Ausfilm supports the safe and ethical development and deployment of AI tools, as well as the need for regulation and guidance to prevent AI use that is risky, unsafe, and unethical.
Ausfilm considers that, when evaluated against the principles outlined in the Proposals Paper, the ethical development and use of AI tools such as REVIZE is low-risk. However, Ausfilm requests greater guidance and assurance for companies on this question, particularly as PDV work can involve the recording and storage of biometric information. 
Ausfilm supports the Government’s use of a principles framework as it is more likely to avoid inadvertently catching low-risk applications. Ausfilm suggests that REVIZE could be used in government guidance as an example of a low-risk activity. If Government considers modifying the principles outlined in the Proposal Paper, it should also consider how these modifications would impact low-risk applications such as REVIZE.
If the Government creates a principles framework, and categories of use are treated separately, Government should strongly consider a category for narrow AI systems used for the creation of professional film and television content. It may be necessary to distinguish content created for curated platforms subject to classification frameworks (such as cinemas, TV and subscription streaming services), from content distributed outside of such frameworks such as via social media. 
If the Government adopts a list-based approach, it would be very important for the list to exclude the use of narrow AI systems such as REVIZE for the creation of professional screen content. 
The screen sector contains sole traders and small, medium, and large businesses. It would be beneficial for the Government to enable developers and deployers to certify or otherwise provide adequate assurance that their tools comply with guardrails established by the Government. This would significantly assist users, particularly sole traders and smaller businesses.
7.  Further comments
Ausfilm notes the concerns that some screen sector creative workers and organisations hold around AI’s rapid development and deployment. AI tools are predicted to disrupt the development, financing, production, and disruption of content: potentially impacting jobs, businesses, and the essence of what it means to create a work. While this submission focuses on specific AI tools currently used in the PDV sector, it will be vital for government policy to broadly encourage innovation while protecting rights, intellectual property, and the ability to create screen stories. 
8.  Conclusion
Ausfilm thanks the Government for the opportunity to provide this feedback. The screen sector is at the leading edge of technological development, and it is important for government approaches to AI to continually adapt to innovations and challenges in the creative industries. 
Ausfilm would be very happy to discuss this submission further. Please contact Patrick May, Ausfilm’s Director of Policy and Research, via patrick.may@ausfilm.com.au

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?

Please provide any additional comments.

3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?
YES the principles give enough clarity and certainty
If you prefer a principles-based approach, what should we address in guidance to give the greatest clarity?
The principles-based approach allows for the greatest coverage and flexibility, but more work is needed to include concrete examples of high-risk use cases in healthcare, law enforcement, and employment. This would help us to understand application areas better. The principles approach needs to clearly focus on the application of AI in a system, rather than the system in its entirety. What is the influence or affect of AI involvement in a system? Is it making decisions which could reinforce biases in the underlying model or is AI simply used to categorise data? The principles provide a good foundation, but for cases where AI is used to translate existing information, further differentiation between AI that generates content and AI that simply translates or disseminates existing information could add clarity. In this case, a principles-based approach remains appropriate but would benefit from detailed guidance on how the principles apply to specific use cases, especially regarding chatbots in the health sector.
4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Yes
If so, how should we define these?
Biometric surveillance: AI systems that use real-time facial recognition in public spaces should be considered for banning due to privacy and racial profiling concerns.
Social and welfare systems: Any AI that uses personal data to make decisions which impact a person’s access to services or welfare, as it poses unacceptable risks of harm.
Non-consensual deepfake content: AI systems that create non-consensual deepfakes for harmful purposes should be banned.
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?

Yes
Please provide any additional comments.

Additionally, ongoing scientific, technical and governmental evaluation should guide the threshold. As GPAI models may become smaller and take the form of agentic systems using smaller AI models working in tandem a FLOPS threshold alone may not adequately capture high-risk GPAI.

Define high-risk against the principles

No
Please provide any additional comments.
The guardrails seem adequate in addressing transparency, accountability, and testing, but they may need reinforcement in areas such as explainability and bias reduction, especially for systems that affect marginalised populations. While transparency and testing are critical, less emphasis on certain areas (like human intervention) may be needed for systems that are not making complex decisions.
Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?
No
Please provide any additional comments
Additional detail added to ensure guardrails clearly capture explainability and bias reduction.
9. How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols to ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property?

10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
No
Which of the guardrails should be amended?
Establish, implement and publish an accountability process including governance, internal capability and a strategy for regulatory compliance Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight Inform end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails
Please provide any additional comments
There should be more clarity on the role of data providers, auditors, and end-users to ensure accountability across the entire AI lifecycle. Developers and deployers should have clear, delineated responsibilities for mitigating risks at different stages, from design to post-deployment monitoring. More clarity on what "public accountability" means in terms of what must be disclosed for transparency is needed. Currently the specific requirements for public facing publishing of accountability and compliance measures is unclear. The guardrails should be clear on how responsibilities are distributed between developers, those who curate the information, and those who deploy the system.
Guardrail 1: While the requirements for governance are clear, what is to be published publicly is unclear. The specific details of accountability in cases where an AI system causes harm is also not clear. It will be important to ensure that this guardrail considers level of risk, different technical implementations of AI and accountability in systems using multiple proprietary AI models or open-source models.
Guardrail 5: While it is recognised that human involvement may in some cases make an AI system less reliable or undermine the efficiencies gained using AI, it is unclear which use cases are covered by this guardrail. It is mentioned that human intervention to reverse a decision made by AI, but it is unclear in what cases this would be required.
Guardrail 6: Current technical solutions for watermarking are not yet robust and it is unclear how this guardrail will differentiate between content generated entirely by AI versus content which is generated by a retrieval augmented generation system. There is a risk that this will place higher quality content generated by retrieval augmented generation on the same level as content generated by large language models.
Guardrail 9: While the documentation outlined in this guardrail is reasonable, it would be helpful to understand the differing levels of documentation required for smaller organisations. It is also unclear what the assessment of human oversight measures entails, and this could severely impact organisations who are developing systems using proprietary large language models for specific tasks. One approach would be to have clear guidelines for human oversight based on the level of risk of the AI system.
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI?
No
How could we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for example low-risk and high-risk GPAI models? 
Risk Differentiation: GPAI models should be classified into low-risk and high-risk categories based on their intended or foreseeable uses. High-risk GPAI, such as those used in healthcare, law enforcement, or national security, should face more stringent oversight, including enhanced testing, auditing, and regular external reviews.
Granular Testing and Monitoring: For high-risk GPAI, more rigorous and ongoing performance assessments should be required. This includes more frequent audits, post-deployment evaluations, and stress testing under diverse real-world conditions.
Human Oversight for High-Risk Applications: High-risk GPAI models should have built-in safeguards, such as requiring human intervention before critical decisions are made, especially in sectors with legal, medical, or safety implications.
Low-Risk GPAI: For low-risk applications, such as those used in customer service chatbots or administrative tools, the guardrails can be relaxed. For instance, instead of comprehensive testing and transparency requirements, businesses could focus on basic testing and self-regulation with occasional external reviews. It is crucial that the specific influence of AI in a system is considered in calculating risk.
12. Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small-to-medium sized businesses applying guardrails?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
Guardrail 10: Conformity assessment by developers of a system could be problematic without an external body involved. Capacity and skills necessary to undertake the assessment would be varied. How would the accountability of a small start-up organisation developing high-risk AI differ from a large and well know corporation? Many developers will be using existing frameworks to combine open-source or proprietary AI models in new ways and it is unclear how risk assessment and accountability would differ for these systems. Some potential approaches are:
Simplified Compliance Pathways: Introduce a tiered regulatory framework where SMEs with low-risk AI models can opt for a simplified compliance pathway. For example, SMEs could submit self-assessment reports or undergo lighter audits, focusing primarily on transparency and basic performance testing.
Government-Supported AI Safety Tools: Provide SMEs with access to government-developed or open-source tools for testing and auditing AI models. This would allow SMEs to meet the guardrail requirements without needing to invest heavily in custom-built compliance systems.
Financial and Technical Support: Offer grants, or financial incentives to SMEs to help them comply with AI regulations. This could include financial support for third-party audits, legal advice on AI ethics, or consulting services for improving transparency and fairness in AI systems.
Exemptions for Low-Risk AI: Create clear exemptions or lighter requirements for SMEs developing AI systems that are low-risk (e.g., those that automate internal administrative tasks or provide general information with no significant legal, health, or safety consequences).
AI Regulatory Guidance for SMEs: Develop easy-to-understand guidance documents and workshops specifically tailored for SMEs. These materials would outline the requirements, provide case studies, and offer templates for necessary documentation, such as compliance reports.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A framework approach – Introducing new framework legislation to adapt existing regulatory frameworks across the economy
What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
The Framework Approach (Option 2) seems to be the best fit for addressing AI in high-risk settings. It allows for broad regulation across different sectors while giving flexibility for future updates. A framework can be developed to address specific high-risk use cases (e.g., healthcare, finance) ensuring a uniform but adaptable structure.
Opportunities:
• Flexibility for future technological advancements.
• Encouraging consistency across sectors, ensuring alignment with international AI regulations (like the EU's AI Act).
• Creating room for Australia to lead in ethical AI innovation by incorporating culturally relevant frameworks, including Indigenous perspectives.
14. Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the Australian Government should consider?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
Option 1 (Domain-Specific Approach) risks creating inconsistent standards across sectors, making it difficult for businesses and organisations to comply when AI systems overlap multiple domains (e.g., healthcare and consumer services).
Option 3 (Whole-of-Economy Approach) may lack the flexibility to address rapidly evolving AI technologies, leading to potential delays in adapting regulations to new innovations.
There’s also a risk of regulatory burden on SMEs under both options if the regulations are too stringent or unclear, especially for lower-risk systems like informational chatbots.
15. Which regulatory option(s) will best ensure that guardrails for high-risk AI can adapt and respond to step-changes in technology?
A framework approach – Introducing new framework legislation to adapt existing regulatory frameworks across the economy
Please provide any additional comments.
• Regular reviews and updates to the framework to reflect the latest technological trends.
• Engaging with international AI governance bodies to ensure the Australian framework aligns with global standards.
• Building flexibility into the framework for low-risk systems, reducing the regulatory burden on smaller businesses while maintaining safeguards for high-risk AI.
• Consultation with Australian organisations working with AI to ensure the framework adapts with technological advancement and encourages innovation in Australia.
16. Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps and inconsistencies with Australia’s existing laws for the development and deployment of AI?
Australia's existing laws (like the Privacy Act) may not be robust enough to handle the unique challenges AI poses, especially regarding the use of personal data in machine learning models or the explainability of AI-driven decisions.
Which regulatory option best addresses this?
A framework approach – Introducing new framework legislation to adapt existing regulatory frameworks across the economy
Please explain why.  
The Framework Approach (Option 2) is best suited to address these gaps. It can integrate with existing laws by specifying how AI systems should comply with privacy regulations and ensuring transparency for algorithmic decisions. This approach allows for:
• Stronger privacy protections by updating existing laws with AI-specific amendments.
• Enabling accountability through clear guidelines on data governance and transparency for both developers and deployers of AI.
• Aligning Australia's laws with international standards (such as GDPR) to prevent discrepancies in cross-border AI deployment.

maintaining flexibility to address Australia's specific context and needs.  Accordingly , we

Response to Questions for Consultation  
Question 1  
Do the proposed principles adequately capture high -risk AI? Are there any principles we 
should add or remove? Please identify any:  
• low-risk use cases that are unintentionally captured   
• categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for defence or 
national security purposes.  
DLC Legal notes that t he government proposes  a principles  and risk-based approach to 
defining high -risk AI, rather than relying on a rigid list -based method. This approach allows 
for context -specific assessment of risks, considering factors such as impacts on human 
rights, health and safety, legal effects, impacts o n groups and cultural rights, as well as 
broader societal, economic, and environmental impacts. This framework provides a 
comprehensive method for assessing risk across different domains.  We recommend 
further consideration be given to whether more could be done with respect to liability and 
adverse consequences arising from end user interaction with AI systems and models.  
We also note that t he proposal recognises  the unique challenges posed by General 
Purpose AI (GPAI) models, particularly in terms of unforeseen applications and risks. The 
proposal suggests applying the guardrails to all GPAI models which we support. The 
proposal also seeks input from stakeholders on whether a subset of these models should 
be defined or classified as high-risk. The approach outlined in the Proposal aligns with 
developments in other jurisdictions, such as the EU, Canada, and the UK, with room to 
consider  Australia's specific context . AI technology is continuously evolving,  and we 
support the Government’s intention to conduct  regular review s of the guardrails and by 
extension, related definitions of high -risk AI, as AI technology advances.    
  
4 
 
We note that t he guardrails are intended to apply to both developers and deployers of high -
risk AI systems throughout the AI lifecycle. However, it is our view that  these guardrails may 
not (yet) sufficiently go far enough to  sufficiently  address broader societal impacts , 
including reducing the effects of bias built into AI technologies such as gender and racial 
bias nor do they (yet) go far enough to incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural 
protocols. There is flexibility and scope in the proposed approach, however, in  our view, 
there is a need for more specific guidance , including non-exhaustive  examples to provide 
clarity on what constitutes high -risk AI together with  more positive concrete measures 
demonstrating how the very real risks of built in bias (or bias by design) will be mitigated . 
On balance,  the proposed approach provide s a robust foundation for capturing high -risk AI, 
with flexibility to adapt as needed. However, its effectiveness will depend on further 
refinement through consultation and ongoing review as AI technology evolves. Specifically , 
consultation to  strengthen certain aspects  around societal impacts and cultural 
considerations . 
Please identify any:  
• low-risk use cases that are unintentionally captured   
• categories of uses that should be treated separately, such as uses for defence or 
national security purposes.  
Low-risk use cases potentially captured:  The Proposal  allows for context -specific 
assessment, which will help avoid unintentionally capturing truly low -risk uses , which may 
be higher in volume . However, there may be a risk  that if the  guardrails are applied to all 
GPAI models , then lower-risk applications of general -purpose AI  may be caught in a bigger 
net than intended . 
Categories that should be treated separately:  The Proposal Paper  doesn’t appear to  
indicate explicit separate treatment for defen ce or national security AI applications. Given 
the sensitive nature of these domains, we recommend  treating them separately or 
providing specific guidance  as to how they should be treated . There may be a need for a 
separate, specific set of guardrails unique to defence and national security.  
Additional principles:  The current principles currently  focus heavily on risks to individuals , 
which is vitally important . However, f or risks to indiv iduals to be  considered in a wholistic 
context we recommend expanding consideration of broader societal or systemic risks from

AI systems , in particular with respect to ameliorating the very real, very tangible 
consequences  of bias built into AI technologies . 
Principles to remove:  We don’t recommend removing  any principles.

about their communities, cultures, and lands. This would provide vital  protection

more concrete, community -defined benefits and mechanisms to ensure those

in its approach to  banning certain AI applications deemed to pose "unacceptable

• AI systems designed to manipulate human behavio ur or exploit 
vulnerabilities ; 
• Biometric identification systems used for real -time surveillance in public 
spaces (with limited exceptions for law enforcement) ; 
• Predictive policing systems based on profiling ; 
• AI systems that categori se people based on sensitive characteristics like 
race, religion, or sexual orientation  etc.  
In defining what constitutes an unacceptable risk  that would  warrant a ban, it is vitally 
important to consider  the potential for serious harm to individuals' rights, health, or safet y; 
threats to democracy, rule of law, or fundamental freedom , lack of human oversight or 
control; privacy violations; risk of large-scale manipulation or exploitation of people . That 
said, we acknowledge that t here are challenges in implementing outright bans , including 
the very nature of  constantly  evolving technologies  makes it challenging to de fine 
boundaries . Any defined boundaries would need to evolve with technology. Further, b lanket 
bans may hinder or prevent legitimate , beneficial uses or innovation in certain contexts. 
Also, certain high-risk applications may have legitimate uses and provided that  proper 
safeguards  are implemented, these should not be automatically discounted simply 
because they are classified high risk.  
An alternative to implementing a ban or  bans could be to impose very stringent 
requirements and oversight on defined, high-risk applications, as the EU does for many use 
cases. There's also a need to consider exceptions for example with respect to national 
security and law enforcement, subject to  strict safeguards.  
In our view, a ny restrictions or prohibitions should be clearly defined, evidence -based, and 
proportionate to the risks . In considering potential bans, we recommend close 
consideration of the EU's list of banned applications as a starting point.  In addition, 
thorough impact assessments should be conducted to identify AI applications that pose an 
unacceptable risk.  Any restrictions, limitations or bans must be precisely defined to 
mitigate unintended consequences . 
We also advocate for a flexible approach that allows for periodic review and adjustment as 
technology (and societal norms ) evolve. We also strongly support the implementation of a 
robust governance framework to assess and manage risks for high -risk AI applications that 
are subject to limitations and / or restrictions .

Question 5  
Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high -risk 
AI, such as general -purpose AI (GPAI)?  
In our view, s ome key points to consider regarding the flexibility of the proposed principles 
to capture new and emerging forms of high -risk AI, including general -purpose AI (GPAI)  
include: 
Principles -based approach:  The UK's approach, as outlined in the white paper  titled ‘AI 
regulation: a pro -innovation approach – policy proposal ’ emphasises a principles -based 
framework rather than rigid definitions or prescriptive rules. This approach is intended to be 
more flexible and adaptable to emerging technologies.  
Defining AI functionally : The UK defines AI based on its functional characteristics of 
"adaptivity" and "autonomy" rather than specific technologies. This allows the framework 
to potentially cover new forms of AI as they emerge  and evolve . 
Focus on risk:   A risk-based approached would direct focus on assessing and mitigating 
risks associated with AI systems  and models , which could also apply to new forms of high -
risk AI as they are developed  and as they evolve . 
GPAI-specific considerations:  The EU AI Act  recognises the unique challenges of general -
purpose AI systems and models and  has introduced specific provisions to address these  
challenges. This suggests that existing principles will likely  need to be adapted or expanded 
to fully capture GPAI risks . It is worth considering this approach in our Australian context, to 
ensure flexibility and adaptability of the principles as AI systems, models and technologies 
evolve.  
Systemic risk threshold:  The EU approach introduces a compute -based threshold for 
identifying GPAI models that present systemic risks. This essentially means that a GPAI 
model shall be presumed to have "high impact capabilities" and present systemic risk 
when "the cumulative amount of computation used for its training measured in Floating 
Point Operations  (FLOPs) is greater than 10^25 , serving as a quan titative criterion to 
determine systemic risk.  Models that exceed this threshold would be deemed high-impact, 
that could pose systemic risks, triggering additional regulatory requirements and scrutiny . 
We suggest this could be a useful model for capturing high -risk GPAI in the Australian 
regulatory  framework.    
  
11 
 
Evolving landscape:  As mentioned elsewhere throughout this paper, t he rapid 
development of AI technologies, particularly GPAI, presents constant and ongoing 
challenges for any regulatory framework. Accordingly, the  principles may need to be 
regularly reviewed and updated to ensure they remain relevant . The UK's approach aims to 
be adaptable, with the ability to modify the definition of AI and the wider regulatory 
framework as needed . We support a similar approach in the Australian context.  
International alignment: There's a clear need for international collaboration on AI 
governance, and alignment with international jurisdictions such as the UK and the EU to  
ensure principles are flexible enough to capture global threats and emerging risks across 
jurisdictions.  
A principles -based approach offers inherent flexibility, however, the challenges posed by 
GPAI and other emerging AI technologies may require specific considerations or additions 
to the principles  over time, as these technologies evolve . Regular review of the principles, 
along with international collaboration, will be necessary to ensure they remain effective in 
capturing new forms of high -risk AI.

regulatory gaps, ensure consistency across sectors, and adapt more easily to rapid

regulatory frameworks.  Further, an AI-specific Act would make it easier to update and

Significantly, an  AI Act could establish dedicated enforcement and monitoring 
mechanisms focused specifically on AI. This would allow for more targeted and responsive   
  
24 
 
oversight as technology changes.  A dedicated Act could more easily incorporate emerging 
concepts like general -purpose AI models, which may not fit neatly into existing regulatory 
frameworks.  
An AI Act would also align with approaches taken by other jurisdictions like the EU AI Act, 
supporting international interoperability.  While Options 1 and 2 could potentially be 
adapted over time, in our view, a purpose -built AI Act appears to offer flexibility and 
responsiveness to keep pace with AI advancements and  would likely make it easier to 
implement consistent updates across the entire AI ecosystem as needed.  
Question 16  
Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps or inconsistencies with Australia’s existing laws 
for the development and deployment of AI? Which regulatory option best addresses this, 
and why?  
DLC views the greatest risks of gaps or inconsistencies in Australia's existing laws for AI 
development and deployment  lie principally in the absence of AI-specific legislation. 
Australia currently does not have laws made specifically for AI. Instead, AI is regulated 
through a patchwork of existing laws that were not designed with AI in mind, which 
inevitably results in there being  gaps. For example, the  Privacy Act 1988  covers some 
aspects of data use in AI, however it doesn’t  not fully address the unique privacy 
challenges posed by AI systems, especially regarding data collection and  use for training AI 
models.  
Similarly,  there are Intellectual Property considerations  not covered by extant legislation . In 
particular regarding the ethical approach to data collection  and obtaining consent of the 
authors of artistic works that might be drawn upon to build the knowledge base of an AI 
system. We know from concerns raised  globally that ChatGPT used thousands of creative 
works without autho r consent to build its knowledge base. For example, a class action 
lawsuit was filed against OpenAI in June 2023 by authors alleging that ChatGPT was trained 
on their copyrighted books without consent or compensation , and The New York Times 
sued OpenAI and Microsoft in December 2023, alleging that their AI models were trained 
on millions of Times articles without permission . These are among many lawsuits seeking 
to hold large language models like ChatGPT accountable for using copyrighted creative 
works in their training data without author consent.    
  
25 
 
We also have strong concerns with risks associated with a lgorithmic bias and 
discrimination . Existing anti -discrimination laws may not adequately address the potential 
for AI systems to produce biased or discriminatory outcomes, especially in areas like 
automated decision -making. Further, t here are currently  gaps in requirements for AI 
developers and deployers to provide transparency about how their systems work and make 
decisions  that could be more robustly captured in a bespoke AI Legislative framework.  
A fundamental question that must be answered if AI is to be truly safe and secure is: “ who 
is (or who should be) responsible for harm caused by  AI systems or when AI systems make 
errors and how that accountability should be enforced ?” Existing laws don’t make clear  
who is (or who should be) the legal entity responsible for harm caused by  AI systems or 
when AI systems make errors  and how that accountability should be enforced . An AI Act is 
an excellent starting point in the building of a robust regime to ensure accountability for AI -
driven decisions .  
We recogni se that the global nature of AI development and use may create gaps in how 
existing Australian laws can be enforced  and in which jurisdictions. Therefore,  global 
cooperation will be an integral part of any AI framework. Similarly, we acknowledge that 
rapid and constant advancements in AI will inevitably  outpace the law, and there is always 
a risk that there will be  gaps as new capabilities like general -purpose AI models  evolve. 
However,  an AI Act , supported by these proposed guardrails and well considered 
regulations will provide a solid foundation  to support innovation, the economy and provide 
a safe and secure -by-design AI framework . In our view, t his approach would address the 
known, identified gaps while maintaining the flexibility needed to adapt to the fast -
changing AI landscape. However, its effectiveness would depend on careful 
implementation and coordination across different regulatory bodies . 
Conclusion  
DLC Legal's response to the Australian Government's proposals for AI guardrails advocate s 
for a risk-based approach focused on high -risk settings and applications, supporting a 
cross-economy AI -specific Act as the most effective regulatory option. In our view, t his 
approach would provide the necessary flexibility and adaptability to keep pace with rapidly 
evolving AI technologies.  Our response emphasi ses the importance of balancing 
innovation with safety and ethical responsibility, suggesting tiered regulations based on 
risk levels and capabilities. We highlight the need for clear accountabilit y structures,   
  
26 
 
transparency in AI development and deployment, and mechanisms to address algorithmic 
bias and discrimination. We underscore  the importance of incorporating Indigenous data 
sovereignty and cultural protocols into the regulatory framework.   
We support  regular review of the guardrails to ensure they remain relevant and effective. 
We also suggest providing clear guidance and Australian context specific use cases to 
assist organisations assess their AI systems against the principles. Our response highlights  
the importance of international alignment and collaboration in AI governance while 
maintaining flexibility to address Australia's specific context and needs.  As AI continues to 
evolve and impact various aspects of society, we believe the proposed approach offers a 
solid foundation for responsible AI development and deployment in Australia. We 
commend the government for its consultation process and believe that continuing this 
engagement with stakeholders will be crucial in developing a clear, balanced approach to 
regulating AI that promotes innovation, mitigates risks, and ensures the safety and well -
being of all Australians.
