4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Yes
If so, how should we define these?
I strongly believe that the Government should consider banning AI systems where technical evaluations show potential for "critical harm", or where "systemic risks" are deemed unacceptable.
The Californian SB1047 bill focused on avoiding "critical harm", defined as mass casualties, at least USD 500 million in damage, or other comparable threats to public safety. Similarly, the EU AI Act describes systemic risks from general-purpose AI, including those that can lead to widespread or catastrophic harm, such as weapons development, persuasion & deception, and self-replication.
Echoing the International Dialogues on AI Safety Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence, I support the call for international coordination to impose certain "red lines" on AI capability, similar to those in SB1047 and the EU AI Act.
If a technical evaluation shows that an AI model could assist in creating cyber, chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapons, or engage in self-replication, deception and, ultimately, loss of control, it should be urgently banned. Legislation should establish an intolerable risk threshold.
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
I believe that Australia should not apply mandatory guardrails to all GPAI models. Instead, the country should impose meaningful obligations on GPAI with systemic risk. This approach will not only contribute to global safety standards but also facilitate AI developers in internalising risks. GPAI that we know is safe is less critical to regulate.
It is important to remember that the risks posed by future highly-capable models are different from those of narrow AI in high-risk applications. Guardrails proportional to the risks posed by the AI system will provide the best balance between safety and innovation.
The RAND report "General-Purpose Artificial Intelligence (GPAI) Models and GPAI Models with Systemic Risk" provides a valuable perspective, suggesting that harmonisation of reporting and evaluation standards across the USA, UK, and the EU could address the unique risks of future models. Australia can contribute to this international norm by adopting a similar approach.
In terms of specifics, mandatory guardrails on GPAI with systemic risks could draw inspiration from SB1047 and include AI evaluation standards, as well as tracking risk management practices and incident mitigations.
7. What are suitable indicators for defining GPAI models as high-risk?
Base on technical capability
What technical capability should it be based on?
Other
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
No
Which of the guardrails should be amended?
Please provide any additional comments
In my opinion, the proposed mandatory guardrails do not distribute responsibility appropriately across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle. We need to ensure that the focal point is on developers and prevent them from shifting risks to others.
The complexity of AI systems as noted by the authors of the MIT AI Risk Repository, makes it challenging to understand how an AI arrived at a decision, and therefore determine who is responsible for the consequences of that decision. In the absence of legal or regulatory incentives, developers may release poorly designed AI systems, leaving those harmed by these systems without recourse.
Furthermore, the "black box" nature of AI systems means that substantive obligations on Australian deployers are unlikely to effectively mitigate risk in many cases. This is because deployers do not have the necessary information to understand or control underlying AI models.
Ultimately, the Government should create incentives that compel AI developers to internalise risks, instead of allowing them to dodge obligations through the opaque nature of AI and legal manoeuvres such as end-user license agreements.
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI?
No
How could we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for example low-risk and high-risk GPAI models? 
I believe that the proposed mandatory guardrails are not sufficient to address the risks of GPAI. Guardrail 1, which relates to accountability processes and compliance, should be expanded.
The discussion paper on page 15 observes that agentic AI might lead to accidents. Therefore, Guardrail 1 should explicitly require developers and deployers of GPAI to report accidents or incidents to the regulator, much like the current practice in the aviation industry. Many domain experts believe that safety incident reporting and security information sharing is the most effective risk mitigation for general-purpose models.
The regulator should also have the powers and obligations to conduct investigations and publish reports that inform ongoing safety practices.
Moreover, Guardrail 1 should include an obligation for AI developers to share models with national AI Safety Institutes. There have been instances where AI developers have made commitments to share models with governments, including Australia, for evaluation, but have either reneged on those agreements or been slow to comply. Regulations should require sharing with regulators to conduct evaluations and other functions.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A whole of economy approach – introducing a new cross-economy AI Act
What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
In my opinion, Australia needs a comprehensive AI Act that can influence the behaviour of overseas AI developers. Research, including from MIT and RAND, suggests that AI developers are best placed to control the most severe risks from AI during model development.
Page 49 of the discussion paper suggests that an AI-specific Act would have enforceable provisions targeting offshore developers, which I believe is necessary. Regulating offshore activity is challenging, but it must be our top priority.
In conclusion, the best regulatory approach would allow established regulators, like the Therapeutic Goods Administration or the Civil Aviation Safety Authority, to lead within their fields of expertise. This would let an Australian AI Act cover any gaps and focus on shaping the behaviour of offshore AI developers.

Australian Copyright Council submission –
Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-Risk Settings: Proposal Paper
2 October 2024

The Australian Copyright Council acknowledges the Traditional Owners and Custodians of the lands on which our office is located, the Gadigal people of the Eora nation, and all Traditional Owners of Country throughout Australia. We pay our respects to all Elders past and present, and recognise their continuing great, creative and cultural expressions.

1.  The Australian Copyright Council (the ACC) is grateful for the opportunity to respond to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources’ (DISR) Proposals Paper on Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI in High-Risk Settings (Proposals Paper) and for the opportunity to have participated in the Proposed Mandatory Guardrails for AI: Creative Industries Roundtable on 30 September 2024.

About the Australian Copyright Council   
2.  The ACC is an independent, not-for-profit, non-government organisation dedicated to promoting understanding of copyright law and its application. The ACC works to foster collaboration between content creators and consumers, representing the peak bodies for professional artists and content creators working in Australia’s creative industries.
3.  The ACC is a unique organisation:  
* it is the only dedicated copyright expert organisation in Australia
* its focus is on copyright as it applies to all art forms
* it provides advocacy, expert advice and free information on copyright issues, and
* it is a membership-based organisation, representing over a million creators. 
4.  The ACC has 24 affiliate member organisations,  representing over a million writers, composers, visual artists, designers, photographers, film directors, performers, choreographers, producers, publishers, record labels and architects working in the Australian creative industries. We understand a number of ACC affiliate members are making their own submissions to the Proposals Paper.
5.  As part of its services, the ACC provides information, education, training and free, written legal advice to those who fall within its guidelines including creators, the staff of libraries, galleries, museums and educational institutions.
Summary
6.  The ACC urges the consideration of issues raised in the implementation of proposed guardrails in the context of the Government’s broader commitment outlined in Revive – Australia’s National Cultural Policy (National Cultural Policy), in particular, the commitment to ‘maintaining a strong copyright framework that works in concert with other legal and policy mechanisms.’. 
7.  It is in these ‘other legal and other policy mechanisms’ that the ACC believes that the AI regulation should lie. The ACC maintains that the Copyright Act, 1968 (Cth) (Copyright Act) has a rigorous framework for balancing of copyright owner rights and user interests.  So, any AI legislative mechanism should sit outside this framework, as a separate AI Act in recognition of existing licensing opportunities embedded in the Copyright Act for the use of copyright material in the training and development of AI systems.
8.  AI regulation including the implementation of mandatory guardrails should be reflective of the recognition that copyright owners may not, in fact, wish to grant permission for the use of their work. There are some sectors, including creators of Intellectual and Cultural Property (ICIP), which are particularly sensitive to use of their work.  In this context, the meaningful application of many of the guardrails requires that ongoing commitment of transparency of use across the AI lifecycle as integral to any AI regulation.
9.  Such AI regulation must apply to all AI systems and services if they are made available in Australia.
10.  In defining the risk of use of copyright material in the development and training of AI across the AI lifecycle, the ACC maintains that the ‘risk of adverse impacts’ on creators’ rights and their ability to consent to the use and receive equitable remuneration for their work, places such use in the high-risk category as outlined in the Proposals Paper.
11.  The ACC therefore supports the Australian government’s proposal to ‘apply mandatory guardrails to all general purpose AI (GPAI) models’ available in Australia.

Background and context
12.  The Proposals Paper comes at a time of other investigations into artificial intelligence (AI) including:
* the ongoing discussions of the Commonwealth Attorney General’s Copyright and Artificial Intelligence Reference Group (CAIRG) which is comprised of members of the creative industries, AI developers, and user groups. Currently, CAIRG is considering several issues which overlap with the Proposals Paper, for example, legal issues concerning copyright and transparency. The ACC is also a member of the CAIRG Steering Committee. 
* the 2024 Joint Select Committee’s Inquiry on the influence and impacts of social media on Australian society (to which the ACC made a submission). 
* the 2024 Senate Select Committee’s Inquiry on Adopting Artificial Intelligence (to which the ACC made a submission).
* the 2023 Department of Industry, Science and Resources’ public consultation on Safe and Responsible AI (to which the ACC made a submission).
* the 2023 House Standing Committee on Employment, Education and Training inquiry into the use of generative artificial intelligence in the Australian education system (to which the ACC made a submission). The ACC also appeared before the Committee on 29 January 2024.
* the 2023 Inquiry into Artificial Intelligence (AI) in New South Wales (to which the ACC made a submission). The ACC also appeared before the Committee on 8 March 2024. 
13.  This submission briefly addresses the following issues explored in the Proposals Paper:
(i)  the proposed principles for defining ‘high-risk AI’
(ii)  the implementation of data governance measures to manage data and provenance including transparency (Guardrails 3, 8, 9)
(iii)  the transparency measures to inform end-users of AI generated content (Guardrail 6).
to the extent that they relate to copyright law.

Introduction – copyright and AI
14.  Enshrined in the Copyright Act, copyright refers to a set of exclusive rights that the copyright owner has over copyright materials including text, images, audiovisual content and published material, for a prescribed duration. 
15.  The first copyright owner is usually (but not always) the ‘author’ or ‘maker’ of such material e.g. a writer who writes a book, an artist who creates illustrations or other artworks, etc.
16.  The exclusive rights of the copyright owner vary depending on the type of copyright material. However, the rights to reproduce material and grant permission to others to use them are common to all types of copyright material.
17.  Reproduction occurs even if the material is converted from a physical format (e.g. a book) to other formats (e.g. an audiobook sound recording or an e-book) and vice versa. This includes where material is converted into a format that is invisible. Partial copies may also be a reproduction if a ‘substantial part’ of the material has been reproduced. A ‘substantial part’ does not necessarily have to be a large portion as a short portion may constitute a ‘substantial part’ if it is ‘vital’, ‘material’ or ‘essential’ to what is being copied or used. 
18.  These Copyright Act reproduction provisions are relevant in the discussion of AI development and training, where the whole or part of copyright materials are converted into machine-readable ‘tokens’.
13.  The right of the copyright owner to grant permission to others to use their material is significant to their livelihood - charging fees or royalties in exchange for permission (or licence) is a common way that copyright owners derive income from their creative work. In this context, copyright is the framework which supports and incentivises the creation of new copyright material.
14.  However, as demonstrated by the series of class actions commenced in other jurisdictions, AI development has involved the use of copyright material without permission and without remunerating the copyright owner. Such use can result in an undermining of the existing copyright framework.  
15.  Other copyright issues raised by AI development and deployment include:
(a)  the unauthorised gathering and use of third-party copyright material in the development and training of an AI platform (the ‘input’) may amount to copyright infringement.
(b)  the potential lack of copyright protection for text, images and music generated by generative AI (the ‘output’) if there is a lack of a human authorship. 
(c)  the potential for copyright infringement if the output reproduces a ‘substantial part' of pre-existing copyright material.

Defining high-risk AI
16.  The ACC submits that the use of copyright material in the AI lifecycle is high-risk based on the proposed principles (Proposed Principles). The ACC accepts that the Proposed Principles must be ‘considered as a whole’ but comments specifically on the following.

* Human rights 

a.	The risk of adverse impacts to an individual’s rights recognised in Australian human rights law without justification, in addition to Australia’s international human rights law obligations.

17.  As the ACC has submitted elsewhere, the act of creation justifies the granting of exclusive rights because ‘a person has a natural property right in the creations of his (sic) mind.’ The creator is central in these justifications for the grant of exclusive rights. This sentiment is also expressed in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights which states that:
Everyone has the right to the protection of the moral and material interests resulting from any scientific, literary or artistic production of which he (sic) is the author.
18.  Whilst Australia may not have domestic human rights legislation in the same form as other jurisdictions,  our international human rights law obligations under Article 15(1)(c) of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights recognises the right of the individual outlined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. 
19.  As a result, the encroachment of a creator’s exclusive rights in the use of their ‘scientific, literary or artistic production(s)’ in the lifecycle of AI, may pose a breach of Australia’s international human rights law obligations, designating this use as high risk.

* Legal effects 

c.	The risk of adverse legal effects, defamation or similarly significant effects on an individual.

20.  As the ACC has previously submitted, the collation of ‘data’ for the development and training of AI platforms has depended on the ‘scraping’ of copyright material without the copyright owner’s permission or remuneration.
21.  The Proposals Paper also places importance on whether it is ‘reasonably possible… to opt out of [such] systems’. Practically, opting out, negotiation or modification of contract terms is unlikely to occur in online services and social media. Acceptance of a platform’s terms and conditions is a prerequisite for use of the platform - potential users have no ability to negotiate contract terms.
22.  Opt out schemes are inherently unfair as they shift the copyright framework’s balance between a copyright owner’s rights and user interests.  Such schemes shift the onus from copyright users having to obtain permission to a copyright owner having to declare their unwillingness to participate in the scraping (or other) system of mass appropriation of content. Practically, an opt out scheme means that the default position is that all uses are permitted unless the copyright owner actively disapproves – silence effectively amounting to consent. 
23.  Scraping and opt out practices, adversely impact the copyright owners’ legitimate interests and conflict with the normal, legal exploitation of their copyright material, resulting in a genuine ‘risk of adverse legal effects’ upon individual copyright owners and the creative sectors. 
24.  These risks are contrary to the Government’s National Cultural Policy which specifically outlines the centrality of copyright to Australia cultural policy, stating ‘Australia’s copyright laws incentivise the creation of new cultural material while also allowing reasonable and equitable use of copyright material in the public interest’.
25.  Individual creators of literary, artistic, musical or dramatic works, and films, have certain moral rights. Moral rights are separate to copyright which, unlike copyright, cannot be assigned or transferred. Creators have three moral rights. These are the right: 
* to be attributed (or credited) for their work
* not to have their work falsely attributed, and
* not to have their work treated in a derogatory way.
26.  Moral rights are therefore about a creator’s relationship to their work and are inextricably associated with an individual creator’s honour and reputation. The potential harm posed by AI systems include the very real risk of harm to individual creators whose work may treated in a way that is prejudicial to the moral rights of the creator.  

* Impacts on groups 

d.	The risk of adverse impacts to groups of individuals or collective rights of cultural groups.

27.  The use of ICIP in the training and development of AI systems affects the collective rights of First Nations peoples in particular. 
28.  The ACC has submitted elsewhere that ICIP rights are First Nations peoples’ rights to their heritage and culture. This includes all aspects of cultural practices, traditional knowledge, and resources and knowledge systems developed by First Nations peoples as part of their Indigenous identity.  
29.  Article 31 of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples includes rights to traditional knowledge and traditional cultural expression. That is, Indigenous people have the right to maintain, develop and control their ICIP. 
30.  While these issues are partially addressed by Australia’s copyright law, the scope of copyright law does not extend to older materials of cultural significance as copyright in artistic works, for example, expires after the designated period, or when the material inherently cannot be protected by copyright e.g. sacred sites. 
31.  The ACC considers that the implementation of guardrails for ICIP must be undertaken in concert with the Office for the Arts’ consultation on standalone ICIP legislation. 

* Systemic impacts 

e.	The risk of adverse impacts to the broader Australian economy, society, environment and rule of law.

32.  From an economic perspective, any benefit of AI do not come without cost. The equity issues arising from the distribution of ongoing income streams flowing to AI services developers which are built on the works of copyright owners, must be considered.  For example, the House of Lords, in reference to large language models (LLMs) recently noted that:
LLMs may offer immense value to society. But that does not warrant the violation of copyright law or its underpinning principles. We do not believe it is fair for tech firms to use rightsholder data for commercial purposes without permission or compensation, and to gain vast financial rewards in the process. There is compelling evidence that the UK benefits economically, politically and societally from upholding a globally respected copyright regime. 
33.  Whilst the potential economic impact on creators’ livelihood of the use of copyright material in the AI lifecycle may be measured, the impact on the Australia’s cultural life is more difficult to quantify.
34.  Whilst the ACC cannot comment further on this point, we note that any dilution, diminution or marginalising of Australian unique stories in whatever form – film, literature, visual art – through the use of copyright material in the AI lifecycle, risks undermining Australia’s National Cultural Policy.

Proposed mandatory guardrails
35.  The ACC supports the Australian Government’s acknowledgement that the preventative guardrails will ‘operate alongside laws and regulatory instruments to hold organisations accountable when harm does occur and help people exercise their existing rights’. 
36.  The ACC supports the view that for the harms already caused, other Government initiatives may apply with a view to compensating those Australians whose content has been used without authorisation.
37.  The ACC also supports the proposal that the guardrails will apply to AI in high-risk settings and GPAI models.
38.  The ACC agrees with the view that all guardrails and transparency obligations should apply to AI services and platforms available in Australia regardless of the origin of the service or platform. 
39.  As a member of the CAIRG and CAIRG Steering Committee, the ACC is working with the Attorney General’s Office looking at issues which touch on those raised in the proposed guardrails. The ACC comments specifically on Guardrails 3 and 6, below.

* Guardrail 3: Protect AI systems and implementing data governance to manage data quality and provenance
40.  The ACC notes that Guardrail 3 is intended to cover issues including:
* the origin and legality of the dataset and collection processes
* documentation of data provenance
* consideration of the principles of Indigenous Data Sovereignty and ICIP
* approaches to data preparation processes, including labelling and categorisation methods,
and intended to complement requirements under the Copyright Act, amongst other legislation.
41.  The threshold issue for this Guardrail 3 is transparency.  The origin and legality of datasets and the provenance of the data which forms these data sets is fundamental to the use of copyright materials in AI systems.  It is this very issue which is the subject of litigation in other jurisdictions where the wholesale scraping of third-party copyright material has been conducted. Without transparency as to origin of data, the legality of datasets in Australia cannot be determined.
42.  Disclosure of provenance of material (with the onus on the user to investigate licensing opportunities) should form part of the labelling and categorising of methods.
43.  The ACC supports the operation of Guardrail 3 in concert with: 
(i)  the transparency obligations in Guardrail 8 allowing copyright owners (and agents managing permission on their behalf) to make informed decisions when deciding whether to grant permission, consistent with the right of copyright owners to assert control over their material, and
(ii)  enabling independent inspection and reporting to ensure compliance with obligations imposed by the Guardrails are met (Guardrail 9).
This will allow for the development of external measures which enable independent oversight.

* Guardrail 6: Inform end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content 
44.  Transparency is also central to a ‘best efforts’ approach requiring organisations to ‘ensure AI-generated outputs, including synthetic text, image, audio or video content, can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated’.
45.  For end-users of GPAI, including generative AI, the copyright issues are:
(a)  the potential lack of protection for works generated by generative AI (the ‘output’) when there is insufficient human authorship, and
(b)  depending on the circumstances, if the generated content reproduces a ‘substantial part’ of existing copyright material (e.g. an artwork that the AI system was trained on), the end-user may have infringed copyright. 

Options for introducing mandatory guardrails
46.  The ACC supports Option 3 – a new separate AI Act to reflect the whole of economy approach that is necessary to properly administer the mandatory guardrails.
47.  This option would allow for an independent AI regulator which could work in concert with other regulators and interact with existing laws including the Copyright Act.

Conclusion
48.  Australia’s copyright framework strikes an appropriate balance between the rights of copyright owners to exploit their own material and user interests. 
49.  This framework, the ACC submits, forms part of the wider legal and policy mechanisms regulating AI - including a standalone AI Act - to apply to all AI services and platforms available in Australia.  
50.  The designation of the use of copyright materials in the AI lifecycle as ‘high risk’ activating the mandatory guardrails must reflect that copyright owners, have the right to grant permission for the use of their work and receive fair compensation.
51.  Ongoing obligations relating to the transparency of use, especially for creators of ICIP is critical for the operation the guardrails.
52.  The ACC thanks the DISR for considering this submission. We look forward to the continuous process of working with the Government and other stakeholders. If the DISR has any further queries or requires further information, please let us know.

4   Consumers Health Forum of Australia  Introduction   
Consumers Health Forum (CHF) is the national peak body representing the interests 
of Australian healthcare consumers and those interested in healthcare consumer 
affairs. CHF works to achieve safe, quality, and timely healthcare for all Australians, 
support ed by accessible health information and systems. At the heart of CHF’s policy 
agenda is consumer -centred care . 
In the context of CHF’s commitment to quality improvement in healthcare , CHF 
supports and recognises  the value of automated decision -making and  discriminative  
Artificial Intelligence  (AI) technologies , which have been used  in healthcare  for many 
decades .  
However,  the sudden rise of generative word modelling , such as ChatGPT , prompts 
CHF to raise  concer ns, as many  features of  generative  AI software  may pose 
significant  risks  to consumers  when used in a healthcare setting . CHF welcomes the 
opportunity to provide a submission  to the Department of Industry , Science and 
Resources proposal paper  “Safe and Responsible Use of AI in Australia ”.  
CHF is invested in ensuring AI use in healthcare is  appropriately regulated : while 
healthcare consumers, healthcare services , and healthcare financing institutions 
could all potentially benefit from the broader  adoption of generative AI, the safety and 
quality  risks  are primarily  borne by consumers.  
In this submission, CHF will provide  the committee  with  healthcare consumer  input on 
the proposed principles  defining  high -risk AI, the  guardrails that would ensure testing, 
transparency and accountability, and the regulatory options to mandate such 
guardrails.  
Background o f CHF’s advocacy  on Artificial 
Intelligence

Making (ADM) and artificial intelligence for several years, including:

Electronic Clinical Decision Making Support (ECDS) software in February 20221. 
Our issue paper - developed through extensive consumer consultation - 
highlighted the importance of governance and oversight of AI at the federal

Ordinary citizens and healthcare consumers must be  involved in all levels of 
governance and the implementation  of legislative  reforms  for generative  AI in 
Australia . 
So far , the formative  process  of reform  has focused  on consulting  and capturing the 
ideas of  the technical experts  that design , deploy  and research  AI – in other words , 
those that are most likely to benefit from broader  applications of AI . CHF recognises

6   Consumers Health Forum of Australia  that their views and input are fundamental , but we a rgue that  there has not been  
sufficient consultation with consumers . As end -users, consumers  are the most 
affected by the shortfall s, loophole s, or regulatory grey area s in which generative AI is 
currently operating and by any that will be  left behind by reform . These are some of 
the consequences  that healthcare consumers are most worried about:  
Consequences for the health consumer  
Health consumers may lose trust in healthcare provider s if they sense that decisions 
about their health are being made  in ways that no one  – except the software  
developers  marketing the software - understands.  This opacity and lack of supervision 
can make health consumers feel uncomfortable and unsafe.  
Generative AI might also lack the nuanced understanding of a health consumer’s 
personal history, values, and preferences that a clinician would typically integrate into 
decision -making. This  change  can lead to decisions that are technically correct  but 
that are not  the best fit for the individual's needs.  
Consumers  are also experienc ing a greater risk of harm : If an AI system makes an 
error, health consumers may be at risk of receiving inappropriate treatment, delayed 
diagnosis, or even life -threatening care outcomes. Without a clinician’s full 
involvement  in validating  outputs , errors may go unnoticed . 
2. Consequences for clinician s 
Clinicians may become overly dependent on AI, eroding their  clinical judgment and 
decision -making skills over time. Relying on AI could make them more hesitant or 
unable to challenge AI -derived recommendations.   
When the worst happens , and AI causes  an error  in clinical management and an  
adverse outcome  for a healthcare consumer , it may also be unclear whether the 
clinician or the AI system was ultimately responsible. Lack of clarity  can lead to 
complex legal and ethical questions about liability and accountability , which will cause 
immense pain to  affected consumers and clinicians . 
3. Consequences for society  
AI systems can inherit and perpetuate biases  already  present in the training data, 
potentially leading to unfair or unequal treatment of different groups of people. This  
bias could exacerbate existing healthcare disparities , widening gaps instead of closing 
them . 
Overuse of AI could also lead to a depersonalised  healthcare  experience , with health 
consumers feeling  like data points  rather  than individuals with unique needs. The    
 
Safe and Responsible use of AI in Australia  – Proposal Paper for Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI 
in high -risk settings   7 human connection , empathy , and understanding , fundamental elements of care 
provision, may be come  weakened  and overlooked . 
Societal trust in healthcare systems could  also decline if people perceive that 
algorithms are making decisions  without appropriate human oversight. Concerns 
about algorithmic errors, transparency, and ethical considerations might lead to  a 
general  feeling of  scepticism and disenfranchisement from the healthcare system . 
Distrust in the healthcare system could then spread to all other domains of society.  In 
Western  democracies, which rely on legitimate power to function, transferring 
decision -making authority from clinicians to generative AI could undermine the 
public's perception of legitimacy in healthcare institutions. Suppose  people feel their 
health is managed by unaccountable algorithms rather than trusted human 
professionals . In that case,  it may weaken the social contract that supports 
democratic governance and legi timate authority in public services.  
For all these  reason s, CHF has been  tirelessly advocating  for healthcare  consumer s to 
be heard . Appropriate resources must be  provided  to consumer organisations  to 
ensure that the Australian public is educated in digital literacy  and that this  new wave 
of transformation does not further deepen the digital divide and inequities in our 
society.  
Key recommendations  
1. Appropriate resources must be provided to consumer organisations  to ensure 
that the Australian public is educated in digital literacy and that this new wave 
of transformation does not further deepen the digital divide and inequities in 
our society.  
2. DISR proposed principles of high -risk AI to include public health risks  to 
physical and mental health (not just individual but also population -level risk)  
3. Proposed guardrails ensuring testing, transparency and accountability of AI to 
be adopted in full  
4. Mandate guardrails for the high -risk use of AI by implementing a whole -of-
economy approach, introducing a new cross -economy AI Act 
 
 
     
 
8   Consumers Health Forum of Australia  Defining high -risk AI  
As advocated in our submission to the  Senate Select Committee on Adopting Artificial 
Intelligence  4, CHF supports the  commitment of the Australian Government to 
establishing  a risk -based legislati on approach  for any new mandatory guardrails for 
the use of AI in high -risk settings.  
CHF  also  supports the DISR proposed principles  that will define the high -risk use of 
generative AI  and explicitly mention  adverse impacts on an individual’s physical or 
mental health.  
 
 
CHF recommends including  a public health definition  of high -risk use of AI  in the DISR 
proposed principles : Due to the extensive reach that automated generative AI would 
have in healthcare , CHF argues that the risks are not just to individual s but also 
systemic.

 DISR Proposed principles  
In designating an AI system as high -risk due to its use, regard must be given t o: 
a. The risk of adverse impacts to an individual’s rights recognised in Australian 
human rights law without justification, in addition to Australia’s international human 
rights law obligations  
b. The risk of adverse impacts to an individual’s physical or mental health or safety  
c. The risk of adverse legal effects, defamation or similarly significant effects on an 
individual  
d. The risk of adverse impacts to groups of individuals or collective rights of 
cultural groups  
e. The risk of adverse impacts to the broader Australian economy, society, 
environment and rule of law  
f. The severity and extent of those adverse impacts outlined in principles (a) to (e) 
above.

accountability of AI  
CHF agrees that the above guardrails should  be fully implemented to ensure that high -
risk use of AI can be monitored and that dev elopers do everything they can to ensure 
that the AI software they design can be  appropriately  monitored and evaluated . 
 
Guardrail  no.5  is essential  for healthcare consumers , as it will address algorithmic 
opacity, that is , the inability to fully observe or understand the inner workings of an AI 
model. If we cannot understand how an algorithm works, how ca n it be audited ? The Proposed mandatory guardrails for high -risk AI at a glance  
Organisations developing or deploying high -risk AI systems are required to:  
1. Establish, implement and publish an accountability process including 
governance, internal capability and a strategy for regulatory compliance  
2. Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate 
risks  
3. Protect AI systems, and implement data governance measures to manage data 
quality and provenance  
4. Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the 
system once deployed  
5. Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful 
human oversight  
6. Inform end -users regarding AI -enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI -
generated content  
7. Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or 
outcomes  
8. Be transparent with other organisations across the AI supply chain about data, 
models and systems to help them effectively address risks  
9. Keep and maintain records to allow third partis to assess compliance with 
guardrails  
10. Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance 
with the guardrails  
    
 
Safe and Responsible use of AI in Australia  – Proposal Paper for Introducing Mandatory Guardrails for AI 
in high -risk settings   11 consequences of algorithmic opacity  are immense in healthcare , as it profoundly  
affects trust.7 Suppose  we cannot understand a decision suggested by an AI mod el 
because of the exceedingly high number of parameters used to reach the suggestion . 
How  can healthcare consumers feel safe and satisfied that it has identified a  correct 
course of  clinical  action?  Guardrail  no.5 provides  Government with  the power  to ask 
firms to  disclose information about their  AI algorithm , should they wish  for it to be 
used in high -risk settings . Knowing that an independent regulatory body has rev iewed 
and understood how an algorithm works will make consumers feel a lot more 
comfortable and safer  about AI being one of the tools used in  the clinical 
management  of their  health . 
 
CHF understands that a k ey objective of better AI regulation is to ensure that some of 
the onus of safety and quality is transferred from deployers of AI  systems to AI 
developers. CHF , however,  believes  that in healthcare , it is ultimately deployers who 
need to ensu re that AI software is safe for use . 
 
CHF maintains its  previously held  position that  the Government  is ultimately 
responsible and should ensure  that processes are in place to audit AI software.  
Similar  to what happens in cybersecurity – where penetration testing is a standard 
practice to find vulnerabilities in a computer system – AI auditing should be standard 
practice and a fundamental step in detecting weaknesses and features that can cause 
harm to consumers. Additionally, mandatory requirement s for AI auditing should 
come with clear standa rds for what counts as an impartial, comprehensive AI audit.  
 
Deployers must also be wary  of healthcare  governance groups commissioning

hired to build the software  might  default to  profit -driven approach es to coding . While 
this will be discussed more in -depth later in this submission,  independent oversight 
and establishing  an independent regulatory body are fundamental  steps to ensure this 
does not happen .

Option 1 – A domain -specific approach  
 
CHF understands the  benefits  of leveraging Australia’s existing laws , such as pre-
existing familiarity with laws, limited disruption  to those regulated, and a faster path to 
context -specific laws.  
 
Consumers , however , have repeatedly  found existing legislation flawed by lack of

For example , some technology and software used in clinical settings , such as note -

It is CHF’s opinion that option 1, being bound by existing law and the enforcement 
powers of existing regulators, would not be able to address  these substantial  critical  
regulatory grey areas  and gaps in enforcement . 
 
Option 2 – Adapting existing regulatory frameworks through framework legislation  
 
CHF understands the advantages of adapting existing regulatory frameworks  and 
that, unlike option 1, it provides a consistent set of definitions and measures to be 
implemented by amending existing regulatory frameworks.  CHF also understands 
that this option allows  businesses and developers in the medical technology industry  
to utilise  their  familiarity with pre -existing regulatory frameworks.  
 
Option 2 , however , presents  to healthcare consumers  the same  unacceptable  
limitation s as Option  1, in which framework legislation would be confined to the scope 
and powers of existing laws . This is simply unacceptable to healthcare consumers, as 
this won’t address key  regulatory  grey areas  and will likely result in the  uneven  
implementation of  amendments . Such an approach - at best  - would happen very 
slowly  and require  substantial  cross -agency  coordination  to be implement ed, 
translating to  “too little, too  late” for healthcare consumers wanting immediate 
protection . 
 
At worst, the patchy and uneven framework application will  translate into losses  for all 
stakeholders involved . High-risk use of AI  will remain  unsafe for consumers,  while 
inconsistent regulatory environments will disorient  developers and deployers . 
Regulatory bodies  will also  be drain ed of  time and resources  to re ctify  implementation 
issues . 
 
All in all,  Option 2 appears to  CHF to  be a high -risk, low -reward option.  
 
Option 3: Introducing a new AI -specific Act  
 
CHF  strongly  supports Option 3 by introducing  a new AI -specific Act , as it will provide 
robust and  uniform legislation that will be implemented across all regulatory 
environments . 
 
A specific AI Act will eliminat e the risk of grey areas exposing healthcare consumers 
to unnecessary risk , especially with healthcare application s of AI that are currently 
used in medical settings but are exempt from  TGA scrutiny and approval .

Option 3 will also ensure greater oversight by establishing  an independent supervisory 
body .  
 
Protecting consumer data within a new AI -
specific Act 
Data safety and privacy are of paramount importance for healthcare consumers. AI is 
bound to collect extensive amounts of data when utilised  in clinical settings, and 
consumers have the right to know where and how these  data are stored and used.  
 
CHF recommends  that the AI-specific Act that would be legi slated as part of option 3  
contains provisions for the safe and private handling of health consumer data.  
 
Data safety : Specific legislation that safeguards data  collected and used by AI  
throughout its entire lifecycle, from data collection to storage to data elimination, 
needs to be implemented.  Recent data  breaches in Australia have highlighted how any 
weakness can result in vast amounts of identified, sensitive data being leaked. The 
stakes are exceptionally high with healthcare data. As such , CHF calls for the 
Government  to leverage protections already in place - such as data and consumer 
protection legislat ion – to create a comprehensive data safety framework for AI in 
healthcare that will protect consumers.  
 
Data guardianship : Legislation must clearly state who can access data collected via AI 
and how data are collected, stored and used. Healthcare consumers' consent for data 
use must be informed and dynamic. Informed consent means that healthcare 
consumers must be notified if their data are about to be used in ways that depart 
from the original use to which they consented. Dynamic consent means that 
consumers must be able – at any time – to modify or withdraw their consent for their 
data being used. Clear proc edures must be in place for data disposal, either by 
ensuring the safe destruction of the data or ensuring that the entity the data is 
transferred to for custody and ownership also meets all safety and privacy 
requirements . To do all this, CHF calls for a comprehensive framework of independent 
data guardianship equipped with the tools to allow for swift, d ecisive  action  in case of 
data and privacy breaches.  
 
Perverse profiting from acquired data : Legislation must also account  for the 
challenges of legislating protections that prevent data from being profited  from . For 
example, private health insurers  must be denied  access to this data , and it should be 
illegal for a private insurer  to refuse a policy or a claim based on AI -collected data.

Inquiry on adopting AI  4 1. Introduction  
In the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence ( AI), the need  for robust , yet flexible,  regulation 
has become evident .  
1.1 The regulation of AI must be underpi nned by human rights principles  
Governments worldwide are grappling with the complexities of integrating AI into our lives while balancing 
its benefits. In this swiftly evolving landscape, the need  for robust yet adaptable regulation is clear .  
AI technologies offer new economic prospects but also raise concerns about potential job displacement s. 
They have the capacity to enhance environmental management and agricultural production, yet they also 
harbour  the risk of propagating harmful misinformatio n campaigns that threaten social cohesion and 
democratic processes.  
Furthermore, the impact of AI on public decision -making processes, which may be subject to judicial 
review, requires careful consideration to guarantee accountability and transparency. In discussions about 
the benefits of AI, it is crucial to highlight the essential role of human rights law and principles as the 
cornerstone of any regulatory framework.  
Neglecting to address AI regulation through a human rights lens not only jeopardi ses indi vidual liberties 
but also exacerbates societal disparities and undermines democratic governance.  
Australia’s  absence of a comprehensive regulatory framework  that is  grounded in human rights law leaves a 
void that private entities will exploit. Allowing cor porations to operate within this policy vacuum poses 
significant risks , particularly as p rofit -driven motives will likely prioriti se lucrative AI applications over 
socially beneficial ones.  
The opacity surrounding AI systems compounds these risks, hinderin g public understanding and oversight. 
Recent instances of malfunction or unfair decision -making highlight the urgent need for comprehensive 
regulatory mechanisms rooted in human rights law.  
Government intervention is essential to ensure that AI advancement s align with broader societal interests 
and ethical imperatives.  
Without decisive action guided by human rights principles, there is a risk of deepening social divides and 
undermining the foundations of a just and inclusive society.  
   
Inquiry on adopting AI  5 2. Human rights and AI regulation  
Human rights law and principles are often overlooked in discussions about AI governance.  
AI governance principles, crafted by companies, governments, civil society, and international organi sations, 
frequently ignore human rights altogether.1 Of those that do mention human rights, only a small fraction, 
approximately 15 percent, actually use them as a guiding framework.2 Moreover, most national AI strategies 
do not deeply consider human rights at all .3 This is unfortunate because human rights law  provides  
established,  clear and specific principles that hold  international legitimacy.  
Emerging from the aftermath of global conflict, the human rights movement was established with the 
explicit goal of preventing human misery  and promoting peace. At the core of human rights law is the belief 
that its principles are not just crucial for averting catastrophe  but also for ensuring that all people can live 
with dignity.4 
Human rights law offer s a robust framework that transcends b orders, providing mechanisms for 
implementation, oversight, and accountability essential for effective governance in the AI era. Their 
importance lies in their capacity to guide ethical decision -making while  fostering  a society where everyone's 
rights are respected.  
In discussions about AI regulation, it's crucial to understand that the focus should not be on whether 
human rights can or should apply to AI. Instead, the emphasis should be on recogni sing how the existing 
human rights framework is inherently r elevant to AI governance.  
2.1 Ethics and AI  
In the discourse surrounding AI regulation, ethics often takes precedence over human rights principles.  
Both ethics and human rights are integral to AI governance, each offering unique but complementary roles. 
While  they might share an overarching aim of restraining state and corporate power and safeguarding 
individual interests, they employ different methodologies. It's imperative to recognise that neither can serve 
as a complete substitute for the other; rather, bo th must be seamlessly integrated into AI regulation 
endeavours.5 
Ethics play a pivotal role in shaping and reinforcing regulation within the AI sphere. However, its 
philosophical underpinnings lead to a lack of standardised norms, resulting in a global abs ence of 
consensus on its precise applicability in AI governance. Relying solely on ethics could pose challenges for 
companies, public bodies, and individuals in understanding what their respective responsibilities are when 
it comes to AI development and de ployment .6  
Additionally, unlike human rights law, ethics lacks mechanisms to ensure accountability. Conversely, 
human rights offer a well -established legal framework that should be regarded as parallel to, rather than 
secondary to, ethics.

Inquiry on adopting AI  6 2.2 Human rights in the digital realm  
Australia, as a party to the major international human rights treaties ,7 is required to guarantee and protect 
the rights enumerated in those treaties to all people in Australia’s jurisdiction , including in the digital 
realm .  The United Nations’ Human Rights Council has issued resolutions requiring that ‘the same rights 
that people have offline must also be protected online ’.8  
Businesses developing or deploying AI technologies  do not have the same obligations  to guarantee and 
protect hum an rights in the way that nation states do. However, international human rights law is not silent 
on the role of businesses in the protection and promotion of human rights.  
The United Nations’ Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights  provides a fra mework to ensure 
that the activities of all businesses, regardless of their size, corporate structure, ownership or location; are 
human rights compliant.9  
The Principles assert that governments must take appropriate measures to ensure that companies and o ther 
non-state entities uphold human rights. Moreover, these principles emphasise that companies , including AI 
developers,  have a duty to respect human rights in all their global operations, including through the 
implementation of due diligence and impact assessments.10 
Companies' understanding of their human rights responsibilities varies, but there is a growing recognition 
that they must address human rights issues. This shift is driven by several factors, including evolving AI 
regulation, pressure from investors, community groups, and the public.11

Inquiry on adopting AI  7 3. Adopting Artificial Intelligence  
3.1 International approaches to mitigate AI risks  
3.1.1 The European Union  
On April 8, 2019, the European Union ’s (EU) High -Level Expert Group on AI introduced the Ethics 
Guidelines f or Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence , which outline  the principles necessary for AI to be 
considered trustworthy.12  
The guidelines emphasise that for AI to be considered trustworthy it must be : 
1) Lawful : AI respect s all applicable laws and regulations, including international, regional and local 
human rights laws.  
2) Ethical : AI respects ethical principles and values.  
3) Robust : AI is robust, resilient and secure in both its technical dimensions  while also accounting for 
the social environment it operates in.  
The Guidelines outline the key requirements that AI systems should meet to ensure trustworthiness. These 
requirements encompass various aspects, including human agency and oversight, technical robustness , 
safety, priva cy, data governance, transparency, non -discrimination, fairness, societal and environmental 
well-being, and accountability.13 
Each requirement is accompanied by specific assessment criteria aimed at evaluating its implementation. 
These criteria include  empowering human decision -making , fostering diversity and inclusivity, promoting 
environmental sustainability  and ensuring accountability and redress mechanisms .14  
In April 2021, the European Commission proposed the EU's first regulatory framework for AI,  known as the 
AI Act  (the Act ). The Act categori ses AI systems based on their risk levels, with more regulation applied to 
higher -risk systems.15 The Act aims to promote trustworthy AI by ensuring respect for fundamental rights, 
safety, and ethical principl es while addressing risks posed by powerful AI models.  
The regulatory framework defines four risk levels for AI systems:16 
Unacceptable Risk:  AI systems posing clear threats to safety, livelihoods, and rights will be banned, these 
include social scoring sys tems or even toys encouraging dangerous behaviour.  
High Risk : This category includes AI used in critical infrastructure, education, the safety components of 
products, employment, public services, law enforcement, migration management, and democratic 
proces ses. High -risk AI systems face strict obligations before market entry, including risk assessment, data 
quality assurance, transparency, documentation, human oversight, and security measures.  
Limited Risk:  Refers to the risks associated with a lack of trans parency in AI use. The Act introduces 
transparency obligations  over limited risk applications  to ensure humans are informed when they are 
interacting with AI so they can take an informed decision to continue to engage or not. For example, 
requiring that  chatbots and AI -generated content  are labelled  as such .

The Act takes a forward -looking approach, designed t o adapt to the rapid evolution of AI technology. It 
emphasises the need for AI applications to remain trustworthy even after they enter the market, requiring 
ongoing quality and risk management by providers to ensure compliance with regulations and laws, 
including human rights law.  
To enforce and implement the Act, the European AI Office was established within the European 
Commission in February 2024. This office is tasked with overseeing enforcement , in collaboration with EU 
member states, with a focus on ensuring that AI technologies respect human rights and foster trust. 
Additionally, it promotes collaboration, innovation, and research in AI among various stakeholders and 
engages in international dialogue to align global AI governance standards.17 
Followin g an agreement reached in December 2023 between the European Parliament and the Council of 
the EU, the AI Act is now in the process of formal adoption and translation. Once published in the Official 
Journal , it will enter into force 20 days later, with ful l applicability after two years.  
The Commission has also launched the AI Pact , a voluntary initiative inviting AI developers to comply with 
key obligations of the AI Act ahead of time, aiming to facilitate a smooth transition to the new regulatory 
framewo rk.18 
3.1.2 Brazil  
Brazil is considering Bill 2338/2023 , which mirrors the EU's AI Act  in its risk -based approach, tailoring 
obligations to the level of risk posed by AI systems.19  
Like the EU Act, Bill 2338/2023  prohibits systems with excessive risk, including those employing 
subliminal techniques to induce harmful behaviour  and those used for social scoring by public authorities.  
Penalties for violating this proposed law range from fines up to R$50,000,000.00 (AUD$ 14,940,532.27) 
per infraction or up to 2% of a companies’ annual revenue, along with other penalties  like the  suspension of 
AI system development or supply.  
3.1.3 Canada  
In June 2022, Canada introduced the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act  (AIDA ) as part of the  Canadian  
Digital Charter Implementation Act .20 
Similar to the EU’s AI Act, the AIDA  proposes a risk -based approach, requiring high -impact AI systems to 
meet safety and human rights standards.  
The Minister of Innovation, Science, and Industry would o versee the AIDA’s enforcement, supported by a 
new AI and Data Commissioner. AIDA also introduces criminal provisions to prevent reckless AI use and 
ensures accountability for AI systems in international and interprovincial trade.  The AIDA is under 
committ ee review in the Canadian House of Common s.

Inquiry on adopting AI  9 3.1.4 Australia  
The University of Technology Sydney's Human Technology Institute has developed an  outline for a model 
law addressing facial recognition technology ( FRT ). This initiative could assist in developing regulation for 
AI more broadly .21  
The model  law aims to restrict or even prohibit the development and deployment of FRT that poses risks to 
human rights while facilitating the use of FRT that aligns with Australia's liberal democratic principles. The 
model  law would primarily target FRT developers and deployers operating within Australia.  
Key objectives of the model law include upholding human rights, adopting a risk -based approach to classify 
FRT applications according to their potential harm, supporting c ompliance among developers and 
deployers, ensuring transparency in FRT usage, establishing effective oversight mechanisms through a well -
resourced regulator, and providing avenues for accountability and redress for people  affected by FRT 
misuse.22  
Addition ally, the  model  law seeks jurisdictional compatibility to ensure consistent application across all 
levels of government and adherence to global standards for international interoperability. By addressing 
these goals, the model law aims to navigate the comp lexities of FRT regulation in a manner that safeguards 
individual rights and fosters responsible technological innovation in Australia.  
3.2 Australia should take a risk -based approach to AI regulation  
The EU's approach, exemplified by the Ethics Guidelines for  Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence  and the AI 
Act, provides a robust framework for regulating AI systems based on their risk levels.  
Brazil's proposed legislation, Bill 2338/2023 , mirrors the EU's approach, demonstrating the international 
recognition of  the importance of risk -based regulation. Similarly, Canada's AIDA  proposes a risk -based 
approach, emphasi sing safety and human rights standards for high -impact AI systems.  
Australia can ensure the responsible development and adoption of AI technologies b y embracing a risk -
based regulatory framework, such as the one proposed by the Human Technology Institute's model law for 
FRT. This approach fosters trust among individuals and businesses, promotes innovation, and encourages 
collaboration on a global scale .

Inquiry on adopting AI  10 4. Recommendation  
As Australians  increasingly embrace AI technologies across various sectors, there is a growing awareness of 
the potential threats they  pose if they are left unregulated .  
While AI holds promise for enhancing efficiency and decision -making, its deployment also raises concerns 
regarding transparency, accountability, and the erosion of democratic principles. In light of this, the Human 
Rights Law Centre recommends the followin g: 
4.1 The Parliament should consider adopting a risk -based approach to AI 
regulation  
Australia should carefully consider adopting a risk -based approach to AI regulation, grounded in 
international human rights law and principles.

Benjamin Archibald
1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
In my view, while the principles provide a practical foundation, they do not sufficiently encompass the characteristics of high-risk AI. I recommend supplementing these principles with a regulatory framework that classifies systems as "high-risk" based on technical evaluations conducted at various stages: pre-training, pre-deployment, and during operation.
AI systems can display unexpected or unintended behaviours, which developers may not always anticipate. Implementing a technical evaluation would help identify and manage these behaviours prior to deployment. Moreover, this would offer clarity in situations where it is uncertain whether an AI system falls within the general principles. This strategy could alleviate the regulatory burden by allowing systems that lack hazardous capabilities to face fewer regulations.
4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Yes
If so, how should we define these?
Yes, I believe certain high-risk use cases warrant consideration for prohibition. Specifically, AI systems with the potential for "critical harm" or that pose "systemic risks," as defined by acceptable standards, should be banned. For instance, California's SB1047 bill defines "critical harm" as resulting in mass casualties, severe financial damage, or other significant threats to public safety.
The EU AI Act emphasizes the systemic risks associated with general-purpose AI, highlighting the possibility of widespread or catastrophic harm. There is an urgent need for international collaboration to establish certain "red lines" regarding AI capabilities, akin to those detailed in SB1047 and the EU AI Act. Immediate action is essential if a technical evaluation indicates that an AI model could facilitate the creation of weapons, engage in deceitful practices, or lead to loss of control.
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
I do not believe the current principles adequately encompass emerging forms of high-risk AI, including GPAI. I propose that Australia adopt the definitions of GPAI and GPAI with systemic risk as outlined in the EU AI Act. These definitions provide a robust and future-proof regulatory framework in line with global standards.
Given the rapid advancement of AI capabilities, we are likely to encounter powerful systems with unforeseen abilities. The distinction made by the EU AI Act between GPAI and GPAI with systemic risk will enable Australia to focus on regulating systems with particularly hazardous capabilities, ensuring the safety of advanced AI technologies.
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
Mandatory guardrails should be proportionately applied to reflect the risks associated with each AI system. This approach balances safety and innovation. I recommend adopting the EU AI Act's strategy of distinguishing between GPAI and GPAI with systemic risk, imposing the most stringent mandatory guardrails on the latter.
The significance of "severity and extent" in a risk-based approach to AI regulation must be taken into account when defining GPAI and instituting specific guardrails. To build public trust, the Government should address the potential catastrophic risks of future GPAI systems with a targeted set of mandatory guardrails. This strategy will encourage a balance between safety and innovation while alleviating regulatory burdens where models are assessed as safe.

8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
I do not believe that the proposed guardrails are sufficiently comprehensive or specific to address the diverse range of risks presented by AI. Historical examples with technologies such as automobiles, aircraft, nuclear weapons, and biotechnology demonstrate that regulation must be tailored to the specific risks associated with each technology. AI presents a new challenge—being both ubiquitous and capable of inflicting catastrophic harm.
A uniform set of guardrails for all high-risk AI systems will inevitably result in instances of both over-regulation and under-regulation. This approach fails to recognize that regulation should be proportional to the risks posed by AI. Consequently, I advocate for a more nuanced strategy, with guardrails tailored to the unique risks associated with advanced AI systems.
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
No
Which of the guardrails should be amended?
Other
Please provide any additional comments
In my opinion, the proposed guardrails do not sufficiently allocate responsibility. Research from the MIT AI Risk Repository and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) indicates that AI developers carry the majority of the risk associated with AI development and usage. This is because the critical decisions that determine the safety and accountability of AI are made during the development phase.
Given the advanced knowledge and understanding of technology companies, it is crucial for effective AI governance that these entities are incentivized to act responsibly. This can be achieved through specific obligations, similar to those established in the EU AI Act, the US Executive Order 14110, or California state bill SB1047, which should be imposed on AI developers operating in Australia.

No
How could we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for example low-risk and high-risk GPAI models? 
I believe that the current proposed guardrails require further refinement to effectively address the risks posed by high-level AI models. We need a precise definition for AI models that may exhibit dangerous behaviours leading to widespread or catastrophic harm. Such behaviours may include weapon development, manipulation and deceit, and self-replication.
Internationally, norms are emerging to define these "red lines," as demonstrated by the EU AI Act Recital 110, SB1047, and the Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence. Once these models are defined, we must establish guardrails to manage the associated risks.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A whole of economy approach – introducing a new cross-economy AI Act
What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
To effectively address the use of AI in high-risk settings, Australia requires an AI Act capable of influencing the actions of overseas AI developers, who are ideally positioned to manage significant risks during the development phase. Regulating offshore activities is a complex issue, but it must remain a priority.
In accordance with the discussion paper, an AI-specific Act with enforceable provisions aimed at offshore developers is essential. Nevertheless, established regulatory bodies, such as the Therapeutic Goods Administration and the Civil Aviation Safety Authority, should continue to oversee their respective areas of expertise. An Australian AI Act should, therefore, focus on addressing gaps and influencing the behaviours of offshore AI developers.

4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?

If so, how should we define these?
I’m concerned about all potential harms from AI systems. However, risks of catastrophic harms clearly warrant special attention. For example, use of AI systems to create bioweapons, lethal autonomous weapons and large-scale cyberattacks on Australia’s water systems, medical systems, democratic systems, security systems, and food systems. I’m clearly not the only Australian that thinks this, given that a “preventing dangerous and catastrophic outcomes from AI” was found to be the top priority when 1,141 Australians were asked ‘what should the government focus on when it comes to Artificial Intelligence’ (Ready Research, 2024). In view of this, I think it is commonsense to ban AI systems that present unacceptable catastrophic risks. I suggest defining these high-risk contexts using the ‘systemic risks’ definition in Recital 110 of the EU AI Act. Benefits of this approach include: (1) consistency with other countries mounts coherent pressure on international AI developers, (2) politically easier to align with the EU’s precedent, (3) administratively easier to align with the EU’s precedent.

13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?

What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
I think an AI Act presents the most promise. The most concerning risks from AI threaten multiple dimensions of Australians’ lives and Australia’s economies. As a result, a domain-specific approach means the most catastrophic risks could ‘fall through the cracks’. For example, in 2021, JBS, the world's larger meat processor paid a $14 million ransom following a cyberattack that blocked its US and Australian operations. The impacts to industry and food supply were relatively limited in this specific case, but the example illustrates that more advanced AI systems threaten Australia’s food supply systems. However, concerningly, in this example, it’s unclear whether such threats to our food supply would be the main responsibility of the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, the Department of Industry Science and Resources, the proposed Minister for Food, the Department of Home Affairs, or another arm of government. An Act AI would also enable Australia to align with other countries in directly pressuring AI developers to address catastrophic risks from AI.

E: Submission to Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high- risk settings consultation 
I
 write to you on behalf of the Australasian College of Dermatologists (ACD) to make  a submission to the Mandatory 
guardrails for AI in high- risk settings consultation, from the perspective of AI -use in dermatology in Australia. ACD 
is Australia’s accredited training body and peak professional and membership organisation for specialists in 
dermatology.  
A
CD supports the development of AI to enhance the practice of dermatology in Australia, and welcomes future 
research on how AI can be utilised in dermatological practice . However, we note that rapid advancements in AI and 
the introduction into dermatological practice create a range of both opportunities and risks to patient care [See 
ACD’s Position Statement on the use of AI in dermatology in Australia ]. R egarding  the proposed mandatory 
guardrails, ACD notes the below areas of consideration by the Department.  
P
otential for AI devices in dermatology  and importance of a regulatory approach 
In dermatology, there is substantial interest in using AI to identify skin lesions from images. As visual pattern 
recognition plays an important role in dermatology, it is an ideal clinical application of AI  [4]. AI software as a 
medical device (SaMD) in particular, has potential to enhance processes in disease screening, diagnostic 
classification and pathology detection, yet regulation is needed to minimise risk  to patients. Given the rapidly 
evolving nature of AI technologies, we support a regulatory rather than legislative approach as this will provide the 
flexibility needed to respond to  the challenges that may emerge in this dynamic environment.  
D
efining high- risk settings and applications  
We note the department’s classification metrics of ‘risk’ in their consultation paper, relating to AI in healthcare, and agree that risk should consider individual patient outcomes  as well as  broader societal and economic impacts. 
In relation to dermatology, therefore, AI -SaMD used in skin cancer classification diagnosis should be considered as 
high -risk due to the potential for misdiagnosis of melanoma, or overdiagnosis o f false positives  leading to 
unnecessary treatment costs.  
A
I tools in high- risk settings require nuanced assessments as associated risks may stem from their workflow or their 
application, rather than the tool itself – which should be considered in risk profiling to ensure safe and effective 
use.  
Fi
rst Nations persons , skin-of-colour , and minimising risk of generalisability  
Often in dermatology, imaging of skin diseases can vary based on device, operator, or population characteristics 
such as age, skin tone, or sun exposure. Poor generalisability results in reduced accuracy when AI models are 
applied to diverse populations.  For AI -SaMD in dermatology , training data bias on gender and ethnicity means that 
models are not generalisable for  under -represented demographics [4,7,10 ]. Specifically for Indigenous Australians, 
who have a lower incidence of skin cancer [3] , using inappropriate datasets in skin cancer AI tools may result in 
false positives ; highlighting the importance of population -specific risk profiling.  Furthermore, First Nations health data is often overreported in ways that is not representative of true health 
experiences  [2,8], which should be a consideration for the department in assessing high -risk environments  and 
ensuring that risk to First Nations people is minimised by AI devices. Ensuring AI models do not overfit or underfit  
[6]when applied to Indigenous and skin- of-color populations is critical. Risk to patients can be minimised if A I
t
echnologie s incorporate Data Sovereignty and Governance principles,  to ensure that their experiences, values, and
rights are respected and reflected.
A
CD notes that  while the inclusion of First Nations  data is necessary  to reduce the risk of harm to First Nations 
peoples , making this a mandatory requirement may inadvertently cause harm by increasing healthcare costs or 
generating unnecessary anxiety  for this group . Furthermore, excluding Indigenous Australians from datasets could 
lead to inaccurate AI assessments of their skin health, thereby widening healthcare disparities.  Instead, a balanced 
approach is required, ensuring Indigenous Australians are represented in AI datasets without imposing undue 
burden.  
E
thical principles  
The ethical use of AI in healthcare must be guided by principles such as transparency, fairness, and non -maleficence  
[1]. The use of AI in healthcare is subject to automation bias, where clinicians may over- rely on AI 
recommendations, even when their own judgment suggests otherwise [ 5,9]. AI decision -making process es—often 
referred to as the "black box" [4 ] phenomenon —further complicates its real- world application, emphasising the 
need for transparent guidelines and continuous monitoring. Addressing these ethical and operational concerns is 
essential for the safe integration of AI into clinical practice.  
ACD would like to thank the Department for the ir consideration of this submission. If you require any further 
information or clarification, please contact Jessica Jaja, Policy Manager, on jessica@dermcoll.edu.au .
