1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
There is insufficient coverage for perpetuality of some AI, especially in relation to deployments that directly or indirectly impact children/youth. Considerations for risks and safety that extend over a lifetime and can possibly impact on subsequent generations requires additional exploration and guidance. These aspects are not usually thought of in risk considerations so would be likely to be overlooked.
Are there any principles we should add or remove?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
As above, in relation to use of AI with children/youth. Unintended consequences may not be apparent for years, even with the best intentions (e.g. use of AI to create bespoke learning packages may have unintended perpetual consequences if not catering for undiagnosed neurodivergence). Guardrails that protect the young and their information must be included. This must include direct usage of AI with children/youth and the use of AI with their information.
Please identify any:
No low-risk use cases that are unintentionally captured.
Categories of uses that must be treated separately are for minors/youth and those that are differently-abled. This collective group of individuals are vulnerable in three ways across all the domains already listed. Two from bias, and one for consequence/impact. This means these groups must be provided additional protections from the elevated risks related to AI use with these individuals.
1. Bias from smaller and more varied data sets. Both minors and differently-abled individuals have less data points to train systems with, and even if they are available, these data points SHOULD be more protected. This means the bias inherent in the training is likely to be of impact.
2, Bias in the base algorithms of the AI systems. When creating programs including AI, developers will draw on assumptions or expectations. With both groups of individuals, these are more varied and usually fall outside the standard assumptions or expectations. For example, children are not expected to have fully developed executive function for decision making, however when this milestone occurs can be widely varied and still be considered normal. Therefore a developer creating a program would build in bias by assuming a level of function.
3. The consequence/impact of AI performing inappropriately for these individuals can be catastrophic. For example, an AI system used for bespoke delivery of education programs to a student may inadvertently cause 'learned helplessness' by not considering different developmental milestones or even undiagnosed neurodivergence. The 'learned helplessness' may go on to impact the student's confidence, development and achievements and worst case impact their mental health and safety.
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
Similar to the above response for minors and differently-abled people, there must also be additional guidance on considerations for bias (data set and assumptions in algorithm creation) and for consequences that need to be culturally aligned.
The capturing of harms must be done in consultation with First Nations elders and leaders. It must be general enough to cover the many Nations across the country and be actionable to further seeking engagement with the appropriate relevant peoples. The principles must include appropriate reference to where AI developers and deployers can contact First Nations representatives to further discuss specific AI uses and use cases. This must take into account the vast and varied First Nation custodians across the country, each with their own unique aspects and unique knowledge of their area of Country. Without consideration of this, the potential harms from AI are compounded by advice that is not appropriate or relevant to the locality of the AI system. If an AI system is to be used Nationally, this must consider all First Nations impacted.
3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?
YES the principles give enough clarity and certainty
If you prefer a principles-based approach, what should we address in guidance to give the greatest clarity?
A principles based approach is preferred as it is less prone to being obsoleted by emerging trends and technologies. However it is vulnerable to interpretation in a manner to avoid responsibility. The vulnerability must be addressed in such a way that responsibility can not be avoided or redirected to a scape-goat.
How can this list capture emerging uses of AI?
Categorisation based on impacts/consequences (both positive and negative) to individuals, groups, and Australia could be used to capture emerging use of AI where the traditional industry domain is unknown. Or the technology itself is unknown. The constant will be that people and the nation will be impacted, therefore by baselining against these constants, changes will be captured.
4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Yes
If so, how should we define these?
High-risk use cases must include those where there is an exclusion of humans in decision making. Or that the system includes humans in decision making however it is not at the appropriate juncture of the decision process flow.
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
Though as above, this can be improved by including greater definition on the consequence/impact to the constants of individuals, groups, and Australia.
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
This will reduce the likelihood of interpretation to not apply the mandatory guardrails. Or that a GPAI model is initially assessed as not requiring guardrails however much later on, it is determined its impact is so great that guardrails should have been applied.
7. What are suitable indicators for defining GPAI models as high-risk?
Define high-risk against the principles
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?
No
Please provide any additional comments.
Recognising the need for flexibility in the framework, there needs to be settings or guidance on commonly understood thresholds, nomenclature and context when requiring transparency and accountability. The current technology environment already has misalignment between developers and deployers/end users in relation to understanding of disclosed functionality or risks. Whether this be due to deliberate lack of transparency or lack of common nomenclature, expectations or understanding between developer industries and user industries (e.g. small medical clinics deploying technology may not have the background to understand product disclosure and description for cloud technologies).
For the requirement for AI testing, transparency and accountability there needs to be additional settings to aid such understanding and reduce deliberate obfuscation of information. The consequence of misunderstanding or obfuscation in high risk settings is multiplied with AI and therefore I think this is essential across the guardrails.
Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?
Yes
What guardrails should we add or remove?
Other
Please provide any additional comments
The additional guardrail requires documentation of deliberate analysis to exclude groups previously identified in this response as having the most impact of perpetual risk from AI whether directly or as a third-party impacted. This means that each use in a high-risk setting regardless of domain will have to explicitly justify why these groups are not impacted, and if they are impacted, how the risks are being managed. This would then need to tie into the guardrails related to informing end-users (in this case the appropriate guardian or safety (e.g. child safety) authority). The initial analysis must be reviewed and updated regularly as the impacted groups from AI are likely to change over time.
It is well known that governance is not always maintained, updated and reviewed for currency. As AI is a fast moving technology, all the guardrails must be amended to include explicit expectations of regular review, update and endorsement by an appropriate organisational authority. Without this expectation, the aspects of accountability will not be as strong as needed.
9. How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols to ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property?
As above with underage or vulnerable groups, the need to explicitly analyse and document why they are not impacted directly or indirectly. When analysis shows impact, inclusion of documented consultation with the appropriate First Nation's groups impacted. There must also be a regular review and update including if initial analysis shows they have not been impacted as this may change over time.
10. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails distribute responsibility across the AI supply chain and throughout the AI lifecycle appropriately?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
On principle, the developers must hold responsibility for appropriate disclosure of their product in a manner and language that is accessible and materially usable by deployers. This is to include the intended use cases, functionalities, scope boundaries, and any known warnings. Deployers are responsible for implementing, using and applying the technology within the bounds identified by the developers and ensure their deployment use case fits within those described by the developer.
The key aspect to this is ensuring the nomenclature and expectations between developer and deployer are designed such that there is no grounds to claim misunderstanding which then would lead to questions in accountability and responsibility.
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI?
No
How could we adapt the guardrails for different GPAI models, for example low-risk and high-risk GPAI models? 
GPAI models change, however end user groups and impacts are relatively static. Adapting the guardrails to focus on the human impacts and assessment of these would go part the way to ensuring the guardrails are sufficient to address risks whilst being more robust to technology changes.
12. Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small-to-medium sized businesses applying guardrails?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
Production of guidance documentation with a focus on human impacts. This can be in the form of a set of questions on a flow-chart or assessment matrix. The aim is to reduce the knowledge gap for small-med business who may not have ready access to technical specialists and enable a consistent application of risk across businesses to aid analysis and decision making.
The use of common English description of human impacts allows such a tool to be more accessible to deployers who may not be as technically minded as developers. It ensures developers categorise and mark their product in a way that can be understood by deployers. As above where it becomes more robust to technology changes, means small-med business are not constantly required to update their knowledge and understanding with technology.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A whole of economy approach – introducing a new cross-economy AI Act
What opportunities should the Government take into account in considering each approach? 
None of the three options are without cons, however AI risk and safety should be viewed similarly to Privacy risk and therefore a whole of economy approach is most applicable. A whole of economy approach allows for the establishment of baseline acceptable human risks especially to underage and vulnerable groups regardless of existing regulatory frameworks for specific industries/domains. It allows for consistency in government management of these in a similar manner such as for Privacy. A whole of economy approach also reduces the burden on small-med business and understanding from end users of personal impacts as there is a level of consistency regardless of industry.
This does not preclude leveraging those existing industry/domain specific frameworks. Contrary, this should be an opportunity to highlight and leverage those frameworks specific to risk and information security that are already established. It would be an opportunity for deliberate analysis on the possibility of wider leveraging of controls from one industry framework that would be pragmatic for another, and uplift of any that are old and require refresh.
The use of existing regulatory bodies should also be incorporated and leveraged.
14. Are there any additional limitations of options outlined in this section which the Australian Government should consider?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
With consideration for human related impacts there needs to be sensitivity around the discussion with regards to different cultural and community groups where impacts may be considered differently or such groups are already vulnerable to discrimination and therefore may require additional protections that don't inadvertently compound discrimination.
15. Which regulatory option(s) will best ensure that guardrails for high-risk AI can adapt and respond to step-changes in technology?
A whole of economy approach – introducing a new cross-economy AI Act
Please provide any additional comments.
As above, focusing on the aspect that is least likely to change with step-changes in technology is the impact to people.
16. Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps and inconsistencies with Australia’s existing laws for the development and deployment of AI?
Where there is contention between the priorities of existing laws and the development of AI. A common example used is the balance between privacy and the need for AI to be trained on real data to be representative of the population.
Which regulatory option best addresses this?
A whole of economy approach – Introducing a new cross-economy AI-specific Act (for example, an Australian AI Act).
Please explain why.  
Regardless of industry/domain, again the human factor (in the example above) for Privacy is a common feature and therefore a whole of economy approach to balancing the need for Privacy and data required for AI would bring consistency.

686Executive Summary
The Pacific Islands comprise a diverse group of nations and territories  
scattered across the Pacific Ocean. They include the Cook Islands, Federated 
States of Micronesia, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Nauru, 
New Caledonia, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, Solomon Islands, 
Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu. These islands face unique challenges such as 
geographic isolation, vulnerability to natural disasters, climate change, labor 
shortages, and the need to preserve their rich cultural heritage. 
Artificial Intelligence (AI), including Generative AI (Gen AI), holds significant 
potential to address these issues by transforming various sectors and 
enhancing the quality of life for Pacific Island peoples. AI can improve disaster 
forecasting and response, enhance healthcare delivery, optimize resource 
management, and promote sustainable development, thereby creating new  
opportunities for growth and resilience in the Pacific Islands.
The current state of AI development in the Pacific Islands varies significantly 
across the region. Some nations are more advanced in their digital 
transformation efforts, having established digital strategies and invested in 
infrastructure, while others are still in the nascent stages of developing and 
adopting these strategies and technologies. The readiness of governments to 
implement AI technologies is also varied, with differing levels of awareness, 
policy frameworks, and regulatory measures in place. 
Insights from global and regional developments underscore the need for 
tailored AI strategies that consider the specific contexts of the Pacific Islands. 
The report emphasizes the importance of building robust digital infrastructure 
and incorporating ethical considerations throughout the AI lifecycle. It 
identifies key lessons learned from other regions, which include the necessity 
of fostering digital literacy among the population, developing comprehensive 
AI governance frameworks, and enhancing regional cooperation to share 
resources and expertise. 
The report includes actionable recommendations for policymakers and 
stakeholders to improve responsible AI governance and deployment in the 
Pacific Islands. Specifically, the report calls for the establishment of a Pacific 
Islands AI Technical Assistance Facility to play a pivotal role in facilitating the 
development and implementation of country-focussed AI strategies, offering 
specialized expertise, and helping to tackle emerging AI challenges through 
capacity-building programs and resource allocation.7

Introduction and Context9Artificial Intelligence (AI) has the potential to transform societies across the 
globe. Its potential applications are vast and varied, with the ability to address 
complex challenges and enhance various aspects of human life. Similarly, 
the benefits of AI are anticipated to contribute to addressing the unique 
challenges faced by the Pacific Islands1, including the tyranny of distance, 
natural disasters, climate change, labor shortages, and cultural preservation. 
However, to fully unlock these benefits, adequate safeguards must be put in 
place to mitigate the potential risks and downsides of AI. 
This report is the fourth in the AI Asia Pacific Institute’s annual series examining 
the state of Artificial Intelligence in the Asia-Pacific Region. The series explores 
the landscape and recent developments of AI governance across the Asia-
Pacific, this time taking a specific focus on the Pacific Islands. The report also 
includes some analysis of Australia and New Zealand as they play significant 
roles in the Pacific Islands through various avenues such as economic assistance, 
regional security, political engagement, and environmental initiatives.
The report presents a preliminary examination of the current global landscape 
of AI development and a review of the preparedness of Pacific Island nations 
for the implementation of responsible AI, including their digital infrastructure 
and related government policies. It also provides initial recommendations to 
policymakers and other stakeholders on how these nations can best govern AI 
to ensure its responsible development and deployment. The research draws 
on a recent project carried out by the AI Asia Pacific Institute for the Association 
of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)2. 
This introduction section delves into the meaning of AI, the potential 
benefits it can bring, and the challenges that must be overcome within the 
unique context of the Pacific Islands.1.0 Research Context101.1 What is AI?
1.2 Generative AIAI refers to the development of computer systems capable of performing 
tasks that usually require human intelligence, ranging from simple rule-based 
activities to complex problem-solving and learning. A subset of AI, Machine 
Learning (ML), enables these systems to improve their performance on specific 
tasks through data exposure, without explicit programming. This learning and 
adaptation ability sets AI apart from traditional systems, allowing it to handle 
unstructured data and dynamic scenarios efficiently. 
AI uses algorithms, mathematical models, and computational power to 
simulate cognitive functions like perception, reasoning, and decision-making, 
with applications such as Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computer 
Vision. The current AI revolution is driven by new methodologies of Machine 
Learning like Deep Learning, Neural Networks, Reinforcement Learning, and 
the significant increase in available data.
Gen AI is a subset of AI capable of generating new content based on  
large amounts of data it has been trained on. Using any kind of data  
for model learning and focusing on the most relevant inputs, Gen AI produces 
outputs in text, image, audio, and video form for various applications. While 
traditional AI can analyze data and provide observations, Gen AI has the 
capability to create something entirely new. Gen AI took the world by storm 
in late 2022 with the release of ChatGPT3, followed by other similar forms of 
Large Language Models (LLMs). With its rapid emergence and accompanying 
risks, it widened the gap between technology and governance, necessitating 
immediate and decisive responses from regulators and policymakers, 
including those from the Pacific Islands.11Table 1.1 presents a summary of the main features of the three main phases of the AI

1.4 High-level Benefits of AIThe lifecycle of AI models, encompassing development and deployment, is a 
multi-stage process with inherent challenges and risks. To reap the benefits 
of AI while mitigating these risks, a holistic approach is crucial. This approach 
integrates ethical considerations, privacy safeguards, and transparency 
throughout the entire lifecycle. The key challenges and risks include:
Data Biases
The initial phase, involving data collection and preprocessing, is susceptible to 
bias if not handled meticulously. These biases can be inadvertently learned by 
the model during training, perpetuating them in the final output.
Lack of Transparency
Deployment of models in the final phase raises ethical concerns due to limited 
transparency and accountability surrounding AI decision-making. This lack of 
clarity can lead to unintended consequences.
Security Concerns
Security risks pose another significant challenge. Malicious actors can exploit 
vulnerabilities through adversarial attacks, manipulating input data to deceive 
AI systems and compromise their integrity.
Data Privacy
When sensitive data is used for training, privacy concerns arise. These 
include questions about data ownership, user consent, and the potential for 
unauthorized access.
AI offers a plethora of benefits across various domains. The ability of AI to 
analyze vast datasets quickly and identify patterns makes it a valuable tool 
in scientific research, drug discovery and climate modelling. For instance, 
McKinsey reported in 2022 that AI-driven drug discovery processes achieve 
a 30 to 50 per cent increase in efficiency for large-scale experiments4, 
while Nature reports an AI-driven climate prediction tool calculates carbon 
emission impacts a million times faster than previous models5. Moreover, 
AI has the potential to address societal challenges, such as poverty,  
inequality, and environmental sustainability, by providing data-driven insights 
and solutions.
Using AI, Stanford University achieved 81-99% accuracy in analyzing poverty 
in regions across Africa, while Carnegie Mellon University is exploring 
opportunities to boost agriculture in poverty-stricken regions6. 13Gen AI, in particular, holds the potential to deliver a wide range  
of high-level benefits:
Enhancing accessibility
The technology is more available, usable and understandable to a broader 
range of users and can be integrated more easily into workflow across multiple 
applications7.  
Developing and consolidating infrastructure
Improved scalability, efficiency, security, and adaptability enable 
organizations to effectively harness the benefits of Gen AI in their  
operations, thus reducing costs and required expertise8.
Consolidating research and development
By enabling the sharing of resources and expertise, this technology accelerates 
the development of new applications, improves quality, and enhances safety. 
This, in turn, speeds up innovation in research and development and provides 
new insights for problem-solving9. 141.5 Key AI Terms

Global and Regional Context162.1 Global Developments
The global market for AI is projected to reach a staggering US$305.90 billion 
in 2024, with an expected annual growth rate of over 15% until 203010. The 
United States currently leads the race, boasting nearly 60% of the world’s top-
tier AI researchers and attracting a staggering $249 billion in private funding. 
China and the United Kingdom follow closely behind, with Israel and Canada 
emerging as rising stars in the AI landscape.
The United States, China, and the European Union emerge as key players 
in the AI landscape, each navigating the path of development alongside 
considerations for responsible governance11.
The US holds the current lead in AI innovation, boasting a strong foundation 
in research and development. Top universities and research institutions attract 
world-class talent, backed by significant private funding. This ecosystem 
fosters groundbreaking discoveries, with nearly 60% of the world’s leading AI 
researchers calling the US home. Additionally, private companies are heavily 
investing in the development of AI.
China is also focussed on AI development. Their government prioritizes AI as a 
national strategic goal, providing substantial public funding and encouraging 
rapid adoption of AI technologies. China excels in areas like data collection 
and real-world implementation. Their massive population provides a readily 
available pool of data, fuelling advancements in areas like facial recognition 
and speech analysis. This approach is pushing the US to innovate even faster, 
creating a dynamic environment for global AI progress.
The governance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a focal point 
globally, especially with the advent of Gen AI widening the gap between 
innovation and governance due to its ability to exacerbate potential risks. AI 
very rapidly sparked substantial interest partly due to its impressive capabilities 
and partly because its risks became more evident, demanding an immediate 
response from regulators and policymakers. 
The European Union is pioneering a regulatory approach to AI governance  
and ethics with its advanced regulations and comprehensive legal  
frameworks. Enacted in March 2024, the EU AI Act categorises AI systems  
based on criteria including human rights, health, safety, and social impact, 
classifying them into unacceptable risk, high risk, and limited or no risk12. As 
the world’s first legal framework for AI, the Act is expected to significantly 
affect global companies that sell or use AI products within the EU, as well as  
serve as a model for global AI governance and ethics.
Emphasising the balance between regulations and the autonomy of 
companies for AI development, the United States does not have a specialized 
federal regulatory framework that comprehensively addresses AI. 17However, to address challenges associated with AI advancement, the U.S. has 
established various AI-related agencies and organizations across different 
sectors and is dedicated to developing a regulatory framework aimed at 
maximising the benefits of AI and mitigating its risks. In October 2023, the 
Biden Administration issued an executive order that provides a comprehensive 
overview of regulations and guidelines for the safe and trustworthy 
development of AI13.
China has officially aligned its AI governance with the advancement of 
universally held values including peace, development, equity, justice, 
democracy, and freedom14. Concurrently, the nation has been actively 
legislating numerous AI regulations at a fast pace. In January 2023, the Deep 
Synthesis Provisions came into effect, establishing comprehensive rules 
governing the creation and use of deepfakes. In August 2023, interim measures 
on generative AI were implemented to ensure that generative AI technologies 
adhere to China’s core socialist values while simultaneously promoting  
non-discrimination, sound intellectual property practices, and corporate 
ethics15.
International efforts are intensifying to establish a unified approach to AI 
governance, focusing on safety, ethics, and responsibility. In May 2023, the 
Hiroshima AI Process was launched to create an international framework 
promoting global governance of safe and trustworthy AI technologies16. 
Additionally, at the UK AI Safety Summit in November 2023, 28 countries 
including the US, China, the UK, and South Korea agreed on a shared 
vision to foster safety and ethical considerations in AI development and 
deployment, which was further discussed at the AI Seoul Summit in 
May 202417. The UN General Assembly adopted the first resolution on AI 
governance In March 2024, promoting ‘safe, secure, and trustworthy’ AI 
systems that also support sustainable development, with backing from  
over 120 member states18.182.2 Regional Developments
2.2.1 Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)
ASEAN member states are at very different stages of digital development 
and AI readiness. This is an important factor underpinning the responsible 
development and use of AI and related technologies. Six of the ten ASEAN 
states—Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and 
Vietnam—have adopted explicit AI strategies. The remaining four, along with 
Timor-Leste, are presently limited to digital policies and strategies with little 
or no reference to AI. While varying significantly in coverage from country to 
country, the AI strategies commonly focus on the development and use of 
AI as a tool to accelerate economic growth and innovation, on building the 
human capacities required to implement AI initiatives, and, to a somewhat 
lesser extent, on strengthening the regulatory ecosystem to underpin the 
responsible use of AI.
ASEAN, as a group is actively navigating the global AI landscape. For instance, 
the ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics19 endorsed in February 2024 
serves as a critical regional initiative, offering recommendations for the 
responsible development and deployment of AI technologies. In September 
2023, the ASEAN Committee on Science, Technology and Innovation (COSTI), 
working through the ASEAN Secretariat, launched an initiative to produce The 
Discussion Paper on the Responsible Development and Use of Generative 
AI in ASEAN, which identifies the most urgent policy, legal and regulatory 
gaps in Gen AI implementation within ASEAN. The discussion paper was 
strongly endorsed in the ASEAN Ministerial Meeting on Science, Technology 
and Innovation (AMMSTI) Statement on Artificial Intelligence (AI) ASEAN  
in June 202420.
Singapore was the first country in Southeast Asia to launch a national AI 
strategy. As a percentage of GDP, Singapore’s government-supported AI 
R&D spending21 is 18 times larger than U.S. R&D spending. The Singapore 
government announced its National AI Strategy in 2019 to map out 
a plan for the development and deployment of scalable, impactful 
AI solutions in key sectors of high value and relevance by 2030. The 
strategy identifies five critical ecosystem enablers to build a vibrant and 
sustainable AI ecosystem: (1) a progressive and trusted environment; (2)  
talent and education; (3) triple helix partnerships22; (4) data architecture; and 
(5) international collaboration23.
Just a week prior to the passing of the EU AI Act, the Personal Data Protection 
Commission (PDPC) of Singapore officially published its Advisory Guidelines 
on the Use of Personal Data in AI Recommendation and Decision Systems. 
They have also launched a discussion paper and a Gen AI Evaluation Sandbox24 
to address governance and trust concerns surrounding this new technology. 
Other member states like Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines are focusing 
on understanding the impact of Gen AI on the future of work and how to best 
prepare their workforce for this evolving landscape.192.2.2 Australia and New Zealand
Australia officially launched the Artificial Intelligence Action Plan in 2021, which 
outlines AI developments through 203025. Managed by the Department of 
Industry, Science, and Resources, this plan saw an investment of $124.1 million 
for 2021-22 and anticipates $75.7 million for 2023-24. The Australian government 
has regularly published discussion papers on AI ethics, including ‘Supporting 
Responsible AI’26 (2023) and ‘Safe and responsible AI in Australia consultation’ 
(2024)27, leading the way in AI governance and ethical advancements. Startups 
like FloodMapp are actively developing technologies to address natural 
disasters within the region28. 
Australia champions the digital transformation of the Pacific Islands through 
collaborations with corporations and international organizations. For instance, 
the Australian government has partnered with the European Union to fund 
the Pacific Digital Economy Programme (PDEP). This initiative fosters digital 
innovations in the Pacific islands through research and technical assistance 
optimised for each specific country29. Further, the country has supported 
Project Olangch, a digitalisation initiative of Palau’s national health sector in 
collaboration with Beyond Essential, an Australian software company. Thanks 
to this effort, Palau could depart from the outdated paper-based system and 
start employing ‘digital health ecosystems’30.
In the absence of a formally documented AI policy like Australia’s, New 
Zealand has developed official government frameworks while also proactively 
supporting digital initiatives in the Pacific Islands. In 2021, New Zealand’s 
National AI Strategy was unveiled at the Aotearoa AI Summit31, detailing a 
five-year plan to align AI development with national values. While no binding 
documents have translated the summit’s content into policy, efforts continue 
across governmental, corporate, and private sectors to enhance AI frameworks 
and technologies. 
The New Zealand government consistently issues guidelines to align AI tool 
usage with the Privacy Act 202032, defines the government’s algorithm use 
in the ‘Algorithm Charter’33, and has released the ‘Generative AI Guidance 
for the Public Sector’34. Moreover, AI Forum, a local NGO, leads responsible 
AI use and governance through its new website, AI Governance. The 
government also actively supports digital development in the Pacific islands. 
For instance, New Zealand spearheaded the Pacific Digital Champions 
Training Program in 202335, a training program that involved Tahiti, Tonga 
and Tuvalu to foster digital capacity for personnel in the tourism sector. 
Further, the country collaborates with the World Bank to finance the 
Kiribati 20-year Plan aiming to overcome barriers to digital connectivity for  
Kiribati’s ICT development36.Chapter 3.

3.3 AI in the Pacific Islands
The Pacific Islands face unique challenges which are critical to their survival 
and development: 
Climate Change
The Pacific Islands are on the frontlines of climate change. Risingsea levels 
and frequent natural disasters, like typhoons and floods, threaten their very 
existence. See Annex 20 for a detailed summary of climate change initiatives 
in the Pacific Islands. For instance, scientists predict Tuvalu could become 
uninhabitable in the next 50 to 100 years42.
Economy
The Pacific Islands struggle with the exodus of skilled workers to New 
Zealand and Australia, resulting in a shortage of skilled labor, which hinders 
economic growth. Additionally, each country exhibits varying levels of 
industrialization and economic size, reflecting diverse economic characteristics 
and scales. The vast distances between Pacific nations further impede  
economic cooperation.25Governance 
The Pacific Islands receive numerous support projects from foreign and 
international organizations, often resulting in overlapping initiatives, 
particularly in foreign direct investment and economic development. Recent 
advancements in AI, including Gen AI, have significant potential to enhance 
the governance efficiency of these islands.
Cultural Preservation 
The Pacific Islands face the challenge of preserving their cultures while 
promoting social and economic development. Maintaining minority languages 
and traditions through education requires significant resources. In the context 
of AI, Gen AI has the potential to threaten intellectual property by not providing 
the royalties that contents from the islands conventionally received.
AI can provide potential solutions and benefits optimised for the unique  
context of each nation in the Pacific Islands - the following provides some 
practical examples: 
3.3.1 Climate Change
Case Study 1: Digital Earth Pacific
Digital Earth Pacific is Pacific Community’s43 analytics platform designed 
to assist Pacific Island nations in enhancing their resilience to natural 
disasters and environmental challenges through data-driven decision-
making. Based on Microsoft’s Planetary Computer, it aggregates vast 
amounts of environmental data collected from satellites and other 
sources and provides timely and precise intelligence that supports 
decision making for relocating communities, managing natural resources,  
and predicting volcanic eruptions44.
Enhanced Disaster Preparedness 
AI helps Pacific Island nations prepare for natural disasters through detailed 
environmental analysis and risk assessment.
Informed Decision-Making
AI empowers Pacific Islands to make informed decisions on disaster response, 
environmental conservation, and urban planning.
Economic and Operational Advancement 
AI boosts economic resilience and operational efficiency by supporting 
preparedness for environmental challenges.26Case Study 2: FloodMapp
FloodMapp, an Australian AI startup, employs machine learning and big data 
analytics to provide real-time, street-level flood forecasts using river and rainfall 
data. This capability is crucial for enabling timely evacuations and strategic 
resource deployment, thereby reducing the impact of floods in regions prone 
to such natural disasters, like the Pacific Islands. Given Australia’s history of 
supporting the Pacific Islands, continued technological partnerships are likely, 
which will not only enhance disaster response capabilities but also strengthen 
the overall resilience of these communities45.
Enhanced Response against Floods 
Real-time Flood-forecasting AI enables timely evacuations and strategic 
resource deployment.
Life and Asset Protection
AI enhances the ability to safeguard lives and property, potentially in Pacific 
Island communities during floods.
3.3.2 Economy
Case Study 3: UN Global Platform for Pacific Islands
An IMF report ‘Tracking Trade from Space: An Application to Pacific Island 
Countries’ introduces a method for tracking trade via satellite-based vessel 
data, specifically applied to Pacific Island countries. These regions, reliant 
on maritime transport and vulnerable to natural disasters, could potentially 
benefit from daily indicators of port and trade activity derived from the UN 
Global Platform. By integrating detailed shipping schedules and specific 
port information via algorithms, Pacific islands countries could potentially fill 
gaps in official data and aid in rapid policy response to economic shifts and 
emergencies like COVID-1946.
Enhanced Economic Monitoring 
AI can provide daily trade indicators that help Pacific Island countries monitor 
economic activities in real-time.
Strategic Planning Support 
AI can aid in the strategic planning and resilience building of maritime regions 
by filling data gaps in official statistics.
Accessibility
UN Global Platform Data, publicly accessible, can be easily employed by the 
Pacific Island community.27Case Study 4: Global Fishing Watch 
Global Fishing Watch employs machine learning to enhance the monitoring of 
marine activities by analyzing Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. This 
approach identifies vessels at higher risk of illegal practices, including forced 
labour. Crucially, this technology supports sustainable fishing in the Pacific, 
where over 50% of the global tuna catch occurs. Strengthening partnerships 
with Pacific Island nations, Global Fishing Watch aims to bolster regional 
fisheries management and sustainability efforts47.
Enhanced Monitoring
AI and Machine Learning can improve the detection of illegal fishing activities 
and forced labour on vessels.
Sustainability Support
AI aids sustainable fishing practices in the Pacific, crucial for the region where 
over 50% of the global tuna catch is sourced.
Economic and Cultural Protection 
AI supports the economies, food security, and cultural identities of Pacific 
Island communities.
3.3.3 Governance
Case Study 5: Safe Use of AI in Public Services
The Australian Government announced a plan to collaborate with Microsoft 
through the Digital Transformation Agency (DTA) to explore the safe and 
responsible use of generative AI in public services. This initiative includes 
a six-month trial of Microsoft 365 Copilot, set to run from January to 
June 2024. The Australian Public Service (APS) is expected to adopt Gen 
AI to enhance productivity and innovation for better service delivery to  
the Australian people48.
Enhanced Productivity 
AI improves the efficiency and output of the Australian Public Service.
Improved Service Delivery 
The integration of AI tools is expected to result in better and more efficient 
services for the Australian public, with the potential of setting benchmarks 
that could be adopted in the Pacific Islands.283.3.4 Culture Preservation 
Case Study 6: Te Hiku Media
Te Hiku Media is developing automatic speech recognition (ASR) models for 
the Māori language, te reo, using AI technology to ensure its preservation. 
Built on Nvidia’s GPUs and employing open-source technologies, the model 
provides high accuracy in transcribing both mono- and bilingual (te reo and 
English) speech. The main goal of this initiative is to preserve, promote, and 
revitalise the te reo Māori language by using AI to capture vast amounts of 
historical and contemporary spoken data from native speakers, and making 
this data accessible for educational and cultural purposes. The application of 
ASR models is expected to inspire the indigenous communities of the Pacific 
Islands to adopt similar technologies to preserve their languages and culture49
Preservation of Heritage 
AI helps to preserve and revitalize indigenous languages, ensuring their 
survival for future generations.
Cultural Empowerment 
AI empowers indigenous communities to control their cultural narratives and 
heritage.
Educational Access

language accessible to its learners.29The Pacific Islands in general have not yet developed systematic and

Chapter 4.
Future Directions, Recommendations 
and Conclusions354.1 Key Lessons Learned
1. Underdevelopment of AI and ICT 
• Pacific Island nations generally lack AI-related strategies and governance 
frameworks, as well as the regulatory structures necessary for AI 
development.
• The region exhibits economic vulnerability and underdeveloped ICT 
infrastructure, posing challenges to AI integration and growth.
• Establishing comprehensive strategies, regulatory frameworks, and 
investing in ICT infrastructure are critical steps for fostering sustainable AI 
development in the Pacific Islands.
2. Weak Awareness of AI
• While there are attempts to introduce AI, most efforts are focused on ICT.
• Most educational and awareness efforts are related to digital technology 
itself, with little focus on AI.
3. Challenges posed for Regional Coordination
• The dispersal and uniqueness of each island state make a one-size-fits-all 
solution difficult.
• The need for more active ICT and AI-dedicated regional bodies and 
initiatives.
• Regional cooperation is often characterized by sporadic, one-off events 
rather than being part of a well-coordinated, continuous strategy that 
fosters long-term linkages and sustained collaboration.
4. Global Cooperation
• Established guidelines from the US, China, and the EU provide a late-mover 
advantage for the Pacific Islands to selectively adopt best practices.
• Australia and New Zealand’s AI strategies and guidelines can serve as useful 
references tailored to the Pacific region.
• Considering the economic vulnerability of the Pacific Islands, economic 
cooperation with international actors and intergovernmental organizations 
is crucial.364.2 Recommendations 
1. Develop Foundational AI Guidelines and Approaches  for the Pacific 
Islands
• Create Comprehensive AI Development Guidance:  
Develop detailed AI development guidance documents tailored to the 
unique conditions of the Pacific Islands. This should be based on thorough 
assessments of the region’s AI ecosystems, taking into account local needs, 
capabilities, and challenges.
• Establish National AI Strategies and Roadmaps:  
Formulate foundational AI strategies and roadmaps for each Pacific Island 
nation, providing clear directions for AI development and integration. These 
strategies should outline specific goals, milestones, and actions needed to 
advance AI in various sectors such as healthcare, education, and disaster 
management, and should build on comprehensive AI diagnostics for each 
country.
• Enhance AI Governance:  
Facilitate the enhancement of AI governance across the Pacific Islands by 
continuously supporting member states to establish adequate regulatory 
frameworks, ethical guidelines, and policies to manage AI development 
and utilization responsibly and sustainably.
• Establish a Pacific Island AI Technical Assistance Facility:  
Undertake the scoping, establishment, and funding of a dedicated facility 
aimed at providing technical and financial support for member-state 
initiatives. This facility will play a pivotal role in facilitating the development 
and implementation of country-focussed AI strategies, offering specialized 
expertise, and helping to tackle emerging AI challenges through capacity-
building programs and resource allocation.
2. Strengthening AI Regulatory Frameworks for the Pacific Islands
• Develop comprehensive and harmonized legislation addressing data 
privacy, consumer protection, and cybercrime to create a robust regulatory 
framework for AI.
• Encourage Pacific Island nations to collaborate on regulatory 
standards, ensuring consistency and facilitating seamless AI  
adoption across the region.
3. Raising Digital Literacy and Awareness
• Develop tailored AI curricula for schools and universities, train educators, 
and create online learning platforms to make AI education accessible, 
especially in remote areas.
• Conduct needs assessments with local stakeholders, promote  
public-private partnerships, and implement pilot projects to develop  
and showcase AI solutions addressing unique local issues like climate 
change and healthcare.• Create Comprehensive AI Development Guidance:

4. Strengthening International and Regional Cooperation
• Foster collaboration with key entities such as ASEAN, and international

UNESCO, and UNDP to deepen ICT and AI partnerships and enhance 
mutual support.
• Cultivate regional ICT and AI cooperation among Pacific Islands by

• Improve interoperability and efficiency of AI-related projects by

are reflective of their unique needs, values, and aspirations, fostering a 
sense of ownership and inclusivity in AI development and deployment.
Annexes
Regional and Country AI Profiles39The Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) is the major Pacific Island intergovernmental 
organization established in 1971, comprising 18 member countries and 
territories from the Pacific region, including Australia, New Zealand, and 
16 Pacific Island nations. Headquartered in Suva, Fiji, the Forum serves as a 
platform for member states to collaborate on regional issues, enhancing 
political and economic cooperation, and fostering collective action. 
PIF’s primary objective is to promote regional stability and prosperity by 
addressing the unique challenges faced by the Pacific islands, including  
their geographical isolation, vulnerability to natural disasters,  
and economic dependencies.
One of the core focuses of the Pacific Islands Forum is sustainable  
development, with a significant emphasis on combating climate change, 
which poses an existential threat to many low-lying island nations. The Forum 
advocates for strong international climate action and supports local adaptation 
and mitigation strategies. Economic development is another critical area, 
where PIF works to enhance trade, investment, and infrastructure development 
through initiatives like the Pacific Agreement on Closer Economic Relations 
(PACER) Plus. These efforts aim to create a more integrated and resilient 
regional economy that can withstand global economic fluctuations.
The Pacific Islands Forum also plays a crucial role in regional security,  
promoting cooperation on maritime security, transnational crime, and 
disaster response. Through frameworks like the Biketawa Declaration, PIF  
has established mechanisms for regional crisis management and peace 
keeping. The Forum engages with international partners and organizations 
to represent the collective interests of its member states on the global stage, 
ensuring that the Pacific voice is heard in global policy dialogues. By fostering 
a spirit of solidarity and shared purpose, the Pacific Islands Forum continues 
to be a vital institution for the advancement of peace, stability, and sustainable 
development in the Pacific region.
Through the Pacific Islands Forum, the Pacific Island Leaders in 2022 
launched the 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent50, an ambitious 
framework designed to guide the collective vision and development priorities 
of the Pacific Islands region over the next three decades. This strategy 
emphasizes the importance of regional solidarity, resilience, and sustainable 
development in addressing the unique challenges faced by Pacific nations. 
Central to the strategy are goals related to climate action, economic growth, 
and environmental stewardship, recognizing the critical importance  
of the ocean and its resources to the livelihoods and cultural heritage  
of Pacific peoples. 
In particular, the 2050 Strategy, under the Thematic Area on Technology 
and Connectivity, calls for: “... a well-connected region that ensures inclusive, 
affordable and accessible air, sea and land transport and ICT technology 
infrastructure and services. Technology and infrastructure is often unaffordable, 
inaccessible, and difficult to maintain. 1. Overview of Regional Initiatives40The adoption of new and emerging sustainable digital technologies requires 
effective partnerships and appropriate regional regulatory arrangements that 
respect the region’s shared values.’’ 
In September 2023, the PIF and ASEAN signed a Memorandum of  
Understanding (MoU) to pave the way for potential cooperation between 
ASEAN and PIF in areas of common interest51. Given the common characteristics 
of selected ASEAN and Pacific Island nations, the general areas outlined in 
the MOU include many that would benefit greatly from consideration of AI 
elements. 
In January 2024, the United States Agency for International Development 
(USAID) initiated the Digital Connectivity and Cybersecurity Partnership (DCCP) 
- Pacific project to bolster internet connectivity in Pacific Island Countries. 
Collaborating with partners such as the Asia Open RAN Academy and USAID 
Indo-Pacific Opportunity Project, the initiative aims to equip the region with a 
skilled workforce and leverage Open RAN technology. This collaborative effort 
seeks to develop a curriculum for regional universities, enhance workforce 
capacity, and support the deployment of Open RAN technology. By enabling 
multiple telecommunications providers to collaborate, this technology extends 
seamless connectivity to areas lacking traditional infrastructure, thereby 
expanding secure digital coverage across the Blue Pacific Continent. With an 
equipped workforce, the initiative aims to extend connectivity to remote and 
low-populated areas, fostering job creation for Pacific Islanders and facilitating 
access to newer services like 5G at competitive rates52.
The Pacific Digital Economy Programme (PDEP) is a collaborative effort 
between the United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF), United 
Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and the United Nations Conference 
on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), aimed at fostering inclusive digital 
economies in the Pacific. Supported by administrative assistance from UNDP, 
PDEP leverages UNCDF’s expertise in digital finance and UNCTAD’s work in 
e-commerce. It operates region-wide research and capacity-building activities 
while providing tailored technical assistance to specific countries. PDEP closely 
collaborates with the Pacific Island Forum Secretariat and various stakeholders 
to create a conducive environment for digital innovation. Funded by the 
Government of Australia and the European Union, the program runs from 2021 
to 2025, contributing to the region’s digital advancement53.
In the midterm review of the program in November 2022, it was found that the 
program proved highly relevant in supporting and fostering an inclusive digital 
economy in the selected countries. Stakeholders noted positive spillover effects 
from the Fintech challenge, leading to increased awareness, knowledge, and 
network expansion. The program’s efficiency was commendable, although 
some bureaucratic processes were deemed time-consuming. Stakeholders 
appreciated the local presence of the program staff in various countries. While 
the program is on track to deliver stakeholder-level outcomes, there’s a need to 
re-evaluate overly ambitious client-level targets. Coherence between various 
activities could be improved, and sustainability efforts should focus on nurturing 
progress and building local capacity. Suggestions were made to enhance 
coherence, effectiveness,and sustainability through strategic partnerships and  
capacity-building initiatives54.41The Smart Villages and Smart Islands initiative in Vanuatu, launched in 
2020, aims to bridge the digital gap in rural areas like Malekula. Led by the 
International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and supported by the Vanuatu 
government and partners, it’s making strides in connectivity, digital skills, and 
tailored services. In 2022, highlights include forming taskforces, enhancing 
solar-powered connectivity, and securing additional funding. Looking forward, 
the focus is on expanding digital literacy training. Positive impacts are already 
visible, such as improved online education access and local businesses using 
digital skills for marketing55.

Australia has no legislation specifically designed to regulate the use of AI. 
Yet, there are existing regulations that have the potential to intersect with 
the AI ecosystem outlining fundamental requirements for AI. These include 
the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth), financial and banking regulations and laws, 
and anti-discrimination Acts’AC (both enacted and upheld by the federal and 
state governments). But most importantly, the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) details 
protections for individuals as it relates to collection, use, disclosure and right 
to access personal information, through regulating government and large 
organizations (those with greater than $3 million AUD p.a turnover). The Act 
Includes 13 privacy principles, covering a variety of dealings with personal 
information, such as cross-border disclosure of personal information and 
disclosure of personal information.

use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) (Discussion Paper). The Discussion Paper, 
informed by the March 2023 Rapid Response Information Report, focused 
on potential legal and practical mechanisms to support the responsible 
development and deployment of AI in Australia.2. Australia43On 17 January 2024, the Australian Government released its interim response

their dedication to embracing digital transformation. This commitment took 
shape during their participation in the Pacific Digital Champions training 
program from 15th-16th August, facilitated by the Pacific Tourism Organisation 
(SPTO) with funding from New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade118.17. Tonga
62Tuvalu’s 2021-2030 National Strategy for Sustainable Development, “Te Kete,” 
prioritizes digital transformation as one of its foremost national outcomes to 
enhance societal well-being. This ambition is manifested through strategic 
initiatives aimed at securing access to cost-effective and dependable 
telecommunication services, promoting e-learning, establishing a secure 
digital space via cybersecurity measures, and crafting a comprehensive legal, 
regulatory, and standards framework to steer digital technology investments 
and applications119.
Tuvalu has no country-specific governing laws around Privacy and Data 
Protection. However, indirect legislations cover the area. For instance, the 
Tuvalu Telecommunications Corporation Act in Section 33 specifies offences 
related to telecommunications, including the modification, interception, and 
unauthorized disclosure of messages120.
In August 2023, the Tuvalu Department of Tourism and its stakeholders 
embraced the opportunity to progress digital transformation, through the 
Pacific Tourism Organisations (SPTO) Pacific Digital Champions training 
program. Funded by the New Zealand Government through its Ministry of 
Foreign Affairs and Trade, the training program is part of the “Pacific Digital 
Tourism Transformation Project” being implemented by SPTO121.
Facing the existential threat of rising sea levels, Tuvalu initiated the Future Now 
Project to preserve its nationhood, governance, and culture through digital 
transformation. The purpose of this initiative is to ensure the continuity of 
state functions and cultural identity, even if the population becomes globally 
dispersed. The project features the creation of a digital twin of Tuvalu, starting 
with the island of Te Afualiku, to capture its physical and cultural landscape. 
Utilising augmented and virtual reality, this project is expected to enable 
future generations of Tuvaluans to interact and maintain their culture in a 
digital realm122.18. Tuvalu6319. Vanuatu
“Vanuatu’s E-Commerce Strategy and Roadmap”, launched by the Ministry 
of Tourism, Trade, Commerce, and Ni-Vanuatu Business, aims to transform 
Vanuatu into a digital-friendly economy by 2026. The strategy focuses on 
improving digital infrastructure, legal frameworks, payment systems, and 
digital skills. The objective of the strategy is the enhancement of trade and 
business growth through e-commerce123.
Vanuatu is actively working towards establishing a data protection law with 
support from the Council of Europe. This effort aims to safeguard personal 
information and enhance digital trust in the country. Although draft bills and 
policies including a National Data Protection and Privacy Policy for 2023 have 
been proposed, they have not yet been enacted into law124. 
In 2020, Vanuatu’s government partnered with the International 
Telecommunication Union (ITU to launch the Smart Villages and Smart Islands 
initiative in the southern region of Malekula, where residents lack access to 
basic services such as healthcare, banking, and reliable power and water 
supply.
The initiative aimed to improve connectivity, build digital skills, and provide 
digital services that are cost-effective and suitable for the community’s needs. 
With support from various UN agencies and organizations, the program has 
made progress in providing digital literacy training, reconnecting villagers to 
the internet, and helping local businesses utilize digital tools for marketing. 
The initiative plans to continue expanding its efforts in 2024, with a focus on 
providing more digital literacy training for villagers, especially for young people, 
women, and people with disabilities. The positive impact of the initiative is 
already visible in the community, with students resuming their studies online 
and villagers using the internet for various purposes. The program’s success 
stories demonstrate Vanuatu’s potential to transform into a “Smart Island” 
through digital transformation at the grassroots level125.6420. Climate Change Initiatives in the Pacific Islands 
Country Climate Change Initiatives
Cook Islands • In 2011, the country established the Climate Change Cook Islands Office 
(CCCI) having moved to coordinate climate change actions across 
government, but it soon became apparent that limited human and financial 
resources were restraining the country’s valiant efforts.
• In February 2016, the Cook Islands became the first country in the Pacific 
to receive GCF readiness support. Since 2016, the Cook Islands has received 
three more readiness grants in 2017, 2018, and 2019, totalling USD 1.9 million.
• The target of 100 percent of electricity generation to be from renewable 
energy sources, is a central component of mitigation initiatives in the Cook 
Islands.
Federated States of 
Micronesia• The Federated States of Micronesia joined the Climate and Clean Air 
Coalition (CCAC) in 2021, committing to action to reduce short-lived climate 
pollutants.
• As the original proponent of the amendment to include HFCs 
(hydrofluorocarbons) under the Montreal Protocol, Micronesia has 
committed to accelerating the HFC phasedown under the Kigali 
Amendment domestically and internationally - helping other countries 
with the implementation of the Montreal Protocol. Work underway in 
Micronesia includes a pilot training institute that prepares refrigeration and 
air conditioning technicians to work with new energy efficient and climate- 
friendly technologies. The country is also mobilizing financing under the 
Kigali Amendment to support more ambitious action.
• Following the Strategic Development Plan, Micronesia developed the 
Climate Change Act in 2014 to address and integrate climate change action 
across ministries. The Climate Change and Sustainable Development 
Council were also established in 2017 to implement the Act.
• The Climate Change Act, adopted by the FSM Congress in late November 
2013 implements the recently adopted Nationwide Integrated Disaster Risk 
Management and Climate Change Policy. It instructs government offices 
and departments to prepare plans and policies consistent with the
• Climate Change Policy by October 2015; it also includes an obligation on the 
President to report to Congress on the progress of implementation of the 
Climate Change, and for the budget request to include one or more lines on 
the implementation of the Climate Change Policy.
Fiji • The Fiji Climate Change Act 2021 was approved by parliament on 
September 23, 2021, and came into force shortly after. The act establishes 
a legal framework for the country’s disaster risk management, adaptation, 
and mitigation actions. It also provides a legal basis for Fiji’s sustainable 
development goals, net-zero emissions target, and commitment to 
environmental protection.
• The National Climate Change Policy is a central policy instrument to protect 
Fiji’s development priorities from current, future and intergenerational 
climate change risks. The NCCP articulates national climate adaptation and 
mitigation objectives and strategies.
French Polynesia • Nationally Determined Contribution - The French Overseas Countries and 
Territories commit an economy-wide plan of limiting the increase in GHG 
emissions to 8.4 percent in 2030 compared to 2016 (6959 KtCO2e). French 
Polynesia states a reduction of 3.7 percent compared to 2016.65Country Climate Change Initiatives
Kiribati • Kiribati as part of Kiribati Climate Change Policy has committed to reducing 
emissions by 13.7 percent by 2025 and 12.8 percent by 2030 compared toa 
“business as usual” (BAU) projection. This is part of Kiribati’s Nationally 
Determined Contribution (NDC).
• The Kiribati Adaptation Program (KAP) is a US$5.5 million initiative that was 
originally enacted by the national government of Kiribati with the support of 
the Global Environment Facility (GEF), the World Bank, the United Nations 
Development Program, and the Japanese Government. Australia later joined 
the coalition, donating US$1.5 million to the effort. The program aims to take 
place over 6 years, supporting measures that reduce Kiribati’s vulnerability 
to the effects of climate change and sea level rise by raising awareness of 
climate change, assessing and protecting available water resources, and 
managing inundation.
Marshall Islands • In 2015, RMI became the first Small Island Developing State to present its 
post-2020 Nationally Determined Contribution. This committed the country 
to a 32 percent reduction of GHG emissions by 2025. The following year, RMI 
also committed to achieving 100 percent renewable energy by 2050.
• In October 2022, The Ministry of Health and Human Services (MOHHS) and 
Ministry of Environment Climate Change Directorate (CCD) of the Republic 
of Marshall Islands (RMI) are partnering with the World Health Organization 
(WHO) to tackle the health impacts of climate change and enhance pre- 
paredness for future health emergencies, including the next pandemic.
• With US$ 399,802 in funding support from the Green Climate Fund (GCF), 
the RMI Government and WHO will also focus on boosting the readiness of 
remote and outer islands of the RMI to protect health and save lives during 
future crises.
Nauru• Republic of Nauru’s Framework for Climate Change and Disaster Risk Re -
duction (RONAdapt) - This framework prioritizes water security, energy se- 
curity, food security, a healthy environment, healthy people, and productive, 
secure land resources.
• Nauru’s Nationally determined contribution (NDC) has been updated to 
include eight thematic areas, including “Loss & Damage”. The country’s goal 
is to reach net-zero emissions by 2050.”
New Caledonia • New Caledonia’s energy transition policy aims to make the territory energy 
self-sufficient and reduce greenhouse gases by at least 70 percent by 2035. 
The Energy Transition Scheme of New Caledonia (STENCS) aims to double 
the share of renewable energy by 2030.
Niue • Niue’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) target for 2020 is 38 per- 
cent of its total electricity generation to come from renewable energy. This 
target is unconditional and not dependent on external funding. However, 
there has been no update on the performance or policy since.
Palau • Palau is a signatory to the Global Methane Pledge (GMP), which commits 
the country to the collective goal of reducing global methane emissions by 
at least 30 percent from 2020 levels by 2030.
• Palau has committed to reducing energy sector emissions by 22 percent by 
2025.
• In 2015, adopted the Palau Climate Change Policy: For Climate and Disaster 
Resilient Low Emissions Development. The policy seeks to work towards low 
carbon emission development, maximize energy efficiency, protect carbon 
sinks, and minimize greenhouse gas emissions.66Country Climate Change Initiatives
Papua New Guinea• Papua New Guinea has increased its level of ambition within its second 
NDC by enhancing the specificity of targets within existing sectors, such as 
energy, and adding in targets for the land use, land use change, and forestry 
sector and adaptation.
• The country aims to achieve carbon neutrality in energy industries by 2030.
• The second NDC is in line with Papua New Guinea’s Vision 2050, as well as 
the Climate Compatible Development Management Policy accords. The 
policy outlines the government’s commitment to be 50 percent carbon- 
neutral by 2030 and entirely carbon-neutral by 2050.
• Papua New Guinea, like many tropical countries, through deforestation, is 
contributing to the release of carbon dioxide, the most critical greenhouse 
gas. WCS PNG is working closely with the Papua New Guinea Government 
to develop and trial a national forest protection initiative known as REDD+ 
(Reduced Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation ― the “+” 
refers to the other benefits of forests). Schemes like REDD+ should not only 
slow the release of carbon dioxide but have the potential to provide tangible 
benefits for forest communities.
Samoa • Samoa’s second Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) aims to reduce 
greenhouse gas emissions by 26 percent by 2030 compared to 2007 
levels, or by 91 Gg CO2e compared to the new reference year. The NDC also 
includes a target to generate 100 percent of electricity from renewable 
energy by 2025.
• Instituted a Samoa Climate Change Policy 2020-2030. This document aims 
at enabling a resilient, safe and prosperous medium-term future for Samoa, 
while meeting the sustainable development goals.
Solomon Islands • The Solomon Islands’ Intended Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 
is a national policy that aims to reduce emissions by 27 percent by 2025 and 
45 percent by 2030, compared to a business-as-usual projection (BaU). The 
NDC also includes a commitment to achieve net zero emissions by 2050.
• Instituted the Solomon Islands National Climate Change Policy (NCCP) 2023- 
2032 and Long Term Low Emission Development Strategy (LT- LEDS). The 
NCCP 2023-2032 allows the Solomon Islands to address climate change, loss, 
and damage (L&D). The policy also aims to strengthen low emission status, 
economic growth, and development.
• Climate and Oceans Support Program in the Pacific Phase 3 (COSPPac3) 
- A 2023–2029 program that supports the Solomon Islands National 
Meteorological Service to provide climate and ocean monitoring and 
prediction services.
• An important contribution at the regional and community level is the Pacific 
Adaptation to Climate Change Project (PACC). The project is designed to 
promote climate change adaptation, and is based on the premise that 
adaptation is a key pre-requisite to sustainable development in Pacific Island 
Countries.67Country Climate Change Initiatives
Tonga • Tonga’s second Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) focuses 
on adapting to climate change, including rising sea levels and higher 
temperatures. The plan includes:
• 2025: 30 percent of the country’s land used for forestry or agro-forestry
• Marine species: Expand the area covered by Marine Protected Areas 
and Special Management Areas to 30 percent of the country’s Exclusive 
Economic Zone
• Greenhouse gas emissions: 13 percent reduction in emissions by 2030 
compared to 2006, through a transition to 70 percent renewable electricity
• Tree planting: Plant one million trees by 2023
• The plan also aims to attract financial support from donors and private 
investors. The projects identified in the plan could reduce greenhouse 
gas emissions by over a million tCO2 by 2030, which would represent a 61 
percent reduction from 2006 levels.
• Instituted the 2035 Climate Change Policy - This policy aims to build 
resilience by redesigning policy to improve people’s ability to respond to the 
effects of climate change.
Tuvalu • In 2022, Tuvalu updated its nationally determined contribution (NDC) to 
climate change, focusing on mitigation and a zero-carbon development 
pathway by 2050. The updated NDC includes the following commitments:
• Reduce greenhouse gas emissions: 100 percent reduction in greenhouse 
gas emissions from the electricity sector by 2030, or almost zero emissions
• Increase energy efficiency: 30 percent increase in energy efficiency in 
Funafuti
• Reduce total GHG emissions: 60 percent reduction in total GHG emissions 
from the entire energy sector by 2030, compared to 2010 levels
• Instituted the National Climate Change Policy 2021-2030; This policy 
considers issues like vulnerability, disaster preparedness, and migration and 
relocation needs.
Vanuatu • NDC: Vanuatu will become 100 percent renewable by 2030, replacing nearly 
all fossil fuel requirements. This will reduce emissions in the energy sector by 
72Gg by 2030.
• In 2022, Vanuatu declared a climate emergency as part of a “climate 
diplomacy push”. The declaration was made ahead of a UN vote on the 
government’s application to have the International Court of Justice protect 
vulnerable nations from climate change.
• The Vanuatu Klaement Infomesen blong Redy, Adapt mo Protekt (Van- 
KIRAP) project is a five-year, USD 22 million project which aims to support 
climate resilient development in Vanuatu through the development, 
communication, and application of climate information services to benefit 
agriculture, fisheries, tourism etc.
