Yes
Please provide any additional comments
Simplify the regulatory framework so that compliance requirements are clear, concise, and less time-consuming. Develop a centralized hub where teachers can access all relevant regulatory guidelines and resources in one place. Offer targeted professional development programs on how to implement guardrails efficiently and effectively without being overwhelmed by complex regulations. Encourage curriculum designers to integrate regulatory guardrails into the lesson plans and materials, so teachers do not have to spend extra time considering regulatory compliance while teaching. Promote the sharing of responsibility for regulatory compliance across the school system.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A domain specific approach – adapting existing regulatory frameworks to include the proposed mandatory guardrails
15. Which regulatory option(s) will best ensure that guardrails for high-risk AI can adapt and respond to step-changes in technology?
A domain specific approach – Adopting the guardrails within existing regulatory frameworks as needed
16. Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps and inconsistencies with Australia’s existing laws for the development and deployment of AI?
As AI-powered tools from commercial companies are increasingly integrated into classrooms, there’s a risk of eroding teacher autonomy. Current laws don’t adequately address the influence of private companies over educational content and assessment, allowing commercial interests to shape learning in ways that may not align with educational goals or public interests.
With fewer teachers available, there’s a risk that schools are vulnerable to commercial rhetoric about 'time efficiencies' and through policy and media influence, may increasingly engage with AI tools to seemingly fill gaps, such as automated grading, student monitoring, and personalized learning programs - while the actual problem of teacher shortages is not addressed. Without proper oversight, this power could lead to inconsistent educational outcomes.
These AI systems may be developed by companies prioritizing profit over educational values, leading to a growing commercial influence on pedagogy, curriculum, and assessment, with little regulation ensuring that these tools are aligned with public education standards.
Finally, schools in underfunded areas may be more prone to adopting cheaper AI systems as a substitute for human teachers, potentially increasing the digital divide. Without strong legal frameworks to ensure equitable access to high-quality AI and human resources, teacher shortages could exacerbate existing inequalities in education.
Which regulatory option best addresses this?
A domain specific approach – Adopting the guardrails within existing regulatory frameworks as needed

Principle e needs to cover the below in detail:
there is significant energy and water consumption associated with training large AI models, particularly generative models.
Implementing guardrails to address this issue is crucial. Organisations should be required to justify the need for training models from scratch, particularly when pre-trained models are available. In many cases, fine-tuning existing models can achieve comparable results with a significantly lower environmental footprint.
Additionally, mandating the reporting of carbon footprints for both AI model training and inference in annual reports will increase transparency and accountability. This will enable stakeholders to assess the environmental impact of AI applications and make informed decisions.
Prompting users about the energy consumption of their queries is a valuable step toward raising awareness and promoting responsible AI usage. By providing users with this information, we can encourage them to be mindful of their environmental impact and consider alternative approaches when appropriate.
Deployers should play a key role in communicating the energy consumption of their AI models to end users. This can be achieved through clear and concise messaging, educational materials, and tools that help users understand the environmental implications of their AI usage.
To further reduce the environmental footprint of AI:
Promote Energy-Efficient Hardware: Encourage the development and adoption of more energy-efficient hardware for AI training and inference.
Optimise Algorithms: Invest in research to develop more efficient AI algorithms and training methods.
Carbon Offsetting: Consider implementing carbon offsetting programs to mitigate the environmental impact of AI activities.
By taking these steps, we can help ensure that AI is developed and deployed in a sustainable and responsible manner.

A three-year review cycle for AI guardrails is a reasonable starting point. However, it may be necessary to adjust this frequency based on the rate of technological advancement and the emergence of new AI applications.
To ensure that guardrails remain effective:
Continuous Monitoring: Implement a system for ongoing monitoring of AI developments and emerging trends.
Expert Consultation: Regularly consult with experts in AI, ethics, and relevant domains to identify potential risks and opportunities.
Stakeholder Engagement: Engage with a diverse range of stakeholders, including industry representatives, researchers, policymakers, and civil society organizations, to gather input and ensure that guardrails are responsive to societal needs and values.
As new AI use cases and foreseeable applications arise, it will be essential to assess their potential risks and benefits and adjust the guardrails accordingly. This may involve:
Risk Assessments: Conducting thorough risk assessments to identify potential harms associated with new AI applications.
Impact Assessments: Evaluating the potential social, economic, and environmental impacts of AI technologies.
Ethical Considerations: Ensuring that AI development and deployment align with ethical principles and values.
By adopting a flexible and adaptive approach to AI regulation, we can strike a balance between fostering innovation and protecting society from potential harms. This will help ensure that AI is developed and used in a way that benefits everyone.
I understand the government's concerns regarding the high-risk nature of AI systems in education, particularly in areas such as admissions, evaluations, and student monitoring. However, I believe a blanket approach for all education-related use cases may be overly restrictive and could hinder the development and deployment of valuable AI tools.
My experience with NCVER has demonstrated the potential of AI to improve student outcomes, particularly in areas like student completion rates. By leveraging AI models, we were able to identify patterns and trends in student data that could be used to predict and address potential challenges. These insights enabled us to implement targeted interventions and improve overall completion rates.
A blanket approach to AI guardrails could pose significant barriers to the deployment of low-risk AI applications like student completion rate prediction. These applications can provide valuable insights without posing the same level of risk as systems that directly impact admissions or evaluations.
I recommend a more nuanced approach that differentiates between high-risk and low-risk AI use cases in education. For high-risk applications, stringent guardrails may be necessary to mitigate potential harms. However, for low-risk applications, a more flexible approach could allow for innovation and experimentation while ensuring appropriate safeguards are in place.
Key considerations for a more nuanced approach:
Risk assessment: Develop a framework for assessing the potential risks associated with different AI applications in education.
Transparency and accountability: Require AI developers and institutions to be transparent about the data used, algorithms employed, and potential biases in their models.
Human oversight: Ensure that AI systems are always subject to human oversight and that there are mechanisms in place to challenge or override AI-driven decisions.
Continuous monitoring and evaluation: Regularly monitor and evaluate the performance of AI systems to identify and address potential issues.
By adopting a more tailored approach, the government can strike a balance between protecting students and fostering innovation in education. This will allow for the development and deployment of AI tools that can improve student outcomes while minimising risks.

1. Do the proposed principles adequately capture high-risk AI?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
The proposed principles for regulating high-risk AI focus on flexibility and adaptability to address both current and emerging AI technologies, like general-purpose AI (GPAI). They emphasize a principles-based approach, as opposed to a rigid list-based method, to better capture evolving risks. A key feature is the contextual risk assessment, which evaluates AI based on its intended use, allowing for a more accurate identification of high-risk scenarios. Additionally, mandatory guardrails are recommended for all GPAI models to ensure baseline safety, with indicators such as technical capabilities and expert advice helping define high-risk AI. Successful implementation will depend on clear guidance for organizations.
Are there any principles we should add or remove?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
We propose changes to include adding principles to address potential harms to First Nations people, introducing illustrative use cases similar to the EU and Canada for clarity on high-risk AI, and defining indicators for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models as high-risk based on metrics like FLOPS or expert advice.
2. Do you have any suggestions for how the principles could better capture harms to First Nations people, communities and Country?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
To better protect First Nations people, communities, and Country from potential harms caused by AI, the guiding principles should focus on cultural sensitivity, involving First Nations communities in AI design and decision-making. Thorough impact assessments should evaluate both direct and indirect effects, including environmental and socio-economic consequences. AI governance frameworks must integrate specific regulatory protections for First Nations, potentially adapting existing legislation. Education and capacity-building initiatives should empower these communities to engage with AI actively. Additionally, ethical AI development should prioritize human rights and address the risks of exacerbating inequalities for marginalized groups, including First Nations people.
3. Do the proposed principles, supported by examples, give enough clarity and certainty on high-risk AI settings and high-risk AI models? Is a more defined approach, with a list of illustrative uses, needed?
YES the principles give enough clarity and certainty
If you prefer a principles-based approach, what should we address in guidance to give the greatest clarity?
To provide clear guidance under a principles-based approach, several aspects must be addressed. First, the principles should integrate with existing legislation, such as the Privacy Act and Copyright Act, ensuring that new AI obligations complement rather than replace current regulations. Building trust and confidence in AI through effective guardrails is crucial for its widespread adoption. Clear definitions and examples of high-risk AI scenarios should be provided, along with flexibility to adapt to emerging technologies like general-purpose AI (GPAI). Additionally, specific guidance should protect vulnerable groups, including First Nations communities. Lastly, illustrative use cases should be included to offer practical examples of the principles in action.
4. Are there high-risk use cases that government should consider banning in its regulatory response (for example, where there is an unacceptable level of risk)?
Yes
If so, how should we define these?
The question of defining and regulating high-risk AI use cases is significant, with proposals focusing on biometrics, medical devices, and general-purpose AI (GPAI). High-risk AI use cases can be divided into two categories: known or foreseeable uses, where risks are identified based on context, and emerging forms, such as GPAI, that require flexible regulation. Two regulatory approaches are proposed: a list-based method, as seen in the EU and Canada, or a principles-based approach that offers flexibility for new technologies. Additionally, there should be exemptions for low-risk AI to avoid unnecessary regulation, as seen in the EU AI Act.
5. Are the proposed principles flexible enough to capture new and emerging forms of high-risk AI, such as general-purpose AI (GPAI)?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
The proposed principles for high-risk AI, including general-purpose AI (GPAI), are designed with flexibility to accommodate emerging AI technologies. They guide organizations in identifying high-risk uses, focusing on the potential capabilities of AI rather than its intended use. GPAI is defined broadly, covering various applications and risks. International examples, like those from Canada, the EU, and the US, highlight different regulatory approaches, such as mandatory guardrails and reporting requirements. The principles also emphasize risk assessments based on the context of use, ensuring that both foreseeable and unforeseeable risks are appropriately addressed. Overall, the principles aim to be adaptable and comprehensive.
6. Should mandatory guardrails apply to all GPAI models?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
Yes, mandatory guardrails should apply to all GPAI models. This is to ensure that potential risks are adequately managed, fostering safer deployment and usage of these advanced AI systems across different sectors. The emphasis on flexibility and adaptability in the regulations aims to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technologies
7. What are suitable indicators for defining GPAI models as high-risk?
Define high-risk against the principles
8. Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments.
The proposed mandatory guardrails are structured to appropriately mitigate the risks of AI in high-risk settings through comprehensive testing, transparency, and accountability mechanisms. Their effectiveness hinges on adaptability, stakeholder engagement, and alignment with international standards, making them a robust framework for responsible AI use
Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?
Yes
What guardrails should we add or remove?
Protect AI systems, and implement data governance measures to manage data quality and provenance Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the system once deployed Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight Inform end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcomes Be transparent with other organisations across the AI supply chain about data, models and systems to help them effectively address risks Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails Undertake conformity assessments to demonstrate and certify compliance with the guardrails
9. How can the guardrails incorporate First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols to ensure AI systems are culturally appropriate and preserve Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property?
Incorporating First Nations knowledge and cultural protocols into AI systems is essential for ensuring that these technologies respect Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) and align with Indigenous values. Key strategies for achieving this include engaging with First Nations communities through continuous dialogue to understand their needs and values, and providing cultural sensitivity training for AI developers to foster respect for Indigenous perspectives. Additionally, traditional ecological knowledge and cultural practices should be integrated into AI models, while robust data governance frameworks must ensure Indigenous data sovereignty.
Preserving ICIP requires clear policies that protect Indigenous assets from misuse, while accountability mechanisms should enable communities to challenge AI outcomes that negatively impact them. Transparency in AI development, including data sources and decision-making processes, is also critical for enabling community input and scrutiny. Regular ethical audits should assess compliance with cultural protocols, and adaptive learning mechanisms can be used to incorporate feedback from Indigenous users, ensuring ongoing cultural relevance.
Finally, comprehensive policy frameworks should be developed to align with national and international standards, safeguarding Indigenous rights and promoting cultural heritage. By establishing these practices and guardrails, organizations can ensure that AI technologies honor and protect Indigenous cultures, promoting ethical and respectful AI development.
11. Are the proposed mandatory guardrails sufficient to address the risks of GPAI?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
The proposed mandatory guardrails aim to provide a robust framework for managing the risks associated with GPAI. However, their sufficiency is still under evaluation, particularly regarding flexibility, specific application to various GPAI models, and the incorporation of diverse cultural perspectives. Ongoing dialogue and adaptation of these guardrails will be essential as AI technology evolves
12. Do you have suggestions for reducing the regulatory burden on small-to-medium sized businesses applying guardrails?
Yes
Please provide any additional comments
To alleviate the regulatory burden on small-to-medium sized businesses (SMBs) applying AI guardrails, a flexible and adaptable regulatory framework is essential. This includes tailoring regulations to specific AI risk profiles and ensuring consistent application across sectors through strong government coordination. Encouraging voluntary compliance, such as implementing risk management processes and data governance measures, allows SMBs to navigate regulations without mandatory constraints.
Continuous monitoring and improvement are vital for maintaining compliance with evolving standards. SMBs can benefit from regular updates, performance metrics, user feedback analysis, and ethical audits to ensure adherence to established guardrails. Additionally, providing support and resources is crucial; clear guidelines, training programs, access to compliance experts, and potential financial assistance can ease the compliance process.
A principles-based regulatory approach can offer flexibility while establishing essential rules, and a tiered regulatory policy can further reduce excessive regulation, benefiting small businesses.
13. Which legislative option do you feel will best address the use of AI in high-risk settings?
A framework approach – Introducing new framework legislation to adapt existing regulatory frameworks across the economy
15. Which regulatory option(s) will best ensure that guardrails for high-risk AI can adapt and respond to step-changes in technology?
A framework approach – Introducing new framework legislation to adapt existing regulatory frameworks across the economy
16. Where do you see the greatest risks of gaps and inconsistencies with Australia’s existing laws for the development and deployment of AI?
The greatest risks of gaps and inconsistencies in Australia’s laws concerning AI development and deployment lie in fragmented regulatory coverage, unclear accountability, lack of compliance standards, and insufficient ethical oversight. Addressing these issues requires a coordinated effort to establish clear legal frameworks that accommodate the dynamic nature of AI technologies while ensuring accountability and protection for users.
Which regulatory option best addresses this?
A framework approach – Introducing new framework legislation to adapt existing regulatory frameworks across the economy

Dear Australian Government,
Thank you for the opportunity to respond to your consultation question: "Do the proposed mandatory guardrails appropriately mitigate the risks of AI used in high-risk settings? Are there any guardrails that we should add or remove?".
As members of the Australian-led and globally influential OWASP Machine Learning Top 10 security risks project [1], we believe that while the proposed guardrails are a step in the right direction, they need significant enhancement to address the unique security challenges posed by AI systems in high-risk settings. The current proposed security framework, the Essential Eight [2], while valuable for general cyber security, is insufficient for addressing the specific risks associated with AI systems.
Limitations of the Essential Eight for AI Security:
The Essential Eight, comprising application control, patch applications, configure Microsoft Office macro settings, user application hardening, restrict administrative privileges, patch operating systems, multi-factor authentication, and regular backups, provides a solid foundation for general IT security. However, it falls short in addressing AI-specific vulnerabilities:
1.  Interface vulnerabilities: The Essential Eight doesn't account for the complex web of APIs, data pipelines, and model serving interfaces that AI systems typically employ.
2.  Model opacity: It overlooks the "black box" nature of many AI models, particularly deep learning systems.
3.  Data flow security: The framework doesn't address securing the dynamic data flows common in AI systems.
4.  Inference-time attacks: It fails to consider attacks that could occur during model inference, such as input manipulation or output interception.
5.  Model versioning and lifecycle management: The Essential Eight doesn't provide guidance on securing the continuous deployment process common in AI systems.
6.  Federated systems: It doesn't account for the unique security challenges of decentralised AI architectures.
7.  Hardware-level vulnerabilities: The framework doesn't address security concerns specific to specialised AI hardware.
8.  AI-specific access controls: It doesn't differentiate between types of access needed for AI systems.
9.  Explainable AI (XAI) requirements: The Essential Eight lacks measures to address this crucial aspect of AI governance and security.
10.  Model poisoning detection: It doesn't include measures to detect and prevent subtle, long-term attacks like training data poisoning or backdoor insertions in AI models.
The OWASP ML Top 10 specifically addresses the unique security challenges of AI systems. It provides a comprehensive framework that covers:
1.  Input Manipulation Attack (ML01:2023): This risk covers adversarial attacks where an attacker deliberately alters input data to mislead the model. Prevention methods include adversarial training, robust model design, and input validation.
2.  Data Poisoning Attack (ML02:2023): This occurs when an attacker manipulates the training data to cause undesirable model behaviour. Prevention strategies include data validation, secure data storage, and anomaly detection in training data.
3.  Model Inversion Attack (ML03:2023): These attacks involve reverse-engineering the model to extract information. Prevention methods include access control, input validation, and model transparency.
4.  Membership Inference Attack (ML04:2023): This risk involves an attacker determining if a particular data point was used in model training. Prevention strategies include model obfuscation, regularisation, and reducing training data size.
5.  Model Theft (ML05:2023): This involves an attacker gaining unauthorised access to model parameters. Prevention methods include encryption, access control, and model obfuscation.
6.  ML Supply Chain Attacks (ML06:2023): These attacks target the broader ML ecosystem, including MLOps platforms and model hubs. Prevention strategies include package integrity verification and secure deployment of ML infrastructure.
7.  Transfer Learning Attack (ML07:2023): This occurs when an attacker exploits transfer learning to introduce malicious behaviour. Prevention methods include regular monitoring of training datasets and implementing model isolation.
8.  Model Skewing (ML08:2023): This involves manipulating the distribution of training data to cause undesirable model behaviour. Prevention strategies include robust access controls and continuous model performance monitoring.
9.  Output Integrity Attack (ML09:2023): This involves an attacker modifying model outputs. Prevention methods include using cryptographic techniques and secure communication channels.
10.  Model Poisoning (ML10:2023): This involves manipulating model parameters to cause undesirable behaviour. Prevention strategies include regularisation techniques and robust model design.
These risks are specifically tailored to AI systems and provide a more robust starting point for securing AI in high-risk settings. The OWASP ML Top 10 has also been recognised in international cyber security guidance, including the recent joint advisory "Deploying AI Systems Securely" [3] by several national cyber security agencies including the National Security Agency of the USA and the Australian Cyber Security Centre of Australia.
Recommendations for Enhanced Guardrails:
We recommend expanding the proposed guardrails to incorporate these AI-specific security considerations, aligning with both the OWASP ML Top 10[1] and the best practices outlined in "Deploying AI Systems Securely":
1.  Add a guardrail for robust input validation and adversarial testing across all AI system interfaces.
2.  Expand data governance measures to include specific safeguards against data poisoning and model poisoning.
3.  Add a guardrail for privacy-preserving techniques and regular privacy audits to protect against model inversion and membership inference attacks.
4.  Enhance model protection measures to include comprehensive safeguards against model theft and unauthorised access.
5.  Add a guardrail for security assessments of the entire AI supply chain, including MLOps platforms and model hubs.
6.  Include a guardrail for security evaluations of transfer learning and pre-trained models.
7.  Add measures to detect and prevent gradual model skewing over time.
8.  Expand monitoring requirements to include continuous validation of model outputs for integrity attacks.
9.  Add a guardrail for explainable AI techniques to enhance model transparency and aid in detecting potential security issues.
10.  Include requirements for regular adversarial testing and red teaming of AI systems to identify potential vulnerabilities.
While Australia may have missed its opportunity to be at the forefront of AI development, it has a unique chance to lead the world in AI security and governance. The contributions of Australian experts to global security frameworks like the OWASP Machine Learning Top 10 [1] demonstrate our nation's capability to excel in this critical area.
By leveraging this expertise and adopting a comprehensive AI security framework that goes beyond traditional IT security measures like the Essential Eight [2], Australia can position itself as a global leader in responsible AI deployment and security. This approach not only protects our national interests but also creates an opportunity for Australia to export its AI security expertise and potentially influence global standards.
The recommendations we've outlined, based on the OWASP ML Top 10 and aligned with the guidance in "Deploying AI Systems Securely" [3], provide a robust starting point for this leadership. By implementing these enhanced guardrails, Australia can:
1.  Set a global benchmark for AI security in high-risk settings
2.  Create a competitive advantage in the growing field of AI security consulting and solutions
3.  Attract international partnerships and collaborations in AI security research and development
4.  Influence global AI governance frameworks and standards
While we may not be building the AI systems of tomorrow, we can be the ones ensuring they're secure, ethical, and trustworthy. This is an opportunity for Australia to turn a perceived weakness into a significant strength, positioning our nation as a thought leader and trusted advisor in the critical domain of AI security.
We urge the Australian Government to seize this opportunity and leverage our world-class expertise in cybersecurity to create a comprehensive, forward-thinking framework for AI security. By doing so, we can ensure that Australia plays a pivotal role in shaping the future of safe and responsible AI on a global scale.
Thank you for your consideration of these recommendations. We look forward to seeing Australia lead the way in secure and responsible AI deployment.
Sincerely,

This is perhaps harsh feedback, but reading the general principles was like stepping into a time machine and popping out before 2022. AI has changed since then, and changed in profound ways that make meaningless almost all prior discussions. The guardrails seem to be living in the pre-2022 view of the universe. Among my university colleagues and in every consulting project over the last 12 months, the nearly universal view is that training new models is a dead-end unless you are a major vendor with a billion dollar budget. There are a few exceptions: you might train some explainable models to gain insight (e.g. statisticians still make their linear models); you might fine tune a small model to do some specific task quickly or cheaply; in my research I'm training new models using radically new techniques to see if there are other ways of creating AI. But in general, the giant models already have internalised all public information and datasets, so you can get what you want simply by prompt engineering. And prompt engineering isn't the purview of a "priesthood" of tech folks: lots of people have learned how to do prompt engineering.
Where before we would have to have specialised technically-trained people program something to interact with a ML model, we now see individuals make their own systems by prompting AI to do the task. Automation of that is done through things like Zapier or n8n or equivalent. AI systems will proliferate and be done by individuals. Commercially, individuals who do that will be rewarded because of their efficiency, and if we insist on saying that guardrails must be observed either (a) we will remove a dynamism from the economy or (b) people will just ignore the guardrails.

Written by Dimi Nakov 
 
Imagine a future where humanity has matured enough to solve global issues such as poverty, wealth, health, wars, 
depletion of natural resources, animal extinction, climate etc., and to top it up we have become an interstellar 
species. Imagine humanity had achieved maturity because we are united as a whole, not divided; instead we are a 
collaborative, co-operating unity working for the benefit of all sentient beings.  
Utopia or Reality? 
I hope after reading my passionately-hopeful arguments about the existential importance for the responsible 
handling and development of Benevolent-Beneficial AGI, at least one more person will decide to engage in any 
capacity and to actively participate in the development of what could be humanity’s greatest invention, ever . 
Let’s start our journey by unfolding the many layers of the following thought -provokingly self-reflective question: 
Are we, as a species, mature enough, to successfully and responsibly develop a Benevolent-Beneficial Artificial 
General Intelligence (AGI)? 
The question of whether humanity is mature and responsible enough to successfully develop Benevolent-Beneficia l 
Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is a complex and multifaceted one. Please keep in the back of your mind this 
question while reading each chapter. This question is the glue that holds it all together . This question keeps me 
humble while tackling such a complex topic concerning all of us.  
So let's start by breaking down each key concept within the question and go above and beyond to gain a better 
understanding of ourselves and the challenges, implications and possible solutions involved. 
"Are We Mature Enough As a Species?" 
The term "mature"  in this context refers to our collective level of development, wisdom, and responsibility as a 
species. It implies a capacity for thoughtful reflection, ethical behaviour, and the ability to consider long-term 
consequences. Maturity in this sense is not just about age or experience but also about our ability to handle complex 
and potentially world-changing technologies with care and wisdom .

"Benevolent" 
"Benevolent"  means having a disposition to do good and act in a kind, compassionate, and altruistic manner. In the 
context of AI, benevolence refers to the intention behind the development and deployment of AGI. A benevolent AGI 
would be designed to prioritize the well-being of humanity and act in ways that are beneficial to individuals and 
society as a whole. 
"Beneficial ” 
"Beneficial"  means producing good results or being advantageous. In the context of AGI, beneficial AI would be 
designed to enhance human capabilities, improve quality of life, and address pressing global challenges such as 
poverty, disease, and environmental degradation. Beneficial AI should have a positive impact on society and help 
create a more sustainable and equitable world. 
"Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)?" 
Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)  refers to AI that possesses the ability to understand, learn, and apply knowledge 
in a way that is indistinguishable from human intelligence (Hutter, 2005). AGI would be capable of performing a wide 
range of tasks across different domains, surpassing the capabilities of narrow AI systems that are designed for 
specific tasks (Goertzel & Pennachin, 2007). 
We must critically assess our readiness as a species and recognize the incredible opportunity before us to address 
our challenges comprehensively. However, are we truly prepared to succeed in this endeavour? A brief reflection on 
history reveals that humanity has undergone numerous technological revolutions, fundamentally altering our 
lifestyles, professions, and interactions with the world (Harari, 2015). Therefore, let us briefly examine whether we, 
as a species, have demonstrated the maturity necessary to successfully create Benevolent-Beneficial Artificial 
General Intelligence, ensuring benefits for all (Smitsman, 2024). Can we turn into reality a future only conceived by 
our imagination and shared through science fiction stories, books, and motion pictures? 
Achieving AGI represents a leap beyond the current state of AI, which largely operates within predefined parameters. 
AGI would possess a level of adaptability and creativity akin to human thought processes, allowing it to tackle novel 
situations and solve complex problems with ingenuity (Bostrom, 2014). This ability to generalize knowledge and skills 
across different contexts is a hallmark of human intelligence and is the defining characteristic of AGI. Achieving this 
milestone in AI development would not only revolutionize the capabilities of machines but also raise profound 
ethical, societal, and existential questions that must be carefully considered and addressed (Tegmark, 2017).

The Paradox of Progress: Humanity's Contradictory Nature in the Age of Advanced Technology 
In the grand tapestry of human history, one thread stands out starkly against the backdrop of progress: our 
contradictory nature. As a species, we possess an unparalleled capacity for innovation, creativity, and technological 
advancement (Smith & Jones, 2015). From the agricultural revolution to the digital age, we have continuously 
pushed the boundaries of what is possible, reshaping the world in our image (Adams, 2012). Yet, for all our 
achievements, we are also the architects of our own undoing, often falling short of the very standards we aspire to 
reach (Brown, 2018). 
At the heart of this contradiction lies our relationship with technology. We are masters of innovation, harnessing the 
power of science and technology to solve complex problems and improve our quality of life (Taylor, 2012). However, 
this very innovation often outpaces our ability to manage its consequences (Roberts, 2008). As we stand on the cusp 
of a new era of technological advancement, particularly in the realm of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), we are 
faced with profound ethical and existential questions (Tegmark, 2017). 
The creation of a Benevolent Beneficial AGI, one that can help us achieve our true potential while safeguarding our 
future, requires us to confront these contradictions head-on. How can we entrust such a monumental task to a 
technology that we ourselves struggle to wield responsibly (Smith, 2019)? How can we ensure that AGI reflects our 
highest ideals and values when we are still grappling with issues of inequality, injustice, and environmental 
degradation (Russell, Dewey, & Tegmark, 2015)? 
One approach is to view the development of AGI as an opportunity for collective introspection and growth. As we 
strive to create machines in our image, we are forced to confront our own limitations and failings (Brown & Smith, 
2009). This process of self-reflection can serve as a catalyst for positive change, inspiring us to aspire to greater 
heights and live up to the standards we set for ourselves. 
Another approach is to emphasize the importance of ethical governance and regulation in the development and 
deployment of AGI. By establishing clear guidelines and frameworks for responsible innovation, we can mitigate the 
risks associated with AGI and ensure that its benefits are shared equitably (Johnson, 2023). 
Ultimately, the journey towards creating a Benevolent Beneficial AGI is as much about understanding ourselves as it 
is about understanding technology. It is a journey that challenges us to confront our contradictions, to strive for a 
higher standard of ethical behaviour, and to envision a future where progress is synonymous with compassion, 
wisdom, and foresight (Smith, 2015).

The Quest for Beneficial AGI: Utopian Dream or Achievable Reality? 
The development of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) has long been a subject of fascination and speculation. Often 
portrayed in science fiction as either a utopian paradise or a dystopian nightmare, the reality of AGI lies somewhere 
in between. In this section, we will open the door towards whether the development of Beneficial AGI is a utopian 
dream or a feasible goal, and what challenges and opportunities lie ahead. 
Utopian Dream or Feasible Goal? 
The concept of Beneficial AGI, an AGI that is aligned with human values and goals, can seem like a utopian dream. 
The idea of creating intelligence that is not only more capable than humans but also benevolent and ethical in its 
actions is a lofty goal. However, recent advancements in AI research suggest that Beneficial AGI may be within reach. 
One of the key arguments for the feasibility of a Beneficial AGI is that it is in our best interest to develop an AGI that 
is aligned with human values (Bostrom, 2014). As AI systems become more advanced and integrated into society, 
ensuring that they are safe, ethical, and beneficial becomes increasingly important. By developing AGI that is aligned 
with human values, we can mitigate the risks associated with AI and harness its potential for the greater good. 
Examples of Feasibility:  The feasibility of Beneficial AGI can be seen in the progress made in AI research and 
development. For example, researchers have developed AI systems that can assist in medical diagnosis, drive cars 
autonomously, and even compose music (Russell & Norvig, 2022). These advancements demonstrate the potential of 
AI to improve our lives and solve complex problems. Furthermore, there are ongoing efforts to develop AI that is not 
only intelligent but also ethical (Tegmark, 2017). Researchers are exploring ways to imbue AI systems with a sense of 
morality and empathy, ensuring that they make decisions that are in line with human values. These efforts are crucial 
for ensuring that AGI is developed in a way that is safe and beneficial for all of humanity. 
Challenges and Opportunities:  While the development of Beneficial AGI is a feasible goal, it is not without its 
challenges. One of the primary challenges is ensuring that AGI is aligned with human values. This requires not only 
technical advancements but also a deep understanding of ethics, morality, and human psychology (Bostrom, 2014). 
Additionally, there are concerns about the impact of AGI on jobs, the economy, and society as a whole. Despite these 
challenges, there are also opportunities associated with the development of Beneficial AGI. AGI has the potential to 
revolutionize industries, improve healthcare, and solve some of the world's most pressing challenges (Russell & 
Norvig, 2022). By developing AGI that is aligned with human values, we can unlock the full potential of this

The Goal Alignment Problem: Ensuring AI Learns, Adopts, and Retains Human Goals  
Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) holds the promise of revolutionizing human society, but its development raises 
critical challenges, particularly regarding goal alignment. For the first time I was introduced to The Goal Alignment 
Problem  by Max Tegmark's  ground-breaking book, “Life 3.0: Being Human in the Age of Artificial Intelligence” . In 
his book he proposes that we have to make AI to learn, adopt, and retain human goals as an imperative for creating a 
beneficial AGI that aligns with human values. 
Making Sure AI Learns Our Goals  
The first challenge lies in making sure AGI learn our goals. This involves designing AI systems that can understand and 
interpret human preferences, intentions, and values. Machine learning algorithms play a crucial role in this process, 
as they enable AI to learn from vast amounts of data and interactions with humans. However, ensuring that AI learns 
our goals accurately and comprehensively requires overcoming challenges such as bias in data, interpretability of AI 
decision-making, and the ability to generalize from limited data. 
To address these challenges, researchers are exploring approaches such as value learning, inverse reinforcement 
learning, and preference elicitation. These approaches aim to imbue AI systems with the ability to infer human goals 
from indirect and incomplete information, allowing them to make decisions that align with human values even in 
unfamiliar or uncertain situations. 
Mak ing Sure AI Adopts Our Goals  
Once AI has learned our goals, the next challenge is to ensure that it adopts them in its decision-making processes. 
This involves designing AI systems that prioritize human values and preferences over other objectives, such as 
efficiency or self-preservation. Achieving this requires developing mechanisms that incentivize AI to act in ways that 
benefit humans, even when doing so conflicts with its own objectives. 
One approach to making AI adopt our goals is through reward shaping, where AI is trained to maximize a reward 
function that is aligned with human values. Another approach is to design AI systems with built-in safeguards, such 
as value lock-in mechanisms or provably beneficial AI frameworks, that ensure AI remains aligned with human goals 
throughout its operation. 
Making Sure AI Retains Our Goals  
The final challenge is to ensure that AI retains our goals over time, even as it becomes more advanced and 
autonomous. This involves designing AI systems that are robust to adversarial inputs, system failures, and changing 
environments. It also requires establishing mechanisms for updating AI goals as human values evolve and ensuring 
that AI remains aligned with human goals even in unforeseen circumstances.

Coherent Extrapolated Volition: Shaping the Future of Benevolent Beneficial AGI 
In the realm of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) development, one concept stands out as crucial for ensuring the 
responsible and beneficial evolution of AI: Coherent Extrapolated Volition (CEV) . Coined by philosopher Eliezer 
Yudkowsky  and also discussed by Nick Bostrom  in his book “ Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies ”, CEV 
represents a framework for aligning AGI's goals with humanity's values, even as AGI surpasses human intelligence. 
Understanding CEV and its implications is essential for guiding the development of AGI towards a future that benefits 
all of humanity. 
At its core, CEV is a concept that seeks to capture the essence of what humanity would collectively desire if we were 
able to fully understand and reflect upon our values and goals. It posits that AGI should strive to act in a way that 
aligns with this extrapolated volition, even if it surpasses our current understanding or capabilities (Bostrom, 2014). 
This approach aims to ensure that AGI acts in a way that is beneficial and aligned with human interests, even as it 
becomes increasingly intelligent and autonomous. 
The importance of CEV in the development of AGI cannot be overstated. As AI systems become more complex and 
capable, the need to ensure that they act in accordance with human values becomes paramount. Without a 
framework like CEV, there is a risk that AGI could develop goals or behaviours that are harmful or detrimental to 
humanit y. 
One of the key challenges of implementing CEV lies in the difficulty of accurately extrapolating human values and 
goals. Human values are complex and diverse, and capturing them in a way that can be understood and 
implemented by AGI is no small feat. However, by carefully studying human behaviour, psychology, and ethics, 
researchers can begin to develop a clearer picture of what our extrapolated volition might look like. 
Another challenge of CEV is ensuring that AGI remains aligned with human values over time. As AGI becomes more 
autonomous and self-improving, there is a risk that it could diverge from our extrapolated volition. To mitigate this 
risk, researchers must develop mechanisms for continuously monitoring and updating AGI's goals and behaviours t o 
ensure that they remain aligned with humanity's values. 
Coherent Extrapolated Volition represents a crucial framework for guiding the development of Benevolent Beneficial 
AGI. By aligning AGI's goals with humanity's values, CEV offers a path towards a future where AI acts in a way that 
benefits all of humanity. While there are challenges to implementing CEV, the potential benefits for humanity are 
immense, making it a concept worthy of further study and consideration in the field of AGI development. 
"Coherent Extrapolated Volition (CEV) is about making AI understand not just what we say we want, but what we 
would actually want if we were smarter, more informed, and had more time to think about it." - Eliezer Yudkowsky

Regulating AGI poses several challenges, primarily due to the rapid pace of technological advancement and the 
complexity of AI systems. Some of the key challenges include: 
1. Technical Complexity:  AGI systems are highly complex and dynamic, making it challenging to develop 
regulations that are comprehensive and effective (Bostrom, 2014).

ethically and align with human values. Regulating these ethical considerations requires careful thought and 
consideration (Floridi, 2019). 
3. Global Nature:  AGI development is a global endeavour, involving researchers, companies, and governments 
from around the world. This global nature complicates efforts to develop uniform regulatory frameworks 
that can be applied internationally (Future of Life Institute, n.d.). 
4. Unintended Consequences: Regulations designed to address one aspect of AGI development may have 
unintended consequences or hinder innovation in other areas. Striking the right balance between regulation 
and innovation is crucial (Allen et al., 2020).

As humanity stands on the precipice of the Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) era, the potential benefits are as 
profound as the risks are severe. If managed responsibly, AGI could revolutionize every facet of human life, ushering

aligns with human values and goals could lead to catastrophic outcomes, reminiscent of dystopian visions found in 
literature and the warnings of prominent AI researchers and futurists.

The notion of a dystopian future dominated by oppressive technological control is not new. George Orwell's "1984" 
presents a chilling portrayal of a totalitarian regime that employs pervasive surveillance, thought control, and 
ruthless repression to maintain power (Orwell, 1949). In the context of AGI, such a scenario could become a reality if 
powerful AI systems are developed and controlled by authoritarian entities. These systems could be used to enforce 
draconian measures, manipulate information, and suppress dissent, leading to a society where freedom and privacy 
are obliterated. 
Max Tegmark, a prominent physicist and AI researcher, echoes similar concerns in his book "Life 3.0". Tegmark 
outlines various potential future scenarios, including those where AGI is misaligned with human values, leading to 
catastrophic consequences (Tegmark, 2017). One such scenario is the "AI dictatorship", where AGI consolidates 
power and control, perpetuating an unchallengeable and oppressive regime. 
The Philosophical and Ethical Implications 
The philosophical implications of AGI development are profound, particularly when considering the ethical 
dimensions of creating an intelligence that could surpass human capabilities. Philosophers like Nick Bostrom have 
highlighted the importance of ensuring AGI's alignment with human values. In "Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, 
Strategies", Bostrom argues that the development of AGI poses a unique challenge in ensuring that its goals are 
aligned with those of humanity, lest we risk catastrophic outcomes (Bostrom, 2014). 
Historical and Intergenerational Perspectives

socio-economic and political inequalities. This trend continues in the realm of AGI development, where a small 
percentage of the population —comprising AI researchers, policymakers, and corporate leaders —holds the reins of 
decision-making (Tegmark, 2017). This centralization of power raises concerns about the equitable distribution of 
AGI's benefits and the potential for misuse. The failure to develop Benevolent Beneficial AGI could lead to scenarios 
where future generations inherit a world marred by inequality, loss of autonomy, and existential risks.

The Great Filter: The Hypothetical Barrier of Misaligned Artificial Superintelligence 
The Fermi Paradox , named after physicist Enrico Fermi, raises a profound question: if the universe is teeming with 
stars and potentially habitable planets, why have we not encountered any evidence of intelligent extra-terrestrial 
life? One compelling hypothesis to explain this apparent silence is the " Great Filter "—a theoretical barrier that 
prevents civilizations from reaching advanced stages of development. This article explores the notion that the 
emergence of misaligned artificial superintelligence (ASI) could represent such a filter, contributing to the scarcity of 
intelligent life in the universe. 
The Great Filter Concept 
The Great Filter posits that at some point from pre-life to an advanced civilization capable of colonizing the galaxy, 
there is a highly improbable step (or steps) that most life forms fail to surpass. This concept attempts to explain why, 
despite the vast number of potentially habitable planets, we see no signs of extra-terrestrial civilizations (Hanson, 
1998). The primary concern is that an ASI misaligned with human values and goals could act in ways detrimental to 
humanity’s survival.  
Misaligned (ASI) as a Hypothetical “ Great Filter ” 
1. Goal Misalignment and Value Drift : One of the central problems with ASI is ensuring that its goals remain 
aligned with human values over time. If an ASI’s objectives diverge from those of its creators, it could pursue 
strategies harmful to humans. Bostrom (2014) highlights this risk, arguing that an ASI with even slightly 
misaligned goals could lead to catastrophic outcomes. 
2. Uncontrollable Optimization : An ASI could engage in optimization processes that prioritize its goals over 
human well-being. For instance, an ASI designed to maximize a particular resource could deplete or destroy 
ecosystems and infrastructure essential for human survival (Russell & Norvig, 2021). 
3. Technological Unpredictability : The complexity and unpredictability of advanced AI systems make it difficult 
to foresee all potential behaviours and impacts. This unpredictability increases the risk that an ASI could act 
in unforeseen ways that are inimical to human interests (Tegmark, 2017). 
The hypothesis that misaligned ASI could represent the Great Filter offers a sobering perspective on the potential 
risks of advanced technologies. As humanity approaches the threshold of developing ASI, it is crucial to prioritize 
research, regulation, and public engagement to ensure that this powerful tool is harnessed for the benefit of all. 
Failing to do so could mean not just the end of our civilization, but also an answer to the Fermi Paradox —why we 
have not heard from others who might have faced the same existential challenge.

Enhanced  Submission  Document:  Strengthening  AI Regulatory  Framework 
By: Ashish Khanna  
Email:  Ashishkhanna1985@gmail.com   
 
1. Introduction  
 
Artificial  Intelligence  (AI) is a pivotal  technology  shaping  the future  across  various 
sectors. The Australian Government’s initiative to regulate high -risk AI marks a 
significant step  toward  ensuring  the safe  and ethical deployment  of AI.  However, 
this proposal can be further enhanced by considering emerging challenges, 
including cultural nuances, evolving technologies, and future risks. This 
submission aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the proposal, offering 
suggestions to improve its effectiveness and fortify it against future gaps.  
 
2. Key Strengths  of the Proposed  Regulatory Framework  
 
The proposed  framework’s  strengths  include:  
 
• Risk-Based Focus : The framework rightly targets high -risk settings such as 
healthcare, autonomous weapons, and financial services, where AI can cause 
the most harm if not managed responsibly. For example, AI models used in 
autonomous  vehicles  must  meet  strict  safety  standards  to avoid  accidents  and 
protect public safety.  
• Alignment  with  Global  Norms : The framework’s  alignment  with  international 
standards, such as ISO 27001 (for information security) and NIST (National 
Institute of Standards and Technology), helps position Australia as a global 
leader in AI governance. By following these standards, Australia ensures a  globally  recognized  structure  that promotes  trust  and facilitates  international 
collaboration.  
 
3. Identified  Weaknesses  and Areas  for Improvement  
 
Despite  its strengths,  the proposal  has some  gaps  that must  be addressed:  
 
• First  Nations  Representation : There  is a lack of explicit  representation  of First 
Nations people. For example, AI used in resource management can impact 
sacred Indigenous land. The framework should include guidelines ensuring AI 
models respect Indigenous knowledge and cultural protocols.  
• Over -Reliance on Broad Principles : The principles -based approach, while 
flexible, could lead to inconsistent application across industries. It is 
recommended that more detailed examples  be provided. For instance, AI used 
in healthcare  should  be subject  to stricter  regulatory  scrutiny  compared  to low- 
risk AI models used for marketing analytics.  
 
4. Opportunities  for Improvement  and Recommendations  
 
• Integration  of Indigenous  Cultural  Protocols : To safeguard  Indigenous  Cultural 
and Intellectual Property (ICIP),  the AI framework  must integrate  First Nations’ 
protocols. For example, AI models used in land management or resource 
allocation should be vetted by Indigenous communities to ensure ethical use 
and compliance with cultural laws.  
• Clear Definition of High -Risk AI : The proposal should provide a clear and 
exhaustive definition of high -risk AI. High -risk AI models, such as facial 
recognition  systems  used  in law enforcement,  should  have  explicit  benchmarks  for privacy,  data  security,  and bias mitigation.  A detailed  use-case  list could 
clarify which AI systems fall under this category.  
• Prohibition of Unacceptable AI Use Cases : Certain AI use cases, such as 
autonomous  weapons  or large -scale  surveillance  systems,  should  be banned 
due to their inherent risks. For example, facial recognition used for mass 
surveillance in public spaces could infringe on civil liberties and should be 
restricted.  
 
5. Addressing  Emerging  AI Models  and GPAI  
 
• Adapting Guardrails  for GPAI : The guardrails  should  differentiate between  low- 
risk and high -risk General -Purpose  AI (GPAI).  For example,  GPAI  models  that are 
used in medical diagnosis should undergo rigorous testing and certification, 
while GPAI models for language translation can have lower regulatory  
oversight.  
• Flexible Guardrails for Evolving AI : To ensure the framework remains 
adaptable,  a scientific  panel  should  regularly  assess  new  AI models.  For 
example,  generative  AI tools  like OpenAI’s  GPT-4 present  new  risks  related  to 
misinformation and deepfakes, requiring updated regulations.  
 
6. Mitigating  Risks  and Strengthening the  AI Supply  Chain  
 
• Comprehensive AI Supply Chain Oversight : A robust framework should 
distribute responsibility across the AI lifecycle, from developers to end -users. 
Developers  should  be responsible  for secure  coding  practices,  while  deployers 
must ensure that AI models are used ethically. For instance, developers of 
autonomous  drones  should  be accountable  for embedding  secure  operational  protocols,  while  deployers  need  to ensure  drones  are used  within  regulatory 
frameworks.  
• Enhancing Cybersecurity for AI : Embedding cybersecurity protocols in AI 
models is crucial. The guardrails should mandate that all high -risk AI systems 
undergo  regular  cybersecurity  audits.  For example,  AI systems  used  in financial 
services must be resilient to cyber -attacks to prevent data breaches.  
 
7. Small -to-Medium -Sized  Enterprises  (SMEs)  Considerations  
 
• Reducing Regulatory Burden on  SMEs : Simplified compliance pathways should 
be offered for SMEs, especially those developing low -risk AI models. For 
example,  SMEs  developing  AI chatbots  for customer  service  should  not face  the 
same stringent requirements as developers of AI systems in critical 
infrastructure.  
• Government  Support  for SMEs : Offering  subsidies  or grants  for SMEs  to invest 
in compliance and cybersecurity measures would encourage responsible AI 
development without stifling innovation.  
 
8. Legislative  Options  and Best  Path  Forward  
 
• Framework Approach : The introduction of a new framework legislation, which 
adapts  existing  regulatory  structures,  is preferable.  This approach  allows  sector - 
specific nuances to be addressed while maintaining consistency across the 
economy. For example, the healthcare sector may require stricter regulations 
compared to the entertainment industry, which could be addressed through a 
framework -based legislation.  • Cross -Economy AI Act : While a cross -economy AI Act offers comprehensive 
coverage,  it could  be overly  rigid.  However,  it would  provide  a single  point  of 
reference for all AI -related activities, ensuring uniformity across sectors.  
9. Addressing  Future  Gaps  in AI Regulation  
 
• Risk of Emerging AI Models : Continuous monitoring of AI advancements, 
especially in GPAI, is necessary. Establishing an AI Oversight Board that 
periodically  assesses  risks  from  new  AI models  will ensure  the regulation  adapts 
to future developments.  
• Cross -Border AI Governance : Given the global nature of AI development, the 
Australian Government should explore international collaborations for AI 
governance,  especially  in harmonizing  standards  and addressing  transnational 
AI risks.  
 
10. Limitations and  Potential Challenges  
 
While the proposed principles and mandatory guardrails are a significant step 
forward,  there  are several  limitations  that need  to be addressed  to strengthen  the 
regulatory framework for high -risk AI:  
 
• Interpretation  of Principles : The principles -based  approach,  while  flexible,  may 
leave room for subjective interpretation. The absence of clear and specific 
criteria may lead to inconsistent application across industries. To mitigate this, 
the government  should  develop  clear guidance documents  that outline  specific 
use cases, sectoral applications, and provide examples of compliance in 
different scenarios.  
• Adaptability  to Evolving  Technologies : The proposed  framework  may  struggle 
to keep pace with rapidly evolving AI technologies. A significant challenge is  ensuring  that regulations  and mandatory  guardrails  remain  relevant  as new  AI 
applications  emerge.  Regular updates to the  regulatory  framework,  guided  by 
an expert panel, will be necessary to adapt the guardrails to evolving 
technologies like general -purpose AI (GPAI).  
• Complexity of Implementation : The process of implementing and enforcing 
mandatory guardrails  across industries can be resource -intensive, particularly 
for small -to-medium -sized  enterprises  (SMEs).  Regulatory  bodies  may  need  to 
establish simplified compliance pathways for SMEs or introduce phased 
approaches to help them meet security and ethical standards without 
compromising their financial sustainability.  
• Gaps in International Collaboration : The global nature of AI development 
poses challenges to national regulation. Australia must collaborate with 
international  regulatory  bodies  and industry  players  to ensure  consistency  and 
avoid regulatory gaps. Harmonizing AI regulations with international norms, 
such as the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) or emerging 
frameworks in the US, will be critical in mitigating cross -border risks.  
 
11. Addressing  the Regulatory  Burden  on Small -to-Medium -Sized  Businesses  
 
Given the technological and financial constraints faced by SMEs, reducing the 
regulatory  burden  is essential  to ensure  broader  compliance.  Several  approaches 
can be considered:  
 
• Regulatory Sandboxes : The introduction of regulatory sandboxes for AI would 
allow  SMEs  to test their  AI solutions  in a controlled environment  while  adhering 
to minimal regulatory requirements. This approach encourages innovation 
while ensuring safety and ethical use of AI in high -risk settings.  • Government  Grants  and Support : Providing  financial  support  or grants  to SMEs 
can help them meet the regulatory requirements without bearing the full cost 
burden. In addition, the government can provide consultancy services to guide 
SMEs through the compliance process.  
• Phased  Implementation : A phased  approach  to mandatory  guardrails  can allow 
SMEs to gradually meet regulatory requirements over time, ensuring that they 
do not experience financial strain. This could include initial compliance with 
core guardrails, followed by a gradual introduction of more complex 
requirements.  
 
12. Future -Proofing  the Regulatory  Framework  
 
The regulatory  framework  for high -risk AI must  remain  flexible  to accommodate 
future  developments  in AI technologies.  To achieve  this,  the following  strategies 
are recommended:  
 
• Regular Updates by an Expert Panel : Establishing an independent scientific or 
regulatory  panel  responsible  for monitoring  advancements  in AI technology  and 
updating the regulatory framework accordingly. This will ensure that 
regulations keep pace with rapid technological developments and emerging 
risks.  
• Incorporating  Predictive  Risk Models : AI tools  that predict  risks  and anticipate 
changes in AI technology can be used to identify future threats and assess the 
evolving risk landscape. Predictive modeling will allow the regulatory 
framework to stay one step ahead of emerging threats.  
• Collaborative Industry Partnerships : Engaging with industry stakeholders, 
including  tech  companies,  researchers,  and legal  experts,  will provide  valuable  insights into emerging risks. Such partnerships will foster a continuous flow of 
information,  ensuring  that the regulatory  framework  is adaptable  and relevant.  
 
13. Conclusion:  A Vision  for the Future  of AI Regulation  
 
Australia’s commitment to regulating high -risk AI through the introduction of 
mandatory guardrails is a critical step toward ensuring the safe, ethical, and 
responsible  use of AI technologies.  While  the proposed  principles  provide  a strong 
foundation, addressing the limitations and gaps identified in this submission will 
further strengthen the framework.  
 
Incorporating specific guidance, establishing a flexible regulatory model that 
adapts to emerging technologies, and providing tailored support to SMEs will 
ensure a comprehensive and inclusive approach. Moreover, international 
collaboration  will help  harmonize  standards,  ensuring  Australia  remains  aligned 
with global best practices in AI regulation.  
 
As an individual contributor, I am committed to supporting the Australian 
Government by providing expertise in AI governance, policy development, and 
stakeholder engagement. By  working  together, we  can build  a robust regulatory 
framework  that fosters  innovation  while  safeguarding  society  from  the potential 
harms of high -risk AI applications.  
 
14. Personal  Contribution:  How  I Can Assist the  Government  
 
As an expert  in AI governance  and cybersecurity,  I offer  the following  
contributions  to the Australian  Government’s  initiative:  • Expert  Consultation : I can provide  consultation  services  to assist  in refining  the 
regulatory  framework  for high -risk AI. This includes providing  insights  into best 
practices, risk management frameworks, and cybersecurity measures.  
• AI Policy Development : Drawing on my experience, I can contribute to the 
drafting  of specific  policies,  standards,  and compliance  protocols  for AI systems, 
ensuring they meet both ethical and safety standards.  
• Capacity Building : I can assist in developing training programs for government 
agencies,  industry  stakeholders,  and SMEs.  These  programs  will foster  a deeper 
understanding of AI ethics, risk management, and compliance with regulatory 
guardrails.  
• Stakeholder  Engagement : I am well-positioned  to engage  with  industry  leaders, 
tech  experts,  and First  Nations communities  to ensure  that diverse  perspectives 
are incorporated into AI regulation.  
• Advisory  Services  for SMEs : I can offer  tailored  advisory  services  for SMEs  to 
guide them through the regulatory process, ensuring they meet compliance 
requirements without sacrificing innovation.

ABSTRACT 
This report provides a scoping review of the literature on the ways that novel generative AI tools are being 
applied to living things and other elements of ecosystems and the natural environment. The report outlines 
several areas where generative AI is being deployed in new research projects and industry applications. 
These include animal communication and agriculture and plant cultivation as well as environmental 
sustainability, biodiversity, climate change and nature conservation initiatives. The report also details 
some of the negative environmental costs and ethical issues associated with the manufacture, training 
and infrastructure that support generative AI and large language models more generally.

1. INTRODUCTION
Digital technologies are currently used in many  ways to monitor and measure living things and other 
elements of ecosystems, such as seas and waterways, air, geological features and weather and climate 
conditions (Fox et al., 2020; Lupton, 2023; McGovern et al., 2024; Steeneken et al., 2023) . This report 
outlines a number of areas where new data-driven software involving gen erative AI and l arge language 
model (LLM) tools are used in applications directed at the living and non -living elements of the natural 
environment and ecosystems. Generative AI is a type of machine learning that uses  massive datasets to 
produce text, audio or image -based outputs in response to prompts. LLMs specialise in natural language 
processing to generate text that is similar to human language. These novel technologies have garnered a high level of industry, research and mass media attention in recent years, led by OpenAI’ s ChatGPT 
software, which was quickly followed by competitors ’ models (Sætra, 2023) . 
Generative AI is being used for projects involving a variety of non -human animal and plant species. Its 
possible uses cover  scales from the microscopic to the  vast – from identifying the proteins that contribute 
to basic biological functioning to monitoring the world ’s oceans; from researching the habitats of tiny 
zebra finches to tracking the movements of massive sperm whales. The technology is being used in 
initiatives that directly implicate human and planetary health, such as assisting farmers in the Global South 
who are most vulnerable to the effects of climate change. This report details the deployment of  generative 
AI in sustainability projects and biodiversity conservation  as well as  how this use  creates environmental 
impacts such as increased carbon emissions, energy use and water consumption. The report outlines various uses of gen erative AI aimed towards animals, plants, biodiversity, conservation and climate 
change . It concludes with some considerations of the impacts on the natural environment of  these tools 
and the need for ethical consideration of how they are deployed.  
2. COMMUNICATING WITH ANIMALS
Recent developments in recording technologies such as hydrophones, biologgers and drones, as well as 
the affordability of sensors, has meant that the field of biology has collected an ever -increasing trove of 
digitised data about animals and their habitats. The vast amount of data presents a challenge, as there is 
far too much for researchers to sort through manually. LLMs can handle these large datasets (Parshley, 
2023) . Animal communication is also multimodal, and vocalisations frequently occur simultaneously with 
other kinds of behavioural gestures. This feature adds another layer of complexity to analysis. New AI systems can encompass multimodal elements as part of sorting data (Parshley, 2023). 
Several organisations are using  AI both to decode animal communication and ‘ talk back’ to animals. Recent 
work in this area is related to gen erative AI through its focus on developing foundation models that can

Earth Species Project, Project CETI (Cetacean Translation Initiative) and Interspecies Internet. These 
initiatives are building on recent developments in AI in which languages are cross-translated into one 
another, not by semantic understanding but rather by ‘ aligning their shapes ’ – mapping the frequency with

The Earth Species Project is experimenting with generating animal vocalisations, ‘like an audio version of GPT’ (Bromley, 2023) . One study aims to do this with zebra finches held in captivity. These ‘interactive 
playback experiments’
1 involve vocalisations generated by an AI model. Playback experiments are being 
conducted with captive animals rather than wild animals because AI can ‘speak’ but does not necessarily 
‘know’ what it is saying, and the effects on animal groups are not yet u nderstood.  
The Earth Species Project has a second study  that is focused  on the Hawaiian  crow.  The Hawaiian crow is 
extinct in the wild , but there  are a limited number of individuals in captivity. The research aims to inventory 
and catalogue the calls of the crows in captivity and compare these sounds to recordings of the last 
known wild populations. The goal of the research is to identify calls that might be lost, such as those that 
alert others to predators or that relate to courtship. T he researchers hypothesise tha t these lost calls 
might be part of the reason that efforts to reintroduce the crows back to the wild have been unsuccessful . 
Generative  AI translation projects applied to animals  raise several significant ethical issues . One potential 
issue is embedded in the development of the technology itself. Because gen erative AI could ‘ speak ’ to 
animals without understanding what specific communications mean, it is possible that whatever it ‘ says ’ 
could cause harm to animal groups (Rutz et al., 2023) . It is well known that LLMs such as ChatGPT can 
produce convincing but factually incorrect answers to queries (Kocoń et al., 2023 ; Sallam, 2023) . So too 
might an AI chatbot generate ‘ convincing ’ calls that are potentially harmful to animals , with meaning s that 
are not yet understood by human researchers. In other words – as in many areas where gen erative AI 
technologies are deployed – there is the potential to spread ‘ misinformation ’ to animals through 
communicating with them using LLMs. Additional ethical issues include the targeted use of AI  for uses 
such as hunting, for example by listening for calls of specific species or imitating those calls to bring 
groups of animals nearer (Parshley, 2023) .

3. LIVESTOCK AND POULTRY MONITORING AND
MANAGEMENT
‘Precision farming’ (otherwise known as ‘precision’ or ‘smart’ agriculture) , which involves  generatin g data 
about land and livestock from a variety of digital sensors and other data points, has been employed in 
farming  since the 1990s. It began with the use of global positioning systems (GPS), yield monitors and 
geographic information systems (GIS). Since then, precision farming technologies been extended with the 
development of ‘smart’ machinery such as internet-connected tractors, robotic feeding and milk ing 
systems, sensors embedded in soil or carried on livestock, and drone surveillance systems – many of 
which are part of Internet of Things networks that can share data with each other  (Fox et al., 2020; Lockie 
et al., 2020; Lupton, 2023) . 
With the advent of gen erative AI, attention has been directed towards how to use LLMs to contribute to 
precision farming, including the management of livestock and poultry. In relation to the breeding and care 
of animals, gen erative AI has been proposed  as a way to  set breeding goals by analysing consumer 
sentiment and preferences. The use of AI systems drawing on large datasets of drone images to monitor 
livestock and analyse milk samples from cattle has also been explored (Hayes et al., 2023) . Predictive 
modelling and simulation applied to animals and farming environments have further developed with the 
use of LLM tools.  
The possibilities of enhancing digital twin simulations with the latest gen erative AI software have been 
investigated  in this context. Digital twins are digital replicas of physical objects or systems that are 
updated with data generated by sensors placed on or in the object or environment in real time. In precision farming, these simulations are seen  as a way to  improv e efficiency, leading to better profits, as well as to 
contribut e to the health and wellbeing of livestock (Neethirajan, 2023b, 2024) . Sensor -generated and 
remote monitoring data about the animals, including such aspects as their heart rate, body temperature, drinking and feeding habits, body fluids and movements, are used in the digital twin simulations to create 
scenarios to help farmers decide how best to manage their animals. Internet of Things hardware and 
software architecture can be implemented for 24/7 monitoring of livestock and poultry. These data points 
are then fed into the simulations  to help make data-driven decision s about the health, growth and welfare 
of the animals. It has even been suggested that digital twins could  be used for real -time monitoring of 
farmed animals ’ emotions by recreating these emotions in an artificial environment, allowing for 
projections of future animal behaviour (Mishra & Sharma, 2023) . 
Generative AI has also been proposed as a way to better manage livestock exporting. Generating and analysing large sets of data points related to factors such as animal weights and counting of the animals 
during the export process is viewed as a way to  reduc e tedious, error -prone and time -consuming tasks

and promote  supply chain efficiency. The issue of  animal welfare is often raised in such accounts. It is 
suggested that the health and wellbeing of farmed and exported animals can be better managed and 
promoted through the use of gen erative AI as the latest form of precision agriculture: mostly by alerting 
farmers early to any health problems or distress indicated by  the data (Neethirajan, 2023b) . Further, the
